A query specifies one index in \(\{1,\ldots,M_N\}\) and returns that symbol encoded in \(\lceil\log_2 M_N\rceil\) bits. The same index always gives the same answer. A query reads one whole symbol, not one arbitrary subset of the proof or an unbounded-length answer. Repeated requests count again toward the query limit. The verifier has no other access to the proof; it may not scan the proof without paying queries. Forming addresses and reading or processing the returned bits count toward its bit running time.

The proof is chosen before \(R\) and is fixed throughout the verification. On a satisfiable formula, the same witnessing proof must be accepted for every random string. On an unsatisfiable formula the error bound holds for every possible proof, including proofs produced with unlimited computation and proofs unrelated to any satisfying assignment. No proof may depend on the subsequently sampled verifier randomness. The verifier may choose later query addresses using earlier answers, as allowed by the existing card; it is otherwise deterministic once the input, random string and oracle are fixed. A standard nonadaptive verifier satisfying these guarantees would in particular meet the target, but nonadaptivity is not an additional requirement here.

Using exactly the displayed proof length, alphabet and random-tape length is a padding convention. Shorter proofs and smaller alphabets can be embedded in these bounds and unused random bits can be ignored. Positive integer exponents absorb constant polynomial factors and logarithmic ceiling effects. The common exponent \(b\) bounds both proof length and alphabet size; it need not be optimal. There is no required relation between \(a,b,c\) beyond positivity. The query bound \(q\) is a fixed integer, while each queried symbol contains \(O(\log(N+2))\) bits. Thus the target permits more than a constant number of proof bits, but not a growing number of queried symbols.

The verifier is a single finite classical program, with no advice, cryptographic assumption, trusted setup, interaction or quantum operations. All of its computation, including parsing, computing the displayed parameters, reading randomness, generating query addresses and computing the decision, must satisfy the polynomial bit-time bound for every valid formula, proof and random string. The construction of a witnessing proof need not be efficient; the assertion is its existence. There is no separate honest prover participating during verification.

Only some fixed positive exponent \(c\) is requested. The question does not demand an optimal exponent, a two-query verifier, an alphabet of constant size, or proof length linear in the formula size. The near-linear-size constant-error PCP problem is a different parameter target.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the constants and uniform verifier, including the two proof/randomness quantifier orders, the resource bounds on every execution, perfect completeness and the stated information-theoretic soundness; or give a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation.

A positive result must achieve polynomial length, polynomial alphabet, logarithmic randomness, constant symbol-query complexity and inverse-polynomial error simultaneously. A constant-error construction, an error exponent tending to zero, a superconstant query bound, or a superpolynomial-size proof is insufficient without an additional proved transformation establishing every required bound. A negative answer must exclude every choice of the fixed constants and every permitted verifier, including adaptive verifiers. Conditional implications under unproved assumptions do not unconditionally decide the target.

title: \(\exists\mathbb{R}\) versus \(\mathrm{NP}\)
summary: The existential theory of the reals asks whether a finite system of polynomial conditions has an exact real solution. Its input is a binary formula, with all coefficient and exponent bits counted in the running-time measure. The question is whether every yes-instance has a polynomial-length binary certificate checked in ordinary polynomial time. Known containments, oracle results and real-valued proof systems leave that discrete-certificate question unresolved in the checked sources. A complete answer must establish or refute ETR membership in NP without restricting possible certificate representations.
formal:
Is \(\exists\mathbb R=\mathrm{NP}\) in the ordinary bit-cost Turing model? Equivalently, is truth of every finitely encoded existential sentence over the ordered real field certifiable by a polynomial-length binary string checked in deterministic polynomial time?

For the language ETR defined below, the concrete target is the existence of one deterministic Turing verifier \(V\) and polynomial bounds \(p,q\) such that, for every binary string \(u\),
\[u\in\mathrm{ETR}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|u|)}:\ V(u,w)=1,\]
with \(V\) halting within \(q(|u|)\) steps on every permitted pair. The question is unconditional and has no oracle or advice.
definitions:
ETR is a language of finite binary strings describing sentences
\[\exists x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\mathbb R:\ \Phi(x_1,\ldots,x_m).\]
Here \(m\ge0\), the entire list of quantified variables is written explicitly, and \(\Phi\) is an explicitly listed finite Boolean formula, using \(\land,\lor,\neg\) and parentheses, whose atomic predicates are \(p=0\) or \(p>0\). Boolean constants true and false are permitted. Each polynomial is a finite monomial list
\[p(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_{j=1}^{s}c_j\prod_{i=1}^{m}x_i^{e_{ij}},\qquad c_j\in\mathbb Z,\quad e_{ij}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}.\]
Every coefficient is a signed binary integer and every exponent is a nonnegative binary integer. Each monomial has its coefficient and its full exponent vector, explicitly delimited. Zero coefficients and repeated monomials are allowed with their usual algebraic meaning. The empty sum is zero and the empty product is one. The convention \(x^0=1\) applies also at \(x=0\). No degree bound is imposed.

Use a fixed finite-alphabet, explicitly delimited encoding of the variable declarations, formula tree, monomial lists, signs and binary integers, then a fixed binary encoding of its symbols. Variable names are indices from 1 through \(m\); no implicit generation of an exponentially long formula is allowed. Let \(L=|u|\) be the entire encoding length, counting every bit of every coefficient and exponent as well as all syntactic structure. Ill-formed strings, invalid indices and unmatched lengths are rejected. With no quantified variables, the sentence has its ordinary closed-form truth value. Inequalities such as \(p\le0\) and comparisons between two polynomials can be expressed with the stated atoms and connectives.

A well-formed string is in ETR precisely when there exists an exact real tuple satisfying its sentence. There is no numerical tolerance or robustness promise. The reals occur as mathematical values of the quantified variables, not as infinite objects supplied to a Turing machine. Binary exponents and coefficients are counted by their bit lengths. This explicit sparse-polynomial representation is polynomially interreducible with the standard arithmetic-term definition of ETR; it does not encode an exponentially long formula by a separate succinct circuit description.

For languages \(A,B\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), a polynomial-time many-one reduction is one total function \(f\) computed by a deterministic multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in \(|u|\), such that \(u\in A\) if and only if \(f(u)\in B\). Define \(\exists\mathbb R\) as all languages with such a reduction to ETR. A language is \(\exists\mathbb R\)-complete when it lies in that class and every language of the class reduces to it in this sense.

Use [NP](definitions.html#p-np), with ordinary binary witnesses and a uniform bit-cost verifier. The program and polynomial bounds are fixed independently of the instance and its length. A verifier must reject every allowed witness on a no-instance and accept at least one on every yes-instance. Every finite-alphabet tape transition costs one; arithmetic on large integers and manipulation of algebraic descriptions are charged their actual bit cost. There is no randomness, oracle, nonuniform advice or exact-real primitive. A witness may encode any finite mathematical certificate with an efficiently checkable interpretation: it need not list a satisfying coordinate tuple or use rational coordinates.

The known inclusion \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\exists\mathbb R\), and closure of NP under these reductions, make class equality equivalent to \(\mathrm{ETR}\in\mathrm{NP}\). Its negation is \(\mathrm{ETR}\notin\mathrm{NP}\). The other known upper bound uses PSPACE, the class decidable by deterministic Turing machines using polynomially many work-tape cells.

For comparison, a constant-free BSS verifier stores exact reals and performs field operations and order tests at unit cost, using only the fixed constants 0 and 1. Restricting its input to bits while allowing polynomially many real witness coordinates gives \(\mathrm{BP}(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}^{0})=\exists\mathbb R\). In the full BSS class comparison, inputs and finitely many fixed machine constants may also be arbitrary reals. That is a different target. The present question asks whether ordinary binary certificates with a bit-cost verifier suffice.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{ETR}\in\mathrm{NP}\) or of \(\mathrm{ETR}\notin\mathrm{NP}\) for the encoding and model above, equivalently proving or refuting \(\exists\mathbb R=\mathrm{NP}\). A positive answer must supply a uniform binary-certificate verification scheme and prove completeness, soundness, a polynomial certificate-length bound and a polynomial bit-time bound for all instances. A negative answer must exclude every such scheme. Showing only that some solutions are irrational, that a chosen coordinate representation needs many bits, or that a particular geometric problem is NP-hard does not exclude other certificate encodings. An oracle separation or a theorem conditional on unequal classes does not settle this unrelativized comparison. The decision target is exact, without numerical approximation tolerance.

title: Polynomial formulas versus linear circuits
summary: The conjecture asks for Boolean functions with linear-size circuits but no polynomial-size formulas. Circuits may reuse intermediate results, while formulas have a tree structure and count repeated variable occurrences separately. The computational basis is binary AND and OR with unary negation, and correctness is exact on every input. The nonuniform separation is equivalent to NC-one being strictly smaller than P/poly, and arbitrarily large violating lengths are sufficient. Known nearly cubic gaps and recent composition results do not yet give the required superpolynomial separation.
formal:
Does there exist a family of total Boolean functions \(f_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), for integers \(n\ge1\), such that
\[\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f_n)=O(n)\qquad\text{but}\qquad \operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f_n)\notin n^{O(1)}?\]
Here \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}\) is minimum bounded-fan-in De Morgan circuit gate count and \(\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}\) is minimum De Morgan formula leaf count. Both are nonuniform and require exact correctness on every input. Precisely, the question asks for one family and a finite constant \(C>0\) satisfying \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f_n)\le Cn\) for all \(n\ge1\), while
\[\forall k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \forall n_0\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists n\ge n_0:\quad \operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f_n)>n^k.\]
For each fixed exponent \(k\), the violation may occur along its own unbounded sequence of lengths.
definitions:
Use the shared [Boolean circuit](definitions.html#boolean-circuits) and [formula leaf-size](definitions.html#formula-size) conventions. For the same total single-output function \(f_n\), \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f_n)\) counts the minimum number of binary AND/OR and unary NOT gates; inputs, constants and wires are free. Fan-out and depth are unrestricted. The quantity \(\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f_n)\) counts the minimum number of variable-leaf occurrences in a formula tree; constants are free, so constant functions have size zero and a literal has size one. Exact correctness is required on every input, and neither quantity imposes a uniform generator.

The sequence of functions, and the optimal circuits and formulas at different lengths, need not have an efficiently computable description. In particular this card does not impose an extra polynomial-time evaluator or uniform circuit-generation algorithm on the family. The source's conjecture is stated using its nonuniform size measures. A family with such extra uniformity would also qualify if it has the required sizes.

The same constant \(C\) bounds circuit size at every length. Allowing finitely many exceptions would be equivalent, since increasing \(C\) absorbs them. The formula condition is equivalent to saying that there do not exist constants \(D>0\), integer \(k\ge1\) and onset \(n_0\) with \(\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f_n)\le Dn^k\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). Thus arbitrarily large violating lengths may depend on the polynomial exponent; the family itself may not. The target asserts no particular exponential or quasipolynomial lower-bound rate.

The two minima compare computations of the same single-output function. Linear circuit size does not bound circuit depth by a logarithm. A size separation using unbounded-fan-in threshold gates, only monotone formulas, or a growing number of outputs is a different statement.

The existence claim is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\subsetneq\mathrm{P/poly}\) for nonuniform Boolean circuit families. Here \(\mathrm{P/poly}\) means \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f_n)\le a(n+1)^b\) for some fixed positive integers \(a,b\), and \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) means a family of binary De Morgan circuits of depth at most \(d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for one constant \(d\); such circuits can be taken polynomial in size. No uniform generation is required in either class. Polynomial-size formulas and logarithmic-depth circuits are equivalent by formula balancing and expansion of a bounded-depth circuit into a tree.

The restriction to linear circuit size does not change this family-existence question. A separating polynomial-size family can be regarded, at lengths \(N_n=a(n+1)^b\), as a function of \(N_n\) variables that ignores the extra variables; at other lengths set the function to a constant. The circuit bound becomes linear, whereas a polynomial formula bound in \(N_n\) would give a polynomial formula bound in \(n\). This is a comparison of nonuniform families and retains the arbitrarily-large-length quantifiers. Conversely, a linear-size family is already in \(\mathrm{P/poly}\). Thus an answer to the equality question has the opposite Boolean polarity from the separation question in this card.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed family-existence claim. A positive answer must specify or mathematically establish the existence of one family satisfying both the single linear circuit bound and failure of every polynomial formula bound. A nonconstructive family can qualify; no efficient generator is part of the target. A negative answer must show that every family with a uniform linear circuit-size constant has some polynomial formula-size bound, whose exponent and coefficient may depend on that family. Proving only one fixed polynomial separation, even with a large exponent, or refuting one candidate family does not settle the question.

title: Is ARRIVAL solvable in polynomial time?
summary: ARRIVAL asks which of two destinations is reached by one token following deterministic alternating switches. The graph and both successor choices are explicit, and every vertex can reach at least one sink in the underlying graph. The target is one deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm, without requiring it to list the token trajectory. Fan and Kim compute the destination for arbitrary explicit cyclic successor lists. Their algorithm takes polynomial bit time even when the token trajectory has exponential length.
formal: Does the deterministic decision problem \(\mathrm{ARRIVAL}\) defined below belong to \(\mathrm{P}\)? Equivalently, is there one deterministic Turing algorithm and constants \(K,c>0\) that, on every valid explicitly encoded switch graph of bit length \(N\), decides whether its token reaches destination \(d_1\) before \(d_0\) within \(K(N+1)^c\) bit steps? The two-destination termination condition and initial switch settings are part of the definition.
definitions:
An instance is \(I=(n,o,s_0,s_1)\), where \(n\ge1\), the ordinary vertices are \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(o\in V\) is the origin, and \(d_0,d_1\notin V\) are two distinct destination symbols. Each successor table is a function \(s_b:V\to V\cup\{d_0,d_1\}\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\). Thus every ordinary vertex has two labelled outgoing arcs, its even arc to \(s_0(v)\) and its odd arc to \(s_1(v)\). These successors may coincide, and self-loops are allowed. The destinations have no outgoing arcs. There are no other edges, weights or choices.

Require that from every ordinary vertex there is a directed path in this switch graph to at least one of the two destinations. A path may use either labelled arc at each vertex for the purpose of checking this condition. It need not follow the token dynamics. This condition is checkable by ordinary reverse graph reachability and guarantees that the actual token process eventually reaches a destination. It does not require that both destinations be reachable from every vertex.

Initially the token is at \(x_0=o\), and every switch bit is zero: \(b_0(v)=0\). If the current position \(x_t\) is a destination, the process stops. Otherwise, writing \(v=x_t\), set
\[x_{t+1}=s_{b_t(v)}(v),\qquad b_{t+1}(v)=1-b_t(v),\]
and leave all other bits unchanged. The successor is selected using the old bit before the bit is flipped. Consequently successive departures from a vertex alternate even, odd, even, odd, starting with even. There is a single token and no player, randomness or external control. The instance is YES if the first reached destination is \(d_1\), and NO if it is \(d_0\).

Encode \(n,o\) and the two length-\(n\) successor tables explicitly using binary integers, with distinguished codes for the two destinations. The input length is \(\Theta(n\log(n+2))\) under this representation, up to fixed delimiters. A graph given by a succinct circuit, a binary multiplicity of initially placed tokens, or an exponentially long switch sequence is not part of this input model. The initial all-zero setting requires no additional table; any fixed initial setting could instead be represented by exchanging the corresponding two successor names.

For an ordinary language rather than a promise problem, reject malformed encodings and well-formed tables failing the reachability condition. Their validity can be checked in polynomial time, so this convention does not alter polynomial-time solvability on the valid instances. Membership in [P](definitions.html#p-np) uses the shared uniform bit-cost convention. The program need only output the answer bit. It is not required to list, or simulate, the token's full trajectory.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that this language is in \(\mathrm{P}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that it is not. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic decision algorithm, prove correctness on every valid graph and polynomial worst-case bit complexity, and handle invalid encodings according to the stated convention. A negative answer must exclude all such polynomial-time decision algorithms; an exponential example for direct token simulation or for one particular algorithm is insufficient. Polynomial time only for a restricted graph class, subexponential time, a randomized algorithm without a deterministic conversion, and succinctly encoded variants do not answer the exact question. No numerical tolerance applies to the Boolean answer or the complexity bound.

title: Linear-size circuits for stable ternary compaction
summary: Stable ternary compaction moves every 2 to the end while preserving the order of all zeros and ones. The question asks whether each input length admits an exact Boolean circuit of size proportional to that length. Circuits may have arbitrary depth and fan-out and may compute freely on the fixed two-bit alphabet encoding. Non-stable compaction and ordinary ternary sorting do not retain the binary sequence required in the answer. The checked short-key sorting advances and conditional or restricted lower bounds do not resolve this nonuniform linear-size question.
formal: Is there a universal constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), stable ternary compaction \(S_n:\{0,1,2\}^n\to\{0,1,2\}^n\) is computable by a Boolean circuit with at most \(Cn\) gates? The function deletes all symbols \(2\), retains all symbols \(0,1\) in their original relative order, and appends the deleted number of \(2\)s on the right. Circuits use the binary alphabet encoding and bounded-fan-in basis specified below, with no depth or uniformity restriction.
definitions: Encode symbols \(0,1,2\) by \(00,01,10\), respectively, using a fixed ordered pair of bits for each input position. A circuit for length \(n\) is a finite acyclic directed Boolean circuit with \(2n\) ordered input bits and \(2n\) ordered output bits. Its non-input gates are binary AND, binary OR, unary NOT and optional constant-0 or constant-1 gates. Each such gate, including a constant gate, contributes one to size. Fan-out is unrestricted. Wires and output designations have no separate cost, and the same gate or input can feed multiple gates and outputs. The circuit is deterministic. It must be correct on every concatenation of valid input encodings; behavior on any input containing a pair \(11\) is unrestricted. For \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\{0,1,2\}^n\), let \(i_1<\cdots<i_m\) be exactly the indices where \(a_i\ne2\). The required output encodes \(a_{i_1}\cdots a_{i_m}\) followed by \(n-m\) copies of \(2\). This definition includes \(m=0\) and \(m=n\). In particular, it preserves the relative order of a \(0\) and a \(1\); it does not sort them against each other. All output positions must be produced by one circuit and their gates are counted jointly. Let \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM+c}}(S_n)\) be the minimum circuit size for the binary-encoded promise function. Here \(\mathrm{DM+c}\) names the local convention above: constant gates count, unlike the free-constant \(\mathrm{DM}\) convention in the shared glossary. The quantifiers are \(\exists C\ge1\;\forall n\ge1\;\exists\mathcal C_n\), with \(|\mathcal C_n|\le Cn\) and exact correctness on all valid inputs. The circuit may depend arbitrarily on \(n\), and no algorithm constructing \(\mathcal C_n\) is required. The circuit may compute on the individual encoding bits; it is not restricted to comparing or routing indivisible records.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM+c}}(S_n)\le Cn\) for some universal \(C\) and all \(n\ge1\), or a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation \(\forall C\ge1\;\exists n\ge1,\ \operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM+c}}(S_n)>Cn\). The negative statement rules out every nonuniform family in the defined unrestricted Boolean model; a lower bound for comparators or indivisible-record routing does not suffice. A conditional result under an additional conjecture settles only that conditional version. A positive answer must retain the original order of the \(0\)s and \(1\)s, with an exact linear size bound rather than a bound multiplied by an unbounded iterated-logarithm factor.

title: Expected linear-time integer sorting for every word length
summary: Integer sorting can inspect the bits of keys instead of treating them only as objects to compare. The question asks for one always-correct randomized word-RAM algorithm taking expected linear time for every permitted word length. The constant must remain uniform when keys occupy much more than logarithmically many bits. Ordinary radix sorting handles smaller universes but its number of passes can grow. This tests whether powerful word operations can completely remove the asymptotic overhead of ordering an arbitrary list of machine words.
formal: Does there exist a uniform Las Vegas word-RAM algorithm and a constant \(C\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), every integer word length \(w\ge\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\), and every list \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\), the algorithm outputs the list in nondecreasing order with expected running time at most \(Cn\)?
definitions: The input occupies n words, with one unsigned w-bit key per word; repeated keys are allowed. The output must contain exactly the input multiset in nondecreasing numerical order, with no stability requirement. The machine is sequential and has w-bit data registers and random-access memory. Unit-cost operations are reads and writes, comparisons, branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication of two words with the product returned in two words, quotient and remainder of two words with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and left or right shifts by a word-specified amount. Shifted-out bits are discarded, and shifts by at least w return zero. Addresses may use a constant number of words to index polynomially many memory cells; all address computation is charged. An operation can generate one fresh independent uniform w-bit random word. These are the only primitive operations; arbitrary-length arithmetic, a built-in sorting operation and free tables are unavailable. All preprocessing, memory initialization performed by the algorithm, and output writes count. A fixed finite program receives n and w; it may select methods according to their values but has no advice depending on them. Las Vegas means every terminating computation is correct and the algorithm terminates with probability one. Expectation is over the internal random choices for each fixed input. C must be independent of both n and w, including when w grows with n.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a single uniform, always-correct Las Vegas program whose expected running time is at most Cn on every admissible (n,w,input), for one C independent of n and w. A negative answer must show that every such sorting program has unbounded expected-time/n ratio over these inputs. A lower bound only for comparison sorting, deterministic programs, or a different word instruction set does not establish that negation.

title: Sorting \(X + Y\)
summary: Given two lists of n numbers, form every sum consisting of one number from each list. The task is to sort these quadratically many sums as quickly as possible. They have substantial inherited order, so they are not an arbitrary collection of unrelated values. The source distinguishes having few comparisons from implementing those comparisons with equally small total running time. Removing avoidable overhead would improve both structured sorting and geometric problems whose events are ordered by pairwise sums.
formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic real-RAM algorithm A and a constant C such that, for every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every \(X=(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}), Y=(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{n})\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}, A\) outputs a permutation \(((i_{1},j_{1}),\ldots ,(i_{n^{2}},j_{n^{2}}))\) of \([n]\times [n]\) satisfying \(x_{i_{r}}+y_{j_{r}}\le x_{i_{r+1}}+y_{j_{r+1}}\) for \(1\le r<n^{2}\), in at most \(Cn^{2}\) unit-cost operations?
definitions: The input consists of n and the 2n exact real numbers in random-access arrays; no sortedness, distinctness, integrality or magnitude bound is promised. All \(n^{2}\) index pairs must occur once in the output, including pairs with equal sums. Ties may appear in any order. A real RAM has exact real registers and cells, supporting copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero reals and comparisons at unit cost. A fixed finite program may use rational constants, with no advice depending on n. It also has integer registers and cells of \(b=d\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for some fixed integer \(d\ge 3\) chosen with the algorithm. Integer instructions are copy, comparison, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b}\), quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts; shifts by at least b return zero. Integer addresses access individual real or integer cells, and each read or write costs one operation. Integer-to-real conversion is permitted, but real-to-integer conversion, floor on reals, extraction of their bits and arbitrary-precision integer operations are not primitives. Memory starts empty apart from the input and fixed program constants; all preprocessing, table construction, address computation and output writes are charged. The algorithm must halt correctly on every input and uses no randomness. Constants C and d are independent of n and of the real values. This is the quadratic-time real-RAM version explicitly asked in the cited necklace paper and identified as the main target in TOPP. Indexed multiset output resolves possible equal sums; allowing repeated input entries does not change the target, since repetitions can be grouped by \(O(n \log  n)\) comparison sorting and expanded within the output budget.
answer_criterion: Give one uniform deterministic program with a proof of exact output correctness and the \(O(n^{2})\) worst-case total-time bound for every real input, or prove that no such program exists in the specified model. Equivalently, a negative answer shows that every correct program has unbounded worst-case running-time/\(n^{2}\) ratio. Neither a bound only on the number of comparisons nor an algorithm restricted to bounded integers resolves this claim.

title: Size-bounded approximate multicommodity-flow sparsifiers
summary: A network has a small distinguished set of terminal vertices and may have many internal vertices. The question asks whether another graph of size depending only on terminal count and positive error can preserve every fractional terminal routing. The replacement graph may use new vertices and need not arise by contraction. Known exact and contraction-based impossibility results have restrictions absent from this question. A positive result would separate the complexity of a network interface from the size and capacity range of its interior.
formal: Does there exist a function \(f:\{2,3,\ldots\}\times(0,1)\to\mathbb N\) such that every finite undirected capacitated graph \(G\) with a labelled set \(T\) of \(k\) terminals admits a finite undirected capacitated graph \(H\), containing the same labelled terminals and at most \(f(k,\varepsilon)\) vertices, for which \[\operatorname{cong}_H(d)\le\operatorname{cong}_G(d)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{cong}_H(d)\] holds simultaneously for every nonnegative terminal demand vector \(d\)? Here \(0<\varepsilon<1\), and new nonterminal vertices and arbitrary capacities in \(H\) are permitted.
definitions:
A capacitated graph has finitely many vertices, undirected edges and strictly positive finite real capacities \(c_e\). Zero-capacity edges may be deleted and parallel edges combined by summing capacities. The terminals are distinct designated vertices. A demand vector assigns a nonnegative real number \(d_{st}\) to each unordered pair of distinct terminals \(\{s,t\}\).

For each terminal pair, assign nonnegative flow amounts to the finitely many simple paths joining the pair, so that their sum is \(d_{st}\). Commodities may split across paths. The load on an edge is the sum of the assigned amounts over all paths using it, regardless of direction or commodity. The congestion of a routing is \(\max_e \operatorname{load}(e)/c_e\). Define \(\operatorname{cong}_G(d)\) as the infimum over all such routings; set it to infinity if some positive demand cannot be routed. Zero demand has congestion zero, including in an edgeless graph. Inequalities involving infinity use the extended nonnegative reals. Integral, unsplittable and directed flow models are not intended.

Equivalently, let \(P_G\) be the set of demand vectors routable with loads at most the capacities. The requirement is \(P_G\subseteq P_H\subseteq(1+\varepsilon)P_G\), where scalar multiplication multiplies every demand coordinate. This fixes the one-sided normalization of quality. A single \(H\) must work for all demands; choosing a different graph after seeing \(d\) is not allowed.

Size means the number of vertices, including terminals. For simple graphs it also bounds the number of edges quadratically, but no bound on the bit complexity of real capacities is required. The bound is uniform over original graph size, topology and capacity magnitudes. This is an existence question: no efficient construction algorithm or computability requirement on \(f\) is added. The graph \(H\) may be entirely new and need not be a minor, quotient, contraction or subgraph of \(G\). Exact preservation corresponds to zero error and is outside the stated positive-error domain.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence statement, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A negative answer must provide fixed \(k\) and fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) for which no finite vertex bound works for all input graphs. Exact-sparsifier lower bounds alone, or lower bounds restricted to contraction-based sparsifiers, do not refute this statement. A positive answer must produce a graph realizing the simultaneous routing inequalities; a non-graph encoding of feasible demands does not suffice.

title: Hypergraph cut sparsifiers with \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) hyperedges
summary: A hypergraph cut counts the total weight of hyperedges meeting both sides of a vertex partition. A cut sparsifier replaces the hypergraph by a smaller weighted hypergraph that approximately preserves every cut at once. The question asks whether O(n/epsilon squared) hyperedges always suffice for multiplicative error epsilon. This matches the natural target from ordinary graphs, while a hyperedge can involve arbitrarily many vertices. The size measure counts hyperedges rather than their total incidence size, making the project specifically about how many distinct multiway interactions must be retained.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that every nonnegatively weighted hypergraph \(H\) on \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge2\), and every real \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\) admit a nonnegatively weighted hypergraph \(H'\) on the same vertices with \(|E'|\le Cn/\varepsilon^2\) and \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{cut}_H(S)\le\operatorname{cut}_{H'}(S)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{cut}_H(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq V\)?
definitions: For \(n\ge2\), write \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A weighted hypergraph \(H=(V,E,w)\) has a set \(E\subseteq\{e\subseteq V:|e|\ge2\}\) and finite nonnegative real weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). For every \(S\subseteq V\), set \(\operatorname{cut}_H(S)=\sum_{\substack{e\in E:\ e\cap S\ne\varnothing,\\e\cap(V\setminus S)\ne\varnothing}}w(e)\). Thus each crossing hyperedge contributes its weight exactly once, regardless of the number of vertices on either side. Empty and singleton edges are omitted because they cross no cut; repeated edges can be merged by summing weights. The approximating hypergraph \(H'=(V,E',w')\) follows the same rules. Its edge set may contain any subsets of the original vertex set, not necessarily original edges; additional vertices are forbidden. Size is \(|E'|\), rather than the sum of edge cardinalities or a bit-encoding length. The same approximation must hold for all cuts simultaneously, and a zero-valued original cut must remain exactly zero. The empty edge set is allowed. This is an existence question with no construction-time, randomness or rational-weight restriction. The constant \(C\) is independent of dimension, accuracy, hyperedge count, maximum edge size and weights.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of this universal existence theorem with one constant \(C\), or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every \(C>0\), some permitted \(n,H,\varepsilon\) has no same-vertex weighted hypergraph meeting both the size and all-cut guarantees. A refutation must allow arbitrary nonnegative replacement hyperedges, not just sampled original edges. A size bound retaining an unbounded logarithmic factor does not establish the stated theorem.

title: Near-linear output-sensitive Subset Sum
summary: The input is an explicit list of positive integers, allowing repetitions, together with an integer threshold. The task is to list every distinct attainable subset sum at most that threshold exactly once, including zero. The question asks for one uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm whose time on every random execution is near-linear in input size plus output size and whose whole output is correct with probability at least two thirds. Known output-sensitive improvements and their 2026 derandomization do not attain this endpoint, which would avoid paying for a large unused numerical range. A complete Lean answer must prove such an algorithm and its guarantees exist or prove their full logical negation in the specified model.
formal:
Is there a uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm that lists all attainable subset sums up to a given threshold in time near-linear in the explicit input size plus the number of distinct output values?

More precisely, for integers \(n,t\ge1\) and an input list \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{1,\ldots,t\}^{n}\), put
\[
S(X,t)=\left\{\sum_{i\in I}x_i:I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\right\}
\cap\{0,\ldots,t\},\qquad q(X,t)=|S(X,t)|.
\]
Does there exist one finite program \(A\), a fixed integer \(d\ge1\), a constant \(C>0\), and an integer \(b\ge0\), chosen independently of every input, such that on the word RAM defined below, with
\[
w=d\left\lceil\log_2(n+t+2)\right\rceil,
\]
both of the following hold for every valid \(n,t,X\)?
\[
\forall r\quad T_{A,d}(X,t;r)
\le C\bigl(n+q(X,t)\bigr)\bigl(\log_2(n+t+2)\bigr)^b,
\]
\[
\Pr_r\!\left[\operatorname{Success}_{A,d}(X,t;r)\right]\ge \frac23.
\]
Here success means that the complete output lists every element of \(S(X,t)\) exactly once and no other value. The time bound applies to every random execution, including unsuccessful executions. The algorithm is not given \(q(X,t)\) or any subset-sum information as additional input.

This card retains the previously selected bounded-error, worst-case word-RAM formulation of the source's near-linear output-sensitive question. Its explicit instruction set and requirement on every random execution are editorial model conventions; the source's expected-time or high-probability bounds are reported separately below.
definitions:
The input is a list of \(n\) positive integers and an integer threshold \(t\), with \(1\le x_i\le t\). Repeated values represent distinct available items, and each index may be selected at most once. Thus the input is an explicitly listed multiset, not a binary encoding of item multiplicities. The empty subset contributes zero. The set \(S(X,t)\) contains distinct integer sums, not a count of subsets. The required output is a finite sequence of \(q(X,t)\) integers in arbitrary order, containing each element of \(S(X,t)\) once. There is no requirement to output witnessing subsets. The threshold is inclusive.

For each fixed choice of \(d\), a word holds an unsigned integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). The input occupies a read-only word array containing \(n,t,x_1,\ldots,x_n\) at addresses \(0,1,\ldots,n+1\), one integer per cell; these values fit in a word. Reading that array at a larger address returns zero. The machine starts at its designated first instruction, with register zero containing \(w\) and all other registers zero. Its separate writable memory consists of word-addressed cells with addresses in the same range, initially zero. Initially zero memory is a machine convention, not an instruction that scans the entire address space. Every initialization performed by the program, and every subsequent memory access, is charged. A computation has a fixed finite control and a fixed finite number of word registers; additional storage uses the charged memory instructions.

Each of the following is a unit-cost instruction on a fixed number of words: copying; reading one addressed input word; loading or storing one addressed writable word; comparing unsigned words and conditional branching; bitwise Boolean operations; logical left or right shifts; addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\); integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor; generating one independent uniform random word; and appending one word to the output. A shift by an amount at least \(w\) returns zero. Arithmetic on larger integers must be implemented using these instructions and is charged accordingly. The program may use fixed integer constants encoded in its finite description, interpreted modulo \(2^w\) when placed in a word. It has no advice, input-dependent tables, or additional oracle instructions. Tables constructed during a run are allowed and all their construction costs count. A halt instruction ends the output sequence and costs one step; an invalid operation, such as division by zero, halts with failure. Output words already appended cannot be withdrawn.

One finite program and one constant \(d\) must serve all \(n,t,X\); neither the program nor its constants may vary with the input parameters. This is the uniformity requirement. All input reads, preprocessing, random-word generation, internal computation and output writes count toward running time. The memory bound comes only from word addressing; no further space restriction is imposed.

For a fixed input and \(d\), let \(r=(r_1,r_2,\ldots)\) be an infinite sequence of independent uniform words from \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\), consumed in order by random-word instructions. This product distribution defines \(\Pr_r\). A deterministic program is permitted as a special case that ignores \(r\). Let \(T_{A,d}(X,t;r)\) be the number of executed instructions, or \(+\infty\) for a nonhalting run. The event \(\operatorname{Success}_{A,d}(X,t;r)\) means that the run halts normally and its output sequence has exactly the required distinct values. Failure includes a missing sum, an extra value, a duplicate, an invalid operation or nontermination. The probability guarantee concerns this single event for the entire output, rather than a separate probability for each attainable value. The condition on time includes even random sequences having probability zero as individual infinite sequences.

The logarithm is base two, and \(b\) is any fixed nonnegative integer. Allowing an arbitrary fixed real exponent \(b\ge0\) would give the same existence question, since rounding that exponent up only enlarges this bound. The notation \(\widetilde O\) used in the context suppresses fixed powers of logarithms in the specified parameters; the displayed bound itself is the exact target. In particular, dependence polynomial in the numerical threshold \(t\), or in \(q(X,t)\) beyond its first power, is not hidden in the target's logarithmic factor.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the formal existence assertion or its full logical negation, using exactly the input, machine, randomness, output and cost conventions above.

A positive answer must specify one finite program \(A\) and constants \(d\ge1\), \(C>0\), and \(b\ge0\), with \(d,b\) integers, and prove for every valid input both the running-time bound on every random execution and probability at least \(2/3\) of the complete correct output. The constants may depend on the program but not on \(n,t,X\). An expected-time estimate or a bound that holds only with high probability does not by itself prove the required bound on every execution.

A negative answer must prove the following full negation. For every finite program \(A\) in the defined model, every integer \(d\ge1\), every constant \(C>0\), and every integer \(b\ge0\), there exist integers \(n,t\ge1\) and a list \(X\in\{1,\ldots,t\}^{n}\) such that
\[
\left[
\exists r\quad
T_{A,d}(X,t;r)>
C\bigl(n+q(X,t)\bigr)\bigl(\log_2(n+t+2)\bigr)^b
\right]
\quad\lor\quad
\left[
\Pr_r\!\left[\operatorname{Success}_{A,d}(X,t;r)\right]<\frac23
\right].
\]
The defeating input may depend on \(A,d,C,b\), so no single fixed instance must defeat all algorithms. A lower bound only for a restricted class of algorithms does not establish this negation. A conditional lower bound proves only its conditional conclusion unless its hypothesis is also established. The target is an exact existence question about an asymptotic resource bound; numerical \(1/100\) approximation does not replace either required proof.

title: Truly subcubic APSP
summary: The input is a directed graph with arbitrary exact real edge weights and no negative cycle, and the output gives the shortest distance for every ordered vertex pair. The target is one uniform randomized algorithm with a fixed positive saving below the cubic exponent, correct on the entire output matrix with probability at least two thirds. Time is charged in a specified comparison-addition real RAM that also permits ordinary logarithmic-size word operations, including all preprocessing and output. Known general algorithms achieve subpolynomial savings, while faster restricted results concern node weights, few outgoing weights, or supplied predictions. Recent restrictions on black-box reductions do not rule out all APSP algorithms, and the inspected sources retain the full target as unresolved.
formal: Is there a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), a fixed rational constant \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), and a fixed constant \(C>0\) such that, on every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with arbitrary real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, \(A\) outputs the entire exact shortest-distance matrix with probability at least \(2/3\), while every run takes at most \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) steps? Here \(n\ge2\), and steps are measured in the comparison-addition real RAM with logarithmic-size index words defined below. The same program, exponent improvement and time constant must work for every graph size and every real weight assignment.
definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input gives \(n\) and an \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix in vertex order. Each entry has a presence flag and, when present, one exact finite real weight. Thus there is at most one edge for each ordered pair; self-loops are allowed. Missing edges have no weight and are represented by the flag, not by a large finite number. There is no bound on the magnitude, sign or precision of a real weight. The graph is promised to have no directed cycle of negative total weight, including negative self-loops.

A finite directed walk \((v_0,\ldots,v_k)\) has weight \(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}w(v_i,v_{i+1})\). The empty walk from a vertex to itself has weight zero. For each ordered pair \((u,v)\), the distance \(d_G(u,v)\) is the minimum weight of a walk from \(u\) to \(v\), or the separate symbol \(+\infty\) if none exists. The no-negative-cycle promise ensures that every reachable minimum is finite and attained; nonnegative cycles can be removed, so a simple path suffices for distinct endpoints. In particular \(d_G(u,u)=0\). Zero-weight cycles and equal shortest distances are allowed. Output consists of all \(n^2\) exact distances in vertex-pair order, each a real value or an unreachable flag. Printing the vertices of every shortest path is not required.

The machine has one fixed finite program and two kinds of random-access memory cell: exact real cells and finite index-word cells. One real-cell load, store or copy, addition, subtraction, or comparison costs one step; comparison returns its trichotomy result as a word. These are the only operations inspecting real values. Real constants built into the finite program are restricted to \(0\) and \(1\); there are no arbitrary advice constants. A real value cannot be converted to its digits, an integer address, or its floor. Multiplication or division of real cells and operations packing several arbitrary reals into one word are not available.

For some fixed integer \(a\ge4\) chosen as part of the program's model, an index word has \(b(n)=\lceil a\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Word loads, stores, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, and addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b(n)}\) cost one step. Unsigned integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one step; division by zero is an invalid computation. A shift of at least \(b(n)\) positions returns zero. Addresses are words. All accessed cells must fit in this address range; a new work cell starts at zero and each access is charged. Word operations can process indices, counters and comparison results; they do not reveal the representation of a real edge weight. The input matrix and initially empty work memory are the only input-dependent initial state.

The randomized instruction obtains one fresh independent fair bit per step. All preprocessing, table construction, memory access, random-bit generation, input reading and output writing are charged to the same runtime. There is no nonuniform table supplied for free, extra prediction, oracle, parallel work unit or quantum operation. The bound is worst case over the input and every coin sequence. For each fixed promised graph, the probability that the whole output matrix is correct must be at least \(2/3\); separate success probabilities for individual entries are insufficient. A deterministic algorithm is included by ignoring the coins.

The bound depends on \(n\), not the bit length or magnitude of weights, because the real operations are exact primitives. This is a classical real-operation question, not an ordinary bit-time algorithm for arbitrary real encodings. Restricting \(\varepsilon\) to rational values in \((0,1]\) preserves existence of a fixed positive exponent saving; any positive saving implies a smaller such rational saving. No behavior is required on graphs violating the no-negative-cycle promise.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated algorithm-existence proposition or its full logical negation in this exact machine model. A positive proof must exhibit one finite uniform program and fixed constants, prove the promised-graph distance semantics and joint correctness probability, and charge every operation to the worst-case \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) bound. A negative proof must rule out every such program and every fixed positive exponent saving, including randomized programs.

A result for bounded integer weights, a restricted graph family, approximate distances, a single source, or additional accurate predictions does not settle this target. Neither does a lower bound restricted to one reduction method or to machines lacking the permitted word operations. An unproved APSP hardness hypothesis cannot serve as the proof of its own consequence here. A bound \(n^3/f(n)\) with only a subpolynomial saving \(f(n)=n^{o(1)}\) does not establish a fixed exponent saving; expected running time alone does not establish the specified worst-case bound. There is no additive or multiplicative error allowance in the distance output.

title: Breaking the \(2^{n}\) barrier for weighted TSP
summary: Exact weighted TSP asks for a cheapest tour through every vertex of a complete undirected graph. This question seeks a uniform classical algorithm with a fixed exponential time base below two. Weights are arbitrary nonnegative integers written in binary, and only polynomial dependence on their total encoding length is allowed. Bounded-error randomization and exponential memory are permitted, but every execution must satisfy the stated worst-case clock. Recent prefactor, structured-weight, time-space and quantum improvements do not establish the full classical guarantee.
formal:
Does exact symmetric weighted travelling salesman admit a classical algorithm with a fixed exponential base below two, allowing bounded-error randomization and polynomial dependence on the input bit length?

Precisely, do there exist a real constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\), positive integers \(K,c,B\) with \(B\ge2\), and one uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm \(\mathcal A\) such that, for every \(n\ge3\) and every complete undirected graph on vertices \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with nonnegative integer edge weights encoded as below, both of the following hold?
\[\Pr[\mathcal A\text{ outputs a minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle}]\ge\frac23,\]
\[\text{number of charged operations on every random execution}\ \le\ K(2-\varepsilon)^n(n+N)^c.\]
Here \(N\) is the total bit length of the explicit input, and the machine model is fixed below using \(B\). All constants and the algorithm precede the quantifiers over the graph, its weights and its encoding length. A deterministic algorithm qualifies as a special case.
definitions:
Instance and encoding. There is one weight \(a_{ij}=a_{ji}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for each unordered pair \(1\le i<j\le n\), and no loops. Weights are exact integers of arbitrary finite bit length. Let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary representation of a nonnegative integer \(t\), without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\). Define the self-delimiting code
\[U(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t).\]
The input is \(U(n)\) followed by \(U(a_{ij})\) in lexicographic order of \((i,j)\), for all \(1\le i<j\le n\). Its length in bits is \(N\). No matrix entry is supplied implicitly by an oracle or by a succinct circuit.

Objective and output. A tour is any permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), interpreted cyclically. Set \(\pi(n+1)=\pi(1)\). Its cost and the optimum are
\[\operatorname{cost}_a(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_{\pi(i),\pi(i+1)},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(a)=\min_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{cost}_a(\pi),\]
where \(S_n\) is the finite set of all such permutations. The graph is complete, so a tour always exists and the minimum is attained. The output is the explicit list of its \(n\) vertex labels, each in \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Any minimum-cost tour is accepted, including any rotation or reversal of one; no uniqueness is required. An invalid list, an explicit failure output, or a suboptimal tour counts as failure. Returning only the optimum value, a bound or an approximate tour is not the required output.

Machine and charges. Use a word RAM whose word length on this input is
\[w=B\left\lceil n+\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil\text{ bits}.\]
The algorithm has one finite program independent of \(n,N\) and all weights. A word is an unsigned integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\); a memory address is one word. The input bits are packed in order into consecutive read-only words, padding the last word with zeros and exposing the true input length. Working memory is initially zero and contains no advice or precomputed tables. Reading or writing one addressed word, copying a word, comparing two words, branching, bitwise Boolean operations, and a left or right shift by a word-specified amount each cost one operation. A shift by at least \(w\) gives zero. Addition, subtraction and multiplication are modulo \(2^w\) and cost one operation; integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one operation. Division by zero is not permitted. A fresh independent fair random bit costs one operation. Outputting a word, including the final partial word, costs one operation.

Integers longer than one word must be represented and processed using multiple charged operations; there is no unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers or exact real numbers. Reading and decoding the input, constructing tables, generating random bits, preprocessing, arithmetic and writing the entire tour are included in the clock. Addressing exponential-size subset tables is allowed by the linear-in-\(n\) word length. There is no separate polynomial-space restriction, and no quantum memory, quantum query, advice string or ideal oracle. The fixed polynomial overhead permitted in \(n+N\) accommodates the bit cost of operations on these finite-width words; this does not assert that sequential simulation of arbitrary random memory access has only polynomial overhead.

Probability and uniformity. For each fixed input the probability is over the machine’s independent fair coin stream. The same success guarantee holds on every input, not just on average over a distribution of weights. The running-time bound holds for every possible coin stream, including unsuccessful executions, so it is a worst-case clock rather than an expected-time bound. The constants \(\varepsilon,K,c,B\) cannot depend on the weights, their range or any property of the instance.

Scope. There is no triangle inequality, Euclidean geometry, bounded-weight, small-doubling or other structural promise. Polynomial dependence on \(N\) is allowed; polynomial dependence on the numerical maximum or sum of the weights is not automatically allowed. The fixed saving \(\varepsilon>0\) cannot tend to zero with \(n\).
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the algorithm-existence proposition or its full logical negation. A positive proof must specify one uniform classical algorithm and fixed constants, prove the worst-case clock including input and output costs, and prove per-instance success probability at least \(2/3\) for an exactly optimal tour. A negative proof must exclude every such algorithm and every permitted choice of constants in the stated randomized word-RAM model. A conditional lower bound settles only that conditional assertion. A restriction on one dynamic-programming framework, a local-search rule or a polynomial-space algorithm does not exclude all allowed algorithms. Faster Hamiltonicity detection, pseudo-polynomial dependence on weight magnitudes, a restricted weight class, approximate optimization or a quantum algorithm does not meet the full positive target.

title: Optimal deterministic restricted-isometry matrices
summary: A restricted-isometry matrix approximately preserves squared Euclidean norms of every vector with at most a specified number of nonzero coordinates. The question asks for one deterministic algorithm producing an explicit rational matrix with \(O(s\ln(eN/s))\) rows and distortion \(1/3\). Its bit running time and complete output length must be polynomial in the ambient dimension, with constants common to every dimension and sparsity. A complete Lean proof must establish the algorithm, its resource bounds and the simultaneous guarantee for all real sparse vectors, or prove unconditional nonexistence in the fixed model. Random optimal matrices, reduced random seeds and coherence-based constructions for restricted parameter families do not meet this uniform deterministic guarantee.
formal:
Do there exist universal constants \(C,B\ge1\), an integer \(b\ge1\), and one deterministic algorithm \(\mathcal A\) with the following property? For every integer pair \(N\ge2\), \(2\le s\le N\), given the pair in binary, \(\mathcal A\) outputs an explicitly listed rational matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times N}\), with an integer row count \(m\ge1\), in at most \(BN^b\) Turing-machine steps, such that
\[m\le C s\ln(eN/s)\]
and
\[\forall x\in\mathbb R^N\text{ with }|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\le s,\qquad \frac23\|x\|_2^2\le\|Ax\|_2^2\le\frac43\|x\|_2^2?\]
The complete binary output must also have length at most \(BN^b\). The constants and the algorithm are common to every pair \((N,s)\).
definitions:
For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\), set \(\operatorname{supp}(x)=\{j\in\{1,\ldots,N\}:x_j\ne0\}\) and \(\|x\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^N x_j^2\). A vector is \(s\)-sparse if its support has size at most \(s\), including the zero vector and all smaller supports. Matrix multiplication has its usual exact real meaning, \((Ax)_i=\sum_{j=1}^N A_{ij}x_j\), with rational entries viewed as reals. The displayed inequalities are the restricted isometry property of order \(s\) with distortion \(\delta=1/3\), for squared Euclidean norms. They must hold simultaneously for every support and every real choice of coefficients; no input distribution, typical-signal exception or probability of correctness is permitted. Columns need not be individually normalized to exactly one, provided the inequalities hold. The matrix is real, not complex.

Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm and \(e=\exp(1)\), so \(\ln(eN/s)=1+\ln(N/s)\), which equals \(1\) when \(s=N\). The real-valued row upper bound is an inequality on the integer chosen by the algorithm; no additional rounding convention is needed. Constants \(C,B,b\) cannot depend on dimension, sparsity, a signal or a support. The case \(s=1\), excluded from the main domain, has the trivial single-row all-ones construction; at \(s=N\), the identity matrix satisfies the geometric requirement. No compression promise such as \(m<N\) is imposed in the dense regime.

Use one fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite alphabet, no advice, randomness or oracle, and ordinary bit-level computation. Time is polynomial in the ambient dimension \(N\), not necessarily in the length of its binary input. In particular, the full matrix must be written; a succinct circuit for entries, an existential matrix description, or a real-number computation with unit-cost exact arithmetic is not the stated output model. All computation and output steps count toward the bound.

For a concrete self-delimiting binary encoding, let \(u(t)=1^k0\operatorname{bin}(t+1)\) for \(t\ge0\), where \(k\) is the length of the binary expansion of \(t+1\) without leading zeroes. The input is \(u(N)u(s)\) with no extra bits. The output is \(u(m)\) followed in row-major order by the \(mN\) rational entries. Encode \(p/q\) by one sign bit, \(u(|p|)\) and \(u(q)\), where \(p\in\mathbb Z\), \(q\ge1\), \(\gcd(|p|,q)=1\), and zero has numerator zero, denominator one and sign bit zero. The sign bit is zero for nonnegative numerators and one for negative numerators. No trailing bits are allowed. This represents every output entry exactly and counts its denominator and numerator lengths. Requiring reduced fractions is an encoding convention, since integer gcd computation is polynomial time. Invalid binary inputs can be rejected without changing the valid-input target; no asymptotic bound is required on malformed encodings.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a uniform deterministic construction exists, or an unconditional proof that it does not in the stated model. A positive answer supplies the finite algorithm and fixed constants and proves termination within the bit-time and output-length bounds, the row inequality and exact RIP for all permitted inputs and all real sparse vectors. The Lean proof must justify any rounding of other representations to the rational output actually printed. A negative answer must rule out every polynomial-time algorithm and choice of universal constants, not just one matrix family or verification method. A conditional lower bound alone is not an unconditional negative answer. Random existence, shorter random seeds, successful numerical recovery, statistical restricted isometry, a different norm, or an asymptotically larger row count does not suffice. This asks whether an algorithm meets the specified exact distortion guarantee; the numerical-target tolerance of 1/100 does not enlarge that guarantee.

title: Subset Sum below the meet-in-the-middle exponent
summary: Subset Sum asks whether some subcollection of given positive integers adds to a target. The classical worst-case benchmark comes from the meet-in-the-middle exponent. The question asks for a fixed positive saving in that exponent with polynomial dependence on binary input length. Bounded-error classical randomization is allowed, with no random-instance promise. Quantum, pseudopolynomial and polynomial-factor improvements do not establish this fixed exponent saving.
formal: Do there exist constants \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), \(c\ge1\) and a uniform classical bounded-error randomized algorithm deciding whether a subset of \(n\) positive integers sums to a nonnegative integer target in \(O(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)n}N^{c})\) worst-case time, where \(N\) is the total binary input length?
definitions: The input is \(n\ge1\), a target \(t\ge0\), and an explicitly listed multiset \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\) of positive integers, all in binary with delimiters; \(N\) is the bit length of that full encoding. Accept if and only if there is \(I\subseteq[n]\) with \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{i}=t\). Each index is used at most once, repetitions of values are permitted, and the empty subset is allowed. Use a uniform random-access machine with \(w=d(n+\lceil\log_{2}(N+2)\rceil)\)-bit words for fixed \(d\ge1\), large enough to address exponential memory. Unit-cost instructions are word read/write, copy, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, comparisons, Boolean operations and shifts; shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword integers are handled through charged component operations. Input packing, preprocessing and memory initialization are charged. Random words are independent and uniform and cost one instruction each. A fixed finite program receives no advice or tables. It answers correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input and the time bound holds on every random execution. Constants are independent of all input values and \(n,N\). Quantum operations and random-instance promises are absent.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one uniform classical randomized algorithm, constants \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), \(c\ge1\), and a constant multiplier meet the stated \(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)n}N^c\) time bound on every random execution and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input, or prove in Lean that no such choices exist. The theorem must allow unrestricted binary magnitudes, repeated positive values, all targets, and the full permitted RAM model.

title: Small Implicit Graph Conjecture
summary: An adjacency labeling scheme assigns each vertex a short binary string from which adjacency can be determined using only two labels. The conjecture asks for logarithmic labels in every hereditary class with at most a factorial times a fixed exponential number of labeled graphs. Hereditary means closed under induced subgraphs, and is weaker than closure under all subgraphs. The monotone case is known, and a 2025 follow-up proves logarithmic-cubed labels for all hereditary small classes. The question isolates when low total information content permits efficient storage in locally decodable vertex descriptions.
formal: Does every hereditary small graph class \(\mathcal C\) admit an adjacency labeling scheme using at most \(K\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits per vertex on every \(n\)-vertex graph in \(\mathcal C\), for some constant \(K\) depending only on \(\mathcal C\)?
definitions: Graphs are finite, undirected and simple. A graph class \(\mathcal C\) is closed under isomorphism; it is hereditary when every induced subgraph of every member also belongs to it. Write \(\mathcal C_n\) for its members with labeled vertex set \([n]\). Small means that there is a constant \(c\geq1\) with \(|\mathcal C_n|\leq n!c^n\) for every \(n\geq1\). A labeling scheme consists of an encoder and a decoder, fixed for the class and all input lengths. The encoder, given an adjacency-matrix encoding of \(G\in\mathcal C_n\), assigns one finite binary label to each vertex. The decoder receives only two labels and returns whether the corresponding distinct vertices are adjacent; it receives no graph description, class-membership oracle, additional table or external value of \(n\). Any size information needed by the decoder must be encoded within the labels. Both are deterministic algorithms, with no imposed time bound; encoding must halt on every graph in the class and decoding must halt on every pair of finite labels. Outside-class encoder behavior is unrestricted. All answers for pairs of vertices of an input member must be exact and simultaneous. Label length is the sole resource being bounded. No polynomial-time recognition of the class is assumed. Monotone, which is a stronger condition, means closed under deletion of both vertices and edges; this question assumes only hereditary closure.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of a labeling scheme and a class-dependent logarithmic length constant for every hereditary small class, or exhibit such a class and prove that no scheme satisfying these conditions exists. No efficient encoding or decoding time is required beyond the source’s algorithmic definition. A result for monotone or weakly sparse classes alone does not settle the universal claim.

title: Four-additive spanners with four-thirds-power size
summary: A spanner retains a subset of graph edges while approximately preserving distances. This card permits an additive increase of at most four edges for every vertex pair. It asks whether the retained subgraph always needs only a constant times n to the four-thirds edges. Only original unweighted edges may be retained. The statement is an existence question independent of construction time.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that every connected simple undirected unweighted graph \(G\) on \(n\ge2\) vertices has a spanning subgraph \(H\) with \[|E(H)|\le Cn^{4/3}\qquad\text{and}\qquad d_H(u,v)\le d_G(u,v)+4\quad\text{for all }u,v\in V(G)?\] Distances count edges. New edges, weights and vertices are not permitted, and no construction-time bound is imposed.
definitions: Each original edge has length one. \(d_{G}(u,v)\) is the minimum number of edges in a path, with \(d_{G}(u,u)=0\). A spanning subgraph H has the same vertex set and a subset of G’s edges, with unchanged unit lengths. If u,v are disconnected in H put \(d_{H}(u,v)=\infty\), so the requirement forces H to be connected. The lower inequality \(d_{H}(u,v)\ge d_{G}(u,v)\) follows from being a subgraph. The cost is number of retained edges; neither construction time nor weights, shortcuts, missing vertices, terminal subsets or faults are part of the model. New weighted edges would be an emulator and are not allowed. Restricting to connected inputs only removes disconnected bookkeeping; applying a universal bound componentwise recovers its usual all-graph form.
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one constant \(C\) suffices for every graph and all vertex pairs. A refutation must give, for every proposed \(C\), a graph for which every spanning subgraph with at most \(Cn^{4/3}\) edges violates the additive bound on some pair.

title: Additive-error exponent of linear-size spanners
summary: A sparse subgraph can increase distances even when all connected components are preserved. The card fixes a constant multiple of the vertex count as the edge budget. It asks for the exponent of the smallest worst-case additive distance error. Every fixed budget coefficient has an answer to absolute accuracy 0.01. New edges and hidden logarithmic increases in the edge budget are not allowed.
formal: For every fixed real edge-budget coefficient \(c\ge1\), determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the exponent \[x_{\mathrm{span}}(c)=\inf\{a\ge0:A_c(n)+1=O_c(n^a)\text{ as }n\to\infty\}.\] Here \(A_c(n)\), defined below, is the largest, over simple undirected unweighted \(n\)-vertex graphs, minimum additive all-pairs distance error of a spanning subgraph with at most \(\lfloor cn\rfloor\) edges and the same connected components. The edge budget is genuinely linear; no hidden logarithmic factor in the budget is allowed.
definitions: For every \(n\geq1\), let \(\mathcal G_n\) be the finite set of simple undirected graphs on \([n]\). Every edge has length one. A spanning subgraph \(H\subseteq G\) has the same vertices, retains only original edges, and must have the same connected components as \(G\). There are no Steiner vertices, shortcut edges or changed edge lengths. Let \[\Delta(G,H)=\max_{u,v:\,d_G(u,v)<\infty}\bigl(d_H(u,v)-d_G(u,v)\bigr),\qquad A_c(n)=\max_{G\in\mathcal G_n}\min_{\substack{H\subseteq G,\ |E(H)|\leq\lfloor cn\rfloor\\ H\text{ preserves components}}}\Delta(G,H).\] Distances count edges. Pairs with \(u=v\) are included, so the maximum is defined and nonnegative even in an edgeless graph. A spanning forest is feasible for \(c\geq1\); thus the quantity is finite. This measures optimal structural approximation, not the running time for finding a spanner; no algorithmic cost bound is imposed. The explicit coefficient \(c\) makes the source’s unspecified linear-size constant a parameter of the target. Define the exponent \[x_{\mathrm{span}}(c)=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \exists n_0\ge1\ \forall n\ge n_0,\ A_c(n)+1\le Cn^a\}.\] For each fixed real \(c\ge1\), the constants may depend on \(c\) and \(a\), but not on the graph or \(n\). Adding one removes zero-value conventions without changing any positive power of growth. A spanning forest has finite distances at most \(n-1\) within its components, so \(0\le x_{\mathrm{span}}(c)\le1\). The infimum need not be attained; no ordinary logarithmic-growth limit is assumed. In particular, exponent zero permits polylogarithmic or other subpolynomial error and does not promise bounded error.
answer_criterion: Supply one explicitly described real-valued function \(a\) on all real \(c\ge1\). Prove in Lean that \(|a(c)-x_{\mathrm{span}}(c)|\le1/100\) at every point of that domain. A pair of [certified bounding functions](definitions.html#numerical-answers) \(L,U\) also qualifies if \(L(c)\le x_{\mathrm{span}}(c)\le U(c)\) and \(U(c)-L(c)\le1/50\) everywhere, with \(a=(L+U)/2\). Use the same edge budget \(\lfloor cn\rfloor\) on both sides.

title: Explicit binary codes with efficient list decoding up to capacity
summary: The question asks for explicit binary codes with efficient list decoding throughout the binary capacity region. For each fixed error fraction and strictly smaller admissible rate, one deterministic pair of programs must work for every message length. The decoder must list all messages consistent with any adversarially corrupted received word in polynomial time. The inherited title and reversed printed rate inequality are corrected explicitly rather than interpreted as a request to exceed capacity. A complete Lean-checked proof must establish the full construction proposition or its logical negation.
formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every pair of rational constants \(\delta,R\) satisfying
\[
 0<\delta<\frac12,\qquad 0<R<1-H_2(\delta),
 \qquad H_2(t)=-t\log_2t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t),
\]
there are uniform deterministic polynomial-time encoding and list-decoding algorithms for binary codes
\[
 E_m:\{0,1\}^{m}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{N(m)}
 \quad(m\ge1),\qquad \frac{m}{N(m)}\ge R,
\]
such that every \(E_m\) is injective and the decoder, on every received word \(y\in\{0,1\}^{N(m)}\), outputs exactly
\[
 \{x\in\{0,1\}^{m}:d_H(E_m(x),y)\le\lfloor\delta N(m)\rfloor\}?
\]
The binary alphabet is fixed even as the gap to capacity tends to zero. The algorithms may depend on the two fixed constants but must handle all message lengths.
definitions:
A binary word is a finite sequence of zeros and ones. Hamming distance \(d_H(u,v)\) counts the coordinates at which equal-length words differ. A code here is an injective encoding of every \(m\)-bit message into a word of a common length \(N(m)\ge m\); it need not be linear or systematic. Its rate is the number of message bits divided by the number of encoded bits.

For each fixed admissible pair \((\delta,R)\), the claimed construction consists of finite deterministic classical multitape Turing programs for an encoder and decoder, constants \(K>0\) and integer \(b\ge1\), and an integer length function \(N(m)\). On an input message \(x\) of length \(m\), the encoder outputs \(E_m(x)\) in at most \(K(m+1)^b\) steps; the output length depends only on \(m\). Thus the length and code construction are effective. On input \((1^m,y)\), where \(y\) has length \(N(m)\), the decoder halts in at most \(K(N(m)+1)^b\) steps. It explicitly lists all qualifying messages, once each, and no others; an empty list is allowed. All reading, code construction, arithmetic, auxiliary computation and output are charged. There is no nonuniform advice, free block-length-dependent code table, external oracle or uncharged preprocessing.

The polynomial output-time bound also bounds the list size polynomially in the block length. No constant list-size bound is imposed. Requiring an exact list is equivalent to allowing additional candidates that can be removed within polynomial time using the encoder and a distance check, provided every qualifying message is included.

The decoder must work for every received word, so the errors may be adversarial. The task is global list decoding, not unique decoding, local decoding, erasure correction or reliable communication only under a random-noise distribution. The code must be binary; a larger alphabet whose size grows as the capacity gap shrinks is insufficient.

The constants, programs and polynomial exponent may depend arbitrarily on the fixed pair \((\delta,R)\). No polynomial dependence on the inverse capacity gap and no single algorithm taking these constants as variable input is requested. Rational constants give a precise countable formulation without changing the strict-slack capacity target: any real pair strictly inside the region is dominated by rational parameters with a slightly larger permitted error fraction and a slightly larger rate. A family is supplied for every message length; it need not attain every possible block length.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must supply the uniform algorithms, encoding injectivity, rate bound, exhaustive decoding correctness and polynomial running-time bounds for every fixed admissible parameter pair. A negative answer must refute this quantified existence assertion; an unproved hardness assumption establishes only a conditional obstruction.

A randomized code construction, inefficient exhaustive decoding, capacity over a variable alphabet, success only on randomly corrupted words, or a construction for only one rate/radius pair does not meet the target. The goal approaches the binary capacity from below; it does not ask to exceed that information-theoretic limit. No numerical tolerance is applied to this existence question.

title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for Steiner Tree
summary: Steiner Tree seeks a minimum-cost tree connecting a specified terminal set in an arbitrary undirected graph with nonnegative rational edge weights. The target is the infimum of approximation ratios achieved by uniform randomized algorithms that always output a feasible tree and run in polynomial time on every random tape. Each ratio bounds expected output cost on every instance, including those with zero optimum, while the algorithm may depend on the chosen ratio.
