Known algorithms approach \(\ln 4\), but the checked hardness bounds are conditional and the bounded later review found no determination of the optimal constant at the requested precision. An accepted answer supplies a real value with a complete Lean proof of absolute error at most \(1/100\), or a certified containing interval of width at most \(1/50\).
formal:
Determine the real constant \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\), the infimum of achievable expected-cost approximation ratios for undirected weighted Steiner Tree under worst-case polynomial running time. For the valid instances \(\mathcal I\) and the uniform randomized, always-feasible algorithms \(\mathcal A\) defined below, put
\[
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ST}}=
\left\{r\in\mathbb R:
r\ge1\ \land\
\exists A\in\mathcal A\ \forall I\in\mathcal I,\
\mathbb E_{\omega}\!\left[\operatorname{cost}_I(A(I;\omega))\right]
\le r\,\operatorname{OPT}(I)\right\},
\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}=\inf\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ST}}.
\]
Supply an unambiguous real value \(a\) and a complete Lean proof that
\[
\left|a-\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\right|\le\frac1{100}.
\]
The algorithm and its polynomial time bound may depend on \(r\), but must work for every valid instance. The expectation concerns output cost, not running time. No complexity assumption is part of the definition. The requested error is additive in this dimensionless approximation ratio.
definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A valid instance \(I=(n,E,R,w)\) consists of a connected simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), a set of terminals \(R\subseteq[n]\) with \(2\le |R|\le n\), and nonnegative rational weights \(w:E\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). An edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices; each pair occurs at most once. Connected means every two vertices are joined by a finite path. The whole graph, terminal list and all weights are explicitly given. There is no restriction on the topology, number of terminals, weight magnitudes, or ratio between positive weights.

A feasible solution is an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) such that the graph on vertex set
\[
W=R\cup\bigcup_{\{u,v\}\in F}\{u,v\}
\]
with edge set \(F\) is connected and has no cycle. Thus the output is one tree containing all terminals; its other vertices may be any subset of the available nonterminals. Its cost and the optimum are
\[
\operatorname{cost}_I(F)=\sum_{e\in F}w(e),
\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(I)=
\min\{\operatorname{cost}_I(F):F\text{ is a feasible solution of }I\}.
\]
Every valid instance has a feasible solution, so the minimum is over a nonempty finite set and is attained. Output edges must be original input edges. Neither new Steiner points outside \([n]\), a separate cost for selected vertices, a set of pairwise connection demands, nor directed edges are part of this problem.

The following encoding fixes the full bit cost. Write each weight uniquely as \(p_e/q_e\), where \(p_e\ge0\), \(q_e\ge1\), and the integers are relatively prime, so a zero weight is encoded as \(0/1\). Order edges lexicographically by their endpoints \(u<v\), obtaining \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\), and order terminal labels increasingly, obtaining \(r_1,\ldots,r_h\). Form one list of integers consisting of \(n\), the explicit vertex list \(1,\ldots,n\), \(m\), the four entries \(u,v,p_{e_j},q_{e_j}\) for each edge \(e_j=\{u,v\}\) in order, then \(h,r_1,\ldots,r_h\). Encode each integer in ordinary binary without leading zeros, with \(0\) represented by one zero. Put a separator \(\#\) between consecutive integers and no trailing separator. Finally encode the three symbols by \(0\mapsto00\), \(1\mapsto01\), \(\#\mapsto10\). The length of the resulting binary string is \(L(I)\). A valid output is the list consisting of \(|F|\) followed by the strictly increasing indices of the selected edges in \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\), using the same integer, separator and binary-symbol encoding. All numerator, denominator, endpoint and output bits count; arithmetic on rational numbers is not a unit-cost operation.

An algorithm is a single probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, a read-only input tape, a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes, and a sequential output tape. The input is delimited by end markers. Each transition reads the scanned symbols, can write one symbol per writable tape, and moves each head by at most one cell; it counts as one step. A transition may additionally read at most one fresh independent fair random bit. The program and tape count do not depend on the input length. There is no advice, oracle, real-arithmetic instruction or uncharged preprocessing. A deterministic algorithm is included by ignoring the random bits.

The set \(\mathcal A\) contains exactly the machines \(A\) for which there exist integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, on every binary input \(z\) and every random sequence \(\omega\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\), the machine halts within \(C(|z|+1)^k\) steps, and on every valid instance and every such sequence its output encodes a feasible solution. Invalid inputs may receive any output within that same bound. The constants \(C,k\) may depend on \(A\), but not on the instance or the random bits. This is a bound on every execution, not merely an expected-time bound.

The random sequence \(\omega\) has the product distribution of independent fair bits; there is no probability distribution on inputs. Since at most \(C(L(I)+1)^k\) bits can be read, the expected cost is the finite average over all bit strings of that length, each with equal probability, disregarding unused bits. Infeasibility has no permitted error probability. The multiplicative bound must hold on every valid instance, with no additive cost term or exception for small inputs. Instances with \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=0\) are included: their expected output cost must be zero. As every finite random execution has positive probability and costs are nonnegative, this requires zero output cost on every execution of such an instance.

Known polynomial-time approximations make \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ST}}\) nonempty; it is bounded below by \(1\), so its infimum is a finite real number. An algorithm attaining exactly \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\) need not exist. In particular, \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}=1\) would mean that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some eligible algorithm achieves ratio at most \(1+\varepsilon\), without requiring an exact algorithm or one program that takes \(\varepsilon\) as an additional input.

For the conditional results in the context, use [P and NP](definitions.html#p-np) and [RP](definitions.html#randomization) as defined in the shared glossary. No equality or separation among these classes is assumed in \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\).
answer_criterion:
An accepted answer supplies an unambiguous real value \(a\) and a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of
\[
\left|a-\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\right|\le\frac1{100}
\]
for precisely the instance class and machine model above. A certified interval \([\ell,u]\) with
\[
\ell\le\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\le u,\qquad u-\ell\le\frac1{50}
\]
qualifies through \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). The value need not be an integer, rational number or decimal expansion; exact determination is welcome but is not required. Merely renaming the defining infimum does not specify an answer.

The proof must respect the infimum's endpoint convention. To establish an upper bound \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\le u\), achievable ratios approaching \(u\) from above suffice; an algorithm achieving \(u\) itself is not required. Equivalently, one may prove that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an eligible algorithm whose expected cost on every instance is at most \((u+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\). A lower bound \(\ell\le\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\) must exclude every eligible algorithm from achieving each ratio \(r\) with \(1\le r<\ell\). For every such \(r\) and algorithm, this requires some valid instance with expected cost strictly greater than \(r\operatorname{OPT}\).

A hardness bound under an unproved complexity assumption proves only the corresponding conditional statement. It does not by itself certify the unconditional constant requested here. A gap for a particular linear-programming relaxation, the worst case of one selected algorithm, a guarantee only for a restricted graph family, or computations on finitely many input sizes do not determine this infimum over all eligible algorithms and all valid instances.

title: Strongly polynomial planar minimum-cost flow
summary: Minimum-cost flow assigns capacity-respecting arc flows that meet prescribed supplies and minimize total cost. The question asks for an asymptotic improvement over the quadratic-times-logarithmic bound on planar graphs. The algorithm must be strongly polynomial, so numerical magnitudes cannot enter its arithmetic-operation bound. A later nearly linear algorithm for polynomially bounded integer data does not by itself meet that requirement. A resolution would show whether planar structure yields a faster exact algorithm independently of the size of the input numbers.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic strongly polynomial algorithm for minimum-cost flow in a planar directed graph whose worst-case number of arithmetic operations and comparisons is \(o(n^{2}\log(n+2))\), where \(n\) is the number of vertices? The algorithm must return an exact minimum-cost feasible flow, or correctly report infeasibility, for all rational capacities, costs and vertex supplies.
definitions: The input is a finite directed graph with vertex set \([n]\), no loops and at most one arc for each ordered pair of vertices; opposite arcs are allowed. The underlying undirected graph is planar, and a combinatorial planar embedding is supplied. Thus the number of arcs is \(O(n)\). Each arc \(a\) has a finite rational capacity \(u_a\geq0\) and rational cost \(c_a\), and each vertex \(v\) has rational supply \(b_v\), with \(\sum_v b_v=0\). All numerators and positive denominators are encoded in binary; no magnitude bound is imposed. A feasible flow assigns rational \(f_a\) with \(0\leq f_a\leq u_a\) and \(\sum_{a\text{ out of }v} f_a-\sum_{a\text{ into }v}f_a=b_v\) at each vertex. Its cost is \(\sum_a c_a f_a\). Strong polynomiality means a bound polynomial in \(n\) on exact rational arithmetic operations, comparisons and index/memory operations, independent of all numeric bit lengths, together with a polynomial bound in total input bit length on every intermediate number’s encoding length. Arithmetic uses addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by nonzero values. The algorithm has finite uniform code and no advice, randomness or oracle. The little-o improvement means that there is a function \(T(n)\) bounding its operation count on every such \(n\)-vertex input with \(T(n)/(n^{2}\log(n+2))\to0\). The source’s instruction to beat the stated bound is interpreted as an asymptotic little-o improvement, not merely a smaller leading constant. The simple planar-network convention prevents arbitrarily many parallel arcs from hiding an unbounded input size in \(n\).
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm with the exact flow guarantee, little-o operation bound and polynomial intermediate bit lengths, or prove that no such deterministic strongly polynomial algorithm exists. A speedup for bounded numerical data, an approximation algorithm, or a lower leading constant at the same asymptotic order does not answer the stated question.

title: Complexity of general vertex-connectivity augmentation
summary: Vertex-connectivity measures how many vertex deletions a graph can withstand before disconnecting. The problem asks for the fewest unit-cost edges that raise this connectivity to an input target. Every missing edge is available, and the target may grow with the graph. Known one-increment algorithms and 2026 parameterized progress do not provide polynomial time for every target. A resolution would clarify the complexity of optimal vertex-failure resilience in the simplest unrestricted augmentation model.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a simple undirected graph \(G\) and a target \(1\leq\lambda<|V(G)|\), computes the minimum number of new edges needed to make \(G\) \(\lambda\)-vertex-connected, when every missing edge is available at unit cost?
definitions: The graph is finite, undirected and simple, with vertex set \([n]\), \(n\geq2\), and an explicit binary adjacency matrix. The integer \(\lambda\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}\) is part of the input, encoded in binary, and need not be fixed. The available links are exactly \(\binom{V(G)}{2}\setminus E(G)\). An augmentation is any subset \(F\) of these links; its cost is \(|F|\), and no new vertices are permitted. The graph \(G+F\) is \(\lambda\)-vertex-connected if deleting any set of fewer than \(\lambda\) vertices leaves a connected graph. The condition \(\lambda<n\) excludes ambiguous conventions on graphs with too few vertices. The optimum is finite because adding every missing edge produces a complete graph. The algorithm must output the exact minimum integer; equivalently it may decide, for a binary budget \(k\geq0\), whether some augmentation has \(|F|\leq k\). The two tasks are polynomial-time equivalent using the finite \(\binom n2\) budget range. Running time is worst-case bit time bounded by one fixed polynomial in the whole input length, with no exponent or multiplicative nonpolynomial dependence on \(\lambda\). The input graph may have arbitrary initial connectivity; there is no promise that the target increases connectivity by only one.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of a deterministic polynomial-time exact algorithm for all target values, or prove that no such algorithm exists. An algorithm polynomial only for fixed target connectivity, a parameterized algorithm exponential in the target or budget, an approximation, or a one-increment result does not meet the guarantee. A proof of NP-hardness alone establishes the implication from a polynomial-time augmentation algorithm to \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). Using this implication for an unconditional negative answer also requires a proof of \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

title: Linear-time exact inversion counting
summary: An inversion is a pair of permutation positions whose values appear in decreasing order. The task is to return the exact total number of such pairs as one integer. The question asks whether one deterministic program can do this in linear worst-case time on a word RAM with logarithmic words. Known approximation and adaptive algorithms do not provide that exact guarantee for every permutation. A STOC 2025 result links faster exact inversion counting to faster packed Dictionary Matching, giving the question broader algorithmic significance.
formal: Do there exist one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm \(A\) and a constant \(C>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\) and every explicitly listed permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(A\) outputs \[\operatorname{Inv}(\pi)=|\{(i,j)\in[n]^2:i<j\ \text{and}\ \pi(i)>\pi(j)\}|\] exactly, using at most \(Cn\) machine instructions in the worst case? The word length and allowed instructions are specified below. The constant and the program must be independent of \(n\) and \(\pi\).
definitions: The input contains \(n\) and the array \(\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(n)\), promised to contain each integer from one through \(n\) exactly once. The output is the single integer inversion count, between zero and \(n(n-1)/2\). Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Choose \(d\ge3\), so the count fits in a word. All constants are independent of the permutation and \(n\). No randomness is allowed. The values are already ranks, so no conversion from arbitrary ordered keys is required. The array has one entry per word; no compressed representation, streaming restriction or comparison-only restriction is imposed. The algorithm may use auxiliary random-access memory, but allocating, initializing and accessing that memory consumes the counted steps. The output is one word containing the exact nonnegative integer. Neither a list of all inverted pairs nor individual per-position counts are required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence assertion or its negation. A positive answer must specify one fixed program and prove its exact count and linear worst-case running time for every legal permutation in the specified model. A negative answer must exclude all such programs and all fixed constants. A relative-error estimate, an algorithm that is linear only on nearly sorted inputs, an expected-time randomized algorithm, or an improvement still superlinear in the worst case does not meet this target. A conditional lower bound establishes only its stated conditional implication.

title: Set-system sparsifiers of size proportional to chain length
summary: A sparsifier retains and reweights a few coordinates while approximately preserving every set’s total weight. The conjecture asks for a support bound proportional to chain length divided by \(\varepsilon ^{2}\). Chain length is measured through the union-closure, so even an incomparable collection of singleton sets can have large chain length. The published upper bound has extra logarithmic factors, which are precisely the remaining loss in the question. A resolution would establish whether this structural parameter completely controls multiplicative sparsification up to a universal constant.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that for every integer \(m\ge 1\), every family \(S\subseteq 2^{[m]}\), every weight vector \(w\in \mathbb{R} \ge 0^{m}\) and every \(0<\varepsilon <1\), there is a reweighting \(\tilde\{w\}\in \mathbb{R} \ge 0^{m}\) with at most \(C\cdot CL(S)/\varepsilon ^{2}\) nonzero coordinates and satisfying \((1- \varepsilon )\sum _{i\in A}w_{i}\le \sum _{i\in A}\tilde\{w\}_{i}\le (1+\varepsilon )\sum _{i\in A}w_{i}\) simultaneously for every \(A\in S\)?
definitions: Here \([m]=\{1,\ldots ,m\}\), and S is any finite collection of subsets, including possibly the empty collection. The support of w̃ is \(\{i:\tilde\{w\}_{i}>0\}\); coordinates outside it are dropped, while retained coordinates may receive arbitrary nonnegative real weights. No normalization such as \(\sum w_{i}=1\) is imposed. Following the source’s witness definition, a chain of length \(\ell\) consists of distinct coordinates \(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{\ell}\) and distinct sets \(A_{1},\ldots ,A_{\ell}\in S\) with \(a_{i}\in A_{i}\) for every i and \(a_{j}\notin A_{i}\) whenever \(i<j\). \(CL(S)\) is the maximum possible \(\ell\), allowing \(\ell =0\). Equivalently, take the union-closure \(U(S)=\{\bigcup T:T\subseteq S\}\), including the empty union; \(CL(S)\) is the largest number of strict inclusions in an ascending chain starting from \(\varnothing\) in \(U(S)\). Thus \(CL(S)=0\) when S is empty or contains only \(\varnothing\). It is not merely the largest chain in the original family. A \((1\pm \varepsilon )\) sparsifier is a reweighting satisfying the simultaneous inequalities in the statement. Sets of original weight zero must retain weight exactly zero. All data and weights are quantified mathematically; the question places no running-time, oracle-access, randomness or bit-complexity requirement on finding w̃. The same C must work independently of m, S, w and \(\varepsilon\). The source allows \(\varepsilon >0\); values \(\varepsilon \ge 1\) admit the zero reweighting, so restricting the nontrivial question to \(0<\varepsilon <1\) preserves it.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal existence bound with one absolute constant C, or refute it by showing that for every C there are a family, weights and an accuracy parameter for which every multiplicative sparsifier needs more than \(C\cdot CL(S)/\varepsilon ^{2}\) coordinates. Bounds with an additional unbounded logarithmic factor do not meet the conjecture; an efficient construction is not required.

title: Complexity of planar 3-edge-colorability
summary: Three-edge-colorability asks whether the edges of a graph can receive three colors with different colors on every pair meeting at a vertex. The selected question asks for the computational complexity of this decision problem on planar graphs. The source studies a sufficient route through augmentation to a planar cubic bridgeless supergraph, where three-edge-colorability follows from the Four-Color Theorem. It also discusses a conjectured characterization for two-connected planar graphs of maximum degree three. A full classification would determine whether the remaining planar cases admit an efficient coloring test or conceal an NP-hard obstruction.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple planar graph \(G\), decides whether its edges can be properly colored with three colors?
definitions: The input graph is undirected, without loops or parallel edges, and encoded by an adjacency matrix on the labeled vertex set \([n]\). The planarity promise means it admits a crossing-free embedding in the plane; no embedding is required as input. A proper three-edge-coloring is a function \(\chi:E(G)\to\{1,2,3\}\) assigning different colors to any two distinct edges with a common endpoint. Graphs may be disconnected, have bridges or isolated vertices, and need not be regular. A vertex of degree greater than three forces rejection, but no other special degree pattern or augmentation promise is imposed. Running time is worst-case bit time \(C(n+1)^k\) for fixed constants on a deterministic Turing machine, with no advice, randomness or oracle. The answer must be exact on every planar input. A total-language version may reject nonplanar encodings, since planarity can itself be tested in polynomial time. This card asks for decision, not for a prescribed structural characterization of all colorable graphs.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm for all planar inputs, or prove that no such algorithm exists. NP-hardness together with a Lean theorem conditional on P ≠ NP establishes conditional intractability and must be labeled as such; it is not by itself an unconditional refutation. Solving only cubic graphs or graphs admitting a particular augmentation is insufficient.

title: Polynomial-time minimum-total-length disjoint paths for fixed k
summary: The graph is undirected and unweighted, with a fixed number k of prescribed terminal pairs. The task is to find vertex-disjoint routes with the smallest possible total number of edges, or report that routing is impossible. Individual routes may need to be longer than their own shortest paths to avoid the others. The source asks for polynomial time at every fixed \(k\ge 3\), allowing the exponent to depend on k. Cao, Qi and Wang solve the related problem in which every route must attain its own shortest-path distance.
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 3\), is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given an undirected unweighted graph G and k prescribed terminal pairs \((s_{i},t_{i})\), outputs pairwise vertex-disjoint paths \(P_{i}\) from \(s_{i}\) to \(t_{i}\) minimizing \(\sum _{i}|E(P_{i})|\), or correctly reports that no such collection exists? Randomized algorithms with success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input are admitted in this reading, consistently with the randomized \(k=2\) baseline cited by the source. Polynomial degree and constants may depend on k; an FPT bound with exponent independent of k is not requested.
definitions: G is a finite simple connected undirected graph with n numbered vertices and unit length on every edge, encoded by an adjacency matrix and the terminal labels. Take the 2k terminals to be distinct; repeated endpoints across different pairs make vertex-disjointness infeasible, and a pair with \(s_{i}=t_{i}\) uses the zero-edge path at that vertex and can be handled separately. A path is a sequence of distinct vertices with consecutive vertices adjacent. Vertex-disjointness includes endpoints and means \(V(P_{i})\cap V(P_{j})=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\). Pairings are fixed: connecting a source to a different pair’s target is not acceptable. Define OPT as the minimum sum of edge counts over all feasible collections and set OPT=∞ when there is none. The output consists of the k vertex sequences of an optimal collection, or an infeasibility answer. For each fixed k the algorithm is a probabilistic Turing machine, with one finite program handling all n and all inputs for that k, running in at most \(C_{k}(n+1)^{c_{k}}\) steps on every random-bit sequence. Constants \(C_{k},c_{k}\) are independent of n. With probability at least \(2/3\) over its independent fair bits, the full output must be correct, including exact optimality. A deterministic algorithm is included as the zero-error case. The formulation asks for polynomial time for each fixed k and does not demand a uniform procedure generating these programs as k varies. The source compares this target with k-DSP, which requires every \(P_{i}\) separately to have length \(\operatorname{dist}_{G}(s_{i},t_{i})\). Such a collection, when it exists, has the smallest possible total length; minimum-total-length routing must also handle inputs where disjoint routes exist but no collection of individually shortest routes exists.
answer_criterion: Establish or refute polynomial-time solvability, with the stated bounded-error allowance, for every fixed \(k\ge 3\). A positive answer must output an exactly optimal collection or detect infeasibility on all inputs. A negative answer must exclude every allowed bounded-error polynomial-time algorithm for at least one fixed \(k\ge3\). Any additional hypothesis used to prove this exclusion must itself be established. Hardness only when k grows with n, an FPT lower bound, approximation, or an algorithm restricted to individually shortest paths does not decide this question.

title: A dichotomy for edge deletion with finitely many forbidden induced subgraphs
summary: The target graph property is specified by a fixed finite list of forbidden induced subgraphs. An instance asks whether deleting at most a supplied number of edges can achieve that property. The question is whether every such fixed-family problem is polynomial-time solvable or NP-complete. The finite-list domain is an explicit specialization of the survey’s broader hereditary-class research direction. A complete dichotomy must cover every finite forbidden family, rather than only single forbidden graphs or parameterized variants.
formal: For every fixed finite family \(\mathcal F\) of finite simple undirected graphs, is the following decision problem either in \(\mathrm{P}\) or \(\mathrm{NP}\)-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions? Given a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) and integer \(k\geq0\), decide whether there is \(S\subseteq E\) with \(|S|\leq k\) such that \(G-S\) has no induced subgraph isomorphic to any member of \(\mathcal F\).
definitions: A simple undirected graph has no loops or parallel edges. For \(U\subseteq V\), its induced subgraph contains every edge of \(G\) with both endpoints in \(U\). Graph isomorphism is an adjacency-preserving bijection of vertex sets. The class of \(\mathcal F\)-free graphs consists of all finite graphs with none of the forbidden induced subgraphs; it is hereditary, meaning closed under taking induced subgraphs. Deleting \(S\) retains all vertices and exactly the edges in \(E\setminus S\). Edges cannot be added, vertices cannot be removed, and every deleted edge costs one. The empty graph and the empty forbidden family are permitted. The input graph uses its adjacency matrix on numbered vertices; \(k\) is binary. The family \(\mathcal F\) is fixed before the input varies and is not part of the input to this decision problem. For each fixed family, its finite graph list may be built into the program, and polynomial exponents and constants may depend on it. A language is in \(\mathrm{P}\) if a deterministic Turing machine decides it in polynomial input length. It is in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if polynomial-size certificates can be checked in polynomial time. A polynomial-time many-one reduction from \(K\) to \(L\) is one deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) on finite binary strings such that \(x\in K\) iff \(f(x)\in L\). NP-completeness means membership in NP and such a reduction from every NP language. Each problem here is in NP because a deletion set can be checked and all induced copies of the finitely many fixed forbidden graphs can be enumerated in polynomial time. The dichotomy is inclusive; it assumes neither \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) nor its negation.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every finite family \(\mathcal F\) satisfies the stated P-or-NP-complete alternative. Alternatively specify one finite family and prove in Lean that its decision problem is neither in P nor NP-complete under the stated reductions. A theorem for a single forbidden graph or a fixed selection of graph classes is insufficient. No separate effective procedure for classifying the family \(\mathcal F\) is imposed by this proposition.

title: Černý conjecture
summary: A synchronizing automaton has an input word that sends all states to one common state. This word resets the system without observing its unknown initial state. The Černý conjecture bounds the shortest reset word by the square of one less than the number of states. The assertion covers every complete deterministic automaton and every finite alphabet. Known extremal examples explain the exact quadratic threshold.
formal: Does every synchronizing complete deterministic finite automaton with \(n\ge1\) states have a reset word of length at most \((n-1)^2\)? The statement quantifies over all finite nonempty alphabets. A reset word sends every possible initial state to the same state, under the transition model below.
definitions: An automaton is a finite transition system \(A=(Q,\Sigma,\delta)\), where \(|Q|=n\ge1\), \(\Sigma\) is a finite nonempty alphabet and \(\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q\) is total. Extend it to words by \(\delta(q,\epsilon)=q\) and \(\delta(q,wa)=\delta(\delta(q,w),a)\). A word \(w\) is a reset word if \(|\{\delta(q,w):q\in Q\}|=1\); its length is its number of letters. Synchronizing means that at least one reset word exists. Its final state is not prescribed. Initial and accepting states play no role, and the empty word handles \(n=1\). There is no strong-connectivity, fixed-alphabet or other structural promise. Partial or nondeterministic automata, and synchronization of only a prescribed subset of states, are different models. No time bound for constructing the word is imposed. In the context, \(T(n)\) denotes the maximum shortest-reset-word length over all such synchronizing automata with \(n\) states; duplicate letter transformations can be removed, so this maximum exists.
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that every synchronizing \(n\)-state automaton has a reset word of length at most \((n-1)^2\), or exhibit a synchronizing automaton and prove that every word up to that length fails to reset it.

title: Sakoda–Sipser problem
summary: Two-way finite automata can reread their input by moving their head in either direction. This project asks whether every n-state nondeterministic machine has an equivalent deterministic two-way machine with polynomially many states. Both machines must agree on all finite words, with no restriction on input length. Rereading sometimes replaces exponentially much one-way memory, but that observation does not supply a general simulation. Resolving the question would quantify how much finite-state succinctness comes from nondeterministic choice once unrestricted revisiting of the input is available.
formal: Do universal constants \(C,k\ge 1\) exist such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every finite nonempty input alphabet \(\Sigma\) and every two-way nondeterministic finite automaton A over \(\Sigma\) with at most n states, there is a two-way deterministic finite automaton D over the same alphabet with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states satisfying \(L(D)=L(A)\)? Equivalence must hold on all finite input words, without a length bound.
definitions: The read-only input tape contains a left endmarker, a word \(w\in \Sigma^{*}\), and a right endmarker. Each automaton has one head, initially on the left endmarker, a finite set Q of states with a designated initial state and designated halting accepting states. In each nonhalting configuration it uses its current state and the scanned symbol to choose a new state and a head displacement in \(\{- 1,0,+1\}\); moves outside the endmarkers are forbidden. A missing transition rejects that branch. A word is accepted if some finite computation reaches an accepting state. Infinite nonaccepting branches do not count as acceptance. For a deterministic automaton there is at most one available transition in each state-symbol pair, and its unique infinite run, if any, rejects. There is no work tape, rewritable input, second head, stack, counter, randomness or advice. State count includes all control and halting states, but the bound is independent of word length and alphabet size. The target is existence of D for each A; computing D from A is not required to take polynomial time. Standard endmarker and stay-put conventions change these state bounds only by polynomial factors.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of universal constants C,k giving an equivalent 2DFA with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states for every n-state 2NFA, or prove that no such constants exist. In the negative direction, every proposed polynomial bound must fail on some source automaton; all language comparisons concern words of every length.

title: Generalized star-height problem
summary: Generalized regular expressions describe regular languages using concatenation, Boolean operations and arbitrary finite repetition. Their star height counts nested repetitions while allowing complementation without an additional height charge. The question asks for a language whose every such description needs at least two nested stars. Ordinary examples with complicated repetitions may simplify drastically when complements are allowed, so inspecting one expression proves little. Establishing a separation beyond height one would reveal a further intrinsic layer of repetition complexity within regular languages.
formal: Does there exist a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\) and a regular language \(L\subseteq \Sigma^{*}\) such that every generalized regular expression denoting L has Kleene-star nesting depth at least two, when complement is allowed without increasing that depth?
definitions: \(\Sigma^{*}\) is the set of all finite words over \(\Sigma\), including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). A regular language is one accepted by a finite deterministic automaton. Generalized expressions are finite expressions built from \(\varnothing , \varepsilon\), and the letters \(a\in \Sigma\) using binary union \(E\cup F\), concatenation EF, complement \(E^{c}\), and Kleene star E*. Their meanings are respectively the empty language, \(\{\varepsilon\}, \{a\}\), language union, all concatenations uv with \(u\in L(E)\) and \(v\in L(F), \Sigma^{*}\setminus L(E)\), and the union of all finite concatenation powers of \(L(E)\), including power zero \(\{\varepsilon\}\). Set \(h(\varnothing )=h(\varepsilon )=h(a)=0, h(E\cup F)=h(\mathrm{EF})=\max \{h(E),h(F)\}, h(E^{c})=h(E)\), and \(h(E*)=h(E)+1\). Define \(h_{g}(L)=\min \{h(E):L(E)=L\}\), which exists because every regular language has an ordinary regular expression. The question is whether \(h_{g}(L)>1\) for at least one such L. There is no bound on expression size, number of complements, union or concatenation depth, automaton size, or alphabet size. Intersection is permitted as the abbreviation \((E^{c}\cup F^{c})^{c}\) and does not add star depth. Backreferences, infinite words, additional predicates and auxiliary alphabets in the final expression are not part of the syntax.
answer_criterion: Prove that some regular language has generalized star height at least two, including a lower bound over all generalized expressions for that language, or prove that every regular language over every finite nonempty alphabet has a generalized expression of star height at most one. Expression size is unrestricted in both alternatives.

title: Decidability of equivalence for unambiguous context-free grammars
summary: An unambiguous context-free grammar has at most one parse tree for every generated word. Two such grammars are given with the promise of unambiguity. The task is to decide whether they generate exactly the same finite words. No deterministic-pushdown or regular-language restriction is imposed. The question asks for a terminating decision procedure without any prescribed complexity bound.
formal: Is it decidable, given two finite context-free grammars \(G_1,G_2\) over the same finite terminal alphabet and promised that both are unambiguous, whether \(L(G_1)=L(G_2)\)?
definitions: A context-free grammar \(G=(V,\Sigma,P,S)\) has finite disjoint sets of nonterminals \(V\) and terminals \(\Sigma\), a start symbol \(S\in V\), and a finite set of productions \(A\to u\), with \(A\in V\) and \(u\in(V\cup\Sigma)^*\). Empty right-hand sides and unit productions are allowed. A parse tree is a finite ordered rooted tree with root \(S\) whose nonterminal nodes expand by productions; its terminal leaves read from left to right form the generated word, possibly empty. The language \(L(G)\subseteq\Sigma^*\) consists of words with such a tree. Unambiguous means at most one parse tree for each word, not at most one order of expanding a fixed tree. Both grammars, alphabet lists and full production strings are explicit finite inputs with binary symbol identifiers and delimiters; duplicate written productions are identified. The decision algorithm is one deterministic Turing machine that terminates on every syntactically valid pair and is correct whenever both grammars satisfy the promise. On pairs violating the promise it may return either answer. Invalid syntax may be rejected. It receives no proof of unambiguity and need not decide that promise. There is no running-time bound, determinism promise for the grammars or restriction to regular or unary languages.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof that such a decision machine exists, or a Lean proof that the promised equivalence problem is undecidable. A result for deterministic pushdown presentations, comparison with only a finite automaton, or a semidecision procedure for inequivalence does not settle the complete two-grammar question.

title: First-order definability of regular tree languages
summary: Can one decide whether a regular language of finite ordered trees has a first-order definition? The automaton is finite input, while the sought sentence must describe its language on trees of every finite size. The logic can inspect labels, descendants and sibling order but cannot quantify over sets of nodes. Known fragment tests and separate necessary or sufficient algebraic conditions leave the full decision problem unresolved. Recent infinite-tree and restricted temporal-logic characterizations do not establish this finite ordered-tree test.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given a finite bottom-up automaton A for finite unranked ordered labeled trees, always halts and decides whether some first-order sentence \(\varphi\) using label predicates, strict descendant and sibling order satisfies A accepts t if and only if \(t\models \varphi\) for every finite input tree t?
definitions: A tree is a finite nonempty set T of finite words over positive integers, containing the empty word \(\varepsilon\), closed under prefixes, and such that \(ui\in T\) implies \(uj\in T\) for \(1\le j\le i\). Its root is \(\varepsilon\); the children of u are \(u1,\ldots ,uk\) in that order. Each node has exactly one label from a nonempty finite alphabet \(\Sigma\). There is no fixed bound on k. \(Desc(x,y)\) means x is a proper prefix of y, so y is a strict descendant of x. \(Sib(x,y)\) means \(x=ui\) and \(y=uj\) for the same parent u with \(i<j\); it orders siblings, not all incomparable nodes. Equality and the unary predicates \(P_{a}(x)\), one per label \(a\in \Sigma\), complete the logical vocabulary. First-order sentences are finite formulas formed from these atomic predicates by Boolean connectives and quantification over individual nodes only, with any finite number of variables and alternations. No quantification over sets, counting quantifier or extra transitive-closure operator is allowed. The parent relation is definable from Desc. The lexicographic order used in the primary paper is equivalent to Desc plus Sib: x precedes y if \(Desc(x,y)\), or some sibling s of t precedes it with s equal to or an ancestor of x and t equal to or an ancestor of y. Conversely Sib is definable from parent and lexicographic order. To fix a finite input presentation, a bottom-up automaton consists of a finite nonempty state set Q, a binary operation ⊕ and identity 0 making \((Q,\oplus ,0) a\) monoid, a table \(\delta _{a}:Q\to Q\) for each \(a\in \Sigma\), and an accepting subset \(F\subseteq Q\). A node labeled a with ordered child states \(q_{1},\ldots ,q_{k}\) receives state \(\delta _{a}(q_{1}\oplus \cdots \oplus q_{k})\); the empty sum is 0. The tree is accepted when its root state lies in F. These finite tables, alphabet and state indices are explicitly encoded in binary; this is an algebraic bottom-up presentation of regular unranked tree languages. The algorithm must work for every valid finite presentation, without a complexity bound beyond termination. The sentence \(\varphi\) may depend on A, but must be a single sentence for all finite trees and all their sizes.
answer_criterion: Prove decidability by an algorithm that terminates correctly on every valid automaton description, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. Recognizing trees with a fixed supplied automaton, deciding whether one supplied sentence agrees with an automaton, or testing definability in a fixed quantifier fragment does not decide existence of an arbitrary first-order definition.

title: Decidability of every level of the dot-depth hierarchy
summary: The dot-depth hierarchy sorts star-free regular languages by how repeatedly concatenation and Boolean operations must be combined. Given a finite automaton and a fixed level, the project asks whether membership in that level can always be decided. The relevant level concerns the simplest possible description of the language, rather than the syntax initially supplied. Deciding star-freeness only establishes membership somewhere in the hierarchy and does not identify a prescribed level. An effective test for every level would connect automaton behavior to precise bounds on logical descriptive complexity.
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), is there an algorithm that, given a deterministic finite automaton over a finite alphabet A, always halts and decides whether its language belongs to \(DD_{k}(A)\), the k-th dot-depth level defined below?
definitions: For each finite nonempty alphabet A, let A* be its finite words, \(\varepsilon\) the empty word, and \(A+=A*\setminus \{\varepsilon\}\). Set \(DD_{0}(A)=\{\varnothing ,\{\varepsilon\},A+,A*\}\). For a class C of languages over \(A, Pol(C)\) consists of all finite unions of marked products \(L_{0}a_{1}L_{1}\cdots a_{r} L_{r}\), where \(r\ge 0\), each \(a_{i}\in A\), and every \(L_{i}\in C; r=0\) gives \(L_{0}\). Let \(Bool(C)\) be closure under finite union, finite intersection and complement relative to A*. Define \(DD_{k+1}(A)\)=Bool(\(Pol(DD_{k}(A))\)). The input automaton is given by finite explicit tables, including its alphabet, initial state and accepting states; its accepted language is \(L(M)\). The question quantifies \(\forall k\exists a\) total Turing algorithm \(A_{k}\forall M\), with \(A_{k}(M)\)=yes exactly when \(L(M)\in DD_{k}(A)\). Each \(A_{k}\) must handle arbitrary finite input alphabets. No polynomial-time or elementary-time bound is requested. This fixes the full integer levels and the four-language level-zero convention; it does not merge distinct concatenation hierarchies or leave the logical signature implicit. Use the [explicit encoding convention](definitions.html#encoding).
answer_criterion: Prove that membership in \(DD_{k}\) is decidable for every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), with each decider handling all finite alphabets, or prove that membership is undecidable for at least one fixed level k. The positive statement does not require an effective procedure that takes k as an additional input.

title: Equivalence of deterministic macro tree transducers
summary: Deterministic macro tree transducers are recursive programs that turn finite ordered trees into other trees. Parameters carry intermediate output pieces, which rules may pass onward or duplicate during processing. The project asks whether two such programs define exactly the same partial transformation on every finite input tree. Testing examples can reveal a disagreement but cannot certify universal agreement without a completeness argument. A general decision procedure would provide an exact equivalence test for an expressive model of structured-data transformation, including cases with very large outputs.
formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given two deterministic macro tree transducers with the same finite ranked input and output alphabets, decides whether they define exactly the same partial function from finite ordered input trees to finite ordered output trees?
definitions: Fix the ordinary inside-out, or call-by-value, semantics. A ranked alphabet assigns a nonnegative arity to each symbol; a tree node has exactly that many ordered children. A transducer has finitely many states q, each with one input-tree argument and \(m(q)\) output-tree parameters, and an initial state \(q_{0}\) with \(m(q_{0})=0\). For each state q and input symbol \(\sigma\) of arity k there is at most one rule \(q(\sigma (x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k}),y_{1},\ldots ,y_{m})\to r\). The finite right-hand side follows the grammar \(r ::= y_{j} | \delta (r_{1},\ldots ,r_{l}) | q' (x_{i},r_{1},\ldots ,r_{m(q' )})\), with \(\delta\) an output symbol of arity l and \(1\le i\le k\). Subtrees and parameters may be copied or deleted, and calls may be nested inside parameter arguments without a fixed nesting bound across instances. On input \(\sigma (t_{1},\ldots ,t_{k})\), evaluate parameter arguments to output trees, then evaluate a call \(q'\) on the indicated child \(t_{i}\) with those parameter values. A missing rule makes the corresponding evaluation undefined, and under call-by-value an undefined argument makes its enclosing evaluation undefined. There is no inspection or pattern matching on parameter trees. Every recursive call processes a proper input child, so evaluation terminates on each finite input, with either a finite tree or undefined. A transducer with a rule for every state/symbol pair is total. There is no regular look-ahead oracle in this chosen syntax. Equality requires identical domains and, on that domain, identical labelled ordered output trees, without identifying different trees by their leaf strings, shapes or origin annotations. Input alphabets, state sets, arities and rules are all part of the finite input to the desired decision algorithm.
answer_criterion: Prove that equivalence of the specified partial deterministic macro tree transducers is decidable by a total algorithm, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. Equivalence requires equality of domains and of the labelled ordered output trees on every input in the common domain.
references: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ipl.2022.106332 | https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.5597 | https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.09163 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22047 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.10270v4 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.03928

title: Equivalence of deterministic higher-order recursion schemes
summary: A deterministic higher-order recursion scheme is a finite typed system of recursive rules that generates a possibly infinite ordered constructor tree. The question asks for one terminating algorithm deciding equality of the complete value trees of any two such schemes. The input orders are arbitrary finite numbers, and equality includes divergence leaves while ignoring internal unfolding steps. Order-one equivalence is decidable, but conditional logical reductions and recent results for other higher-order models do not settle this unrestricted target. A resolution would establish the boundary of exact behavioral comparison for higher-order recursive tree generators.
formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which, on every pair \((G,H)\) of finite deterministic higher-order recursion schemes over the same finite ranked alphabet, halts and decides whether \[\operatorname{Tree}(G)=\operatorname{Tree}(H)?\] Both schemes may have arbitrary finite type order, with their orders supplied by their finite descriptions. Equality is exact equality of the possibly infinite ordered value trees, including the nullary divergence symbol \(\bot\). No safety or productivity promise is imposed.
definitions:
A ranked alphabet \(\Sigma\) is a finite set of terminal symbols with ranks \(r(a)\in\mathbb N\). Simple types are finite expressions generated by a base type \(o\) and the arrow constructor \(\tau\to\sigma\), associating to the right. A terminal of rank \(r\) has the type with \(r\) arguments of type \(o\) and result \(o\); rank zero means type \(o\). A scheme has a finite set of typed nonterminals, one distinguished start nonterminal \(S:o\), and exactly one rule \[F x_1\cdots x_k\longrightarrow t\] for each nonterminal \(F:\tau_1\to\cdots\to\tau_k\to o\). Here the distinct variables \(x_i:\tau_i\) are the only variables allowed in \(t\), and \(t:o\) is a finite well-typed applicative term over terminals, nonterminals and these variables. Terms are symbols or applications \(uv\), with \(u:\alpha\to\beta\) and \(v:\alpha\) giving \(uv:\beta\); application associates to the left. Rules may be mutually recursive and may duplicate or discard parameters. There are no data tests, constructor equations, pattern matching or nondeterministic alternatives. No syntactic restriction called safety is required.

Starting at the closed ground term \(S\), expose the head constructor by repeatedly replacing a fully applied head nonterminal \(F u_1\cdots u_k\) by \(t[u_1/x_1,\ldots,u_k/x_k]\). When a terminal head \(a u_1\cdots u_{r(a)}\) is exposed, output a node labeled \(a\) with the ordered child trees obtained in the same way from the ground terms \(u_i\). If the head unfolding never exposes a terminal, output a single \(\bot\) node with no children. In particular, unfolding does not require finishing a constructor's arguments before exposing that constructor. This defines \(\operatorname{Tree}(G)\) over \(\Sigma\cup\{\bot\}\). A node address is a finite sequence of positive integers specifying successive child positions, starting with the empty address at the root. A terminal of rank \(r\) has precisely children numbered \(1,\ldots,r\), and \(\bot\) has none. Equality means the same set of addresses and the same label at every address. The number of unfolding steps and the names of internal nonterminals are not observable.

Type order is defined by \(\operatorname{ord}(o)=0\) and \(\operatorname{ord}(\tau\to\sigma)=\max\{\operatorname{ord}(\tau)+1,\operatorname{ord}(\sigma)\}\). A scheme's order is the maximum order of its nonterminals; the two input orders need not agree. An input explicitly lists the finite alphabet and ranks, type syntax trees, nonterminal symbols, start symbols and rule syntax trees, with binary indices and delimiters. Well-typedness and the syntactic conditions are effectively checked; invalid descriptions are rejected. The sought machine must work uniformly over all valid encodings, alphabets, finite orders and rule sizes. It returns an exact Boolean answer, without approximation, random error, an oracle, or any additional time or space requirement beyond termination.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of decidability or undecidability of the input language defined above. A positive answer must supply one effective algorithm and prove its termination and correctness on every valid pair, including equal infinite trees and divergent schemes, uniformly in the finite input orders. A negative answer must prove that no total computable decider exists; undecidability for one fixed order already suffices for this unrestricted problem. A positive algorithm only for a restricted order or safety class, model checking of one tree, or a theorem conditional on another unresolved decision problem is not a full positive answer. No finite-depth approximation to tree equality is accepted.

title: Linear-time minimization of deterministic finite automata
summary: A deterministic finite automaton can be minimized by merging reachable states that accept exactly the same continuation words. The question asks whether every complete automaton over any fixed alphabet of at least two letters can be minimized in deterministic linear worst-case word-RAM time. The output must be an explicit smallest automaton recognizing exactly the original language, and all preprocessing and output work count. Classical algorithms take O(n log n) time, while known logarithmic-factor lower bounds concern partition refinement rather than every algorithm in the stated model. A resolution would determine whether the extra logarithmic cost reflects the general problem or the structure of its classical algorithms.
formal: For every fixed alphabet size \(a\ge2\), is deterministic minimization of complete finite automata over \([a]=\{0,\ldots,a-1\}\) possible in \(O(n)\) worst-case time on the word-RAM defined below? More explicitly, the target is \[\forall a\ge2\ \exists M_a,C_a,n_a\ \forall n\ge n_a\ \forall A\text{ with }n\text{ states},\quad M_a(A)\text{ outputs a smallest equivalent complete DFA in at most }C_a n\text{ steps}.\] Here \(M_a\) is a single finite program independent of \(n\); \(C_a\) and \(n_a\) may depend on \(a\), and \(n_a\ge a\) may be assumed. The task is exact language-preserving minimization, with no prescribed canonical naming of output states.
definitions:
For \(n\ge1\), an input DFA is \(A=([n],[a],\delta,s,F)\), where \(\delta:[n]\times[a]\to[n]\) is total, \(s\in[n]\), and \(F\subseteq[n]\). Its explicit input consists of \(n\), \(s\), the \(an\) transition targets, and \(n\) accepting-state bits, one target or bit per input word. Extend \(\delta\) to finite words by \(\delta^*(q,\varepsilon)=q\) and \(\delta^*(q,ub)=\delta(\delta^*(q,u),b)\). The recognized language is \(\{u:\delta^*(s,u)\in F\}\). The output is an explicit complete DFA \(B=([k],[a],\delta',s',F')\), \(1\le k\le n\), recognizing exactly that language, with \(k\) minimal among all complete DFAs over the same alphabet. Unreachable input states may be discarded; no equivalence partition for them is required. Both input and output transitions are explicitly represented.

Use one sequential deterministic word-RAM with word length \(w=\lceil2\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), addressed word memory and finitely many registers. Reading or writing one addressed word, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), Boolean bit operations, shifts by an amount less than \(w\), comparisons and conditional branches each cost one step. No arbitrary-precision arithmetic, oracle instruction or externally supplied lookup table is available. The finite program may depend on the fixed alphabet size but not on the input size. All algorithmic preprocessing, auxiliary-table construction, initialization and output writing are charged to the running time; memory beyond the input has a fixed blank initial value. The asymptotic target is considered for \(n\ge n_a\ge a\), so the explicit \(an\)-word transition table fits the chosen word address space. Finitely many smaller sizes for each fixed alphabet are finite exceptions to the asymptotic claim. This spells out the input-addressing convention without changing the saved logarithmic word formula. The cost is in word operations, not bit operations: the input uses \(\Theta(n)\) words for fixed \(a\). There is no randomization, expected-time qualification, distribution on inputs, language approximation or promise on the transition graph.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed proposition or its logical negation, including correctness, minimality, explicit output and the stated RAM cost. A positive proof must cover every fixed \(a\ge2\) by a uniform-in-\(n\) finite program and fixed constants. A negative proof must establish that for some fixed \(a\ge2\), every correct program in this full RAM model fails an \(O(n)\) worst-case bound: no constants \(C,n_0\) work for all sufficiently large inputs. A lower bound restricted to partition refinement, a comparison model or one particular minimization algorithm does not prove this negation. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional version.

title: Decidability of the nondeterministic tree-automaton index problem
summary: The input automaton recognizes a language of infinite binary trees. Acceptance requires one run whose every branch satisfies parity. The target asks whether the language can use a specified interval of priorities. The replacement may have arbitrarily many finite states. Recent characterizations do not by themselves decide the general index problem.
formal: Is it decidable, given a nondeterministic parity automaton A on infinite full binary trees and a nonempty integer priority interval J={i,…,j}, whether some nondeterministic parity tree automaton over the same alphabet, using only priorities in J, recognizes exactly the same language as A?
definitions:
An input tree is a function from finite binary strings to a supplied finite nonempty alphabet Sigma. An automaton has a finite state set Q, an initial state q0, a transition relation Delta contained in Q×Sigma×Q×Q, and a map assigning a nonnegative integer priority to each state. A run labels every tree node by a state, starts with q0, and at each node obeys one transition specifying the left and right child states. A run accepts if, on every infinite branch, the largest priority appearing infinitely often is even. A tree is accepted if at least one accepting run exists. Missing transitions simply preclude a run.

All tables and priorities are explicit finite input data; i and j are binary integers with 0≤i≤j. The sought automaton may have any finite number of states and need not use every priority in J. Equivalence quantifies over all infinite Sigma-labelled binary trees. The decision algorithm is a total Turing machine with no complexity bound. The max-even convention is fixed for both automata; shifting or reversing priorities must preserve this convention and the target interval.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked decision procedure for all such inputs, or prove undecidability. A characterization with an undecided boundedness condition is insufficient. Results restricted to deterministic, alternating or word automata do not answer the nondeterministic tree problem.

title: Separating words problem
summary: Two distinct binary strings are given at the same length. A separating deterministic finite automaton must accept exactly one of them. The question asks whether a logarithmic number of states always suffices. The automaton may depend on both strings and has no restriction on other inputs. This is stronger than merely asking whether the polynomial growth exponent is zero.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that any two distinct binary words of length \(n\ge1\) can be distinguished by a deterministic finite automaton with at most \(C\log_2(n+1)\) states? Distinguishing means accepting exactly one of the two words, with unrestricted behavior on all other words. The automaton may depend on the pair, and its complete one-pass transition model is defined below.
definitions:
The parameter \(n\) is a positive integer and both words have exactly \(n\) symbols. A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) consists of a finite nonempty set \(Q\), one initial state \(q_0\), a total transition function \(\delta:Q\times\{0,1\}\to Q\), and an accepting set \(F\subseteq Q\). It reads its word once from left to right, starting at \(q_0\), applies \(\delta\) for each symbol and accepts exactly when its final state lies in \(F\). There are no epsilon transitions, auxiliary storage or external position counters. All states, including any rejecting sink, count toward size. The automaton may depend on the pair of words, and either orientation of acceptance is allowed. Its behavior on other words is unrestricted. The minimum is finite, since a DFA can recognize a singleton word, and the maximum is over a finite nonempty set of pairs. No efficiency requirement is imposed on finding the automaton.

Precisely, write
\[
s(n)=\max_{\substack{u,v\in\{0,1\}^n\\u\ne v}}
\min\bigl\{|Q|:\text{a DFA with state set }Q\text{ accepts exactly one of }u,v\bigr\}.
\]
The maximum and minimum use the model above. A complete DFA recognizing one fixed length-\(n\) word has at most \(n+2\) states, so \(1\le s(n)\le n+2\).

The assertion \(s(n)=O(\log n)\) is expressed for all positive lengths using \(\log_2(n+1)\). One universal constant must cover every length and every pair of distinct words; no efficiency bound is imposed on constructing the separating automaton.
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one constant \(C\) works for every pair of distinct equal-length binary words. To refute the bound, show that for every \(C>0\) some pair requires more than \(C\log_2(n+1)\) states.

title: Primitive words and context-freeness
summary: A primitive word is nonempty and is not a power of any shorter nonempty word. The language contains all such words over a fixed finite alphabet with at least two symbols. The conjecture says that no context-free grammar generates exactly this language. Grammars may be ambiguous, so unique-parse limitations would not settle the question. A 2026 paper still states this grammar-expressibility question as open.
formal: For every finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) with \(|\Sigma|\ge2\), is the language \[\operatorname{Prim}(\Sigma)=\{w\in\Sigma^+ : \text{there are no }u\in\Sigma^+,\ k\ge2\text{ with }w=u^k\}\] not context-free?
definitions: An alphabet is a finite set of symbols. A word is a finite sequence of symbols; \(\Sigma^*\) includes the empty word and \(\Sigma^+\) excludes it. The power \(u^k\) is the concatenation of \(k\) copies of \(u\), where \(k\) is an integer. All one-letter words are primitive. A context-free grammar consists of a finite set \(V\) of nonterminals disjoint from \(\Sigma\), a start symbol \(S\in V\), and a finite set of rules \(A\to x\) with \(A\in V\) and \(x\in(V\cup\Sigma)^*\). Its language is the set of all terminal words derivable from \(S\) by finitely many applications of rules. Empty productions, unit productions and ambiguity are allowed. The assertion is that no such grammar has language exactly \(\operatorname{Prim}(\Sigma)\), for every allowed alphabet. It concerns all word lengths, with no algorithmic size or running-time parameter. Nonprimitive words are excluded even when their repeated root is itself nonprimitive.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof that the primitive-word language is non-context-free for every finite alphabet of size at least two, or a Lean counterexample consisting of an allowed alphabet and a context-free grammar generating exactly its primitive words. Excluding only unambiguous grammars, deterministic grammars or grammars of bounded size is insufficient.

title: Complement closure of conjunctive languages
summary: Conjunctive grammars combine concatenation, union and intersection. The question asks whether their languages are closed under complement over the same alphabet. The grammar semantics uses the least fixed point of positive language equations. A complement may need a completely different grammar with no prescribed size bound. Known non-closure for unambiguous linear grammars does not settle the full conjunctive class.
formal: For every finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) and every conjunctive grammar G over it, does there exist a conjunctive grammar H over the same terminal alphabet with \[L(H)=\Sigma^*\setminus L(G)\,?\]
definitions: A conjunctive grammar has a finite terminal alphabet \(\Sigma\), a disjoint finite set N of nonterminals, a start symbol S, and finitely many rules \(A\to\alpha_1\mathbin{\&}\cdots\mathbin{\&}\alpha_k\), with \(k\ge1\) and \(\alpha_i\in(\Sigma\cup N)^*\). Interpret a terminal as its singleton language, a word of symbols as concatenation of their languages, a conjunction as intersection, and alternative rules for A as union. The language tuple is the least fixed point of these monotone equations, equivalently the union of their iterations starting with empty nonterminal languages. An empty right-hand-side word denotes \(\{\varepsilon\}\); a nonterminal with no rules denotes the empty language. No negation appears in the grammar. The complement is relative to all finite words over the declared alphabet, including the empty word. H may use arbitrarily many new nonterminals and rules. The target is closure of the language class: no computable transformation, grammar-size bound, linearity or unambiguity requirement is added. Boolean grammars may use negation and have different semantic issues; their complement properties do not provide a conjunctive grammar automatically. Linear conjunctive grammars restrict each conjunct to at most one nonterminal and are not the full class in this question.
answer_criterion: Prove the closure statement in Lean, with an equivalent conjunctive grammar for every input language, or give a conjunctive grammar and prove that its complement has no conjunctive grammar whatsoever. Showing that a complement is not context-free, not linear, or not unambiguous does not prove non-closure of the full conjunctive class.

title: Dense periodic behavior in surjective one-dimensional cellular automata
summary: A local rule updates every site of a two-sided infinite configuration. Surjectivity guarantees a predecessor for every configuration. The conjecture asks whether every finite observation extends to a temporally periodic configuration. Spatial periodicity and eventual periodicity are different requirements. Known special cases and reformulations do not automatically cover every surjective rule.
formal: For every finite nonempty alphabet A, radius r≥0 and local rule \(f:A^{2r+1}\to A\), let \(F:A^{\mathbb Z}\to A^{\mathbb Z}\) be defined by \(F(x)_i=f(x_{i-r},\ldots,x_{i+r})\). If F is surjective, must its temporally periodic configurations be dense in \(A^{\mathbb Z}\)?
definitions:
A configuration is a two-sided infinite sequence of letters. Give A the discrete topology and A^Z the product topology: specifying finitely many coordinates gives a basic open cylinder. Surjectivity means every configuration y has a preimage x with F(x)=y. Temporal periodicity means F^p(x)=x for some positive integer p, which may depend on x. Density means that every finite word u over A occurs, at coordinates 0 through |u|−1, in some temporally periodic x. This cylinder condition is equivalent to topological density.

The target does not require x to be periodic under spatial translation. Joint spatial and temporal periodicity is a stronger stated property and must not replace the requested condition without a proved implication. Eventual temporal periodicity also differs from periodicity from time zero. The full shift includes every A-valued sequence; no forbidden-word subshift, special algebraic alphabet or reversibility promise is imposed.
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that every surjective local rule satisfies the cylinder condition, or give an explicit finite local rule, prove it is surjective, and exhibit a finite cylinder containing no temporally periodic configuration. Failure of spatial periodicity or of a particular period alone is insufficient.

title: Exponential complementation lower bounds for unambiguous automata
summary: An unambiguous automaton has at most one accepting run for each word. Its complement must accept exactly the words that the input automaton rejects. The card asks whether some binary inputs require exponentially many complement states at arbitrarily large sizes. The output is allowed to be an arbitrary nondeterministic automaton. The target concerns representation size rather than the time to build the complement.
formal: Can complementing a binary unambiguous finite automaton require exponentially many states even if the complement may be represented ambiguously? For \[C(n)=\max_A\min\{|Q_B|:L(B)=\{0,1\}^{*}\setminus L(A)\},\] where \(A\) ranges over binary unambiguous automata with between one and \(n\) states and \(B\) over binary nondeterministic automata, does \[\exists c>0\ \forall N\ge1\ \exists n\ge N,\qquad C(n)\ge2^{cn}\] hold?
definitions:
Both kinds of automaton are finite tuples \((Q,\{0,1\},\Delta,I,F)\), where \(Q\) is the state set, \(I,F\subseteq Q\) are the initial and final state sets, and \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\{0,1\}\times Q\) is a transition relation. Multiple initial states, missing transitions, unreachable states and empty initial or final sets are allowed. There are no epsilon transitions or duplicate parallel transitions.

An accepting run on a word \(a_1\cdots a_m\) is a state sequence \(q_0,\ldots,q_m\) with \(q_0\in I\), \(q_m\in F\), and \((q_{i-1},a_i,q_i)\in\Delta\) for every \(1\leq i\leq m\). A word belongs to the language if it has an accepting run. For the empty word the accepting runs are the states in \(I\cap F\). The input automaton is unambiguous when each word has at most one accepting run; there is no restriction on the number of rejecting runs.

Only the number of states is charged, not transitions, the alphabet description or computation used to construct the automaton. Up to state renaming there are finitely many eligible inputs. Determinization and complementation give an output with at most \(2^{n}\) states, so the minimum and maximum defining \(C(n)\) exist.

The function \(C(n)\) is the worst-case minimum complement size defined in the statement. The lower bound asks for arbitrarily large input-size bounds, not for a hard example at every size. The constant \(c\) is universal; the automaton may depend on the size bound. No construction-time bound is imposed.
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one positive \(c\) gives \(C(n)\ge 2^{cn}\) for arbitrarily large state budgets \(n\), even when the complement automaton may be ambiguous. A refutation shows that for every \(c>0\), eventually \(C(n)<2^{cn}\).

title: A \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}/\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) dichotomy for visibly pushdown languages
summary: A visibly pushdown automaton reads finite words whose letters prescribe its stack operations. The target concerns well-matched inputs and nonuniform Boolean circuit families. It asks whether every recognized language is either in constant-depth threshold circuits or complete for logarithmic-depth bounded-fan-in circuits. Hardness uses constant-depth truth-table reductions, and the alternatives may overlap. The source’s partial classification for the weaker class AC0 does not settle this dichotomy.
formal: For every visibly pushdown language \(L\) of well-matched finite words, is \(L\in\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) or is \(L\) complete for \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) under constant-depth truth-table reductions? The circuit families and reductions are nonuniform, as defined below; the alternatives are inclusive.
definitions: The alphabet is a fixed finite disjoint union \(\Sigma=\Sigma_{\mathrm{call}}\cup\Sigma_{\mathrm{ret}}\cup\Sigma_{\mathrm{int}}\). A word is well-matched when every prefix has at least as many calls as returns and the whole word has equally many. A deterministic visibly pushdown automaton has finite control states, a finite stack alphabet with a bottom marker, an initial state and designated final states. It reads one letter per step, starting with just the bottom marker. A call pushes one non-bottom symbol, a return pops one symbol, and an internal letter leaves the stack unchanged; the finite transition table may inspect the state, letter and stack top. Acceptance requires a final control state and a stack containing just the bottom marker. Words that are not well-matched are rejected. Missing transitions reject. A language recognized by such an automaton is a visibly pushdown language (VPL); the automaton is fixed, while word length grows. Letters use a fixed-length injective binary code, and invalid codes are rejected. A nonuniform circuit family has one Boolean circuit for each input length, with no requirement that a machine generate the circuits. In \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\), circuits have polynomial size and constant depth and may use NOT and unbounded-fan-in AND, OR and majority gates. A majority gate returns one precisely when more than half its inputs are one. In \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\), circuits have polynomial size, depth \(O(\log(n+2))\), and AND and OR gates of fan-in at most two, together with NOT gates. Constants and polynomial exponents may depend on the fixed language. The reduction \(K\leq_{\mathrm{cd}}L\) consists of nonuniform constant-depth polynomial-size Boolean circuits with AND, OR and NOT gates and polynomial-length oracle gates for membership in \(L\). No directed path goes from an oracle output to an oracle input. The circuit decides \(K\), and its size includes the oracle-query wires. Completeness means \(L\in\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) and \(K\leq_{\mathrm{cd}}L\) for every \(K\in\mathrm{NC}^{1}\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated alternative for every VPL. Alternatively specify a VPL and prove in Lean both that it is outside \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) and that it is not \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\)-hard under the stated reductions. The target does not additionally require an algorithm assigning automata to the alternatives. A classification using a different reduction or uniformity convention must establish that it implies this proposition.

title: Equivalence of discounted-sum automata
summary: A discounted-sum automaton assigns a convergent weighted value to each infinite run, with later weights geometrically discounted. Its value on an infinite word is the supremum over all runs carrying that word. The question asks for exact decidability of equality of two such functions for every input rational discount factor shared by the automata. Known results for constant functions, reciprocal-integer factors, finite words and transition-dependent discounting have different scopes. A resolution would determine whether arbitrary nondeterministic quantitative specifications in this basic model can be compared algorithmically.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that always halts and decides, given a rational \(\lambda\) with \(0<\lambda<1\) and two total nondeterministic discounted-sum automata \(\mathcal A,\mathcal B\) over the same finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), whether \[\forall w\in\Sigma^\omega,\qquad \mathcal A(w)=\mathcal B(w)?\] Both automata have rational transition weights and use the same discounted-sum value function \(\operatorname{DSum}_{\lambda}\). Their word values are the suprema of their run values. The input factor is arbitrary rational, with no reciprocal-integer restriction.
definitions: Such an automaton is \(\mathcal A=(Q,q_0,\Sigma,E,\gamma)\), where \(Q\) is a finite nonempty state set, \(q_0\in Q\), \(E\) is a finite set of transitions with source, target and label in \(Q,Q,\Sigma\), and \(\gamma:E\to\mathbb Q\) gives their weights. Parallel transitions, including differently weighted transitions with the same endpoints and label, are allowed. Totality means that every pair \((q,a)\in Q\times\Sigma\) has at least one outgoing transition. There are no empty-label transitions, final-state tests, fairness requirements or restrictions on which infinite runs count. For an infinite word \(w=a_0a_1\cdots\), a run \(\rho=e_0e_1\cdots\) starts at \(q_0\), consecutive transitions have matching endpoints, and \(e_i\) has label \(a_i\). Set \[\operatorname{DSum}_{\lambda}(\rho)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\lambda^i\gamma(e_i),\qquad \mathcal A(w)=\sup_{\rho\text{ a run of }\mathcal A\text{ on }w}\operatorname{DSum}_{\lambda}(\rho).\] If \(W=\max_{e\in E}|\gamma(e)|\), every series converges absolutely and has absolute value at most \(W/(1-\lambda)\); totality ensures a nonempty run set, so the supremum is a finite real number. Nondeterministic choices are optimized separately for each complete word. No single online strategy is required to select them. All finite sets and transition tables are explicit, and rational weights and the common multiplier \(\lambda\) are encoded as signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. The deciding machine takes these finite descriptions, not an infinite word as an oracle input. It must answer correctly on every well-formed pair and every allowed factor, without a resource bound. Equality is exact equality of real-valued functions on all infinite words; this yes-or-no decidability question has no approximation tolerance.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one total computable algorithm decides the stated equality for every encoded input, or prove in Lean that no such algorithm exists. A positive result must handle arbitrary rational \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), unrestricted finite nondeterminism, signed rational weights and all infinite words under supremum semantics. A result for deterministic or functional automata, reciprocal-integer factors, finite words, or comparison up to a positive tolerance does not settle the full target. A negative result obtained by permitting different discount factors on different transitions does not settle this single-factor problem.

title: Deciding pattern avoidance over a prescribed alphabet
summary: A pattern identifies blocks that must repeat consistently. An occurrence substitutes a nonempty word for each variable. The question asks whether an infinite word over a prescribed finite alphabet can avoid every occurrence. The desired algorithm must halt on all pattern and alphabet-size inputs. Known questions about depth or unrestricted alphabet size are not the same decision problem.
formal: Is the following set decidable: pairs (p,k), where p is a nonempty finite word of variables and k≥2, such that there exists an infinite word \(w\in\{0,\ldots,k-1\}^{\mathbb N}\) containing no nonerasing substitution instance of p as a contiguous factor?
definitions:
The input pattern is an explicitly written finite sequence of variable identifiers; only equality of identifiers matters. The integer k is encoded in binary.
