A nonerasing substitution maps every variable occurring in p to a nonempty finite word over the k-letter alphabet and extends to p by concatenation. Repeated occurrences of a variable receive the same word; different variables may receive the same word. A forbidden occurrence is an interval of consecutive positions in w whose word equals h(p) for some such substitution h. The infinite word is one-sided, indexed by the nonnegative integers, with no computability, morphic-generation or eventual-periodicity requirement. It may use fewer than k symbols.

Decidability asks for a single deterministic Turing machine that halts on every valid finite pair and answers yes exactly when such an infinite avoiding word exists. No running-time bound is imposed. The question fixes the available alphabet size as part of the instance; testing whether some unspecified finite alphabet permits avoidance is a different decision problem. Partial words with holes and abelian pattern occurrences are also outside this target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked total decision procedure with equivalence to the stated infinite-word existence property, or a complete undecidability reduction whose outputs are valid pairs of the specified kind. A procedure that decides only avoidability over some finite alphabet, or verifies one proposed infinite construction, is insufficient.

title: Nondeterminism versus determinism with two two-way heads
summary: Two read-only heads move in both directions on a marked input tape. Nondeterministic control can choose among enabled transitions. The target asks whether that choice recognizes a language unavailable to deterministic control with the same two heads. Heads cannot directly sense that they coincide. Acceptance permits nonterminating rejecting runs and does not impose a state-size bound.
formal: Is there a finite alphabet Sigma and a language L⊆Sigma* recognized by a nondeterministic two-way two-head finite automaton but by no deterministic two-way two-head finite automaton, under the nonsensing model below?
definitions:
The input tape is read-only and contains a left endmarker, the finite input, and a right endmarker. A machine has finitely many states and two labelled heads. Initially both heads scan the first input symbol, or the right endmarker for empty input. A transition depends only on the current state and the ordered pair of scanned symbols; it chooses a new state and, for each head, a movement in {−1,0,1}. Heads cannot move outside the endmarkers. There is no extra predicate testing whether the heads occupy the same position: seeing identical symbols does not reveal coincidence.

A run accepts if it is finite and halts in an accepting state with no enabled transition. A word is accepted by a nondeterministic machine when at least one run accepts. Other runs may reject or continue forever. A deterministic machine has at most one transition per state and scanned-symbol pair; it need not halt on words outside its language. The finite control may be arbitrarily large but is fixed independently of input length. Neither machine has a work tape, counter, stack, advice or extra head. The question compares language classes, not state-size blowups for simulating a specific machine.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked language separation, including a nondeterministic recognizer and a proof excluding every deterministic two-head recognizer, or prove equality of these two language classes in Lean. A simulation using more heads or a separation only for one-way input is insufficient.

title: Recognizing good-for-games and good-for-MDP automata
summary: Good-for-games automata admit one online deterministic resolution that accepts every word in their language. Good-for-MDP automata preserve optimal acceptance probabilities when composed with every finite Markov decision process. The project asks matching complexity classifications for GFG parity recognition with unbounded priority count and GFM Büchi recognition. Lehtinen, Prakash and Skrzypczak establish NP-completeness for good-for-games parity recognition. For good-for-MDP Büchi recognition the known bounds still range from PSPACE-hardness to EXPTIME membership.
formal: Determine the exact worst-case computational complexity of each of the following two recognition languages: \[\mathrm{GFG}_{\mathrm{par}}=\{\langle\mathcal A\rangle:\mathcal A\text{ is a good-for-games parity automaton}\},\qquad \mathrm{GFM}_{\mathrm B}=\{\langle\mathcal A\rangle:\mathcal A\text{ is a good-for-MDP Büchi automaton}\}.\] The input is an explicit finite nondeterministic automaton, and the number of parity priorities is unbounded and part of the first input. The requested classification is for each language separately, with matching complexity-class upper and hardness bounds under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The source's two recognition tasks are retained; no particular class membership conjecture is substituted for either classification.
definitions:
An automaton has a finite nonempty state set \(Q\), a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), an initial state \(q_0\), and a complete transition relation \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\Sigma\times Q\). Completeness means that every state and letter admit a transition; a rejecting sink handles missing transitions. A run on \(w=a_0a_1\cdots\) follows transitions \((q_i,a_i,q_{i+1})\) from \(q_0\). A parity automaton has a map \(p:\Delta\to\mathbb N\) and accepts a run when the largest priority appearing infinitely often is even. A Büchi automaton has a marked set \(F\subseteq\Delta\) and accepts a run when transitions in \(F\) occur infinitely often. Its language \(L(\mathcal A)\) contains the words with some accepting run. A good-for-games (GFG) automaton admits a single deterministic rule that selects each next transition using only the finite input prefix read so far, so that its induced run accepts every \(w\in L(\mathcal A)\). The rule may remember the entire past; it cannot inspect future letters. One rule must work on all words.

A finite Markov decision process (MDP) over \(\Sigma\) has finite state and action sets \(S,U\), an initial state \(s_0\), a nonempty set \(U(s)\) of enabled actions at each state, a label \(\ell(s,u)\in\Sigma\), and a distribution \(P(s,u,\cdot)\) on \(S\) for each enabled pair. Distribution entries are real numbers in \([0,1]\) summing to one. A policy maps the observed finite history of states and actions to a distribution on the enabled actions. It generates a path by choosing \(u_i\), emitting \(\ell(s_i,u_i)\), and sampling \(s_{i+1}\) using \(P\); products of these conditional probabilities give the path measure. Define \[V_{\mathrm{sem}}(M,\mathcal A)=\sup_\pi\Pr_M^\pi[\ell(s_0,u_0)\ell(s_1,u_1)\cdots\in L(\mathcal A)].\] In the product with \(\mathcal A\), a policy observes the joint state \((s_i,q_i)\), chooses an enabled pair consisting of \(u_i\) and a transition \((q_i,\ell(s_i,u_i),q_{i+1})\), then samples \(s_{i+1}\) from \(P(s_i,u_i,\cdot)\). Thus the automaton choice precedes that next random state and sees no future. Let \(V_{\mathrm{syn}}(M,\mathcal A)\) be the supremum, over all such history-dependent randomized product policies, of the probability that the selected automaton run satisfies its Büchi condition. The automaton is good-for-MDP (GFM) if \(V_{\mathrm{syn}}(M,\mathcal A)=V_{\mathrm{sem}}(M,\mathcal A)\) for every finite MDP over its alphabet and every initial MDP state. The product policy may depend on the MDP. This is exact equality of probabilities, without approximation or a probability-one promise.

Only the automaton is input to recognition; MDPs, policies and GFG rules are quantified objects. States, letters and transitions are explicitly enumerated; indices and priorities use binary integers with delimiters. Input size \(n\) is the total bit length, and invalid descriptions are rejected. The alphabet size, graph size and number of priorities are not fixed parameters. Computational bounds use uniform Turing machines and worst-case resource use over inputs of length at most \(n\), with exact acceptance and no randomized error. A polynomial-time many-one reduction from a language \(X\) to \(Y\) is a total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) with \(x\in X\iff f(x)\in Y\). A language is \(\mathcal C\)-complete if it belongs to \(\mathcal C\) and every language in \(\mathcal C\) reduces to it in this sense. Use the shared definitions of [P and NP](definitions.html#p-np), [PSPACE](definitions.html#space) and [EXP, also called EXPTIME](definitions.html#exponential-time).
answer_criterion: Give Lean-checked matching complexity classifications for both recognition languages with the specified explicit input encoding and reduction convention. For each claimed complete class \(\mathcal C\), prove the resource upper bound and \(\mathcal C\)-hardness. Any other class used in the answer must have an independent machine/resource or logical definition, not a definition that merely renames this recognition problem or the collection of problems reducible to it. The precision requested is complexity-class completeness under polynomial-time many-one reductions, not an exact leading constant in running time. An isolated improvement of one bound, an algorithm requiring a fixed priority count, or a result only for one recognition language is partial progress. Numerical approximation of the MDP values is not the acceptance criterion.

title: Isomorphism of tree-automatic ordinals without addition
summary: Finite tree automata describe a domain and its order relation. The input is promised to be a well-order. The task is to decide whether two such orders have the same ordinal type. No automaton for addition or ordinal notation is supplied. A known decision result with addition does not automatically solve this order-only promise problem.
formal: Is there an algorithm which, given two injective finite-tree-automatic presentations promised to describe well-orders using only their domain and strict order relations, decides whether those well-orders are isomorphic?
definitions:
A code is a finite rooted ordered binary tree with labels in a finite alphabet. Every node has either zero or two children. A finite bottom-up tree automaton assigns a state to a leaf from its label, and to an internal node from its label and its children’s states; acceptance means the root receives a designated accepting state in some run. A presentation consists of an automaton for a language D of codes and an automaton for the relation < on D. To recognize a pair, read their convolution: use the union of their tree domains and pad a missing component by a new blank symbol.

Codes are the elements themselves, so distinct accepted trees represent distinct elements; no quotient or equality automaton is supplied. The promise is that < is a strict linear order on D and every nonempty subset of D has a least element. Empty D is allowed and denotes ordinal zero. The promise is semantic, not a finite proof or ordinal notation attached to the input. Isomorphism means existence of a bijection between the domains preserving and reflecting <. Only domain and order automata are supplied: there is no presentation of ordinal addition.

A decision procedure must halt and be correct on every pair satisfying the promise. It may behave arbitrarily on inputs violating it. No complexity bound is requested, and the task does not include deciding whether an arbitrary presentation is well-founded.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked promise-decision algorithm with termination and correctness on all well-order presentations, or a complete undecidability proof whose reduction always produces valid well-order presentations. A procedure requiring an additional automaton for ordinal addition does not meet the input specification.

title: Deterministic separability of nondeterministic timed languages
summary: The input is a pair of nondeterministic timed automata describing finite event sequences with real timestamps. The question is whether a terminating algorithm can decide the existence of a deterministic timed separator accepting the first language and rejecting the second. Input automata may use invisible epsilon steps, while the separator has no such steps and may use any finite number of clocks. The known decidability theorem fixes the separator’s clock count and therefore does not answer this unrestricted question. Either a general decision procedure or an undecidability proof must be checked in Lean for the stated timed-word model.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given two nondeterministic timed automata \(A,B\) with epsilon transitions over the same finite alphabet, always halts and decides whether there exists a deterministic timed automaton \(S\) such that \(L(A)\subseteq L(S)\) and \(L(S)\cap L(B)=\varnothing\)? Languages contain finite timed words. The separator may use any finite number of clocks and any finite integer constants: no resource bound is supplied or fixed in advance.
definitions:
A finite timed word over a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) is \((a_1,t_1)\cdots(a_n,t_n)\), where \(n\geq0\), \(a_i\in\Sigma\), and \(0\leq t_1\leq\cdots\leq t_n\) are real timestamps. Equal timestamps and the empty word are allowed.

A timed automaton has finite sets of locations \(Q\), clocks \(X\), initial locations \(I\subseteq Q\), final locations \(F\subseteq Q\), and transitions \((p,a,\phi,Y,q)\). Here \(a\in\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}\), \(Y\subseteq X\), and \(\phi\) is a Boolean combination of true, false, \(x\mathrel{\sim} z\), and \(x-y\mathrel{\sim} z\), with clocks \(x,y\), integer \(z\), and \(\sim\in\{=,<,\leq,>,\geq\}\). There are no location invariants. All sets, transitions and guard formulas are explicitly encoded, with signed binary integer constants.

A run starts at time 0 in an initial location with all clocks zero. Time may advance by any nonnegative real amount, adding that amount to every clock. A transition can then fire when its guard is true; it changes the location and resets precisely the clocks in \(Y\) to zero. Its label and absolute firing time form an event. A finite run is accepting when its final location belongs to \(F\). The language \(L(A)\) consists of the timed words obtained from accepting runs by deleting all epsilon-labeled events and preserving the timestamps of all other events. Arbitrarily many but finitely many epsilon steps, including before the first and after the last visible event, are allowed.

A deterministic separator has exactly one initial location, no epsilon transitions, and at most one enabled transition for each location, input letter and clock valuation. Incomplete transition relations are permitted and a missing transition rejects. Equivalently one can merge overlapping guards when their target location and reset set coincide. The number of locations, number of clocks and magnitudes of constants can all depend on the input pair.

The decision algorithm is one ordinary deterministic Turing machine on the finite descriptions and must halt on every valid pair; no complexity bound or disjointness promise is imposed. A pair with intersecting languages necessarily has answer no. Malformed descriptions can be rejected.
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of decidability for this input model and unrestricted finite separators, or a Lean-checked proof of its undecidability. Decidability for each fixed clock bound does not supply a decision algorithm for the unrestricted problem; the algorithm must also terminate on negative instances.

title: Universality of unambiguous register automata over ordered integers
summary: A register automaton reads letters paired with integer data and retains finitely many integer values. Its transitions may compare stored values, input values and named constants, and may guess new values. Unambiguity promises at most one accepting run for every word. The question asks whether one can decide that every finite data word is accepted. Known algorithms over equality or dense rational order do not by themselves settle the selected discrete-integer model.
formal:
Is universality decidable for unambiguous register automata with guessing over \((\mathbb Z,<,=)\) and finitely many named integer constants? Given a finite automaton description in the model below, promised to have at most one accepting run on every finite data word, must there be an algorithm deciding whether
\[L(\mathcal A)=(\Sigma\times\mathbb Z)^*?\]
The finite alphabet, number of registers, control states, guards and binary-encoded constants are all part of the input. This card makes the guessing convention explicit, using the relational register model discussed in the cited literature. Its main target is the decidability part of the source question; a tight complexity classification is a further question if the answer is positive.
definitions:
The automaton has a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), a finite set of control states \(Q\), one initial state \(q_0\), a set \(F\subseteq Q\) of accepting states, and \(k\ge0\) registers with values in \(\mathbb Z\). All registers initially contain zero. This fixed initialization is part of the selected convention; integer constants, including zero, are available in guards. A data word is any finite sequence \((a_1,z_1)\cdots(a_m,z_m)\), where \(a_i\in\Sigma\) and \(z_i\in\mathbb Z\). The empty word is included.

For each control-state pair and input letter, the transition table specifies a quantifier-free Boolean formula \(g\) built using true, negation and conjunction from atoms \(u=v\) and \(u<v\). Terms \(u,v\) are the current input datum, an old register value \(r_i\), a proposed new register value \(r'_i\), or one of the finitely many integer constants in the description. Disjunction can be expressed using negation and conjunction. There is no addition, successor, multiplication or arbitrary numerical predicate in a guard. Parallel descriptions of the same transition relation are combined by disjunction.

From state \((q,\bar r)\) on input \((a,z)\), the automaton may move to any \((q',\bar r')\) for which the corresponding guard is true over the ordinary integers. Thus new register values may be nondeterministically guessed; they are not required to be copies of the input or old values. The transition relation may have infinitely many successors. Each transition consumes exactly one input letter, with no epsilon moves. A run is its sequence of control states and register tuples, starting at \((q_0,0,\ldots,0)\). It accepts if its control state after the last input letter is in \(F\). Acceptance depends on the existence of such a run, and no condition is imposed on final register contents. Different syntactic guard clauses producing the same sequence are not counted as different runs.

Unambiguity means that every word has at most one initialized accepting run, including all guessed values. There may be many rejecting or partial runs. In particular, a universal unambiguous automaton has exactly one accepting run for every word. This is a semantic promise on the supplied description, not a claim that all transition choices are unique.

Descriptions use finite binary encodings of states, letters, register indices, guard syntax and signed integer constants. A decision procedure is one deterministic Turing machine that halts and returns the correct universality answer on every description satisfying the promise. Its behavior on ambiguous or malformed descriptions is unrestricted, and it need not verify the promise. There is no complexity bound, bound on the number of registers, or bound on constant magnitudes beyond finiteness.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of decidability in this promised class, or prove that no such decision procedure exists. A positive answer must cover arbitrary finite register counts and named integer constants, with the specified guessing transitions. An undecidability reduction must produce unambiguous automata. Algorithms over rational data, over equality alone, or for a fixed restricted register model do not settle this integer-order target.

title: Skolem problem
summary: The Skolem problem asks whether one terminating algorithm can decide if any given integer linear recurrence ever has a zero term. The input lists its order, coefficients and initial values in binary, with no restriction on order or repeated characteristic roots and no upper bound on the index. Every single term can be computed, but a decision procedure must also finish when the infinite sequence has no zero. The question is a basic exact reachability problem in linear dynamics with connections to program verification and automata. A complete Lean proof must establish decidability or undecidability for all inputs; conditional termination, low-order algorithms and density-one index sets do not settle that target.
formal: Is there a single deterministic Turing machine which, for every input consisting of an integer \(k\ge1\), integer coefficients \(c_0,\ldots,c_{k-1}\), and integer initial values \(u_0,\ldots,u_{k-1}\), halts and correctly decides whether \(u_t=0\) for some integer \(t\ge0\), where the infinite sequence is uniquely defined by \[u_{t+k}=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_j u_{t+j}\qquad(t=0,1,2,\ldots)?\] The order \(k\) is part of the input and is unrestricted; no time or space bound is requested.
definitions: Use input alphabet \(\{0,1,+,-,\#\}\). For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(\operatorname{bin}(a)\) be its ordinary base-two expansion without leading zeros, with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\). Encode an integer \(z\) by a plus sign followed by \(\operatorname{bin}(z)\) if \(z\ge0\), and by a minus sign followed by \(\operatorname{bin}(-z)\) if \(z<0\); negative zero is invalid. A valid input is \(\operatorname{bin}(k)\), then exactly \(k\) signed coefficient fields in order, then exactly \(k\) signed initial-value fields in order, separated by one \(\#\) between consecutive fields, with no other symbols or trailing separator. The first field has \(k\ge1\). Output 1 means that a zero occurs at some nonnegative index, including among the initial values; output 0 means that every term at a nonnegative index is nonzero. The machine must halt with one of these two outputs on every valid input and reject every malformed input with output 0. This decidable syntax convention does not affect the underlying decidability question. A deterministic Turing machine has one finite transition table, a finite alphabet and finitely many work tapes; it has no randomness, external oracle, advice or input-dependent program. The sequence values are exact integers with no bound on their magnitude, and the same fixed coefficients apply at every index. The listed recurrence need not have the smallest possible order. Coefficients and initial values may vanish, all may be zero, and \(c_0=0\) is allowed; forward evolution is still uniquely defined. In particular, neither distinct characteristic roots nor a non-degeneracy assumption is promised. No upper bound on the index of a possible zero is supplied. This is a discrete-time existence-of-a-zero question, with indices \(0,1,2,\ldots\); negative or real-valued indices and nonnegativity of all terms are different targets.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a total decision machine exists, with termination and correctness for every valid input and rejection of malformed strings, or a Lean-checked proof that no such machine exists. Equivalently, the language of valid encodings whose sequences contain a zero must be proved decidable or undecidable. A negative answer must rule out every total deterministic decider, not merely give an input on which one proposed program fails. A positive answer has to decide both the zero and zero-free cases uniformly over all orders; a semidecision procedure, a bounded-index algorithm, a theorem for a fixed order, or conditional termination under an unproved number-theoretic assumption does not settle the full target. A complexity lower bound such as NP-hardness does not prove undecidability. No polynomial bound, bound on the first zero, or enumeration of the entire zero set is required as the output.

title: Parity games in polynomial time
summary: A parity game is a finite arena in which two players choose an infinite path, and the least priority recurring infinitely often decides the winner. The target asks whether one uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm decides the winner from every specified starting vertex. The card specifies arbitrary vertex ownership, full-history strategies, binary priorities and the complete bit-cost model. OpenAI computes exact values for finite priority mean-payoff games in deterministic polynomial bit time. Paying one for even priorities and zero for odd priorities makes the value determine the parity winner.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(C,c\geq1\) such that, for every encoded finite parity game \(G\) and starting vertex \(s\), \(A\) decides whether Even has a winning strategy from \(s\) within \(C(N+1)^c\) steps, where \(N\) is the full input length defined below?
definitions:
A parity game has vertices \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq1\), an edge relation \(E\subseteq V\times V\), an owner function \(o:V\to\{\mathrm{Even},\mathrm{Odd}\}\), and priorities \(p:V\to\mathbb N\), where \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Each vertex has at least one outgoing edge; self-loops are allowed. The designated start is \(s\in V\). An infinite play is a sequence \((v_i)_{i\geq0}\) with \(v_0=s\) and \((v_i,v_{i+1})\in E\) for every \(i\). The owner of \(v_i\) chooses \(v_{i+1}\); ownership need not alternate along an edge. Both players see the entire finite history and there are no chance moves. Let \(I=\{d\in\mathbb N:p(v_i)=d\text{ for infinitely many }i\}\). This set is finite and nonempty. Even wins precisely when \(\min I\) is even, and Odd wins otherwise.

A strategy for a player assigns a legal successor to every finite valid history ending at a vertex owned by that player. A play is consistent with the strategy if it follows the prescribed successor at each such vertex. Even has a winning strategy from \(s\) if there exists a strategy for which every consistent infinite play starting at \(s\) is won by Even. Strategies and infinite plays are quantified mathematical objects; neither is supplied as input. A positional strategy depends only on the current vertex, but the target does not assume positionality in its definition.

For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(a+1)\), where \(b\) is the length of the binary expansion without leading zeroes. Encode a game by \(1^n0\), followed by its \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row order, \(n\) owner bits (0 for Even and 1 for Odd), then \(\operatorname{code}(p(1)),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(p(n)),\operatorname{code}(s)\), with no trailing bits. The input length \(N\) includes every priority bit. Invalid encodings are rejected within the same polynomial time bound. The machine is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, finite tape alphabet and no oracle or advice; each transition costs one step. All arithmetic and input processing count toward time. The same \(A,C,c\) must work for every arena and all priority values, with no fixed bound on the number or magnitude of priorities.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-verified proof of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a uniform algorithm and prove its termination, correctness for all valid games and polynomial bit-time bound, including rejection of malformed inputs. A negative answer must exclude every such polynomial-time decider for the full problem. A lower bound for a particular algorithm, automaton representation or restricted collection of methods does not prove that negation. Bounds whose polynomial exponent depends on the number of priorities, experimental performance, and conditional theorems do not settle the unconditional target.

title: Word equations with linear length constraints
summary: Word equations require substitutions of finite strings that make all supplied concatenations identical. Here the same substitution must also satisfy a conjunction of integer linear constraints on total string lengths. The target is one always-terminating decision algorithm for arbitrary finite inputs, including empty substitutions and unrestricted variable occurrences. Known restricted decision results and partial termination criteria do not settle this combination, and stronger letter-count predicates describe a different problem. A resolution would establish whether complete exact solving is possible for this basic fragment of string constraints, before imposing efficiency requirements.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine which halts on every input consisting of a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), a finite system of word equations \(U_i=V_i\) and a finite conjunction of integer linear equalities and inequalities on variable lengths, and answers YES exactly when they admit a simultaneous solution in the free monoid \(\Sigma^*\)? The alphabet, equations, variables and arithmetic coefficients are all part of the input. No bound on the running time is prescribed.
definitions: The alphabet \(\Sigma\) is a finite nonempty set of constant letters. The finite set of variables \(X=\{X_1,\ldots,X_k\}\) is disjoint from \(\Sigma\); \(k\) may be zero. Each side \(U_i,V_i\) is an explicitly written finite word over \(\Sigma\cup X\), including the empty word. A substitution \(\sigma:X\to\Sigma^*\) assigns one finite word to each variable and extends by concatenation while fixing each constant letter. Every occurrence of a variable receives the same word, and empty substitutions are allowed. Each equation requires literal equality \(\sigma(U_i)=\sigma(V_i)\). The length \(|w|\) of a word is its number of letters. Each arithmetic atom has the form \(\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_j|\sigma(X_j)|\le b\) or \(\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_j|\sigma(X_j)|=b\), with signed binary integer coefficients and constants. Every supplied atom must hold for the same substitution as every equation. Empty lists of equations or constraints are allowed and mean the empty conjunction. Alphabet and variable symbols have finite identifiers; equation sides are explicit lists and arithmetic atoms are explicit coefficient lists. Nothing is given as a circuit or a compressed word. The machine is one uniform program over all input sizes, alphabet sizes, variable counts, equation counts and coefficient values; it halts on both positive and negative instances. Malformed inputs may be rejected. Only existential choice of the substituted words is involved. There is no variable-times-variable product of lengths, individual-letter count, regular-language predicate, string-to-integer conversion or universal string quantifier. Nonempty-variable requirements are expressible by \(-|\sigma(X_j)|\le-1\), but they are not imposed unless present in the input. This is exact satisfiability, with no random error, oracle, numerical tolerance or complexity bound.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that a total computable YES/NO procedure exists for exactly the encoded input class above, or that no such procedure exists. A positive answer must verify termination on every input and equivalence of YES with existence of one simultaneous substitution satisfying all word and arithmetic constraints. It need not output a substitution or satisfy a time bound. A negative answer must prove noncomputability for this length-only existential conjunction problem; a result using extra predicates, stronger quantification, or a failure of one particular procedure does not suffice. Acceptance is exact and has no numerical tolerance. This editorial audit does not supply a Lean formalization.

title: A logic capturing polynomial time
summary: Is there an effective logic for all polynomial-time properties of finite unordered structures? Its sentences must describe properties unchanged by renaming domain elements. Each sentence must compile effectively to an evaluation algorithm with a polynomial time bound. Fixed-point logic captures polynomial time when an order is supplied, but that is a different input model. Current candidate and restricted-class results leave the general existence question open.
formal: Does there exist a logic L with decidable syntax and isomorphism-invariant semantics on finite relational structures such that its sentences define exactly the polynomial-time decidable Boolean properties, and an effective compiler maps each sentence to a correct polynomial-time evaluation algorithm with a polynomial running-time bound?
definitions: A finite relational vocabulary \(\tau\) lists finitely many relation symbols with fixed positive arities. A finite \(\tau\)-structure A has a nonempty finite domain and interprets each r-ary symbol as a subset of \(A^{r}\). An isomorphism is a bijection between domains that preserves and reflects every relation. For computation, label the n domain elements by \([n]\) and encode the domain explicitly together with all relation tables in binary. Different labelings of the same abstract structure are permitted; the input supplies no distinguished order relation. A Boolean property is an isomorphism-closed class of structures of one vocabulary. It is in PTIME when one deterministic Turing machine decides membership for every encoding in time polynomial in its length. The logic has a decidable set of finite binary sentence encodings with their vocabularies. Each sentence \(\varphi\) has a truth value \(A\models \varphi\) invariant under isomorphism. One total computable compiler, given a valid \((\tau ,\varphi )\), outputs a deterministic machine \(M_{\varphi}\) and integers \(C_{\varphi},k_{\varphi}\ge 1\) such that \(M_{\varphi}\) decides \(A\models \varphi\) in at most \(C_{\varphi}(N+1)^{k_{\varphi}}\) steps on every valid input structure encoding of length N. Finally, for every finite \(\tau\) and every PTIME Boolean property Q of \(\tau\)-structures, some fixed \(\tau\)-sentence \(\varphi\) satisfies \(A\models \varphi\) exactly when \(A\in Q\) for all finite A. Neither sentence construction from an arbitrary machine nor polynomial-time compilation is required. The exponent may depend on the sentence. No uniform polynomial bound for the combined input \((\varphi ,A)\) is imposed. The same syntax and compiler must work across vocabularies; no oracle, advice or externally chosen ordering is supplied to the semantics.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a formalism satisfying decidable syntax, invariant semantics, effective polynomial-time compilation and expressive completeness for every finite relational vocabulary. A negative resolution proves that no formalism can satisfy all these requirements. Failure of one named logic, capture on a restricted class of structures, or capture with an additional input order does not decide general existence.

title: Internal semisimplicial types in ordinary HoTT
summary: Semisimplicial types organize vertices, edges, triangles and higher-dimensional fillers with compatible shared boundaries. Ordinary homotopy type theory can describe any fixed finite collection of these stages externally. The project asks for one internal family indexed by natural numbers, together with compatible maps forgetting the highest stage. Higher identities carry data, so specifying all coherence requirements uniformly is harder than listing equations in ordinary set-based mathematics. Such a construction would provide an internal foundation for important higher-dimensional structures without extending the stated type theory.
formal: In the fixed ordinary HoTT theory T below, can one define a single internal family \(S:\mathbb{N} \to U_{1}\) and restriction maps \(r_{n}:S(n+1)\to S(n)\) whose finite stages are equivalent, compatibly with restriction, to the canonical finite semisimplicial telescopes \(D_{n}\)?
definitions: Fix T to be intensional Martin–Löf type theory with dependent function and pair types \(\Pi ,\Sigma\), identity types with their J eliminator, empty and unit types, finite coproducts, natural numbers and W-types, a cumulative predicative sequence \(U_{0}:U_{1}:\cdots\) closed under these constructors, and univalence for these universes. Also allow propositional truncation and homotopy pushouts with their ordinary dependent eliminators and propositional computation rules for path constructors, as in the HoTT book. There is no equality reflection, axiom K/UIP, resizing, choice, excluded middle, second equality type, display modality, or additional primitive for semisimplicial types. The question concerns definability in this specified theory; a negative result would apply to this theory, not automatically to every possible extension called HoTT. Define an external, finite family of syntactic telescopes as follows. \(D_{0}\) is \(U_{0}\), with element \(A_{0}\). Given data \(d=(A_{0},\ldots ,A_{j- 1})\) in \(D_{j- 1}\), form \(B_{j}(d)\), the dependent type of labelled boundaries of a j-simplex: for every nonempty proper subset F of \(\{0,\ldots ,j\}\), in increasing cardinality and then lexicographic order, choose a label \(x_{F}\) in \(A_{|F|- 1}\) evaluated on the labels of all nonempty proper subfaces of F. Identify F with \(\{0,\ldots ,|F|- 1\}\) by its increasing enumeration when supplying these arguments. For singleton F this means \(x_{F}:A_{0}\). Set \(D_{j}=\Sigma (d:D_{j- 1})(B_{j}(d)\to U_{0})\), whose last field is \(A_{j}\), and let \(p_{j}:D_{j+1}\to D_{j}\) forget the last field. This describes an ordinary finite T-expression for each external integer j; it does not postulate an internal function \(j\mapsto D_{j}\). The required output is finite closed T-terms \(S:\mathbb{N} \to U_{1}\) and \(r:\Pi (n:\mathbb{N} )(S(n+1)\to S(n))\), together with a metatheoretic proof that for every external j there are T-terms \(e_{j}:S(j)\)≃\(D_{j}\) and homotopies \(e_{j}\circ r_{j} \sim  p_{j}\circ e_{j+1}\). Here j inside T denotes its numeral, ≃ is the usual type equivalence, and ~ is pointwise identity. No judgmental equality between \(S(j)\) and \(D_{j}\) is required. The equivalences classify the full type-valued telescopes, with arbitrary \(U_{0}\)-small simplex types and no fixed truncation bound.
answer_criterion: Prove that the specified theory T admits finite closed terms S and r together with the external stagewise equivalences and compatibility homotopies required above, or prove that no such terms and witnesses exist in T. The positive conclusion must hold at every external finite stage and allow arbitrary \(U_{0}\)-small simplex types.

title: Tarski’s exponential function problem
summary: Tarski’s exponential function problem asks whether one terminating algorithm can decide every first-order sentence about the standard real numbers with their full exponential function. The input is finite symbolic syntax with no arbitrary real constants or real-number oracle, and quantifiers range over all reals. Acceptance requires a complete Lean-checked proof of total correct decidability or a proof of undecidability, with no time bound and no unresolved extra hypothesis. The question extends decidable polynomial real arithmetic and already controls conditional verification results for restricted weighted automata. Macintyre–Wilkie’s conditional theorem and the checked June2026 axiomatization still rely on the real Schanuel hypothesis; restricted model completeness is a different conclusion.
formal: Is the first-order theory of the standard real exponential field \(\mathbb R_{\exp}=(\mathbb R;0,1,+,-,\times,<,\exp)\) decidable? Precisely, does there exist one ordinary deterministic Turing machine \(D\) which halts on every encoded first-order sentence \(\varphi\) in this fixed language and outputs \(1\) exactly when \(\mathbb R_{\exp}\models\varphi\), and \(0\) otherwise? The exponential function is defined on all real numbers, and the required conclusion is unconditional.
definitions: The domain is the standard field \(\mathbb R\), with its usual constants, addition, unary additive inverse, multiplication and strict order. Equality is a logical symbol. Here \(\exp(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}x^j/j!\), the standard real exponential, with \(0!=1\); it is not an input function or an oracle available to the machine. Terms are finite expressions formed from variables \(v_i\), \(i\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), the constants \(0,1\), unary negation and exponentiation, and binary addition and multiplication. Atomic formulas are term equalities or strict inequalities. Formulas are formed using negation, conjunction, disjunction and the quantifiers \(\exists v_i\) and \(\forall v_i\). Every quantifier ranges over all of \(\mathbb R\), regardless of the index \(i\); indices name variables, not integer-valued inputs. Binding has its usual nested scope, with the nearest enclosing quantifier on a given variable binding that occurrence. A sentence is a formula with no free variables, and truth uses the ordinary real operations and ordinary first-order semantics. Arbitrarily many variables, nested exponentials and arbitrary finite quantifier alternations are allowed. There are no names for arbitrary real parameters, integer predicates, trigonometric functions or additional input operations. For a fixed finite-alphabet encoding, write a variable as v[b], where b is the usual binary expansion of its nonnegative index, with no leading zero except for the index zero itself. Use literal strings 0 and 1 for constants, and the prefix term forms -(t), exp(t), +(t,u) and *(t,u). Formula forms are =(t,u), <(t,u), not(phi), and(phi,psi), or(phi,psi), exists(v[b],phi) and forall(v[b],phi), with the indicated parentheses and commas and no spaces; t,u stand for terms and phi,psi for formulas, not literal tokens. Thus all inputs are finite strings over a fixed finite alphabet of these characters. To make D total on all strings, malformed encodings and formulas with free variables must be rejected with output 0. D has finite control and finitely many ordinary work tapes, has no oracle, noncomputable real constant, advice or random choices, and is the same machine for every input length, number of variables and quantifier pattern. No running-time or space upper bound is imposed beyond halting.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a single total deterministic Turing machine exists and has the stated exact truth behavior, or a complete Lean-checked proof that the language of true encoded sentences is undecidable by ordinary Turing machines. In the positive direction, termination and correctness must hold for every finite input, with the stated rejection convention on invalid strings. In the negative direction, the proof must rule out every candidate total decider, not merely refute one proposed algorithm or one recursively specified axiom system. A computably equivalent precise syntax may be used if its effective correspondence with the card’s encoding and sentence semantics is proved. A procedure that is correct whenever it terminates but lacks a universal termination proof does not meet the positive criterion. Deciding only a syntactic fragment qualifies only if the proof also establishes decidability of the full stated theory. Neither assuming Schanuel’s conjecture nor assuming another unresolved hypothesis is an unconditional resolution; the hypothesis would itself have to be proved in the accepted Lean development. Numerical evaluation with any fixed precision, bounded search for real solutions, or a time-complexity lower bound does not replace this exact decidability target.

title: Positivity problem for linear recurrences
summary: An integer linear recurrence gives a finite rule for generating an infinite sequence. The positivity problem asks whether every term is nonnegative, with the recurrence order included in the input. Computing a long prefix cannot certify the answer because a negative term may appear arbitrarily late. Characteristic roots can combine growth and oscillation, making exact sign control depend on subtle arithmetic relationships. A terminating decision procedure would provide a basic verification tool for linear discrete dynamics, while a negative result would establish limits even in this elementary setting.
formal: Does there exist a Turing machine that, on every input consisting of an integer \(d\ge 1\), integer initial values \(u_{0},\ldots ,u_{d- 1}\), and integer coefficients \(a_{0},\ldots ,a_{d- 1}\), halts and decides whether \(u_{n}\ge 0\) for every \(n\ge 0\), where \(u_{n+d}=\sum _{i=0}^{d- 1}a_{i} u_{n+i}\)? The order d is part of the input and has no fixed upper bound.
definitions: All integers are given exactly in signed binary, and the coefficient and initial-value lists are explicit. The recurrence is homogeneous and its coefficients are constant in n. The requested property includes every term from \(u_{0}\) onward and allows zero terms. Coefficients may be zero, including \(a_{0}\); the decision procedure must accept these inputs as well. No promise of distinct characteristic roots, reversibility, eventual nonnegativity, or bounded order is imposed. The recurrence supplied need not be of minimal order. Computation uses the ordinary Turing model, with no real-number or number-theoretic oracle. No polynomial-time or other specified running-time bound is required, but the machine must halt for both possible answers. A simple sequence has a minimal characteristic polynomial with no repeated complex roots. Use the [explicit encoding convention](definitions.html#encoding).
answer_criterion: Prove that nonnegativity of every term is decidable for integer linear recurrences of arbitrary input order, by a machine halting on both positive and negative instances, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. The property is \(u_{n}\ge 0\) for all \(n\ge 0\), including the initial values.

title: Simple stochastic games in polynomial time
summary: A simple stochastic game combines choices of a maximizing player, choices of a minimizing player and fair random branching. The project asks for a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm deciding whether the optimal probability of reaching a target exceeds a given rational threshold. OpenAI gives a deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm for the exact value of turn-based games with binary rational transition probabilities. Making the target absorbing and paying one on every step there makes each play’s mean payoff equal to its reachability indicator. Comparing the exact start value with the input threshold also handles equality.
formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time decider that, given a finite simple stochastic game \(G\), start vertex \(s\) and binary rational \(r\in[0,1]\), accepts exactly when \(v_G(s)>r\)? Here \(v_G(s)=\sup_\sigma\inf_\tau\Pr_s^{\sigma,\tau}[\text{eventually reach sink }1]\). Time is measured in the total encoded bit length of the game, start vertex and threshold.
definitions: The vertices are partitioned into Max, Min, random, and two distinct terminal sinks 0 and 1. Every nonterminal vertex has two listed successor slots; slots may have the same successor. At a Max or Min vertex its owner chooses a slot. At a random vertex each slot is chosen with probability \(1/2\), independently at each visit. Both players observe the complete finite history and the current vertex. Strategies may use history and private randomness; there is no bound on play length. Reaching 1 gives Max payoff one; reaching 0, or playing forever without reaching 1, gives payoff zero. Min minimizes the same expected payoff that Max maximizes. No promise of almost-sure termination is imposed. All vertices, ownership labels and successor indices are explicit; \(r=a/b\) is exact with binary integers \(0\le a\le b\) and \(b>0\). Equality \(v_{G}(s)=r\) is a NO instance. The algorithm is an ordinary uniform deterministic Turing algorithm; its polynomial bound has universal constants independent of the game and threshold. Use the [explicit encoding convention](definitions.html#encoding).
answer_criterion: Prove that the exact threshold language \(\{(G,s,r):v_{G}(s)>r\}\) belongs to P, or prove that it does not. The polynomial-time algorithm must handle arbitrary finite games, including nonterminating plays, and reject equality to the threshold.

title: Mean-payoff games in polynomial time
summary: Two players control different vertices of a finite integer-weighted graph and choose an infinite path from a specified start. Max wins when the lower limit of the average weight is nonnegative against every history-dependent strategy of Min, including exact equality zero. The question is whether the resulting binary-input winner language has one deterministic decider running in polynomial bit time on all inputs. OpenAI’s game algorithm computes exact values and optimal policies for both players in polynomial bit time on binary rational inputs. With one outcome per action and equal priorities, comparing the start value with zero decides the stated game.
formal:
Is the exact mean-payoff winner language \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\) defined below in deterministic polynomial time?

A valid instance is a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge1\), at least one outgoing edge at every vertex, a partition \(V=V_{\mathrm{Max}}\sqcup V_{\mathrm{Min}}\), an integer weight function \(w:E\to\mathbb Z\), and a start vertex \(s\in V\). Its encoding is in \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\) exactly when
\[\exists\sigma\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{Max}}\ \forall\tau\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{Min}},\qquad
\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}w(v_t,v_{t+1})\ge0,\]
where \(v_0=s\) and the unique infinite play \((v_t)_{t\ge0}\) follows the two strategies. Weights have the binary encoding specified below, and equality zero counts as winning for Max. Give a complete Lean proof of \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\in\mathrm{P}\) or of \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\notin\mathrm{P}\).
definitions:
The edge set is a subset of \(V\times V\); self-loops are allowed and duplicate edges are not listed. Every listed edge has one arbitrary integer weight, possibly negative or zero. Either ownership set may be empty, and edges may connect vertices of the same owner. There are no chance vertices, additional agents, hidden information, simultaneous moves, fairness constraints, or extra payoff coordinates. Every vertex has a successor, so no finite-play convention is needed.

A finite history from \(s\) is a nonempty vertex sequence \(h=(s=v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_t)\) following edges of \(E\). A strategy of Max assigns to every such history ending in \(V_{\mathrm{Max}}\) a successor \(v\) with \((v_t,v)\in E\); define a strategy of Min analogously. The sets of these total deterministic history-dependent functions are \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{Max}}\) and \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{Min}}\). Neither player sees future choices. A strategy may depend on the complete known instance and entire finite history; the problem statement places no memory or computability restriction on strategies. For any pair, the play is uniquely determined by recursion. A positional strategy means that the selected successor depends only on the current vertex; positional optimality is an established theorem, not an additional promise on the instance.

For \(T\ge1\), set \(a_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}w(v_t,v_{t+1})\). The lower limit means
\[\liminf_{T\to\infty}a_T=\sup_{N\ge1}\inf_{T\ge N}a_T.\]
It is a finite real number because \(|a_T|\le W\), where \(W=\max(1,\max_{e\in E}|w(e)|)\). The average need not converge for arbitrary history-dependent play. A negative finite prefix is allowed: this objective imposes no lower bound on the running cumulative sum and no prescribed initial energy budget. The payoff is not a discounted sum or a finite-window average.

For a concrete binary encoding, let \(b(u)\) be the binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(u\), without leading zeros and with \(b(0)=0\). Define \(B(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\). Encode an integer \(z\) by \(B(\zeta(z))\), where \(\zeta(z)=2z\) for \(z\ge0\) and \(\zeta(z)=-2z-1\) for \(z<0\). This is a signed binary representation with a uniquely recoverable sign and magnitude; it is not unary in \(|z|\).

The input is \(B(n)B(m)B(s)\), followed by the \(n\) ownership bits in vertex order, and then \(m=|E|\) triples \(B(u)B(v)B(\zeta(w(u,v)))\), listing edges in increasing lexicographic endpoint order. Ownership bit one denotes Max and zero denotes Min. The complete string must satisfy the stated graph and encoding conditions, with no trailing bits. All other binary strings are rejected and are outside \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\). Let \(L\) denote the complete input length. Input validation and the translation to ordinary explicit adjacency-list signed-binary representations are polynomial-time operations; these representation conventions do not impose a graph or weight promise.

Membership in \(\mathrm{P}\) means that there are a finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that for every binary string \(x\), \(A(x)\) halts within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) bit steps, outputting one exactly when \(x\in\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\). The same program and constants must work for every size, graph, weight assignment and start vertex. Input reading, validation, arithmetic, storage access and output all count. There is no advice, randomization, game-solving oracle or unit-cost operation on arbitrarily large integers. The polynomial may depend on the fixed program but not on \(n,m,W\) or the instance. The output is only the exact winner bit; the task does not require printing an infinite strategy or play.

There is no bound on \(W\) in terms of \(n\) or \(m\). Its contribution to the input is logarithmic, so a bound polynomial in \(n,m,W\) is pseudopolynomial and need not be polynomial in \(L\). A rational threshold \(a/b\), with binary integers \(a\) and \(b>0\), gives an equivalent decision model: the weights \(bw(e)-a\) have polynomial encoding length and their nonnegative mean threshold expresses the original threshold. Thus fixing the threshold to zero retains the binary-weight complexity question.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of either
\[\exists A\ \exists C,d\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*},\quad
 A(x)\text{ halts within }C(|x|+1)^d\text{ steps and outputs }\mathbf1_{\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}}(x),\]
or its logical negation, with the machine and language definitions above. A positive proof must establish the exact game semantics, correctness on every valid instance, rejection of invalid encodings, and the full polynomial bit bound. A negative proof must rule out every deterministic polynomial-time decider, rather than only a particular local-improvement rule, representation, certificate family or algorithmic framework.

A pseudopolynomial bound, a polynomial bound only after random perturbations, a randomized expected-time guarantee, or an algorithm for a restricted graph or weight family does not answer the full question. A polynomial number of arithmetic operations alone is insufficient if intermediate integers require superpolynomial bit length. A strongly polynomial algorithm with polynomially bounded bit representations would suffice but is more than required. There is no approximation tolerance or unproved complexity hypothesis in the target.

title: FO model checking on hereditary monadically dependent graph classes
summary: First-order model checking evaluates a vertex-quantified logical sentence on an explicitly given finite graph. The question asks for a uniform deterministic algorithm on each hereditary effectively monadically dependent class, with computable parameter dependence and a sentence-independent graph-size exponent. Effective monadic dependence bounds the powerset graphs obtainable through short formulas with arbitrary unary vertex markings. The algorithm receives no graph decomposition or class-membership certificate, and must work for all sentences on its fixed class. Hereditary independent classes have a hardness theorem and effectively stable classes have algorithms, while the July 2026 radius-one results leave the full positive direction open.
formal:
For every hereditary effectively monadically dependent class \(\mathcal C\) of finite simple undirected graphs, is first-order model checking fixed-parameter tractable with a computable parameter dependence?

Precisely, does every such \(\mathcal C\) admit a single deterministic algorithm \(A_{\mathcal C}\), a total computable function \(f_{\mathcal C}:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and a constant integer \(d_{\mathcal C}\ge0\) such that, for every \(G\in\mathcal C\) and every first-order graph sentence \(\varphi\), the algorithm outputs whether \(G\models\varphi\) within
\[f_{\mathcal C}(|\varphi|)\,(|V(G)|+1)^{d_{\mathcal C}}\]
steps? The algorithm receives only the graph and the sentence, in the encodings below, and must halt on every input. The exponent may depend on the class but not on the sentence. The effective structural hypothesis is the computable powerset-obstruction bound defined below.
definitions:
Graph class and promise. A finite simple undirected graph has a finite vertex set and a symmetric irreflexive adjacency relation \(E\); the empty graph is permitted. A class \(\mathcal C\) is closed under graph isomorphism. It is hereditary if \(G[S]\in\mathcal C\) for every \(G\in\mathcal C\) and every \(S\subseteq V(G)\), where \(G[S]\) retains exactly the edges with both endpoints in \(S\). The class is fixed before the algorithm is chosen, not given as part of an instance. No decision procedure for membership in the class is assumed. Correctness and the displayed time bound are required only when the input graph belongs to the class. On other inputs the algorithm may return either answer, but must halt.

First-order syntax and truth. The graph signature has equality and a binary adjacency symbol, with variables \(x_i\) indexed by \(i\in\mathbb N\). Formulas are built from atoms \(x_i=x_j\), \(E(x_i,x_j)\), negation, binary conjunction, and existential quantification \(\exists x_i\); other connectives and universal quantification are abbreviations expanded into this syntax. A sentence has no free variables. Atoms are interpreted using actual equality and graph adjacency; Boolean operations have their usual truth tables, and quantifiers range over all vertices. On the empty graph an existential statement is false and a universal statement is true. The query language has no unary predicates, vertex order, arithmetic, function symbols or set quantification. Write \(G\models\varphi\) for truth of the sentence.

Encoding and computation. For a nonnegative integer \(i\), let \(\ell\) be the binary length of \(i+1\), and encode it as \(U(i)=1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(i+1)\), where the last part has exactly \(\ell\) bits. Encode \(G\) with labeled vertex set \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) as \(U(n)\) followed by its upper-triangular adjacency bits, in lexicographic order of pairs \(i<j\). All these bits are supplied explicitly. Formulas use prefix syntax: tags 000, 001, 010, 011, 100 respectively stand for equality, adjacency, negation, conjunction and existential quantification. An atom tag is followed by \(U(i)U(j)\), negation by one encoded subformula, conjunction by two in order, and the existential tag by \(U(i)\) and one subformula. The parameter \(|\varphi|\) is this binary length, including variable indices. A valid input concatenates the graph code and one sentence code; invalid inputs may be rejected. An algorithm is a finite deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite tape alphabet and no oracle, advice or randomness; time counts its transitions. Polynomial simulation overhead between the usual explicit graph representations and finite-word computational models can be absorbed in the class-dependent exponent and parameter function.

Unary expansions for the structural condition. For this purpose only, allow additional unary symbols \(P_j\), \(j\in\mathbb N\), with atom \(P_j(x_i)\) encoded by tag 101 followed by \(U(j)U(i)\). Each formula uses finitely many such symbols. They are interpreted independently as arbitrary vertex subsets; they may overlap. Their names and variable indices are included in formula length. There are no additional parameters or constant symbols.

Transduction. Let \(\theta(x_0,x_1)\) be any formula in this expanded syntax whose only possible free variables are \(x_0,x_1\). Given \(G\), choose arbitrary interpretations of all unary symbols used in \(\theta\). On the same vertex set, form an undirected graph by putting an edge between distinct \(u,v\) exactly when \(\theta(u,v)\lor\theta(v,u)\) holds in that expansion of \(G\). Finally keep any subset of vertices and take the induced graph on it. Denote by \(T_\theta(G)\) the set of all graphs obtainable in this way, up to isomorphism. Colors are discarded in the output. There is no copying of vertices or tuple-valued output domain in this definition.

Monadic dependence and its effective version. A class is monadically dependent when no single formula \(\theta\) produces every finite simple graph among the outputs \(T_\theta(G)\) as \(G\) ranges over the class. To state the quantitative promise, for an integer \(s\ge1\) let \(P_s\) be the bipartite powerset graph with disjoint vertex sets \(\{a_1,\ldots,a_s\}\) and \(\{b_S:S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,s\}\}\), and edges exactly \(a_i b_S\) with \(i\in S\). It has \(s+2^s\) vertices and no edges within either part.

The class \(\mathcal C\) is effectively monadically dependent if there is a total computable function \(b:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that
\[\forall\theta\ \forall G\in\mathcal C:\quad P_{b(|\theta|)}\notin T_\theta(G).\]
Absence means that no choice of unary predicates and retained vertex subset yields a graph isomorphic to that powerset graph. The bound is uniform over all formulas of the given length, all graphs in the class, and all their colorings. It is the effective dependence-function convention of Mählmann’s Definition 12.24, which in particular implies monadic dependence. The finite program computing \(b\) may depend on \(\mathcal C\).

Uniformity of the requested algorithm. For each class, one finite program \(A_{\mathcal C}\) must handle all input sentence lengths. It may depend on the class and its effective dependence witness, but receives neither a class-membership certificate nor a graph decomposition on an instance. The quantifiers are class-wise existence of the algorithm, computable function and exponent; no single procedure that accepts arbitrary descriptions of classes and constructs their algorithms is required. There is no prescribed growth rate for \(f_{\mathcal C}\), beyond total computability.
answer_criterion:
Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish, for every class satisfying the hereditary and effective-dependence promises, one total deterministic algorithm and one computable parameter bound with a sentence-independent polynomial exponent, for the specified graph-and-sentence input model.

A negative answer must establish a particular hereditary effectively monadically dependent class for which no such algorithm, computable parameter function and fixed exponent work. In particular, every candidate total deterministic algorithm and bound must fail on some graph in that class and some sentence, either in correctness or in running time. An obstruction applying only to one proposed algorithm, an ineffective class, or a restricted decomposition method is insufficient. A conditional hardness result alone does not refute this unconditional target unless its additional assumption is also proved. Structural existence theorems, a different algorithm for each sentence length, randomized algorithms, or algorithms supplied with extra decompositions do not by themselves meet the criterion.

title: Asser’s problem
summary: The spectrum of a first-order sentence is the set of positive sizes of its finite models. Asser’s problem asks whether the complement of every such set is again a first-order spectrum. The representing sentence may use a new vocabulary and must work at all sizes simultaneously, with no effective construction required. The general question is equivalent to closure of nondeterministic single-exponential time under complement for binary-encoded sizes. Two-variable counting spectra are understood, while reductions to three-variable graph inputs and later restricted-logic results leave the general question open.
formal:
Is the class of finite first-order spectra closed under complement within the positive integers?

For every finite relational vocabulary \(\tau\) and every first-order sentence \(\varphi\) over \(\tau\), does there exist a finite relational vocabulary \(\sigma\) and a first-order sentence \(\psi\) over \(\sigma\) such that
\[\forall n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:\quad \bigl(\exists\text{ an }n\text{-element }\sigma\text{-structure satisfying }\psi\bigr)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \neg\bigl(\exists\text{ an }n\text{-element }\tau\text{-structure satisfying }\varphi\bigr)?\]
The vocabulary and sentence \((\sigma,\psi)\) may depend on \((\tau,\varphi)\), but must work simultaneously for every positive size \(n\). They need not use the original vocabulary. No effective procedure for obtaining \(\psi\), or bound on its length, is required.
definitions:
Vocabulary and syntax. A finite relational vocabulary is a finite, possibly empty list \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) of distinct relation symbols with specified positive integer arities \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\). There are no function or constant symbols. Equality is a logical symbol and is always available. Variables are drawn from a countable supply. Formulas are finite expressions built from equality atoms \(x=y\), relation atoms \(R_i(x_1,\ldots,x_{a_i})\), negation, conjunction, and first-order existential quantification; other Boolean connectives and universal quantification have their usual equivalent definitions. Variables in an atom may repeat. A sentence has no free variables. Neither the number of symbols, their arities, the number of variables nor quantifier depth has a fixed global bound.

Structures and semantics. A structure over \(\tau\) consists of a nonempty finite domain \(A\) and, for each symbol \(R_i\), an arbitrary interpretation \(R_i^A\subseteq A^{a_i}\). Equality is actual equality of elements. A relation atom holds under a variable assignment exactly when the assigned tuple belongs to its interpreted relation; equality, Boolean operations and existential quantification are evaluated in the usual way, with quantified variables ranging over elements of \(A\). Write \(\mathcal A\models\varphi\) when a sentence is true in this structure. There is no built-in order, arithmetic, graph condition or fixed interpretation of a relation. A sentence may itself require such properties.

Spectrum. Define
\[\operatorname{Spec}(\varphi)=\{n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:\exists\mathcal A,\ |A|=n\text{ and }\mathcal A\models\varphi\}.\]
The existence quantifier ranges over all interpretations of all symbols at that size. One may fix the domain to \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), since relabeling does not affect truth. The target is
\[\operatorname{Spec}(\psi)=\mathbb Z_{>0}\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(\varphi).\]
Only cardinalities are retained; the spectrum does not count how many models or isomorphism types exist at a size. Empty and infinite structures are outside this definition, and the complement does not include zero.

Scope. The restriction to relational vocabularies preserves the ordinary class of first-order spectra: finite-arity functions and constants can instead be represented by relations, together with first-order conditions enforcing their graph or unique-value interpretation on the same domain. No second-order quantifiers over relations or arbitrary external numerical predicates are added to the representing sentence. The target is an existence statement about finite formulas and their entire sets of model sizes. It imposes no computational model, sentence-construction resource bound or model-search algorithm requirement.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed universal complement-closure statement or its full logical negation. A positive proof must establish a single representing first-order sentence for the whole positive-integer complement of each input spectrum; the new vocabulary is unrestricted except for finiteness and the stated relational syntax. A negative proof must establish a first-order spectrum whose complement is not the spectrum of any first-order sentence over any permitted finite vocabulary. Equivalently, for that input sentence, every candidate representing sentence must fail at some positive size, which may depend on the candidate. Checking finitely many sizes, ruling out a fixed vocabulary or variable bound, or showing that literal sentence negation fails is insufficient. The theorem must be unconditional unless it also proves every additional assumption used.

title: NP membership of word-equation satisfiability
summary: A word equation asks whether replacing each variable by a finite word can make its two sides identical. The selected target is whether satisfiability of unrestricted plain word equations belongs to NP. A positive answer needs polynomial-size certificates and one polynomial-time verifier, without prescribing how a solution is represented. The problem is NP-hard and has a nondeterministic linear-space algorithm, while a 2026 source still lists NP membership as open. The overlapping word-unification card is merged here, with its original record retained in the archive.
formal:
Let \(\mathrm{WE}\) be the language of encodings of satisfiable word equations \(u=v\) over finite free monoids, as defined below. Is
\[
\mathrm{WE}\in\mathrm{NP}?
\]
Explicitly, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(V\), a constant \(C\ge1\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that \(V\) halts on every pair of bit strings \((e,w)\) within \(C(|e|+|w|+1)^k\) steps and, for every valid equation encoding \(e\) of length \(N\),
\[
e\in\mathrm{WE}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{*}\ 
\bigl(|w|\le C(N+1)^k\ \text{and}\ V(e,w)=1\bigr)?
\]
The verifier rejects invalid equation encodings. The same machine and constants work for all alphabets, equations and variable sets.
definitions:
For an integer \(a\ge1\), the constant alphabet is \(\Sigma=\{a_1,\ldots,a_a\}\). Its free monoid \(\Sigma^*\) is the set of finite words, including the empty word \(\varepsilon\), with concatenation as the operation. Concatenation is associative and \(\varepsilon\) is its identity; distinct letters do not commute by assumption.

The variable set is \(\mathcal X=\{X_1,\ldots,X_r\}\), disjoint from \(\Sigma\), where \(r\ge0\). An equation is a pair \(u,v\in(\Sigma\cup\mathcal X)^*\). Both sides are explicitly written token sequences. A solution assigns one word \(\sigma(X_i)\in\Sigma^*\) to each variable, fixes every constant letter, and extends by concatenation. The equation is satisfiable exactly when \(\sigma(u)=\sigma(v)\) for some assignment. All occurrences of a variable receive the same word. Empty words, repeated variables, variables on both sides, and equations with empty sides are allowed. There are no length constraints, regular-language restrictions, inverse symbols or inequalities.

One precise binary encoding is as follows. Write \(1^a0\,1^r0\,1^{\ell_u}0\,1^{\ell_v}0\), where \(\ell_u=|u|\) and \(\ell_v=|v|\) count tokens. Follow this header by all tokens of \(u\) and then all tokens of \(v\). Each token is encoded in \(b=\lceil\log_2(a+r+1)\rceil\) bits: code \(i\) for \(a_i\) and code \(a+j\) for \(X_j\). Codes outside \(1,\ldots,a+r\) are invalid. There must be exactly \(\ell_u+\ell_v\) token blocks and no trailing data. Thus
\[
N=a+r+\ell_u+\ell_v+4+b(\ell_u+\ell_v).
\]
This explicit encoding fixes bit complexity without allowing compressed input equations.

Use [NP](definitions.html#p-np), with precisely the soundness and completeness quantified above. A certificate is any finite binary string. It need not contain the substituted words explicitly, and no particular compressed representation is prescribed. A satisfiable input must have some short accepting certificate; an unsatisfiable input must have none.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of \(\mathrm{WE}\in\mathrm{NP}\). A positive answer must specify the verifier and prove the polynomial time and certificate bounds together with soundness and completeness for every input. A negative answer must prove that no such verifier exists; failure of one certificate format or long explicit solutions is insufficient. This binary target has no numerical \(1/100\) tolerance. Results only for boundedly many variables, bounded occurrences, or added constraints do not decide the full statement.

title: Decidability of multiplicative-exponential linear logic and branching VASS reachability
summary: Can an algorithm decide whether a given sequent has a proof in multiplicative-exponential linear logic? This logic keeps track of how each assumption is used, and its exponential modalities allow an assumption to be reused or discarded. In the equivalent counter formulation, a branching rule combines several child configurations and reachability asks whether a finite tree produces an exact target. Reductions in both directions have been known since 2004. In July 2026, Bizière, Leroux and Sutre gave a decision procedure for branching reachability, settling both formulations.
formal: Is provability decidable in propositional multiplicative-exponential linear logic (MELL)? Given a finite sequent \(\Gamma\), the algorithm must halt and decide whether \(\vdash\Gamma\) has a derivation in the calculus below. Equivalently, is exact reachability decidable for branching vector addition systems with states (branching VASS)? Given a finite system of input dimension \(d\) and a target \(q(x)\), decide whether a finite derivation tree has root \(q(x)\).
definitions:
MELL. Use finite formula trees. Leaves are atoms \(p_i\), their dual literals \(p_i^\perp\) for \(i\ge 0\), or units \(1,\bot\). The constructors are tensor \(A\otimes B\), par (⅋), written \(A\mathbin{\mathrm{par}}B\), and the modalities \(!A,?A\), with arbitrary nesting. A sequent is a finite multiset of formulas. A comma denotes multiset union. The one-sided cut-free calculus has two axioms, \(\vdash p_i,p_i^\perp\) and \(\vdash 1\). From \(\vdash\Gamma,A\) and \(\vdash\Delta,B\), tensor derives \(\vdash\Gamma,\Delta,A\otimes B\). From \(\vdash\Gamma,A,B\), par derives \(\vdash\Gamma,A\mathbin{\mathrm{par}}B\). From \(\vdash\Gamma\), the unit rule derives \(\vdash\Gamma,\bot\). Dereliction takes \(\vdash\Gamma,A\) to \(\vdash\Gamma,?A\). Weakening takes \(\vdash\Gamma\) to \(\vdash\Gamma,?A\). Contraction takes \(\vdash\Gamma,?A,?A\) to \(\vdash\Gamma,?A\). Promotion takes \(\vdash ?\Gamma,A\) to \(\vdash ?\Gamma,!A\), where every formula in \(?\Gamma\) has outermost symbol \(?\). Contexts may be empty. A derivation is a finite tree built from these rules. Input sequents list the formula trees explicitly with binary atom indices.

Branching VASS. The input specifies a finite nonempty state set \(Q\), a dimension \(d\ge 1\), and finitely many rules \((S,a,q)\) with \(S\subseteq Q\), \(a\in\mathbb Z^d\), and \(q\in Q\). A configuration \(q(x)\) has \(x\in\mathbb N^d\), with zero allowed. To apply a rule, supply a child \(s(x_s)\) for each \(s\in S\). The parent is \(q(a+\sum_{s\in S}x_s)\), provided every output coordinate is nonnegative. An empty \(S\) gives a leaf \(q(a)\) under the same condition. A target is reachable if it occurs at the root of a finite tree of rule applications. Rules may be reused. The system, child-state sets and target are explicit, and all coordinates are in binary.
answer_criterion: Give a decision procedure for either formulation and prove that it halts and answers correctly on every valid input, or prove undecidability. The established reductions carry either answer to the other formulation. The reachability target is exact and the dimension is part of the input.

title: Decidability of Presburger arithmetic with primes
summary: Presburger arithmetic describes the standard integers using addition and order and has a decidable first-order theory. This question adds a predicate for positive primes and asks for one algorithm deciding every sentence, with arbitrary quantifier alternation. The resulting language can express prime-pattern claims such as twin primes and Goldbach’s conjecture. Nieuwveld proves unconditionally that addition and the positive primes already have an undecidable first-order theory over the natural numbers. Restricting quantifiers to nonnegative integers transfers this result to the ordered integers in the question.
formal: Is the full first-order theory of the fixed structure \[\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{Pr}}=(\mathbb Z;0,1,+,-,<,\mathrm{Pr})\] decidable, where \(\mathrm{Pr}(n)\) means that \(n\ge2\) is a positive prime? Equivalently, does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which halts on every finite encoded sentence \(\varphi\) of this language and returns YES exactly when \(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{Pr}}\models\varphi\)? The question is unconditional and permits arbitrary finite first-order quantifier alternation.
definitions: All variables range over the standard integers \(\mathbb Z\). The symbols \(0,1,+,-,<\) denote their usual constants, addition, unary negation and strict order. The predicate \(\mathrm{Pr}\) is false for negative integers, zero and one; for \(n\ge2\), it is true exactly when the only positive divisors of \(n\) are \(1\) and \(n\). This defines the intended predicate in the mathematical metatheory; multiplication and variable divisibility are not additional symbols of the input language. Terms are variables, integer numerals, sums and negatives. Atoms are term equality, strict inequality and \(\mathrm{Pr}(t)\); formulas use the ordinary Boolean connectives and individual-variable \(\exists,\forall\). A sentence has no free variables. Arbitrary signed integer numerals and multiplication by a specified integer coefficient are harmless abbreviations for expressions in this language, not products of two variables. Inputs are explicit finite syntax trees with variable identifiers and numerals encoded in binary. Malformed encodings may be rejected. The machine is uniform over all formula lengths, variable counts and alternation depths, with no prescribed resource bound, randomness or oracle. It must give exact truth in this one intended structure, rather than satisfiability over arbitrary structures or provability from an unspecified axiom set. There is no numerical tolerance. Removing the definable unary-negation symbol does not change decidability: its graph is \(x+y=0\).
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that such a total computable truth classifier exists, or that none exists. A positive proof must formalize finite syntax, satisfaction in the standard integer structure, the algorithm, termination on every sentence and correctness in both truth directions. A negative proof must establish noncomputability of this exact full theory.
