A result conditional on an unproved number-theoretic hypothesis must discharge that hypothesis to meet the unconditional criterion. Deciding a quantifier-restricted fragment or testing the primality of a supplied integer does not cover the target. No Lean formalization is supplied by this editorial review.

title: Scott-continuous lambda models with theory \(\lambda \beta\)
summary: Scott's continuous semantics interprets untyped lambda terms using mathematical domains and continuous functions. The project asks whether some model identifies exactly the pairs of terms related by beta-conversion. Beta-conversion expresses equality generated by applying functions to arguments and substituting those arguments into their bodies. Many semantic constructions validate additional equations, so soundness for beta-reduction alone does not answer the question. An exact model would show whether this influential notion of continuous meaning can distinguish every pair of terms that the basic operational equations keep separate.
formal: Do there exist a pointed directed-complete partial order \(D\) and Scott-continuous maps \(F:D\to[D\to D]\) and \(L:[D\to D]\to D\) with \(F\circ L=\mathrm{id}_{[D\to D]}\), such that two finite untyped lambda terms have equal interpretations in every environment exactly when they are beta-convertible?
definitions:
Terms are built from countably many variables using application \(MN\) and abstraction \(\lambda x.M\), up to renaming bound variables. Beta-convertibility \(=_\beta\) is the least congruence containing \((\lambda x.M)N=_\beta M[N/x]\), using capture-avoiding substitution.

A directed subset is nonempty and each pair of its elements has an upper bound in the subset. The partial order \(D\) has a least element and suprema of all directed subsets. A Scott-continuous function is monotone and preserves directed suprema. The function space \([D\to D]\) contains all such functions ordered pointwise.

An environment \(\rho\) assigns an element of \(D\) to each variable. Write \(I_\rho(M)\) for the interpretation of a term. Define
\[I_\rho(x)=\rho(x),\qquad I_\rho(MN)=F(I_\rho(M))(I_\rho(N)),\qquad I_\rho(\lambda x.M)=L\bigl(d\mapsto I_{\rho[x:=d]}(M)\bigr).\]
The target is \((\forall\rho,\ I_\rho(M)=I_\rho(N))\iff M=_\beta N\) for every \(M,N\). The domain may have arbitrary cardinality and need not be algebraic or effectively presented. Only \(F\circ L\) must be the identity. These are set-based models with the full Scott-continuous function space.
answer_criterion: Prove that a pointed dcpo and continuous retraction F,L satisfying the stated exact-theory condition exist, or prove that none exist. A negative answer must cover all such dcpos, without assuming an effective presentation, algebraicity or extensionality.

title: Barendregt–Geuvers–Klop conjecture
summary: A pure type system specifies a typed lambda calculus through a uniform collection of formation rules. Weak normalization means that every well-typed term has some terminating reduction path. The conjecture asks whether that global property forces every reduction path of every well-typed term to terminate. A term may have both a normalizing route and a divergent route in less constrained rewriting settings, so the type-system hypothesis is essential. A proof would connect existence of normal forms with unrestricted evaluation termination across a broad family of typed calculi.
formal: For every pure type system \((S,A,R)\) defined below, does weak normalization of every typable term imply strong normalization of every typable term?
definitions:
A pure type system has sorts \(S\), axioms \(A\subseteq S^2\) and product rules \(R\subseteq S^3\). The finite terms are variables, sorts, applications \(tu\), abstractions \(\lambda x:B.t\), and products \(\Pi x:B.C\), up to renaming bound variables. Variables come from a countably infinite set. A context is a finite sequence of declarations of distinct variables. The typing judgment is the least relation satisfying the following rules, with \(s,s_1,s_2,s_3\) ranging over sorts and each fresh declaration using a new variable.

For \((s_1,s_2)\in A\), derive \(\varnothing\vdash s_1:s_2\). From \(\Gamma\vdash B:s\), derive \(\Gamma,x:B\vdash x:B\) for fresh \(x\). Weaken \(\Gamma\vdash t:B\) to \(\Gamma,x:C\vdash t:B\) if \(\Gamma\vdash C:s\) and \(x\) is fresh.

From \(\Gamma\vdash B:s_1\), \(\Gamma,x:B\vdash C:s_2\) and \((s_1,s_2,s_3)\in R\), derive \(\Gamma\vdash(\Pi x:B.C):s_3\). From \(\Gamma,x:B\vdash t:C\) and \(\Gamma\vdash(\Pi x:B.C):s\), derive \(\Gamma\vdash(\lambda x:B.t):(\Pi x:B.C)\). From \(\Gamma\vdash t:(\Pi x:B.C)\) and \(\Gamma\vdash u:B\), derive \(\Gamma\vdash tu:C[u/x]\). Finally, from \(\Gamma\vdash t:B\), \(\Gamma\vdash C:s\) and \(B=_\beta C\), derive \(\Gamma\vdash t:C\).

One beta step contracts \((\lambda x:B.t)u\) to \(t[u/x]\) at any subterm, including inside annotations and product types. Substitution avoids capture, and \(=_\beta\) is the reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure of these steps. A term is typable if it has a type in some finite context. Weak normalization means each typable term has a finite reduction to a term with no beta redex. Strong normalization means every reduction from every typable term is finite. Both notions include open terms. The system may be infinite, undecidable or nonfunctional.
answer_criterion: Prove that every pure type system in which all typable terms are weakly beta-normalizing is strongly beta-normalizing, or exhibit a pure type system that is weakly normalizing for every typable term but has a typable term admitting an infinite beta-reduction sequence.

title: Decidability of unification in the basic modal logic K
summary: Basic modal logic K interprets formulas on arbitrary accessibility relations between possible worlds. The problem asks whether it is decidable that a finite formula has a substitution instance valid at every world of every such model. Substitutions act simultaneously on all input variables, may introduce new variables, and leave no designated parameters fixed. Frames may be finite or infinite, and no reflexivity or transitivity condition is imposed. The requested algorithm must halt on every input; its time and the size of a possible substitution have no prescribed bounds.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that halts on every finite modal formula \(\varphi\) and decides whether there exists a substitution \(\sigma\) for its propositional variables such that \(\sigma (\varphi )\) is valid on every Kripke frame?
definitions: Formulas are finite expressions generated by variables \(p_{i} (i\in \mathbb{N} ), \perp\), negation, conjunction and the unary operator □; other Boolean connectives and ◇ are abbreviations. Variable indices use binary notation and formulas are supplied as fully written syntax trees. A substitution assigns a finite formula to each variable occurring in \(\varphi\), may use new propositional variables, and extends simultaneously through the connectives and □; it does not substitute recursively inside its newly inserted formulas. There are no distinguished parameters that must remain unchanged. A frame is a nonempty set W with an arbitrary relation \(R\subseteq \mathrm{W}\times \mathrm{W}\), finite or infinite. A valuation assigns a subset of W to every variable. Satisfaction uses the usual truth tables, ⊥ is false everywhere, and \(w\models\)□\(\psi\) iff \(v\models \psi\) for all v with wRv. Validity means satisfaction at every world in every frame with every valuation. This is the basic normal modal logic K, with no reflexivity, transitivity or seriality requirement on R. The substitution is existentially quantified without a length bound. Only its existence is decided; no running-time bound or output unifier is required. Malformed formula encodings are rejected.
answer_criterion: Give a total decision procedure correct for every finite formula in the stated language, or prove that no such Turing machine exists. The unbounded substitution and arbitrary-frame semantics must remain those of parameter-free, single-modality K.

title: Decidability of termination for one-rule string rewriting
summary: A one-rule string system repeatedly replaces one fixed substring by another. The question is whether an algorithm can decide if every reduction sequence from every finite starting word eventually stops. Replacement positions are unrestricted, and the rule and alphabet are part of the input. Known decision procedures cover special rule families, while an August 2026 note still lists the arbitrary one-rule question as open. The answer must prove decidability or undecidability in Lean for global termination, rather than only termination from one supplied word.
formal: Is global termination of a one-rule string rewriting system decidable? The input is a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) and two explicitly written words \(\ell,r\in\Sigma^{*}\). Define \(u\to v\) when \(u=x\ell y\) and \(v=xry\) for some \(x,y\in\Sigma^{*}\). Decide whether there exists no infinite sequence \(w_0\to w_1\to w_2\to\cdots\) of finite words. The quantifier includes every starting word and every choice of replacement position.
definitions:
The alphabet is a finite nonempty set listed by distinct binary symbol indices. Both sides of the rule are explicit finite sequences of these symbols, including possibly the empty word \(\varepsilon\). No variables, compressed word descriptions, contexts supplied as inputs, or additional rewrite rules occur.

One rewrite step chooses one contiguous occurrence of \(\ell\) and replaces it with \(r\), preserving the prefix \(x\) and suffix \(y\). If \(\ell=\varepsilon\), any boundary in a word, including its ends, is an occurrence. A rule application counts as a step even when the resulting word is identical to the original word. Thus \(\ell=r\) admits a constant infinite reduction sequence from \(\ell\).

Global termination means that for every \(w_0\in\Sigma^{*}\) there is no function \(w:\mathbb{N}\to\Sigma^{*}\) with first value \(w_0\) and \(w_i\to w_{i+1}\) for all \(i\geq0\). There is no fixed leftmost or rightmost evaluation strategy. Requiring only that each word has some terminating sequence would be a different property.

Decidability asks for a single deterministic Turing machine that halts on every valid finite description and outputs yes exactly for globally terminating systems. No running-time bound is imposed. Malformed descriptions can be rejected. The rule itself varies across instances; neither its length nor the alphabet size is a fixed constant.
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of a total decision algorithm for all one-rule systems in this model, or a Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. Deciding termination from one supplied start word, analyzing one strategy, or handling a restricted family of rules alone is insufficient.

title: Commutativity of the full probabilistic powerdomain monad
summary: Continuous valuations generalize probability distributions on ordered semantic domains. The question asks whether the order of two integrations can always be exchanged. The selected variant uses subprobability mass and the Scott topology of the dcpo product. Minimal valuations form a smaller class for which separate positive results are available. Separation from that class does not by itself refute the interchange equation.
formal: Editorial subprobability variant: for all dcpos X,Y, all continuous subprobability valuations mu on X and nu on Y, and every Scott-continuous \(f:X\times Y\to[0,\infty]\), must \[\int_X\!\left(\int_Y f(x,y)\,d\nu(y)\right)d\mu(x)=\int_Y\!\left(\int_X f(x,y)\,d\mu(x)\right)d\nu(y)\,?\] This is commutativity of the full continuous-subprobability valuation monad.
definitions:
A dcpo is a partially ordered set in which each nonempty directed subset has a supremum. A directed set is one in which every finite subset has an upper bound within the set. A Scott-open subset is upward closed and, whenever a directed supremum belongs to it, contains an element of that directed set. A map is Scott-continuous when it is monotone and preserves directed suprema. X×Y has the componentwise dcpo order and its Scott topology; do not substitute a potentially different topological product of Scott spaces. The target [0,infinity] has its usual order and Scott topology.

A continuous subprobability valuation mu assigns a number in [0,1] to each Scott-open U, with mu(empty)=0, mu(X)≤1, monotonicity, modularity mu(U)+mu(V)=mu(U union V)+mu(U intersection V), and preservation of suprema of directed families of open sets. For a nonnegative Scott-continuous h define its integral by the layer-cake formula integral_0^infinity mu({x:h(x)>t}) dt, allowing infinity. Iterated integrals in the statement use this definition.

The monad orders valuations pointwise; its unit sends x to the Dirac valuation U↦1 if x∈U, zero otherwise. For a Scott-continuous kernel K:X→V(Y), extension maps mu to U↦integral_X K(x)(U)dmu(x). These definitions specify the same independence-interchange question through the displayed Fubini identity. All continuous valuations of total mass at most one are allowed, not just finite combinations of Dirac valuations or their directed-supremum closure, called minimal valuations. Choosing total mass at most one is an explicit specialization; the card does not claim equivalence with every unbounded-mass convention.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed identity for the entire stated domain, or explicit dcpos, continuous subprobability valuations and a Scott-continuous integrand with different iterated integrals. A nonminimal valuation alone is not a counterexample, and commutativity proved only for minimal valuations does not settle the full class.

title: Univalence, impredicativity and propositional resizing
summary: An impredicative universe supports quantification over types without the usual increase in universe size, while univalence connects equivalence with equality. Propositional resizing adds the requirement that large propositions have equivalent small representatives. The source asks for a model of type theory supporting all three features together. Its cubical assembly construction provides univalence and impredicativity but fails resizing, and a related positive model weakens identity and dependent-product structure. Constructing a model with the intended ordinary type-theoretic rules would clarify whether these attractive foundational principles can coexist without sacrificing essential forms of dependent reasoning.
formal: Does there exist a nondegenerate model of ordinary dependent type theory, with the type formers and computation rules specified below, containing a univalent impredicative universe \(U\) of data types into which every homotopy proposition can be resized?
definitions: A model is a set-based category with families: it has contexts and substitutions forming a category with an empty terminal context, types over each context, terms of each type, and context extension \(\Gamma.A\) classifying a substitution into \(\Gamma\) together with a term of its reindexed type \(A\). Reindexing of types and terms obeys identity and composition strictly. Type-forming operations, constructors and eliminators commute strictly with reindexing. Require dependent products \(\prod_{x:A}B(x)\), dependent sums \(\sum_{x:A}B(x)\), intensional identity types \(\operatorname{Id}_A(a,b)\), empty and unit types, binary coproducts, and natural numbers. Products have abstraction and application with the usual judgmental beta and eta equations; sums have pairing, projections and dependent elimination with their usual computation equations. Identity types have reflexivity and the unrestricted dependent eliminator \(J\), whose reflexivity computation equation holds judgmentally. Empty, unit, coproduct and natural-number types have their usual dependent eliminators and judgmental constructor equations. Also require function extensionality: the canonical map from an identity of dependent functions to their pointwise identities is an equivalence. Judgmental equations are equalities of the interpreted operations, rather than merely inhabited identity types. Nondegenerate means that the interpreted empty type has no closed term. A Tarski universe is an ambient type \(U\) with a decoding family \(\operatorname{El}:U\to\mathrm{Type}\). It has codes for empty, unit, binary coproduct and natural-number types and is closed under dependent sums and identity types of decoded small types. It is impredicative when, for every ambient type \(A\) and family \(b:A\to U\), the dependent product \(\prod_{x:A}\operatorname{El}(b(x))\) has a code in \(U\). These coding operations and their decoding identifications must be specified and stable under substitution; decoded closure may hold up to specified isomorphism. The domain \(A\) need not itself have a code in \(U\). There is no requirement that \(U\) code itself. Write \(\operatorname{isProp}(P)=\prod_{x,y:P}\operatorname{Id}_P(x,y)\). A type is contractible if it has a point identified with every point; a map is an equivalence if every fiber \(\sum_x\operatorname{Id}(f(x),y)\) is contractible. Univalence means that, for all \(a,b:U\), the canonical transport map \(\operatorname{Id}_U(a,b)\to\operatorname{Equiv}(\operatorname{El}(a),\operatorname{El}(b))\) is an equivalence. Propositional resizing means that for every ambient type \(P\), in every context with a term of \(\operatorname{isProp}(P)\), there is a small proposition code \(p:U\) and an equivalence \(P\simeq\operatorname{El}(p)\), uniformly under substitution. These are internal structures of the model; external equivalence of isolated fibers is insufficient. No particular assembly, cubical or path-category presentation, no Church’s thesis and no higher inductive types are required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a model exists, specifying its semantic structures and verifying all rules, closure, univalence, resizing and nondegeneracy; or prove in Lean that no such model exists. A merely postulated model, a model with only propositional universes, or a model validating only weaker identity or dependent-product computation rules does not satisfy this formulation. A failure of resizing in one candidate model is not a universal nonexistence proof.

title: Decidability and completeness of concurrent Kleene algebra with parallel iteration
summary: Concurrent Kleene algebra describes finite partially ordered executions using choice, sequential and parallel composition, and iteration. The card asks both whether refinement is decidable and whether its valid inequalities follow from the stated axioms when both sequential and parallel iteration are allowed. Refinement preserves events and labels while permitting extra ordering, and parallel iteration allows arbitrarily many concurrent copies. Decision and completeness results for expressions without parallel iteration do not settle the full-signature questions retained here. A resolution would establish the algorithmic and proof-theoretic limits of algebraic reasoning about unbounded finite concurrency.
formal: Settle both parts of the source question for the full concurrent Kleene-algebra signature, including unbounded finite parallel iteration. For finite expressions \(e,f\), write \(e\preceq f\) when \(\downarrow\llbracket e\rrbracket\subseteq\downarrow\llbracket f\rrbracket\), using the pomset refinement semantics below. (1) Is there a total computable procedure deciding \(e\preceq f\) on every pair of such expressions? (2) Are the stated Kleene-algebra axioms for both products, together with weak interchange, complete for this semantics: \[\forall e,f,\quad e\preceq f\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathsf{CKA}\vdash e+f=f?\] The already settled fragment without parallel iteration is recorded in the context. The two remaining questions are separate: neither an algorithm alone nor an axiomatic completeness theorem alone is a complete answer to this paired target.
definitions:
An input supplies a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) and two finite syntax trees generated by \[e ::= 0\mid1\mid a\ (a\in\Sigma)\mid e+e\mid e\cdot e\mid e\parallel e\mid e^*\mid e^\dagger.\] The alphabet and syntax trees have explicit finite encodings, with labels represented by binary indices; no succinctly shared circuits, numerical iteration counts or bound on nesting is imposed. A pomset is a finite partially ordered set of events labelled in \(\Sigma\), considered up to label-preserving order isomorphism. The empty pomset interprets \(1\), the singleton labelled \(a\) interprets \(a\), and \(0\) denotes the empty language. A sequential product \(P\cdot Q\) uses disjoint copies and places every event of \(P\) before every event of \(Q\); a parallel product \(P\parallel Q\) uses disjoint copies with no additional cross-order. Lift products to sets by taking every pair, and interpret \(+\) as union. The language of \(e^*\) is the union of all finite sequential products of members of \(\llbracket e\rrbracket\); \(e^\dagger\) is the analogous union of finite parallel products. Both include the empty product. These are finite executions of unbounded size, not infinite executions. A pomset \(P\) refines \(Q\), written \(P\sqsubseteq Q\), if there is a bijection from the events of \(Q\) to those of \(P\) preserving labels and every order comparison in \(Q\); \(P\) may add further comparisons. Put \(\downarrow L=\{P:\exists Q\in L,\ P\sqsubseteq Q\}\), ranging over all finite pomsets. Thus \(e\preceq f\) equivalently says every pomset of \(\llbracket e\rrbracket\) refines some pomset of \(\llbracket f\rrbracket\). For example, \(a\cdot b\preceq a\parallel b\).

The proof system \(\mathsf{CKA}\) uses ordinary finite equational reasoning (reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, substitution and congruence) and the following axiom and inference schemas on arbitrary full-signature terms. Write \(x\le y\) as an abbreviation for \(x+y=y\). Addition is associative, commutative and idempotent, with identity \(0\). For each pair \((\circ,\star)\in\{(\cdot,*),(\parallel,\dagger)\}\), the product is associative, has identity \(1\), has absorbing element \(0\), distributes over addition on both sides, and satisfies \[1+x\circ x^\star=x^\star=1+x^\star\circ x.\] Its induction rules are \[x\circ y\le y\ \Longrightarrow\ x^\star\circ y\le y,\qquad y\circ x\le y\ \Longrightarrow\ y\circ x^\star\le y.\] Parallel product additionally commutes. Finally impose weak interchange \[(x\parallel z)\cdot(y\parallel w)\le(x\cdot y)\parallel(z\cdot w).\] Premises of induction rules must themselves be derived; no extra assumptions about the input letters are available. Soundness holds for the downward-closed pomset semantics. The decision question requires exact deterministic halting answers, with no error allowance, oracle or complexity bound.
answer_criterion: Provide complete Lean-checked resolutions of both parts, with a separate conclusion for each. Decidability requires a total computable classifier for the displayed semantic preorder and a correctness proof; undecidability requires a proof that no such classifier exists. Completeness requires derivability of every valid refinement inequality from exactly the stated finite-proof schemas. Incompleteness requires a valid inequality and a proof of its nonderivability, for example through a fully verified algebraic countermodel to derivability. A proof for terms omitting \(\dagger\), or for plain language equality before refinement closure, is partial. A theorem about validity in all continuous models does not by itself prove completeness of the specified finitary axioms.

title: Greedy CDCL without restarts versus resolution
summary: A resolution refutation derives the empty clause by repeatedly combining clauses on opposite literals. This card asks whether any such supplied proof can be translated in deterministic polynomial time into a greedy clause-learning search on the same formula without restarts. The legal search must process conflicts and unit clauses immediately and may backjump only as justified by a learned asserting clause. Known simulations with relaxed propagation or preprocessing, and newer generalized backtracking results, do not establish this exact claim. A resolution would show whether restarts change the polynomial proof-generating power of idealized greedy SAT search.
formal: Does greedy CDCL without restarts p-simulate resolution in the asserting-learning model below? Precisely, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(M\), a constant \(C>0\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\) such that for every finite CNF formula \(F\) and every valid resolution refutation \(\pi\) of \(F\), on the explicit binary input \((F,\pi)\) of length \(L\), \(M\) halts within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps and outputs a legal greedy CDCL refutation of the same \(F\), without restarts, of at most \(C(L+1)^k\) bits? The single program and polynomial must work for all formulas and supplied proofs.
definitions:
Literals are \(x_{i}\) or \(\neg x_{i}\) for \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,n\}\); clauses are sets of literals and F is a finite set of clauses. A resolution inference derives \((C\setminus \{x\})\cup (D\setminus \{\neg x\})\) from clauses C containing x and D containing \(\neg x\). A refutation is a finite sequence ending in the empty clause, each entry being an input clause or an inference from earlier entries, with parent indices and pivot recorded. Variable indices and pointers use binary notation. Clause and formula encodings explicitly list their literals.

A CDCL state consists of a database D containing F and an ordered trail of assignments to distinct variables of F. Each assignment is marked either as a decision or with its reason clause in D. Its decision level is the number of decisions up to that assignment. Initially \(D=F\) and the trail is empty. A clause is falsified if all its literals are false on the trail; it is unit if exactly one literal is unassigned and all others are false. The following priority of actions is mandatory.

If D has a falsified clause, a conflict must be processed before any other action. At decision level zero the run ends with UNSAT. Otherwise choose a falsified clause K and a trivial resolution analysis: start with K and repeatedly resolve the current clause with a reason clause recorded on the current trail, using a distinct pivot at each step. Every intermediate clause must be falsified by the current trail. Stop at a nonempty asserting clause C, meaning that exactly one of its variables has the current highest decision level. The trace records the full analysis. Add C to D and erase the suffix of the trail whose decision levels exceed a, where a is the maximum level of the other literals of C, or zero if there are none. Then perform one legal unit propagation and return to the conflict-first priority check.

If there is no conflict but a unit clause exists, choose such a clause, assign its unassigned literal to true, record that clause as the reason, and repeat the priority check. Only when neither conflicts nor units exist may a new decision assign either value to an unassigned variable. At such a stable state the run may first delete any subset of learned clauses, retaining all input clauses and all reasons appearing on the current trail, and must then make a decision. A satisfying complete trail ends with SAT, not a refutation. There is no independent operation clearing or shortening the trail: backjumping is allowed only after a conflict and only to the assertion level.

All choices of decisions, unit reasons, conflict clauses, trivial asserting analyses and permitted deletions are free components of the output trace. No fixed branching heuristic or first-UIP policy is imposed. No new variables, preprocessed replacement formula, unrecorded learned axioms or restarts are permitted. The only learned clauses are those derived by the recorded conflict analyses. The trace length counts all clauses, literals, assignments, analysis steps and pointers in an explicit binary encoding, so expensive analysis cannot be hidden in one step. This is the restart-free instantiation of the Vinyals model with arbitrary trivial asserting learning. The requested p-simulation is a uniform translation supplied with \(\pi\); mere existence of a short trace, or finding one from F alone, is a different claim.

The input promise is that the explicitly recorded resolution derivation is a valid refutation of the supplied formula; correctness is required for every promised input, including a formula already containing the empty clause. Invalid encodings or derivations may be rejected. All computation and output costs use ordinary sequential bit time. Choices made by the translator are deterministic and fully recorded, with exact clause and Boolean semantics; no randomness, numerical approximation, oracle or nonuniform advice is available. The model permits a conflict-justified backjump to level zero, which does not count as an independent restart.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof of the displayed uniform p-simulation or its logical negation. A positive answer must formalize the finite clause encoding and resolution proof checker, the stated CDCL state and transition system, and a computable translator with a polynomial bit-time bound, proving that every valid input proof yields a trace on the original formula ending in the permitted UNSAT state. The trace must obey conflict and propagation priority, trivial asserting analysis, assertion-level backjumps, deletion restrictions and the absence of restarts. A negative answer must rule out all such uniform polynomial-time translators; a lower bound for one fixed heuristic or a different backtracking policy is insufficient. Existence of polynomial-size traces alone does not supply the required efficient translator. Conditional theorems settle only their stated conditional variants unless their premises are also proved. No proof-assistant verification of either answer is claimed by this editorial review.

title: Deciding MSO-definable choice on the infinite binary tree
summary: An MSO formula relates two arbitrary subsets of the infinite binary tree. A uniformizer must select one valid output wherever any output exists. The selection itself must be defined by a single MSO formula. The task is to decide whether such a formula exists for a given relation. Finite-cross-section results and examples without choice do not alone give that decision procedure.
formal: Given a monadic second-order formula \(\varphi(X,Y)\) over the full infinite binary tree, is it decidable whether there is an MSO formula \(\theta(X,Y)\) defining a partial function with exactly the same domain as \(\varphi\) and with graph contained in \(\varphi\)?
definitions:
The tree domain is \(\{0,1\}^*\), including the empty word. Its signature contains the two labelled child relations \(\operatorname{child}_0(u,u0)\) and \(\operatorname{child}_1(u,u1)\), and equality. First-order variables range over nodes and monadic second-order variables over all subsets of nodes, finite or infinite. Formulas use Boolean connectives and quantification of either kind. The input has exactly the indicated two free set variables and no other free variables or external set parameters.

For each subset X, write \(R_X=\{Y:\mathcal T\models\varphi(X,Y)\}\). A candidate \(\theta\) must satisfy: for all X,Y, \(\theta(X,Y)\) implies \(\varphi(X,Y)\); and for every X with \(R_X\) nonempty, there is exactly one subset Y satisfying \(\theta(X,Y)\). When \(R_X\) is empty, \(\theta\) has no witness. The same finite formula \(\theta\) must work for all X. There is no causality, finite-state transducer, cardinality bound on \(R_X\), or definability restriction on X. The decision algorithm is an ordinary Turing machine on formula syntax and must halt on every formula. It need only decide existence; producing \(\theta\) is an optional stronger result.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked terminating decision algorithm and proof of equivalence to existence of the specified formula \(\theta\), or prove this existence problem undecidable. Showing that some relations lack uniformizers does not prove that recognizing the uniformizable relations is undecidable.

title: Satisfiability with two variables and one transitive relation
summary: Sentences use only two variable names but may reuse them arbitrarily. One binary predicate must be transitive in every admissible model. Models may be finite or infinite and equality is available. The requested procedure must decide satisfiability for all such sentences. Finite-model and restricted partial-order results leave this broader target distinct.
formal: Is satisfiability decidable for first-order sentences with equality, only two reusable variable symbols, and one distinguished binary relation required to be transitive, when models may be finite or infinite?
definitions:
The input is a finite sentence over a finite vocabulary of unary and binary relation symbols, one of which is distinguished as T. There are no function symbols, constants or counting quantifiers. Only x and y may appear as variables, but quantifiers can bind and reuse them at arbitrary nesting depth. All Boolean connectives and ordinary existential and universal quantifiers are permitted. Equality has its usual interpretation.

A model is any nonempty structure in which T satisfies: for all elements a,b,c, T(a,b) and T(b,c) imply T(a,c). This semantic restriction may use three elements even though the input sentence has two variables. Reflexivity, irreflexivity, antisymmetry and totality are not required. All other predicates are unrestricted. The question is whether a total Turing machine can decide existence of such a model for every input sentence; neither model size nor running time is bounded. An infinite model is a valid witness even if no finite model exists.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked decision algorithm for unrestricted satisfiability or prove undecidability. Deciding only existence of finite models, or only sentences with guarded existential witnesses, does not meet this target.

title: Perfect matching in NC
summary: Perfect matching seeks pairwise disjoint edges that cover every vertex of a graph. The question asks for a deterministic parallel algorithm on general graphs with polynomially many processors and polylogarithmic running time. Sequential polynomial-time algorithms do not supply this bound because their matching updates may depend on earlier choices. General graphs also contain odd cycles, which require coordination beyond the constraints that suffice in bipartite graphs. The saved card distinguishes this target from the nearby bipartite advance and asks whether compatible matching decisions can be organized efficiently in parallel without randomness.
formal: Do there exist constants \(C,a,b>0\) and a logspace-uniform family of Boolean circuits which, on the adjacency matrix of every n-vertex simple undirected graph, output a perfect matching or correctly report that none exists, with at most \(C(n+2)^{a}\) gates and depth at most \(C(\log _{2}(n+2))^{b}\)?
definitions: The input is the \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix of a graph on \([n]\), with symmetry and zero diagonal promised. A perfect matching is a set of edges with exactly one edge incident to each vertex. Output is a flag and an \(n\times n\) binary incidence matrix for the chosen matching; when the flag reports nonexistence the remaining output bits are ignored. The empty graph has the empty perfect matching. Circuits use fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\), fan-in-one NOT, constants 0,1 and unrestricted fan-out. Depth counts gates on the longest input-output path and size counts gates; the \(n^{2}\) output positions are specified as part of the description. A deterministic Turing transducer on unary input \(1^{n}\) writes the description using \(O(\log _{2}(n+2))\) work bits, with read-only input and write-only output. Constants and generator are fixed across n; every valid input must receive an exact answer. No randomness, oracle, advice, bipartiteness or other structural graph promise is supplied.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of the stated logspace-uniform polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth search circuits on all simple undirected graphs, or prove that no such family exists. A negative answer rules out every fixed choice of the size and depth exponents and constants. An algorithm only for bipartite graphs, or one using quasipolynomial circuit size or catalytic auxiliary memory, does not meet the specified positive criterion.

title: Distributed Lovász Local Lemma in \(O(\log  \log  n)\) rounds
summary: The distributed Lovasz Local Lemma seeks an assignment avoiding many bad events, each depending on only a bounded number of other events. Processors know local portions of this dependency structure and communicate in synchronous LOCAL rounds. The question asks for \(O(\log  \log  n)\) rounds with high probability when the dependency degree is constant and the probability criterion has sufficiently strong constant polynomial slack. The guarantee must bound the worst finishing time over all nodes. An algorithm that achieves only a small average finishing time would leave the central coordination issue unresolved for the last remaining bad events.
formal: Does there exist an integer \(c\ge 2\) such that, for every fixed integer \(d\ge2\), a uniform randomized LOCAL algorithm \(A_{d}\) and a constant \(K_{d}\) solve every n-event variable Lovász Local Lemma instance of dependency degree at most d and maximum bad-event probability p with \(p\cdot d^{c}<1/2\), within \(K_{d}(1+\log _{2}\log _{2}(n+2))\) rounds, with probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\) of avoiding all bad events simultaneously?
definitions: There are \(n\ge 2\) bad events, each a predicate on a specified finite subset of finitely many mutually independent variables. Each variable has a finite nonempty alphabet and a rational probability distribution; event predicates and distributions are given by finite tables. Variables occurring in no event can be omitted. Two distinct event nodes are adjacent exactly when their variable sets intersect; this graph is the communication network. Its maximum degree is at most d. The number p is the largest probability of an event under the product of the specified distributions. Each node initially knows n,d, its own event table, its variables and their distributions, its neighbours and their identifiers. Node identifiers are distinct integers in \([n^{2}]\); shared variables have consistent names. Use [synchronous LOCAL rounds](definitions.html#distributed-rounds) with unrestricted terminating local computation. Nodes have private independent fair random bits. A single finite program is used at all nodes, independently of n and the instance. Each node outputs one value for each of its variables. Success requires agreement on shared variables and falsity of every event. The round bound holds on every random tape; the success probability is over all node coins for each fixed instance and identifier assignment. Constants and the algorithm may depend on d; the slack exponent c is chosen before d. No preprocessing using the full instance is supplied. The factor \(1/2\) removes the low-degree ambiguity recorded in the source conjecture.
answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed integer \(c\ge 2\) admits, for every fixed \(d\ge 2\), algorithms \(A_{d}\) and constants \(K_{d}\) with the stated round and global-success bounds on all eligible instances. Alternatively, prove that for every candidate c there is a fixed d for which no such algorithm and constant exist. An obstruction at one slack exponent alone does not refute the existential choice of c. Bounds averaged over nodes, expected round bounds, or a higher fixed power of log log n do not meet the stated guarantee.

title: One-cycle versus two-cycles conjecture
summary: The input graph is promised to be one large cycle or two equal-sized cycles. Its edge list is spread across machines with sublinear local memory and linear total memory. Machines can exchange arbitrary coded messages with any other machines, subject to per-round volume limits. The conjecture requires logarithmically many rounds for every uniform high-probability algorithm in this model. The identical local degrees and edge counts make the global arrangement of the components the essential information.
formal:
Is the following conjecture true? For every fixed sublinear local-memory exponent \(0<\delta<1\), every uniform randomized MPC algorithm \(A\) that distinguishes a single cycle of length \(n\) from two disjoint cycles of length \(n/2\), with high probability and linear total memory as specified below, requires \(\Omega(\log n)\) worst-case synchronous rounds. More precisely, for every fixed positive integer confidence parameter \(h\), there must be constants \(c_{A,h}>0\) and \(n_{A,h}\) such that
\[T_A(n,h)\ge c_{A,h}\log_2 n\]
for every even \(n\ge n_{A,h}\). Correctness has probability at least \(1-n^{-h}\) on each promised graph and every admissible initial placement of its edge list.
definitions:
The input is an edge list of a simple undirected graph with vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), for even \(n\ge6\). It is promised to consist either of one cycle through all \(n\) vertices or of exactly two disjoint cycles, each through \(n/2\) vertices. Every edge appears once as its pair of endpoints; the orientation of that pair and list order are arbitrary. Both cases have exactly \(n\) edges and degree two at every vertex. The vertex names carry no order around a cycle. Inputs outside the promise impose no correctness requirement.

Here is a fixed finite-word version of linear-total-space MPC. For a fixed \(\delta\), use \(p(n)=\lceil n^{1-\delta}\rceil\) machines, indexed from one to \(p(n)\). For each fixed \(h\), the algorithm may choose constants \(K_h\ge4\) and an integer \(B_h\ge2\), independent of \(n\). A word has \(B_h\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits. Each machine can store at most \(K_h\lceil n^\delta\rceil\) words, including its input, work state and communication buffers. Thus the sum of memory capacities is \(O(n)\) words for fixed \(h,\delta\). Initially each edge record is placed on one machine, and every placement fitting these local capacities is allowed. Other mutable memory is initially blank. Each machine knows \(n,p(n),h\) and its own index; fixed model parameters are part of the program.

Each synchronous round allows arbitrary finite local computation within that memory and communication with arbitrary other machines. Each machine sends at most \(K_h\lceil n^\delta\rceil\) words in total and receives at most that many; words may encode arbitrary information rather than whole graph records. Recipient addresses count as part of the communicated data. The algorithm must respect both send and receive bounds on every promised input and every random tape. Messages arrive before the next round. Local computation must terminate but has no time bound. Machines have private independent fair random bits and may additionally use a common read-only fair random tape; random bits retained for later use occupy memory. There is no further advice or oracle.

All machines execute one finite program with their indices as input. The program is uniform over \(n,h\); it can depend on the fixed exponent. It suffices to quantify over rational \(\delta\in(0,1)\), so all machine counts and capacity bounds are effectively specified: any fixed smaller real exponent is dominated by a rational exponent below one, and a lower bound for every rational exponent covers it. Constants in the resource bounds may depend on the program and fixed confidence parameter, but not on the input or placement.

Machine one must eventually output ONE or TWO. On every promised input and placement, the output must be correct with probability at least \(1-n^{-h}\), jointly over all random bits. No machine may exceed the resource bounds even on a tape leading to an incorrect answer. Let \(T_A(n,h)\) be the supremum of the number of synchronous rounds until this output, over all promised inputs with exactly \(n\) vertices, all initial placements and all random tapes. Eligible algorithms have finite \(T_A(n,h)\) for each \(n,h\). The target is a worst-case round bound, not expected time.

High probability means that every fixed positive integer \(h\) can be requested as an input parameter; integer parameters also imply every fixed real failure exponent. The lower-bound constants may depend on \(h,\delta,A\). No component-stability, comparison-only or indivisible-record restriction is imposed. In particular, graph distance does not bound the distance a message can travel between machines.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the universal logarithmic lower bound or of its full negation. A uniform \(o(\log n)\)-round algorithm for one fixed \(\delta<1\), with the stated correctness and space bounds for every fixed confidence parameter, suffices to refute it. The literal negation can also be witnessed by failure of the eventual lower bound along an unbounded subsequence; a refutation need not be little-o at every size. A bound only for restricted encodings, component-stable algorithms, geometric embeddings or larger total memory does not prove the stated conjecture.

title: Explicit superconstant lower bounds in the congested clique
summary: Can a graph predicate that is easy to compute centrally require a number of congested-clique rounds tending to infinity? Each processor initially knows its incident graph edges and can send a different logarithmic-size message to every other processor in each round. Only one decision bit is required, and local computation is unrestricted. Known hard-function counting and hierarchy arguments do not provide the required centrally polynomial-time predicate. Broadcast bounds and the known two-round MST limitation do not resolve this unicast one-bit target.
formal: Does there exist a Boolean predicate \(P\) of finite simple undirected graphs on \([n]\), decidable from the full adjacency matrix by one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, such that every uniform deterministic unicast congested-clique algorithm computing \(P\) has worst-case round complexity \(R_{A}(n)=\omega (1)\)? Only node 1 is required to output the decision bit, and the input, bandwidth and limiting convention are fixed below.
definitions: For each \(n\ge 2\), the communication network is the complete graph on processors \(1,\ldots ,n\). The input is a separate simple undirected graph G on the same labeled vertex set. Initially processor v knows n, its identifier v and the \(n- 1\) adjacency bits for edges incident to v in G. No other input or certificate is supplied. In a synchronous round every processor performs a finite, otherwise unrestricted amount of local deterministic computation and sends a separate message of at most \(\operatorname{ceil}(\log _{2} n)\) bits to each other processor; all messages arrive before the next round. Local memory is unrestricted. All processors execute one fixed finite algorithm with their identifiers and n as inputs; no nonuniform advice, randomness, oracle or free communication is allowed. The cost counts communication rounds only, not local computation. Node 1 must halt with \(P(G)\) on every input; requiring all nodes to receive this one bit changes the cost by at most one round. \(R_{A}(n)\) is the maximum number of rounds until node 1 outputs, over all n-vertex input graphs. The statement \(R_{A}(n)=\omega (1)\) means that for every integer \(B\ge 1\) there is N such that \(R_{A}(n)>B\) for every \(n\ge N\); it is stronger than a lower bound at only infinitely many sizes. The chosen predicate may depend on vertex labels, as in Korhonen–Suomela’s graph-language model. “Explicit” is fixed by the source proposal’s centralized polynomial-time condition: one deterministic Turing machine computes P on every adjacency matrix within \(C(n+1)^{k}\) steps for constants C,k independent of n. There is no polynomial bound imposed on processors’ local work. A constant multiple of log n message bits can be simulated by a constant factor more rounds and does not change the \(\omega (1)\) target.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a single graph predicate with a proved centralized polynomial-time decision procedure and proves the displayed \(\omega (1)\) lower bound against every correct uniform deterministic protocol in the specified model. A negative resolution proves the logical negation of that existence statement. A two-round lower bound, a lower bound for broadcast messages or restricted local computation, or a hard predicate without the centralized polynomial-time guarantee does not settle the target.

title: Sublogarithmic distributed MIS
summary: Vertices must choose a maximal independent set using only communication along graph edges. The LOCAL model allows arbitrarily long messages and unlimited finite local computation. The question asks for a randomized round count that is little-o of the logarithm of the graph size. Success must hold jointly with arbitrarily high fixed polynomial confidence on every graph and identifier assignment. Recent algorithms handle graphs without short cycles, while the unrestricted graph case remains the selected target.
formal:
Does there exist one uniform classical randomized LOCAL algorithm \(A\), taking a positive integer confidence parameter \(h\), such that for every fixed \(h\ge1\), on every \(n\)-vertex simple undirected graph with \(n\ge2\), its vertex outputs form a maximal independent set with probability at least \(1-n^{-h}\), and its worst-case elapsed round count \(T_A(n,h)\) satisfies
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{T_A(n,h)}{\log_2 n}=0?
\]
The guarantee ranges over all degrees, all valid distinct identifier assignments and all port numberings. Local computation, storage and message lengths are unrestricted; vertices have private random bits and may know \(n\) and the maximum degree.
definitions:
The network is the input finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\); disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are included. Vertex \(v\) eventually outputs a bit \(b_v\). Set \(I=\{v:b_v=1\}\). Independence requires that no edge have both endpoints in \(I\), and maximality requires that every vertex outside \(I\) have a neighbor in \(I\). Maximal does not mean maximum cardinality. For the one-vertex graph the algorithm must output its vertex, without an asymptotic restriction beyond finite time.

Vertices have pairwise distinct identifiers in \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\). Each vertex initially knows its own identifier, its degree, the identifiers of its neighbors, the exact \(n\), the exact maximum degree \(\Delta\), and \(h\). An arbitrary port numbering bijectively labels each vertex's incident edges by the integers from one to its degree. The two endpoints need not give an edge the same port number. Knowing neighbors initially instead of after an identifier-exchange round changes the count by at most one round and does not change the little-o target.

The LOCAL model runs in synchronous rounds. Each vertex can send a different finite binary message of arbitrary length along each incident edge, with messages delivered before the next round. There are no other channels, graph preprocessing, advice strings or shared random tape. Each vertex runs the same finite program with its own sequence of independent fair random bits. Local storage and intermediate computation are unbounded but must be finite and terminate on every random tape between rounds. The program is uniform over \(n,\Delta,h\) and vertex identifiers. After a vertex emits its output it may send fixed dummy messages until all vertices have finished.

For fixed \(n,h\), \(T_A(n,h)\) is the supremum of the number of elapsed rounds until all outputs are available, over every graph with exactly \(n\) vertices, identifiers, ports and random tapes. This supremum must be finite. The displayed success probability concerns the entire output labeling simultaneously on each particular input, not each vertex separately. The time guarantee holds even on tapes on which the output is wrong.

The limit means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) and every fixed integer \(h\ge1\), some \(n_0\) has \(T_A(n,h)\le\varepsilon\log_2n\) for every \(n\ge n_0\). The threshold may depend on \(h,\varepsilon\) and the program, but not on the graph, degrees or identifiers. Positive integer confidence parameters suffice for every requested real constant failure exponent. No common bound uniform in unbounded \(h\) is required. This explicit confidence-input convention realizes the saved high-probability requirement.

A bound on awake rounds, expected rounds, node-average rounds, or graphs avoiding short cycles is not the all-input worst-case elapsed-round bound in the question.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of such a uniform algorithm, including maximality, joint success probability and the little-o limit for every fixed confidence parameter; or prove the negation of this existential statement in the specified model. A lower bound for a restricted algorithmic technique, a sublogarithmic bound only for some graph classes, or a merely expected-time bound does not settle the target.

title: Logarithmic-round deterministic maximal independent set
summary: The vertices of an arbitrary graph must deterministically choose a maximal independent set. They can exchange unlimited finite messages along edges, but their identifiers may be adversarial. The target is a number of rounds bounded by one constant times the logarithm of the graph size. The guarantee must hold uniformly over all degrees and identifier assignments. Known polylogarithmic algorithms and nearly logarithmic lower bounds leave this sharper upper-bound milestone open in the checked sources.
formal:
Do there exist one uniform deterministic LOCAL algorithm \(A\) and an absolute constant \(C>0\) such that on every finite nonempty simple undirected graph with \(n\) vertices, and every valid identifier assignment and port numbering, all vertices output the membership bits of a maximal independent set within
\[C\log_2(n+2)\]
synchronous communication rounds? Vertices may know \(n\) and the maximum degree. No random bits are available, and the constant is independent of graph degree.
definitions:
The network is the input graph \(G=(V,E)\), which can be disconnected and can have isolated vertices. Its maximum degree \(\Delta\) may be any integer from zero to \(n-1\). A set \(I\subseteq V\) is independent if no edge has both endpoints in \(I\). It is maximal if every vertex outside \(I\) has a neighbor in \(I\). This is inclusion maximality, not maximum cardinality. Each vertex outputs exactly one bit indicating its own membership, and the joint labeling must satisfy both conditions on every instance.

Identifiers are arbitrary pairwise distinct integers from \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\). At a vertex of degree \(d\), its incident edges receive distinct local ports \(1,\ldots,d\); port numbers at the two endpoints need not agree. Initially a vertex knows its own identifier, its degree and ports, the identifiers of its neighbors, the exact \(n\) and the exact \(\Delta\). Supplying neighbor identifiers initially saves at most the one round required to exchange them.

In each LOCAL round every vertex may perform an arbitrary finite deterministic local computation and send a separate finite binary message to each neighbor. The message lengths and local working memory are unrestricted. Messages arrive before the next round. Communication is possible only along graph edges; there is no centralized graph preprocessing, shared memory, nonuniform advice or external oracle. Every local computation terminates. All vertices execute one finite program independent of the graph size, with the listed information as input.

A halted vertex has fixed its output and may subsequently send dummy messages. The round count is elapsed synchronous time until all vertices have output, not the sum of their work or a count of active rounds. The displayed bound includes all graphs, identifiers, ports and degrees simultaneously. The use of \(\log_2(n+2)\) handles the one-vertex case; after changing the constant it is equivalent to an eventual \(O(\log n)\) guarantee on \(n\ge2\).

For a correct algorithm \(A\), let \(T_A(n)\) be the largest elapsed round count on the allowed instances of exactly \(n\) vertices. The question is \(\exists A\,\exists C>0\,\forall n\ge1:T_A(n)\le C\log_2(n+2)\). Its negation must exclude every correct uniform deterministic program, not merely algorithms using a particular decomposition or rounding method.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction and analysis of a correct uniform deterministic algorithm with the displayed bound, or a proof of the full negation. A polylogarithmic bound with exponent greater than one, a randomized algorithm, a degree-dependent constant, or a result restricted to a special graph family is insufficient.

title: Almost-linear-work parallel exact maximum flow
summary: The task is exact maximum flow in an arbitrary directed graph with polynomially bounded integer capacities. Every arc must receive an explicit integral flow value, and the entire output must be correct with probability at least two thirds. The desired uniform parallel algorithm has almost-linear total work and subpolynomial depth on every execution. Recent DAG reductions and dense-instance algorithms clarify the problem without supplying this simultaneous endpoint. A complete Lean-checked answer must meet both resource bounds for every fixed polynomial capacity range, without restricting the graph family.
formal:
For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), do there exist one uniform randomized priority-CRCW PRAM algorithm \(A_a\), constants \(C_a\ge1\) and \(B_a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge a+3}\), and a function \(h_a:\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\to[1,\infty)\) with
\[
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\log h_a(N)}{\log N}=0,
\]
such that the following holds? On every explicitly given directed graph with \(n\ge2\) vertices, \(m\) arcs, distinct terminals \(s,t\), and integral capacities \(0\le u_e\le n^a\), the algorithm outputs an exact integral maximum flow with probability at least \(2/3\), and every execution satisfies
\[
 W\le C_a(m+n)h_a(m+n),\qquad
 D\le C_a h_a(m+n).
\]
Here \(W\) is total work and \(D\) is parallel depth in the word model below. In asymptotic notation the requested simultaneous bounds are \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) work and \((m+n)^{o(1)}\) depth.
definitions:
The vertex set is \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Input memory contains \(n,m,s,t\) and an explicit ordered array of arcs \(E\), each with its two endpoint labels and integer capacity. There are no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. The range is \(0\le m\le n(n-1)\), and isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and zero capacities are permitted. No planarity, acyclicity, density or expansion promise is assumed. The fixed integer \(a\) specifies the admitted capacity regime and may be built into the program.

A feasible output is an integer \(f_e\) for every original arc, in input order, such that \(0\le f_e\le u_e\) and
\[
 \sum_{(v,z)\in E}f_{(v,z)}=
 \sum_{(z,v)\in E}f_{(z,v)}
 \quad(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}).
\]
Its value is outgoing flow minus incoming flow at \(s\). It must maximize that value over all feasible flows. Integral capacities admit an integral maximum flow. Any maximizing flow is acceptable, but the entire arc vector must be output explicitly. A maximum-flow value, a cut or an implicit flow alone is not the required output. If no positive flow is possible, the exact optimum is zero.

The computational model is a synchronous parallel random-access machine with shared memory and priority concurrent reads and writes (priority CRCW PRAM). Simultaneous reads of one cell are allowed. If multiple processors try to write one cell in a round, the lowest-index writer succeeds. Each active processor executes at most one word-RAM instruction per round, using its own local registers and the shared memory. Processor identifiers and memory addresses are word values. Processors follow one finite program with their identifiers available; there is no input-length advice or precomputed table. Processor activation and all program-controlled initialization count as work; a hidden computation cannot be assigned to an uncharged processor. Initially only the explicit input and fixed machine constants are present, and unused memory and registers are zero.

Words have length
\[
 w=B_a\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil.
\]
Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, copying, comparisons, branches, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. A shift by at least \(w\) positions returns zero. Each processor may generate a fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit word in one instruction; all such random words are mutually independent. Operations on longer integers are implemented by multiple charged instructions. There are no unit-cost arbitrary-precision arithmetic operations or real-number oracles. The chosen \(B_a\) must accommodate every processor identifier and address used by the algorithm.

Work \(W\) is the sum of all executed processor instructions, including activation, input access, preprocessing, random generation and output writes. Depth \(D\) is the number of synchronous rounds until the complete output is available. Both resource bounds must hold on every execution, including executions returning an incorrect answer. Correctness means that the whole vector is feasible and exactly optimal, with probability at least \(2/3\) over the machine's coins for each fixed input. The success probability is not averaged over graphs, and resources are not merely bounded in expectation. Deterministic algorithms are allowed as a special case.

The program, word constant, multiplicative constant and overhead function may depend on \(a\), but not on the graph, its input ordering or its capacities. One algorithm for the fixed \(a\) must achieve the asymptotic bounds over all sizes. In particular, for every \(\delta>0\), its work is eventually at most \((m+n)^{1+\delta}\) and its depth at most \((m+n)^\delta\), after increasing a size threshold depending only on \(a,\delta\). Allowing a different algorithm for each \(\delta\) would be a different claim. The overhead function is an analytic bound, not advice supplied to the machine.

Subpolynomial depth is the requested target; polylogarithmic depth would suffice but is not required. The same computation must have almost-linear total work. An algorithm with small depth and polynomially more work, or with almost-linear work and a fixed positive power of \(n\) in its depth, does not meet the simultaneous endpoint. Using \(m+n\) accounts explicitly for the vertex set even when the graph contains few arcs.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence claim or its logical negation.

A positive answer must cover every fixed capacity exponent \(a\), with a uniform algorithm for that exponent, the simultaneous worst-case work and depth bounds, and the per-input probability of an exact explicit integral maximum flow. A result with stronger bounds also qualifies if it supplies this full output and model guarantee.

A negative answer must prove that for at least one fixed \(a\) no admissible algorithm and constants satisfy the target. A conditional obstruction, a lower bound for one algorithmic framework, or a difficulty confined to a more demanding capacity model does not establish the unconditional negation. An approximation algorithm, a restricted graph-family result, or a reduction to another task alone is insufficient unless the remaining task is also solved with the required resources.

title: Optimal exact single-source shortest paths in CONGEST
summary: Single-source shortest paths asks every vertex to learn its exact distance from one source in a weighted network. In CONGEST, each edge carries only a logarithmic number of bits per communication round. The target is a randomized algorithm using roughly \(\sqrt{n}\) plus the hop diameter D rounds, ignoring polylogarithmic factors. The graph is undirected and connected, with nonnegative polynomially bounded integer edge weights. Achieving this bound would combine global distance propagation with the bandwidth limits of the network at the scale identified by the saved problem statement.
formal: For every fixed integer \(b\ge 1\), do there exist constants \(K,c>0\) and a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm which, on every connected simple undirected graph with \(n\ge 2\) vertices, integer edge weights in \([0,n^{b}]\) and a designated source s, makes every vertex output its exact weighted distance from s in at most \(K(\sqrt{n}+D)(\log _{2}(n+2))^{c}\) rounds on every execution, with simultaneous correctness probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\)? Here D is the diameter of the unweighted graph.
definitions: A path length is the sum of its edge weights; the distance is the minimum path length, and the source distance is zero. D is the maximum over vertex pairs of the minimum number of edges on a path between them. The graph itself is the [CONGEST network](definitions.html#distributed-rounds). In each synchronous round, each endpoint of each edge can send at most \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits to the other endpoint, for a constant B depending only on b. Nodes initially know n,b, the source identifier, their own identifiers, and the identifiers and weights of incident neighbours. Identifiers are distinct integers in \([n^{2}]\). Local computation and memory are unrestricted, but each local computation between rounds terminates. Nodes use independent private fair random bits. One finite program, allowed to depend on b, runs at all nodes; no global graph description, advice, routing tables or preprocessing is supplied. The graph, weights, source and identifiers are fixed before randomness is drawn. Output at v is an ordinary binary integer for \(\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\), stored locally. The guarantee concerns all vertices together, over all coins. All communication, including finding termination and any preprocessing, counts in the round bound. K,c,B are independent of n,D and the instance; no value of D is initially supplied.
answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed weight exponent b there is a single uniform algorithm meeting the stated \(O((\sqrt{n}+D)\operatorname{polylog} n)\) round bound on every execution and the simultaneous \(1- n^{- 3}\) correctness probability on every eligible network. Alternatively, prove that this is impossible for at least one fixed b, for every choice of algorithm and fixed constants K,c,B. An approximation guarantee, an \(n^{o(1)}\) overhead not bounded by a fixed power of log n, or a result for only one diameter regime is not the stated affirmative answer.

title: Directed reachability with nearly linear memory and polylogarithmic passes
summary: Directed reachability in a stream asks whether one vertex can reach another when graph edges arrive in an adversarial order. Nearly linear memory in the vertex count cannot store every edge of a dense graph. The question asks for a randomized algorithm using only polylogarithmically many passes and n times a polylogarithmic number of memory bits. Simple repeated scans can propagate reachability one step at a time, taking many passes on badly ordered paths. The project is to combine a small memory footprint with far fewer scans without relying on favorable edge order.
formal: Do there exist constants a,b,C and a uniform randomized streaming algorithm that decides directed s–t reachability on every n-vertex graph using at most \(Cn(\log (n+2))^{a}\) bits of memory and \(C(\log (n+2))^{b}\) passes, with success probability at least \(2/3\) for every adversarially ordered edge stream?
definitions: The input is a finite simple directed graph on the labelled vertex set \([n], n\ge 2\), with distinct designated vertices s,t. The algorithm knows n,s,t before reading the edges. Each directed edge occurs once in an insertion-only stream, in an arbitrary order fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits. Each pass scans this same stream in the same forward order. The input is read-only: there are no adjacency queries, random-access reads, sorting operations on external storage, or writable auxiliary streams. All mutable working storage counts toward the bit bound; fresh independent random bits may be read from a one-way random source. The memory and pass bounds hold on every execution. Computation between successive input items is unrestricted but must terminate; no running-time bound beyond termination is imposed. A yes answer means that there is a directed path from s to t in the input graph. The constants and algorithm are independent of n, the graph, and the edge order.
answer_criterion: Prove that one uniform randomized decision algorithm has simultaneous \(O(n \log ^{a}(n+2))\)-bit space and \(O(\log ^{b}(n+2))\)-pass bounds for fixed constants a,b on every execution, and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every fixed graph and edge order. Alternatively, prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. Ruling out a fixed pass count, requiring the output of a path, or restricting computation between stream items does not establish the stated negation.

title: Depth-first search in NC
summary: A depth-first-search forest records the parent choices of recursive graph exploration. For an undirected graph, it is a rooted spanning forest in which every graph edge joins a vertex to one of its ancestors. The problem asks for a deterministic, uniformly specified parallel computation that constructs any such forest with polynomial resources and polylogarithmic depth. Randomized NC algorithms and deterministic results for restricted graph classes are known, but those guarantees do not settle the general target. A solution would show whether this basic search structure can always be built efficiently in parallel without random choices.
formal: Does there exist a logspace-uniform family of deterministic Boolean circuits of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth that, on the adjacency matrix of every finite simple undirected graph, outputs a valid depth-first-search forest? The roots and the order of visiting neighbors may be chosen freely for each input.
definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) the input is the \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-diagonal adjacency matrix of a graph G on \(V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). The output is a parent array \(p\in \{0,\ldots ,n\}^{n}\), with 0 denoting a root. If \(p(v)\ne 0\), require \(\{v,p(v)\}\in E(G)\); repeatedly taking parents must reach 0 from every vertex. These parent edges define a rooted forest, and each connected component of G must be spanned by one of its trees. A vertex u is an ancestor of v if u lies on the tree path from v to its root. The forest is a DFS forest if, for every edge \(\{u,v\}\in E(G)\), one endpoint is an ancestor of the other. For undirected graphs this is exactly the class of forests produced by recursive depth-first search under some choices of roots and neighbor orders. Encode each parent entry in \(\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Each circuit \(C_{n}\) has \(n^{2}\) input bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) output bits, uses AND and OR gates with at most two inputs and NOT gates with one input, and has size at most \(O(n^{c})\) and depth at most \(O((\log _{2}(n+2))^{k})\), for fixed constants c,k independent of n and G. Logspace uniformity means that one deterministic Turing machine, given \(1^{n}\), writes the description of \(C_{n}\) while using \(O(\log (n+2))\) working space, excluding its read-only input and write-only output tapes. Correctness is required on every valid adjacency matrix; behavior on other bit strings is unrestricted. The empty graph has the empty output. No randomness or input-length-specific advice is supplied. NC here refers to computing a valid encoded output, rather than deciding a Boolean language.
answer_criterion: Construct one circuit family satisfying all the stated correctness, uniformity, size and depth requirements, or prove that no such family exists. The output may be any valid DFS forest. A randomized algorithm, a quasipolynomial-size circuit family, an algorithm only for a restricted graph class, or a lower bound for one prescribed traversal order does not settle this question.

title: Two-dimensional sandpile prediction in NC
summary: A stable rectangular array contains at most three grains at each cell and is surrounded by an infinite empty lattice. Adding one grain triggers simultaneous topplings, each sending one grain in each of the four cardinal directions. The question asks whether a specified cell ever topples, without giving a time bound in the input. The desired computation uses one uniform family of polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth Boolean circuits on the full explicit input. Known results for other dimensions, weighted grids, boundary sinks or alternating update schemes do not settle this precisely specified planar question.
formal: Is the language \(\mathrm{SP}_2\) defined below in logspace-uniform \(\mathrm{NC}\)? An instance explicitly supplies a finite stable rectangular array of sand grains and cells \(p,q\) inside that rectangle. Extend the array by zero to all of \(\mathbb Z^2\), add one grain at \(p\), and accept exactly when \(q\) eventually topples under the simultaneous four-neighbor rule. The question concerns one uniform circuit family with polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth for all input lengths.
definitions:
Let \(W,H\ge1\), let \(B=\{0,\ldots,W-1\}\times\{0,\ldots,H-1\}\), let \(c:B\to\{0,1,2,3\}\), and let \(p=(p_x,p_y),q=(q_x,q_y)\in B\). Define \(\bar c(v)=c(v)\) on \(B\) and \(\bar c(v)=0\) elsewhere in \(\mathbb Z^2\). Set \(c_0(v)=\bar c(v)+\mathbf1_{\{v=p\}}\). With
\[
E=\{(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)\},
\]
define, for every integer \(t\ge0\) and every \(v\in\mathbb Z^2\),
\[
c_{t+1}(v)=c_t(v)-4\mathbf1_{\{c_t(v)\ge4\}}+
\sum_{e\in E}\mathbf1_{\{c_t(v-e)\ge4\}}.
\]
Here \(\mathbf1_A\) is \(1\) when assertion \(A\) holds and \(0\) otherwise. Every unstable cell topples once per simultaneous round; its threshold and the number of grains sent to each neighbor are fixed. The required output is \(1\) exactly when \(\exists t\ge0:\ c_t(q)\ge4\). All cells outside the supplied rectangle participate in the same dynamics. There is no absorbing boundary, periodic identification, missing neighbor or cell-dependent weight.

For a nonnegative integer \(z\), let \(s(z)\) be its ordinary binary expansion without leading zeros, using \(s(0)=0\), and let \(b(z)=|s(z)|\). Encode \(z\) as \(1^{b(z)}0s(z)\). A valid binary input is the concatenation of these codes for \(W,H,p_x,p_y,q_x,q_y\), followed by exactly \(2WH\) bits encoding the entries of \(c\): list rows in increasing \(y\), and within each row increasing \(x\), using \(00,01,10,11\) for \(0,1,2,3\). Dimensions must be positive and the encoded coordinates must belong to \(B\). Strings not meeting these conditions are rejected. Let \(N\) be the complete binary string length, including all array entries. Extra zero rows or columns are permitted, but their entries still count; this is not a sparse or succinct configuration encoding.

Membership in logspace-uniform \(\mathrm{NC}\) means that there exist fixed integers \(a,k\ge1\), a fixed real \(K\ge1\), and a deterministic finite Turing-machine program generating a Boolean circuit \(C_N\) from the unary input \(1^N\), for every \(N\ge0\). It must halt, use at most \(K\log_2(N+2)\) work-tape cells, and write an explicit gate-and-wire description to a write-only output tape. Its input tape is read-only. The circuit has \(N\) input bits and one output, uses AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates of fan-in one and constants \(0,1\), has at most \(K(N+2)^a\) gates and depth at most \(K(\log_2(N+2))^k\), and decides \(\mathrm{SP}_2\) exactly on all length-\(N\) strings. Gate descriptions use binary indices in topological order and specify the output gate. There is no advice or oracle. The constants, circuit generator and gate basis are independent of the instance. Randomized error is not allowed; no time \(t\) is supplied as part of the instance.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of membership of this language in the specified uniform circuit class, or a complete Lean proof that no such circuit family and generator exist. Polynomial sequential simulation alone is insufficient. A proof of P-completeness under logspace reductions would imply nonmembership only with the additional assumption that P differs from NC; it is not an unconditional negative answer.

title: Optimal measurements and near-linear decoding for universal ℓ₂/ℓ₁ sparse recovery
summary: A fixed matrix compresses every real signal to a short vector of linear measurements. The decoder must work for all signals with error controlled by the best k-sparse ℓ₁ tail divided by √k. The conjecture combines O(k log(en/k)) measurements with near-linear deterministic decoding. The arithmetic model permits input-independent polynomial preprocessing but charges decoding accesses. Faster results with an ℓ₁ reconstruction error or only per-input randomized success do not meet this target.
formal: Do there exist absolute constants \(C,B>0\), \(a\geq0\), and a deterministic recovery scheme such that, for every \(n\geq1\) and \(1\leq k\leq n\), one fixed matrix \(A_{n,k}\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(m\leq Bk\log_2(en/k)\) permits recovery from \(A_{n,k}x\) in at most \(Bn\log_2^a(n+2)\) operations, with \[\|x-\widehat x\|_2\leq \frac{C}{\sqrt{k}}\min_{z:\,|\operatorname{supp}(z)|\leq k}\|x-z\|_1\] simultaneously for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\)?
definitions: The support of a vector is the set of its nonzero coordinates; a vector is \(k\)-sparse if its support has size at most \(k\). The norms are \(\|v\|_1=\sum_i|v_i|\) and \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\). The minimum in the statement is the sum of absolute values outside the \(k\) largest-magnitude coordinates of \(x\); ties may be broken arbitrarily. The decoder receives \(n,k\), the exact real measurement vector \(y=A_{n,k}x\), and read-only access to the fixed description of the scheme. It receives neither \(x\) nor its support, and must output all \(n\) coordinates of \(\widehat x\). The output need not itself be sparse. Measurements are linear and selected independently of the unknown signal. We use the real-arithmetic model: real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero number, square root of a nonnegative number, comparison, and access to an addressed stored entry each cost one operation; ordinary integer index operations cost one as well. The decoder is one fixed algorithm, with polynomial-size read-only advice depending only on \(n,k\), including the matrix and any preprocessing data. Reading advice is charged. Advice generation and forming the original measurement vector are outside the requested decoding bound. No polynomial-time explicit matrix construction is required.
