Once the scheme is fixed its decoder is deterministic and the guarantee holds for all real signals; a matrix chosen by the probabilistic method is admissible only if a single fixed choice works for all signals. Constants, the polynomial advice exponent and the decoding exponent are independent of \(n,k,x\). Measurements are noiseless; no additional post-measurement perturbation is included.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked construction or existence proof of a scheme meeting both resource bounds and the universal mixed-norm error guarantee in the specified arithmetic model, or prove that no such scheme exists. A guarantee holding with high probability separately for each input, an ℓ₁/ℓ₁ error bound, or optimal row count with slower decoding is insufficient.

title: Fast merging of summaries for symmetric streaming computations
summary: The input statistic is a total Boolean function invariant under reordering the stream. A streaming program computes it using polylogarithmic memory and time per item. The selected question asks for equally efficient local summaries and merging on every binary aggregation tree. A known simulation preserves small space but can use superpolynomial merge time. The target excludes promise and randomness separations and does not require identical intermediate summaries.
formal: Does every total, order-invariant Boolean stream function computable deterministically in polylogarithmic space and polylogarithmic time per item also admit a deterministic summary scheme with polylogarithmic message size, working space, and time per merge, correct for every binary merge tree? The uniform families, input lengths and costs in this question are specified below.
definitions: For each integer \(N\geq2\), let \(f_N\) map every nonempty sequence over \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\) of length at most \(N\) to one bit. Totality means every such sequence is in its domain. Order invariance means permuting any sequence leaves its value unchanged; it is stronger than merely swapping two players. A streaming algorithm is one fixed deterministic program given \(N\) in binary, which starts with an initialized state, reads one item at a time, and produces \(f_N(x)\) when the stream ends. There must be constants \(B,c\), depending on the family but not \(N\), for which initialization, each update and final output take at most \(B\log^c(N+2)\) steps, and the stored state and temporary workspace use that many bits. A merge scheme consists of three fixed deterministic programs: a map \(\Phi_N\) from one item to a summary, a map \(\mu_N\) from two summaries to a summary, and a decoder \(\eta_N\) from a summary to a bit. Summaries may include their represented length. For every valid sequence and every rooted binary tree whose leaves are its items in any order, apply \(\Phi_N\) at the leaves, \(\mu_N\) at internal nodes and \(\eta_N\) at the root. The resulting bit must equal \(f_N(x)\). Intermediate summaries may depend on the tree; only the decoded answer must be invariant. Each message, workspace and invocation time is bounded by \(B_1\log^{c_1}(N+2)\), for constants depending on the family. Time means steps of a standard deterministic multitape Turing machine on binary representations; input and output tapes have the usual sequential access. The programs receive \(N\) and their local arguments, with no advice or precomputed data depending on \(N\). Both models are exact and deterministic. The conclusion is existence of a merge scheme for each streaming-computable family, not a promised efficient compiler from arbitrary program descriptions.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal simulation, including the time, memory and arbitrary-tree guarantees. Alternatively give a total symmetric family with a qualifying streaming algorithm and prove that no qualifying merge scheme exists. A slow merge procedure with short messages, a separation using a promise, or a private-randomness separation does not decide this specified question.

title: Wait-free exact FIFO queues in Common\(_{2}\)
summary: The question asks for an exact FIFO queue shared by any fixed finite number of processes. Every process may enqueue and dequeue, and each operation must finish in finitely many of its own steps despite other processes stopping. Only read/write registers and Test&Set bits are supplied. Relaxed queues and algorithms that merely guarantee system-wide progress do not meet this requirement. The checked 2026 impossibility concerns strong linearizability, so the ordinary Common\(_{2}\) question remains open in the cited sources.
formal: For every fixed number \(n\ge 2\) of asynchronous processes, is there a deterministic wait-free linearizable implementation of an initially empty, unbounded FIFO queue using only atomic read/write registers and atomic Test&Set bits? Every process may perform both Enqueue and Dequeue, repeatedly and in any order. The implementation must satisfy exact FIFO semantics in every execution, including executions with arbitrary delays and crashes. This is the source’s Common\(_{2}\) question; “some objects with consensus number two” is not a free choice of base types that could include the desired queue itself.
definitions: There are n sequential processes with distinct identifiers \(1,\ldots ,n\). Each invokes a new high-level operation only after its previous one returns. The scheduler interleaves atomic shared-memory steps arbitrarily; a process may stop forever at any point. A register stores a finite value and supports atomic Read and Write. A Test&Set object is a bit initially 0 whose atomic operation returns the old bit and sets it to 1; arbitrarily many initially fresh objects and registers are available. Private computation and storage are allowed. No bound on memory growth or on the number of operations in a history is imposed, but every performed step manipulates finitely represented data. No Compare&Swap, stronger atomic multi-object operation, or queue base object is supplied. Sequential queue state is a finite sequence of values from \(\{0,1\}^{*}\). \(Enqueue(v)\) appends a new occurrence of v and returns an acknowledgement. Dequeue removes and returns the first occurrence if one exists; otherwise it returns a distinguished EMPTY symbol outside the value set and leaves the queue empty. Equal values may be enqueued multiple times, but each enqueue occurrence may be removed only once. Linearizability means that each finite concurrent history can be completed by responses to some pending invocations and deletion of the others, so that its completed operations have a legal sequential FIFO order preserving each process’s order and real-time order: an operation that returns before another is invoked precedes it. Wait-freedom means that any invoked operation whose process continues taking steps returns after finitely many of that process’s own steps, regardless of other processes’ speeds or failures. No promise that another process will take a step is available. The algorithm may depend on the fixed n; the question does not require one implementation for infinitely many simultaneously participating processes. Common\(_{2}\) denotes types implementable for every finite n from registers and two-process-consensus power; the cited model paper states the queue question equivalently using Test&Set. Equal consensus numbers alone do not assert mutual implementability.
answer_criterion: Construct and prove correct such a deterministic implementation for every finite n, or prove impossibility for some finite n in this model. Both exact linearizability and individual wait-free progress are required. A lock-free implementation that permits starvation, a restriction on the number of enqueuers or dequeuers, duplicated removal of an occurrence, weak-empty responses, bounded histories, or a stronger atomic base type does not meet the target. An impossibility result only for strong linearizability does not rule out ordinary linearizability.

title: One-pass approximation scheme for random-order streaming matching
summary: Edges of an arbitrary fixed graph are presented in a uniformly random order. The algorithm sees the stream once and must retain a nearly maximum matching. The space target is nearly linear in vertices for each fixed accuracy. Existing constant-factor improvements do not constitute a full approximation scheme. The explicit accuracy dependence prevents confusing shrinking-error lower bounds with this target.
formal:
Is there one uniform randomized streaming algorithm, an integer \(c\ge0\) and a total computable function \(g:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to\mathbb N_{>0}\) with the following guarantee? For every \(n\ge1\), every simple undirected graph \(G\) on \([n]\), and every rational \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\), the algorithm takes \(\varepsilon\) as input and reads the edges once in uniformly random order. On every run it uses at most \(g(\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil)n(\log_2(n+2))^c\) working bits and returns a matching \(M\) of \(G\). Over the edge order and the algorithm’s coins,
\[\Pr\bigl[|M|\ge(1-\varepsilon)\nu(G)\bigr]\ge2/3.\]
definitions:
G is any fixed simple undirected graph on a known labelled vertex set [n]. Its m distinct edges arrive once each in a uniformly random permutation, independently of the algorithm’s coins. The adversary may choose G but not condition the stream order on those coins. The algorithm receives \(n\) in binary and the numerator and positive denominator of the reduced fraction \(\varepsilon\) on separate read-only binary inputs. It reads edges sequentially without rewinding, and outputs an actual edge set M after the final edge. A matching has no two edges sharing a vertex; \(\nu(G)\) is the largest matching cardinality.

Space includes stored edge endpoints, counters, retained random bits, and the final output buffer. The output must be a valid matching on every run; the approximation may fail with probability at most 1/3, over both permutation and internal randomness. All copies of the read-only parameters retained in working memory count toward the space bound. The program, the space coefficient function \(g\) and the logarithmic exponent \(c\) are fixed before the accuracy and graph are chosen. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) is demanded, and no processing-time target beyond termination is imposed. Thus the question is about space at each fixed positive accuracy, not an exact matching algorithm obtained by setting \(\varepsilon\) to 1/n at uniform near-linear cost.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof with one algorithm, one exponent \(c\) and one computable bound \(g\) satisfying the displayed guarantees on the entire domain, or prove the negation of that statement. A lower bound using a sequence \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon(n)\) must rule out the permitted dependence on \(\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\).

title: LOCAL coloring below square-root degree dependence
summary: A proper coloring with \(\Delta+1\) colors always exists for a graph of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\). The question asks whether a uniform deterministic LOCAL algorithm can find one in \(O(\Delta^{1/2-\varepsilon}+\log^* n)\) rounds for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). Any positive constant saving in the degree exponent qualifies, however small, and it must be independent of both graph size and degree. Processors must reduce a large identifier-based palette without causing conflicts among adjacent vertices acting simultaneously. Crossing the square-root degree barrier would improve local coordination while preserving the small dependence on total network size.
formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), one uniform deterministic LOCAL algorithm \(A\), and a constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every supplied integer degree bound \(\Delta\ge2\), and every finite simple undirected \(n\)-vertex graph of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\), the algorithm produces a proper vertex coloring with colors in \(\{1,\ldots,\Delta+1\}\) within
\[
C\bigl(\Delta^{1/2-\varepsilon}+\log^*n\bigr)
\]
synchronous communication rounds? The guarantee must hold for every assignment of distinct identifiers from \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\) and every local port numbering. All vertices know \(n\) and \(\Delta\); the same \(\varepsilon,A,C\) must work for all these inputs.
definitions:
The network is exactly the input graph. Graphs may be disconnected and may have isolated vertices, but have no loops, parallel edges, weights or additional structural promises. A supplied \(\Delta\) is any upper bound on all degrees, not necessarily the exact maximum. Proper coloring means that every vertex outputs one allowed color and the two endpoints of each edge output different colors. There is no demand that all colors be used.

Each vertex runs the same finite deterministic program, initially knowing its own identifier, its degree, the local names of its incident ports, and \(n,\Delta\). Port names bijectively number the incident edges at each vertex; names at opposite ends need not agree. The identifier range \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\) fixes the polynomial-ID convention explicitly. Identifiers may be assigned adversarially and may be used arithmetically; no order-invariance restriction is imposed. The initial state contains no global graph description, advice or preprocessing result.

In one synchronous LOCAL round, each vertex sends an arbitrary finite binary message along each incident edge, possibly a different message to each neighbor, and then receives all messages sent to it in that round. Local computation and memory are unbounded, but the program must complete its local steps and eventually output at every vertex. There is no bandwidth restriction, randomness, shared random tape or communication along nonedges. Initially exchanging neighbor identifiers, if needed, costs at most one round and is absorbed by the requested bound. Once all vertices have output, the coloring is final. Elapsed rounds to the last output are counted, rather than total messages, local work or average node time.

The function \(\log^*n\) counts successive base-two logarithms until the value is at most one. The fixed constant \(\varepsilon\) is chosen before all graph parameters. It is not an accuracy input; the task does not demand one algorithm for every requested saving. A saving that tends to zero as \(n\) or \(\Delta\) grows is insufficient. Constants hidden in the guarantee cannot depend on graph size, degree bound, port numbering or identifiers.

The target retains only an additive iterated-logarithmic dependence on graph size. A bound polynomial in \(\log n\), even if independent of \(\Delta\), does not establish it in all degree regimes. This is vertex coloring in deterministic LOCAL; results for edge coloring, randomized algorithms, special graph families or massively parallel computation have different guarantees.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of an algorithm and some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) meeting the stated uniform round bound, or of the logical negation of this existence statement. The improvement may be arbitrarily small but must be one positive constant independent of both \(n\) and \(\Delta\). A negative answer must rule out every positive constant exponent saving in the stated model. Improving a logarithmic factor while retaining degree exponent \(1/2\), or allowing the saving to tend to zero with input size, does not meet the target. There is no prescribed minimum saving and no numerical \(1/100\) answer tolerance for this proposition.

title: Full random walks with near-linear streaming space
summary: The problem asks for one entire random-walk trajectory in a directed graph presented as an edge stream. The start is known in advance, and the number of steps is at most the number of vertices. The output distribution must be within 1/100 in total variation of the true joint distribution of all visits. Near-linear bit space and a fixed polylogarithmic number of passes must suffice for every graph and edge order. Known constant-pass tradeoffs and improved dense-graph samplers do not settle this general target.
formal:
Can a randomized graph-streaming algorithm sample a whole \(L\)-step random walk, for every \(1\le L\le n\), with total-variation error at most \(1/100\), near-linear bit space and polylogarithmically many passes?

More precisely, do there exist one uniform algorithm \(A\), constants \(C_s,C_p>0\) and fixed nonnegative integers \(a,b\) with the following property? For every unweighted directed graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), every start \(s\), every \(1\le L\le n\) and every fixed ordering of its edges, \(A\), knowing \(n,L,s\) before reading the stream, uses at most
\[C_s n\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^a\text{ bits and }\left\lceil C_p\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^b\right\rceil\text{ passes}\]
and outputs a tuple \((Y_0,\ldots,Y_L)\) whose distribution \(\nu_{G,s,L}\) satisfies
\[\|\nu_{G,s,L}-\mu_{G,s,L}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le1/100?\]
Here \(\mu_{G,s,L}\) is the joint distribution of the ordinary directed random walk starting at \(s\), with the absorbing convention at a vertex of out-degree zero defined below.
definitions:
The graph has the known labeled vertex set \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(n\ge1\), and edge set \(E\subseteq V\times V\). There are no multiple copies of an edge; self-loops are allowed. Both directions between distinct vertices may be present independently. Every edge has unit weight. The stream explicitly lists each directed edge once as a binary pair, in an arbitrary fixed order. Empty streams, isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and graphs with highly unequal degrees are allowed. The number of edges need not be known in advance.

For a vertex \(v\), its out-neighbor set is \(N^+(v)=\{w:(v,w)\in E\}\) and its out-degree is \(d^+(v)=|N^+(v)|\). A true random walk starts with \(X_0=s\). At every step, conditional on the complete history so far, if \(d^+(X_i)>0\), then \(X_{i+1}\) is chosen uniformly from \(N^+(X_i)\). New choices are independent conditional on the successive current vertices. Repeated visits and repeated traversal of an edge are permitted; this is not a simple path.

At a vertex of out-degree zero, define \(X_{i+1}=X_i\). This absorbing convention ensures that a length-\(L\) tuple is defined for every input. It is equivalent to adding a self-loop only at each zero-out-degree vertex. The convention is stated explicitly rather than leaving a uniform choice from an empty set undefined. It does not replace directed transitions elsewhere by undirected ones or add restarts from another vertex.

Equivalently, define the transition probabilities \(K_G(v,w)\) as \(1/d^+(v)\) when \(d^+(v)>0\) and \((v,w)\in E\), as one when \(d^+(v)=0\) and \(w=v\), and as zero otherwise. The desired law on \(V^{L+1}\) is
\[\mu_{G,s,L}(v_0,\ldots,v_L)=\mathbf1_{\{v_0=s\}}\prod_{i=0}^{L-1}K_G(v_i,v_{i+1}).\]
The integer \(L\) counts transitions, so the output lists \(L+1\) vertices including the start. The parameters \(n,L,s\) are explicitly available before the first pass. Only one sampled trajectory is requested.

For distributions \(\mu,\nu\) on this finite tuple space, total variation means
\[\|\nu-\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\frac12\sum_{\omega\in V^{L+1}}|\nu(\omega)-\mu(\omega)|.\]
This compares the complete joint distributions, including dependencies between visits. Correct endpoint probabilities or correct single-time marginals alone do not establish the requirement. The output law averages over all internal random choices. The bound is not a probability that a numerical estimate is accurate, so a separate two-thirds-success convention is not substituted for it. Any probability assigned to an impossible trajectory is part of the total-variation error.

The algorithm returns an explicit tuple in \(V^{L+1}\), with initial vertex \(s\), after processing its passes. It must include every intermediate vertex, not just the endpoint, selected checkpoints, transition counts, a random seed or a program for reconstructing a longer object. The tuple may be assembled in working memory and then written to a final output tape. Its \(O(L\log(n+2))\) bits fit inside the allowed near-linear class because \(L\le n\); all working storage used to assemble it is counted.

A pass reads the full edge sequence from beginning to end. Between passes the algorithm may rewind and keep its working memory, but the sequence and its order remain the same. It cannot change the edge list, jump to an old edge, query an adjacency list or ask for a random neighbor except through computations on information acquired from the stream. There is no uncounted external scratch storage. This is an insertion-only arbitrary-order stream, not a randomly ordered or deletion stream.

Use one finite uniform randomized program for all parameter values. It may draw independent fair random bits. All mutable information counts toward bit space, including edge samples, labels, counters, retained randomness, intermediate structures and the assembled output. Old random choices can be reused only through information retained within that space. Pass and memory bounds hold on all executions. The algorithm must produce its tuple with probability one; no additional bound on local running time is imposed. The input graph and its edge ordering are fixed independently of the random choices.

The constants and logarithmic exponents in the statement do not depend on \(n,L,s,G\), its edge order or the random choices. Since \(L\le n\), a fixed polynomial in \(\log(n+2)\) and \(\log(L+2)\) is bounded by a fixed power of \(\log(n+2)\). Thus the displayed pass bound expresses the source's polylogarithmic target in the selected length range. In background bounds, \(\widetilde O\) and \(\widetilde\Omega\) hide fixed logarithmic factors; the target itself specifies their permitted form.

Knowing the start before reading the graph is important. A preprocessing summary that must later support any as-yet-unknown start has a stronger requirement. A lower bound for that stronger preprocessing task does not automatically apply to the present algorithm. Likewise, a theorem with a fixed constant pass count cannot be evaluated at a growing polylogarithmic pass count unless its uniform dependence on that parameter is proved.

The source asks broadly for faster simulation and separately for endpoint-distribution estimation and the most likely endpoints. This card selects the full trajectory, fixed total-variation accuracy, unweighted directed input and length range \(1\le L\le n\). It retains the known-start and near-linear-space, polylogarithmic-pass objective.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that an algorithm and fixed constants satisfying every condition above exist, or a complete Lean-checked proof that they do not. A positive answer must bound the total variation of the entire explicit output tuple and account for memory and passes on every graph and edge ordering. A negative answer must rule out all fixed logarithmic exponents \(a,b\) in the selected resource bounds, with the start known before streaming. Constant-pass lower bounds, lower bounds only for unknown-start preprocessing, endpoint-only samplers, results on dense graphs or bounds allowing a polynomial factor in \(L\) do not resolve this target. The tolerance \(1/100\) is the specified statistical distance between distributions, not an additive error on asymptotic resource bounds.

title: Fault-adaptive Byzantine agreement at optimal resilience
summary: The historical question asks for binary strong Byzantine agreement with the optimal honest-majority resilience threshold. Communication must use at most a constant times n(f+1) words when only f processes are actually corrupted. The synchronous model includes authenticated channels, adaptive corruptions and trusted ideal threshold signatures. A published PODC 2026 theorem provides the required protocol and also an adaptive bound on decision rounds. The reviewed historical card is therefore preserved in the resolved archive rather than listed as an open problem.
formal:
Does there exist a uniform deterministic synchronous protocol and an absolute constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(t\ge0\), with \(n=2t+1\) named processes and trusted ideal signature setup as defined below, the protocol solves binary strong Byzantine agreement against every adaptive adversary corrupting at most \(t\) processes, and every execution with \(f\le t\) actual corruptions has total communication at most
\[
C\,n(f+1)
\]
words sent by processes while they follow the protocol? The protocol receives \(n,t\), identities and the setup, but not the eventual value of \(f\). The bound includes communication after a process decides. No bound on the number of rounds is imposed beyond eventual decision by every never-corrupted process.
definitions:
Processes have distinct identities \(1,\ldots,n\), know the membership and threshold \(t\), and each starts with one input bit. Every pair has a reliable authenticated channel. Time is divided into synchronous rounds known to all processes. A message sent by a noncorrupted process to another noncorrupted process is delivered by the end of that round. A send to each of several recipients is charged separately; there is no free broadcast primitive.

An adversary may choose which processes to corrupt as the execution develops, after observing communication, with at most \(t\) distinct processes ever corrupted. Corruption is permanent and reveals the process’s state and signing capability. Corrupted processes may send inconsistent messages, omit messages, or stop. They cannot impersonate an uncorrupted sender or create signatures forbidden by the ideal signing interface. Honest messages already sent retain the stated reliable-delivery guarantee. Let \(f\) be the total number of distinct processes corrupted during the execution. Correct processes for agreement, termination and validity are those never corrupted.

Each correct process must eventually decide one bit, once and irrevocably. Agreement requires that all such decisions are equal. Strong unanimity requires that, if every correct process’s original input is the same bit \(b\), their decision is \(b\), regardless of the inputs and messages of corrupted processes. With mixed correct inputs, either bit is permitted.

The trusted setup occurs before the measured execution and supplies public verification information and private signing capabilities. Ordinary signatures are publicly verifiable and can be produced only by the named signer; once produced, they may be copied and forwarded. For any publicly specified threshold \(q\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), an ideal threshold-signature instance permits each process to create a share on a specified message. Shares from at least \(q\) distinct processes on that same message can be combined locally into one constant-size publicly verifiable certificate. A certificate can be created only from the required distinct shares, or copied if already available. Corrupted signers can provide their own shares on arbitrary messages. This idealization rules out forgery exactly; it does not assert unconditional security of a physical cryptographic implementation. Setup and local signature operations incur no communication charge beyond transmitting their inputs or outputs.

A word carries a constant number of input bits, ordinary signatures, signature shares or threshold certificates, together with \(O(\log(n+2))\) ordinary control bits. These constants are fixed independently of \(n,t,f\). An arbitrary list of signers, values or certificates is charged for all its contents; compression into one threshold certificate is allowed only through the stated interface. Every nonempty message costs at least one word. Local computation is unrestricted. A protocol is uniform if a single finite algorithm specifies each process’s behavior from its identity, input, parameters, setup and local history. It uses no random choices outside the ideal setup.

The communication measure counts every word sent while a process is uncorrupted, including words sent by a process that is later corrupted, and all permitted protocol traffic after decisions. Arbitrary traffic sent after corruption is excluded. The bound holds in every allowed execution, not merely in expectation or in the worst case \(f=t\). The case \(t=0,n=1\) is included.
answer_criterion: A positive benchmark answer requires a complete Lean-checked protocol, correctness proof and uniform \(C n(f+1)\) word bound in the specified ideal model. A negative answer would require a Lean-checked impossibility proof for this quantified assertion. The target is binary existence with an asymptotic resource guarantee, so no numerical \(1/100\) tolerance applies. Published mathematics now gives the positive answer; this archived record does not claim that the protocol has already been formalized in Lean.

title: Linear-round weighted APSP in CONGEST
summary: Every node in a weighted network must learn its exact distance to every other node. Messages are limited to logarithmically many bits per edge and round, with communication only along the input network. The target is a uniform randomized algorithm using a truly linear number of rounds and succeeding globally with constant probability. A linear lower bound and a randomized near-linear upper bound are known, leaving factors hidden by polylogarithmic notation. A complete answer must prove the literal linear bound or rule it out in this same model.
formal:
For every fixed integer \(b\ge1\), does there exist a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm and a constant \(C_b\) that, on every connected simple undirected \(n\)-vertex graph with integer edge weights in \(\{0,\ldots,n^b\}\), outputs all exact weighted distances at their respective vertices within \(C_b n\) communication rounds, with probability at least \(2/3\) that all outputs are correct simultaneously?

The bound must hold on every execution, for all \(n\ge2\). “Linear” means \(O(n)\) with no factor growing with \(n\); a bound \(\widetilde O(n)=O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) does not meet the target.
definitions:
The communication network is the input graph \(G=(V,E,w)\). It has \(n\ge2\) vertices, no loops or parallel edges, is connected, and has nonnegative integer edge weights. For a fixed \(b\), each weight lies between 0 and \(n^b\) inclusive and is represented in binary. A vertex is a processor with a unique identifier in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). It initially knows \(n\), \(b\), its own identifier, the identifiers of its neighbors and the weights of its incident edges, but no other part of the topology or other edge weights. The requirement holds for all labelled graphs and therefore all assignments of these identifiers. The usual polynomial-size identifier range is equivalent for this target because identifiers can be renamed in \(O(n)\) rounds.

Computation is synchronous. In each round each endpoint of each edge can send the other endpoint a message of at most \(B_b\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits, for a fixed constant \(B_b\). Both directions operate independently and different neighbors may receive different messages. All messages sent in a round arrive before the next round. Communication is allowed only along edges of \(G\); there are no additional links between non-neighbors. Edge weights affect shortest-path lengths, not message latency or bandwidth. Local storage and finite local computation are unrestricted and uncharged; only the number of communication rounds is counted. The local rules form one finite, computable program, fixed for all \(n\) and inputs, with no topology-dependent advice or preprocessing.

Randomized processors use independent private fair random bits. For every fixed graph, weights and identifier assignment, probability is over these bits. By the prescribed worst-case round deadline every processor must halt and produce its output; an invalid or incomplete output counts as failure. The success event requires all vertices' entire distance tables to be correct in the same execution, with probability at least \(2/3\). Deterministic algorithms are included as a special case. No average over graphs or identifier assignments is used.

For vertices \(u,v\), define
\[d_G(u,v)=\min_{P:u\leadsto v}\sum_{e\in P}w(e),\qquad d_G(u,u)=0.\]
The minimum may be taken over simple paths, since weights are nonnegative. Each vertex \(v\) must output the labelled table \(\{(u,d_G(u,v)):u\in V\}\). Distances are finite integers of at most \((n-1)n^b\); zero-weight edges and equal-length alternative paths are allowed. The output is the exact distance table, without a requirement to list every path. Output and retained local tables are local memory, not extra communication channels.

The constants, bandwidth bound and program may depend on \(b\), but not on \(n\), graph density, diameter, individual weights or the random choices. At most \(C_b n\) rounds are allowed on every execution. There is no message-count bound beyond the per-edge per-round bandwidth. The source's linear-time question is retained literally. The explicit bounded-error convention uses one fixed constant global success probability; it does not impose an additional failure probability tending to zero with \(n\). The source's nonnegative polynomially bounded integer-weight setting includes the zero-weight edges used in its lower-bound example.

The proposition's negation says that for some fixed \(b\), no such uniform bounded-error algorithm has a linear worst-case round bound on all instances. It does not demand an \(\Omega(n^{1+\delta})\) lower bound for a fixed positive \(\delta\); a rigorously unavoidable unbounded logarithmic or slower factor could already refute linear time. The notation \(\widetilde O(n)\) suppresses polylogarithmic factors and therefore must not be read as \(O(n)\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated linear-round existence proposition. A positive answer must give, for every fixed weight exponent \(b\), a uniform protocol with the stated bandwidth, worst-case \(C_b n\) deadline and simultaneous exact correctness probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. A negative answer must rule out every such protocol for at least one fixed \(b\), preserving the communication and randomness conventions. A near-linear bound with an unbounded factor, approximate distances, a result only for unweighted graphs, a deterministic-only lower bound, or an algorithm with communication links outside the input graph is insufficient. Neither an expected-time bound alone nor a per-vertex success probability alone supplies the stated guarantee. The target is exact asymptotic linearity; numerical error tolerance does not apply.

title: Subquadratic metric TSP cost estimation below factor two
summary: A metric TSP cost query algorithm asks for distances between selected pairs of labeled points. The question asks whether some fixed approximation factor below two is achievable with a subquadratic number of queries on every metric. The algorithm is randomized and only needs to output a cost estimate, with success probability at least two thirds. Nearly linear MST-weight estimation gives the factor-two baseline, while stronger TSP estimates are known for special metrics or with extra spanning-tree information. The target separates sparse access to a global optimum value from the information needed to construct an explicit tour.
formal:
Do there exist an absolute constant \(\delta\in(0,1)\) and a classical randomized distance-query algorithm that estimates the minimum traveling-salesperson tour cost of every \(n\)-point metric within a factor \(2-\delta\), using \(o(n^2)\) distance queries?

For a metric \(d\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge3\), define
\[\operatorname{TSP}(d)=\min_{\pi\in\mathfrak S_n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}d\bigl(\pi(j),\pi(j+1)\bigr),\qquad \pi(n+1)=\pi(1).\]
The algorithm knows \(n\) and can request \(d(i,j)\) for any chosen pair of labels. Its output \(Z\) must satisfy
\[\Pr\!\left[\operatorname{TSP}(d)\le Z\le(2-\delta)\operatorname{TSP}(d)\right]\ge\frac23\]
for every input metric. Only the number of oracle calls is bounded; the output is a cost estimate and need not describe a tour.
definitions:
The input consists of a known integer \(n\ge3\), the labels \([n]\), and an oracle for a function \(d:[n]\times[n]\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). It is promised that \(d(i,j)=0\) exactly when \(i=j\), that \(d(i,j)=d(j,i)\), and that
\[d(i,k)\le d(i,j)+d(j,k)\quad\text{for all }i,j,k\in[n].\]
Thus all off-diagonal distances are finite positive real numbers. The triangle inequality and symmetry are input promises, not properties that the algorithm must verify. Metrics are arbitrary: no Euclidean embedding, dimension bound, integer-distance restriction, bounded aspect ratio or distribution on inputs is supplied.

One query consists of specifying labels \(i,j\in[n]\) and receiving the exact real distance \(d(i,j)\). It costs one oracle call. Queries may depend on earlier replies and on the algorithm’s private randomness. Repeated calls are charged again. Diagonal values are known to be zero; allowing a paid diagonal call gives no additional information. The metric remains fixed throughout the execution and is chosen independently of the random bits.

The algorithm is uniform: a single finite program works for every \(n\). To specify computation with exact real oracle replies, use a classical real-register machine with rational program constants, ordinary finite control, integer counters, and exact real arithmetic and comparisons. Allowed real operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by a nonzero value; registers may store queried distances and calculated real values. Randomness consists of independent fair bits, which may be used to select labels. Integer computation, local arithmetic, storage and random-bit generation are not charged to the query budget. They must define an algorithm that halts with probability one on each input. No advice depending on the metric or on \(n\), quantum queries, further metric oracle, precomputed spanning tree or access to unqueried matrix entries is available.

This is a query-complexity question, so there is no polynomial-time or subquadratic-time requirement on the computation between calls. In particular, the original source’s suggestion of subquadratic total time is a stronger aspiration, not an additional condition for answering its primary query question. A positive solution with such a time bound would also solve this card, provided it meets all the stated guarantees.

The output \(Z\) is one real value. On a successful execution it is an upper estimate at most \(2-\delta\) times the optimum. An equivalent lower-estimate convention would require \(\operatorname{TSP}(d)/(2-\delta)\le Z'\le\operatorname{TSP}(d)\); multiplication by the fixed approximation factor converts between the conventions without oracle calls. The algorithm may fail to meet the interval on at most one third of its random executions. Success is required for each metric individually, not merely on average over an input distribution.

The query bound is worst case over inputs and random executions, apart from null-probability exceptional executions. Formally, there must exist \(q:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that every \(n\)-point input uses at most \(q(n)\) oracle calls with probability one, and
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{q(n)}{n^2}=0.\]
The constant \(\delta\), the program and this bound are independent of all distance values. There is no hidden dependence on the ratio of the largest to the smallest positive distance. For finitely many small \(n\), all pair distances may be queried without affecting the limit. The little-o condition is weaker than demanding \(O(n^{2-\gamma})\) for some fixed \(\gamma>0\); both a fixed polynomial saving and a genuine slower asymptotic saving would qualify.

The quantifier order is \(\exists\delta\;\exists A\;\exists q\;\forall n\ge3\;\forall d\), followed by probability over the execution of \(A\). The improvement \(\delta\) must be a positive constant; an approximation factor approaching two from below as \(n\) grows is insufficient. The card asks whether any such constant improvement exists, not for the largest possible improvement or a full approximation-query tradeoff.

A tour is a cyclic ordering of all labels, using each exactly once before returning to the start. The cost includes that closing edge. The oracle describes the complete metric, so each tour edge costs the queried distance itself; no separate underlying graph path needs to be output. \(\mathfrak S_n\) is the set of all permutations of \([n]\). The finite minimum in the definition of \(\operatorname{TSP}(d)\) is attained and is strictly positive.

For background, a spanning tree is a connected acyclic graph on all labels, and \(\operatorname{MST}(d)\) is the minimum sum of its edge distances. The familiar inequalities \(\operatorname{MST}(d)\le\operatorname{TSP}(d)\le2\operatorname{MST}(d)\) explain the factor-two threshold. Estimating the weight of an MST does not give its edges. A graphic metric is the shortest-path distance metric of a connected unweighted undirected graph. A \((1,2)\)-metric has every off-diagonal distance equal to one or two. Both are special classes of the general metric inputs here.

This is not a streaming task: a stream reveals entries in an imposed order, whereas the algorithm here chooses each pair it queries. A result that is given a minimum spanning tree as additional input, or promises a spanning tree of unit-distance edges, concerns additional information or structure absent from the target. Full-input approximation algorithms may also use quadratically many distance entries, regardless of their approximation ratio.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of an absolute \(\delta>0\), a uniform classical randomized algorithm and a worst-case query bound \(q(n)=o(n^2)\) with the stated success probability for every metric. A positive answer must prove the cost guarantee, the uniform little-o bound independent of the metric’s scale and aspect ratio, and almost-sure halting in the specified oracle model. It need not output a tour or run in subquadratic total time. A negative answer must refute this quantified existence statement for randomized adaptive algorithms; a lower bound only for deterministic algorithms, near-exact approximation, or a specific algorithm is insufficient. Positive results restricted to graphic or \((1,2)\)-metrics, or assuming an MST is supplied, do not resolve the arbitrary-metric target. Experimental success rates, conditional computational hardness and an improvement that vanishes with \(n\) do not establish the required result.

title: Work-efficient parallel approximate flow
summary: The question concerns parallel approximation of maximum flow in undirected graphs with vertex capacities. Each vertex limits the total traffic through it, and the algorithm must explicitly output a feasible flow between the two named terminals. The flow value must be within a factor of one plus the requested inverse-polylogarithmic error of optimum. The target combines nearly-linear total processor work with polylogarithmic parallel depth. The ordinary edge-capacitated version has such an algorithm; this card asks only for the vertex-capacitated version.
formal:
Does undirected vertex-capacitated maximum flow admit a uniform randomized parallel \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation with nearly-linear total work and polylogarithmic depth?

Given an undirected graph with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges, distinct terminals \(s,t\), and nonnegative vertex capacities, the algorithm must output a feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow of value at least \(\mathrm{OPT}/(1+\varepsilon)\), where \(\mathrm{OPT}\) is the maximum feasible flow value. It must use \((n+m)\operatorname{polylog}n\) work (total processor operations) and \(\operatorname{polylog}n\) depth (parallel steps), with success probability at least \(2/3\).

The polynomially bounded capacities, inverse-polylogarithmic accuracy regime, uniformity and word-PRAM model are quantified below.
definitions:
An input graph \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, simple and undirected, with \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(n\ge2\), \(m=|E|\), and distinct named terminals \(s,t\). It is supplied by an explicit edge list; disconnected graphs and zero capacities are allowed. For each undirected edge \(\{u,v\}\), a flow has nonnegative values \(f_{uv},f_{vu}\). Put
\[
\mathrm{out}_f(v)=\sum_{w:\{v,w\}\in E}f_{vw},\qquad
\mathrm{in}_f(v)=\sum_{w:\{v,w\}\in E}f_{wv}.
\]
Require \(\mathrm{in}_f(s)=\mathrm{out}_f(t)=0\) and \(\mathrm{in}_f(v)=\mathrm{out}_f(v)\) for \(v\notin\{s,t\}\). The value is \(F=\mathrm{out}_f(s)=\mathrm{in}_f(t)\). Fractional flows are allowed. Internal circulations may occur but consume vertex capacities.

Each \(v\) has capacity \(U_v\ge0\). Its load is \(\mathrm{out}_f(v)\) if \(v\ne t\), and \(\mathrm{in}_f(t)\) if \(v=t\). Require load at most \(U_v\) for every vertex, including both terminals. Edges impose no additional capacity bounds; only the vertex loads constrain feasibility. Equivalently, in a decomposition into directed simple terminal paths, every unit uses capacity at each vertex on its path, including its endpoints; removable internal circulations do not improve the optimum.

\(\mathrm{OPT}\) is the maximum \(F\) over feasible real flows. Zero flow is feasible, and instances with \(\mathrm{OPT}=0\) must also be handled. The output explicitly lists rational values for both orientations of every edge. On a successful run all feasibility inequalities hold exactly and \(F\ge\mathrm{OPT}/(1+\varepsilon)\); no vertex-capacity violation is permitted.

Here is an explicit polynomial-data and inverse-polylogarithmic-accuracy convention. For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), allow integral vertex capacities \(U_v\in[0,n^a]\). Let
\[
L=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil,\qquad
\varepsilon=1/q,\quad q\in\mathbb N,\quad 2\le q\le L^a.
\]
Input numbers, labels and \(q\) are encoded in binary. The same algorithm must cover every fixed \(a\); it receives the numerical instance and \(q\), not advice or a precomputed structure for the graph. Reciprocal-integer accuracies specify the source's inverse-polylogarithmic regime: intermediate accuracies can be met by requesting a smaller reciprocal accuracy. This does not require a fully polynomial bound for arbitrary inverse accuracy outside that regime.

Use a synchronous priority-CRCW word PRAM: processors execute one fixed finite program, have labelled shared-memory words, can read concurrently, and simultaneous writes to one location retain the value of the lowest-numbered writing processor. Use the [integer word instructions](definitions.html#ram) at width \(w\). Each processor may generate one independent fair bit in one step. A word has \(w=C_a L\) bits for a fixed constant \(C_a\); larger integers and rational numerators or denominators use multiple words and their operations are charged accordingly. There is no exact-real or arbitrary-precision unit-cost primitive. Work counts all processor operations, including input handling and output; depth is the number of synchronous steps. The algorithm must halt within the stated bounds on every random tape and succeed with probability at least \(2/3\) on each valid input.

Nearly-linear work and polylogarithmic depth mean that, for every fixed \(a\), there are constants \(K_a>0\) and \(k_a\in\mathbb N\), independent of the graph, its numerical data and \(q\), such that
\[
\mathrm{work}\le K_a(n+m)L^{k_a},\qquad
\mathrm{depth}\le K_a L^{k_a}.
\]
These are explicit editorial model conventions for the source's parallel resource question. They count the finite precision needed by an actual implementation. Polynomially many processors without the work bound, or a subpolynomial factor that is not bounded by a fixed power of \(L\), is insufficient.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of this existence assertion for undirected vertex-capacitated maximum flow. A positive answer must specify one uniform algorithm and establish exact capacity feasibility, the approximation guarantee, per-instance success probability and simultaneous work/depth bounds for every fixed data-and-accuracy exponent \(a\). A negative answer must rule out such an algorithm in the stated model. The question is binary; there is no additional numerical \(1/100\) tolerance. A theorem about the optimum value alone must also supply the required flow output, and a capacity-violating bicriteria result alone does not meet the stated feasibility guarantee.

title: Sharp register lower bound for obstruction-free set agreement
summary: Set agreement lets processes decide at most k distinct values that were actually proposed. Obstruction-freedom guarantees completion when one process eventually runs alone. The question asks whether n minus k plus one shared registers are always necessary. It concerns one invocation, named processes and arbitrarily large read/write registers. The matching known upper bound makes this a sharp space conjecture.
formal: For every integer pair \(n>k\ge1\), must any deterministic obstruction-free one-shot \(k\)-set-agreement protocol for \(n\) named processes use at least \(n-k+1\) shared atomic read/write registers? Equivalently, is \(R(n,k)\ge n-k+1\) throughout the domain, with \(R\) and the register, validity and progress conventions below? The matching upper bound is known; no restriction on register width or local computation is added.
definitions:
Fix \(n>k\ge1\). There are \(n\) processes with distinct known identifiers \(1,\ldots,n\); each knows \(n,k\) and initially knows only its own input in \([n]\), not other processes' inputs. A protocol may depend on \(n,k\), and is given by finite deterministic programs with unbounded private storage and no bound on finite local computation. No uniform procedure generating protocols for different \(n,k\) is required. A process may invoke the task at most once; it participates when it invokes, and may decide at most once, after which it stops. Any subset may participate.

The only communication is through a fixed array of \(r\ge0\) shared multiwriter/multireader registers with common names \(1,\ldots,r\). Every process can read and write every register. A register stores a finite binary string of unrestricted length; one atomic read returns its entire current string, and one atomic write replaces that string. Initial shared contents may depend on \(n,k\) and the protocol but are fixed independently of the input assignment and participation. All shared storage is in these counted registers. A scheduled process takes a local computation step, including invocation or decision, or performs one atomic read or write with a finite local update; no stronger shared primitive, random choice, clock, or failure detector is supplied.

An execution is any finite or infinite interleaving of such steps; a process may stop forever at any point, representing a crash, with no fairness or timing assumption. In every finite execution prefix, each decided value must be the input proposed by a process that has already invoked, and at most \(k\) distinct values may have been decided.

Obstruction-freedom requires that, from every reachable configuration, every participating undecided process \(p\) decides after finitely many further own steps if only \(p\) is scheduled thereafter. Other processes may subsequently resume, so safety must also hold under every extension. Register widths, private storage and running time are uncharged.

Define \(R(n,k)\) as the least integer \(r\) for which a protocol satisfies these requirements for every assignment of inputs and every schedule. A finite sufficient \(r\) is known, so this minimum exists.
answer_criterion: Prove the register lower bound in Lean for all \(n>k\ge1\) under the stated validity and obstruction-freedom requirements, or give one admissible pair and a correct protocol using at most \(n-k\) registers.

title: Bipartite maximal matching with polynomial-in-degree volume
summary: A maximal matching is a collection of disjoint edges to which no additional edge can be added. A vertex query may inspect the graph only by following ports from vertices it has already visited. The input supplies the two sides of the bipartite graph, and separate queries must describe one consistent matching. The question asks for one deterministic algorithm whose visited volume is polynomial in the degree bound and independent of graph size. The February 2026 primary list retains this question between known linear and superpolynomial degree-dependent bounds.
formal: Do there exist universal constants \(C>0\), \(k\in\mathbb N\) and one uniform deterministic local-query algorithm which, on every finite simple bipartite graph of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\), answers each vertex query after visiting at most \(C(\Delta+1)^k\) distinct vertices, such that all answers together specify one maximal matching? A proper two-coloring of the input graph is supplied. The bound has no dependence on the number \(n\) of graph vertices.
definitions: The input is a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(n=|V|\ge1\), an integer bound \(\Delta\ge1\) with \(\deg(v)\le\Delta\) for all vertices, an injective identifier map \(V\to[n^2]\), and a proper coloring \(\chi:V\to\{0,1\}\) satisfying \(\chi(u)\ne\chi(v)\) on every edge. At each vertex \(v\), the incident edges have an arbitrary fixed bijective port numbering by \(\{1,\ldots,\deg(v)\}\); the two endpoints’ port numbers need not agree. A query rooted at \(v\) initially knows only \(n,\Delta\), the identifier, degree and color of \(v\), and its port index set. Its visited set starts as \(\{v\}\). It can adaptively probe port \(j\) of any visited vertex \(w\), thereby learning the corresponding neighbor \(u\), its identifier, degree, color and the reciprocal port of that edge at \(u\). This adds \(u\) to the visited set. Revisited vertices are recognized by their identifiers and counted only once. A probe does not reveal unvisited vertices behind other ports. The explored vertices form a connected set; direct probes of arbitrary identifiers are forbidden. The volume is the number of distinct visited vertices, including the root, at termination. Temporary memory and local computation are unrestricted but finite. Each rooted query starts afresh, with no preprocessing, shared mutable state or information retained from earlier queries. One finite deterministic program must work for all sizes, degree bounds, graphs, identifier assignments, port orders and supplied proper colorings. It receives no advice or randomness. It outputs either an unmatched symbol \(\bot\) or one local port at its root. For the outputs to describe a matching, whenever \(v\) selects its port leading to \(u\), the separate query at \(u\) must select the reciprocal port leading to \(v\). Let \(M\) be the selected undirected edges. Maximality requires that every edge in \(E\) has an endpoint incident to an edge of \(M\). Equivalently, no further edge can be added to \(M\) while keeping all selected edges vertex-disjoint. Maximum cardinality is not required. The same matching must result for every order of queries, and repeating a query must give the same answer. The constants \(C,k\) are independent of all input parameters, including \(\Delta\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction and correctness/volume proof for the quantified algorithm, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A negative result must rule out every universal polynomial degree bound for every correct uniform deterministic algorithm in this connected, stateless model. An algorithm with a factor depending on \(n\), randomized or expected volume guarantees, an oracle allowing arbitrary jumps, a method requiring preprocessing, or an approximation to maximum matching that need not be maximal does not establish the positive statement. A linear-in-degree lower bound alone does not establish the negative statement.

title: Polylogarithmic-space streaming Euclidean MST estimation
summary: Points arrive one at a time in Euclidean space, and the goal is to estimate the cost of connecting them by a minimum spanning tree. The algorithm gets one insertion-only pass and may keep only memory polynomial in the dimension and the logarithmic input parameters. It should return a constant-factor estimate with probability at least two thirds for every input order. The cited paper leaves a gap between its sublinear-space constant-factor result and this smaller memory budget. The question asks how compactly one can summarize global geometric connectivity, without requiring the summary to output the tree itself.
formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized one-pass insertion-only streaming algorithm A and absolute constants \(C\ge1\), \(K\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), \(d\ge1\), \(\Delta\ge2\), and every stream of n distinct points in \(\{0,\ldots,\Delta\}^{d}\), A uses at most
\[K\bigl(d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\lceil\log_2(\Delta+2)\rceil\bigr)^k\]
bits of working memory and returns a rational estimate Z satisfying
\[\Pr[\operatorname{MST}(X)\le Z\le C\operatorname{MST}(X)]\ge 2/3?\]
The stream order is arbitrary and fixed independently of the algorithm’s private random bits. The output estimates total Euclidean MST cost; it need not describe a tree. For polynomially bounded integer coordinates, the required space is \(\mathrm{poly}(d\log n)\), as in the community proposal.
definitions:
The point set X consists of the n distinct inserted vectors. Coordinates are nonnegative integers given in binary, and the parameters n,d and the bound \(\Delta\) are supplied before the stream. The graph is complete on X; an edge between x and y has weight \(\|x-y\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^{d}(x_j-y_j)^2)^{1/2}\). The quantity \(\operatorname{MST}(X)\) is the minimum sum of edge weights over all spanning trees of this graph. It is a real number even though the input coordinates are integers.

The algorithm is one fixed finite probabilistic Turing-machine program with a read-once input stream, private independent fair random bits, working tapes, and an output tape used only for the final rational estimate. An input record may be buffered, with those bits charged to memory. All retained state, counters, random seeds and postprocessing workspace count toward the space bound, on every input and every random tape. Consumed input cannot be revisited, and there are no deletions, extra passes, random-order promise, external storage, nonuniform advice or real-number registers. The machine must halt on every random tape; no separate update-time or total-time bound is imposed. The probability is over its coins for each fixed stream. The constants and exponent do not depend on n,d or the coordinate bound.

Dependence polynomial in the bit length of coordinates makes the finite-input convention explicit. In particular, for each fixed integer b and \(\Delta\le n^b\), the bound has the proposal’s \(\mathrm{poly}(d\log n)\) form. The logarithmic coordinate factor is recorded rather than silently treating arbitrary reals as constant-size words. The target allows d to grow, including \(d=\Theta(\log n)\); a bound exponential in d does not qualify. The approximation constant can be any fixed finite C. Requiring the estimate to lie above the true cost is a normalization: a two-sided constant-factor estimate can be rescaled at the cost of changing C. Neither an explicit tree nor a \(1+\varepsilon\) approximation is required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm satisfying the stated memory, pass and probability bounds for some absolute finite approximation constant, or prove the negation for every such algorithm and constants. An \(n^{\varepsilon}\)-space algorithm for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), a factor growing with n, a multiple-pass algorithm, or a lower bound excluding only constants near 1 does not settle this target.

title: Strongly polynomial linear programming
summary: A rational linear program minimizes a linear objective subject to linear equalities and nonnegative variables. The question asks for one deterministic exact solver using polynomially many scalar arithmetic operations depending only on the numbers of variables and constraints. Intermediate rational values must have bit lengths polynomial in the full input length, and the computation must admit an exact polynomial-time bit implementation. The solver must distinguish infeasibility, an objective unbounded below and a finite attained optimum on every input, without matrix or conditioning promises. OpenAI gives a strongly polynomial solver for general rational linear programs with all three outcomes.
formal:
Does there exist one deterministic algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,d,C',e\) with the following guarantee for every \(m,n\ge1\), \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\)? For the linear program
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x: x\in\mathbb R^n,\ Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},\]
the algorithm returns an exact rational optimal vector, or correctly reports infeasibility or an objective unbounded below. It uses at most \(C(m+n+1)^d\) elementary operations in the rational arithmetic model below, and every numerical value during the computation has binary encoding length at most \(C'(N+1)^e\), where \(N\) is the full input bit length. The same program and constants must work for all dimensions and coefficient values.
definitions:
The input contains the dimensions and the complete dense lists of entries of \(A,b,c\), including zeros. Each rational is supplied as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Their lengths, the dimensions and the delimiters all contribute to \(N\). No rank, nondegeneracy, strict-feasibility, boundedness, coefficient-size or conditioning promise is imposed. The variables range over the real numbers; rational input guarantees that a finite optimum, when the feasible set is nonempty and the objective bounded below, has a rational optimal vector.

Computation uses one fixed finite arithmetic-RAM program with rational registers, integer addresses and finite control. One scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero rational, exact comparison, register read/write or copy costs one operation. Conditional branches, elementary integer index arithmetic and comparisons, and data transfers also count. Index operations are integer addition and subtraction; indirect addressing accesses one location at a time. Indices start from dimensions or fixed integer constants and are manipulated by these index operations. A rational coefficient or computed rational cannot be reinterpreted as an address. Each scalar entry of a vector or matrix operation must be charged separately. All preprocessing, memory access, feasibility testing and production of the output count. A scalar rational input read or output write counts once at this arithmetic level; transferring its individual binary digits is accounted for by the bit implementation.

The program may contain finitely many fixed rational constants. It has no oracle, advice, randomness, floor or integer-part primitive, square-root primitive, or instruction inspecting the binary digits, numerator, denominator or encoding length of a rational register. Comparisons and arithmetic act on exact rational values, not floating-point approximations. Here the binary size of a rational is the combined length of its signed numerator and positive denominator in lowest terms. The bound also covers integer indices and the output. Reduction to lowest terms specifies representation and exact bit simulation; it supplies no additional operation with which the arithmetic program can extract numerator or denominator data. The elementary rational operations must admit an exact implementation on a binary multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in their operand lengths. Thus the dimension-only operation bound together with the polynomial numerical-size bound yields total bit time polynomial in \(N\); the bit-time bound is not required to be independent of \(N\).

Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). An infeasibility answer is correct exactly when \(F=\varnothing\). An unbounded-below answer is correct exactly when \(F\ne\varnothing\) and
\[\forall M\in\mathbb R\ \exists x\in F,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x<M.\]
Otherwise the algorithm must return \(x^*\in F\cap\mathbb Q^n\) with
\[\forall y\in F,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x^*\le c^{\mathsf T}y.\]
Any optimal vector is allowed when several exist; an optimal basis is not required. An unbounded feasible region can still have a finite minimum, and must then receive an optimal-vector output. Infeasibility and unboundedness outputs are distinct tags, not an approximate numerical infinity. The operation bound depends only on \(m+n\); neither coefficient magnitudes, their bit lengths, numerical conditioning nor a requested accuracy may enter it.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this algorithm-existence statement or of its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a finite deterministic program, prove its correct exact output in all three cases for every rational input, and prove both a single dimension-only polynomial operation bound and a single polynomial bound on numerical encoding lengths, with an exact polynomial-time bit implementation.

A negative answer must prove that no program with any fixed constants \(C,d,C',e\) satisfies all these requirements on every input. An exponential example for one pivot rule or a restricted class of interior-point methods does not exclude every algorithm in the specified model. A guarantee restricted to special matrices, fixed dimension, well-conditioned or strictly feasible inputs, or an approximate optimum does not settle the question. This is a yes/no existence target; the benchmark's numerical approximation tolerance does not replace exact optimization or either complexity bound.
