title: Komlós conjecture
summary: Komlós asks whether every collection of real vectors of Euclidean norm at most one can be assigned signs so that every coordinate of their sum is bounded by one universal constant. The dimensions and entries are arbitrary, and the same complete choice of signs must control all coordinates simultaneously. The positive answer requires some finite constant, without determining the best one or giving an efficient algorithm. Such a theorem would imply the Beck–Fiala discrepancy bound and strengthen rounding and optimization guarantees. A complete Lean proof must establish the universal bound or unbounded discrepancy; the 10 September 2026 preprint claims the full positive bound, but this review has not independently verified its proof.
formal: Is there a real constant \(C>0\) such that for every pair of integers \(m,n\ge1\) and every matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^m A_{ij}^2\le1\) for each \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), there exists a single sign vector \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) for which \[\max_{1\le i\le m}\left|\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j\right|\le C?\] The constant must be independent of both dimensions and all matrix entries.
definitions: For a real vector \(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_m)\), its Euclidean norm is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\), and its maximum-coordinate norm is \(\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|\). The columns \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) of \(A\) may be any vectors in \(\mathbb R^m\) with \(\|v_j\|_2\le1\), including zero vectors and vectors with negative or irrational entries. The signed sum is \(Ax=\sum_j x_jv_j\), where every one of the \(n\) coefficients is exactly \(-1\) or \(1\). Define the combinatorial discrepancy \(\operatorname{disc}(A)=\min_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}\|Ax\|_\infty\); this minimum is attained because there are finitely many sign vectors. The proposition asks for a universal upper bound on this number over all such matrices. The same chosen \(x\) must satisfy every row inequality simultaneously, though it may depend on the full matrix. The column norm bound is individual, not an average across columns; there is no row norm, row-count, rank or sparsity restriction. All matrices are finite, with arbitrary positive dimensions. The task is existence of some finite constant, not determination of the optimal constant and not an algorithm for finding the signs. There is no bit encoding or computational-time restriction on the entries or the sign choice. A fractional vector in \([-1,1]^n\), a vector with unassigned zero coordinates, or independent choices of signs for different rows does not constitute the required witness.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition with a specified finite real constant \(C>0\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\) there exist positive integers \(m,n\) and a real matrix \(A\) with all column Euclidean norms at most one, such that for every \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) there is a row \(i\) satisfying \(|\sum_j A_{ij}x_j|>C\). Equivalently, a negative answer proves that these discrepancies are unbounded; the dimensions and matrix may depend on \(C\), without an efficient construction requirement. A fixed finite lower bound on the necessary constant does not refute the conjecture. A bound that grows with a dimension, a partial coloring, or a result limited to sparse, random or nonnegative matrices does not prove the universal target. No optimization of the positive constant is required.

title: Nearly linear-time solution of general sparse linear systems
summary: A sparse linear system explicitly stores only the nonzero matrix entries and its right-hand side. The question asks whether every nonsingular rational system with polynomial conditioning can be approximately solved in nearly linear time in the number of nonzeros. Coefficient lengths and residual accuracy are bounded on a logarithmic scale, and the output must list every rational coordinate. The fixed word-RAM model charges preprocessing, precision, randomness and output, with a worst-case time bound and success probability at least two thirds. Known structured solvers and general improvements over matrix multiplication motivate the target but do not provide its universal near-linear guarantee.
formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized classical algorithm \(A_c\) and constants \(C_c,K_c\ge1\), \(d_c\ge0\), all integers, with the following guarantee? Every promised input consists of \(n\ge2\), a nonsingular rational matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\) with \(m\) nonzero entries, a nonzero vector \(b\in\mathbb Q^n\), and an integer \(1\le p\le c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\). Every input numerator magnitude and positive denominator has at most \(c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) binary digits, and
\[\kappa_2(A)\le n^c.\]
On every run, \(A_c\) must halt within
\[C_c m\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil^{d_c}\]
word operations in the model below, with word length \(w=K_c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). With probability at least \(2/3\), its explicit rational output \(\widehat x\in\mathbb Q^n\) must satisfy
\[\|A\widehat x-b\|_2\le2^{-p}\|b\|_2.\]
The constants and the finite program may depend on \(c\), but must work for all promised dimensions, matrices, right-hand sides and accuracies. Matrices may be nonsymmetric and indefinite.
definitions:
The input explicitly gives \(n,m,p\) in binary, followed by an unordered list of \(m\) triples consisting of a row index, a column index and a nonzero rational value, with distinct positions in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}^2\), and then all \(n\) entries of \(b\). Unlisted matrix entries are zero. Rational numbers are signed binary integer numerators and positive binary integer denominators; reduced fractions are not required. The binary length of zero is one, and a sign is stored separately. Fixed separators specify the list boundaries and integer lengths. Nonsingularity implies \(n\le m\le n^2\), so the total encoding has \(O_c(m\log n)\) bits. The parameter \(c\) specifies the family of promises, rather than an additional runtime input. The algorithm need not verify the promises; guarantees are required only on inputs satisfying them.

For a real vector \(z\), \(\|z\|_2=(\sum_i z_i^2)^{1/2}\). Define \(\sigma_{\max}(A)=\max_{\|z\|_2=1}\|Az\|_2\), \(\sigma_{\min}(A)=\min_{\|z\|_2=1}\|Az\|_2\), and \(\kappa_2(A)=\sigma_{\max}(A)/\sigma_{\min}(A)\). The minimum is positive for nonsingular \(A\). The requested error is relative residual error for this exact rational input, with \(\varepsilon=2^{-p}\). It is not a promise that the approximate vector has the same relative forward error as the residual.

The word RAM has a fixed finite program and a fixed finite number of registers, each holding an unsigned \(w\)-bit word. Input is stored as an explicit binary string packed into a read-only word array. Working memory consists of \(w\)-bit cells addressed by \(w\)-bit words and initially zero; no input-dependent advice or precomputed table is supplied. A step performs one read or write, comparison, conditional branch, addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\), unsigned quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operation, or logical shift of a word. A shift by at least \(w\) positions returns zero. Address computations use the same instructions. One fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit word costs one step. Longer integers occupy multiple cells and use multiple operations. No instruction acts on an arbitrary real number or arbitrary-length integer at unit cost.

The output is a length-delimited explicit list of \(n\) signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Every output word must be written, and all its bits occupy the output encoding. Input processing, preprocessing, any auxiliary matrices, numerical precision, randomness and output cost are included in the stated time bound. The clock is a worst-case bound on every choice of random words, not an expected bound. Probability refers only to the algorithm's independent randomness for each fixed input. An invalid output counts as failure. Uniformity means one program for each fixed \(c\), without dependence on \(n\) or on the particular input; no extra effective procedure generating programs from \(c\) is requested.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition, or of its full logical negation, in this word-RAM model. An affirmative proof must establish the algorithm, its worst-case clock and its success guarantee for every fixed \(c\) and every input in the associated promise family. A negative proof must establish that for some fixed \(c\), no finite program and constants satisfy all these guarantees. It must exclude all algorithms in the stated model, rather than only a chosen iterative method or preconditioner. A result restricted to one structured matrix family, a different output representation or an uncharged real-arithmetic model does not meet the target.

title: Exact semidefinite feasibility in polynomial time
summary: The input is a fully listed rational affine symmetric matrix whose dimension and number of real variables are both unbounded. The target is a deterministic polynomial bit-time decision of whether some real substitution makes the matrix positive semidefinite. Singular feasible points, irrational-only feasible parameters, unbounded sets and infeasible instances at zero distance from the cone are included. Known approximation and exact-duality results retain assumptions or model distinctions, and the September 2026 source still states the unrestricted exact complexity as open. A complete Lean proof must establish one polynomial-time decider or exclude all such deciders; it need not output a feasible point or optimization value.
formal:
Does exact semidefinite feasibility belong to \(\mathrm{P}\) in the ordinary Turing model? The input is an explicitly listed tuple of symmetric rational matrices
\[A_0,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n},\qquad n\ge1,\ m\ge0,
\]
and the required output is \(1\) if and only if
\[\exists x\in\mathbb R^m\quad A_0+\sum_{i=1}^{m}x_iA_i\succeq0.\]
More precisely, do there exist one deterministic finite-program Turing machine \(M\) and positive integers \(a,d\) such that, for every input string of total binary encoding length \(N\), \(M\) halts within \(a(N+1)^d\) steps and correctly decides the language defined below? Both matrix dimension and number of variables are unbounded input parameters. No numerical promise or approximation tolerance is supplied.
definitions:
The input lists \(n,m\) in binary and then all \((m+1)n^2\) entries of the matrices in row order. An entry is a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator, with fixed separators; separators and sign symbols have fixed binary encodings and count toward \(N\). Numerators and denominators need not be relatively prime. All entries, including zeroes and both symmetric halves, are explicitly written; the input is not a circuit, oracle or abbreviated prescription for larger matrices. The language contains exactly the valid encodings with \(n\ge1\), \(m\ge0\), matching dimensions, symmetric matrices and a feasible real vector. Malformed strings, zero denominators and nonsymmetric matrix lists are rejected. Equivalent conventional explicit integer/list encodings differ only by polynomial overhead.

A real symmetric matrix \(B\) is positive semidefinite, written \(B\succeq0\), when \(z^{\mathsf T}Bz\ge0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\). Zero eigenvalues are allowed. The variable \(x\) ranges over all real vectors, not only rational ones. For \(m=0\), the sum is zero and the unique vector in \(\mathbb R^0\) is feasible precisely when \(A_0\succeq0\). For a valid general input, output \(0\) means that no real feasible vector exists.

The computation model is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with fixed finite tape alphabets and one transition charged per time step. Input access, arithmetic on binary strings, intermediate computations, memory access and output are all charged. The algorithm has no oracle, advice, randomness or unit-cost operations on arbitrary exact real numbers. Its time constants are fixed independently of the matrices, their dimensions and their entries. The only output is the decision bit; it need not write a feasible point, an algebraic representation of one, an optimum value or an infeasibility certificate.

The domain includes feasible sets with empty interior, singular feasible matrices, unbounded feasible sets and infeasible affine matrix families at distance zero from the positive semidefinite cone. In particular, there is no positive-definite-feasibility promise, no known containing radius or interior ball, and no lower bound on conditioning or distance to feasibility. Strict feasibility would require a vector producing a positive definite matrix, meaning \(z^{\mathsf T}Bz>0\) for every nonzero \(z\); it is not assumed here. 'Exact' refers to the correct membership bit on every input, including these boundary cases, rather than to numerically accurate matrix entries.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of membership of this language in \(\mathrm{P}\), or of its negation. An affirmative proof must give one deterministic algorithm and one universal polynomial bit-time bound, and prove that its decision agrees with real feasibility for every valid input, with rejection of invalid encodings. A negative proof must rule out every deterministic polynomial-time decider in this model. Failure of one numerical method, exponential size of an explicit witness, or a conditional hardness reduction with an unproved assumption is insufficient. A decision procedure may use arbitrary internal methods, but a guarantee for approximate feasibility, strictly feasible inputs, bounded regions or fixed dimensions does not establish the complete target.

title: Single-exponential dependence on dimension for integer programming
summary: The input is an explicit system of rational linear inequalities whose variables must all be integers. The task is exact feasibility, with no boundedness, rank or coefficient-size promise. The question asks for one deterministic algorithm with a fixed exponential base in the number of variables and a fixed polynomial dependence on input length. The checked general randomized bound and recent determinant-dependent bound do not supply that guarantee. An accepted answer must give a complete Lean-checked construction or unconditional impossibility proof in the bit-computation model.
formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\), an integer constant \(c\ge1\), and one uniform classical deterministic Turing machine \(A\) such that, for every pair of integers \(m,n\ge0\), every explicitly given rational matrix \(Q\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) and every rational vector \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\), the machine correctly decides whether
\[
 \exists x\in\mathbb Z^n\quad Qx\le b
\]
within at most
\[
 2^{Cn}(N+1)^c
\]
bit operations, where \(N\) is the total binary encoding length of the input? The inequalities are componentwise, and there is no boundedness or coefficient-size promise beyond the finite explicit encoding.
definitions:
The dimension parameter \(n\) is the number of integer variables, and \(m\) is the number of inequalities. Both are supplied with the input. The matrix entries and right-hand-side entries are given exactly as signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators, with explicit lengths or delimiters; entries need not be reduced to lowest terms. The entire matrix is listed in row-major order, followed by \(b\). The encoding length \(N\) includes all coefficients, dimensions, signs, denominators and delimiters. There is no succinct circuit or oracle representation of the inequalities.

The inequality \(Qx\le b\) means
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{n}Q_{ij}x_j\le b_i
 \quad\text{for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}.
\]
Every coordinate of \(x\) must be an integer, with no a priori bound on its magnitude or sign. Nonnegativity restrictions are present only if encoded among the inequalities. The underlying real polyhedron may be empty, unbounded, lower dimensional, or contain lines; the matrix may be rank deficient. No bound is imposed on the number of inequalities, determinant magnitudes or width of the feasible region. There is no objective function.

For \(n=0\), \(\mathbb Z^0\) contains the single empty vector, and feasibility means \(0\le b_i\) for every row. For \(m=0\), the conjunction of inequalities is empty and the instance is feasible. These conventions also cover the completely empty system.

The output is one exact Boolean answer: YES if an integer solution exists, and NO otherwise. Producing a feasible point or a separate infeasibility certificate is not required by this decision target. A positive answer cannot be based solely on real feasibility or on satisfying relaxed or numerically perturbed inequalities.

The computation uses a fixed finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program, independent of \(m,n,N,Q,b\). Time is the number of bit-level machine steps. All reading, parsing, exact integer or rational arithmetic, storage operations and output are charged. Arithmetic on an arbitrarily large number is not one operation. Randomness, nonuniform advice, real-number primitives and uncharged optimization or separation oracles are not available.

The constants \(C\) and \(c\) are universal for that one program. In particular, the polynomial exponent on \(N\) may not depend on \(n\), and the exponential base may not grow with \(n\), coefficient magnitude or the number of rows. A polynomial factor in numerical coefficient or determinant magnitude can be exponential in its binary encoding length and therefore is not automatically permitted. Any implementation that uses such a factor must prove that its full bit cost nevertheless meets the displayed bound on every input.

The phrase single-exponential dependence on dimension refers to the factor \(2^{Cn}\). Bounds of the form \((\log(n+2))^{Dn}\) with a fixed \(D>0\) have a growing base and do not meet that dependence as stated. A family of unrelated algorithms, one for each fixed dimension, also does not suffice without one uniform machine and the required universal bounds.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated deterministic algorithm's existence or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation.

A positive answer must establish exact feasibility decisions and the total bit-operation bound for every encoded rational system, including unbounded and lower-dimensional cases. If the method first converts the input to another formulation, its cost, encoding growth and dependence on the number of integer variables must all be accounted for. An optimization algorithm is sufficient only if its proved guarantees include this feasibility task and the specified bound.

A negative answer must rule out every admissible uniform deterministic program and all fixed constants \(C,c\) in the statement. A lower bound conditional on ETH, \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) or another unproved assumption does not establish this unconditional negation. Excluding subexponential time \(2^{o(n)}\) does not exclude the requested single-exponential bound.

A randomized algorithm, an algorithm restricted to bounded coefficients or a special block structure, an approximate integer-feasibility procedure, or a bound exponential in a different parameter does not decide the selected target without a proved extension.

title: Crouzeix’s sharp numerical-range inequality
formal: Does the inequality \[\|p(A)\|_2\le 2\max_{z\in W(A)}|p(z)|\] hold for every integer \(n\ge1\), every complex matrix \(A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\) and every scalar polynomial \(p\in\mathbb C[z]\)?
definitions:
The numerical range is \(W(A)=\{x^*Ax:x\in\mathbb C^n,\ \|x\|_2=1\}\), where \(x^*\) denotes conjugate transpose. The vector norm is Euclidean, and the induced matrix norm is \(\|B\|_2=\max_{\|x\|_2=1}\|Bx\|_2\). For \(p(z)=\sum_{j=0}^m c_jz^j\), set \(p(A)=\sum_{j=0}^m c_jA^j\) with \(A^0=I\). Compactness of \(W(A)\) ensures that the scalar maximum exists.

The constant 2 must work for every dimension, scalar polynomial and matrix, including nonnormal and nondiagonalizable matrices. The inequality is an assertion about complex matrices, with no input-encoding convention. Allowing a matrix of polynomials \([p_{ij}]\) of arbitrary block size yields the stronger complete conjecture.
answer_criterion: A Lean proof of the universal scalar-polynomial inequality establishes the affirmative answer recorded below. Its sharpness follows by taking \(p(z)=z\) and the \(2\times2\) matrix with a single nonzero entry \(J_{12}=1\). Then \(\|J\|_2=1\) and \(\max_{z\in W(J)}|z|=1/2\).

title: Polynomial-time simplex pivot rule
summary: Primal simplex maximizes a rational linear objective by exchanging one entering and one leaving basis column at a time. The question asks for one deterministic rule that reaches an optimality-certifying basis from every supplied feasible basis in polynomial total bit time. Each pivot must have positive entering reduced cost and follow the exact minimum-ratio test, with tied and zero-length degenerate pivots included. The rule may inspect all numerical data and use history, but every computation and basis exchange must fit the same polynomial input-length bound. OpenAI’s diameter lower bound is in the number of facets, while the pivot bound here is in the full binary input length.
formal:
Does there exist one deterministic primal-simplex algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that the following holds for every promised rational input \((A,b,c,B_0)\)? The linear program is
\[\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in\mathbb R^n,\ x\ge0\},\]
where \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) has full row rank, \(1\le m\le n\), the maximum is finite, and \(B_0\) is any supplied feasible basis. Starting at exactly \(B_0\), the algorithm must reach and output a feasible basis \(B_t\) whose nonbasic reduced costs are all nonpositive, using only the legal improving pivots below, in at most \(C(N+1)^d\) total bit operations. Here \(N\) is the binary length of the complete input, including \(B_0\).
definitions:
The input explicitly lists \(m,n\), every entry of \(A,b,c\), and the \(m\) distinct column indices of \(B_0\). Rationals are encoded by signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators; \(N\) includes all entries, signs, dimensions, basis indices and delimiters. The feasible set may be unbounded, but its objective is promised to have a finite maximum. The supplied basis makes it nonempty. There is no nondegeneracy, small-coefficient or conditioning promise. No guarantee is required for inputs violating these promises.

Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A basis \(B\subseteq[n]\) has size \(m\) and invertible submatrix \(A_B\), whose columns are ordered by increasing index. Coordinates of \(x_B\), \(c_B\), and vectors indexed by \(B\) use this same order. Its basic solution \(x(B)\in\mathbb Q^n\) is
\[x(B)_B=A_B^{-1}b,\qquad x(B)_j=0\quad(j\notin B).\]
The basis is feasible exactly when \(x(B)_B\ge0\) coordinatewise. For a nonbasic index \(j\notin B\), its reduced cost is
\[r_j(B)=c_j-c_B^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-1}A_j,\]
where \(A_j\) is column \(j\) of the original matrix.

A legal pivot chooses an entering index \(j\notin B\) with \(r_j(B)>0\). Set \(a=A_B^{-1}A_j\), with coordinates \(a_k\) indexed by \(k\in B\), and set
\[I=\{k\in B:a_k>0\},\qquad
\theta=\min_{k\in I}\frac{x(B)_k}{a_k}.\]
The finite-maximum promise ensures \(I\ne\varnothing\) for such an entering index. Choose any leaving index \(i\in I\) attaining this minimum and replace the current basis by
\[B'=(B\setminus\{i\})\cup\{j\}.\]
This is one pivot. Ties in the ratio test are decided by the algorithm. The new basic solution has coordinate \(\theta\) at \(j\), coordinates \(x(B)_k-\theta a_k\) at the old basic indices, and zero at the other nonbasic indices. If \(\theta=0\), the pivot is degenerate: it changes the basis while keeping the represented point and objective value unchanged. Such pivots are permitted and count in full. A positive step increases the objective by \(\theta r_j(B)\). An exchange with zero or negative entering reduced cost is not a legal pivot here.

The computation is one finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program over fixed finite tape alphabets. Every tape transition counts toward the bit-time bound. There is no advice, oracle or randomization. All arithmetic is exact; arithmetic on long integers or fractions, basis updates, comparisons, preprocessing, helper computations, memory access and output are charged at their bit cost. The program may inspect the entire numerical input and keep any history that fits within its total time bound. In particular, it is not restricted to a local or memoryless choice rule or to ordinal rankings of the entering variables.

At designated pivot events the program maintains a current feasible basis, initially exactly \(B_0\). Its entire sequence \(B_0,B_1,\ldots,B_t\) must follow the exchanges just defined on the supplied \(A,b,c\). Other computations cannot reset this current basis, skip intermediate pivots, alter the objective or constraints, or substitute an extended formulation. The rule may perform charged computations about other bases or auxiliary problems, but they do not themselves move the current basis. The terminal condition is
\[r_j(B_t)\le0\quad\text{for every }j\in[n]\setminus B_t.\]
Together with feasibility this certifies that \(x(B_t)\) is an exact maximizer. Reaching a vertex with optimal objective value is not a substitute for this basis condition. If \(B_0\) already satisfies it, zero pivots are allowed; when \(m=n\), the condition is vacuous. The question concerns optimization from a supplied feasible basis, not phase-I construction of that basis. One program and one pair of constants must serve all inputs and all permitted starting bases.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of such a program, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must verify legality of every basis exchange, feasibility throughout, exact terminal reduced costs and a single worst-case polynomial bound on the complete bit computation, including pivot selection and degenerate steps, for every promised input and initial basis.

A negative proof must rule out every finite deterministic program and every fixed polynomial bound in this model. It may establish unavoidable long paths or unavoidable computation needed to choose pivots, but a lower bound restricted to particular rankings, memory restrictions, one pivot rule, or a nonlinear objective does not establish that universal negation. Merely proving that some short path exists without an efficient uniform algorithm is insufficient for a positive answer. Expected or smoothed time, approximate optimality, and a polynomial number of pivots with unbounded selection cost also do not meet the target. No numerical approximation tolerance applies to this yes/no statement.

title: Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture
summary: A clutter is a finite family of sets with no redundant containing member. Its packing property requires unweighted packing–covering equality in every deletion and contraction minor. The conjecture asks whether this already implies equality for every nonnegative integer capacity vector. Weighted packings may repeat members within those capacities. Recent source results cover finite ground-set sizes and restricted families, while retaining the general question.
formal: Does every finite clutter with the packing property have the max-flow min-cut property? Equivalently, if every deletion/contraction minor satisfies unweighted integral packing–covering equality, must weighted integral packing–covering equality hold for every nonnegative integer weight vector?
definitions:
A clutter \(\mathcal C\) on a finite ground set \(E\) is a family of subsets of \(E\), no one properly containing another. Its original members are nonempty; the empty family is allowed. A cover is a set \(T\subseteq E\) meeting every member, and \(	au(\mathcal C)\) is its minimum cardinality. A packing is a family of pairwise disjoint members; \(
u(\mathcal C)\) is its maximum cardinality. Deleting an element removes it from the ground set and discards all members containing it. Contracting an element removes it from the ground set and from every member, then keeps only inclusion-minimal members. A minor is obtained by any finite sequence of these operations, including the empty sequence. The packing property is \(	au(\mathcal D)=
u(\mathcal D)\) for every minor \(\mathcal D\). For the empty family both numbers are zero. For the degenerate minor \(\{\varnothing\}\), set both numbers to \(+\infty\): no cover exists and arbitrarily many copies of the empty member can be packed. These conventions give no obstruction from degenerate minors. For an original clutter and capacities \(w\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{E}\), define \[	au_w(\mathcal C)=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in T}w_e:T\subseteq E	ext{ is a cover}ight\},\qquad 
u_w(\mathcal C)=\max\left\{\sum_{F\in\mathcal C}y_F:y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{\mathcal C},\ \sum_{F
i e}y_F\le w_e	ext{ for every }e\in Eight\}.\] Multiplicities \(y_F\) allow repeated packed members, and every copy consumes one unit of capacity at each of its elements. Both optima are finite because original members are nonempty. The max-flow min-cut (MFMC) property is equality of these optima for every nonnegative integer capacity vector; the weights and ground-set size have no fixed upper bound.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal implication, or of its logical negation. An affirmative answer must establish \(\tau_w(\mathcal C)=\nu_w(\mathcal C)\) for every clutter with the packing property and every nonnegative integer vector \(w\). A negative answer must exhibit a finite clutter and such a vector with \(\tau_w(\mathcal C)>\nu_w(\mathcal C)\), and verify the packing property for every minor. A finite census, a proper subclass theorem, or fractional duality alone is insufficient.

title: P-matrix linear complementarity in polynomial time
summary: The problem asks for nonnegative rational vectors linked by a linear equation, with at least one zero in each paired coordinate. The input matrix is promised to have every nonempty principal minor strictly positive, which guarantees a unique solution for every right-hand side. The question is whether one deterministic algorithm always finds that exact solution in polynomial time measured in the full binary input length. A complete Lean proof must supply that uniform algorithm and bound or rule out every such polynomial-time algorithm without adding a promise-recognition task. OpenAI’s strongly polynomial algorithm covers monotone linear complementarity, and a P-matrix can have an indefinite symmetric part.
formal:
Does there exist one uniform deterministic algorithm that solves every rational P-matrix linear complementarity problem in polynomial bit time? More precisely, are there a deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, on every explicitly encoded rational input
\[n\in\mathbb N_{>0},\qquad M\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n},\qquad q\in\mathbb Q^n,\]
the machine halts within \(B(N+1)^k\) steps, where \(N\) is the full input length defined below, and whenever \(M\) is a P-matrix it outputs \(z,w\in\mathbb Q^n\) satisfying
\[w=Mz+q,\qquad z_i\ge0,\quad w_i\ge0,\quad z_iw_i=0\quad(1\le i\le n)?\]
A P-matrix has strictly positive determinant for every nonempty principal submatrix. No certificate of this promise is supplied, and the algorithm need not recognize it. The constants \(B,k\) and the program are shared by all dimensions and all rational coefficients.
definitions:
Matrix promise. Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For a nonempty subset \(S\subseteq[n]\), the principal submatrix \(M[S,S]\) consists of the rows and columns with indices in \(S\), both in increasing order. Thus the promise is
\[\operatorname{Pmat}(M)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\forall\varnothing\ne S\subseteq[n],\ \det M[S,S]>0.\]
Here the determinant is the usual alternating sum of products, evaluated exactly over \(\mathbb Q\). Strict positivity is essential. There is no symmetry, sparsity, triangularity, positive-semidefiniteness or nondegeneracy assumption. In particular, a valid solution may have both \(z_i=w_i=0\) in some coordinate.

Equations and output. The matrix product is \((Mz)_i=\sum_{j=1}^nM_{ij}z_j\), and all inequalities use the ordinary rational order. With \(z,w\ge0\), coordinatewise complementarity is equivalent to \(z^Tw=\sum_{i=1}^n z_iw_i=0\). A solution is the complete pair of vectors, with exact rational coordinates. An interval, floating-point vector or small residual is not an exact solution under this task. The guarantee is a search guarantee: returning only a yes/no answer about existence is insufficient.

Binary encoding. To make the bit model definite, encode a nonnegative integer \(t\) by
\[u(t)=1^{b(t)}0\,\operatorname{bin}(t+1),\qquad b(t)=\lfloor\log_2(t+1)\rfloor+1,\]
where \(\operatorname{bin}(t+1)\) is its binary expansion without leading zeroes, of length \(b(t)\). The initial run of ones specifies that length. A rational number is written uniquely as \(p/d\), with \(p\in\mathbb Z\), \(d\in\mathbb N_{>0}\) and \(\gcd(|p|,d)=1\), and is encoded by a sign bit, then \(u(|p|)\), then \(u(d)\). The sign bit is zero for nonnegative \(p\), including zero, and one for negative \(p\). Thus zero uses numerator zero and denominator one. The input concatenates \(u(n)\), all \(n^2\) entries of \(M\) in row-major order, and the \(n\) entries of \(q\). Every entry, including a zero entry, is explicitly present. A syntactically valid input has exactly this form and no trailing bits. Its total binary length is \(N\). The output concatenates the \(n\) rational encodings of \(z\), followed by those of \(w\), in index order; \(n\) is already known from the input. Other usual explicit binary rational encodings are polynomially equivalent to this convention.

Computation. The same finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program is used for every input. One transition costs one step. Reading input, rational arithmetic, comparisons, intermediate representations and writing the entire output are all charged. There are no oracles, real-number unit-cost operations, randomness, nonuniform advice or free preprocessing. The polynomial time bound applies to every syntactically valid rational input, including matrices that fail the P-matrix promise. On those nonpromised inputs any halting output is allowed; detecting a violated principal minor is not required. Behavior on malformed input strings is unrestricted. A polynomial bound only on promised inputs is equivalent for this existence question, since a known polynomial bound can be enforced with a clock and arbitrary output after timeout. The bound may depend polynomially on coefficient bit lengths through \(N\); this is not a demand for a strongly polynomial number of arithmetic operations independent of those lengths.

Quantifier order. The question is \(\exists A\,\exists B,k\,\forall(n,M,q)\) with the time guarantee above and correctness whenever \(\operatorname{Pmat}(M)\). Coefficient magnitudes, dimension, degeneracy and numerical conditioning may vary without restriction; they do not permit selecting a different program or polynomial for each input.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of this algorithm-existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish one program, one polynomial bit-time bound and exact correctness on every promised input, including degenerate instances. Any internal approximation procedure must be proved to recover and output the exact rational solution within that bound. A negative answer must show that every uniform deterministic machine with a polynomial time bound on all syntactically valid rational inputs fails to output the required solution on some P-matrix instance. Exponential examples for one pivot rule, hardness of recognizing P-matrices, a lower bound in a restricted oracle model, or a conditional complexity-theoretic barrier alone do not prove that negation. An algorithm for a proper matrix subclass or with an uncontrolled condition-parameter factor does not establish the positive answer.

title: Polynomial-time integer programming with bounded subdeterminants
summary: The determinant of every square submatrix is bounded by a fixed constant. The matrix may be dense and the number of variables grows with the input. The target is polynomial bit complexity for each fixed determinant bound. Infeasible and unbounded instances require explicit correct outcomes. Known sparse-matrix results have assumptions absent from this card.
formal: For every fixed integer \(\Delta\ge1\), is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for integer linear optimization \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), on inputs for which every square submatrix of A has determinant of absolute value at most \(\Delta\)?
definitions:
The matrix A is integral with m rows and n columns, and b and c are integral vectors of lengths m and n. All entries, signs and dimensions are explicitly encoded in binary; \(N\) is the total input bit length. Every square submatrix of each size 1 through min(m,n) is covered by the determinant promise, including singular submatrices. There is no restriction on the number of nonzero entries per row or column, and n is not fixed.

For each fixed \(\Delta\), the algorithm must run in at most \(C_\Delta(N+1)^{k_\Delta}\) bit operations for constants depending only on \(\Delta\). Thus this is a polynomial-time question for each fixed parameter value, not a strongly polynomial or fixed-parameter-tractable running-time requirement. Correctness is only required on promised matrices; recognizing the promise is not part of the task. The output is INFEASIBLE if no integral feasible point exists, UNBOUNDED if feasible objective values have no lower bound, and otherwise an integral feasible minimizer and its exact objective value. The vectors and values use binary encodings.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithmic existence proof for every fixed Delta with the stated bit-time bounds and all three outcomes, or refute it. An algorithm with an additional row-sparsity restriction or fixed dimension does not settle the question; an obstruction that invokes an additional complexity hypothesis settles the negative answer only if that hypothesis is proved.

title: Linear bound in the flatness theorem
summary: A full-dimensional convex body contains no integer point in its interior. Its width is measured in nonzero integer directions without unit normalization. The conjecture bounds that width by a universal constant times dimension. Boundary integer points and nonsymmetric bodies are allowed. An October 2026 preprint improves the remaining logarithmic factor but does not remove it.
formal: Does a universal real constant C>0 exist such that, for every integer n≥1 and every compact convex set \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) with nonempty interior and \(\operatorname{int}(K)\cap\mathbb Z^n=\varnothing\), its lattice width satisfies \(w(K)\le Cn\)?
definitions: The lattice is the standard integer lattice. For a nonzero integer direction \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), directional width is \(\max_{x\in K}\langle z,x\rangle-\min_{x\in K}\langle z,x\rangle\); lattice width w(K) is the infimum of these widths over all nonzero integer z. Directions are not normalized to Euclidean unit length. Compactness makes the extrema finite; full dimensionality excludes empty-interior degeneracies. Integer points on the boundary are allowed. No symmetry, polyhedral representation, rationality or smoothness is assumed. C is independent of n and K. This is an existence bound, not a request to compute the smallest C.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a universal linear bound, or prove its negation by showing that for every C>0 some admissible dimension and body have width exceeding Cn. Improving the logarithmic factor without removing it does not settle the target.

title: Limited-memory convex optimization
summary: First-order convex optimization learns about an objective through queries returning its value and a subgradient. The source asks how the number of queries needed for a prescribed accuracy changes when the algorithm has limited working memory. It highlights methods with strong oracle complexity whose stored geometric information can require quadratic space in dimension. The question is whether that memory cost is inherent or can be traded away without losing the optimal query rate. A sharp tradeoff would distinguish information acquired from the oracle from information that must remain available between optimization steps.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the deterministic first-order oracle complexity \(T(d,M,\varepsilon)\) of minimizing a globally convex, Euclidean \(1\)-Lipschitz function with a global minimizer in the unit ball, when only \(M\) bits can be retained between queries. The target is the entire tradeoff for integers \(d\geq1\), \(M\geq0\) and real \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/4\), including the parameters for which \(T(d,M,\varepsilon)=\infty\).
definitions: Let \(\mathcal F_d\) contain all convex functions \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) such that \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq\|x-y\|_2\) for every \(x,y\), and such that some global minimizer \(x_*\) satisfies \(\|x_*\|_2\leq1\). A subgradient at \(x\) is a vector \(g\) with \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\) for every \(y\in\mathbb R^d\). A query at any \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) returns the exact pair \((f(x),g)\) for any valid subgradient; correctness is required for every sequence of such choices. An \(M\)-bit, \(t\)-query algorithm consists of deterministic maps \(\phi_i:\{0,1\}^M\to\mathbb R^d\), \(\psi_i:\{0,1\}^M\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\to\{0,1\}^M\) for \(1\leq i\leq t\), and \(\zeta:\{0,1\}^M\to\mathbb R^d\). Starting with \(s_0=0^M\), it queries \(x_i=\phi_i(s_{i-1})\), receives \((f(x_i),g_i)\), and sets \(s_i=\psi_i(s_{i-1},f(x_i),g_i)\). Its final output is \(\zeta(s_t)\); for \(t=0\) it is \(\zeta(s_0)\). All maps may depend on \(d,M,t,\varepsilon\), but not on the unknown function. They are unrestricted mathematical maps: computing an update can use arbitrary real operations and temporary memory. Only the retained state is limited; there is no runtime, uniformity or computability requirement on these maps. The iteration index is implicit in the maps and is not charged to memory. Define \(R(d,M,t)=\inf_A\sup_{f\in\mathcal F_d,\,(g_i)}[f(\zeta(s_t))-\min_x f(x)]\), and \(T(d,M,\varepsilon)=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:R(d,M,t)\leq\varepsilon\}\), with the minimum of the empty set equal to infinity. The infimum over algorithms need not be attained: \(R\leq\varepsilon\) means that for every \(\eta>0\) some algorithm has worst-case error at most \(\varepsilon+\eta\). Queries and outputs are not restricted to the unit ball.
answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular characterization \(G(d,M,\varepsilon)\in[0,\infty]\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of \(cG\leq T\leq CG\) throughout the stated domain, for fixed \(c,C>0\). Prove exactly which parameters have infinite complexity. The memory argument and requested accuracy must be those stated, without an unstated constant enlargement of memory or accuracy. Upper bounds must respect the infimum convention. Resolving only optimal-query memory requirements or one accuracy regime is not a characterization of the full tradeoff.

title: Smale’s seventh problem
summary: Smale's seventh problem concerns placing N points on the unit sphere so that their logarithmic interaction energy is nearly minimal. The target is an algorithm running in time polynomial in N. Its output energy may exceed the global minimum by only a universal constant times log N. This is an additive energy guarantee, which requires more precise control than merely producing visually well-distributed points. A construction with a rigorous bound would connect efficient computation with the equilibrium behavior of many mutually repelling particles on a curved surface.
formal: Do there exist real constants \(C,K>0\), an integer \(k\ge1\), and one deterministic real-number algorithm \(A\) in the model below such that, for every integer \(N\ge2\), \(A(N)\) outputs distinct points \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\in S^2\) in at most \(KN^k\) operations and satisfies \(E_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\le E_N^{\ast}+C\ln N\)?
definitions: Let \(S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2=1\}\). For distinct points define \(E_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N)=-\sum_{i\ne j}\ln\|x_i-x_j\|_2\), counting ordered pairs; configurations with collisions have energy \(+\infty\). Let \(E_N^{\ast}\) be the infimum over all \(N\)-tuples on \(S^2\). Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm and \(\|\cdot\|_2\) is Euclidean distance. Use one deterministic finite real-arithmetic program with a fixed finite list of real constants independent of \(N\). The machine has exact real registers, finite control and tapes; each scalar copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero register, sign test, or tape movement costs one operation. It may allocate storage, charging the operations that use it, and has no primitive logarithm, square root, floor, randomness or optimization oracle. The input integer \(N\) is supplied as one exact real value. Output is the explicit list of \(3N\) coordinates, all required to lie exactly on the sphere. Time is polynomial in \(N\), not in \(\log N\); this is a real-number computation model, not a bit-cost model. The energy inequality is a mathematical condition on the output, and the machine need not evaluate that energy.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of one permitted real-arithmetic program and constants \(C,K,k\), independent of \(N\), satisfying both the time and energy guarantees for every integer \(N\ge2\), or prove in Lean that no such program and constants exist. The output must lie exactly on the sphere. Expected energy under a distribution, finitely many solved cardinalities, or a larger asymptotic additive error does not meet this criterion.

title: Woodall’s conjecture
summary: A dicut is a nonempty one-way boundary in a directed graph, and a dijoin is a set of arcs meeting every dicut. The smallest dicut bounds how many pairwise disjoint dijoins can exist. Woodall’s conjecture states that this bound is always attained in the unweighted setting. The card allows parallel arcs, fixes the nontrivial connectivity regime and keeps the statement separate from the false weighted generalization. A proof or counterexample would settle a longstanding integral packing–covering equality beyond known constant-factor and graph-class results.
formal: For every finite weakly connected loopless directed multigraph \(D\) that is not strongly connected, let \(\tau(D)\) be the minimum size of a directed cut. Do there exist \(\tau(D)\) pairwise arc-disjoint dijoins in \(D\)? All arcs have unit capacity, and a dijoin must meet every directed cut. Equivalently, can the arcs be colored with \(\tau(D)\) colors so that every directed cut contains every color?
definitions:
A directed multigraph is a finite vertex set \(V\), a finite set \(A\) of individually distinguished arcs, and two maps \(\operatorname{tail},\operatorname{head}:A\to V\). For every arc its tail differs from its head. Parallel arcs and arcs in both directions between the same vertices are allowed. Weak connectivity means that every two vertices are connected after forgetting arc directions. Strong connectivity means that every ordered pair of vertices is joined by a directed path, including a path of length zero from a vertex to itself. The graph is assumed weakly connected and not strongly connected, so in particular it has at least two vertices.

For \(\varnothing\ne U\subsetneq V\), define
\[
\delta^+(U)=\{a\in A:\operatorname{tail}(a)\in U,\ \operatorname{head}(a)\notin U\},
\qquad
\delta^-(U)=\{a\in A:\operatorname{tail}(a)\notin U,\ \operatorname{head}(a)\in U\}.
\]
A directed cut, also called a dicut, is \(\delta^+(U)\) for such a set \(U\) with \(\delta^-(U)=\varnothing\). The hypotheses ensure that the family of dicuts is nonempty and none of its members is empty. Thus
\[
\tau(D)=\min\{|\delta^+(U)|:\varnothing\ne U\subsetneq V,\ \delta^-(U)=\varnothing\}
\]
is a well-defined positive integer. Parallel arcs are counted separately.

A dijoin is a subset \(J\subseteq A\) such that \(J\cap B\ne\varnothing\) for every dicut \(B\). A family \(J_1,\ldots,J_{\tau(D)}\) is pairwise arc-disjoint when \(J_i\cap J_j=\varnothing\) for all \(i\ne j\). It need not cover all arcs. No arc has a weight, capacity zero or capacity greater than one. This is an existence assertion, without an algorithm, running-time bound, randomness, approximation or restricted graph class.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that every graph in the stated domain has \(\tau(D)\) pairwise arc-disjoint dijoins, or exhibit a finite graph in that domain and give a complete Lean proof that no such family exists. The target is the universal min–max assertion; it is not a numerical approximation to a packing value. A constant-fraction guarantee, a fractional packing, a theorem for a proper subclass or a counterexample requiring zero-capacity arcs does not settle it.

title: Superpolynomial semidefinite extension complexity of perfect matching
summary: The perfect-matching polytope is the convex hull of the incidence vectors of perfect matchings in a complete graph of even order. A semidefinite lift represents that polytope exactly as an affine image of an affine slice of a real positive semidefinite cone. The question asks whether the required matrix order is unbounded by every polynomial in the number of graph vertices, allowing arbitrary real coefficients and separate representations at each size. Exponential bounds for linear lifts and coordinate-symmetric semidefinite formulations leave this unrestricted representation question unresolved in the checked sources. A complete Lean proof must establish the full lower-bound assertion or prove that one polynomial bounds exact semidefinite lifts for the entire family.
formal:
Is the semidefinite extension complexity of the perfect-matching polytopes of complete graphs unbounded by every polynomial in the number of vertices? Precisely, is
\[
\forall B,b\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\quad
\exists n\in\mathbb N\quad
\bigl(n\ge2\ \land\ 2\mid n\ \land\
\operatorname{xc}_{\mathrm{SDP}}(P_n)>Bn^b\bigr)
\]
true, for the exact real semidefinite lifts defined below?

This is a statement about the existence of representations, with arbitrary real coefficients and no symmetry or efficient-construction requirement. The quantifiers ask whether no single polynomial bounds the entire family; they do not require a specified exponential rate or a lower bound holding at every sufficiently large even size. Integer constants express the same assertion as the inherited formulation with every pair of positive real constants \(C,c\).
definitions:
For each even integer \(n\ge2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let
\[
E_n=\{\{i,j\}:i,j\in[n],\ i<j\},
\]
and let \(K_n=([n],E_n)\) be the finite simple undirected complete graph. A perfect matching is a subset \(M\subseteq E_n\) in which every vertex belongs to exactly one edge. Its incidence vector \(\chi^M\in\mathbb R^{E_n}\) has coordinate one on edges in \(M\) and zero on all other edges. Define
\[
P_n=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^M:M\text{ is a perfect matching of }K_n\}.
\]
The convex hull of a finite set consists of all weighted sums of its elements with nonnegative real weights summing to one. Thus \(P_n\) includes exactly those convex combinations, with one coordinate for each of the \(\binom n2\) edges.

For a positive integer \(r\), let
\[
\mathbb S^r=\{Y\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}:Y^{\mathsf T}=Y\},
\qquad
\mathbb S^r_+=\{Y\in\mathbb S^r:\forall z\in\mathbb R^r,\ z^{\mathsf T}Yz\ge0\}.
\]
An affine subspace of \(\mathbb S^r\) is a translate of a real linear subspace. An affine map into \(\mathbb R^{E_n}\) has the form \(\pi(Y)=A(Y)+a\), with \(A\) real linear and \(a\in\mathbb R^{E_n}\). A size-\(r\) semidefinite lift of \(P_n\) is a pair \((L,\pi)\), where \(L\subseteq\mathbb S^r\) is an affine subspace and \(\pi:\mathbb S^r\to\mathbb R^{E_n}\) is affine, satisfying the exact equality
\[
P_n=\pi(L\cap\mathbb S^r_+).
\]
The quantity \(\operatorname{xc}_{\mathrm{SDP}}(P_n)\) is the least positive integer \(r\) admitting such a pair. Every finite polytope has a finite such representation, so this minimum exists. Restricting sizes to positive integers also fixes the convention for the singleton \(P_2\).

Size means the order of this single positive semidefinite matrix, not the number of scalar entries or inequalities. If several positive semidefinite blocks are used, their block-diagonal combination counts their total order. Coefficients of \(L\) and \(\pi\) may be arbitrary real numbers. No bit-length bound, computability condition, uniform algorithm producing the representations, or efficient numerical procedure is imposed. The lifted feasible set need not be bounded or strictly feasible. No invariance under permutations of graph vertices or matrix coordinates is required. The condition \(Y^{\mathsf T}=Y\) is ordinary matrix symmetry and does not impose such an invariance requirement. Approximate outer representations do not meet the exact equality.

The inherited card uses affine projection maps. The cited survey defines lifts using linear projection maps; these conventions differ by at most one in matrix order and hence give the same polynomial-boundedness question. The original thesis asks about the polytope of all matchings, including nonperfect ones. Its family has polynomial-size exact semidefinite lifts if and only if the complete-graph perfect-matching family does, so the retained target is a polynomially equivalent formulation of the source question, not a claim that those polytopes are identical.
answer_criterion:
Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated proposition or its full logical negation, for exactly the objects and size convention above.

A positive answer must prove that for every \(B,b\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) there is an even \(n\ge2\) for which no exact semidefinite lift has matrix order at most \(Bn^b\). This includes all real affine slices and affine projection maps, without imposing symmetry, uniformity, strict feasibility or coefficient restrictions.

A negative answer must prove
\[
\exists B,b\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\quad
\forall n\ge2\text{ with }2\mid n\quad
\exists r\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists L\subseteq\mathbb S^r\ \exists\pi:\mathbb S^r\to\mathbb R^{E_n}\quad
\bigl(r\le Bn^b\ \land\ L\text{ is affine}\ \land\pi\text{ is affine}\
\land\ P_n=\pi(L\cap\mathbb S^r_+)\bigr).
\]
The polynomial is common to all sizes, while the representations may depend arbitrarily on \(n\); an efficient construction algorithm is not additionally required.

A lower bound for linear lifts, coordinate-symmetric semidefinite formulations, a fixed relaxation hierarchy, or a restricted coefficient field is insufficient by itself. An approximation result or an efficient matching algorithm is not an exact semidefinite representation. Conditional results must also establish any extra hypothesis needed for the unconditional target. This is an asymptotic representation-existence proposition, so no additive numerical tolerance replaces its quantified bounds.

title: Nearly quadratic oracle complexity for convex-body volume
summary: A convex body is known only through membership answers and concentric ball bounds. The goal is a constant-relative-error estimate of its volume with constant success probability. The target is nearly quadratic expected classical query complexity, including queries used for rounding. Checked general upper bounds remain larger, while a recent preprint gives a nearly quadratic lower bound. The question asks for the optimal information scale of high-dimensional volume estimation.
formal: Is there a randomized classical membership-oracle algorithm such that, for every fixed \(a\ge1\), every \(n\ge2\), and every convex body \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) with \(B_2^n\subseteq K\subseteq n^a B_2^n\), it returns \(V\) satisfying \[\Pr[|V-\operatorname{vol}_n(K)|\le\operatorname{vol}_n(K)/10]\ge2/3\] using at most \(C_a n^2(\log(2+n))^{c_a}\) membership queries in expectation? The polynomial-radius promise and origin are supplied; no isotropic position or uniform-sampling oracle is given.
definitions:
A convex body is a compact convex set with nonempty interior, and \(B_2^n=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_2\le1\}\). Volume means n-dimensional Lebesgue measure. More generally, supplied concentric radii \(r,R\) and center \(z\), with \(R/r\le n^a\), can be rescaled to this normalization; volume scales by \(r^n\). The exponent \(a\) is fixed independently of dimension, and the constants may depend on it.

The only access to the unknown body is the exact bit indicating whether a queried real point belongs to \(K\), including its boundary. Queries can be adaptive and randomized. The information model permits measurable choices of exact real points and arbitrary measurable computation between queries, all of which are uncharged. Every membership answer costs one query. No separation, optimization, boundary, quantum-superposition or conditional-sampling oracle is available. Randomness belongs to the algorithm; the body itself is adversarially fixed.

The algorithm must terminate almost surely. Both its expected query bound and success guarantee hold for each eligible body. An expected bound is the selected interpretation of oracle complexity, rather than a bound on every random tape. Preprocessing, rounding and production of auxiliary samples must pay for all membership queries they use. In particular, one cannot assume an isotropic transformation has already been found for free.

The relative accuracy \(1/10\) and probability \(2/3\) are fixed constants in the computational task. The TCS500 benchmark's absolute \(1/100\) rule for numerical answers does not replace this algorithmic success condition. The target bounds information from the oracle, not total arithmetic operations or the bit length needed to represent continuously distributed query points.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of an algorithm with the stated uniform relative-accuracy and expected-query guarantees, or its negation in the classical query model. A bound assuming free isotropic rounding, a quantum algorithm, or an estimate for a constant-dimensional high-precision regime does not suffice. A matching-order lower bound alone does not prove the requested upper bound.

title: CLS versus FP
summary: CLS describes total search tasks motivated by continuous local improvement. The source proves that it is exactly the intersection of PPAD and PLS, two classes based on different existence principles. The equivalent discrete question gives one succinct path problem and one succinct local-search problem and asks for a solution to either. The requested algorithm must be deterministic and polynomial in the length of both circuit descriptions. A resolution would determine whether the common part of these two search classes is computationally tractable.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{CLS}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}\)? Equivalently, does a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm solve the following Either-Solution problem: given an End-of-Line instance and an independent Localopt instance, return a valid solution of at least one of them?
definitions:
Every circuit is an explicitly encoded acyclic Boolean circuit with fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}, \mathrm{NOT}\), constants, listed wires and ordered input/output nodes. An End-of-Line instance consists of \(S,P:\{0,1\}^{n}	o \{0,1\}^{n}, n\ge 1\), satisfying \(P(0^{n})=0^{n}\) and \(S(0^{n})
e 0^{n}\). An accepted output is a bit string \(v\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) with \(P(S(v))
e v\), or with both \(v
e 0^{n}\) and \(S(P(v))
e v\). In particular \(v=0^{n}\) is permitted only for the first condition. A Localopt instance consists of \(T:\{0,1\}^{m}	o \{0,1\}^{m}\) and \(V:\{0,1\}^{m}	o \{0,1\}^{r}\), with \(m,r\ge 1\). Treat V’s output as an unsigned binary integer; an accepted local-search output is w with \(V(T(w))\ge V(w)\). The joint instance contains both independent sets of circuits; n,m,r may differ. A solution is a tag selecting one instance and a string meeting that instance’s condition. On malformed encodings or failure of the two easily checkable End-of-Line conditions, output INVALID; on a valid joint instance INVALID is forbidden. The algorithm must halt within one fixed polynomial in the combined encoded length, including all circuit input/output nodes. It receives no advice, randomness or oracle. Total NP search problems are polynomially bounded input-output relations with polynomial-time verifiable outputs and at least one output for each input. A reduction maps an input to an instance and transforms every valid answer back to a valid original answer, using deterministic polynomial time for both maps. PPAD and PLS are the classes reducing to End-of-Line and Localopt respectively. The source proves that the either-solution problem is complete for their intersection and that CLS=PPAD∩PLS. These equalities give the stated equivalent discrete formulation of \(\mathrm{CLS}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}\); no new smoothness or numerical promise is introduced.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one uniform deterministic algorithm always returns a permitted answer within a fixed polynomial in the combined input bit length, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Solving both component instances is not required. A restricted-circuit algorithm, a randomized algorithm alone, or a conditional hardness implication does not establish either unconditional answer to \(\mathrm{CLS}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}\).

title: Polynomial-time linear convergence for geodesically convex optimization
summary: Geodesically convex optimization replaces straight segments with shortest paths on a Riemannian manifold. The question asks for a deterministic first-order algorithm with query complexity polynomial in dimension and logarithmic in inverse accuracy. It also requires polynomial arithmetic work per query, so a powerful but computationally intractable geometric oracle would not suffice. The source develops an ellipsoid-like approach for constant-curvature spaces and identifies obstacles on more general manifolds. A solution would extend the efficient precision dependence of Euclidean convex optimization to curved spaces while respecting the cost of manipulating their geometry.
formal: In the geometric arithmetic model below, is there a deterministic first-order algorithm and absolute constants \(C,a,b>0\) that minimize every Lipschitz geodesically convex function on a strongly geodesically convex ball in a complete Riemannian manifold, using at most \(C(d+\zeta)^a\lceil\log(2/\varepsilon)\rceil\) objective-oracle queries and at most \(C(d+\zeta)^b\) additional operations between consecutive queries? Here \(d\) is the manifold dimension, \(\zeta=r\sqrt K/\tanh(r\sqrt K)\), with value one at \(K=0\), and the required additive objective error is \(\varepsilon Lr\). The same polynomial overhead bound applies before the first query and after the last.
definitions: The input consists of a complete connected smooth \(d\)-dimensional Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\), \(d\geq1\), a reference point \(x_0\), a radius \(r>0\), a Lipschitz bound \(L>0\), a sectional-curvature bound \(K\geq0\), and real \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\). All sectional curvatures lie in \([-K,K]\). The distance \(\operatorname{dist}\) is the infimum of lengths of connecting curves in the given Riemannian metric. The closed ball \(D=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x_0,x)\leq r\}\) is promised strongly geodesically convex: every two points of \(D\) have a unique minimizing geodesic in \(\mathcal M\), and its whole segment lies in \(D\). If \(\gamma\) is such a segment parametrized on \([0,1]\) at constant speed, the unknown function \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) satisfies \(f(\gamma(t))\leq(1-t)f(\gamma(0))+tf(\gamma(1))\), and \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\operatorname{dist}(x,y)\). A function query at \(x\in D\) returns \(f(x)\) exactly and any tangent vector \(g\in T_x\mathcal M\) satisfying \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\rangle_x\) for every \(y\in D\); correctness is required for every valid sequence of returned subgradients. Here \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\) is the initial velocity at time zero of the unit-time minimizing geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\). Only functions and subgradient oracles meeting these conditions are inputs. The output must be a point \(\widehat x\in D\) with \(f(\widehat x)-\min_D f\leq\varepsilon Lr\). Completeness makes the closed bounded ball compact, so this minimum exists. The algorithm has no access to a formula for \(f\). For computational access to geometry, points and tangent vectors are exact typed objects supplied by a geometric oracle; the input includes an orthonormal basis of \(T_{x_0}\mathcal M\). The available geometric operations are: distance between points; inner product of two vectors in one tangent space; linear combination of such vectors; \(\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)\), the time-one point of the geodesic with initial velocity \(v\); \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\) for \(x,y\in D\); and parallel transport of a tangent vector along the explicitly specified geodesic \(t\mapsto\operatorname{Exp}_x(tv)\), \(0\leq t\leq1\). Each such operation is charged \((d+1)^3\) units, irrespective of point or vector magnitude. Object storage and access cost one unit; objects cannot be inspected except by these operations. Exact real scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, square root on nonnegative arguments, exponential, logarithm on positive arguments, comparisons and integer indexing operations each cost one unit. There is no floor or extraction of bits from a real register. All computation, including geometric operations, is charged apart from the separately counted function queries. One uniform finite program must work for every admissible manifold, basis, oracle and parameter tuple. There is no randomization, integral oracle, convex-hull oracle or free optimization subroutine.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm with the required uniform objective accuracy, logarithmic query dependence on inverse accuracy, and polynomial overhead independent of inverse accuracy, or prove that no such algorithm exists in the stated access model. A query bound with an uncomputable geometric step, a theorem only for a particular manifold, or an additional logarithmic factor in the query count does not meet the target. A negative result must allow the full list of geometric primitives provided here.

title: Optimal approximation for nonmonotone submodular maximization over a matroid
summary: The input is a nonnegative submodular set function and one matroid, accessed through exact value and independence oracles. The goal is to choose an independent set with a large objective value, even though adding elements can reduce that value. The target is the supremum of expected approximation factors achievable by a uniform randomized algorithm using polynomially many total oracle-model operations. The checked literature gives a 0.401 approximation and a 0.478 value-query barrier, with the general gap explicitly retained in a March 2026 source. A benchmark answer must determine that optimal real ratio within 1/100 and prove the claimed accuracy in Lean without assuming that the supremum is attained.
formal:
Determine the optimal expected approximation ratio for maximizing a nonnegative, not necessarily monotone submodular set function subject to one matroid independence constraint, in the polynomial-time oracle model specified below.

For an instance \(J=(n,f,\mathcal I)\), write
\[
\operatorname{OPT}(J)=\max\{f(S):S\in\mathcal I\}.
\]
Let \(\mathscr A\) be the class of uniform randomized oracle algorithms defined below: each always outputs an independent set and has a polynomial bound on its total number of elementary operations, on every valid instance and every random tape. Define
\[
\mathcal R=\left\{\alpha\in[0,1]:
 \exists A\in\mathscr A\ \forall J\
 \mathbb E_{\omega}\!\left[f\!\left(A^{f,\mathcal I}(n;\omega)\right)\right]
 \ge \alpha\,\operatorname{OPT}(J)\right\},
\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}=\sup\mathcal R.
\]
The universal quantifier ranges over every finite ground-set size, every nonnegative submodular function on that ground set, and every matroid on it. The approximation constant and algorithm are chosen before the instance. The target is the real number \(\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\); it is not assumed that an algorithm attains the supremum. Supply a real answer \(a\) with a Lean-checked proof that
\[
|a-\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}|\le \frac{1}{100}.
\]
definitions:
For \(n\in\mathbb N_{0}\), the ground set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\), and \(2^{[n]}\) denotes its power set. The objective is a function \(f:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) satisfying
\[
f(S)+f(T)\ge f(S\cup T)+f(S\cap T)
\quad\text{for all }S,T\subseteq[n].
\]
This is submodularity. Monotonicity would additionally require \(f(S)\le f(T)\) whenever \(S\subseteq T\); no such requirement is imposed. Nonnegativity applies to every subset, including infeasible ones. No normalization \(f(\varnothing)=0\) is required.

A matroid independence family \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^{[n]}\) satisfies three axioms: \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\); every subset of an element of \(\mathcal I\) belongs to \(\mathcal I\); and if \(S,T\in\mathcal I\) with \(|S|<|T|\), then some \(t\in T\setminus S\) satisfies \(S\cup\{t\}\in\mathcal I\). An output is any set in \(\mathcal I\), and need not be maximal. The rank, defined as \(\max_{S\in\mathcal I}|S|\), is unrestricted. A cardinality constraint is the special case \(\mathcal I=\{S:|S|\le k\}\).

The input explicitly supplies the integer \(n\) in binary, with zero represented by the single bit zero. Sets supplied to or returned by an oracle are represented by their \(n\)-bit incidence vectors. Two exact oracles are available: a value oracle returns the real number \(f(S)\), and an independence oracle returns the bit indicating whether \(S\in\mathcal I\). The oracles remain fixed throughout a run. Neither the full table of \(f\) nor a list of all independent sets is supplied, and there is no oracle for a continuous extension, its derivatives, or an optimum.

Fix the following exact-real oracle computation convention. An algorithm is one finite program with finite control, finitely many ordinary bit tapes and finitely many tapes of exact real cells. It may contain finitely many rational constants, each specified by a signed integer numerator and a positive integer denominator. Initially work tapes are blank or zero. Elementary instructions are ordinary bit-tape read/write and one-cell head moves; one-cell real-tape head moves; copying or loading a real cell; addition, subtraction, multiplication or division of a fixed finite number of currently addressed real cells; exact comparison of two such cells; obtaining one independent fair random bit; or one of the two oracle calls. Each instruction costs one operation. Division must have a nonzero divisor on every valid run. The query incidence vector must already have been written on the query tape; reading and writing its bits are charged by the bit-tape instructions. An oracle answer is deposited in a designated real cell or bit cell in one operation. Outputting the final incidence vector is also charged. Real cells have no instruction for inspecting a binary expansion or converting an arbitrary real directly into an integer.

This is a unit-cost exact-arithmetic oracle model: the size parameter is \(n\), and real answers are not charged by a bit length. All computation between queries is counted. Programs have no advice depending on \(n\) or the instance, no arbitrary real constants, and no other oracles. This explicit convention completes the source's polynomial-time/value-oracle formulation; it does not assert equivalence to a bit-complexity model for rational objectives.

Formally, \(A\in\mathscr A\) means that there are integers \(C\ge1\) and \(q\ge0\), fixed for that program, such that for every valid \(J=(n,f,\mathcal I)\) and every random tape \(\omega\), the program makes only valid operations and queries, halts within \(C(n+1)^q\) elementary operations, and outputs an \(n\)-bit vector encoding a member of \(\mathcal I\). Thus both its number of oracle queries and its other work are polynomially bounded. No feasibility error is allowed. The expectation in the guarantee concerns objective value, not feasibility or running time.

The random tape consists of independent fair bits, so each specified prefix of length \(r\) has probability \(2^{-r}\). For a program with the above clock, at most \(C(n+1)^q\) bits are read; its expected value is consequently a finite average over that many fair bits, with unused bits ignored. If \(\operatorname{OPT}(J)=0\), the multiplicative guarantee is automatically satisfied; no quotient by zero is used. Always returning the empty set guarantees factor zero, so \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty and its supremum is well-defined in \([0,1]\).
answer_criterion:
Supply a specified real number \(a\), or an unambiguous expression defining it, and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of
\[
|a-\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}|\le \frac{1}{100}
\]
for exactly the instance class and algorithm class above. Merely restating the supremum that defines \(\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\) is not a determination.

A certified interval is sufficient: give \(l,u\in[0,1]\), prove
\[
l\le\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\le u,\qquad u-l\le\frac{1}{50},
\]
and use \(a=(l+u)/2\). To make explicit what both sides mean, the lower bound can be certified by proving
\[
\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists A\in\mathscr A\
\forall J\
\mathbb E_{\omega}[f(A^{f,\mathcal I}(n;\omega))]
\ge(l-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(J).
\]
The upper bound can be certified by proving
\[
\forall\varepsilon>0\ \forall A\in\mathscr A\
\exists J\
\mathbb E_{\omega}[f(A^{f,\mathcal I}(n;\omega))]
<(u+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(J).
\]
Membership in \(\mathscr A\) includes the full program, uniform polynomial clock and unconditional feasibility requirements from the definitions. In the lower statement the program and its polynomial constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(J\); the upper statement ranges over every such program and all possible polynomial degrees. This permits approaching a supremum without attaining it.

Exact determination is welcome but is not mandatory. A guarantee for a subclass of matroids or objectives, for deterministic algorithms alone, or for polynomially many queries with unrestricted computation does not by itself determine this target. Nor does an upper bound assuming an unproved complexity separation constitute the unconditional upper certificate above.

title: Superlinear randomized query lower bounds for submodular minimization
summary: A value oracle answers exact evaluations of an unknown submodular set function. The randomized algorithm must find a true global minimizer on every input with constant success probability. The question asks whether the worst-case query requirement grows faster than every constant multiple of the ground-set size. Neither numeric evaluation cost nor local computation is charged. Known deterministic and parallel-round lower bounds do not settle this randomized total-query question.
formal: Let \(R(n)\) be the minimum worst-case number of value-oracle queries needed by a randomized algorithm to find an exact minimizer of every real-valued submodular function on \(n\) elements, with success probability at least \(2/3\). Is \(R(n)=\omega(n)\), meaning \(R(n)/n\to\infty\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
definitions: The ground set is \([n]\), and a function \(F:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) is submodular if \(F(A)+F(B)\geq F(A\cup B)+F(A\cap B)\) for all subsets \(A,B\). No monotonicity, nonnegativity, symmetry or normalization is promised. A query specifies any subset \(S\) and receives its exact real value \(F(S)\). The algorithm may adapt later queries to all previous values and its own random choices. Its final answer is a subset \(S_*\) satisfying \(F(S_*)\leq F(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq[n]\); any minimizer is acceptable, including the empty or full set. For every fixed valid oracle \(F\), the probability of a correct output is at least \(2/3\). In the definition of \(R(n)\), a cost bound \(q\) requires at most \(q\) oracle calls on every input and every outcome of the random choices, not just in expectation. Arbitrary finite local computation and exact operations on the oracle answers are free. The algorithm has no direct access to a formula, table or circuit for \(F\). We use classical randomized query complexity: for each dimension, random coins select a deterministic adaptive query procedure, independently of \(F\); the maps and distributions must define measurable success events. An algorithm may depend on \(n\), so lower bounds also apply to nonuniform choices. The value magnitudes and their bit encodings do not enter the query cost. Exhaustively querying all \(2^n\) subsets shows that \(R(n)\) is finite. A superlinear lower bound means that for each real constant \(C>0\), all sufficiently large \(n\) satisfy \(R(n)>Cn\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked superlinear lower bound in the specified randomized bounded-query model. Alternatively prove the negation of that growth statement: a fixed constant C and infinitely many dimensions admit correct algorithms using at most Cn queries. An O(n)-query algorithm for all dimensions would suffice for a negative answer but is stronger than the logical negation. A deterministic lower bound, a lower bound on parallel rounds, or hardness only for finding a nonempty proper minimizer does not establish the target.

title: Input-sparsity relative spectral low-rank approximation
summary: Spectral low-rank approximation seeks a rank-k representation whose largest directional error is near the best possible. The source asks for a relative-error guarantee in time equal to reading the nonzero matrix entries plus a term linear in n and polynomial in k over epsilon. That speed is available in the cited comparison for Frobenius error, which aggregates squared errors instead of controlling the worst direction. The spectral target is therefore substantially stronger. A solution would make sparse-matrix compression fast while protecting against a large error concentrated in one singular direction.
formal: Is there a randomized algorithm and absolute constants \(C,b>0\) that, for every real \(n\times n\) matrix \(A\), integer \(1\leq k<n\) and rational \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\), returns \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}\) with orthonormal columns such that \[\|A-ZZ^{\mathsf T}A\|_2\leq(1+\varepsilon)\min_{\operatorname{rank}(B)\leq k}\|A-B\|_2\] with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(C\operatorname{nnz}(A)+Cn(k/\varepsilon)^b\) operations?
