definitions: The matrix is given as a list of its nonzero entries, each with its row index, column index and real value; unspecified entries are zero and index pairs do not repeat. The integer \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)\) is the length of this list. The spectral norm is \(\|D\|_2=\sup_{\|x\|_2=1}\|Dx\|_2\). For singular values \(\sigma_1(A)\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_n(A)\geq0\), the optimum on the right is \(\sigma_{k+1}(A)\). Orthonormality means \(Z^{\mathsf T}Z=I_k\), so \(ZZ^{\mathsf T}\) is an orthogonal projection of rank \(k\). The output is the explicit matrix \(Z\); forming the generally dense product \(ZZ^{\mathsf T}A\) is not required. All real input matrices are included, with no gap, conditioning, spectral-decay, positivity or distributional promise. If \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\leq k\), the required residual is exactly zero on a successful run. The selected arithmetic model is a uniform real RAM with unit-cost addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, square root of a nonnegative value, real comparison, and indexed memory access. Registers store exact reals or integer indices; integer indexing arithmetic is charged, and no real-to-integer floor or bit extraction is a free primitive. Independent fair random bits and independent standard normal real samples are available at unit cost. This explicitly adopts the ideal arithmetic and sampling convention used in randomized numerical linear algebra; bit complexity is not the target. The operation bound includes reading the input, all preprocessing, random sampling and writing the output, and must hold on every random run. Only correctness may fail with probability at most one third, separately for each fixed input. A single algorithm and the same constants work for all parameters; \(n\geq2\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proofs of its probability guarantee and stated arithmetic running time, or prove that no such algorithm exists in this model. The coefficient of the nonzero-entry term must be an absolute constant: multiplying that term by k, inverse accuracy or logarithms of n misses the target. Frobenius-norm error, additive spectral error, extra output rank, or a bound conditional on a singular-value gap does not establish the displayed claim.

title: Gap-entropy conjecture
summary: The arms have independent Gaussian rewards with unit variance and a unique best mean. The benchmark averages expected sample cost over arm relabelings and takes an infimum over globally correct algorithms. The conjecture predicts that cost from the total inverse-square gaps and the entropy of their scale distribution. It differs from asking one algorithm to attain the benchmark on all instances without an adaptation cost. A 9 September 2026 preprint claims the precise formula; its proof has not been independently certified in this review.
formal: Are there absolute constants \(0<c\leq C<\infty\) such that, for every Gaussian best-arm instance \(I\) defined below and every \(0<\delta<1/10\), \[cH(I)\bigl(\log(1/\delta)+\operatorname{Ent}(I)\bigr)\leq L(I,\delta)\leq CH(I)\bigl(\log(1/\delta)+\operatorname{Ent}(I)\bigr)?\] Here \(L\) is the order-oblivious instance-wise optimum over globally correct sampling algorithms, not the performance of one algorithm required to attain the bound on every instance.
definitions: An instance has \(n\geq2\) independent arms with distributions \(\mathcal N(\mu_i,1)\), unknown means \(\mu_i\in[0,1]\), and a unique largest mean \(\mu_*\) at index \(*\). Each pull of arm \(i\) reveals a fresh independent sample from its distribution. An adaptive sampling algorithm knows \(n\) and \(\delta\), chooses pulls using earlier samples and independent internal randomness, and eventually outputs an arm index. It is \(\delta\)-correct if on every valid instance it stops almost surely and outputs its unique best arm with probability at least \(1-\delta\). Local computation is unrestricted; the resource is total number of pulls, and expectations include sampling noise and algorithmic randomness. Algorithms are measurable so that these probabilities and expectations are defined. Let \(T_A(I)\in[0,\infty]\) be the expected number of pulls. If \(S_n\) is the set of all permutations of arm labels and \(\pi I\) is the corresponding relabeled instance, define \(L(I,\delta)=\inf_A (1/n!)\sum_{\pi\in S_n}T_A(\pi I)\), where the infimum ranges over algorithms correct on every instance of the same Gaussian model. The infimum is taken separately for each \(I,\delta\): an algorithm selected for favorable performance at I must nevertheless remain correct on all other instances. It need not attain the infimum. For each suboptimal arm, set \(\Delta_i=\mu_*-\mu_i\in(0,1]\), and \(H(I)=\sum_{i\ne *}\Delta_i^{-2}\). For integers \(r\geq0\), set \(G_r=\{i\ne *:2^{-(r+1)}<\Delta_i\leq2^{-r}\}\), \(H_r=\sum_{i\in G_r}\Delta_i^{-2}\), and \(p_r=H_r/H(I)\). The gap entropy is \(\operatorname{Ent}(I)=\sum_{r:p_r>0}p_r\log(1/p_r)\), with natural logarithms. Only finitely many groups are nonempty. The constants in the conjecture are independent of n, all means, the number of gap scales and δ.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of both uniform constant-factor bounds, or prove that no such universal pair of constants exists. A result only as δ tends to zero with the instance fixed, only for dyadic gaps or monotone algorithms, or an algorithm with an extra closest-gap term does not by itself prove the displayed claim about L. The recent claimed proof must meet the same mathematical and Lean-checking requirement.

title: Constant-factor entrywise \(\ell_1\) rank-\(k\) approximation with variable \(k\)
summary: The task compresses a rational matrix while measuring error by the sum of absolute entrywise differences. The output must have rank at most the supplied rank and approximate the best real matrix of that rank. Both the approximation factor and polynomial-time exponent must remain independent of the rank. Known fixed-rank approximation schemes do not meet this joint polynomial-time requirement. The question asks whether an absolute constant-factor guarantee is possible with explicit rational output.
formal: Do a uniform randomized polynomial-bit-time algorithm \(A\) and an absolute constant \(C\ge1\) exist such that, for every rational matrix \(M\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\) and input integer \(0\le k\le\min(m,n)\), \(A\) returns rational factors \(U\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times k}\), \(V\in\mathbb{Q}^{k\times n}\) satisfying \[\|M-UV\|_1\le C\operatorname{OPT}_k(M),\qquad \operatorname{OPT}_k(M)=\min_{\substack{B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\\\operatorname{rank}(B)\le k}}\|M-B\|_1,\] with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input?
definitions: \(m,n\ge 1\); dimensions, k and each signed rational numerator and positive denominator are explicitly encoded in binary. The input length N counts the whole dense matrix description. \(\|W\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}|W_{ij}|\) is the entrywise norm; rank is matrix rank over \(\mathbb{R}\). The optimum is over all real \(m\times n\) matrices of rank at most k and is attained, since a minimizing sequence can be confined to a bounded closed sublevel set. The output consists of binary rational entries of U and V; for \(k=0\) their product denotes the zero matrix. There is a single polynomial P such that A halts within \(P(N)\) Turing-machine steps on every input and every random tape, including the time to write its factors. Therefore the factors have polynomial total encoded length; no unit-cost exact real arithmetic or implicit algebraic-number oracle is available. The approximation factor C and polynomial exponent are independent of m,n,k and entry magnitudes. The probability is over independent fair algorithm coins for each fixed input. Only the displayed multiplicative error is allowed. In particular, when \(\operatorname{rank}(M)\le k\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}_{k}(M)=0\), success requires exact equality \(UV=M\). When the optimum is positive the output need not be an exact real minimizer: the task asks for rational factors meeting the constant-factor inequality. This is the explicit rational bit-model completion of the imported approximation question, not a claim that optimal real factors are rational or efficiently computable.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof that such an algorithm and absolute factor exist with the stated uniform bit bounds, or a Lean proof of their nonexistence. A factor depending on the rank, a polynomial exponent depending on the rank, output rank above the requested rank, or uncharged exact-real computation does not meet this criterion.

title: Log-squared query complexity of fixed-dimensional Tarski fixed points
summary: The input is oracle access to a monotone function on a finite grid of fixed dimension. Each query reveals one full function value, and any exact fixed point is acceptable. The question asks whether the worst-case deterministic query count is bounded by a squared logarithm of side length in every fixed dimension. A March 2026 result establishes that bound in dimension four while leaving the general fixed-dimension question unresolved. Resolving the target would clarify the information needed for monotone fixed-point search without also requiring fast internal computation.
formal: For integers \(n\ge2\) and \(k\ge1\), let \(Q(n,k)\) be the minimum worst-case number of deterministic adaptive value queries needed to find a fixed point of an unknown monotone function \(f:[n]^k\to[n]^k\), where \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Is \[\forall k\ge1\ \exists C_k>0\ \forall n\ge2:\quad Q(n,k)\le C_k(1+\log_2 n)^2?\] A query at \(x\in[n]^k\) reveals the entire vector \(f(x)\) at cost one. Arbitrary finite computation between queries is allowed. The constant \(C_k\) may depend on \(k\) but not on \(n\) or \(f\); no polynomial bound on its dependence on \(k\) is required.
definitions: The grid \([n]^k\) consists of all integer vectors with \(k\) coordinates in \([n]\). Its order is coordinatewise: \(x\le y\) means \(x_i\le y_i\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\). The oracle promise is that \(x\le y\) implies \(f(x)\le f(y)\). A fixed point is a vector \(x\) with exact equality \(f(x)=x\); any fixed point is an acceptable output, with no least or greatest requirement. For given \(n,k\), a deterministic oracle decision tree is finite. Each internal node names a query vector and has branches indexed by possible returned vectors; the next query depends only on \(n,k\) and the preceding transcript. Each leaf outputs a vector that is a fixed point for every promised oracle consistent with that leaf. Paths inconsistent with every promised oracle impose no correctness requirement. The tree’s cost is the maximum number of internal nodes on the path followed by any promised oracle. \(Q(n,k)\) is the minimum such cost over all correct trees, with a separate tree allowed for each pair \(n,k\). Thus no uniform or efficient construction of the optimal trees is built into the target. The only access to the unknown function is through the counted queries; no table, circuit, auxiliary advice about \(f\), randomness or quantum query is provided. Reading or manipulating a returned vector and other finite internal computation do not add query cost. Monotonicity on this finite complete lattice guarantees existence of a fixed point. Every logarithm in the bound has base two.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed bound or its negation. A positive answer must establish correct decision trees with the stated worst-case query bound for every fixed dimension and every side length. A negative answer must show that there exists one fixed \(k\) such that, for every \(M>0\), some \(n\ge2\) satisfies \(Q(n,k)>M(1+\log_2 n)^2\). A logarithmic exponent that increases with \(k\), or a lower bound whose contradiction requires \(k\) to increase with \(n\), does not settle the assertion. The target places no bound on internal computation time; a query-efficient result need not yield a polynomial-time algorithm for succinctly encoded functions.

title: First-order convergence to local minimax optima
summary: In sequential minimax optimization, one player minimizes a smooth function of x while a second player maximizes it in y. A local minimax point respects this order using shrinking neighborhoods whose radii may differ for the two players. The selected variant asks for one deterministic method with exact function-value and gradient queries whose finite limits are local minimax points for almost every initialization. The same method must converge locally to every strict local minimax point, so avoiding convergence everywhere is not a valid answer. Existing convergence theorems retain extra hypotheses or weaker derivative-based targets, and the exact variant and limits of the current source review are explicitly recorded.
formal:
Consider sequential minimax optimization \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^p}\max_{y\in\mathbb R^q} f(x,y)\), with \(p,q\ge1\), \(f\in C^2(\mathbb R^{p+q},\mathbb R)\), and a supplied constant \(L>0\) satisfying
\[\|\nabla f(z)-\nabla f(w)\|_2\le L\|z-w\|_2\qquad\text{for all }z,w\in\mathbb R^{p+q}.\]
Does there exist one uniform deterministic first-order oracle method, in the model below, that produces iterates \(z_k=(x_k,y_k)\) from every initial point and has both of these properties for every such \(p,q,f,L\)?

First, for Lebesgue-almost every initial point \(z_0\), whenever the complete sequence \((z_k)_{k\ge0}\) converges to a finite point \(z^*\), that point is a local minimax point in the neighborhood definition below. Second, every strict local minimax point has an open neighborhood of initial points from which the method converges to that point. The second requirement excludes a method that satisfies the first merely by never converging.
definitions:
The order of play is fixed: \(x\) is the minimization variable and \(y\) is the maximization variable. All norms are Euclidean. A point \(z^*=(x^*,y^*)\) is a local minimax point if there exist \(\delta_0>0\) and a function \(h:(0,\delta_0]\to[0,\infty)\), with \(\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}h(\delta)=0\), such that for every \(0<\delta\le\delta_0\) and all \(x,y\) with \(\|x-x^*\|_2\le\delta\) and \(\|y-y^*\|_2\le\delta\),
\[f(x^*,y)\le f(x^*,y^*)\le
 \max_{\|y'-y^*\|_2\le h(\delta)} f(x,y').\]
The closed maximization ball is nonempty and compact, so the maximum exists. The radius function may depend on \(f,z^*\). There is no additional bound on \(h(\delta)/\delta\), no restriction to a Hessian range, and no assumption of concavity in \(y\). In particular, local minimax does not mean a simultaneous local Nash equilibrium or a global minimax solution.

A stationary point satisfies \(\nabla f(z^*)=0\). Define its Hessian blocks
\[A=\nabla^2_{xx}f(z^*)\in\mathbb R^{p\times p},\quad
 B=\nabla^2_{yy}f(z^*)\in\mathbb R^{q\times q},\quad
 C=\nabla^2_{xy}f(z^*)\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}.\]
A strict local minimax point here means a stationary point satisfying
\[B\prec0,\qquad A-CB^{-1}C^{\mathsf T}\succ0.\]
For a symmetric matrix, positive definiteness means that its quadratic form is positive on every nonzero vector; negative definiteness is defined with a negative sign. These sufficient conditions imply the neighborhood definition above. They define the points at which attraction is required, not a promise on every stationary point or every local minimax point of the input. Degenerate and non-strict points remain subject to the first, limit-selection requirement.

A first-order oracle queried at \(z\in\mathbb R^{p+q}\) returns the exact pair \((f(z),\nabla f(z))\). The function is available only through this oracle, not through its formula, a Hessian oracle, a maximization oracle or a best-response oracle. A method is one fixed finite real-arithmetic program supplied with \(p,q,L,z_0\), initialized with empty history and fixed rational constants. It uses scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero numbers, exact comparisons, branching, copying, and integer loop/address operations. Real registers cannot be inspected digit by digit. Oracle calls may be adaptive, at points computed from the supplied data and earlier replies. Finite differences or other numerical quantities computed from finitely many permitted replies are allowed; direct derivative queries above first order are not.

The program may retain finite history and use iteration-dependent or adaptively chosen parameters. On every permitted input and after every finite iteration count it must finish the finite work needed to produce the next iterate, using finitely many elementary operations, stored values and oracle calls. No infinite inner loop, exact limit operation, uncharged auxiliary oracle, function-dependent advice or external randomization is allowed. Auxiliary storage is finite at each finite stage but need not have a fixed bound over the infinite run. This is an asymptotic convergence question: no polynomial iteration bound, oracle-complexity rate or bit-complexity bound is requested. The real oracle and exact arithmetic are part of the model, not claims about finite-precision implementation.

For precision, let \(z_k^{f,L}(u)\) be the sequence produced from initial point \(u\), with dimensions understood and \(z_0^{f,L}(u)=u\). The first guarantee means that, for each \(p,q,f,L\), there exists a set \(E_{f,L}\subseteq\mathbb R^{p+q}\) of Lebesgue outer measure zero such that
\[\forall u\notin E_{f,L}\ \forall z^*,\quad
 \lim_{k\to\infty}z_k^{f,L}(u)=z^*
 \ \Longrightarrow\ z^*\text{ is a local minimax point of }f.\]
The one exceptional set must cover all possible bad limits, not a separate uncountable union of exceptions for individual points. Equivalently, the same implication must hold almost surely for every initialization distribution with a density with respect to Lebesgue measure. The algorithm itself is deterministic.

The second guarantee means that for every strict local minimax point \(z^*\), there exists \(r>0\), depending on \(f,L,z^*\), such that
\[\forall u\in\mathbb R^{p+q},\quad
 \|u-z^*\|_2<r\ \Longrightarrow\ \lim_{k\to\infty}z_k^{f,L}(u)=z^*.\]
Every start uses the same program initialization; no target point or attracting radius is supplied to it. The requirements permit divergent or nonconvergent runs outside these local basins. They concern limits of the full sequence, not every subsequential accumulation point, and do not require global convergence or attraction to every non-strict local minimax point.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of a method meeting both guarantees, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must specify one finite oracle program, establish that it produces every next iterate after finite work, prove the common measure-zero exception statement for every permitted objective and every valid supplied \(L\), and prove local attraction at every point satisfying the strict Hessian conditions.

A negative proof must exclude every method in this specified oracle model from satisfying the conjunction. Counterexamples only to gradient descent-ascent, extragradient or another named update do not exclude every method. A method that never converges, convergence only to stationary points or second-order necessary-condition points, local linear stability without the stated limit guarantees, or a theorem assuming additional curvature or neighborhood-radius restrictions does not meet this target. No finite iteration rate is demanded, and the benchmark's numerical tolerance does not replace exact convergence or exact local minimaxity.

title: Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture
summary: The KLS conjecture asks for a universal Poincaré inequality for every log-concave probability distribution with zero mean and identity covariance. Every locally Lipschitz function of finite variance and gradient energy must have its variance bounded by that energy times one constant independent of the dimension and distribution. The target includes uniform distributions on convex bodies and requires no symmetry, independence or positive curvature assumption. Its equivalent expansion principle connects high-dimensional geometry and concentration with the analysis of sampling algorithms. A complete Lean proof must establish the universal bound or its unbounded-counterexample negation; radial, quadratic and dimension-dependent improvements do not settle the full target.
formal: Does there exist a real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every isotropic log-concave probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and every locally Lipschitz function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) with \(\int f^2\,d\mu<\infty\) and \(\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu<\infty\), \[\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)\le C\int_{\mathbb R^n}\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)?\] The same constant must work for all dimensions, measures and admissible functions. This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
definitions: All norms and derivatives are Euclidean, with \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2)^{1/2}\). Here a log-concave probability measure has a Lebesgue density \(\rho(x)=e^{-V(x)}\) of integral one, where \(V:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is measurable and convex; \(e^{-\infty}=0\). Convexity means \(V((1-s)x+sy)\le(1-s)V(x)+sV(y)\) for all \(x,y\) and \(0<s<1\), using the extended-real convention on the right. Thus \(d\mu(x)=\rho(x)\,dx\). Isotropy means finite second moments and \(\int x_i\,d\mu=0\), \(\int x_i x_j\,d\mu=\delta_{ij}\) for every \(i,j\), where \(\delta_{ij}=1\) if \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. Equivalently, the mean vector is zero and the covariance matrix is the identity. Isotropy excludes measures supported on a proper affine subspace, so no lower-dimensional singular case is omitted by using a density. Locally Lipschitz means that every point has a neighborhood on which \(|f(y)-f(z)|\le L\|y-z\|_2\) for some finite \(L\); the neighborhood and constant may depend on the point. Such a function has a Euclidean derivative outside a Lebesgue-null set, and \(\nabla f\) is the vector of its partial derivatives there; set it to zero where the derivative does not exist. This choice on the null set does not affect integration against \(\mu\). Write \(\bar f=\int f\,d\mu\), which is finite by the second-moment assumption, and \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)=\int(f-\bar f)^2\,d\mu\). The gradient energy is the integral of \(\|\nabla f\|_2^2\). Define \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu)\) as the infimum of all \(a\ge0\) for which the displayed inequality holds with \(a\) for every admissible function, with infimum of the empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). The question asks whether these constants are uniformly bounded; it does not ask for their optimal universal value. No symmetry, product structure, differentiability of \(V\), bounded support or positive lower bound on its curvature is assumed. Uniform laws on full-dimensional convex bodies are included after isotropic normalization; a convex body is a compact convex set with nonempty interior. The problem is an analytic existence statement, with no oracle, encoding or algorithmic-time requirement.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal Poincaré inequality with some finite real \(C>0\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\), there exist an integer \(n\ge1\), a measure \(\mu\) satisfying all stated log-concavity and isotropy conditions, and an admissible locally Lipschitz \(f\) of finite second moment and finite gradient energy such that \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)>C\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu\). The dimension, measure and function may depend on \(C\). A single violation for one proposed numerical constant does not refute existence of some larger universal constant. A dimension-dependent bound, or a theorem restricted to linear, radial or quadratic functions or a narrower class of measures, is insufficient unless the proof also establishes the entire stated target. No optimal value of \(C\) is required. An equivalent geometric statement can qualify only with a Lean-checked implication proving this proposition or its negation; cited but unproved conjectural dependencies do not complete acceptance.

title: Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair conjecture
summary: The GNRS conjecture asks whether weighted graphs excluding a fixed minor have shortest-path metrics that embed into \(\ell_1\) with bounded distortion. The bound may depend on the excluded graph but must be independent of graph size and all edge lengths. One map must preserve every pairwise distance, with no required algorithm or target-dimension bound. The equivalent routing formulation predicts a constant concurrent-flow versus cut gap for arbitrary demands. The checked restricted-family results leave the general conjecture, including its planar case, unresolved.
formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every finite simple graph \(H\), there exists a real constant \(C_H\ge1\) such that, for every nonempty finite connected simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with no \(H\) minor and every edge-length function \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{>0}\), there exist an integer \(m\ge1\) and a map \(f:V\to\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[
d_{G,w}(u,v)\le
\sum_{j=1}^{m}|f(u)_j-f(v)_j|
\le C_H\,d_{G,w}(u,v)
\qquad\text{for every }u,v\in V?
\]
The constant may depend only on \(H\). The dimension and map may depend on the whole weighted graph, with no bound on dimension or on the time needed to construct them.
definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph consists of a finite vertex set and a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices, called edges. Connected means every pair of vertices is joined by a path. A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if deleting vertices or edges and contracting edges, followed by removal of loops and duplicate edges, can produce a graph isomorphic to \(H\). Exclusion concerns the underlying unweighted graph.

The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths. The shortest-path distance \(d_{G,w}(u,v)\) is the minimum length of a path from \(u\) to \(v\), and \(d_{G,w}(u,u)=0\). Positivity and finiteness make this a finite metric. A one-vertex graph is allowed and satisfies the target trivially.

The target space is finite-dimensional \(\ell_1^m\): the vector space \(\mathbb R^m\) with distance \(\|a-b\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^m|a_j-b_j|\). The first inequality fixes a noncontracting normalization, and the second allows expansion by at most \(C_H\). Allowing an arbitrary common scaling factor instead gives the same distortion notion.

All edge lengths are arbitrary positive real numbers. Neither graph size nor the ratio of the largest to the smallest edge length may affect \(C_H\). There is no requirement that the graph or its lengths be efficiently encoded, since this is a mathematical existence question. All pairs must satisfy the inequalities simultaneously for the same map.

The source also allows zero edge lengths and hence zero distances between different vertices. That convention is equivalent for this conjecture: contract each component of zero-length edges, retain the shortest parallel edge when necessary, and map the original vertices through this quotient. The quotient is still a minor of the original graph. The positive-length statement above avoids treating distinct points at distance zero as a metric space.

No Euclidean target, restriction to selected terminals, average-distance guarantee, or transformation of the distances by a power is part of this statement. Here a terminal, when used in the context, simply means a selected vertex whose distances must be preserved.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must obtain a finite constant for every fixed excluded minor, uniformly over all weighted graphs in that class and all vertex pairs. It need not determine the best constant or construct the embeddings efficiently. A negative answer must give one fixed graph \(H\) such that for every real \(C\ge1\), some finite connected positively weighted \(H\)-minor-free graph admits no map into any finite-dimensional \(\ell_1\) space satisfying both inequalities with factor \(C\). Failure at one fixed distortion value is insufficient if a larger uniform value remains possible. This binary existence claim has no additive numerical tolerance.

title: Unknot recognition in polynomial time
summary: The input is an explicit finite crossing diagram of a tame knot. The question asks whether a deterministic algorithm can recognize the unknot in polynomial bit time. Both unknottedness and knottedness have polynomially verifiable certificates, which does not itself give such an algorithm. A September 2026 preprint claims a positive solution using locally minimal bridge presentations. The review has not independently certified that claim, so the card retains uncertain scientific status.
formal:
Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(M\), a real constant \(C>0\), and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every valid explicit knot-diagram encoding \(D\) of bit length \(N\), the machine halts within \(C(N+1)^k\) steps and outputs
\[
M(D)=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{the knot represented by }D\text{ is ambient isotopic to the unknot}?
\]
It must output zero for every nontrivial knot. The same machine and constants must work for all diagrams, without auxiliary certificates or advice.
definitions:
The \(3\)-sphere is \(S^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\sum_{i=1}^4x_i^2=1\}\), equivalently the one-point compactification of \(\mathbb R^3\). A tame knot is an embedded circle in \(S^3\) that can be carried by an ambient isotopy to a finite polygonal embedded circle in \(\mathbb R^3\). Wild embeddings are excluded.

An ambient isotopy is a continuous map \(H:S^3\times[0,1]\to S^3\) such that each \(H_t=H(\,\cdot\,,t)\) is a homeomorphism and \(H_0\) is the identity. Two knots have the same type if some such \(H_1\) takes one onto the other. The unknot is the type of a round planar circle. Knots are not given an orientation.

A knot diagram is a plane drawing of one immersed circle with finitely many transverse double crossings and a choice of overpassing strand at every crossing. The drawing determines a tame knot by separating the two strands locally in the third coordinate. Its input representation is combinatorial, so real coordinates are unnecessary.

For a diagram with \(n\ge1\) crossings, encode a connected graph with \(n\) vertices and four half-edges at each vertex. A half-edge is one end of an edge; an explicitly listed pairing of the \(4n\) half-edges forms the edges. Loops and parallel edges are allowed. At every vertex list the four incident half-edges in cyclic order, and mark which of the two opposite pairs is overpassing. The other pair is underpassing. Also designate one face as the outer face.

The cyclic orders must define a cellular embedding in the sphere: replace each vertex by an oriented disc, join paired half-edges by bands respecting the orders, and cap each resulting boundary circle by a disc. The resulting surface must be a sphere. Equivalently for this connected rotation system, its face cycles must give Euler characteristic \(n-2n+f=2\), where \(f\) is their count. The outer face gives a plane drawing.

Following edges and continuing through the opposite half-edge at each crossing must trace a single unoriented closed component. Thus the representation describes a knot, not a multi-component link. A separate fixed code represents the crossing-free circle. All indices, pairings, cyclic lists and crossing bits are written explicitly in binary with fixed delimiters. They can be checked combinatorially in polynomial time; malformed encodings may be rejected.

The parameter \(N\) is the length of the supplied finite encoding. A standard indexing uses \(O(n\log(n+1))\) bits, with the crossing-free code handled separately. It is neither the smallest possible crossing number of the knot nor the length of a compressed program describing a larger diagram.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic Turing-machine program with finitely many tapes. A step reads and writes a bounded number of tape symbols; arbitrary-length integer operations are not unit-cost operations. It receives no spanning disc, invariant, simplification sequence, random bits, oracle or length-dependent advice. The required output is one bit, not an isotopy or diagram simplification.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must establish the algorithm’s correct answer on every valid diagram and one polynomial worst-case bit-time bound. A negative proof must exclude every deterministic polynomial-time recognizer in this input model, rather than only a selected algorithm or simplification rule. Short certificates, polynomial-length move sequences and successful finite experiments do not by themselves prove deterministic polynomial running time. The existence statement is binary and has no numerical approximation tolerance.

title: Planar k-set growth exponent
summary: A planar k-set is a k-point subset that a line strictly separates from the remaining points. The point set has no three collinear points and otherwise arbitrary real coordinates. The card asks for the exponent of k after factoring out the linear number-of-points term. The exponent must be located within absolute error 0.01 using bounds uniform in both parameters. Exact counts and growing logarithmic factors are not part of the answer.
formal: Determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the exponent \[x_{\mathrm{kset}}=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall 1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\ K_2(n,k)\le Cn(k+1)^a\}.\] Here \(K_2(n,k)\) is the largest number of distinct \(k\)-point subsets strictly separable by a line in an \(n\)-point planar set with no three collinear points. Its full definition is below. The bound must be uniform in both integer parameters. Logarithmic factors and exact extremal counts are not requested.
definitions:
For a finite set \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^2\), let
\[
\mathcal S_k(P)=\bigl\{S\subseteq P:\ |S|=k,\ 
\exists(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}\ 
\exists t\in\mathbb R:\ 
a x+b y<t\ \forall(x,y)\in S,\ 
a x+b y>t\ \forall(x,y)\in P\setminus S\bigr\}.
\]
For integers \(n\ge2\) and \(1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), define
\[
K_2(n,k)=
\max_{\substack{P\subseteq\mathbb R^2,\ |P|=n\\
                 \text{no three points of }P\text{ are collinear}}}
|\mathcal S_k(P)|.
\]


The plane \(\mathbb R^2\) has arbitrary real coordinates. A point set contains distinct points. General position here means exactly that no three points lie on one affine line; there is no grid, precision, distribution or convex-position restriction.

The affine line \(a x+b y=t\) has nonzero normal vector \((a,b)\). The strict inequalities in the definition place all points of \(S\) on one side and all other points on the opposite side. In particular the separating line contains no input point. A member of \(\mathcal S_k(P)\) is a k-set. Each subset is counted once, regardless of how many lines separate it.

The maximum is well-defined: every count is an integer between zero and \(\binom nk\), and there are general-position point sets of each permitted size. Thus the set of attained counts is a nonempty finite set of integers even though coordinates range over infinitely many possibilities.

Complementing subsets gives the same count for \(k\) and \(n-k\). Sizes zero and \(n\) each give one subset, so the stated domain captures the nontrivial range. The target is a combinatorial extremal function, not the time complexity of listing k-sets.

In the context, a directed j-edge joins two input points and has exactly \(j\) other points strictly to its left. For even \(n\), an undirected halving edge has \((n-2)/2\) other points on each side of its supporting line. The line through this edge is not a strict separator, since it passes through two points. The requested exponent is \[x_{\mathrm{kset}}=\inf\{a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}:\exists C>0\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall 1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\ K_2(n,k)\le C n(k+1)^a\}.\] The integer parameter domain is the same as above. The coefficient \(C\) may depend on \(a\), but not on either parameter or the point configuration. The cited upper bound ensures \(0\le x_{\mathrm{kset}}\le1/3\). The infimum need not be attained. Thus a value zero permits subpolynomial dependence on \(k\) and does not assert a linear bound \(O(n)\). This records the exponent of the dependence on subset size after factoring out the linear dependence on the number of points; it does not assert a two-sided power-law asymptotic.
answer_criterion: Supply \(a\) and prove \(|a-x_{\mathrm{kset}}|\le1/100\) in Lean. For each feasible exponent, one coefficient \(C\) must work for every legal pair \((n,k)\). To exclude an exponent, show that every proposed \(C>0\) fails at some such pair. The infimum need not be attained. A [certified enclosing interval](definitions.html#numerical-answers) of width at most \(1/50\) also suffices via its midpoint.

title: Polynomial Hirsch conjecture
summary: The polynomial Hirsch conjecture asks for a universal polynomial bound on the edge-graph diameter of every pointed polyhedron. The parameters are dimension and number of facets, with arbitrary real coordinates and both bounded and unbounded regions allowed. OpenAI constructs bounded simple rational polytopes whose edge-graph diameter exceeds every fixed polynomial in the facet count. Their dimension grows more slowly than every positive power of the facet count. These examples disprove the proposed bound even for bounded polytopes.
formal:
Is the following proposition true? There exist a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that for every integer \(d\ge1\) and every nonempty, full-dimensional, pointed convex polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), writing \(n\) for its number of facets,
\[
\operatorname{diam}G(P)\le C(n+d)^k?
\]
The same \(C\) and \(k\) must work for all dimensions, all facet counts and all real coefficients defining \(P\). Both bounded and unbounded polyhedra are included.
definitions:
A polyhedron is a set \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Ax\le b\}\), where \(A\) is a real matrix with finitely many rows, \(b\) is a real vector of matching length and inequalities are coordinatewise. Its affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing it. Full-dimensional means this affine hull is \(\mathbb R^d\); a polyhedron in a larger ambient space is considered in its own affine hull.

Pointed means that there are no \(x\in P\) and nonzero \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) for which \(x+tv\in P\) for every \(t\in\mathbb R\). A nonempty pointed polyhedron has at least one vertex. A bounded polyhedron is called a polytope.

A nonempty proper face is a set \(P\cap\{x:a\cdot x=\beta\}\), where \(a\ne0\), the dot denotes the usual real inner product and \(a\cdot x\le\beta\) for all \(x\in P\). Face dimension means the dimension of its affine hull. A facet is a face of dimension \(d-1\); \(n\) counts the distinct geometric facets, not duplicate or redundant rows of a chosen inequality description. A vertex is a face consisting of one point.

The undirected graph \(G(P)\) has the vertices of \(P\) as its graph vertices. Two distinct vertices are adjacent exactly when the segment joining them is a one-dimensional face. Such a segment is a bounded edge. An unbounded one-dimensional face contributes no new graph vertex and no edge to infinity.

A graph path is a finite sequence of vertices with successive terms adjacent, and its length is its number of edges. Distance is the minimum path length between a pair of vertices, and diameter is the largest such distance. These polyhedral graphs are finite, nonempty and connected; a graph with one vertex has diameter zero. Distances count edges of unit cost, not their Euclidean lengths.

The coefficients may be arbitrary real numbers, and no simplicity, general-position or nondegeneracy hypothesis is imposed. The constants cannot depend on coordinate values or an encoding length. Paths may use edges in either direction; no objective function, monotonicity condition or algorithm for finding a path is specified. Polynomiality requires one exponent independent of dimension.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must supply universal \(C>0\) and integer \(k\ge1\) and cover every permitted polyhedron and vertex pair. A negative proof must show that for every real \(C>0\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), some permitted \(d\)-dimensional polyhedron with \(n\) facets has a pair of vertices at graph distance greater than \(C(n+d)^k\). Refuting one fixed linear expression, requiring a long path under one pivot rule, or bounding a different notion of distance is insufficient. This binary existence question has no numerical approximation tolerance.

title: Logarithmic \(\ell_1\) distortion lower bound for planar Earth Mover Distance
summary: Earth Mover Distance is the minimum cost of transporting one probability measure into another. The input measures live on a planar square grid with Euclidean transport costs. The question asks whether every embedding of the whole measure space into ell-one incurs at least logarithmic distortion. Arbitrary nonlinear embeddings and all real probability weights are permitted. The retained 2026 resolution proves this lower-bound target, whose Lean formalization remains a valid benchmark answer.
formal: Do there exist universal constants \(c>0\) and \(n_0\ge2\) such that \[D(n)\ge c\log_2 n\qquad\text{for every integer }n\ge n_0?\] Here \(D(n)\), defined below, is the least bi-Lipschitz distortion into \(\ell_1\) of the space of all probability measures on \(\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}^2\), equipped with Earth Mover Distance using Euclidean ground distances.
definitions:
For \(n\geq2\), a probability measure is a vector \(\mu:X_n	o[0,1]\) with \(\sum_x\mu(x)=1\); all real weights are allowed. For two such vectors put \[W_n(\mu,
u)=\min_\pi\sum_{x,y\in X_n}\|x-y\|_2\pi(x,y),\] where \(\pi(x,y)\geq0\), \(\sum_y\pi(x,y)=\mu(x)\) for each \(x\), and \(\sum_x\pi(x,y)=
u(y)\) for each \(y\). The minimum exists because the set of transport plans is a nonempty compact polytope. Thus unit total mass is transported, with cost equal to distance rather than squared distance. The space \(\ell_1\) consists of real sequences \(z=(z_i)_{i\geq1}\) with \(\sum_i|z_i|<\infty\), and norm \(\|z\|_1=\sum_i|z_i|\). Define \(D(n)\) to be the infimum of all \(D\geq1\) for which a single map \(F\) from the whole probability simplex on \(X_n\) into \(\ell_1\) satisfies \(W_n(\mu,
u)\leq\|F(\mu)-F(
u)\|_1\leq D W_n(\mu,
u)\) for every pair \(\mu,
u\). Allow arbitrary nonlinear maps; the lower inequality normalizes scale and ensures injectivity. No restriction to distributions of bounded support size, uniform weights or a fixed denominator is imposed. No linearity, sketch length, algorithmic runtime or finite output dimension is required. Finite-dimensional \(\ell_1\) maps remain admissible by padding with zeros. The infimum need not be attained; matching constant-factor bounds do not require an optimum-achieving map. If no finite-distortion map exists, the infimum is infinity, although the cited upper bound rules this out for each finite grid.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof that \(D(n)\ge c\log_2 n\) at every sufficiently large grid size for one \(c>0\). The matching logarithmic lower bound is recorded below among the dated results.

title: Lang–Plaut problem
summary: A doubling metric has uniformly limited local branching: each ball can be covered by a bounded number of smaller balls. The Lang–Plaut problem considers such a metric when it already sits inside a Hilbert space. It asks whether the points can be represented in some finite-dimensional Euclidean space while changing all distances by only a bounded factor. Both dimension and distortion should depend only on the doubling constant. The issue is whether intrinsic metric simplicity suffices to eliminate an infinite-dimensional ambient representation.
formal: For every integer \(K\geq2\), do there exist a finite integer \(N(K)\geq1\) and a finite real constant \(D(K)\geq1\) such that every \(K\)-doubling subset \(X\) of real Hilbert space admits a map \(F:X\to\mathbb R^{N(K)}\) satisfying \[\|x-y\|_2\leq\|F(x)-F(y)\|_2\leq D(K)\|x-y\|_2\qquad(x,y\in X)?\]
definitions: It suffices to use the real Hilbert space \(\ell_2=\{(x_i)_{i\geq1}:\sum_i x_i^2<\infty\}\), with norm \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_i x_i^2)^{1/2}\). A doubling subset of any Hilbert space is separable and isometrically identifies with a subset of this space. Give \(X\subseteq\ell_2\) the restricted Hilbert distance. It is \(K\)-doubling if, for every \(x\in X\) and \(r>0\), the closed ball \(B_X(x,r)=\{y\in X:\|x-y\|_2\leq r\}\) is covered by at most \(K\) closed balls \(B_X(z,r/2)\) with centers \(z\in X\). No boundedness, closedness, compactness or finiteness of \(X\) is assumed. Empty sets and singletons cause no difficulty. The codomain has its ordinary Euclidean norm. The displayed lower inequality makes the map injective and fixes its arbitrary scale; without that normalization, distortion is the product of the Lipschitz constants of a map and its inverse on its image. The functions \(N,D\) must be chosen before \(X\), and may depend only on \(K\), not on the number of points, diameter, aspect ratio or ambient Hilbert dimension. The embedding may be nonlinear and may be chosen separately for each \(X\). There is no algorithm, continuity beyond the displayed bounds, or prescribed polynomial dependence on \(K\) required. Distances themselves must be preserved within these factors; replacing them by a power smaller than one changes the target.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal statement in Lean, or give a complete Lean-checked refutation with a fixed doubling bound for which no uniform pair of finite dimension and distortion bounds works. Equivalently, the qualitative Lang–Plaut formulation can be settled by proving that every doubling Hilbert subset has some finite-dimensional bi-Lipschitz embedding, or by exhibiting one that has none; the source proves the equivalence with the quantitative formulation. A restriction to linear maps, snowflaked distances, or bounds growing with the number of points does not resolve the question.

title: Weak \(\varepsilon\)-net size exponent
summary: A weak epsilon-net hits every convex set containing a sufficiently large fraction of the input points. Its chosen points may lie anywhere in Euclidean space. The question asks how the worst-case net size grows as a power of inverse accuracy. The exponent is requested to absolute error 0.01 in every fixed dimension. The target imposes no algorithmic construction requirement and ignores logarithmic factors.
formal: For every fixed integer \(d\ge2\), determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the exponent \[x_{\mathrm{net}}(d)=\inf\{a\ge0:f_d(\varepsilon)=O_d(\varepsilon^{-a})\text{ as }\varepsilon\downarrow0\}.\] The function \(f_d(\varepsilon)\), defined below, is the worst-case minimum cardinality of a weak \(\varepsilon\)-net hitting all convex sets that contain at least an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of a finite point set in \(\mathbb R^d\). Net points may lie outside the input set. The requested answer concerns the exponent, with no requirement to determine logarithmic factors.
definitions: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be any nonempty finite set of distinct points, and let \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\) be real. A weak \(\varepsilon\)-net is a finite set \(N\subset\mathbb R^d\) such that \(N\cap C\ne\varnothing\) for every convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) satisfying \(|P\cap C|\geq\varepsilon|P|\). A set is convex if it contains the segment joining any two of its points. All convex ranges, including unbounded and lower-dimensional ones, are allowed; no restriction to halfspaces, simplices or a given finite family is made. Equivalently it is enough to hit \(\operatorname{conv}(Q)\) for every \(Q\subseteq P\) with \(|Q|\geq\lceil\varepsilon|P|\rceil\), so using only closed convex ranges gives the same condition. Net points can lie anywhere in \(\mathbb R^d\) and need not belong to \(P\). Put \(w(P,\varepsilon)=\min\{|N|:N\text{ is a weak }\varepsilon\text{-net for }P\}\) and \(f_d(\varepsilon)=\sup_{P\subset\mathbb R^d,\,0<|P|<\infty}w(P,\varepsilon)\). The minimum exists since \(N=P\) is feasible. The supremum ranges over every size and configuration with the same fixed dimension and accuracy; a bound depending on \(|P|\) is not a bound on \(f_d\). The weak-net theorem ensures \(f_d(\varepsilon)<\infty\). There is no general-position, rational-coordinate, uniform-measure-on-space, algorithmic or randomized guarantee in the target: the only measure is the uniform counting measure on the given finite set. The problem measures extremal cardinality, not construction time. For each fixed integer \(d\ge2\), define \[x_{\mathrm{net}}(d)=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \exists\varepsilon_0\in(0,1/2]\ \forall\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_0],\ f_d(\varepsilon)\le C\varepsilon^{-a}\}.\] Constants may depend on \(d\) and \(a\), but not on the accuracy or point set. The classical polynomial upper bound and inverse-accuracy lower bound give \(1\le x_{\mathrm{net}}(d)\le d\), so every requested value is a finite real number. The infimum need not be attained; a polylogarithmic factor in \(1/\varepsilon\) does not change the exponent. Different fixed dimensions may use different constants, with no uniform bound on their growth requested.
answer_criterion: Supply one explicitly described real-valued function \(a\) on all integers \(d\ge2\). Prove in Lean that \(|a(d)-x_{\mathrm{net}}(d)|\le1/100\) at every point of that domain. A pair of [certified bounding functions](definitions.html#numerical-answers) \(L,U\) also qualifies if \(L(d)\le x_{\mathrm{net}}(d)\le U(d)\) and \(U(d)-L(d)\le1/50\) everywhere, with \(a=(L+U)/2\). The weak-net asymptotics take \(\varepsilon\) to zero at each fixed dimension.

title: Decidability of PL four-sphere recognition
summary: The input is a finite simplicial complex promised to be a closed combinatorial four-manifold. The question asks whether one deterministic algorithm can recognize the standard PL four-sphere on every such input. There is no time bound, but both termination and a correct binary answer are mandatory. Topological equivalence, finite experimental classifications and heuristics that may remain inconclusive do not supply this guarantee. The checked sources retain dimension four as the unresolved boundary in PL sphere recognition.
formal:
Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(M\) with the following property? For every finite abstract simplicial complex \(K\), encoded by its facets as below and promised to be a nonempty closed combinatorial \(4\)-manifold, \(M\) halts and outputs a bit satisfying
\[
M(\operatorname{enc}(K))=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
K\cong_{\mathrm{PL}}\partial\Delta^5.
\]
Here \(\partial\Delta^5\) is the standard PL \(4\)-sphere. Output zero is required on every promised input that is not PL homeomorphic to it. There is no running-time or space bound, and connectedness is not part of the promise.
definitions:
A finite abstract simplicial complex \(K\) is a finite family of finite subsets of a finite vertex set \(V\), containing the empty set and closed under taking subsets. Its members are faces; inclusion-maximal faces are facets. The dimension of a nonempty face \(\sigma\) is \(|\sigma|-1\). Pure dimension four means that all facets have exactly five vertices.

Vertex labels are distinct nonnegative integers. The input lists each facet once, sorting labels increasingly within facets and sorting the facet lists lexicographically. Each label is written in binary with no leading zero except for the label zero itself. A fixed separator between labels and a second separator between facets make this a finite string over a fixed alphabet. The full complex is the family of all subsets of the listed facets, and its vertex set is their union. Renaming vertices does not affect the correct answer.

The geometric realization \(|K|\) is the subset of \(\mathbb R^V\) consisting of vectors \((t_v)_{v\in V}\) with \(t_v\ge0\), \(\sum_vt_v=1\), and \(\{v:t_v>0\}\in K\). Each face is realized as the convex hull of its coordinate unit vectors. A finite simplicial subdivision is a finite triangulation of this realization by simplices contained in old simplices, whose union on each old simplex equals that simplex.

Two finite complexes are piecewise-linearly homeomorphic, written \(K\cong_{\mathrm{PL}}L\), when they admit finite subdivisions that are simplicially isomorphic. A simplicial isomorphism is a bijection on vertices taking faces to faces in both directions. Equivalently, their realizations have a homeomorphism that is affine on the simplices of suitable finite subdivisions.

The simplex \(\Delta^q\) is the complex of all subsets of a set of \(q+1\) vertices. Its boundary \(\partial\Delta^q\) consists of all proper subsets of that vertex set. The standard PL \(j\)-sphere is \(\partial\Delta^{j+1}\), up to PL homeomorphism.

The link of a vertex \(v\) is
\[
\operatorname{lk}_K(v)=
\{\sigma\in K:v\notin\sigma,\ \sigma\cup\{v\}\in K\}.
\]
In this card, a nonempty closed combinatorial \(4\)-manifold means a finite pure four-dimensional complex for which every vertex link is PL homeomorphic to \(\partial\Delta^4\). Multiple connected components are allowed. No orientation, simple-connectivity, homology-sphere or prior topological-sphere promise is imposed.

A deterministic Turing machine has a finite transition rule, finite tape alphabet and finitely many tapes; it starts with the encoded complex on its input tape. Halting with output one means acceptance, and halting with output zero means rejection. Termination and correctness are required on all and only promised inputs; behavior on malformed strings or complexes outside the promise is unrestricted. The same finite machine must work for complexes of every size.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of the stated machine or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish termination and the exact PL classification on every promised input, without additional unproved hypotheses. A negative answer must establish that every deterministic Turing machine has a promised input on which it either fails to halt with a bit or gives the wrong bit. A lower bound ruling out only polynomial time, a procedure that can return “unknown,” or a classifier proved correct only on a finite census does not settle this target. This is a binary decidability statement with no numerical approximation tolerance.

title: \(2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\) lower bound for binary edit distance in \(\ell_1\)
summary: Binary edit distance counts unit-cost insertions, deletions and substitutions. One map of all length-n strings into a finite-dimensional l1 space must preserve every distance within a common multiplicative distortion. The dimension, real coordinates and computation needed to obtain the map are unrestricted. The question asks whether every such embedding has distortion at least \(2^{c\sqrt{\log_2 n}}\) for some universal \(c>0\) and every sufficiently large \(n\). The cited logarithmic lower bound and \(2^{O(\sqrt{(\log n)(\log\log n)})}\) upper bound do not decide this specific threshold.
formal:
For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)\) be the infimum distortion of embeddings of all length-\(n\) binary strings, with unit-cost edit distance, into finite-dimensional \(\ell_1\). Distortion measures the worst multiplicative change in any distance after a common rescaling; its precise all-pairs definition is below.

Do there exist an absolute real constant \(c>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge2\) such that
\[
D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)\ge 2^{c\sqrt{\log_2 n}}
\qquad\text{for every integer }n\ge n_0?
\]
This is the assertion that binary edit distance requires \(\ell_1\) distortion at least \(2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\).
definitions:
Let \(X_n=\{0,1\}^n\), the set of all \(2^n\) binary strings of length \(n\). The distance \(\mathrm{ED}(x,y)\) is the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to transform \(x\) into \(y\), each at cost one. Inserted and substituted characters are binary, and intermediate strings may have any finite length. For \(v\in\mathbb R^m\), the \(\ell_1\) norm is \(\|v\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^m|v_i|\).

Define the optimal distortion by
\[
D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)=\inf\bigl\{D\in[1,\infty):\ \exists m\in\mathbb N_{\ge1},\ \exists f:X_n\to\mathbb R^m,\ \exists a>0,\ \forall x,y\in X_n,\ a\,\mathrm{ED}(x,y)\le\|f(x)-f(y)\|_1\le D a\,\mathrm{ED}(x,y)\bigr\}.
\]
The dimension \(m\) is any finite positive integer, coordinates are arbitrary real numbers, and the map need not have an efficient or computable description. There is no bound on dimension or construction/evaluation time, and no requirement for a uniform algorithm across different \(n\). The same map \(f\) and positive scale \(a\) must satisfy both inequalities simultaneously for all pairs in \(X_n\); \(f,m,a\) may depend on \(n\). The infimum ranges over all such choices and need not be attained. Every finite metric space has a finite-distortion embedding into some finite-dimensional \(\ell_1\), so \(1\le D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)<\infty\).

All logarithms in the target are to base two. The constants \(c\) and \(n_0\) in the proposed lower bound must be independent of \(n\), the dimension and the embedding. The assertion concerns every sufficiently large string length, not just an infinite subsequence. Its exponent contains \(\sqrt{\log_2 n}\), with no additional \(\log\log n\) factor.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed lower-bound assertion or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish constants \(c>0\) and \(n_0\ge2\) for which the lower bound holds for every integer \(n\ge n_0\), against all unrestricted finite-dimensional \(\ell_1\) embeddings in the definition. A negative answer must prove
\[
\forall c>0\;\forall N\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\;\exists n\in\mathbb N_{\ge N}:\quad
D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)<2^{c\sqrt{\log_2 n}}.
\]
A single exceptional length does not refute the asymptotic assertion. This is an exact yes/no target; neither a matching upper bound nor optimization of the constant \(c\) is required. A lower bound restricted to a chosen dimension or family of maps does not establish the claim for unrestricted embeddings.

title: Near-linear-time exact Euclidean minimum spanning trees
summary: A Euclidean minimum spanning tree connects the input points with minimum total edge length. The complete graph is implicit in the point coordinates. The question asks for exact computation in time equal to the number of points times a fixed power of its logarithm. The guarantee must hold deterministically in every fixed dimension at least three. Approximate trees and expected-time bounds alone do not meet this target.
formal: For every fixed integer \(d\ge3\), is there one deterministic algorithm \(A_d\), a constant \(C_d>0\), and an integer \(a_d\ge1\) that compute an exact Euclidean minimum spanning tree of any \(n\ge2\) distinct points in \(\mathbb R^d\) in at most \[C_d n\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^{a_d}\] worst-case steps in the real-arithmetic model below? The input is an array of coordinates \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\). The output is a list of \(n-1\) index pairs forming a connected acyclic graph \(T\) minimizing \(\sum_{\{i,j\}\in T}\|p_i-p_j\|_2\). The program and constants may depend on fixed \(d\), but not on \(n\) or the coordinates.
definitions: The Euclidean distance is \(\|p-q\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d(p_j-q_j)^2)^{1/2}\). Coordinates are arbitrary exact reals; there is no general-position, bounded-spread or unique-optimum promise. Any minimum tree is a correct output. The complete graph and its edge weights are implicit, so reading every possible edge is not a required part of the input. For each fixed \(d\), the algorithm is one finite deterministic program for all \(n\) and all coordinates, with rational constants, exact real registers and indexed memory. Each operation \(+,-,\times,/\) on its domain, nonnegative square root, comparison, copy, indexed read or write costs one step. Addresses and counters are integers of \(O_d(\log(n+t+2))\) bits after \(t\) steps, with ordinary arithmetic and comparisons charged per word operation. There is no floor or bit extraction from real registers, advice depending on the input size, or geometric oracle. All input access and output steps count. Worst-case time is the supremum over all valid size-\(n\) inputs. Constants and programs may depend on fixed \(d\), but not on \(n\) or the coordinates; no simultaneous polynomial dependence on variable dimension is requested.
answer_criterion: For each fixed \(d\ge3\), prove in Lean that a deterministic algorithm returns an exact minimum spanning tree within the stated worst-case real-arithmetic bound. A refutation must exclude every such algorithm and exponent for at least one fixed dimension.

title: Dürer’s conjecture
summary: The input is a convex three-dimensional polytope. Its faces may be separated only along original edges. The output sought is one connected planar net. Distinct face interiors must not overlap. Allowing cuts across faces or disconnected pieces gives a different problem.
formal: For every bounded three-dimensional convex polytope \(P\subset\mathbb R^3\) with nonempty interior, is there a connected edge unfolding whose distinct face interiors do not overlap in the plane?
definitions: A convex polytope is the convex hull of a finite set of real points. Its faces here are its maximal two-dimensional facets, and adjacent facets share an entire polytope edge. Choose a spanning tree of the facet adjacency graph. Make separate copies of all facets and glue only the pairs of matching edges selected by that tree, retaining the edge identifications inherited from \(P\). An edge unfolding is a map of this glued polygonal surface to \(\mathbb R^2\) whose restriction to each copied facet is a Euclidean isometry and whose restrictions agree on glued edges. Require images of the relative interiors of distinct facets to be disjoint. Contacts between boundary points are permitted; cuts may run only along original polytope edges. The glued surface and its image are connected. This is a geometric existence statement with arbitrary real coordinates, not an algorithmic runtime claim.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every convex polytope in the stated domain has a spanning tree of facet adjacencies and compatible planar facet isometries with pairwise disjoint relative interiors, or prove a counterexample in Lean: one such polytope for which every permitted gluing tree and planar realization fails. No algorithmic runtime or stricter boundary-injectivity claim is required.

title: Near-linear-time exact planar Euclidean matching
summary: A perfect matching pairs every planar input point with one other point. Its objective is the sum of the ordinary Euclidean lengths of all pairs. The question asks for an exact deterministic algorithm in near-linear worst-case time. No red-blue bipartition or general-position promise is supplied. Squared lengths and approximate matchings define different objectives.
formal: Is there one uniform deterministic algorithm and universal constants \(C>0\), \(a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) that compute a minimum-length perfect matching of any \(2n\) distinct points in \(\mathbb R^2\), for every \(n\ge1\), in at most \[Cn\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^a\] worst-case steps in the exact real-arithmetic model below? The output is a list of \(n\) unordered index pairs, each index occurring once, minimizing \(\sum_{\{i,j\}\in M}\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}\). The input consists only of the coordinates, with no bipartition or geometric promise.
definitions: The coordinates are arbitrary real numbers supplied in an indexed array. No general-position, bounded-spread, coordinate-precision or unique-optimum promise is made; any minimizing matching is acceptable. An algorithm is one finite deterministic program, valid for every input size, with rational program constants, no advice and no oracle. It has exact real registers and an indexed memory. A real arithmetic operation \(+,-,\times,/\) on its domain, a nonnegative square root, a comparison, a register copy, or an indexed read or write costs one step. Integer addresses and loop counters use ordinary arithmetic and comparisons on \(O(\log(n+t+2))\)-bit words after \(t\) steps, with a program-dependent constant in this word bound; there is no floor, bit extraction from reals, or operation that solves an entire optimization problem. Input access, memory operations and output are charged. Running time is the supremum of the number of steps over all valid inputs of the given size. All programs must halt and be correct on every valid input. This fixes the conventional geometric arithmetic interpretation of the source; it is not a bit-complexity question about sums of square roots. The main problem is unrestricted perfect matching: no red/blue partition is supplied.
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one deterministic algorithm computes a minimum-length perfect matching within the stated worst-case time for all planar point sets, or that every proposed algorithm and bound fail on an admissible input.

title: Decidability of contractibility for finite two-dimensional complexes
summary: The input is a finite simplicial complex made of vertices, edges and triangles. Decide whether expansions and collapses can transform it into a single vertex. Intermediate complexes may be larger and higher-dimensional than the input. The algorithm must halt with a correct answer on every input, but no efficiency bound is imposed. This recognition problem differs from limiting expansions to dimension three or using collapses alone.
formal: Is there an algorithm that, on every finite nonempty simplicial complex \(K\) of dimension at most two, halts and decides whether \(K\) is simple-homotopy equivalent to a point? Equivalently, can contractibility of all such \(K\) be decided?
definitions:
A finite abstract simplicial complex is a finite collection of nonempty finite vertex sets, called simplices, closed under taking nonempty subsets. A simplex with \(r+1\) vertices has dimension \(r\). The input explicitly lists its simplices, or equivalently its maximal simplices and their vertex labels. The promise is that every simplex has at most three vertices. Edges and triangles need not form a manifold or embed in Euclidean three-space.

An elementary collapse removes a pair \((\sigma,\tau)\) of simplices, where \(\sigma\) is a codimension-one face of \(\tau\) and the only simplex properly containing \(\sigma\) is \(\tau\). An elementary expansion is the inverse: add such a pair so that the result is again a simplicial complex and that pair could be collapsed immediately.

Simple-homotopy equivalence to a point means that a finite sequence of expansions and collapses takes \(K\) to a complex consisting of a single vertex. New vertices may be introduced; intermediate complexes may be larger and have dimension greater than two. There is no prescribed bound on the number of moves, number of vertices or intermediate dimension. Relabeling vertices has no mathematical effect.

For comparison with the topological formulation, the geometric realization \(|K|\) is obtained by gluing an ordinary Euclidean simplex for each face along its common subfaces. It is contractible if its identity map can be continuously deformed to a constant map: there exist \(p\in|K|\) and a continuous
\[H:|K|\times[0,1]\longrightarrow |K|,\qquad H(x,0)=x,\quad H(x,1)=p.\]
For a finite complex, being contractible is equivalent to having the simple-homotopy type of a point, as recalled in the sources.

The algorithm is a single deterministic Turing machine acting on the finite encoding. It must give the correct yes/no answer and terminate on both contractible and noncontractible inputs. No polynomial-time or other running-time bound is required. There is no promise that \(K\) is already contractible or simply connected, and no contraction certificate is supplied.

This is specifically recognition of the simple-homotopy type of a point. The card does not ask to decide equivalence of an arbitrary pair of complexes. It also does not restrict allowed moves to collapses alone, or impose a fixed expansion budget.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a total decision algorithm for this input class, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A procedure that eventually finds a contraction on yes-instances but may run forever on no-instances is insufficient. A hardness theorem ruling out efficient algorithms does not establish undecidability.

title: Constant-distortion Steiner point removal
summary: Steiner point removal starts with a weighted graph and a designated set of terminals whose mutual distances matter. The goal is to delete the other vertices through graph-minor operations, leaving a graph on exactly those terminals. Its edges may be reweighted, but terminal distances should never shrink and should grow by at most a universal factor. The same guarantee must work regardless of how many terminals the input contains. This asks whether graph topology and useful terminal geometry can both survive an extreme reduction in representation size.
formal: Is there an absolute constant \(C<\infty\) such that, for every finite connected undirected graph \(G\) with nonnegative real edge lengths and every terminal set \(K\subseteq V(G)\) with \(|K|\geq2\), there is a reweighted terminal-preserving minor \(H\) with vertex set exactly \(K\) satisfying \[d_G(s,t)\leq d_H(s,t)\leq C\,d_G(s,t)\qquad(s,t\in K)?\]
definitions: The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths, and \(d_G\) is the minimum path length between its endpoints. Zero-length edges are allowed, so distinct terminals can have distance zero; the displayed inequalities then require their distance in \(H\) to be zero too. To specify precisely the terminal-preserving minor condition, choose pairwise disjoint nonempty connected vertex sets \(B_t\subseteq V(G)\), one for each \(t\in K\), with \(B_t\cap K=\{t\}\). The graph \(H\) is a simple graph on the labeled set \(K\); an edge \(st\) of \(H\) is permitted only if some edge of \(G\) joins \(B_s\) to \(B_t\). Not all such permitted edges have to be kept, and vertices outside the branch sets may be deleted. Thus vertices can be deleted, edges deleted or contracted, and parallel edges or loops removed, but no two terminals are identified and no surviving vertex is a nonterminal. Each edge of \(H\) may receive an arbitrary new nonnegative real length, independent of the original length of an edge witnessing its adjacency. This is a topological minor relation with allowed reweighting, not a requirement that contraction preserve inherited edge lengths. Define \(d_H\) by shortest paths and as infinity for disconnected pairs; the guarantee forces finite terminal distances. Both inequalities must hold simultaneously for all pairs in one chosen minor. The same \(C\) must work independently of the numbers of vertices, edges and terminals, graph topology, edge-length magnitudes and aspect ratio. The target is existential and imposes no construction-time, input-encoding or randomness requirement on a proof of existence.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of such a universal constant and the required rooted minor for every input in Lean, or prove its negation: for every finite \(C\), some graph and terminal set admit no minor meeting all the inequalities. A family with unbounded necessary distortion is a valid negative answer; a single fixed lower bound on the constant is not. Expected distortion for each pair, additional surviving Steiner vertices, or a guarantee only in a restricted graph class does not settle the statement.

title: Polynomial-time recognition of the 3-sphere
summary: The input is an explicit finite simplicial complex promised to triangulate a closed connected PL three-manifold. The question asks whether one deterministic algorithm can recognize the standard three-sphere in time polynomial in the total input bit length. The polynomial bound must hold on all binary inputs, while correct answers are required on the promised manifold inputs. Sphere recognition is decidable and has polynomially verifiable positive certificates, with the checked negative-certificate result depending on the generalized Riemann hypothesis. The 2026 K3 problem list retains the polynomial-time question, whose resolution would also affect the complexity of unknot recognition.
formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm deciding whether a finite simplicial triangulation of a closed connected piecewise-linear \(3\)-manifold is piecewise-linearly homeomorphic to the standard \(3\)-sphere?

Precisely, let \(\mathcal P\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) be the promised encodings below, and let \(S(x)\) assert that the encoded complex is PL-homeomorphic to \(\partial\Delta^{4}\). Does there exist one uniform deterministic Turing machine \(M\), an integer \(C\ge1\), and an integer \(d\ge0\) such that
\[
\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*}\ \exists b\in\{0,1\}\
\left[
H_{M}\bigl(x,C(|x|+1)^{d},b\bigr)
\ \land\
\bigl(x\in\mathcal P\ \Rightarrow\ (b=1\Longleftrightarrow S(x))\bigr)
\right]?
\]
Here \(H_{M}(x,t,b)\) means that \(M\) halts within \(t\) transitions with output bit \(b\). The running-time bound holds on every binary string, including malformed encodings and inputs outside the manifold promise; correctness is required on \(\mathcal P\). The machine and both polynomial constants are fixed before the input is chosen.
definitions:
A finite abstract simplicial complex on \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is a collection \(K\) of subsets of \([m]\), closed under taking subsets and containing every singleton. Its elements are simplices; a simplex with \(r+1\) vertices has dimension \(r\). A tetrahedron is a simplex with four vertices.

An input complex is given by integers \(m\ge4\) and \(N\ge1\), and \(N\) distinct tetrahedra
\(\tau_{j}=\{v_{j1},v_{j2},v_{j3},v_{j4}\}\), where
\[
1\le v_{j1}<v_{j2}<v_{j3}<v_{j4}\le m.
\]
The quadruples are listed in strictly increasing lexicographic order, and every vertex in \([m]\) occurs. Define
\[
K_{x}=\{\sigma\subseteq[m]:\ \sigma\subseteq\tau_{j}
\text{ for some }j\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\}.
\]
All lower-dimensional faces are implicit. Thus the listed tetrahedra are exactly the maximal simplices. There are no coordinates, edge lengths or geometric drawings in the input.

Fix a binary encoding as follows. For a nonnegative integer \(r\), let \(b(r)\) be the ordinary binary representation of \(r+1\), with no leading zero, and let \(\ell=|b(r)|\). Encode \(r\) by \(1^{\ell}0b(r)\). The input string is the concatenation of the codes of \(m,N\), followed by the codes of \(v_{11},v_{12},v_{13},v_{14},v_{21},\ldots,v_{N4}\) in that order, with no trailing bits. A syntactically valid string parses uniquely and obeys the preceding inequalities, ordering and vertex-coverage conditions. Set \(L=|x|\), the total number of input bits. Since every vertex occurs, \(m\le4N\); these explicit encodings have length \(O(N\log(N+2))\).

The geometric realization is the polyhedron
\[
|K|=\left\{(a_{1},\ldots,a_{m})\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{m}:
\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}=1,\ 
\{i:a_{i}>0\}\in K\right\}.
\]
Each abstract simplex is realized as the convex hull of its coordinate unit vectors. A finite geometric simplicial complex is a finite collection of convex hulls of affinely independent finite point sets, containing all their faces, with the intersection of any two simplices empty or a common face. A subdivision of a realization \(|K|\) is such a geometric complex with underlying set \(|K|\), each of whose simplices is contained in an original simplex, and for which every original simplex is the union of simplices of the subdivision. New vertices may be arbitrary real points; they are not additional input data.

Two finite complexes are PL-homeomorphic if they have finite subdivisions whose abstract simplicial complexes are isomorphic. An isomorphism is a bijection of their vertices carrying simplices to simplices in both directions; its affine extension on each simplex supplies the piecewise-linear homeomorphism. There is no required bound on the size of these subdivisions in the definition of the topological property. For \(r\ge1\), \(\Delta^{r}\) is the full simplex on \(r+1\) vertices and \(\partial\Delta^{r}\) consists of all its proper faces. The standard PL \(3\)-sphere is \(|\partial\Delta^{4}|\); the standard PL \(2\)-sphere is \(|\partial\Delta^{3}|\).

For a vertex \(v\) define its link by
\[
\operatorname{lk}_{K}(v)=
\{\sigma\in K:v\notin\sigma,\ \sigma\cup\{v\}\in K\}.
\]
A link has as its vertex set the union of its simplices; when realizing it, use those vertices as the coordinate indices. The same definitions apply to any finite vertex set by replacing \([m]\) with that set. The promise set \(\mathcal P\) consists of syntactically valid strings such that the graph with vertex set \([m]\) and edges the two-element simplices of \(K_{x}\) is connected, and every vertex link is PL-homeomorphic to \(\partial\Delta^{3}\). This is the simplicial formulation of a closed connected PL \(3\)-manifold: finite realization gives compactness, and the spherical-link condition gives the local manifold condition without boundary. No orientation, homology calculation, fundamental-group presentation or certificate of the promise is supplied. Nonorientable manifolds are permitted by the promise. For every binary string \(x\), define \(S(x)\) to be false if \(x\) is not syntactically valid, and otherwise to mean that \(K_{x}\) is PL-homeomorphic to \(\partial\Delta^{4}\).

The machine model is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with finite control, one read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes. Its tape alphabet is \(\{0,1,\#,\square\}\), with \(\square\) blank. Tape cells have nonnegative integer indices and every head initially scans cell zero. The input tape initially holds exactly \(x\) followed by blanks. One transition reads the symbols under the heads, changes the state, writes at most one symbol on each work tape and moves each head by at most one cell; a left move at cell zero stays there. The two halting states output zero and one, respectively. Each transition costs one unit, so all parsing and arithmetic are charged at the bit level. The number of tapes, state set and transition table are independent of \(L\). There is no advice, randomness, oracle or unit-cost operation on unbounded integers.

An answer of one is required for every promised triangulation of the standard PL sphere, and an answer of zero for every other promised manifold. For all other binary strings either bit is permitted, but the same uniform polynomial time bound is mandatory. Neither efficient performance on sampled inputs nor an algorithm restricted to a proper subclass of the promised manifolds meets this definition.
answer_criterion:
