Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed existence proposition, including one machine, its uniform polynomial clock on all binary strings and both correctness directions on \(\mathcal P\), or a complete Lean proof of its full logical negation.

Explicitly, the negative answer must prove
\[
\forall M\ \forall C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall d\in\mathbb N_{0}\
\exists x\in\{0,1\}^{*}
\]
such that, writing \(t=C(|x|+1)^{d}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\bigl(\neg H_{M}(x,t,0)\land\neg H_{M}(x,t,1)\bigr)\\
&\quad\lor\
\left[
x\in\mathcal P\ \land\
\left(
\bigl(H_{M}(x,t,1)\land\neg S(x)\bigr)
\lor
\bigl(H_{M}(x,t,0)\land S(x)\bigr)
\right)
\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus every candidate machine and polynomial clock must fail either the total time bound or correctness on a promised input. The witness input may depend on the candidate and clock. A lower bound for one algorithm, a conditional complexity implication, NP or coNP membership, or a proof of decidability alone does not decide this unconditional target.

title: Linear-size universal point sets for planar graphs
summary: One point set is selected for each graph size. Every planar graph of that size must have a straight-line drawing using some of those points. Vertex assignments may depend on the graph. The question asks whether only linearly many points suffice. Results for subclasses do not settle the universal requirement.
formal: Does there exist a universal real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), some set \(U_n\subset\mathbb R^2\) of at most \(Cn\) distinct points supports a crossing-free straight-line drawing of every simple planar graph on \(n\) vertices?
definitions: The point set \(U_n\) is chosen as a function of \(n\) before the graph is supplied. For each finite simple undirected planar graph \(G\) with vertex set \([n]\), there must be an injective map \(\phi:V(G)\to U_n\). Every edge is drawn as the closed line segment between its endpoint images. Two edge segments may intersect only at the image of a shared endpoint, and the relative interior of an edge may contain no vertex image. Unused points in \(U_n\) are allowed. The injection may depend on \(G\); the same prescribed correspondence of labels to points is not required. The graph need not have a prescribed planar embedding. Coordinates are arbitrary reals, and no grid-size, computability or runtime constraint is imposed. A planar graph means one admitting a plane embedding by arcs with these same incidence and nonintersection requirements.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that a constant \(C>0\) and sets \(U_n\) with the stated universal drawing property exist for every \(n\), or prove the logical negation in Lean: for every \(C>0\), some \(n\) has the property that every point set of size at most \(Cn\) fails to support at least one simple planar graph on \(n\) vertices. The point set precedes the graph in the quantifiers, and each successful drawing may choose its own vertex assignment.

title: Flip graph connectivity in three dimensions
summary: A tetrahedralization divides the convex hull of a fixed three-dimensional point set into tetrahedra. A local flip replaces two tetrahedra by three, or reverses that replacement, while retaining the same five vertices. The question asks whether every pair of tetrahedralizations can be joined by such moves when no four input points are coplanar. All intermediate meshes must keep every original point as a vertex at its original coordinates. Regular tetrahedralizations are known to be connected, but the unrestricted geometric question remains open in the checked sources.
formal:
For every finite point set \(P\subset\mathbb R^3\) with \(|P|\ge4\) and no four points coplanar, is the graph of all geometric tetrahedralizations of \(P\) connected under \(2\leftrightarrow3\) bistellar flips?

A tetrahedralization must use exactly the vertices \(P\), consist of straight, nondegenerate tetrahedra meeting along common faces, and cover \(\operatorname{conv}(P)\). A legal flip replaces two tetrahedra filling a convex triangular bipyramid by the three tetrahedra with the same five vertices and the same union, or performs the reverse replacement. Every intermediate tetrahedralization must retain all points of \(P\) as vertices.

Equivalently, for every such \(P\) and every pair \(T,T'\) of its tetrahedralizations, must there exist a finite sequence \(T=T_0,T_1,\ldots,T_m=T'\) in which each consecutive pair differs by one legal flip?
definitions:
The set \(P\) is finite and consists of distinct points with arbitrary real coordinates in ordinary three-dimensional Euclidean space. General position here means that every four distinct points are affinely independent, equivalently that no four lie in a common plane. Together with \(|P|\ge4\), this ensures a three-dimensional convex hull and nonzero volume for every tetrahedron with four vertices in \(P\). Points may lie in the interior of \(\operatorname{conv}(P)\); they are not assumed to be in convex position. No additional condition on cospherical points is imposed.

For a finite set of points \(A\), its convex hull \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\) is the set of all convex combinations of points of \(A\), with \(\operatorname{conv}(\varnothing)=\varnothing\). A geometric tetrahedron with vertex set \(A\subset P\), \(|A|=4\), is the closed set \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\). Its faces are the convex hulls of subsets of its vertices, including vertices, edges, triangles, the tetrahedron itself and the empty face.

A tetrahedralization is a collection \(T\) of four-element subsets of \(P\) satisfying all of the following conditions. Every point of \(P\) belongs to some member of \(T\). The union of the corresponding closed tetrahedra is \(\operatorname{conv}(P)\). For every \(A,B\in T\),
\[\operatorname{conv}(A)\cap\operatorname{conv}(B)=\operatorname{conv}(A\cap B).\]
Thus different tetrahedra have disjoint interiors and any intersection is their common face; overlaps, crossing faces and hanging vertices inside another tetrahedron are excluded. All faces of the tetrahedra are understood to belong to the resulting simplicial complex. This is a full geometric triangulation, not merely an abstract complex homeomorphic to a ball. No extra vertices, curved faces or gaps in the convex hull are allowed.

The local replacement can be specified by five distinct points \(a,b,c,d,e\in P\). They must all be vertices of their convex hull, and that hull must be the convex triangular bipyramid formed by the two tetrahedra \(\{a,b,c,d\}\) and \(\{a,b,c,e\}\) sharing triangle \(abc\). In particular, \(d\) and \(e\) are on opposite sides of the plane of \(a,b,c\). Write
\[U_2=\bigl\{\{a,b,c,d\},\{a,b,c,e\}\bigr\},\qquad U_3=\bigl\{\{a,b,d,e\},\{b,c,d,e\},\{c,a,d,e\}\bigr\}.\]
These are the two tetrahedralizations of this bipyramid: \(U_2\) uses the interior triangle \(abc\), while \(U_3\) uses the interior edge \(de\). A \(2\)-to-\(3\) flip is allowed when \(U_2\subseteq T\) and
\[T'=(T\setminus U_2)\cup U_3\]
is a tetrahedralization of the same \(P\), with the replaced tetrahedra and the new tetrahedra having exactly the same geometric union. A \(3\)-to-\(2\) flip is the inverse operation under the same conditions. Requiring both configurations to be valid tetrahedralizations makes the local move compatible with all tetrahedra outside the replaced region.

The flip graph \(\mathcal F(P)\) is the finite undirected graph whose vertices are these tetrahedralizations and whose edges join pairs related by one such flip. Reversing a legal move is legal. Connectivity means that every pair of graph vertices can be joined by a finite path. The path may have length zero when the two tetrahedralizations coincide. No polynomial bound, sharp diameter, monotonicity condition or prescribed target triangulation is part of the proposition.

Only \(2\)-to-\(3\) and \(3\)-to-\(2\) moves are permitted. A \(1\)-to-\(4\) move inserts an interior vertex into a tetrahedron, and a \(4\)-to-\(1\) move removes a vertex; neither is allowed, even if the point is restored later. Points cannot be moved or perturbed along a path. Allowing such operations changes the graph under study.

The quantifier order is \(\forall P\;\forall T,T'\;\exists m\ge0\;\exists(T_i)_{i=0}^m\). All tetrahedralizations and all intermediate coordinates refer to the same fixed geometric point set. A negative answer consists of a set meeting the general-position hypothesis and two valid tetrahedralizations in different components, with a proof that no finite legal path joins them. Merely showing that one particular greedy rule gets stuck, or displaying an abstract nonrealizable tetrahedral complex, is insufficient.

Regular tetrahedralizations are a special class mentioned in the known results. A tetrahedralization \(T\) is regular if there is a height assignment \(w:P\to\mathbb R\) such that, for each \(A\in T\), an affine function \(\ell_A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R\) equals \(w\) on the four points of \(A\) and is strictly below \(w\) at every point of \(P\setminus A\). These are the tetrahedralizations obtained by projecting the simplicial lower hull of the lifted points. The target includes nonregular tetrahedralizations as well. It is an exact geometric existence question; there is no coordinate encoding, running-time or approximation tolerance to optimize.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of connectivity for every finite point set in the stated general position. A positive proof must establish a finite legal \(2\leftrightarrow3\) path between every pair of full geometric tetrahedralizations, with all intermediate complexes using the same point coordinates and vertex set. No efficient path-finding algorithm or polynomial path length is required. A negative proof must establish the general position and geometric validity of a counterexample and prove that two tetrahedralizations lie in different components of its full flip graph. A result only for regular triangulations, higher-dimensional point sets, abstract complexes, or paths that remove or add vertices does not settle the target. Numerical experiments and approximate coordinate pictures alone are insufficient.

title: Optimal input-sparsity subspace embeddings
summary: An oblivious subspace embedding chooses a random linear map without knowing the subspace it must preserve. With high probability, the map must preserve the norms of all vectors in each fixed target subspace at once. The question asks for optimal output dimension together with a precise logarithmic-over-accuracy bound on nonzeros per column. These two parameters control compression quality and the arithmetic cost of applying the embedding to sparse data. The checked 2026 result approaches the target with remaining sub-polylogarithmic factors and does not settle the exact conjecture.
formal: Is the optimal-dimension sparse oblivious subspace-embedding conjecture true? Precisely, does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge1\) such that for every pair of integers \(n\ge d\ge1\) and every \(0<\varepsilon,\delta\le1/3\), there are an integer \(m\) and a probability distribution \(\mathcal D\) over real \(m\times n\) matrices with \[1\le m\le\left\lceil C\,\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon^2}\right\rceil,\qquad s=\left\lceil C\,\frac{\log(d/\delta)}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil,\] such that every matrix in the support has at most \(s\) nonzero entries per column and, for every \(d\)-dimensional linear subspace \(W\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[\Pr_{\Pi\sim\mathcal D}\bigl[\ \forall x\in W:\ (1-\varepsilon)\|x\|_2\le\|\Pi x\|_2\le(1+\varepsilon)\|x\|_2\ \bigr]\ge1-\delta?\] The row and column-sparsity bounds must hold simultaneously, with no additional growing factors.
definitions: The ambient dimension is \(n\), the subspace dimension is \(d\), and the reduced dimension is \(m\). All logarithms are natural logarithms; changing the base changes only the universal constant. For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^n x_j^2)^{1/2}\). A linear subspace \(W\) is closed under real linear combinations and has a basis of exactly \(d\) linearly independent vectors. Its embedding is the linear map \(x\mapsto\Pi x\). The distribution is a Borel probability measure on the finite-dimensional real matrix space and is supported on matrices satisfying the per-column sparsity bound. Different matrix entries need not be independent; neither a particular sparsity pattern nor a particular distribution of nonzero values is prescribed. The same \(\mathcal D\), chosen from \(n,d,\varepsilon,\delta\) alone, must satisfy the probability guarantee for every fixed \(W\). It cannot depend on a basis or other information about \(W\). The order of quantifiers is \(\forall(n,d,\varepsilon,\delta)\ \exists(m,\mathcal D)\ \forall W\); this does not require one sampled matrix to succeed simultaneously for all subspaces. Inside the success event, however, the inequalities must hold simultaneously for every vector of the chosen subspace, rather than separately with fresh randomness for each vector. The failure probability is \(\delta\) for the entire subspace. The statement is distributional existence, with one universal dimension/sparsity constant, and does not require a finite-bit sampling algorithm or bit-complexity bound for arbitrary real entries. This is the explicit dimension-and-sparsity conjecture underlying the source’s input-sparsity application-time discussion. The accuracy and confidence regime \(0<\varepsilon,\delta\le1/3\) is fixed explicitly; neither parameter is assumed to be inverse polynomial in \(d\). There is no restriction relating \(n\) to the desired row bound, and \(m\) is permitted to exceed \(n\) when the parameter bound does. For an \(n\times d\) input matrix \(A\), \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)\) denotes the number of its nonzero entries. Column sparsity controls the number of scalar contributions needed to form \(\Pi A\); this motivates the running-time terminology but is not an extra end-to-end bit-time requirement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the quantified existence statement, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must give the simultaneous row and column-sparsity bounds for all stated parameter values and a distribution independent of the target subspace. Constants may not depend on \(n,d,\varepsilon,\delta\). Bounds with extra logarithmic or sub-polylogarithmic factors, only inverse-polynomial failure probabilities, or only inverse-polynomial accuracy do not establish this exact target. A construction chosen after examining the subspace, a guarantee for a finite list of vectors, or a failure example for a single proposed distribution does not settle the general conjecture.

title: Klee’s measure running-time exponent
summary: Klee’s measure problem computes the volume covered by a union of axis-aligned boxes. Overlaps count once, and the requested volume is exact. The card asks for the optimal deterministic running-time exponent in every fixed dimension at least three. Each exponent must be certified to absolute error 0.01. Logarithmic factors and a fastest algorithm attaining the infimum are not required.
formal: For each fixed integer \(d\ge3\), determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the optimal deterministic running-time exponent \[x_{\mathrm{Klee}}(d)=\inf\{a\ge0:\text{some uniform exact algorithm has worst-case time }O_d(n^a)\}.\] The task is to compute the exact \(d\)-dimensional volume of the union of \(n\) explicitly given axis-aligned boxes in the real-RAM model below. Programs and constants may depend on fixed \(d\), but not on the coordinates or input size. Logarithmic factors in running time are not part of the numerical answer.
definitions: An input is a list of \(n\ge 0\) closed boxes \(B_i=\prod_{j=1}^d[a_{ij},b_{ij}]\), specified by their 2dn finite real endpoints, with \(a_{ij}\le b_{ij}\). Overlaps, coincident endpoints, duplicate boxes and zero side lengths are allowed. The output is the exact Lebesgue measure of \(\bigcup_i B_i\), returned as a real number; the empty union has volume zero. For clarity, the real-RAM convention here is deterministic computation with exact real registers, unit-cost copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, comparisons and branching. Random access is through integer addresses. Control and address registers have \(O(\log (n+2))\) bits, with any fixed constant factor depending on the algorithm and d; standard arithmetic, comparison, Boolean and shift operations on these words cost one unit. Integers can be converted to real registers, but real values can affect integer control only through comparisons: no floor, bit extraction or arbitrary real-to-integer conversion is available. A program is finite and independent of n and the coordinates; any hard-coded real constants must be algebraic and finitely specified. Input reads, output writes, preprocessing, memory operations and control steps count. Worst-case time is the maximum over all endpoint lists of size n, regardless of coordinate magnitude. No randomness, approximation tolerance, oracle or precomputed advice depending on n is supplied. For a correct uniform deterministic program \(A\) in fixed dimension \(d\), let \(t_{A,d}(n)\) be its worst-case time on \(n\) boxes. Define \[x_{\mathrm{Klee}}(d)=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists A\ \exists C>0\ \exists n_0\ge1\ \forall n\ge n_0,\ t_{A,d}(n)\le Cn^a\}.\] A different uniform program may be selected for each fixed dimension and each exponent bound, but not for each input length. Elementary input access and the cited algorithm give \(1\le x_{\mathrm{Klee}}(d)\le d/2\). The infimum need not be attained; in particular a value does not prescribe matching logarithmic factors. A lower bound must concern every permitted exact program, without an unproved complexity assumption.
answer_criterion: Supply one explicitly described real-valued function \(a\) on all integers \(d\ge3\). Prove in Lean that \(|a(d)-x_{\mathrm{Klee}}(d)|\le1/100\) at every point of that domain. A pair of [certified bounding functions](definitions.html#numerical-answers) \(L,U\) also qualifies if \(L(d)\le x_{\mathrm{Klee}}(d)\le U(d)\) and \(U(d)-L(d)\le1/50\) everywhere, with \(a=(L+U)/2\). Use the specified exact real-RAM model at each fixed dimension. Lower bounds must cover all permitted uniform exact algorithms for that dimension.

title: Truly subquadratic exact Euclidean bipartite matching
summary: The input is two equally sized labelled sets of points in the Euclidean plane. The task is to find an exactly minimum-length one-to-one red-blue matching in truly subquadratic time. The card fixes a real-arithmetic model and permits bounded-error randomization on every fixed input. Fast approximation and faster stochastic-input algorithms have different guarantees. A solution would show whether planar geometry alone removes a polynomial part of the quadratic exact-optimization cost.
formal: Does there exist a uniform algorithm and absolute constants \(\delta,C>0\) that, for every \(n\ge1\) and every pair of labelled planar point lists \(R=(r_1,\ldots,r_n)\), \(B=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)\), returns a permutation \(\pi\in S_n\) minimizing \(\sum_{i=1}^n\|r_i-b_{\pi(i)}\|_2\), using at most \(Cn^{2-\delta}\) operations in the real-arithmetic model below, with probability at least \(2/3\) on each input? Deterministic algorithms qualify. Coordinates are arbitrary real numbers and there is no separation, spread or grid promise.
definitions:
The input consists of the two explicit lists of coordinate pairs in \(\mathbb R^2\); coincident points remain distinct labelled objects. A feasible matching pairs each red label with exactly one blue label and conversely. Its edge length is \(\|(x,y)-(u,v)\|_2=\sqrt{(x-u)^2+(y-v)^2}\). The output is the list of matched labels, and any minimizer is acceptable when several matchings tie. Squared Euclidean lengths define a different objective.

The editorial computational convention is a uniform real RAM with exact addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero value, comparison and nonnegative square root, each costing one operation. Reading or writing one register, branching, and drawing a fair random bit also cost one. Integer registers are used for addressing and ordinary control; no operation extracts an arbitrarily long binary expansion of a real in one step. Input reals are accessed as atomic coordinates, so this is an arithmetic-operation question rather than a finite-bit encoding theorem. The program is finite and independent of the input size.

The stated operation bound is worst-case over inputs and random choices; success probability refers only to the algorithm's coins on each fixed input. A successful output must attain the exact minimum, not merely an approximation to its cost. This bounded-error convention explicitly resolves the imported draft's unspecified randomization convention. The exponent improvement and constant must be independent of all coordinates, including the ratio between largest and smallest nonzero distances. An estimate containing an uncontrolled coordinate-dependent factor does not meet the bound. No preprocessing of a supplied table of all red-blue distances is free: the given input has only \(4n\) real coordinates.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm with the displayed operation and success guarantees, or a Lean-checked refutation in this specified model. A positive answer includes exact optimality on the successful event and one fixed exponent improvement for every input. A negative answer must exclude every such algorithm and every positive fixed improvement, rather than exhibit a bad case for a particular method. Approximate matching, a guarantee only for random point sets, or a grid-dependent time bound does not establish the proposition.

title: Polygon visibility graph recognition
summary: A polygon's visibility graph records which pairs of vertices can be joined by a segment lying inside the polygon. The source supplies both a candidate graph and a Hamiltonian cycle specifying the intended polygon boundary. It asks for an efficient decision procedure for whether a simple polygon realizes exactly that information. Choosing coordinates must satisfy visibility and obstruction requirements simultaneously. The problem tests whether a combinatorial record of sight lines contains enough accessible structure to reconstruct a genuine geometric environment.
formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and a cyclic order \(C=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) of its vertices, decides whether some simple polygon with these labelled vertices in boundary order \(C\) has visibility graph exactly \(G\)? Here \(n\geq3\), the graph is given by its complete adjacency matrix and the cyclic order by an explicit list. Both visible and nonvisible pairs must be realized, and the polygon has no holes or additional vertices.
definitions: A realization assigns distinct points \(p_i\in\mathbb R^2\) to the labels. The union of the segments \([p_{v_i},p_{v_{i+1}}]\), with indices cyclic modulo \(n\), must be a simple closed polygonal curve: consecutive segments meet only at their common endpoint and nonconsecutive segments are disjoint. Let \(P\) be this curve together with its bounded complementary component. Vertices \(i\ne j\) are visible exactly when the entire closed segment \([p_i,p_j]\) is contained in \(P\). Visibility along the boundary is allowed, including through other labelled collinear vertices; redundant collinear boundary vertices are permitted as long as the curve remains simple. This closed-region convention is explicit and no general-position promise is imposed. The graph must contain every edge of the specified boundary cycle, otherwise the answer is no. Malformed matrices, a nonsymmetric matrix, loops, a nonpermutation order or \(n<3\) are rejected. The input is a binary encoding of the full matrix and list, of length \(N\); one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine must decide correctly in at most \(K(N+1)^a\) steps for fixed \(K,a\). Real coordinates are existential mathematical witnesses, with no rationality, grid-size or bit-length restriction. The requested algorithm returns a Boolean answer and need not produce coordinates.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the language of realizable graph/order pairs belongs to \(\mathrm{P}\), or that it does not, for the exact polygon and visibility conventions above. A positive answer must establish correctness and a polynomial worst-case bit-time bound for one uniform decision algorithm on every encoding. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm; an NP-hardness or \(\exists\mathbb R\)-hardness result alone does not prove nonmembership in \(\mathrm{P}\) without the corresponding separation. A necessary graph condition, recognition of a special polygon class, or recognition with extra geometric data is insufficient.

title: Near-quadratic Voronoi complexity of lines in three dimensions
summary: Each point in three-dimensional space has a set of nearest input lines. Connected regions with the same nearest-line set form the diagram’s cells. The question counts cells of all dimensions. The proposed bound is arbitrarily close to quadratic. The Euclidean metric and the specified nondegeneracy convention are essential parts of this formulation.
formal: For every real \(\varepsilon>0\), does there exist a real \(C_\varepsilon>0\) such that every regular Euclidean Voronoi diagram of \(n\ge2\) distinct affine lines in \(\mathbb R^3\), under the exact stratum convention below, has total complexity at most \(C_\varepsilon n^{2+\varepsilon}\)?
definitions: A line is the set \(\ell_i=\{p_i+tv_i:t\in\mathbb R\}\), where \(p_i,v_i\in\mathbb R^3\) and \(v_i\ne0\). Distances are ordinary Euclidean point-to-line distances. For every nonempty \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), define \(V_I\) to be the set of points whose set of nearest lines is exactly \(\{\ell_i:i\in I\}\). Regular means that \(V_I\) is empty for \(|I|>4\), and for \(1\le|I|\le4\) each nonempty \(V_I\) is a smooth embedded manifold of dimension \(4-|I|\). The cells counted are the connected components of every nonempty \(V_I\), including unbounded components and zero-dimensional components. Let \(b_0(V_I)\) be the number of such components, with \(b_0(\varnothing)=0\); total complexity is \(\sum_{\varnothing\ne I\subseteq[n]}b_0(V_I)\). These semialgebraic sets have finitely many connected components. The statement is an extremal mathematical bound; no bit encoding or construction algorithm for real coordinates is required. The constants depend only on \(\varepsilon\), not on the lines or their coordinates.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated bound for every \(\varepsilon>0\) on all diagrams in the defined regular class, or prove its logical negation in Lean: some \(\varepsilon_0>0\) has unbounded total complexity divided by \(n^{2+\varepsilon_0}\) over that class. The count must include connected components in all four dimensions, including unbounded ones. A bound only for four sites, one ruled-surface family, vertices alone, or a different metric does not establish the full statement.

title: Fast Johnson–Lindenstrauss transforms for sparse vectors
summary: A Johnson–Lindenstrauss map reduces dimension while approximately preserving the length of each fixed vector with high probability. The question asks for the optimal output dimension together with application time proportional to input sparsity plus output length, up to logarithms of the ambient dimension. The map is chosen independently of the input, and the guarantee must hold for all distortion and failure-probability parameters. Known sparse and fast structured transforms do not by themselves provide this full combination, and the separate short-seed objective has been removed. A resolution would clarify whether geometric compression can be performed almost at the cost of reading and writing sparse data.
formal:
Do there exist absolute constants \(C_1,C_2>0\), an integer \(q\ge0\), and uniform sampling and application algorithms with the following property? For every integer \(d\ge1\) and every \(0<\varepsilon,\delta<1/2\), the sampling algorithm produces an input-independent representation of a random linear map \(A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k\), where
\[
1\le k\le\min\{d,\lceil C_1\varepsilon^{-2}\log_2(1/\delta)\rceil\}.
\]
For every fixed \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), its distribution satisfies
\[
\Pr_A\bigl[(1-\varepsilon)\|x\|_2\le\|Ax\|_2
                 \le(1+\varepsilon)\|x\|_2\bigr]\ge1-\delta.
\]
Given a sampled representation and the list of the \(s\) nonzero coordinates of any \(x\), the application algorithm must return all coordinates of \(Ax\) in at most
\[
C_2(s+k)\bigl(\log_2(d+2)\bigr)^q
\]
operations in the arithmetic model below, for every sampled representation and input. The same constants and algorithms must work for all parameters. The matrix distribution is independent of \(x\), including its support.
definitions:
The Euclidean norm is \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d x_i^2)^{1/2}\), and \(s=\|x\|_0=|\{i:x_i\ne0\}|\) is input sparsity. The input is an arbitrary-order list of distinct indices in \(\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and their nonzero real values, together with \(d\). Coordinates absent from the list are zero. Reading this list and writing the dense length-\(k\) output count toward application time. The zero vector is included, with \(s=0\).

A sampled object represents one genuine linear map on all of \(\mathbb R^d\), not a map chosen after seeing the support or magnitudes of the input. The application algorithm must evaluate that map exactly in real arithmetic. The approximation concerns preservation of length, not numerical evaluation of the matrix product. The probability statement is for each vector fixed independently of the sampled map; it does not claim that one dimension-reducing map preserves every vector simultaneously. No promise bounds the ratio of the largest coordinate to the norm.

Use an arithmetic RAM: a real value occupies one cell, and addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero value, square root of a nonnegative value, and comparison each cost one operation. Memory access and operations on integer indices of logarithmic size in the allocated storage also cost one. There is no floor operation on arbitrary real values, arbitrary real-to-integer decoding, or oracle for matrix-vector multiplication. The programs are finite and uniform, with rational built-in constants; \(\varepsilon,\delta\) are real parameter inputs. This is an arithmetic-operation question, not a bound on the bit complexity of arbitrarily precise real coordinates.

The distribution and its representation may be prepared before the input vector is provided. To fix the construction convention, the sampler uses independent fair bits, has expected time and storage bounded by a fixed polynomial in \(d+\varepsilon^{-1}+\lceil\log_2(1/\delta)\rceil\), and terminates with probability one. It outputs a finite read-only representation used by the application algorithm. Setup work is independent of the input vector and is not included in per-vector application time; any subsequent work on the vector, including an input-dependent transformation or preprocessing, is included. Application time is a worst-case bound, not an amortized bound over a favorable collection of vectors. All sampler outcomes with positive probability must define an evaluable map. No logarithmic bound on the number of random bits is requested.

The output dimension \(k\) is selected from the parameters and is fixed before drawing the map. The ceiling handles integer dimensions, and the cap at \(d\) allows the identity when the usual dimension bound would exceed the ambient dimension. The phrase optimal dimension refers to the order of the displayed upper bound, not its best leading constant. The exponent \(q\) and time constant are independent of error and failure probability. In particular, an extra factor depending on \(\varepsilon^{-1}\) or \(\log(1/\delta)\) cannot be hidden in the input-sparsity term unless it is absorbed by the displayed bound.

The source has a separate question about generating the map with \(O(\log(d/\delta))\) random bits. The formulation omits that additional objective. The setup convention above makes the retained application question precise without reinstating the short-seed target.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the uniform existence assertion, including the distribution, dimension bound, pointwise probability guarantee and worst-case sparse-input application bound in the stated model. An affirmative answer must cover every parameter choice and arbitrary real input vector; a result only for constant distortion, constant failure probability, dense inputs, or special coordinate distributions is insufficient. A negative answer is the full negation and must cover every allowed construction and application algorithm, rather than one chosen sparse-matrix family. A proof about the omitted seed-length objective does not answer this card. The benchmark's numerical-value tolerance does not weaken the prescribed asymptotic guarantees.

title: Exact planar Euclidean maximum TSP
summary: The problem asks for an exactly longest closed Euclidean tour through rational points in the plane. The output is an ordering of all points, and edge crossings are allowed. One deterministic algorithm must run in time polynomial in the full binary length of all coordinates. Approximation schemes and exact algorithms for polygonal norms do not settle this Euclidean bit-complexity question. A resolution would clarify how the choice of geometry and exact arithmetic affects optimization complexity.
formal:
Is there a deterministic algorithm that finds an exactly longest Euclidean tour through any finite set of rational points in the plane in time polynomial in the full binary input length?

For an explicitly listed set \(P=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)\) of distinct points in \(\mathbb Q^2\), with \(n\ge3\), define the length of a cyclic ordering \(\pi\) by
\[\ell_P(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt{(x_{\pi(i)}-x_{\pi(i+1)})^2+(y_{\pi(i)}-y_{\pi(i+1)})^2},\qquad \pi(n+1)=\pi(1).\]
Do there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\), a constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(a\ge0\) such that, on every valid input of bit length \(B\), the machine returns a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfying
\[\ell_P(\pi)=\max_{\sigma\in S_n}\ell_P(\sigma)\]
within \(C(B+1)^a\) bit operations?
definitions:
The input is a finite list of coordinates \(p_i=(x_i,y_i)\). Each coordinate is a signed binary integer numerator divided by a positive binary integer denominator. Use a fixed self-delimiting encoding of these integers and the list. The bit length \(B\) counts all numerators, denominators and delimiters, as well as the number of points. The coordinates may have arbitrarily many bits. There is no bound on their magnitude, denominators, aspect ratio or minimum separation beyond what the finite input specifies. Equivalent ordinary binary encodings change polynomial time only by polynomial factors.

The points are pairwise distinct. Collinear triples, an entirely collinear set and other degeneracies are allowed. No general-position or convex-position promise is imposed. The algorithm must work for all \(n\ge3\). A machine may reject malformed encodings, repeated points or lists shorter than three; this validation must also take polynomial time. These validity conventions do not permit rejecting any valid instance because its coordinates are numerically difficult.

The symbol \(S_n\) denotes the set of all permutations of the point indices. A tour visits every input point exactly once in that order and then returns to its starting point. Its edges are the straight segments between consecutive points, and its total length is the sum of their ordinary Euclidean lengths. Every pair of points is an available connection. There is no separate graph of allowed edges, and there are no obstacles.

The word “planar” restricts the locations of the points to two-dimensional Euclidean space. It imposes no noncrossing requirement on the tour. Segments may intersect, overlap on collinear inputs or pass through other points; the visits in the tour are specified by its permutation. Cyclic rotations and reversals represent the same undirected cycle, but the output may be any representing permutation. If several tours attain the maximum, any one is acceptable.

The output is the explicit list of \(n\) indices in a maximizing order. It need not include the optimum length, an approximation to that length, a square-root expression or a certificate independently checking optimality. Its size is polynomial in \(B\). Exactness refers to maximizing the real-valued sum in the statement, even though the output itself is a finite combinatorial object.

Use a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with finite alphabet and finite program. The constants \(C,a\) are fixed for the entire algorithm, independent of the input length, coordinates and arrangement. All arithmetic, storage, comparisons and output operations are charged by their bit cost. An operation involving arbitrarily large integers or algebraic numbers is not a unit-time primitive. The machine has no exact-real arithmetic oracle and no oracle comparing sums of square roots. Randomized algorithms, advice depending on input length and machines whose polynomial exponent depends on the input do not satisfy this definition.

Each squared edge length is rational, but its square root can be irrational. Distinct tours can also have equal total lengths. A proposed algorithm must justify any precision or exact arithmetic it uses within its polynomial bit bound. A polynomial bound on the number of real-arithmetic operations alone does not provide that justification. Conversely, returning an optimal permutation is not defined to include solving every separate comparison problem for arbitrary sums of square roots.

The objective is the sum of all edge lengths. It differs from minimum-length TSP, from finding a longest spanning path without the closing edge, and from maximum scatter TSP, which maximizes the shortest edge in the tour. Replacing Euclidean distance by squared Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance or a polygonal norm also changes the optimization problem.

A polynomial-time approximation scheme supplies, for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), a tour of length at least \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(P)\), where \(\operatorname{OPT}(P)=\max_{\sigma\in S_n}\ell_P(\sigma)\). Its polynomial exponent or constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\). This does not give exact optimization by simply choosing an unspecified tiny error: the separation between unequal tour lengths and the resulting computation cost would both need proof.

The original source asks broadly for the complexity of finding a maximum tour and mentions a conjecture of NP-hardness. This card selects, the specific existence question for a polynomial bit-time exact-tour algorithm on rational planar inputs. NP-hardness means that a polynomial-time reduction would make this optimization task at least as hard as every problem in NP, with the reduction and output access specified. Such a theorem can establish a conditional obstruction under \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\); NP-hardness alone does not prove the unconditional nonexistence quantified here.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the uniform deterministic algorithm in the statement, including correctness on every valid input, handling of exact ties and a polynomial bound in the full bit length. Alternatively, give a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. A negative answer must quantify over every deterministic machine and every fixed polynomial bound. An approximation scheme, a real-arithmetic algorithm without a bit-cost analysis, a result only for a restricted point configuration or a three-dimensional hardness theorem does not settle this target. A planar NP-hardness reduction is substantial progress but gives an unconditional negative answer only together with a proved premise sufficient to rule out the algorithm. There is no additive or multiplicative tolerance: the returned permutation must attain the exact maximum.

title: Linear-size sample compression
summary: Sample compression keeps labeled examples and a short side message from which a fixed decoder recovers every original training label. The conjecture asks for a bound linear in VC dimension, uniformly across all Boolean concept classes. This card counts both retained examples and side bits, and permits arbitrary predictors and unlimited computation. Cai and coauthors obtain a near-quadratic bound for every class. Whether a linear number of examples and side bits always suffices remains open.
formal: Is there a universal integer \(C\ge1\) such that every nonempty Boolean concept class \(H\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X}\) on an arbitrary set \(X\), with finite VC dimension \(d\ge1\), admits a labeled sample compression scheme with nonnegative integer kernel and side-information bounds \(k,b\) satisfying \[k+b\le Cd?\] The scheme is exact on every finite \(H\)-realizable sample, stores an unordered subset of labeled sample records plus \(b\) bits, and may reconstruct a predictor outside \(H\). Its compressor, reconstructor, \(k\), and \(b\) may depend on the complete class, but the same scheme and bounds must work for all sample sizes. Only \(C\) must be universal. This preserves the card’s previously selected linear-size, counted-side-information formulation.
definitions: A concept is a total Boolean function on \(X\). A finite set \(U\subseteq X\) is shattered by \(H\) if \(\{h|_U:h\in H\}=\{0,1\}^{U}\); the VC dimension is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A finite labeled sample is a finite set \(S\subseteq X\times\{0,1\}\). It is \(H\)-realizable if some \(h\in H\) agrees with every pair in \(S\); in particular, a realizable sample has no contradictory labels at the same point. The empty sample is allowed. A scheme consists of deterministic set maps \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\). For every realizable \(S\), \(\kappa(S)=(T,z)\), where \(T\subseteq S\), \(|T|\le k\), and \(z\in\{0,1\}^{b}\). The reconstruction \(\rho(T,z):X\to\{0,1\}\) is a total predictor satisfying \[\rho(\kappa(S))(x)=y\qquad\text{for every }(x,y)\in S.\] The reconstructor is defined for all possible finite labeled kernels of size at most \(k\) and all \(b\)-bit strings, with consistency required only on actual compressed messages. It receives no original sample, sample size, omitted point, original index or ordering of retained examples. One retained labeled example costs one unit, even on a domain whose points have no finite binary descriptions; each side-information bit costs one unit. The retained set is unordered. A finite side alphabet \(I\) instead of bit strings costs \(\lceil\log_2|I|\rceil\) bits. Allowing variable-length strings of bounded length changes this linear-size question only by a constant factor if their lengths are encoded as part of the message. The compressor is required only on realizable samples. Reconstruction need not be proper, stable under deletion of unused records, computable, efficient, or measurable. No randomness or data-distribution promise is involved. Dimension zero is omitted from the display because a nonempty such class has one pointwise labeling and admits a scheme storing nothing. All classes of positive finite dimension, not just finite domains or finite classes, are included.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the stated universal linear bound, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must provide a single universal constant and, for each class, a valid compressor and reconstructor with the counted size bound holding on every realizable sample. A negative answer must show that for every integer \(C\ge1\), some class of positive finite VC dimension admits no such scheme of size at most \(Cd\). A lower bound against only proper, stable, efficient, or otherwise restricted reconstruction does not refute this unrestricted target. Neither does failure of a particular embedding construction. Free side information or free ordering of retained points is outside the model. The requirement is exact consistency and linear size with a universal constant; it asks for no additive numerical approximation.

title: Learning parity with noise in polynomial time
summary: The card asks whether a hidden parity vector can be recovered efficiently from uniform examples whose labels are independently flipped. The noise rate is any fixed rational below one half, with a separate uniform polynomial-time learner allowed for each rate. Success requires the entire secret vector with probability at least two thirds for every secret and dimension. Known subexponential algorithms, storage bounds, conditional reductions and structured physical experiments do not establish the unrestricted polynomial-time assertion or its negation. The completed card preserves the assessed importance and gives exact computation, sampling and Lean proof requirements.
formal: For every fixed rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\), does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that exactly recovers every hidden parity vector from independent uniform examples with independent label noise of rate \(\eta\)? More explicitly, is the following assertion true? \[\forall\eta\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1/2)\ \exists A_\eta,\ C_\eta,k_\eta\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall s\in\{0,1\}^n:\quad \Pr[A_\eta^{\operatorname{EX}_{n,s,\eta}}(1^n)=s]\ge\frac23,\] where every execution takes at most \(C_\eta(n+1)^{k_\eta}\) bit-computation steps, including all example requests and output writing, and \(\operatorname{EX}_{n,s,\eta}\) returns a fresh pair \[ (a,b),\qquad a\sim U_n,\quad e\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\eta),\quad b=\langle a,s\rangle\oplus e.\] All vectors, errors and machine coins are independent except for the displayed dependence of each label on its input and the same fixed secret. This retains the existing every-fixed-rate, every-secret search-LPN target.
definitions:
The domain \(\{0,1\}^n\) is the vector space \(\mathbb F_2^n\), where addition is coordinatewise modulo two. The parity \(\langle a,s\rangle=(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i s_i)\bmod2\) is the XOR of exactly those input coordinates where \(s_i=1\); \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two. \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution giving each input vector probability \(2^{-n}\), and \(e\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\eta)\) means \(\Pr[e=1]=\eta\). The secret is arbitrary, fixed before the samples and coins are drawn, and unchanged throughout one execution. Each call returns an independent sample under that fixed secret, including a fresh error bit. The learner may decide when to request more samples based on its previous observations, but cannot choose \(a\), observe the error bit, obtain a clean label, or query a coherent quantum example.

\(A_\eta\) is one classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine using fair independent coins and the specified example oracle. It receives the dimension in unary. The fixed rational rate may be built into the machine; there is no promise that one common algorithm or common exponent works uniformly over rates approaching one half with \(n\). The machine, positive integer constant \(C_\eta\), and positive integer exponent \(k_\eta\) are chosen before \(n\) and \(s\). They may depend on \(\eta\), but have no length-dependent advice. All reading, storing, revisiting examples, computation and output bits are charged; the oracle’s internal sample generation is not charged, and one request costs at least one step. The worst-case bound holds for all possible example and coin histories, not just in expectation. Thus time, samples and stored bits are polynomially bounded, while unrestricted repeated access to stored data is allowed. No single-pass or small-memory constraint is imposed.

The output is exactly one \(n\)-bit vector \(\widehat s\); malformed output is failure. Success means \(\widehat s=s\), not merely low noisy-label error or an unspecified prediction advantage. The probability is over the entire training sample stream and learner randomness for each fixed secret, with no distributional promise on \(s\). Neither \(s\) nor the sample inputs are promised sparse. Fixed confidence \(2/3\) is retained. The target is the existence of a polynomial-time search procedure, rather than the quantitative size of the best subexponential exponent or a numerical approximation requiring a precision convention.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or its complete logical negation. A positive result must supply a machine and polynomial resource bound separately for every fixed rational noise rate, and prove exact recovery with the stated probability for every dimension and secret. A negative result must exhibit at least one fixed rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\) for which every candidate machine and polynomial bound fail on some dimension and secret, either in the resource guarantee or in recovery probability. Hardness only for a rate depending on \(n\), a restricted statistical-query or small-memory learner, sparse inputs, quantum examples, or under an unproved computational assumption is not the unconditional negation. Recovering a hypothesis with some advantage is sufficient only together with a proved conversion meeting the exact-secret criterion and the same polynomial-resource requirements.

title: Polynomial-time distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
summary: A DNF is a disjunction of conjunctions of possibly negated Boolean variables, with the number of terms bounded by the supplied size parameter. The learner sees only independent noiseless labeled examples from an arbitrary unknown distribution and must run in one polynomial in dimension, term bound and the stated accuracy/confidence parameters. Its output may be any explicitly written deterministic Boolean circuit whose predictions have small distributional error with high probability. Polynomial sample complexity is available, while known improper-learning lower bounds remain conditional and recent positive results use restricted distributions, stronger query access or different output guarantees. A solution needs a complete Lean proof of the full uniform learner guarantee or a negation covering every allowed learner and polynomial bound.
formal:
Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and absolute positive integers \(a,d\) such that the following holds for every pair of integers \(n,s\ge1\), every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) representable by a DNF with at most \(s\) terms, every probability distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), and every pair of integers \(t,b\ge2\)? Given only \((n,s,t,b)\) and access to independent labeled examples \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim D\), the learner halts within
\[a(n+s+t+b+1)^d\]
steps on every run and outputs an explicitly encoded deterministic Boolean circuit \(h\) on \(n\) inputs such that
\[\Pr\!\left[\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}D(x)\,\mathbf 1[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge1-2^{-b}?\]
The outer probability includes the learner’s coins and sampled examples. Membership queries, equivalence queries and descriptions of \(f\) or \(D\) are not supplied. The output need not be a DNF; it must be an efficiently evaluable circuit as defined below.
definitions:
A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation, \(1\le i\le n\). A term is the conjunction of a subset of literals with at most one sign for each variable; the empty conjunction equals \(1\). A disjunctive normal form (DNF) is the disjunction of finitely many terms; the disjunction with no terms equals \(0\). Contradictory terms may be removed and repeated literals or terms ignored without increasing size. The size bound \(s\) counts terms, each of arbitrary width at most \(n\). The learner receives an upper bound \(s\), not a representation or a promise that the minimum DNF has exactly \(s\) terms. Both negated and unnegated literals are allowed.

The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and unit-cost transitions. The integer parameters are in canonical binary notation with separators. The runtime is polynomial in their displayed values, not merely their encoding lengths. Apart from the example oracle, it has no oracle or advice and performs no quantum operations. Reading parameters, processing samples, generating random bits, storing data, arithmetic and writing the entire hypothesis all count toward the same worst-case time bound. Internal random bits are independent unbiased coins, independent of the example stream.

Each example-oracle request returns a fresh independent pair \((x,f(x))\) from the same fixed \(D\) and target \(f\). The learner can choose when to request or reuse an obtained example, but cannot choose or condition the next sampled point. Transferring its \(n+1\) bits costs \(n+1\) steps, and subsequent processing is also charged. One may equivalently supply an infinite independent example stream and charge for each read example. All answers are noiseless. The algorithm receives neither point probabilities nor a sampling program for \(D\). The distribution is an arbitrary assignment of nonnegative real masses summing to one on the finite Boolean cube; no product structure, uniformity, smoothness or efficient samplability is promised. Thus finite exact sampling is an idealized access model, and the cost of implementing a sampler for \(D\) is not part of the learning task.

A hypothesis is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with input wires \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), constants \(0,1\), binary AND/OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output wire. It is encoded by its full topologically ordered gate list, gate types and binary indices of preceding wires, with separators, followed by the output index. The output is always valid circuit syntax. The number of written bits is bounded by the learner’s runtime; evaluation on any new \(n\)-bit input uses ordinary deterministic circuit evaluation, with time polynomial in \(n\) and the written circuit length. It uses no example oracle, target oracle or new randomness. A circuit that only describes a procedure for generating a much larger circuit is not an explicit output in this convention. No abstention output is allowed at prediction time.

The inner sum is the prediction error on a fresh point drawn from \(D\). The outer probability is over the finite sample/coin experiment bounded by the clock. The guarantee is required separately for every fixed \(f,D,n,s,t,b\); the same program and constants must work for all of them. No worst-case correctness on every point is required. With \(\varepsilon=1/t\) and \(\delta=2^{-b}\), the requirement is the usual polynomial dependence on \(n,s,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta)\). Other \(0<\varepsilon,\delta<1\) are covered by rounding to reciprocal-integer accuracy and dyadic confidence at least as strong as requested. These encodings retain the original PAC target without an input representation for arbitrary real numbers.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence proposition or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify one learner and universal polynomial bound, establish valid explicit circuit output and the all-run time bound, and prove the stated error/confidence inequality for every target, distribution and parameter choice. A negative proof must rule out every uniform learner and every fixed polynomial bound in this model. It must cover arbitrary circuit hypotheses, not only proper learners that return DNFs or a restricted algorithm class. A conditional lower bound whose computational assumption is left unproved, an algorithm with membership queries, a guarantee only for a special distribution or constant number of terms, and a superpolynomial runtime do not establish either full answer.

title: Efficient learning of well-separated Gaussian mixtures
summary: The card asks for globally learning well-separated spherical Gaussian mixtures with both polynomial samples and polynomial computation. The weights, centers and unequal component scales are hidden, and all must be recovered to the source’s stated relative accuracy up to one permutation. The source’s efficient local refinement requires initialization that its sample-efficient procedure does not find in polynomial time. Later algorithms improve separation or dimension dependence but retain assumptions or parameter costs that do not meet the full target. A Lean resolution must establish or refute one uniform end-to-end learner under the explicit separation, access and arithmetic-cost conventions.
formal: Is there an end-to-end polynomial-time, polynomial-sample algorithm for learning the parameters of well-separated spherical Gaussian mixtures at the source’s square-root-logarithmic separation scale? More precisely, do there exist one uniform randomized learner \(A\) and universal constants \(C_{\rm sep},B,a\ge1\) such that the following holds for every integer \(k\ge3\), \(d\ge1\), \(s\ge k\), \(R\ge1\), \(t\ge3\)? For every mixture \[P=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\pi_i N(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2 I_d),\qquad \pi_i\ge1/s,\quad \frac{\max_i\sigma_i}{\min_i\sigma_i}\le R,\] whose means satisfy \[\|\mu_i-\mu_j\|_2\ge C_{\rm sep}\max\{\sigma_i,\sigma_j\}\sqrt{\log(sR)}\quad(i\ne j),\] the learner, given only \(d,k,s,R,t\) and independent unlabeled samples from \(P\), returns \(k\) estimated component parameters with probability at least \(2/3\) for which some permutation \(\tau\) of \([k]\) satisfies, for every \(i\), \[\frac{|\widehat\pi_{\tau(i)}-\pi_i|}{\pi_i}\le\frac1t,\qquad \frac{\|\widehat\mu_{\tau(i)}-\mu_i\|_2}{\sigma_i}\le\frac1t,\qquad \frac{|\widehat\sigma_{\tau(i)}-\sigma_i|}{\sigma_i}\le\frac1{t\sqrt d}.\] Require at most \(B(d+k+s+R+t)^a\) samples and total arithmetic operations, including output. The learner receives no initial estimates of the means, weights or variances. It need not attain the source’s sharper near-linear sample bound; the selected question asks for polynomial sample complexity and polynomial time simultaneously.
definitions:
Here \(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_k>0\) sum to one, \(\mu_i\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(\sigma_i>0\). The covariance matrix of component \(i\) is \(\sigma_i^2 I_d\), so \(\sigma_i\) is a standard deviation, not a variance. To draw an observation, select an index with probabilities \(\pi_i\) and then draw from that component; the index is never revealed. Different observations and learner coins are independent. Each component’s coordinates have independent variance \(\sigma_i^2\), but both its center and scale are unknown. Weights need not be equal and scales need not coincide. There is no bound on the absolute centers or on the common absolute scale, no general-position or linear-independence assumption on centers, and no target-specific advice.

\([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), \(I_d\) is the identity matrix and \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_j v_j^2)^{1/2}\). The logarithm is natural. The same constant \(C_{\rm sep}\) applies to every instance and is independent of requested accuracy. In the balanced equal-scale special case \(s=k,R=1\), the separation is a constant times \(\sqrt{\log k}\) standard deviations. For general mixtures, the source’s separation (14) uses \(\sqrt{\log(\rho_\sigma/\pi_{\min})}\), where \(\rho_\sigma=\max_i\sigma_i/\min_i\sigma_i\) and \(\pi_{\min}=\min_i\pi_i\). The public integers \(s,R\) are conservative bounds on \(1/\pi_{\min}\) and \(\rho_\sigma\); the displayed separation is imposed with those supplied bounds. Rounding each true quantity upward increases it by at most a factor of two, absorbed by the universal separation constant. This is an explicit public-parameter convention for the source’s polynomial-resource question, not a restriction to balanced or known-variance mixtures.

All five integer parameters are supplied in unary. Accuracy is \(\varepsilon=1/t\); these reciprocal tolerances express arbitrary precision within a constant factor. The output is a finite list \((\widehat\pi_i,\widehat\mu_i,\widehat\sigma_i)_{i=1}^k\) with positive estimated scales, nonnegative weights summing to one, and real mean vectors. Its component order is immaterial: the same permutation must match all three parameter types. The loss is parameter recovery in the displayed relative/scaled units. Merely producing a distribution close in total variation, a good partition for some observations, or a sampler with a different representation does not by itself meet this output requirement.

Use a finite uniform exact-real register program, with rational constants in its fixed code. Copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division guarded at zero, comparison, branching, square root of a nonnegative number, and each random fair bit cost one operation. Integer control, input reading, register access and writing each output real are counted. Loading a \(d\)-coordinate observation costs \(d\) operations. The program has no component-label oracle, chosen-input density oracle, exact-moment oracle, free optimization procedure, floor/digit extraction or arbitrary real advice. Its single polynomial bound must hold for every target, sample history and coin history; the success guarantee accounts for the randomness. Constants, program and polynomial exponent are common to all parameters. The source does not specify coordinate-bit precision; this declared real-arithmetic convention does not assert an equivalent finite-bit algorithm. Any finite-precision version needs its own sample representation and justified rounding/error analysis.

The time bound explicitly allows polynomial dependence on the weight and scale-ratio bounds, while the separation depends on their logarithm. It is not polynomial time if the exponent on dimension or component count grows with \(k\), \(t\), or a separation parameter. A family of algorithms at separation \(\log^{1/2+c}k\) with constants or exponents depending on a fixed \(c>0\) does not imply a single algorithm at \(c=0\).
answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof of the uniform existence proposition or its negation. A positive proof must include global initialization from unlabeled samples, every component’s mean/weight/scale guarantee under one permutation, the stated success probability, and a universal polynomial bound for samples and all arithmetic/output costs. A local convergence theorem with accurate starting parameters is not enough. A negative result must rule out every learner and universal constants for some allowed parameters and mixture, rather than merely a particular iterative method. A computational assumption must remain a hypothesis unless proved. Larger asymptotic separation, fixed component count, equal variances only, or a weaker distribution-learning output is not a complete answer. The requested parameter accuracy is explicitly \(1/t\), with the dimension factor in the standard-deviation error retained.

title: One-way functions from hardness of learning P/poly
summary: The card asks whether failure of efficient worst-case circuit learning already implies ordinary one-way functions. The learner receives independent noiseless examples under any input distribution and must output a small ordinary Boolean predictor. A one-way function is uniformly easy to evaluate but has negligible inversion probability for every efficient uniform adversary at all sufficiently large lengths. Known reverse connections impose efficiently sampled targets, low computational depth, different learning-length quantifiers or a different description-approximation problem. The completed card preserves the unrestricted implication and records those distinctions while leaving its current status uncertain.
formal: Does worst-case computational hardness of distribution-free PAC learning of polynomial-size Boolean circuits from random labeled examples imply the existence of one-way functions? Precisely, let \(\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\) be the size-parameterized uniform learning assertion below, and let \(\mathsf{OWF}\) mean the existence of an ordinary uniformly computable one-way function secure against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter. The target is \[\neg\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathsf{OWF}.\] Equivalently, would the nonexistence of all such one-way functions guarantee an efficient learner for every target circuit and every example distribution? Hardness here is the failure of efficient learning in the worst case over targets and distributions; no efficiently samplable distribution of hard target descriptions, depth promise on those descriptions, or hardness reduction from SAT is assumed.
definitions:
Fix ordinary acyclic one-output Boolean circuits with two-input AND/OR gates, one-input NOT gates and constants, together with a standard effective binary encoding. For integers \(n\ge1\), \(s\ge n+1\), let \(\mathcal C(n,s)\) be all functions \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) represented by such a circuit with at most \(s\) input nodes and gates in total. Polynomial-size circuit families, with no uniform construction requirement across lengths, form \(\mathrm{P/poly}\). The public bound \(s\) exposes the source’s usual polynomial-in-target-size learning convention; the hidden target description is not an input to the learner.

\(\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\) means that there exist one randomized classical Turing machine \(A\) and one polynomial \(p\) such that, for all \(n,s\) as above, all integers \(a,b\ge3\), all \(f\in\mathcal C(n,s)\), and all probability distributions \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), the following holds. Given \(1^n,1^s,1^a,1^b\) and access only to independent examples \((x,f(x))\), \(x\sim D\), the machine runs for at most \(p(n+s+a+b)\) steps on every execution and outputs a deterministic ordinary Boolean circuit \(h\) with \[\Pr_{A,\,\text{examples}}\left[\Pr_{x\sim D}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le1/a\right]\ge1-1/b.\] The outer randomness consists of the training draws and independent fair machine coins; the inner draw is fresh. Example requests, reading their bits, all computation and output bits count toward the bound. The hypothesis may have size larger than \(s\), but its description and evaluation remain polynomially bounded by the learning time. It needs no further samples or access to \(f\) when evaluated. It is not required to reconstruct the target circuit, identify a unique representation, or be a member of the size-\(s\) class. This avoids imposing proper learning at the prescribed size. The learner has no membership queries, equivalence queries, nonuniform advice or code for sampling \(D\). The example source supplies independent draws even for distributions with no short sampling program. Labels are noiseless values of one fixed target. Arbitrarily large inverse-error and inverse-failure parameters \(a,b\) express ordinary PAC accuracy/confidence. Worst-case hardness is the logical negation of this uniform guarantee, not a lower bound against one particular learner or one restricted type of output.

\(\mathsf{OWF}\) means that there exist a polynomial-time computable length function \(\ell\) and one deterministic polynomial-time machine \(F\) giving maps \(F_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^{\ell(n)}\), such that for every uniform randomized polynomial-time machine \(I\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), there is \(N_{I,k}\) for which, for all \(n\ge N_{I,k}\), \[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,I}\big[I(1^n,F_n(x))\in\{0,1\}^n\ \land\ F_n(I(1^n,F_n(x)))=F_n(x)\big]\le n^{-k}.\] In this display the inverter is run once and its returned string is reused in both tests. \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution on \(n\)-bit strings, independent of inverter coins. Equivalently the event says that the one returned string is any length-\(n\) preimage of \(F_n(x)\), not necessarily \(x\) itself. Invalid output is failure. Evaluation of the family is uniform in \(n\), with no secret key, trapdoor or advice; \(1^n\) tells the inverter the input length. Its running time is polynomial in \(n\). The probability bound is negligible: it is eventually below every inverse power. This is the ordinary all-sufficiently-large-lengths strong one-way notion, not only security on infinitely many lengths. These uniformity and length conventions are made explicit because later learning characterizations use several different variants. No efficient transformation with a specified runtime overhead between witnesses is additionally requested; the target is the existential implication itself.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed implication in Lean, or prove its logical negation \(\neg\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\land\neg\mathsf{OWF}\). A positive result must derive a single uniform one-way family with negligible inversion probability at all sufficiently large lengths from the stated unrestricted worst-case learning failure. It may equivalently prove a distribution-free learner from nonexistence of such families, but the learner must handle every target and distribution, not merely a samplable average or a special low-description-complexity promise. A result giving only an auxiliary-input primitive or infinitely-often security is a different conclusion unless its upgrade to the stated notion is proved. An oracle-relative separation or a limitation on a specified reduction method alone does not refute the ordinary implication. This is an existence question with exact logical quantifiers, not a numerical approximation problem.

title: Learning Boolean juntas from uniform random examples
summary: A Boolean junta depends on at most k hidden coordinates of an n-bit input. The card asks for a single learner with time polynomial in n, 2^k and inverse prediction error from independent uniform noiseless examples. The output may be any efficient Boolean circuit and need not recover the exact relevant set. Known faster-exponent algorithms and results using smoothing, monotonicity, membership queries or correlated examples do not meet this full guarantee. The completed card preserves its earlier approved target and importance, identifies the original source, and specifies the exact uniform quantifiers for a Lean proof or refutation.
formal: Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and universal positive integers \(B,C\) such that every Boolean \(k\)-junta on \(n\) variables can be learned from independent uniform noiseless examples in time polynomial in \(n,2^k\) and inverse error? Explicitly, for all integers \(n\ge1\), \(0\le k\le n\), \(t\ge3\), and every \(k\)-junta \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), the learner receives \(1^n,1^k,1^t\) and an independent-example oracle \(\operatorname{EX}_f\). Every execution takes at most \(B(n+2^k+t)^C\) steps and outputs an ordinary Boolean circuit \(h\) for which \[\Pr_{A,\,\operatorname{EX}_f}\left[\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23.\] The exponent \(C\), constant \(B\) and machine are independent of \(n,k,t,f\). This preserves the existing full \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon)\) target; it is not merely a separate polynomial-time statement for every fixed \(k\).
definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A \(k\)-junta is a Boolean function for which there exist an unknown subset \(S=\{i_1<\cdots<i_r\}\subseteq[n]\), \(r\le k\), and an arbitrary Boolean table \(g:\{0,1\}^r\to\{0,1\}\) such that \[f(x)=g(x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_r})\quad\text{for all }x\in\{0,1\}^n.\] Neither \(S\) nor \(g\) is given to the learner. No monotonicity, sparsity of the truth table or lower bound on variable influence is assumed. For \(k=0\), the class consists of the two constant functions, using the unique empty input to \(g\). The public \(k\) is only an upper bound on the number of relevant coordinates; it need not be the minimal support size.

\(U_n\) gives each binary vector probability \(2^{-n}\). Each call to \(\operatorname{EX}_f\) supplies a new pair \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim U_n\), independent of all previous draws and the learner’s fair random coins. The unknown target is fixed before the data are drawn. The learner can request further independent examples adaptively, but cannot choose their inputs, obtain membership-query labels, or request coupled or neighboring examples. Labels are exact noiseless bits. The outer probability measures confidence over the complete learning execution; the inner probability is zero-one prediction error on a fresh independent input. Reciprocals of positive integers suffice to represent arbitrary desired positive error tolerances up to polynomial rounding overhead. The fixed confidence is \(2/3\).

The output is a finite acyclic ordinary Boolean circuit on the \(n\) input bits, using two-input AND/OR gates, one-input NOT gates and constants with a fixed effective binary encoding. It may depend on all coordinates and need not itself be a \(k\)-junta; this is improper learning. It is evaluated without the training oracle and with no stored target-dependent state other than its output description. The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine, with no advice, receiving the displayed public integers in unary. All example reading, computation, stored-data access, fair random bits and output writing count in the worst-case bit-time bound, which also bounds the number of example requests and output length. The example generator’s internal sampling cost is not charged. Circuit evaluation is polynomial in the written circuit size under this encoding. Repeated access to stored examples and any polynomial amount of memory within the time bound are allowed. The requirement is predictive approximation; it does not require identifying the exact relevant set, giving a minimum representation or recovering every truth-table entry.

Polynomial dependence on \(2^k\) permits an exponential dependence on the number of relevant variables, since an arbitrary \(k\)-bit table already has \(2^k\) entries. It excludes a degree of \(n\) that grows with \(k\). For every fixed \(c>0\), the displayed guarantee would in particular be polynomial in \(n,t\) for all \(k\le c\log_2 n\); an algorithm that only handles each constant \(k\) with its own exponent need not satisfy it. The accuracy target is the explicitly bounded rational error \(1/t\); the problem asks for exact existence of the learner and universal exponent rather than a numerical optimal value.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof that such \(A,B,C\) exist, or prove the complete negation: for every proposed uniform machine and universal constants, some allowed \(n,k,t,f\) violates the worst-case resource bound, finite hypothesis condition or the stated PAC probability. A positive answer must handle all Boolean junta tables and all support sizes up to \(n\) with one exponent independent of \(k\). A learner using membership queries, correlated random-walk examples, a randomly perturbed marginal distribution, or only monotone targets does not meet the specified interface. A statistical-query, limited-memory or specified-neural-training lower bound does not exclude every allowed machine. Conditional cryptographic hardness must retain its unproved premise and is not the unconditional negation. Neither exact support recovery nor a prescribed proper output is an additional obligation.

title: Learning decision trees from uniform random examples in polynomial time
summary: The card asks for a polynomial-time learner for every small Boolean decision tree from independent uniform labeled examples. The tree is hidden and the learner receives neither chosen-input labels nor its representation. A successful learner may return any efficient Boolean circuit with the requested prediction error and two-thirds confidence. Known smoothed, query-based and representation-aware results provide different guarantees and do not settle this passive learning target. The completed card preserves its importance and scope while making the accuracy encoding, resource bounds and full Lean proof criterion explicit.
formal: Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and universal positive integers \(B,C\) such that, for every \(n,s\ge1\), \(t\ge3\), and every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) represented by a decision tree with at most \(s\) nodes, \(A\), given \(1^n,1^s,1^t\) and independent uniform examples labeled by \(f\), runs on every execution for at most \(B(n+s+t)^C\) steps and outputs a Boolean circuit \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr_{A,\,\mathrm{examples}}\left[\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23?\] The hypothesis may be an arbitrary efficiently evaluable circuit. The target remains the previously selected polynomial-time sample-only uniform-PAC question; reciprocal-integer error \(\varepsilon=1/t\) makes the accuracy encoding explicit.
definitions:
A Boolean decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node is labeled by a coordinate index in \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and has two children, with outgoing edges labeled zero and one; each leaf is labeled by an output bit. On input \(x\), evaluation follows the edge specified by the queried bit at each internal node until it reaches a leaf, whose bit is the output. Coordinates may occur repeatedly and there is no depth, monotonicity, balance, or randomness promise on the hidden tree. Size counts all nodes, as in the existing card. A full branching binary tree with \(\ell\) leaves has \(2\ell-1\) nodes, so the leaf-count convention used by the backdoor-defense source changes this polynomial-size question only by a constant factor. The size bound and input dimension are public; the target tree, its structure and its node labels are not supplied.

\(U_n\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Each example request yields a fresh independent \((x,f(x))\), \(x\sim U_n\), under one fixed target. Labels are exact and noiseless. Requests may be scheduled adaptively, but the learner cannot choose the input to be labeled or require correlations between successive inputs. In particular, there is no membership oracle, equivalence oracle or free access to the tree representation. The learner uses independent fair random bits and no length-dependent advice. Its guarantee is required for every target tree, rather than for a random tree or a randomly perturbed input distribution. The outer probability is confidence over the training draws and internal coins; the inner error probability concerns a fresh independent uniform input.

An output hypothesis is a finite acyclic circuit on the same \(n\) bits, using two-input AND/OR, one-input NOT and constant gates in a fixed effective binary encoding. It need not be a tree or have size at most \(s\). The output is evaluated without further samples, the hidden target or any unreported target-dependent state. This is improper predictive learning, not exact tree identification or minimum-size reconstruction. The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with unary public parameters; every bit operation, request, example read, stored-data access, random bit and output bit is counted. One fixed worst-case bound applies across all parameters and sample histories; the same bound also limits sample count and output length. Circuit evaluation takes polynomial time in the written circuit size. The example source’s internal sampling cost is not charged.
