Unlimited computation on polynomially many examples does not meet the requirement.

The error parameter ranges over \(1/t\), \(t\ge3\). For any desired real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), choosing \(t=\max\{3,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\}\) yields error at most \(\varepsilon\) with only polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\). Thus this encoding retains the ordinary arbitrary-accuracy learning target without treating an arbitrarily long rational spelling as a constant-cost input. Fixed confidence \(2/3\) is retained. The universal polynomial has no degree depending on \(s\), tree depth, the particular target or the accuracy parameter. The problem is a yes/no existence statement; there is no unspecified numerical optimization precision.
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that the stated uniform learner and universal polynomial bound exist, or prove their logical negation: every proposed machine and constants fail for some allowed dimension, size, accuracy and target, in either the worst-case resource guarantee or the PAC success condition. A positive answer must use only independent uniform labeled examples and cover every target tree. Proper-learning hardness, minimum-consistent-tree hardness, or a lower bound for one greedy heuristic does not rule out the allowed arbitrary circuit output. A result under an unproved computational assumption proves only the corresponding conditional negation. Membership-query learning, random-tree learning, smoothed-distribution learning and correlated-example algorithms have different access or target promises and are not accepted as a resolution of the displayed statement.

title: Polynomial-time density learning of Gaussian mixtures
summary: The learner receives independent observations from a mixture of at most k nondegenerate Gaussians in d dimensions. It must output another such mixture whose whole distribution is close in total variation, without reconstructing the original components. The question asks for a uniform algorithm with time polynomial jointly in k and d for each fixed accuracy, using explicitly specified exact-real arithmetic. Polynomial sample sufficiency coexists with statistical-query lower bounds and conditional computational hardness, neither of which is silently treated as an unconditional resolution. Newer positive results with bounded parameters, fixed component counts or growing dimension exponents do not establish the full target.
formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that properly learns every mixture of at most \(k\) nondegenerate Gaussian distributions on \(\mathbb R^d\), to any fixed total-variation accuracy, in time polynomial jointly in \(k\) and \(d\)? Precisely, is there one algorithm \(A\) in the arithmetic model below such that, for every integer \(t\ge3\), there are integers \(C_t,a_t\ge1\) for which the following holds for all integers \(k,d\ge1\) and all \(P\in\mathcal G_{k,d}\)? Given \(k,d,t\) and independent samples from \(P\), the algorithm uses at most \(C_t(k+d)^{a_t}\) operations and outputs a description of \(\widehat P\in\mathcal G_{k,d}\) satisfying \[\Pr[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,\widehat P)\le1/t]\ge2/3.\] The time bound holds on every execution and includes sampling and writing the output. Its constants are uniform over all mixture parameters. No polynomial dependence on \(t\) is required: this card asks the source's joint polynomial dependence on the number of components and dimension at each fixed accuracy.
definitions: For a positive integer \(d\), a nondegenerate Gaussian distribution \(N(\mu,\Sigma)\) has mean \(\mu\in\mathbb R^d\) and a symmetric positive-definite matrix \(\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\). Positive definite means \(v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v>0\) for every nonzero \(v\in\mathbb R^d\). Its density at \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) is \[(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right).\] The class \(\mathcal G_{k,d}\) consists of all distributions \(P=\sum_{i=1}^k w_iN(\mu_i,\Sigma_i)\), where \(w_i\ge0\), \(\sum_iw_i=1\), and each component satisfies the preceding conditions. Zero weights allow fewer than \(k\) components; repeated components are allowed. Means, covariance eigenvalues and component separation have no upper or lower promises beyond positive definiteness, and positive weights have no prescribed minimum. If \(p,q\) are the densities of \(P,Q\), their total variation distance is \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\int_{\mathbb R^d}|p(x)-q(x)|\,dx,\] where integration is with respect to Lebesgue measure. The learner has no access to the hidden component label or parameters. Each sampling request returns a fresh independent vector drawn from \(P\). The output consists of \(k\) weights, \(k\) means and \(k\) positive-definite covariance matrices, describing a valid member of the same class on every execution. This requirement is called proper learning. No correspondence between true and output components is required. The success probability is over all sampled vectors and the algorithm's independent fair random bits. Computational convention: \(A\) is one finite program, with rational constants and no nonuniform advice, using exact real registers together with a Turing work tape. Allowed real operations are copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero value, square root of a nonnegative value, and order or equality comparisons; each costs one operation. Reading or writing a real register costs one operation; a sample vector costs \(d\) operations. Each fair random bit and each ordinary tape step costs one operation. Integer inputs use binary encoding. Undefined arithmetic operations are forbidden. Each output scalar must be written and charged. No integration, optimization, density-evaluation or arbitrary-function oracle is available. The density formula defines the mathematical distribution, not an extra primitive of the program. This explicit arithmetic convention measures computation on real observations; it does not claim polynomial bit complexity for an unspecified finite-precision encoding.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the algorithm-existence statement or of its logical negation in the stated model. An affirmative proof must establish validity of the proper output, total execution bound and uniform total-variation guarantee for every allowed mixture and every accuracy parameter. A negative proof must rule out all algorithms in the specified arithmetic model, rather than only statistical-query algorithms or one proposed method. A conditional hardness theorem must be identified with its additional hypothesis and does not by itself settle this unconditional yes/no target. Learning with a fixed number of components, recovering component parameters under separation assumptions, or returning only an arbitrary sampler does not establish the requested statement. The reciprocal-accuracy parameter belongs to the learning guarantee; it is not a single numerical answer to be approximated at the benchmark's default tolerance.

title: NP-hardness of improper learning of \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\)
summary: The question asks whether SAT reduces to agnostic learning of general polynomial-size Boolean circuits. The learning oracle receives a circuit sampling labeled examples and returns an approximately optimal hypothesis. The returned hypothesis may use an arbitrarily larger fixed polynomial size than the comparator circuits. The reduction must work with every valid oracle reply and without additional cryptographic assumptions. A June 2026 follow-up gives related conditional hardness, leaving the unconditional target unresolved.
formal: Is there an integer \(a\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(b\ge a\), there are an integer \(r\ge1\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time oracle reduction \(R_b\) which decides SAT with success probability at least \(2/3\) using the following agnostic circuit-learning oracle? A query is a Boolean sampling circuit producing a distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^{m}\times\{0,1\}\). Every oracle reply must be a circuit \(h\) of size at most \((m+1)^{b}\) satisfying \[L_D(h)\le\min_{g\in\operatorname{SIZE}_{m}((m+1)^{a})}L_D(g)+(m+1)^{-r}.\] The reduction must succeed for every sequence of valid replies. The exponent \(r\), reduction and its running-time polynomial may depend on \(b\), but not on the SAT instance. No cryptographic or unproved complexity assumption is part of the target. This selects the source's agnostic, efficiently samplable-distribution reduction formulation.
definitions:
A Boolean circuit is an explicitly listed directed acyclic graph with named input wires, constant zero and one wires, fan-in-two AND and OR gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, and named output wires. Its size is its number of noninput gates, including constant gates. Gate types and predecessor indices are encoded in binary in topological order; all input and output counts are explicit. Write \(\operatorname{SIZE}_{m}(s)\) for the binary functions on \(m\) input bits computed by one-output circuits with at most \(s\) gates. A language is in \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\) if its restriction to each input length is computed by a circuit family with polynomial size; those circuits need not be generated uniformly.

A sampling-circuit query has some number \(q\ge0\) of random input bits and \(m+1\) output bits, with \(m\ge1\). Uniform independent bits in \(\{0,1\}^{q}\) induce the joint distribution \(D\); the first \(m\) outputs are the example and the last is its label. Labels may be noisy and need not be realizable by a small circuit. The risk is \(L_D(h)=\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}[h(x)\ne y]\). The oracle returns the full description of a predictor satisfying the displayed excess-risk guarantee. An answer always exists because the smaller comparator family is finite, contains constant functions, and is included in the allowed output family. The oracle itself has no computational restriction. It may select different valid circuits based on the query history; the reduction must work for all such selections, not only for a favorable learning rule.

The reduction is a randomized multitape Turing machine using independent fair bits. For each fixed \(b\), one polynomial in the SAT input bit length bounds its running time on every random tape and response history, counting construction of all sampling circuits and reading all reply descriptions; oracle computation is uncharged. Queries may be adaptive and may have different \(m,q\). In particular, the entire sampling circuit and every reply must have polynomial encoding length in the reduction's input length. The reduction may inspect hypothesis descriptions and evaluate them; it has no additional oracle or advice. SAT uses an explicit syntax-tree encoding of AND, OR and NOT formulas, with malformed encodings rejected. Probability of a correct SAT answer is over the reduction's coins, for each fixed input and each valid response policy.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such an exponent \(a\) and reductions exist, or a proof of the negation. A positive answer must cover every polynomial output-size exponent \(b\ge a\), allowing the stated dependence of the reduction on \(b\). Hardness only when the predictor is restricted to the target size, or only under an additional cryptographic assumption, does not suffice. A negative answer must rule out the displayed family of reductions, not merely one restricted reduction technique.

title: Quasipolynomial accuracy exponent for Gaussian agnostic halfspace learning
summary: The learner receives Gaussian examples labeled by an arbitrary fixed Boolean function. Its predictor must perform almost as well as the best affine halfspace. The question asks whether the dimension exponent can grow only logarithmically with inverse excess error. Training and prediction evaluation are both charged in the specified real-arithmetic model. Statistical-query restrictions or general stochastic labels cannot silently replace this model.
formal: Do there exist constants \(C,K>0\) and one uniform randomized learner in the real-arithmetic model below such that, for every dimension \(n\ge2\), rational inverse excess error \(t\ge3\), and permitted Boolean target, its training cost plus output-evaluation cost is at most \[K n^{C\log_2 t}\] on every execution, and it succeeds with probability at least \(2/3\)? The target labels are deterministic: for every measurable \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\{-1,+1\}\), a learner sees independent \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim\gamma_n=N(0,I_n)\), and must output a predictor \(h\) such that \[\Pr\left[\operatorname{err}_f(h)\le\operatorname{OPT}_n(f)+\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23,\qquad \operatorname{err}_f(h)=\Pr_{x\sim\gamma_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)],\] where \[\operatorname{OPT}_n(f)=\inf_{w\in\mathbb R^n,\ b\in\mathbb R}\Pr_{x\sim\gamma_n}[\operatorname{sgn}(\langle w,x\rangle+b)\ne f(x)].\]
definitions:
\(\gamma_n\) is the Borel probability measure on \(\mathbb R^n\) with density \((2\pi)^{-n/2}\exp(-\|x\|_2^2/2)\) with respect to Lebesgue measure; its coordinates are independent standard normal random variables. A halfspace predictor has the form \(x\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(\sum_i w_i x_i+b)\), with real coefficients and threshold and \(\operatorname{sgn}(z)=+1\) for \(z\ge0\), otherwise \(-1\). Constant predictors are allowed by \(w=0\). Affine halfspaces follow the source’s introductory definition, which includes a constant term; its later notation sometimes suppresses that term. No margin, bounded coefficient encoding, sparsity or homogeneity assumption is added. The infimum in \(\operatorname{OPT}_n(f)\) does not presume an available optimum or supply its value to the learner.

The unknown target \(f\) is any Borel-measurable Boolean function, fixed before the examples and learner coins are drawn. It need not itself be a halfspace. Each oracle request returns an independent Gaussian vector with its exact value under the same \(f\); the learner cannot choose the sampled point, inspect code for \(f\), ask for a label at a selected point, or query the optimum. There is no independent stochastic label distribution conditional on \(x\) in this literal target-function formulation. The outer success probability includes all sample draws and internal randomness; error is measured on a fresh Gaussian input. The learner may output an improper predictor. The source uses \(L^1\) notation: for \(\{-1,+1\}\)-valued \(h,f\), \(\mathbb E|h-f|=2\operatorname{err}_f(h)\). Thus excess disagreement \(1/t\) is excess \(L^1\) loss \(2/t\), not \(1/t\). This exact factor is kept separate from asymptotic runtime notation.

Computational convention: use one finite uniform real-arithmetic register program, with rational constants in its fixed code, integer control and rational public parameters \(n,t\). It can copy real registers, apply \(+,-,\times,\div\) to a constant number of registers, compare their values, branch and generate a fair random bit, each at unit arithmetic cost. Division by zero must be handled by a comparison before division. Discrete control, register access and writing an output instruction each cost one step. Sampling and loading an \(n\)-coordinate labeled example costs \(n+1\) units. The oracle supplies exact real coordinates; no cost for internally generating a Gaussian real is attributed to the learner. There is no floor, digit-extraction primitive, arbitrary real advice, optimization oracle, expectation oracle or decision oracle for general properties of real numbers. Uniformity means the same finite program works for all \(n,t,f\), with no length-dependent constants or advice.

The output is a finite acyclic arithmetic-and-comparison circuit on \(n\) real inputs, built from the same operations, Boolean choices and sign tests. Constants may be stored real values computed during training. It must define a total \(\{-1,+1\}\)-valued predictor on every real input, with each division guarded when its denominator vanishes. Output writing and each stored real coefficient are charged one unit per written item. Evaluation cost is the number of circuit operations; it is included in the resource measure. Such circuits give measurable predictors and need no further examples or target access after training. There is no requirement that the output be a halfspace, and no fixed polynomial degree or circuit-size restriction beyond the stated time bound.

For a learner \(A\), let \(\tau_A(n,t)\) be the supremum over every allowed target, sample history and coin history of its training cost plus the evaluation cost of its output circuit, with nontermination or invalid output charged infinite cost. This exact-real arithmetic model is an explicitly stated convention completing the source’s continuous-example interface. It does not assert a theorem translating arbitrary real computations to the bit model. Exact Gaussian examples have no finite binary representation in general, and the 2014 question specifies neither a rounding oracle nor a coordinate-bit budget. A separate bit-complexity variant would need those definitions and a proof that rounding preserves the learning guarantee for arbitrary measurable targets. Numerical rounding is therefore not silently included as a free primitive in the present arithmetic target.
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that a single learner achieves the stated excess error with probability at least \(2/3\) within the joint training and evaluation bound \(Kn^{C\log_2 t}\). A refutation must exclude every proposed learner and pair of constants on the stated Gaussian model.

title: Fully polynomial learning of halfspace intersections under Gaussian and uniform inputs
summary: The card asks separately whether intersections of a variable number of affine halfspaces can be learned efficiently under Gaussian and uniform Boolean-cube inputs. The desired polynomial bounds cover dimension, intersection size, inverse accuracy, training and prediction. Labels come only from independent noiseless examples, and the output predictor may lie outside the target class. The surrounding margin theorem and newer subexponential, bounded-width and proper-learning results do not supply the requested uniform polynomial guarantee. A Lean resolution must prove or refute the full learner-existence statement in each explicitly defined computational model.
formal: Resolve the following two distribution-specific questions, separately. For \(D_n=\gamma_n=N(0,I_n)\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and for \(D_n=U_n\), the uniform measure on \(\{-1,+1\}^n\), does there exist a uniform randomized learner \(A_D\) and constants \(B_D,C_D\ge1\) such that, for all integers \(n,k\ge1\), \(t\ge3\), and all intersections \(f\) of at most \(k\) affine halfspaces, \(A_D(n,k,t)\), using only independent examples \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim D_n\), outputs a predictor \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr\!\left[\Pr_{x\sim D_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23\] in total training, output-writing and evaluation cost at most \(B_D(n+k+t)^{C_D}\)? The Gaussian branch uses the explicit real-arithmetic convention below; the Boolean-cube branch uses bit computation. The learner may be improper. Both the number of halfspaces and inverse accuracy are variable parameters: a polynomial whose exponent depends on \(k\) or \(t\) does not answer either branch affirmatively. A full resolution reports an answer to each branch, rather than treating failure of one as a classification of both.
definitions:
An affine halfspace has Boolean value \(+1\) when \(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i+b\ge0\), and value \(-1\) otherwise, for arbitrary real \(w_1,\ldots,w_n,b\). Its boundary is included in the positive side. An intersection has value \(+1\) exactly when all its component inequalities hold; otherwise it has value \(-1\). The intersection with no components is the constant positive function. All coefficients and the number of nonredundant inequalities are hidden; only the upper bound \(k\) is supplied. No coefficient-size, margin, balance or homogeneity promise is added. On the cube, the function is simply the restriction of those inequalities to the finite domain; their real coefficients are not input strings whose sizes the learner must read.

\(\gamma_n\) has independent standard normal coordinates, with joint density \((2\pi)^{-n/2}\exp(-\|x\|_2^2/2)\). Under \(U_n\), each of the \(2^n\) sign vectors has mass \(2^{-n}\). The appropriate distribution is known to its learner, but the target is unknown. Each example is an independent draw with the exact noiseless target label. The learner cannot ask for labels at chosen points, inspect the target description, or query conditional distributions. The inner probability is disagreement on a fresh example; the outer probability includes training examples and the learner’s random coins. The error tolerance is \(\varepsilon=1/t\), with integer \(t\) supplied in unary together with \(n,k\). These reciprocal tolerances define arbitrary requested accuracy up to a constant factor without introducing an uncounted rational encoding length. Confidence is fixed at \(2/3\); neither branch promises perfect recovery of coefficients.

For the cube, \(A_U\) is one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a source of independent fair bits and an example tape. Writing a labeled example costs \(n+1\) bit operations. The output is an ordinary finite acyclic Boolean circuit, using AND, OR and NOT gates and constants, evaluated on the input signs encoded as bits. Training, reading, output length, and worst-case output evaluation time are all counted. The polynomial bound must hold on every sample and coin history. The same program and constants must work for every \(n,k,t,f\), with no advice depending on input length.

For the Gaussian branch, use one finite real-register program whose fixed constants are rational. Copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division with an explicit zero-denominator guard, comparison, branching, and generating a fair bit have unit cost; discrete control, register access and output writing are also charged. Loading one exact labeled Gaussian vector costs \(n+1\) units. Integer control and the unary public parameters do not supply any infinite advice. There is no floor or digit extraction, optimization oracle, expectation oracle or oracle deciding general real-number properties. The output is a finite acyclic arithmetic-and-comparison circuit with constants computed during training and a total Boolean sign output. Every division must be guarded so evaluation is defined on every input. Its stored constants, instructions and worst-case evaluation operations are counted in the same polynomial bound; it requires no further target access. This permits any such efficiently evaluable predictor, including ones outside the intersection class. All these predictors are Borel measurable.

The real-arithmetic convention explicitly fills the source’s unspecified continuous-input cost interface. Exact Gaussian coordinates need not have finite binary representations, so this branch does not silently claim an equivalent finite-bit learning theorem. Conversely the discrete branch uses actual bit costs and Boolean outputs. A result stated in a different computational model must justify the transfer before it resolves the corresponding branch. Independent programs and constants for the two branches are allowed; each program must be uniform over its own parameters.
answer_criterion: Give Lean proofs deciding the displayed uniform-existence proposition for each of \(D=\gamma\) and \(D=U\). A positive proof supplies one learner, universal polynomial constants, termination/resource bounds, a valid finite predictor and the learning guarantee for every parameter and target. A negative proof negates that full existence statement: for every candidate learner and polynomial constants, show a violating parameter/target or resource requirement. A conditional lower bound proves only the corresponding implication unless its assumption is also established. A restriction to statistical-query learners, proper hypotheses, fixed \(k\), a positive margin or a different sample source does not by itself resolve these propositions. State the model transfer for any invoked bound. The answer is a pair of exact truth values; no numerical approximation or unspecified asymptotic exponent counts as a resolution.

title: Distribution-free improper learning of two unrestricted halfspaces
summary: One threshold is efficiently learnable from labeled examples, but the target here combines two thresholds. Examples follow any fixed distribution on the Boolean cube and no positive margin is promised. The learner receives a bound on target description length and may output any efficiently evaluable classifier. Hardness for proper learners or growing numbers of halfspaces does not settle this two-halfspace target. The question asks for a uniform polynomial-time guarantee across all distributions and permitted target descriptions.
formal: Is there a single randomized learner that, for every distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), every target \(f\) expressible as the intersection of two integer-weight halfspaces of total description length at most a supplied bound \(B\), and every rational \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), uses only independent labeled examples from \(D\) to output a Boolean circuit \(H\) with \(\Pr_{x\sim D}[H(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(2/3\), in time polynomial in \(n+B+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon)\)?
definitions: A halfspace is \(h(x)=1\) exactly when \(\sum_{i} w_{i} x_{i}\ge \theta\), with \(w_i,\theta\in\mathbb{Z}\) in signed binary; equality is positive. The target f is the conjunction of two such predicates. Its description length is the bit length of a list of both weight vectors and thresholds, using self-delimiting binary integers. The learner receives n and B in unary and a rational \(\varepsilon\) with \(0<\varepsilon <1/2\) in binary. It is promised that f has at least one such description of length at most B, but receives neither that description nor its weights. An example oracle returns independent pairs \((x,f(x))\) with x sampled from an arbitrary fixed distribution D on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\). The learner receives only these labeled examples and its own independent fair coins. Each oracle call costs at least \(n+1\) steps to receive its bits; all further work is charged in Turing-machine bit steps. Membership queries, advice and descriptions or probability evaluations of D are absent. There must be a fixed polynomial P such that on every random tape the running time, and hence sample count and output length, are bounded by \(P(n+B+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon))\). Output a deterministic Boolean circuit \(H:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\) in the explicit \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) basis. The success condition is \(\Pr_{\mathrm{samples,coins}}[\Pr_{x\sim D}[H(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon]\ge2/3\), uniformly over \(n,B,\varepsilon ,D\) and every promised f. Circuit evaluation costs polynomial time in its output encoding. The hypothesis need not be an intersection of halfspaces. Encoding an arbitrary deterministic polynomial-time evaluator by its Boolean circuit preserves this unrestricted efficient-output convention.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof constructing and bounding a learner under all the stated quantifiers, or a Lean proof that none exists. Proper-learning hardness and statistical-query lower bounds do not exclude all allowed learners. A margin promise, a restricted input distribution or membership queries would change the problem.

title: Square-root multiclass regret from Littlestone dimension
summary: An online learner predicts a label and then observes the correct one. Regret compares its expected mistakes with the best fixed hypothesis in hindsight. Littlestone dimension measures the depth of binary prediction trees realizable by the class. The question asks for a universal square-root dimension-times-horizon regret bound. The constant cannot grow with the number of labels, even for infinite label spaces.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every pair of nonempty sets \(X,Y\), every nonempty class \(H\subseteq Y^X\) of Littlestone dimension at most \(d\), and all integers \(T\ge d\ge1\), the minimax expected regret satisfies \[R_T(H)\le C\sqrt{dT}?\] Infinite instance and label sets are allowed, and no regularity or computability restriction on the class is added. For the prediction game defined below, \[R_T(H)=\inf_A\ \sup_{(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_T,y_T)\in X\times Y}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^T(1-p_t(y_t))-\min_{h\in H}\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbf1\{h(x_t)\ne y_t\}\right\}.\] Here \(p_t=A_t((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_{t-1},y_{t-1}),x_t)\) is a probability distribution on labels. The infimum ranges over all causal prediction rules, without computational restrictions.
definitions: A hypothesis \(h\in H\) assigns a label from \(Y\) to each instance in \(X\). A depth-\(r\) Littlestone tree is a complete binary tree with an instance at each internal node and two distinct labels from \(Y\) on that node's outgoing edges; the pair of labels may vary by node. The tree is shattered if every root-to-leaf path has one fixed hypothesis agreeing with all its edge labels on its instance points. The dimension \(\operatorname{Ldim}(H)\) is the largest shattered depth, or infinity if depths are unbounded. On each round the adversary presents \(x_t\), the learner supplies \(p_t\), and the adversary then reveals \(y_t\). The learner observes the actual label before the next round and is charged expected zero-one loss \(1-p_t(y_t)\). It does not observe future instances. The adversary may react to \(p_t\); loss is the displayed expectation, not a reaction to a sampled label. The sequence need not be realizable by any hypothesis. The comparator is one fixed hypothesis chosen in hindsight, whose minimum loss exists since the possible losses are integers from zero to \(T\). A distribution here is a function \(p:Y\to[0,1]\) satisfying \(\sum_{y\in Y}p(y)=1\), with this sum defined as the supremum of sums over finite subsets. It automatically has at most countable positive support. This atomic convention does not increase the best possible regret relative to arbitrary probability measures with measurable singletons: any missing atom mass can be assigned to one fixed label, increasing no zero-one loss. All histories and rules are arbitrary set functions, so no topology or measurability structure on \(X,H\) is required. Rules may know \(H\) and \(T\), need not be proper, and have no runtime, memory, computability or finite-description bound. Infima and suprema need not be attained. Dimension zero means all hypotheses agree pointwise and zero regret is attainable. The range \(T\ge d\) avoids the separate saturation regime because cumulative regret cannot exceed \(T\). All requested comparison constants must be independent of the instance and label spaces, class, dimension and horizon.
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that \(R_T(H)/\sqrt{dT}\) has a universal upper bound over the classes and horizons specified above, or prove that this ratio is unbounded on that domain.

title: Algorithmic threshold for the symmetric binary perceptron
summary: The symmetric binary perceptron seeks a sign vector satisfying many random Gaussian two-sided constraints. The conjecture places the efficient-search density at the scale of the squared margin, allowing fixed powers of its reciprocal logarithm. The card defines a supremum over uniform polynomial-time algorithms and states its exact real-arithmetic convention. The input dimension tends to infinity at each fixed margin and density before the margin approaches zero. Stable-algorithm barriers, a sign-matrix algorithm and conditional lattice reductions each have limits that prevent treating them as a full resolution.
formal:
Does the Gaussian symmetric binary perceptron's polynomial-time search threshold satisfy
\[\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)=\widetilde\Theta(\kappa^2)\qquad\text{as }\kappa\downarrow0?\]
Precisely, are there constants \(C\ge1\), an integer \(a\ge0\), and \(\kappa_0\in(0,1/2]\) such that for every rational \(\kappa\in(0,\kappa_0]\),
\[\frac{\kappa^2}{C(\log(1/\kappa))^a}\ \le\ \alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)\ \le\ C\kappa^2(\log(1/\kappa))^a?\]
For fixed margin \(\kappa>0\) and density \(\alpha>0\), an instance is an \(\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\)-by-\(n\) matrix \(G\) with independent standard Gaussian entries. A successful search returns \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^n\) with
\[\max_{1\le i\le\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor}\left|\sum_{j=1}^{n}G_{ij}\sigma_j\right|\le\kappa\sqrt n.\]
The threshold is the supremum of fixed rational densities at which a uniform polynomial-time algorithm succeeds with probability tending to one as \(n\to\infty\), in the real-arithmetic model specified below.

The polylogarithmic tolerance restores the tilde lost in the imported excerpt. To make the source's informal efficient-algorithm class definite on exact Gaussian inputs, this card explicitly selects rational-constant randomized real-arithmetic computation. It does not assert equivalence with every discretized or machine-specific version of the conjecture.
definitions:
The dimension \(n\) ranges over positive integers. Margin \(\kappa\) and density \(\alpha\) are positive rational constants held fixed while \(n\) tends to infinity; write \(M=\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\). The \(Mn\) entries of \(G\in\mathbb R^{M\times n}\) are mutually independent with probability density \((2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-t^2/2)\) on \(\mathbb R\). A feasible output is a full vector of \(n\) signs satisfying every displayed two-sided constraint. When \(M=0\), every sign vector is feasible. A failure symbol, a malformed vector or an infeasible vector counts as failure. No conditioning on satisfiability or planting of a hidden solution is performed.

The normalization is by \(\sqrt n\), the square root of the number of variables, and the density is constraints divided by variables. The symbol \(\kappa\) denotes the allowed absolute margin. All constraints are symmetric around zero; there is no one-sided inequality in place of the absolute value. This is the Gaussian version, not a matrix of independently uniform signs. For a nonzero row count the maximum is the usual infinity norm; the empty maximum is taken to be zero.

A permitted algorithm has a finite program with rational numerical constants and finite discrete control, real registers with exact arithmetic, and integer registers for array addresses and loop counters. It can read the supplied matrix, copy values, apply addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, and branch on equality or order comparisons. Integer-address arithmetic is addition, subtraction and comparison; addresses used must be valid nonnegative integers. Each such instruction, register access, input access, output instruction and branch costs one operation. There is no floor, bit-extraction operation on a real register, arbitrary function oracle or infinite program-specific real constant. Division by zero must be handled by an explicit branch, not a source of extra computational power.

For internal randomness, the program may request independent fair bits or independent standard Gaussian real samples, each in one operation. These samples are independent of the input matrix and of all prior samples. The algorithm can be deterministic by making no random requests. There must be constants \(D>0\), \(d\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\) such that it halts after at most \(D(n+1)^d\) operations on every real input matrix of the required dimensions and every sequence of random choices, returning either a sign vector or failure. Space and all input inspection count through these operations. The finite program and constants may depend on the fixed rational pair \((\alpha,\kappa)\), but not on \(n\) or on the sampled matrix. No advice string depending on \(n\) is provided. Exact real arithmetic is a declared computational convention; operation count is not a bound on finite-precision bit complexity.

Let \(\mathcal D_\kappa\subseteq\mathbb Q_{>0}\) be the set of densities \(\alpha\) for which such an algorithm \(A\) exists with
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr_{G,R}\bigl[A(G;R)\text{ returns a feasible sign vector}\bigr]=1.\]
Here the probability is over both the independent Gaussian entries and the algorithm's permitted internal randomness. The convergence need not have a supplied rate. The algorithm must be one uniform program for the full sequence of dimensions at the fixed parameter pair, rather than a different program at every dimension. Define
\[\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)=\sup\bigl(\mathcal D_\kappa\cup\{0\}\bigr)\in[0,+\infty].\]
The supremum need not be attained; this definition does not assume an algorithm at the threshold or an all-input guarantee. The main conjecture includes a finite upper bound for sufficiently small margins. Showing algorithms whose densities approach a claimed lower endpoint can establish a lower bound on the supremum even if no endpoint algorithm exists.

In the displayed asymptotic claim, \(\log\) is the natural logarithm and \(\kappa\) approaches zero through positive rationals. The constants \(C,a,\kappa_0\) are chosen once before all those margins. The limit in \(n\) defining the threshold is taken first, separately for each fixed pair. No polynomial dependence of the running-time coefficient or exponent on \(1/\kappa\) is imposed. A statement for a shrinking margin \(\kappa(n)\), or for one fixed value such as \(\kappa=1\), is a different quantifier regime.

The two sides have different meanings: the lower side concerns the existence of successful algorithms at enough densities; the upper side bounds the success densities of every permitted polynomial-time algorithm. A geometric obstruction proved only for algorithms satisfying an additional stability property is not an upper bound for this unrestricted class. Failure to achieve success tending to one does not require success to tend to zero; there may be nonvanishing success or different subsequential behavior.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed two-sided polylogarithmic envelope for the defined threshold. A positive answer must establish both inequalities with one set of fixed constants in the declared computational, input-distribution and order-of-limits conventions. A refutation must exclude every permitted choice of those constants, rather than only a selected logarithmic exponent or the stronger claim with no logarithmic loss. Bounds restricted to stable algorithms, experiments, existence of solutions without efficient search, or a result conditional on an unproved lattice hardness assumption do not alone settle the statement. The benchmark target is the asymptotic conjecture, so the numerical 1/100 tolerance does not replace its logarithmic-factor precision.

title: Littlestone-dimension regret bounds for unrestricted classes
summary: A learner predicts binary labels while an adversary supplies instances and then labels. Its regret is the expected number of errors beyond those of the best fixed concept on the same sequence. The question asks whether every class of finite Littlestone dimension has regret of square-root order in dimension times horizon, with universal constants. The sharp known theorem uses a minimax regularity assumption, and later primary sources explicitly leave removal of that assumption open. A complete Lean answer must establish the universal two-sided bound for arbitrary classes or refute it under the same prediction model.
formal: Do universal real constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) exist such that, for every nonempty set \(\mathcal X\), every nonempty Boolean concept class \(\mathcal H\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal X}\) of finite Littlestone dimension \(d\ge1\), and every integer horizon \(T\ge d\), the optimal adversarial online regret satisfies \[c\sqrt{dT}\le R_T(\mathcal H)\le C\sqrt{dT}?\] Here \[R_T(\mathcal H)=\inf_A\ \sup_{(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_T,y_T)\in\mathcal X\times\{0,1\}}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell(p_t,y_t)-\min_{h\in\mathcal H}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf1\{h(x_t)\ne y_t\}\right\},\] where \(p_t=A_t((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_{t-1},y_{t-1}),x_t)\in[0,1]\), \(\ell(p,0)=p\), and \(\ell(p,1)=1-p\). The infimum ranges over all such causal prediction rules. No restriction of countability, topology, compactness, or measurability is imposed on \(\mathcal X\) or \(\mathcal H\). The unresolved issue in the source is whether the upper bound holds with this full generality; the matching lower scale is already known.
definitions: A concept \(h\) assigns one binary label to every instance. A complete binary tree of depth \(r\) has one instance from \(\mathcal X\) at each internal node and its outgoing edges labeled 0 and 1. The tree is shattered by \(\mathcal H\) if every root-to-leaf path has a concept whose labels on that path's nodes equal its edge labels. The Littlestone dimension \(d\) is the largest shattered depth. Each horizon-specific rule \(A=(A_1,\ldots,A_T)\) is an arbitrary family of set functions from labeled histories and the current instance to \([0,1]\); it may depend on the whole class and on \(T\). The number \(p_t\) is a probability of predicting label 1, so \(\ell(p_t,y_t)\) is the expected zero-one mistake loss. No probability distribution on the arbitrary instance space is required: regret is defined directly by the displayed supremum of finite sums. Equivalently, the adversary presents \(x_t\), the learner chooses \(p_t\), and the adversary then supplies \(y_t\); the charged loss is \(\ell(p_t,y_t)\), not an adversary's reaction to a sampled binary prediction. The learner sees the label before the next round. Future instances and labels are unavailable. The sequence need not be realizable by any concept; comparison is to the best single concept in hindsight. The minimum comparator loss exists because the class is nonempty and losses are integers in \(\{0,\ldots,T\}\). The infimum over rules and supremum over sequences need not be attained. Running time, memory, computability, and finite descriptions of the class or rules are unrestricted; the predictor need not choose a concept from the class. The constants must be independent of the domain, class, dimension, and horizon, and logarithmic factors may not be hidden. The restriction \(T\ge d\) is essential to this square-root formulation because regret is at most \(T\); the omitted dimension-zero case has a single distinct concept and zero regret.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal two-sided statement, or its logical negation, in Lean under the stated arbitrary-set prediction model. For a positive answer, supply universal constants and prove both bounds, using any previously formalized lower-bound result with matching hypotheses. If an optimal rule does not attain the infimum, rules approaching the upper bound arbitrarily closely suffice. A negative answer must refute the existence of universal constants: for every proposed pair \(0<c\le C<\infty\), some class and allowed horizon violate a bound. In view of the known universal lower bound, the outstanding mathematical task is the upper bound or classes with unbounded ratio \(R_T(\mathcal H)/\sqrt{dT}\). A result with a class-dependent constant, an extra logarithmic factor, or an added regularity hypothesis does not settle the question. This is an exact constant-factor asymptotic claim, not an additive numerical approximation.

title: Sample-optimal Gaussian graphical model learning in polynomial time
summary: The problem asks whether sparse Gaussian conditional-independence graphs can be recovered in polynomial time with an information-theoretically optimal number of independent samples. The statement allows arbitrary means and condition numbers and requires every edge and nonedge to be identified correctly. Sample optimality is defined by a minimax benchmark that retains degree, normalized edge strength and confidence without assuming a universally sharp formula. Known degree-dependent algorithms, structural-subclass results, conditional hardness and trajectory-based algorithms each address a different part of the question. A Lean resolution must establish or refute one uniform algorithm with both a universal sample factor and a fixed polynomial arithmetic-time bound.
formal: Can general Gaussian conditional-independence graphs be learned in uniform polynomial time using, up to a universal constant factor, the information-theoretically optimal number of independent observations? For integers \(p\ge2\), \(1\le d\le p-1\), \(r\ge2\), and rational \(0<\kappa<1\), let \(\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)\) be the Gaussian family defined below and let \(m^*(p,d,\kappa,r)\) be its minimax sample count for exact graph recovery with failure probability at most \(2^{-r}\), allowing unrestricted measurable estimators. Is there one uniform randomized algorithm \(A\) and constants \(C,B,a\ge1\) such that, for every parameter choice and every \(P\in\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)\), \(A(p,d,\kappa,r)\) returns its exact graph with probability at least \(1-2^{-r}\), draws at most \(\lceil C m^*(p,d,\kappa,r)\rceil\) independent samples, and uses at most \[B\bigl(p+d+\lceil\kappa^{-1}\rceil+r+L\bigr)^a\] real-arithmetic operations, including sample loading and output, where \(L\) is the binary encoding length of \(\kappa\)? The exponent and constants must be independent of every parameter and of the unknown distribution. This retains the general sample-optimal computational question from the source’s conclusion; bounded-degree recovery is already treated there. The minimax definition does not presume that the commonly quoted \(d\log p/\kappa^2\) sample scale is sharp in all joint parameter regimes.
definitions:
A member \(P\) of \(\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)\) is \(N(\mu,\Sigma)\), where \(\mu\in\mathbb R^p\) is arbitrary, \(\Sigma\) is a real symmetric positive definite \(p\times p\) covariance matrix, and \(\Theta=\Sigma^{-1}\) is its precision matrix. Its undirected graph has vertices \([p]=\{1,\ldots,p\}\) and an edge \(\{i,j\}\), for \(i\ne j\), exactly when \(\Theta_{ij}\ne0\). Every vertex has at most \(d\) neighbors, and every edge satisfies \[\frac{|\Theta_{ij}|}{\sqrt{\Theta_{ii}\Theta_{jj}}}\ge\kappa.\] This normalized precision entry is the magnitude of the corresponding partial correlation. For an empty graph the edge condition holds vacuously. The parameters are upper and lower promises, not assertions that degree equals \(d\) or minimum strength equals \(\kappa\). No eigenvalue, condition-number, variance, sign-pattern, incoherence, faithfulness, treewidth or walk-summability restriction is imposed. The learner is not given \(\mu,\Sigma,\Theta\), or a graph representation.

An observation is an entire vector \(X\in\mathbb R^p\) drawn from \(P\); observations are independent and identically distributed. The graph-recovery loss is zero exactly when all off-diagonal zero/nonzero decisions are correct, and one otherwise. Estimating covariance entries to a numerical tolerance is a different task. The probability in the guarantee includes the observations and internal randomness. The public failure tolerance is \(2^{-r}\); allowing all integers \(r\ge2\) keeps confidence variable. The graph output is its \(p\times p\) symmetric binary adjacency matrix with zero diagonal.

For a fixed \((p,d,\kappa,r)\), define \(m^*\) as the least nonnegative integer \(m\) for which some Borel-measurable randomized estimator from \((\mathbb R^p)^m\) to the finite set of labeled undirected graphs satisfies \[\inf_{P\in\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)}\Pr_{X_1,\ldots,X_m\sim P}[\widehat G(X_1,\ldots,X_m)=G(P)]\ge1-2^{-r}.\] Randomization is an independent infinite fair-bit sequence, and the estimator must be measurable jointly in data and that sequence. It may depend arbitrarily on the four public parameters and has no computation bound; this defines an information benchmark, not a computational oracle. If the set of such sample counts were empty, set \(m^*=+\infty\); known finite sample upper bounds exclude that case for this family. The target algorithm receives neither \(m^*\) nor an optimal estimator. Its sample limit must hold on every possible observation and coin history, even if it adaptively decides when to stop. Padding an early stop with unused observations makes comparison with fixed-size estimators unambiguous.

Computation uses an explicitly chosen standard exact-real arithmetic convention. One finite uniform register program has rational constants in its code, discrete control and fair random bits. Copying, \(+,-,\times,\div\), comparison, branching and each control or output operation cost one unit; any division must be guarded at a zero denominator. Loading one observed vector costs \(p\) units. The algorithm outputs only finite bits for the adjacency matrix. It has no access to conditional samples, a Markov transition trajectory, matrix entries of the unknown distribution, exact expectations, optimization oracles, arbitrary real advice, floor/digit extraction, or an oracle deciding general real-number properties. The positive integers \(p,d,r\) are public unary inputs and \(\kappa\) is supplied by positive coprime binary numerator and denominator, with total bit length \(L\). Reading and translating these inputs are counted. The displayed worst-case operation bound applies to all sample and random-bit histories, not just in expectation.

This convention makes the source’s continuous-observation computational question precise without asserting equivalence to finite-bit Gaussian data. Exact Gaussian coordinates are generally not finite binary strings; the source does not prescribe a rounding budget. In particular, allowing arbitrary condition numbers in the distribution is material to numerical implementation. Any finite-precision result, or computational hardness assumption in another machine model, needs a justified relation to this arithmetic convention before it resolves the displayed proposition. Polynomial time means a single fixed exponent for variable \(d\); \(p^{O(d)}\) is insufficient. Sample optimality means a universal multiplicative factor, with no suppressed dependence on \(d,\kappa,r\) or logarithmic loss.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof of the existence proposition or its full negation. An affirmative result must supply one uniform algorithm and constants, prove exact graph recovery over the entire promised Gaussian family, prove the universal constant-factor comparison with the defined information-theoretic minimum, and verify worst-case sample and arithmetic-time bounds. A negative result must rule out every such learner and constants on some allowed parameters or distribution. A conditional computational obstruction remains conditional unless its hypothesis is also proved. A \(p^{O(d)}\) method, a result only for a fixed degree, a polynomial-time method using more than a universal-factor sample overhead, or a theorem with extra spectral/sign assumptions does not suffice. Neither does learning from a Glauber trajectory establish the independent-observation guarantee. A closed form for \(m^*\) is useful but is not assumed in advance; any claimed closed form must be proved uniformly in its stated regime. The answer is an exact yes/no theorem, not a numerical estimate of a covariance matrix.

title: Nontrivial agnostic membership-query learning of \(\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\)
summary: The card asks whether constant-depth modular circuits admit agnostic membership-query learning with a superpolynomial-factor saving over exponential time. Inputs are uniform, labels may be arbitrary and stochastic, and each chosen query receives a fresh conditional label. The target keeps the source’s exponentially small correlation slack and its literal one-third full-learning success guarantee. Known positive results restrict the circuit class or relax the optimum-error comparison and do not establish the full ACC⁰ target. A Lean answer must prove the complete uniform algorithmic assertion or its unconditional negation under these exact resource and accuracy conventions.
formal: Can polynomial-size constant-depth modular circuits be agnostically learned under uniform inputs using membership queries in time \(2^n/n^{\omega(1)}\)? Precisely, for every fixed depth bound \(d\ge1\), fixed modulus \(m\ge2\), and fixed integer size exponent \(k\ge1\), do there exist one uniform randomized oracle Turing machine \(A_{d,m,k}\), an integer \(n_0\), and a saving function \(\sigma:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to[0,\infty)\) such that \(\sigma(n)/\log_2 n\to\infty\) and the following holds? For every \(n\ge n_0\) and every joint distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\times\{-1,+1\}\) whose first marginal is uniform, \(A_{d,m,k}\), given \(1^n\) and the conditional-label oracle described below, runs in worst-case time at most \(2^{n-\sigma(n)}\) and outputs a hypothesis \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr\left[\operatorname{corr}_D(h)\ge \max_{c\in\operatorname{ACC}_{d,m,k}(n)}\operatorname{corr}_D(c)-2^{-n^{99/100}}\right]\ge\frac13,\qquad \operatorname{corr}_D(g):=\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim D}[g(x)y].\] All machine coins and oracle responses are included in this probability. The success constant \(1/3\) is the literal consequence of the source’s full-learning convention \(1-\delta\) and its assignment \(\delta=2/3\); it is recorded explicitly rather than silently exchanged with the separate weak-learning convention.
definitions:
An \(\operatorname{ACC}_{d,m,k}(n)\) circuit is a finite acyclic circuit with \(n\) input bits, constants, unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates, one-input NOT gates, and unbounded-fan-in \(\mathrm{MOD}_m\) gates. A \(\mathrm{MOD}_m\) gate returns one exactly when the number of its one-valued inputs is divisible by \(m\). There are at most \(d\) gates along each input-to-output path and at most \(n^k\) internal gates and wires in total. Its output bit is converted to \(-1,+1\) by \(b\mapsto2b-1\). Fix an effective binary encoding of gates and their ordered incoming wires. These fixed-depth, fixed-modulus, polynomial-size classes give the usual \(\mathrm{ACC}^0\) target when the fixed parameters vary. Gate-count versus wire-count conventions change polynomial size exponents only; the question quantifies over every exponent. The parameters are fixed before input length and may determine the learner and its saving; neither depth nor modulus grows with \(n\). Hidden comparator circuits may be chosen independently at different lengths and need not form a uniformly constructible family. No target circuit description is given to the learner.

The joint distribution \(D\) is otherwise arbitrary. For each chosen query \(z\in\{0,1\}^n\), the oracle returns one fresh label sampled from \(D(Y\mid X=z)\), independently of its earlier samples conditional on the submitted queries. Queries may adapt to previous answers, and repeated queries need not agree. The uniform marginal gives every \(z\) positive probability, so all conditional label distributions are defined. Labels may be deterministic, stochastic, noisy, or inconsistent with every comparator circuit; no realizability promise is made. The learner knows the uniform marginal and can itself draw uniform inputs. It has no sampler description for the label probabilities, equivalence oracle, circuit advice, or oracle access to an optimal comparator. Correlation lies in \([-1,1]\), and the maximum exists because the comparator set is finite and nonempty. For \(\{-1,+1\}\)-valued functions, zero-one error equals \((1-\operatorname{corr})/2\); thus the displayed correlation slack is excess prediction error at most \(2^{-n^{99/100}}/2\), rather than a multiplicative approximation to optimum error.

The output is a finite description of an ordinary Boolean circuit with AND, OR and NOT gates, interpreted as \(h:\{0,1\}^n\to\{-1,+1\}\). The hypothesis need not be an ACC circuit, have depth \(d\), or have size \(n^k\); this is improper learning. Its description is counted in the learner’s running time, and it is evaluated without further training queries. Using ordinary finite circuits makes the usual effectively evaluable hypothesis convention explicit. All query writing and reading, fair random bits, bit computation and output writing count toward worst-case running time; one submitted label is one oracle response, and the oracle’s internal generation cost is not charged. Consequently the number of queries is bounded by the same time. There is no real-arithmetic unit-cost computation in the learner. The exponential accuracy threshold is a mathematical success condition fixed by \(n\), not an exact irrational input that must be encoded or compared by the machine.

The expression \(2^n/n^{\omega(1)}\) means that a single learner for each fixed \((d,m,k)\) has a saving \(\sigma(n)\) whose ratio to \(\log_2 n\) tends to infinity: for every real \(B>0\), eventually \(\sigma(n)\ge B\log_2 n\). The saving is a runtime-bound witness, not an additional oracle or input. Finite exceptional lengths are allowed. A fixed-factor improvement or division by one fixed power of \(n\) is insufficient. Polynomial factors in an otherwise qualifying time can be absorbed into a smaller saving with the same limit. No efficient procedure for constructing the learner uniformly from the fixed depth, modulus and size exponent is additionally requested.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the displayed existence statement, or of its full logical negation: some fixed \((d,m,k)\) admits no uniform learner with the stated eventual superlogarithmic saving and correlation guarantee simultaneously for all uniform-marginal label distributions. A positive answer must meet the specified shrinking accuracy, the literal full-learning success constant, the conditional-query interface and worst-case total time, including a finite evaluable output. Constant-error learning, realizable-only learning, a fixed polynomial-factor saving or a multiplicative optimum-error factor does not meet this agnostic target. A lower bound against a restricted query method or a conditional cryptographic obstruction is not the unconditional negation unless the additional assumption is also proved. This is an exact asymptotic yes/no statement, not a request to approximate a numerical quantity.

title: Linear conditional-information bounds for VC learning
summary: The card asks whether every finite-VC binary class has a proper learner whose whole output has conditional information only linear in the dimension. The same learner must achieve expected training error within a universal square-root dimension-to-sample-size term of the best hypothesis on every sample. The information experiment reveals two candidates per training position and measures what the output says about the hidden choices. Known negative results concern stricter realizable training guarantees, while other optimal generalization analyses use different information bounds. A directly relevant FOCS 2026 paper is accepted but its theorem text was not located, so the completed formulation retains uncertain current status.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(c>0\) such that the following holds? For every nonempty Boolean hypothesis class \(H\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X}\) of finite VC dimension \(d\ge1\), and every integer \(n\ge d\), there is a proper randomized learner \(A:(X\times\{0,1\})^n\to H\) satisfying both \[\forall P,\quad \operatorname{CMI}_{P}(A)\le cd\] and \[\forall s\in(X\times\{0,1\})^n,\quad \mathbb E_{W\sim A(s)}\widehat L_s(W)\le\inf_{h\in H}\widehat L_s(h)+c\sqrt{d/n}?\] The first quantifier ranges over all labeled-data distributions in the measurable model below, including nonrealizable distributions. The second ranges over every deterministic sample, including samples with conflicting labels. The same learner must satisfy both guarantees; it may depend on \(H,n\), but not on \(P\). This is the original source’s main agnostic Conjecture 6, recovered from the imported introduction excerpt, not its different realizable or improper variants.
definitions:
A hypothesis is a total function \(h:X\to\{0,1\}\). A finite set \(V\subseteq X\) is shattered if every map \(V\to\{0,1\}\) is the restriction of a hypothesis in \(H\); the VC dimension is the supremum of sizes of shattered finite sets. For a labeled sequence \(s=((x_i,y_i))_{i=1}^n\), its empirical zero-one loss is \(\widehat L_s(h)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{h(x_i)\ne y_i\}\). Samples are ordered and may contain repeated points. Proper means that every output is a member of \(H\), rather than an arbitrary Boolean predictor. The expected empirical loss averages only the learner’s private randomness, with the input sequence held fixed. There is no running-time, finite encoding, efficient evaluation, or finite/countable-domain restriction.

The following explicit measurable-kernel convention makes the source’s probability notation meaningful. Equip \(X\) and the hypothesis space \(H\) with sigma-algebras for which evaluation \((h,x)\mapsto h(x)\) is jointly measurable; binary labels have all subsets. The statement quantifies over such measurable presentations of the classes. A randomized learner is a probability kernel from the product sample space into \(H\): for each input it assigns a probability distribution on \(H\), and probabilities of measurable output events vary measurably with the input. Deterministic learners are included. All distributions \(P\) on the labeled product space are allowed. This is a stated probability-interface convention, not a finite-domain specialization, a premise that a measurable empirical-risk minimizer exists, or a claim about nonmeasurable learning rules. It should be retained explicitly in a formalization.

For \(\operatorname{CMI}_{P}(A)\), draw a supersample \(\widetilde Z=(Z_{i,b})_{1\le i\le n,\ b\in\{0,1\}}\) of \(2n\) independent labeled examples from \(P\), and independently draw a uniformly random selector \(B\in\{0,1\}^n\). Let \(\widetilde Z_B=(Z_{i,B_i})_{i=1}^n\), then draw \(W\) from the kernel \(A(\widetilde Z_B)\) using no access to the unselected examples. Define \[\operatorname{CMI}_{P}(A)=I(W;B\mid\widetilde Z)=n-H(B\mid W,\widetilde Z)\] in bits. Here \(H(B\mid W,\widetilde Z)=\mathbb E[-\sum_{b\in\{0,1\}^n}p_b\log_2 p_b]\), where \(p_b=\mathbb E[\mathbf1\{B=b\}\mid\sigma(W,\widetilde Z)]\), and \(0\log_2 0=0\). This finite-selector definition uses conditional expectation and does not need pointwise conditional densities on arbitrary domains. The quantity lies between zero and \(n\). It measures the complete hypothesis-valued output \(W\) under its stated measurable structure, not merely the labels it predicts on the supersample and not the learner’s unreleased random seed. Changing logarithm base only rescales the universal constant. The learner cannot see \(P\), the supersample or selector as additional inputs. The accuracy slack and information constant are uniform over all classes, dimensions and sample sizes; a bound with an extra \(\log n\), or with a class-dependent constant, is a different assertion.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of Conjecture 6 in the explicitly stated probability convention, or prove its logical negation. A positive answer supplies one universal \(c\) and a proper probability kernel for every admitted \(H,n\), with the distribution-uniform CMI bound and pointwise empirical-loss bound both established. A negative answer must show that for every proposed \(c>0\), some admitted class and sample size defeat every proper kernel: either some distribution violates the information bound, or some deterministic sample violates the expected empirical-loss bound. A counterexample only to exact consistency or to empirical loss \(O(d/n)\) does not refute the allowed \(O(\sqrt{d/n})\) slack here. A generalization bound using a different information quantity, an improper output, or a distribution-dependent learner does not prove this claim. The target is existence with universal constants, not a numerical quantity requiring additive approximation.

title: PAC learning of finite automata under the uniform distribution
summary: The card asks whether every finite automaton can be learned efficiently from uniformly sampled words labeled only by acceptance. The learner knows the word length, alphabet and state bound and may return any efficient predictor. It must achieve every requested accuracy and confidence using polynomial time without membership queries or state information. A published local-pseudorandom-generator assumption rules out even weak improper learning on uniform binary words, and a 2026 source retains that premise. The completed card records this conditional negative answer while preserving the original unconditional question and its exact Lean decision criterion.
formal: Are deterministic finite automata efficiently PAC learnable from independent uniformly distributed words and their acceptance bits? Use the ordinary finite-word, fixed-length uniform model. Does there exist one randomized classical Turing machine \(L\) and one polynomial \(p\) such that, for every alphabet size \(q\ge2\), word length \(n\ge1\), state bound \(s\ge1\), integers \(a,b\ge3\), and deterministic finite automaton \(M\) with at most \(s\) states over \(\Sigma_q=\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\), the following holds? Given \(1^q,1^n,1^s,1^a,1^b\) and access only to independent examples \((w,M(w))\) with \(w\sim U_{q,n}\), \(L\) runs in worst-case time at most \(p(q+n+s+a+b)\), and outputs a finite predictor \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr_{L,\,\mathrm{examples}}\left[\Pr_{w\sim U_{q,n}}[h(w)\ne M(w)]\le\frac1a\right]\ge1-\frac1b?\] The predictor may use any efficiently evaluable representation; it need not be an automaton. A 2021 theorem rules out this guarantee under a specified local-pseudorandom-generator assumption, already for binary alphabets. This card retains the unconditional algorithm-existence question, while recording that published conditional negative answer explicitly.
definitions:
A deterministic finite automaton is a tuple \(M=(\Sigma_q,Q,q_0,F,\tau)\) with a nonempty finite state set \(Q\), \(|Q|\le s\), initial state \(q_0\in Q\), accepting states \(F\subseteq Q\), and a total transition function \(\tau:Q\times\Sigma_q\to Q\). Starting at \(q_0\), it reads the letters of a finite word from left to right and updates its current state by \(\tau\); \(M(w)=1\) exactly when its final state lies in \(F\), and otherwise \(M(w)=0\). The target transition table, states and accepting set are hidden. The public value \(s\) is an upper bound on the number of states, not the full target description. The source’s size convention is state count. A complete transition-table encoding has length polynomial in \(s\) and \(q\), so the explicit polynomial dependence on both parameters accounts for that representation.

\(U_{q,n}\) assigns probability \(q^{-n}\) to every word in \(\Sigma_q^n\); equivalently its \(n\) letters are independent and uniform in \(\Sigma_q\). Each oracle request supplies a fresh independent word and its deterministic acceptance bit under the same fixed \(M\). The learner may request more independent examples adaptively but cannot select the word to be labeled. It sees neither the final state nor the sequence of intermediate states. There are no membership queries, equivalence queries, counterexamples, nonuniform advice or random-target assumption. The guarantee must hold for every automaton, including arbitrarily chosen transition graphs and accepting sets. Randomness in the outer probability comes only from examples and the learner’s independent fair coins; the inner probability is error on a fresh uniform word. This is the realizable PAC model with noiseless labels. Parameters \(1/a\) and \(1/b\) range over inverse integers, which suffice to express every desired positive accuracy and failure tolerance by rounding downward.

For a concrete hypothesis interface, encode each letter in \(\lceil\log_2 q\rceil\) bits and let the output be an ordinary Boolean circuit on the resulting \(n\lceil\log_2 q\rceil\) bits. Its output on valid word encodings is \(h(w)\); values on unused letter codes are irrelevant. The circuit may use two-input AND/OR, one-input NOT and constant gates with a fixed effective binary encoding. Its description is written within the learning-time bound and is evaluated without examples or access to the target. This expresses unrestricted improper efficient prediction: the output is not constrained to at most \(s\) states or to a minimal consistent automaton. Uniformly polynomial-time evaluable finite predictors have ordinary polynomial-size circuit representations under the usual bit-computation convention. All bit operations, reading examples, fair random bits and output writing count toward the one polynomial bound, as does the number of example requests. The example oracle supplies the promised distribution; its own sampling computation is not charged. The same machine and polynomial work for all displayed parameters, lengths and targets.

Uniformity refers to words of the specified length, not to an impossible probability measure assigning equal mass to all of \(\Sigma_q^*\). The learner may depend on the public \(n\), and its guarantee is only over words of that length. Exact identification of the complete infinite regular language, prediction simultaneously at every length by one output, geometric length mixtures, and real-valued limit-average behavior on infinite words are different tasks. The arbitrary-finite-alphabet convention follows the source’s DFA and \(U^n\) definitions; the later hardness theorem applies already when \(q=2\). Computational efficiency is essential: the question does not merely ask for a finite or polynomial information-theoretic sample bound.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of \(L,p\) with the complete uniform guarantee in Lean, or prove its logical negation: for every proposed machine and polynomial, some allowed parameters and target violate the runtime, finite-output or PAC condition. A positive answer must allow every target automaton and observe only independent acceptance-labeled uniform words. A result for random transition graphs, additional state labels, membership queries or only a fixed bounded state count does not meet the statement. A negative answer under the local-PRG assumption is a conditional theorem and must retain that premise; it does not by itself prove the unconditional negation. Hardness of finding a smallest consistent DFA also does not exclude an arbitrary efficient predictor. The yes/no assertion has exact logical quantifiers and rational error/confidence tolerances; no numerical optimum is being approximated.

title: Minimax sample complexity of proper agnostic online reinforcement learning
summary: The learner interacts with an unknown finite-horizon MDP through complete episodes. It must select a nearly best policy from a supplied finite class. The target is a two-sided estimate of one plus the worst-case number of episodes, including policy classes that need zero samples. State layers, binary actions, terminal rewards and constant confidence are fixed explicitly. This quantitative proper-learning variant is marked as a narrowing of the source’s characterization question.
formal:
For proper agnostic online reinforcement learning in the finite episodic model below, determine \(N(\Pi,H,\varepsilon)+1\) up to universal constant factors. Supply one function \(g\) of the given policy tables, layers, start state, horizon and accuracy, and constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) such that
\[c\,g(\Pi,H,\varepsilon)\le N(\Pi,H,\varepsilon)+1\le C\,g(\Pi,H,\varepsilon)\]
for every legal finite instance description and every real \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\). Here \(N\) is the minimax number of training episodes. This is the TCS500 benchmark’s quantitative finite-state version of the source question.
definitions:
An instance description specifies a horizon \(H\ge1\), finite nonempty disjoint state layers \(S_1,\ldots,S_H\), a designated initial state \(s_0\) in \(S_1\), a fixed action set {0,1}, and a nonempty finite class \(\Pi\) of deterministic policies. A policy is a table assigning one action to every state; the layer identifies time. The learner receives all these tables. The unknown MDP has arbitrary stochastic transitions from layer h to h+1, and a terminal reward in [0,1] whose distribution depends on the last state and action. Earlier rewards are zero. All probability distributions may have arbitrary real probabilities. The value \(V(\pi)\) is expected terminal reward from \(s_0\).

Each episode starts afresh at \(s_0\) and follows the actual transitions for H steps. The learner observes visited states, chosen actions and the terminal reward. During training it may choose arbitrary randomized actions based on the entire history, including previous episodes. It cannot reset to an intermediate state, sample a chosen transition or inspect the transition/reward tables. There is no computation or policy-evaluation cost restriction: this is statistical complexity with measurable randomized learning rules.

\(N(\Pi,H,\varepsilon)\) is the least nonnegative integer N for which some such rule, after at most N complete episodes, outputs a member \(\hat\pi\) of \(\Pi\) with \(V(\hat\pi)\ge\max_{\pi\in\Pi}V(\pi)-\varepsilon\) with probability at least 2/3, for every MDP on these layers. The layer sets and start state are understood as part of \(\Pi\)’s description. N is finite, since testing every policy separately is allowed.

The required answer supplies an explicit expression or structural parameter g of the policy tables, layers, H and \(\varepsilon\), and universal constants c,C>0 with \(cg\le N+1\le Cg\) for every description. A definition merely repeating the optimization over learners and MDPs is not a determination. The added one handles classes learnable without samples. This narrows the broad characterization request to a specified minimax quantity; dependence on state count is not prohibited in the expression. It fixes proper output, binary actions and terminal rewards rather than silently treating all online RL models as equivalent.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked characterization by one explicitly described \(g\), with matching bounds for \(N+1\) and constants independent of the full instance and accuracy. A singleton policy class has \(N=0\), so the bounds must cover \(N+1=1\) there. Prove the upper bound using episodic online access and a policy in the given class. Prove the lower bound for every allowed learner. The local definitions specify which structural characterizations qualify.

title: Dimension complexity of distribution-independent SQ learning
summary: The question asks whether successful distribution-independent statistical-query learning forces low dimension complexity. The learner may adapt bounded expectation queries to previous noisy answers. Its guarantee must hold for every distribution, target and valid response rule. The desired conclusion is one deterministic feature map representing the entire class exactly in dimension proportional to the query count divided by squared tolerance. Recent conditional results impose additional structure and do not establish the unrestricted implication.
formal: Is there a universal constant \(C>0\) with the following property? For every nonempty set \(X\), every nonempty binary concept class \(\mathcal H\subseteq\{-1,+1\}^{X}\), every integer \(m\ge1\), tolerance \(0<\tau<1\) and error \(0\le\varepsilon<1/4\), suppose a single randomized statistical-query learner makes at most \(m\) queries of tolerance \(\tau\) and, for every input distribution \(D\), target \(h\in\mathcal H\) and admissible oracle response rule, returns \(\hat h\) with \(\mathbb E[\Pr_{x\sim D}(\hat h(x)\ne h(x))]\le\varepsilon\). Must \(\operatorname{dc}(\mathcal H)\le C m/\tau^{2}\)? The learner is selected before the distribution, target and oracle replies. The constant is independent of all these objects and of the accuracy, domain size and class.
definitions:
Use the discrete measurable structure \(2^{X}\) on an arbitrary domain, and quantify over all countably additive probability measures on it. A tolerance-\(\tau\) query is an arbitrary bounded function \(q:X\times\{-1,+1\}\to[-1,1]\); its answer is any real \(v\) satisfying \(|v-\mathbb E_{x\sim D}q(x,h(x))|\le\tau\). Queries may depend on previous answers and an internal random seed independent of the instance. A response rule can depend on the public history, including the current query, but observes the hidden seed only through that history. It must obey the tolerance at every history that can occur for the fixed distribution and target. The guarantee holds for every such rule, with expectation over the learner's seed. Require the interactions and their resulting loss to be measurable, so that the stated expectations exist. These measurable-interaction conventions specify the source's abstract oracle model. Query count is the resource: there is no restriction on computation between queries, description length, adaptivity, or the class containing the output predictor. There are no free samples or additional distribution information.

The dimension complexity is the least integer \(d\ge0\) for which there is one map \(\phi:X\to\mathbb R^{d}\) such that, for each \(h\in\mathcal H\), some \(w_h\in\mathbb R^{d}\) satisfies \(h(x)=\operatorname{sgn}_{+}(\langle w_h,\phi(x)\rangle)\) for every \(x\in X\). Here \(\operatorname{sgn}_{+}(z)=+1\) when \(z\ge0\), and \(-1\) otherwise, and the inner product is the sum of coordinatewise products. Put \(\operatorname{dc}=+\infty\) if no finite dimension works. The feature map is deterministic, shared by all targets, and independent of \(D\); no construction or efficiency requirement is imposed on it. Offsets require a coordinate of the feature map. The representation must be exact at every point, even though the learner's premise allows positive expected error.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the universal implication, or of its negation. A positive answer must supply a universal finite \(C\). A negative answer must show that no such constant works: for every \(C>0\), exhibit or prove the existence of a class and admissible learner parameters satisfying the premise but with \(\operatorname{dc}(\mathcal H)>Cm/\tau^{2}\). An infinite dimension example also qualifies. A result assuming extra rank, margin or distribution conditions, or allowing only approximate or random feature representations, does not establish the stated implication.

title: Recursive teaching dimension conjecture
summary: A finite concept class can be studied through both its VC dimension and its recursive teaching dimension. VC dimension measures the ability to realize label patterns, while recursive teaching measures how examples can identify concepts through successive elimination. The question asks whether one universal constant always bounds recursive teaching dimension by that constant times VC dimension. The same constant must work for every finite class. The project seeks a direct quantitative link between the complexity of learning from samples and the information needed for structured teaching.
formal: Does there exist a universal real constant \(K>0\) such that, for every finite set \(X\) and every finite Boolean concept class \(\mathcal C\subseteq\{0,1\}^X\), \[\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)\leq K\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)?\] Both dimensions are the combinatorial quantities defined below. The constant must be independent of the number of concepts, the domain size and the class itself.
