title: Unleveled fully homomorphic encryption from LWE alone
summary: Fully homomorphic encryption evaluates Boolean computations on encrypted bits and returns a compact encrypted result. The question asks for one classical key-generation procedure that needs no advance bound on the depth of those computations. The only hardness premise is the specified ordinary polynomial-modulus LWE assumption, without independent circular security. Security must hold against polynomial-size nonuniform classical adversaries who also see the evaluation key. A complete Lean-checked answer must establish the entire implication and its uniform correctness and compactness guarantees, or refute it.
formal:
Does the ordinary polynomial-modulus decisional Learning With Errors assumption specified below imply the existence of a classical compact fully homomorphic public-key encryption scheme whose keys are generated without a bound on the size or depth of the circuits subsequently evaluated?

The scheme must be secure against nonuniform polynomial-size classical adversaries given both its encryption and evaluation keys. Its only hardness assumption may be the stated ordinary LWE assumption; no independent circular-security or key-dependent-message assumption is allowed.
definitions:
Fix the following precise LWE hypothesis. For every integer \(c\ge3\), let \(q_c(d)\) be the least prime at least \(d^c\). For every positive integer-valued polynomially bounded sample-count function \(M(d)\), sample independently
\[
 A\leftarrow\mathbb Z_{q_c(d)}^{M(d)\times d},\qquad
 s\leftarrow\mathbb Z_{q_c(d)}^d,\qquad
 u\leftarrow\mathbb Z_{q_c(d)}^{M(d)}
\]
uniformly, and let the coordinates of \(e\) be independent integers with probability proportional to \(\exp(-\pi z^2/(4d))\), reduced modulo \(q_c(d)\). Here \(\mathbb Z_q\) is the ring of integers modulo \(q\). The hypothesis is that the distributions
\[
 (A,As+e\bmod q_c(d))\quad\text{and}\quad(A,u)
\]
are computationally indistinguishable against every family of nonuniform classical randomized circuits of size polynomial in \(d\). That is, the absolute difference of their acceptance probabilities is negligible in \(d\). The integer \(c\) and the polynomial sample bound are fixed before \(d\) grows. A distinguisher may know them and \(d\). The noise is the discrete Gaussian \(D_{\mathbb Z,2\sqrt d}\); no encryptions of secrets, correlated auxiliary hints or circular-security statements are included in this assumption.

Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in the security parameter of each experiment. Circuit size counts gates, input bits and private random bits, using fan-in-two Boolean gates and unary negation. Nonuniform means that each circuit may be chosen independently at each parameter value, with no efficient procedure producing the family. These are classical adversaries, not quantum ones.

The requested scheme has one fixed tuple of uniform classical algorithms
\[
 \operatorname{Gen}(1^\lambda)\to(pk,evk,sk),\quad
 \operatorname{Enc}(pk,b)\to c,\quad
 \operatorname{Eval}(evk,F,c_1,\ldots,c_t)\to c_F,\quad
 \operatorname{Dec}(sk,c)\to b.
\]
All algorithms may also receive \(1^\lambda\) implicitly. Generation, encryption and evaluation may use fresh independent fair random bits; decryption is deterministic. Generation and bit encryption have polynomial worst-case bit running time in \(\lambda\). Evaluation runs in time polynomial in \(\lambda\) and its complete input length. The model is an ordinary multitape Turing machine; no ideal cryptographic oracle is available.

Plaintexts are bits. The circuit \(F\) is explicitly given by its gate list, has \(t\) inputs and one output, and uses fan-in-two AND and OR and unary NOT. The generation algorithm receives no circuit, circuit-size bound or depth bound. There is one fixed polynomial \(P\) bounding the lengths of \(pk,evk,sk\), fresh bit ciphertexts and evaluated one-bit ciphertexts, as well as the time for decrypting these ciphertexts, by \(P(\lambda)\). This bound is independent of \(F\), its input count and its depth. All auxiliary public material is included in \(pk,evk\).

For every fixed polynomial \(p\), there must be a negligible function \(\mu_p(\lambda)\) such that, for every circuit \(F\) with size and input count at most \(p(\lambda)\) and every vector of input bits, independently encrypting those bits, evaluating \(F\), and decrypting yields \(F(b_1,\ldots,b_t)\) with probability at least \(1-\mu_p(\lambda)\). The probability includes all coins of generation, encryption and evaluation. Fresh bit decryption has negligible error as well. The algorithms and \(P\) are fixed before choosing \(p\). Thus one key-generation algorithm supports every polynomial circuit bound; choosing a large fixed polynomial depth during setup does not meet the quantifiers.

Security means that for every nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit family \(T_\lambda\),
\[
 \left|\Pr[T_\lambda(pk,evk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,0))=1]
       -\Pr[T_\lambda(pk,evk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,1))=1]\right|
\]
is negligible in \(\lambda\). Each experiment generates a fresh key tuple and fresh encryption and adversary randomness. Since the public key allows arbitrary further encryptions, this is bit-message chosen-plaintext indistinguishability. The requested theorem must derive this security from the precise LWE hypothesis above. It is not a request to prove LWE hardness unconditionally.

There is no external trusted setup, subsequent secret-key assistance, random oracle or additional hardness premise. Bootstrapping and public encryptions involving secret-key bits are permitted if their security is proved from ordinary LWE. In particular, the absence of a circular-security assumption is a requirement on the proof, not a ban on a syntactic form of evaluation key. Polynomial hardness of LWE is the assumption: subexponential hardness, functional encryption and obfuscation may not simply be assumed independently.

The correctness condition is evaluation of one arbitrary polynomial-size circuit on fresh ciphertexts. A stronger guarantee for indefinitely composing new evaluations on already evaluated ciphertexts is not an extra requirement here. The related TCS-6871 instead asks for an operational reduction from worst-case polynomial-factor GapSVP, allowing quantum computation in that reduction; it has a different stated foundation.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked construction of one scheme, its uniform running-time and compactness bounds, the correctness guarantee for every polynomial circuit-size bound, and a proof of its security from exactly the specified LWE hypothesis; or give a complete Lean-checked refutation of that implication.

An additional circular-security, functional-encryption, obfuscation or stronger-hardness assumption does not meet the positive target. A construction with depth-dependent setup, a quantum evaluator or noncompact decryption also does not qualify. Breaking one proposed scheme, or separating one restricted class of black-box reductions, does not refute the general existence implication. A negative answer must refute the implication from the stated LWE assumption to existence of the scheme. Any further premise used for that refutation must also be established. Numerical approximation tolerance does not weaken these asymptotic security, correctness and resource requirements.

title: Sub-square-root share-size exponents in perfect secret sharing
summary: Secret sharing lets authorized groups reconstruct a secret while unauthorized groups learn nothing. The target asks for a universal bound \(K\cdot 2^{cn}\) bits per share for every n-party access structure, with \(c<1/2\) and a one-bit secret. Perfect reconstruction and privacy are required, and nonlinear schemes are allowed. Nir’s August 2026 preprint states a \(2^{0.496n+o(n)}\) bound that would meet this target. The claimed resolution is recorded with uncertain status because its proof has not been independently verified in this review.
formal: Do there exist real constants \(K>0\) and \(0<c<1/2\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\) and every monotone access structure \(\Gamma\) on \([n]\) with \(\varnothing \notin \Gamma\) and \([n]\in \Gamma\), there exists a perfect secret-sharing scheme for a uniform one-bit secret with \(\max _{i} \log _{2}|S_{i}|\le K\cdot 2^{cn}\), where \(S_{i}\) is the finite alphabet of participant i’s share?
definitions: \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). An access structure \(\Gamma \subseteq 2^{[n]}\) is monotone when \(A\in \Gamma\) and \(A\subseteq B\subseteq [n]\) imply \(B\in \Gamma\). A scheme is a joint probability distribution of a secret B uniform on \(\{0,1\}\) and shares \(X_{i}\in S_{i}\), where each \(S_{i}\) is a finite nonempty set. For each \(A\in \Gamma\) there is a deterministic map \(r_{A}:\prod _{i\in A}S_{i}\to \{0,1\}\) such that \(r_{A}((X_{i})_{i\in A})=B\) with probability one. For each \(A\notin \Gamma\), the conditional distributions of \((X_{i})_{i\in A}\) given \(B=0\) and \(B=1\) are identical. This is exact reconstruction and perfect information-theoretic privacy, with arbitrary collusion within A. Share size is the base-two logarithm of its alphabet cardinality, not its Shannon entropy or the sum over participants. It is normalized by the secret size of one bit. There is no linearity, field, threshold, computation-time or uniform construction requirement. The scheme may depend on the whole finite access structure. K,c must be universal. Rounding \(\log _{2}|S_{i}|\) up to an integer encoding length changes K only by an absolute factor.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that some universal \(K>0\) and \(0<c<1/2\) satisfy the stated worst-share bound for every permitted access structure, or prove the logical negation in Lean. A negative answer must show that for every such \(K,c\) some access structure admits no perfect scheme with that bound, allowing all finite share alphabets and all joint distributions in the definition. The object quantified over is a general scheme; it need not be linear or efficiently constructed.

title: Existence of one-way functions
summary: Do classical one-way functions exist without an unproved hardness assumption? A polynomial-time function with negligible inversion success against every uniform classical polynomial-time adversary, or a proof that none exists. Complete candidates and complexity-theoretic equivalences are known; their required hardness has not been proved. An unconditional existence or impossibility theorem. Would establish or rule out the basic computational asymmetry behind many cryptographic primitives.
formal: Does there exist a total deterministic polynomial-time computable function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to \{0,1\}^{*}\) such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every integer \(d\ge 1\), there is \(n_{0}\) with \(\Pr [f(I(1^{n},f(X)))=f(X)]\le n^{- d}\) for all \(n\ge n_{0}\), where X is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and the probability also includes the independent random coins of I?
definitions: The security parameter \(n\ge 1\) is given in unary as \(1^{n}\). A single deterministic Turing machine computes f on every finite binary string in time polynomial in its input length. Each inverter I is one classical randomized Turing machine with a worst-case polynomial running-time bound; its input contains \(1^{n}\), so its running time and output length are polynomial in n. It receives \(f(X)\), not X, and has no advice, oracle or secret information. An output Y succeeds exactly when \(f(Y)=f(X)\); any preimage is accepted, even one of a different length from X. An explicit failure output is unsuccessful. No injectivity, permutation property or length preservation is imposed. Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in \(n\). The threshold \(n_{0}\) can depend on I and d. Security is averaged over the uniformly sampled input and the inverter’s coins, and must hold for all sufficiently large n, not merely an infinite subsequence.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves, without an unproved computational hardness assumption, that at least one f satisfies the stated efficiency and inversion bound. A negative resolution proves that every polynomial-time f has a polynomial-time inverter whose success is non-negligible: for some \(d\ge 1\) it exceeds \(n^{- d}\) for infinitely many n. A conditional construction or a failure of one particular candidate does not decide existence.

title: Exponential share-size lower bounds for perfect secret sharing
summary: Secret sharing distributes a secret so that prescribed groups can reconstruct it and all other groups learn nothing. The question asks whether some policy at every sufficiently large participant count forces a positive exponential number of bits in at least one share. The secret is one bit, and all finite, perfectly private schemes are allowed. Known exponential lower bounds for restricted schemes do not settle this unrestricted question. A resolution would identify a basic storage limit of information-theoretic access control.
formal:
An access structure specifies which groups of participants may recover a secret; a perfect scheme gives exact recovery to those groups and no information to all other groups. Precise definitions appear in Model & notation. Is the following proposition true?
\[
\exists c>0\ \exists n_0\ge1\ \forall n\ge n_0\ \exists\Gamma_n\subseteq 2^{[n]}:
\quad\forall\text{ perfect schemes for }\Gamma_n,\qquad
\max_{i\in[n]}\log_2|\mathcal S_i|\ge 2^{cn}.
\]
Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the secret is one uniform bit, \(\Gamma_n\) is a monotone access structure with \(\varnothing\notin\Gamma_n\) and \([n]\in\Gamma_n\), and \(\mathcal S_i\) is participant \(i\)'s finite share alphabet. Here \(n_0\) is an integer, and the constants are universal. Sharing and reconstruction may be nonlinear and computationally unbounded.
definitions:
A monotone access structure \(\Gamma\subseteq 2^{[n]}\) is a collection of authorized subsets such that \(A\in\Gamma\) and \(A\subseteq B\subseteq[n]\) imply \(B\in\Gamma\).

A perfect scheme is a joint probability distribution of a uniform secret \(B\in\{0,1\}\) and shares \(X_i\in\mathcal S_i\), where every \(\mathcal S_i\) is finite and nonempty. For each authorized \(A\), a deterministic map from \(\prod_{i\in A}\mathcal S_i\) to \(\{0,1\}\) recovers \(B\) with probability one. For every unauthorized \(A\), the distributions of \((X_i)_{i\in A}\) conditioned on \(B=0\) and on \(B=1\) are identical. Arbitrary joint distributions are allowed; there is no field or linearity restriction.

The cost of a share is \(\log_2|\mathcal S_i|\) bits, and the scheme's cost is the largest of these costs. This measures alphabet size, not Shannon entropy. Rounding to an integer encoding length does not change the exponential-existence question. The access structures need not be efficiently recognizable, and the schemes need not be uniformly constructible. The statement concerns all sufficiently large integer participant counts, with one positive constant \(c\) chosen first.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified exponential lower bound, or a complete proof of its logical negation. A lower bound restricted to linear schemes or to bounded-complexity reconstruction does not meet the universal scheme quantifier. A merely superpolynomial lower bound does not establish the stated exponential bound.

title: Polylogarithmic communication for two-server private information retrieval
summary: A user wants one bit from a database replicated at two servers that do not communicate. Each individual server must learn nothing about which bit was requested. The question asks whether one round can use only a fixed power of the logarithm of the database size in total bits. Correctness and privacy are perfect, while local computation is unrestricted. The known subpolynomial protocols leave a substantial gap to this communication target.
formal:
Private information retrieval lets a user recover a selected database bit without revealing its index to either server. Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge2\), a classical one-round two-server protocol with perfect correctness and perfect privacy has total communication at most
\[
C(\log_2 n)^k
\]
bits for every database \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), requested index \(i\in[n]\), and outcome of the user's randomness? The two servers each hold the entire database and do not communicate or collude. Model & notation specifies the protocol and exact privacy requirement. There is no computational hardness assumption or bound on local computation.
definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For each \(n\), a protocol specifies a nonempty finite randomness set \(\mathcal R_n\), query maps \(Q_{1,n},Q_{2,n}\), deterministic answer maps \(A_{1,n},A_{2,n}\), and a deterministic recovery map \(D_n\). Queries and answers are finite binary strings. The user samples \(r\) uniformly from \(\mathcal R_n\), independently of the database, and sends \(q_j=Q_{j,n}(i,r)\) to server \(j\). The server sends back \(a_j=A_{j,n}(x,q_j)\). There is one query and one answer per server. The user starts with only \(n,i,r\), with no database-dependent advice or shared secret.

Perfect correctness means \(D_n(i,r,a_1,a_2)=x_i\) for every \(x,i,r\). Perfect privacy means that for each \(j\in\{1,2\}\) and all \(i,i'\in[n]\), the random strings \(Q_{j,n}(i,r)\) and \(Q_{j,n}(i',r)\) have identical distributions. Since answers are deterministic functions of a server's database and query, this also protects its entire view. The servers follow the protocol; robustness to false answers and confidentiality of the rest of the database from the user are not required.

The cost is the maximum of \(|q_1|+|q_2|+|a_1|+|a_2|\) over all \(x,i,r\), where \(|w|\) is the bit length of a string \(w\). Protocol descriptions may depend on \(n\) but not on \(x\) or \(i\). There is no uniformity or local-running-time restriction. The same constants \(C,k\) must work for every database size; they cannot grow with \(n\). Answers may contain more than one bit.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such a protocol family and universal constants exist, or prove the logical negation. Privacy must be exact against each computationally unbounded individual server. The bound includes both queries and both answers in the worst case. Computational privacy, database-dependent client preprocessing, or a growing number of servers changes the target.

title: Sub-two-thirds exponent for random-function inversion
summary: Preprocessing sees a randomly chosen function and stores a short string before an inversion challenge arrives. The decoder then evaluates the function at adaptively chosen inputs and tries to find any preimage of the challenge. The question asks for a fixed positive improvement below exponent \(2/3\) in both advice length and oracle queries. Success is required on half the inputs for half the functions, with no restriction on preprocessing or local computation. This isolates a longstanding limit of generic cryptanalysis with preprocessing.
formal:
An inverter stores a short advice string about a function before seeing the output it will be asked to invert. Can both its stored advice and its number of later function evaluations beat the exponent \(2/3\) by a fixed positive amount?

Precisely, do there exist real constants \(0<\varepsilon<2/3\), \(C>0\), and an integer \(N_0\ge2\) such that, for every integer \(N\ge N_0\), there is a deterministic classical advice map \(P_N\) and adaptive oracle decoder \(D_N\), as defined in Model & notation, with
\[
s_N\le C N^{2/3-\varepsilon},\qquad
t_N\le C N^{2/3-\varepsilon},
\]
and
\[
\Pr_{f\sim U(\mathcal F_N)}\!\left[
\Pr_{x\sim U([N])}\!\left[
f\bigl(D_N^f(f(x),P_N(f))\bigr)=f(x)
\right]\ge\frac12\right]\ge\frac12?
\]
Here \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\), \(\mathcal F_N\) is the set of all functions from \([N]\) to \([N]\), and \(U(E)\) means the uniform distribution on a finite nonempty set \(E\). The nonnegative integers \(s_N\) and \(t_N\) count advice bits and bound oracle queries, respectively. Finding any preimage counts as success.
definitions:
For each \(N\), preprocessing is an arbitrary map \(P_N:\mathcal F_N\to\{0,1\}^{s_N}\), where \(\mathcal F_N\) contains all \(N^N\) functions. The map sees the complete function before the challenge is chosen. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and only its \(s_N\)-bit output persists to the query phase.

The decoder receives a challenge \(y\in[N]\) and an advice string. It may query the oracle at an input \(z\in[N]\) and obtain \(f(z)\). Each new query can depend on the challenge, advice and all previous answers. It halts after at most \(t_N\) queries on every oracle and input, and outputs an element of \([N]\). Its computation between queries and temporary workspace are unrestricted. This is an advice-length versus query-count model, not a bound on all working memory or elapsed computation time.

The maps and decoding rules may depend on \(N\); no algorithm generating them uniformly is required. The decoder is fixed before \(f\) is sampled: it can depend on the sampled function only through the advice and the oracle replies. A uniformly random function has independent uniform values at its \(N\) inputs. For at least half of these functions, decoding must work on at least half of the independently uniform inputs \(x\) when challenged with \(f(x)\). The target does not sample \(y\) uniformly from the whole codomain, and it does not restrict \(f\) to permutations.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) permits the stated family and success probabilities, or prove the logical negation. A logarithmic saving at exponent \(2/3\) does not meet the fixed-exponent target. A negative answer must cover arbitrary advice maps and adaptive decoders in the stated model, not only a named inversion method.

title: Oblivious transfer from public-key encryption
summary: Oblivious transfer lets a receiver obtain one of two bits while hiding its choice from the sender. The receiver’s full view must reveal no more than its choice and the selected bit. The question asks whether ordinary public-key encryption alone implies such a classical protocol with static semi-honest standalone security. The card permits polynomial interaction and use of algorithm code, while fixing uniform simulators and nonuniform polynomial-size distinguishers. Oracle barriers and recent constructions with extra sampling, rerandomization or decoding assumptions do not settle the unrestricted implication.
formal:
In the classical plain model, does the existence of public-key encryption secure against chosen-plaintext attacks imply the existence of 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious transfer secure against static semi-honest corruption of either party?

Let \(E\) assert the existence of the bit-encryption scheme defined below, and let \(T\) assert the existence of the two-party protocol and simulators defined below. The target is the unrelativized implication
\[E\ \Longrightarrow\ T.\]
All honest algorithms and simulators are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time classical machines; security is against arbitrary nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit families. The implication may use the full code of the encryption algorithms, non-black-box reasoning and polynomially many messages. It must not assume an additional property of encryption unless that property is proved to follow from the stated premise.
definitions:
Common conventions. The security parameter \(\lambda\ge1\) is provided as the unary string \(1^\lambda\). Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in \(\lambda\). An algorithm is uniform probabilistic polynomial time if it has one fixed finite multitape Turing-machine program and a bound \(K(L+1)^d\) on its bit steps for every input of total length \(L\) and every sequence of independent fair random bits, for some fixed positive integers \(K,d\). Reading, arithmetic, coin generation and all output bits are charged. Malformed inputs may be rejected but must satisfy the clock. There is no advice, ideal oracle, quantum resource or uncharged preprocessing.

For polynomial-length random bit strings \(X_\lambda,Y_\lambda\), write \(X_\lambda\approx_c Y_\lambda\) when for every Boolean circuit family \((D_\lambda)\) of polynomially bounded description length,
\[\left|\Pr[D_\lambda(X_\lambda)=1]-\Pr[D_\lambda(Y_\lambda)=1]\right|\]
is negligible in \(\lambda\). Such a family need not be uniformly generated. It may hardwire polynomial-length auxiliary information, including the input sequence under consideration. Deterministic circuits with binary AND/OR gates, unary NOT gates and constants suffice; private random coins could equivalently be allowed. Encodings expose actual string lengths, with zero padding to a common polynomial bound for the distinguisher. Tuples and messages are encoded by their number of components and each component's length followed by its bits. Nonnegative lengths use \(U(t)=1^\ell0s\), where \(s\) is the canonical binary expansion of \(t\), \(\ell=|s|\), and zero uses \(s=0\).

Public-key encryption. A scheme consists of three uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms, with public code:
\[(pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathrm{KeyGen}(1^\lambda),\quad z\leftarrow\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,m),\quad \widehat m\leftarrow\mathrm{Dec}(1^\lambda,sk,z).\]
Keys and ciphertexts are ordinary finite bit strings; \(m\in\{0,1\}\), and decryption returns a bit or a failure symbol \(\bot\). All invocations use fresh independent coins. Keys generated at parameter \(\lambda\), honest ciphertexts and their encodings have polynomial length in \(\lambda\). Correctness requires one negligible function \(\mu_E\) such that for every \(\lambda\) and both message bits,
\[\Pr[\mathrm{Dec}(1^\lambda,sk,\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,m))\ne m]\le\mu_E(\lambda),\]
where the probability includes fresh key-generation, encryption and any decryption randomness.

IND-CPA security for bits means
\[(pk,\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,0))\ \approx_c\ (pk,\mathrm{Enc}(1^\lambda,pk,1)),\]
with fresh keys and encryption coins in each experiment. The secret key is not given to the distinguisher. The encryption algorithm is public, so polynomially many encryptions chosen by an attacker can be computed locally. No decryption oracle is available. For this bit-message case the two displayed challenge distributions specify the chosen-plaintext confidentiality requirement. The assertion \(E\) is existence of any scheme satisfying this correctness and security, without algebraic, rerandomization, key-sampling or ciphertext-sampling promises.

Oblivious transfer. The sender \(S\) receives private bits \((m_0,m_1)\), and the receiver \(R\) receives a private choice bit \(c\). Both receive \(1^\lambda\), have independent private fair coins, and exchange a finite ordered sequence of classical messages directly. There is one fixed protocol, with polynomially many bit steps per party, messages and communicated bits on every honest execution and every random-tape choice. Equivalently, all these quantities are bounded by some \(B(\lambda)=K(\lambda+1)^d\) independent of the inputs. The receiver outputs \(y\in\{0,1,\bot\}\); the sender has no output. Correctness requires a negligible \(\mu_T\) such that
\[\forall\lambda\ \forall(m_0,m_1,c)\in\{0,1\}^3:\quad\Pr[y=m_c]\ge1-\mu_T(\lambda).\]
The failure symbol counts as an error. There is no requirement of two rounds or constant rounds.

Static semi-honest corruption means that at most one party is designated corrupted before execution, then follows the prescribed algorithm with the prescribed coin distribution while retaining all information it sees. It may afterwards apply any polynomial-size computation to this information. It does not modify messages, bias its randomness, change its input during the protocol or erase data to satisfy a security condition. The real view \(\operatorname{View}_S\) includes the sender's input, its complete random tape and all sent/received messages. The real view \(\operatorname{View}_R\) includes the receiver's input, its complete random tape, all messages and its final output. A fixed polynomial number of fair bits may be sampled at the start and unused bits retained. Internal computation is determined by the input, coins and messages and is thus recoverable from the view.

Privacy requires two fixed uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulators \(\operatorname{Sim}_S,\operatorname{Sim}_R\). For every sequence of input triples \((m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda},c_\lambda)\), the following ensemble pairs must be computationally indistinguishable:
\[\operatorname{View}_S(1^\lambda,m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda},c_\lambda)\ \approx_c\ \operatorname{Sim}_S(1^\lambda,m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda}),\]
\[\operatorname{View}_R(1^\lambda,m_{0,\lambda},m_{1,\lambda},c_\lambda)\ \approx_c\ \operatorname{Sim}_R(1^\lambda,c_\lambda,m_{c_\lambda,\lambda}).\]
The source of randomness on the left is an honest interaction of both parties; each right-hand experiment uses the simulator's own fresh coins. Input sequences need not be efficiently computable. The sender simulator receives no choice bit; the receiver simulator receives no unchosen message. The simulators precede the quantifiers over sequences and distinguishers, and have worst-case polynomial clocks rather than merely expected polynomial time. The assertion \(T\) is existence of a protocol and simulators satisfying these requirements.

The plain model supplies no common reference string, random oracle, trusted third party or hardware, and no pre-shared correlated randomness or secret. It permits only the independent randomness and communication just described. The security task is one standalone execution with static passive corruption; malicious deviation, adaptive corruption, fairness, guaranteed delivery against abort and universal composability are not additional requirements.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(E\Rightarrow T\) or its full logical negation. A positive proof must obtain the specified uniform protocol and simulators, establish all polynomial clocks and communication bounds, and prove correctness and both privacy ensembles from the encryption premise alone. Non-black-box use of encryption code and non-black-box security arguments are permitted. The literal negative answer is \(E\land\neg T\) in the ordinary, unrelativized model. An oracle world with encryption but no OT, a lower bound on black-box reductions, an attack on one protocol or a failure at a prescribed round count does not prove that negation. Any extra sampling or rerandomization property used by a proposed construction must also be derived from the premise.

title: Key agreement from one-way functions
summary: A one-way function is easy to compute and hard for every efficient classical algorithm to invert on a random input. Key agreement asks two initially independent parties to produce the same secret by exchanging only public messages. The target asks whether the existence of any one-way function already implies such a uniform classical protocol, allowing arbitrary non-black-box constructions. The keys must agree with negligible error and remain indistinguishable from independent uniform keys even when an efficient observer sees the whole transcript. Oracle barriers do not refute this unrestricted implication, while a claimed positive construction of public-key encryption from 2023 remains unverified in this review.
formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical two-party key-agreement protocol in the plain public-channel model below? The parties must output \(\lambda\)-bit keys with negligible disagreement, and either honest key must be computationally indistinguishable from an independent uniform key given the entire public transcript. This is the unrelativized existence implication, allowing arbitrary constructions and security proofs, including those that inspect the program implementing the one-way function.
definitions:
The security parameter is an integer \(\lambda\geq1\), given as the unary string \(1^{\lambda}\). Every algorithm has one finite program for all parameters and is a classical Turing machine operating on bits; no nonuniform advice or oracle is available. A probabilistic polynomial-time (PPT) algorithm uses independent fair random bits and has a polynomial worst-case running-time bound on every input and every random tape. For standalone algorithms, the bound is in the total input length. Machine steps, reading and writing bits, and producing outputs all count. Each algorithm may have its own fixed polynomial bound. Tuples of bit strings use the prefix-free component encoding \(s\mapsto1^{|s|}0s\); a finite list is encoded by its number of components in the same encoding, followed by its encoded components, with integers represented in binary without leading zeros except for zero itself. Any explicitly proved polynomial-time equivalent encoding is acceptable.

Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in \(\lambda\). A one-way function is a total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that, for every uniform classical PPT inverter \(I\), the function \(\Pr[\,|Y|=\lambda\ \land\ f(Y)=f(X)\,]\) is negligible, where \(X\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) and \(Y=I(1^{\lambda},f(X))\). The probability includes the independent coins of \(I\). A failure output or a string of the wrong length is an unsuccessful inversion; recovering any preimage of the stipulated length suffices. The function need not be injective or length preserving. Its program is public.

A candidate protocol consists of two uniform interactive machines \(A,B\). On the common input \(1^{\lambda}\), they start with independent private coins and no other secret or correlated input. They exchange finite classical bit strings through a noiseless public channel. Fix the conventional alternating-message execution, with \(A\) first and empty messages permitted; public termination flags indicate when each machine has finished. A polynomial in \(\lambda\), fixed for the protocol, bounds the combined computation, messages, message lengths, and execution length on every pair of honest random tapes. Both parties always terminate with strings \(K_A,K_B\in\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\). The public transcript \(T\) is the finite ordered list of messages with sender labels, message boundaries and termination flags, encoded as above. Private working tapes and private coins are not part of \(T\). Communication occurs only through these messages; there is no additional timing channel. No trusted setup, preshared secret, correlated randomness, random oracle, quantum computation or quantum communication is permitted.

Correctness means that \(\Pr[K_A\ne K_B]\) is negligible in \(\lambda\), over independent honest coins. Passive secrecy means that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(D\) outputting a bit, the advantage
\[\left|\Pr[D(1^{\lambda},T,K_A)=1]-\Pr[D(1^{\lambda},T,U_{\lambda})=1]\right|\]
is negligible, where each experiment runs the honest protocol and \(U_{\lambda}\) is an independent uniform element of \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\). The coins of \(D\) are independent of all other randomness. Correctness makes the same requirement with \(K_B\) equivalent. The eavesdropper sees the whole transcript and the public programs but does not modify messages. Its polynomial running time allows it to store the entire polynomial-length transcript: there is no extra storage bound. Negligibility is required eventually at all sufficiently large parameters, not just along a subsequence; its thresholds may depend on the adversary. The quantifier order is: if some \(f\) satisfying one-wayness exists, then some single pair \((A,B)\) satisfying the resource bound, correctness and secrecy against every such \(D\) exists. No uniform compiler from descriptions of functions to protocols, black-box interface, fixed number of rounds or perfect correctness is imposed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish an unrelativized protocol satisfying all of the specified correctness, secrecy, uniformity and cost requirements from the one-way-function premise alone. A negative answer must establish that a one-way function exists and that no protocol in the stated class satisfies both correctness and secrecy. Failure of a particular protocol, an oracle separation, a restriction to black-box reductions, a result assuming perfect correctness, or an attack with polynomially many oracle queries but unbounded computation does not establish that negation. Additional unproved cryptographic assumptions and security only at infinitely many parameters do not settle the full target.

title: One-way permutations from one-way functions
summary: A one-way permutation is an efficiently computable bijection whose inverse is hard to compute on a random input. This card asks whether ordinary one-way functions imply an efficiently generated public-key family of such permutations. Every generated key must define a permutation of the whole Boolean cube, while inversion hardness is averaged over honest keys and uniform inputs. Known black-box barriers do not settle this unrestricted implication, and the recent full-domain construction uses stronger assumptions. A complete Lean-checked answer must prove this exact existence implication or its ordinary-model negation.
formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function secure against every nonuniform polynomial-size classical adversary imply the existence of an efficiently generated public-key family of one-way permutations on full Boolean cubes, with the same adversary convention? Require a bijection on the entire cube for every key the generator can output, and negligible inversion probability averaged over an honestly generated public key and a uniform input. No trapdoor is required.
definitions:
All inputs and outputs are finite binary strings. Uniform polynomial time means one finite classical Turing program with a polynomial worst-case bit-operation bound in its input length. Randomized programs use independent fair random bits within that bound. A nonuniform polynomial-size adversary is a family of polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with polynomially many random input bits allowed. Its description and any auxiliary advice have polynomial length in the security parameter and may depend on that parameter, but not on independently sampled secret experiment coins.

A function \(\mu:\mathbb N\to[0,1]\) is negligible if, for every integer \(a\ge1\), there exists \(N_a\) such that \(\mu(n)\le n^{-a}\) for all \(n\ge N_a\).

The premise is that a single deterministic polynomial-time program computes a family
\[
 f_n:\{0,1\}^n\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{\ell(n)},
\]
where \(\ell(n)\) is a nonnegative integer, polynomially bounded and computable in polynomial time from \(1^n\), such that every nonuniform polynomial-size randomized family \(I_n\) has negligible success probability in the following experiment. Sample \(X\) uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^n\), give \((1^n,f_n(X))\) to \(I_n\), and declare its output \(Z\) successful exactly when \(Z\in\{0,1\}^n\) and \(f_n(Z)=f_n(X)\). Any preimage counts. The function's description is public, and no injectivity or subexponential hardness is assumed.

The desired permutation family consists of a fixed polynomially bounded integer function \(m(n)\ge n\), computable in polynomial time from \(1^n\), a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm \(\operatorname{Gen}(1^n)\to pk\), and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluation algorithm \(\operatorname{Eval}(1^n,pk,x)\). Let \(K_n\) be the support of Gen: the finite set of keys that occur with positive probability. For every \(n\ge1\) and every \(pk\in K_n\), evaluation on the whole input cube defines a map
\[
 \pi_{n,pk}:\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m(n)},
 \qquad \pi_{n,pk}(x)=\operatorname{Eval}(1^n,pk,x),
\]
and this map must be a bijection. Equivalently, for each output in that cube there is exactly one input in the cube with that output. This is an exact structural property for every generated key, not a property permitted to fail on a negligible fraction of keys or inputs.

One-wayness requires that, for every nonuniform polynomial-size randomized adversary \(A_n\), the probability of the event
\[
 Z=A_n(1^n,pk,\pi_{n,pk}(X))\in\{0,1\}^{m(n)}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \pi_{n,pk}(Z)=\pi_{n,pk}(X)
\]
is negligible in \(n\), where \(pk\leftarrow\operatorname{Gen}(1^n)\), \(X\) is independently uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\), and adversary coins are independent. An incorrectly sized or malformed output fails. Each adversary may have its own polynomial resource bound and negligible success bound. The public key and all algorithm descriptions are available to the adversary; the generator's private coins are not supplied.

Full domain refers to each permutation's input and output sets, both the complete Boolean cube. It does not require \(K_n\) to contain all strings of some length, to have efficiently recognizable membership, or to be independent of the construction's building blocks. No requirement is imposed on bijectivity for keys outside \(K_n\), although the evaluation program must still terminate within its polynomial bound on all inputs. No inverse algorithm, secret trapdoor, key recovery or hardness for every individual key is demanded. A trapdoor construction would qualify if its public family has the required properties and satisfies the stated security.

All algorithms and security guarantees are classical. The implication is about existence in the ordinary model with no ideal oracles. It may use the full description of an underlying one-way function, and its polynomial bounds may depend on that function. It is not restricted to a black-box compiler or reduction and assumes no obfuscator, additional cryptographic primitive or stronger security level.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence implication, supplying uniform generation and evaluation, the length function, every-key bijectivity and the negligible inversion bound against all stated adversaries; or give a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation in the ordinary computational model.

A restricted-domain permutation or merely injective length-expanding function does not satisfy the target. Additional assumptions must themselves be derived from ordinary one-way functions. An oracle separation or exclusion of a class of black-box constructions is a barrier, not a refutation of this unrestricted implication. Proving that ordinary one-way functions do not exist would establish the implication vacuously, not refute it. No numerical approximation tolerance applies.

title: Collision-resistant hashing from one-way functions
summary: The problem asks whether the existence of ordinary one-way functions implies a publicly keyed collision-resistant hash family. Honest algorithms are uniform and polynomial-time, while security must hold against every polynomial-size nonuniform classical circuit family. The hash compresses two security-parameter lengths to one, and an attacker chooses both colliding messages after seeing the freshly sampled public key. A complete Lean proof must establish the unrestricted existence implication or prove its negation, including the existence of a one-way function and the failure of every eligible hash family. Known oracle separations, stronger product-hardness constructions and the 2026 multicollision and interactive-argument results leave this ordinary-model implication unresolved.
formal:
In the ordinary classical computational model, is the following existence implication true?
\[\bigl(\exists f\;\operatorname{OWF}(f)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \bigl(\exists\operatorname{Gen},H\;\operatorname{CRH}(\operatorname{Gen},H)\bigr).\]
The predicates are defined below. The honest functions and algorithms are uniform and polynomial-time, and security is against every nonuniform family of polynomial-size classical Boolean circuits. The hash family has a freshly sampled public key \(k\) and maps \(H_k:\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\to\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) for every positive integer security parameter \(\lambda\). Both members of a proposed collision may be chosen after the key is known. The implication permits unrestricted constructions and proof techniques, including use of a one-way function's implementation.
definitions:
Parameters and computation. All strings are finite binary strings. The security parameters \(n,\lambda\) range over the positive integers, and \(1^n\) denotes the unary string of \(n\) ones. Honest algorithms are ordinary Turing machines with one fixed finite program, no advice and no oracles. Deterministic algorithms have polynomial bit running time in the total input length. A probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm additionally uses independent fair random bits and has a polynomial running-time bound on every random tape; it therefore uses at most polynomially many random bits. The polynomial and its degree are fixed for each program, independent of the parameter and sampled inputs.

Adversaries. A nonuniform polynomial-size circuit family \((A_n)_{n\ge1}\) consists of finite acyclic Boolean circuits over AND, OR, NOT and constant gates, with fan-in at most two and unrestricted fan-out. Size counts all gates and input and output wires, including random input wires. There are constants \(C,d\in\mathbb N_{>0}\) such that each size is at most \(C(n+1)^d\). A randomized circuit receives independent uniform bits on its random wires. Circuit descriptions may be arbitrary functions of the parameter and the fixed public honest programs; no algorithm generating the family is required. They are fixed before the fresh challenge or hash key is sampled. Each family has its own polynomial bound.

Finite-string encoding. To supply a string \(z\) of length at most an integer bound \(P\) to a fixed-width circuit, use \(\operatorname{enc}_P(z)\): the binary representation of \(|z|\), padded to exactly \(\lceil\log_2(P+1)\rceil\) bits, followed by \(z\) and enough zero bits to fill a \(P\)-bit data field. Bounds used below are positive integer-valued polynomials. This encoding reveals the string and its length and adds only polynomial overhead. In particular, variable-length function outputs and public keys are not supplied as a length-regularity promise.

Negligibility. Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in the security parameter of each experiment.
The threshold may depend on the exponent and the adversary, as well as on the fixed primitive. Security must hold eventually for every parameter, not merely on an infinite subsequence. No fixed inverse-polynomial or constant error is allowed.

One-way function. A candidate \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) is total and uniformly deterministic polynomial-time computable. Fix a positive integer-valued polynomial \(p\) bounding \(|f(x)|\) whenever \(|x|=n\). In its inversion experiment, sample \(X\) uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^n\), independently sample the circuit's random wires \(R\), and compute exactly once
\[Y=A_n(1^n,\operatorname{enc}_{p(n)}(f(X));R)\in\{0,1\}^n.\]
Define \(\operatorname{Inv}_{f,A}(n)=\Pr[f(Y)=f(X)]\). Then \(\operatorname{OWF}(f)\) means this probability is negligible for every permitted family \(A\). Any preimage of the challenge of length \(n\) is accepted; recovery of the original \(X\) is not required. Restricting the circuit output to \(n\) bits only removes invalid answers, which could always be replaced by a fixed \(n\)-bit candidate. The choice of the polynomial padding bound does not change security because valid encodings with different bounds can be converted in polynomial time.

Publicly keyed hash family. A candidate consists of a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time generator \(\operatorname{Gen}(1^\lambda)\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluator \(H(1^\lambda,k,x)\). There is a fixed positive integer-valued polynomial \(q\) such that every generated key has length at most \(q(\lambda)\). For every key in the support of the generator and every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\), the evaluator outputs exactly \(\lambda\) bits. Write \(H_k(x)=H(1^\lambda,k,x)\) when the parameter is understood. No evaluator property is required for keys outside that support. The key need not be uniform over all strings; its actual distribution is the output of the generator. It is fully public, and evaluation needs no secret.

Collision experiment. Independently sample the generator's random tape \(S\) and the adversary's random wires \(R\), set \(k=\operatorname{Gen}(1^\lambda;S)\), and compute exactly once
\[(x,x')=B_\lambda(1^\lambda,\operatorname{enc}_{q(\lambda)}(k);R)\in\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\times\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}.\]
Define
\[\operatorname{Coll}_{\operatorname{Gen},H,B}(\lambda)=\Pr[x\ne x'\ \land\ H(1^\lambda,k,x)=H(1^\lambda,k,x')].\]
The predicate \(\operatorname{CRH}(\operatorname{Gen},H)\) means this probability is negligible for every permitted circuit family \(B\). The adversary can compute the public evaluator within its circuit budget and select both inputs as functions of the key. It does not receive the generator's private random tape. Fixed-width candidate outputs again lose no successful attacks.

Scope of the implication. Existence of any one-way function in this model is the only cryptographic hypothesis. The conclusion is existence of some secure hash family; it need not be a particular proposed transformation applied to every one-way function. There is no requirement that a single algorithm transform arbitrary program descriptions into hash-family descriptions. No random oracle, trusted setup, quantum computation, extra hardness assumption or stronger exponential-security requirement is supplied. The all-parameter, nonuniform security and exact factor-two compression conventions are retained from the inherited card.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication or its logical negation. A positive proof must establish the existence of the specified public-key generator and evaluator from the one-way-function hypothesis alone, including uniform polynomial-time computability, exact compression for every generated key, and negligible collision success against every nonuniform polynomial-size circuit family. All transformations of parameters and security guarantees used in that proof must be justified. A proof may use function implementations and need not be black-box.

The logical negation requires proving both that a one-way function exists and that no hash family satisfying this model exists. For the latter assertion, every pair of uniform polynomial-time programs meeting the hash syntax must admit a permitted circuit family with nonnegligible collision probability. Equivalently, for each such pair there must be an adversary and a fixed \(c\in\mathbb N_{>0}\) whose success exceeds \(\lambda^{-c}\) for infinitely many \(\lambda\). Merely proving that a chosen construction fails, even for one secure one-way function, is insufficient.

An oracle world separating these primitives or an impossibility theorem restricted to black-box reductions establishes a barrier, not this ordinary-model negation. Target-collision resistance, resistance only to finding three or more colliding inputs, injective noncompressing functions, security only for uniform adversaries or only infinitely often, and constructions assuming quantitative product hardness do not meet the full conclusion. This is an exact yes-or-no implication, with no additive numerical tolerance on the security requirement.

title: Fully homomorphic encryption from public-key encryption
summary: Fully homomorphic encryption permits evaluating Boolean circuits over encrypted input bits. The question asks whether its existence follows from ordinary public-key encryption alone. Key generation must work without a supplied circuit-depth bound, and decryption cost must remain independent of the evaluated circuit. The scheme must remain secure with its evaluation key public. Known black-box barriers and implications from additional primitives do not settle this unrestricted existence implication.
formal: Does the existence of IND-CPA-secure public-key bit encryption imply the existence of an IND-CPA-secure, compact, unleveled fully homomorphic bit-encryption scheme for every polynomial-size Boolean circuit, with the algorithms and security convention below?
definitions:
All algorithms are uniform probabilistic Turing machines with worst-case polynomial bit running time in their explicit input lengths; decryption is deterministic. The security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. An adversary is a nonuniform family of randomized Boolean circuits of size polynomial in \(\lambda\), including its advice and random-input nodes. All random bits are independent and fair. A function \(
u:\mathbb{N}	o [0,1]\) is negligible when for every positive integer a there exists \(\lambda _{0}\) such that \(
u (\lambda )\le \lambda ^{- a}\) for all \(\lambda \ge \lambda _{0}\). Security is quantified separately over every such adversary family, with a negligible bound allowed to depend on the family. A public-key bit-encryption scheme consists of \(Gen(1^{\lambda})=(pk,sk), Enc(pk,b)=c\) for \(b\in \{0,1\}\), and \(Dec(sk,c)\in \{0,1,\perp\}\). There is one negligible \(

e b]\le
u(\lambda)\), over key generation and encryption. In the IND-CPA experiment Gen is run, the adversary receives pk and selects bits \(b_{0},b_{1}\) and a state, an independent uniform \( eta \in \{0,1\}\) is chosen, \(c=Enc(pk,b_{ eta})\) is returned, and the adversary outputs \( eta '\). Require \(|\Pr[ eta\prime= eta]-1/2|\) to be negligible. The adversary may perform any polynomial number of public encryptions on its own before and after the challenge. There is no decryption oracle. Bit encryption suffices; longer messages are represented by bit lists. For FHE, Gen outputs (pk,evk,sk); the evaluation key evk is public and is included with pk in the IND-CPA experiment. Gen receives no circuit size or depth bound. Eval(evk,\(C,c_{1},\ldots ,c_{t}\)) outputs one ciphertext for a circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^{t}	o \{0,1\}\), encoded as an acyclic \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) circuit with listed wires. For every polynomial s there is a negligible \(

The scheme must also correctly decrypt fresh encryptions. Multiple output bits mean separate output ciphertexts, so compactness scales linearly with output length. Only the usual one-evaluation correctness contract is required; no circuit privacy or additional guarantee for arbitrary malformed or previously evaluated ciphertexts is imposed.
