title: Polynomial-time private release of all marginals
summary: A marginal query asks what fraction of database rows match a pattern on selected attributes. The card asks for one private synopsis that answers all exponentially many such queries with error tending to zero as the dimension grows. Both creating the synopsis and evaluating a short query must use polynomial time, with only polynomially many input rows. Known interactive, synthetic-data and Gaussian-factorization results impose different resource or output requirements and do not settle this target. A complete Lean answer must prove the specified uniform existence statement or rule out every mechanism and evaluator satisfying it.
formal: Do there exist an integer \(C\ge1\), a function \(\alpha:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to[0,1]\) with \(\lim_{d\to\infty}\alpha(d)=0\), a uniform randomized mechanism \(M\), and a uniform deterministic evaluator \(E\) satisfying the following statement? For every integer \(d\ge2\), put \(n=d^{C}\). For every explicitly given database \(D\in(\{0,1\}^{d})^{n}\), \(M(d,D)\) runs in worst-case time polynomial in \(n+d\), satisfies \((1,1/(100n^{2}))\)-differential privacy under replacement of one row, and outputs a finite binary synopsis \(S\). With probability at least \(2/3\) over \(M\)'s random bits, this one synopsis satisfies \[\left|E(d,S,J,a)-q_{J,a}(D)\right|\le\alpha(d)\] simultaneously for every \(J\subseteq[d]\) and \(a\in\{0,1\}^{J}\). The evaluator runs in worst-case time polynomial in \(d+|S|\), outputs a binary-encoded rational, and has no further access to the database. The synopsis may be arbitrary: it need not be synthetic data or describe a consistent probability distribution.
definitions: \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). A marginal query \((J,a)\) asks for the fraction of rows agreeing with the assignment \(a\) on the coordinates in \(J\): \[q_{J,a}(D)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1\{\forall j\in J,\ D_{ij}=a_j\}.\] All orders \(0\le|J|\le d\) are included; the empty query equals one. Each query can be encoded as a length-\(d\) word over \(\{*,0,1\}\), indicating omitted coordinates or required bits; fix any constant-length binary encoding of these symbols. Thus there are \(3^{d}\) queries with descriptions of length \(O(d)\). The database is an ordered \(n\)-by-\(d\) bit matrix. For every ordered pair of equal-size databases \(D,D'\) differing at one row and every set \(O\) of binary output strings, privacy requires \[\Pr[M(d,D)\in O]\le e\Pr[M(d,D')\in O]+1/(100n^{2}).\] It is a guarantee on the whole synopsis distribution. \(M\) and \(E\) are ordinary classical multitape Turing machines with no advice, oracle or shared private database state; \(M\) uses independent fair bits. One fixed polynomial bounds its time, output length and number of random bits on every execution. One fixed polynomial bounds the evaluator's time on every valid query and synopsis. The probability of simultaneous accuracy is required separately for every database, with no input-distribution promise. All of \(C,\alpha,M,E\) and their polynomial bounds are chosen before \(d,D\). The convergence condition means that for every real \(\eta>0\), there is \(d_0\) such that \(\alpha(d)\le\eta\) for all \(d\ge d_0\); no computable convergence rate or procedure for evaluating \(\alpha\) is required. Error is an absolute error in a row fraction in \([0,1]\), not in the unnormalized count. These are the concrete synopsis, privacy and sample-size conventions already selected for this card in September 2026; they are not claimed equivalent to every interactive or fixed-order variant of the source question.
answer_criterion: Prove this existence statement or its logical negation in Lean. A positive answer must exhibit the fixed uniform machines, exponent, polynomial resource bounds and vanishing error function and prove both privacy and simultaneous accuracy on every valid database. A negative answer must exclude all such choices; hardness only under an unproved cryptographic assumption proves the corresponding conditional obstruction, not the unconditional negation. Fixed positive error, accuracy only for most queries or typical databases, a polynomial number of interactive queries, or a runtime polynomial in the exponential number of all query answers does not meet the stated criterion. The target is the existence of a vanishing-error polynomial-time synopsis, rather than a numerical value requiring additive \(1/100\) determination.

title: Chosen-ciphertext security from ordinary public-key encryption
summary: Ordinary public-key encryption hides a chosen challenge message from an attacker who can encrypt messages independently. Full chosen-ciphertext security must still hide it when the attacker adaptively obtains decryptions of every other ciphertext. The question asks whether the weaker primitive alone implies the existence of the stronger one in the plain model. One fixed scheme must tolerate every polynomial attack bound, and the construction may use the original algorithms in an unrestricted way. A complete Lean-checked answer must establish this existence implication or refute it in the ordinary computational model.
formal: Does the existence of an IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption scheme imply the existence of an IND-CCA2-secure public-key encryption scheme in the plain model, with correctness and classical security as defined below, against all nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries? The sole premise is ordinary chosen-plaintext-secure public-key encryption, and the conclusion is full adaptive chosen-ciphertext security with no fixed bound on an attacker's polynomial number of decryption queries.
definitions:
A public-key encryption scheme consists of one fixed triple of uniform classical algorithms
\[
 \operatorname{Gen}(1^n)\to(pk,sk),\qquad
 \operatorname{Enc}(pk,m)\to c,\qquad
 \operatorname{Dec}(sk,c)\to m\text{ or }\bot .
\]
Here \(n\ge1\) is a security parameter, and keys, messages and ciphertexts are finite binary strings. The symbol \(\bot\) is distinct from every message. Gen and Enc use independent fair random bits; Dec is deterministic. Each algorithm is a finite Turing program with worst-case time polynomial in its full input length, including \(n\), which may be included in the keys. In particular, Gen has polynomially bounded output length. Encryption supports arbitrary binary messages; decryption is defined and halts on every ciphertext string, with malformed encodings rejected. The algorithms use no external oracle or advice.

Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in \(n\). Correctness requires that, for every polynomial length bound \(p\), some negligible function \(\mu_p\) satisfies
\[
 \max_{|m|\le p(n)}
 \Pr_{(pk,sk)\leftarrow\operatorname{Gen}(1^n),\ \operatorname{Enc}}
 [\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m))\ne m]
 \le\mu_p(n).
\]
The maximum includes the empty message. Neither perfect correctness nor recovery of the encryption randomness is required.

An adversary is a nonuniform family of classical polynomial-size computations with polynomially many fair random bits and polynomial-size advice. Advice can depend on \(n\), but not on the independently sampled keys, challenge bit or honest encryption coins. Total running time, state, message lengths, oracle-query lengths and number of queries are bounded by some polynomial in \(n\) that may depend on the adversary. Equivalently, these are polynomial-size Boolean circuits with the specified adaptive oracle interfaces. Arbitrary polynomial-size auxiliary information independent of the fresh experiment is included in the advice.

In the IND-CPA experiment, generate \((pk,sk)\), give \((1^n,pk)\) to the first stage \(A_1\), and let it output two equal-length messages \(m_0,m_1\) and a state \(\sigma\). Choose an independent uniform bit \(b\), form \(c^*=\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m_b)\) with fresh coins, and give \((1^n,pk,\sigma,c^*)\) to \(A_2\), which outputs a bit \(\widehat b\). Its advantage is
\[
 \left|\Pr[\widehat b=b]-\frac12\right|.
\]
The probability includes all key-generation, challenge-encryption, challenge-bit and adversary randomness. The quantification is over adversaries obeying the equal-length challenge rule and producing a bit; failures to follow this syntax may instead be defined to yield an independent fair guess. Both stages can compute arbitrary encryptions themselves using the public algorithm, so a separate encryption oracle is unnecessary. The scheme is IND-CPA secure if this advantage is negligible for every adversary just defined.

The IND-CCA2 experiment is the same except for adaptive decryption access. Before the challenge, \(A_1\) may query any ciphertext \(c\), receiving \(\operatorname{Dec}(sk,c)\). After it chooses the messages and receives \(c^*\), \(A_2\) has the oracle
\[
 \mathcal D_{sk,c^*}(c)=
 \begin{cases}
 \bot,&c=c^*\text{ as binary strings},\\
 \operatorname{Dec}(sk,c),&c\ne c^*.
 \end{cases}
\]
Every later query may depend on the challenge and all earlier answers. The exclusion applies only after the challenge is issued; it does not retroactively invalidate a pre-challenge query. Any different string is permitted, even if it encodes related data or decrypts to the challenge plaintext. The scheme is IND-CCA2 secure if the same advantage is negligible for every such two-stage adversary.

For each security notion, one fixed scheme must satisfy the definition for every polynomially bounded adversary. The scheme cannot be chosen after fixing a maximum number of decryption queries. Its negligible bound may depend on the adversary. All security is classical; no quantum adversary is requested.

The plain model provides no ideal random oracle, externally supplied common reference string, trusted hardware or separate setup. The recipient's own random key generation is allowed. The question is an implication between existence statements. A resulting scheme may use the descriptions of the starting algorithms, change all formats and incur any fixed polynomial overhead. No particular compiler, black-box access discipline or preservation of the starting efficiency is required.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that an IND-CPA scheme implies an IND-CCA2 scheme satisfying the precise definitions, with proofs of uniform implementation, polynomial running time, correctness and security; or give a complete Lean-checked proof of the negation of this existence implication in the ordinary computational model.

Breaking a particular CPA scheme under chosen-ciphertext attack does not disprove the existence of a different secure scheme. A separation restricted to black-box constructions, or relative to an oracle, is not a negative resolution here. Additional trapdoor, proof-system, pseudorandomness or setup assumptions must themselves follow from the sole premise. Security only before the challenge, only against an a priori bounded number of decryption queries, or only against ciphertext modification without the stated decryption access is insufficient. No numerical approximation tolerance applies.

title: Pseudorandom functions from worst-case hardness of learning
summary: A learning algorithm receives query access to an unknown function and must output a circuit that predicts it accurately on uniformly random inputs. The question asks whether failure of efficient learning forces an efficiently sampled pseudorandom function family in the same circuit class. The premise permits a different hard target for each learner and does not assume a common samplable distribution of hard targets. Both the learner and the sampler are uniform polynomial-time algorithms, and security permits adaptive chosen queries. The source’s nonuniform exponential-regime theorem and the checked later qualified results do not establish this implication.
formal:
For every circuit class
\[
\mathcal C\in\{\mathrm{AC}^0,\ \mathrm{AC}^0[p]\ (p\text{ any fixed prime}),\
\mathrm{ACC}^0,\ \mathrm{TC}^0,\ \mathrm{NC}^1,\
\mathrm{Formula},\ \mathrm{Circuit}\},
\]
does the following implication hold?
\[
\neg\operatorname{Learn}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathcal C)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{PRF}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathcal C).
\]
Here learning means uniform randomized polynomial-time improper learning under the uniform input distribution, with adaptive membership queries. The conclusion is a uniformly polynomial-time samplable family of functions computed by polynomial-size \(\mathcal C\)-circuits, secure against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time oracle distinguisher. Both notions are defined below.

The hypothesis is only worst-case failure of learning: each candidate learner may fail on its own target function. No efficiently samplable common distribution of hard targets is assumed.
definitions:
All targets are Boolean functions on \(\{0,1\}^n\), with \(n\ge2\). Circuits are finite directed acyclic graphs with input bits, optional constants, and a single Boolean output. Size counts wires; depth is the longest input-to-output gate path. Negation gates have one input. General \(\mathrm{Circuit}\) uses AND and OR gates of fan-in at most two and NOT gates, with unrestricted depth. \(\mathrm{Formula}\) uses the same basis but has a tree of gates, with no reuse of a gate output. \(\mathrm{NC}^1\) uses that bounded-fan-in circuit basis with depth at most \(d\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) for a fixed integer \(d\).

For \(\mathrm{AC}^0\), AND/OR gates may have unbounded fan-in and depth is at most a fixed integer \(d\). The class \(\mathrm{AC}^0[p]\) additionally permits a gate testing whether the number of ones among its inputs is divisible by the fixed prime \(p\). For \(\mathrm{ACC}^0\) the same definition permits any fixed integer modulus \(m\ge2\); the modulus does not grow with \(n\). The class \(\mathrm{TC}^0\) instead additionally permits unweighted majority gates, which output one when at least half their inputs are one. Negations and constants are allowed in all classes. These conventions specify classes of target functions; targets need not themselves be uniformly generated.

A fixed polynomial subfamily is specified by an integer \(k\ge1\), the wire bound \(n^k\), and, where relevant, fixed \(d\) and \(m\). Write \(\mathcal C_{\theta,n}\) for the resulting set of \(n\)-input functions, where \(\theta\) collects these fixed constants. For \(\mathrm{AC}^0[p]\), \(p\) is fixed as part of the choice of class.

The assertion \(\operatorname{Learn}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathcal C)\) means that for every fixed \(\theta\) there is one probabilistic oracle Turing machine \(L_\theta\) and a polynomial \(P_\theta\) with the following property. For every \(n\ge2\), integer \(q\ge2\), and \(f\in\mathcal C_{\theta,n}\), the machine \(L_\theta^f(1^n,1^q)\) halts within \(P_\theta(n,q)\) steps on every execution and, with probability at least \(2/3\), outputs a finite ordinary Boolean circuit \(h\) satisfying
\[
\Pr_{x\leftarrow\{0,1\}^n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le 1/q.
\]
It may adaptively query any \(n\)-bit input and receive its exact value under \(f\); writing queries and the hypothesis counts toward its time. The hypothesis need not belong to \(\mathcal C\), and the target circuit description is not supplied. The polynomial running-time bound also holds for every other Boolean oracle. There is no advice depending on \(n\). Negating this definition gives the hardness premise with its quantifiers, including the possibility that the hard target depends on the learner and on \(n\).

The assertion \(\operatorname{PRF}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathcal C)\) means that for some fixed \(\theta\), some polynomial-time computable seed length \(a(n)\le n^r\), and a single deterministic polynomial-time sampler \(S\), every \(S(1^n,s)\), \(s\in\{0,1\}^{a(n)}\), describes a circuit for a function \(f_{n,s}\in\mathcal C_{\theta,n}\). The sampler runs in polynomial time in \(n\), including writing its entire output. It may be a general polynomial-time algorithm; only the sampled functions are required to have the stated \(\mathcal C\)-circuits.

For every uniform probabilistic oracle Turing machine \(D\) running in polynomial time in \(n\), the advantage
\[
\left|
\Pr_{s\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{a(n)}}[D^{f_{n,s}}(1^n)=1]
-
\Pr_{g\leftarrow\mathcal F_n}[D^g(1^n)=1]
\right|
\]
is negligible in \(n\), where \(\mathcal F_n\) is the set of all Boolean functions on \(n\) bits with its uniform distribution. Both probabilities include \(D\)'s random bits. The same sampled function answers all queries consistently. The distinguisher may choose polynomially many queries adaptively but does not receive the seed or circuit description. A nonnegative function \(\eta(n)\) is negligible when for every integer \(j\ge1\), \(\eta(n)\le n^{-j}\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Security is eventual at all lengths, not merely on an unspecified infinite subsequence.

The implication is asked in the ordinary, unrelativized model. It does not require a black-box construction or an algorithm that extracts a sampler from a description of a hardness proof. This card fixes the uniform polynomial-time meaning of the source’s broader question; its exponential and nonuniform theorem is recorded separately as context.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed implication for the specified classes and quantifiers. A proof must obtain the efficiently sampled same-class family from the stated learning-hardness premise alone. Assuming a samplable hard target distribution, proving only a nonuniform or exponential-time dichotomy, or supplying a conditional PRF candidate does not suffice. A refutation must establish a failure of this implication in the stated unrelativized model; a relativizing or black-box barrier alone is not a refutation. This is a binary implication question, with exact security and learning quantifiers; numerical \(1/100\) slack does not alter them.

title: Low-noise LPN hardness from Nearest Codeword hardness
summary: Binary Nearest Codeword asks whether a given target lies within a specified Hamming distance of a linear code. The proposed implication uses worst-case difficulty of that decision problem to rule out a uniform distinguisher for one low-noise LPN regime. The LPN experiment has a random secret, a random matrix, n-squared samples and inverse-square-root noise at square dimensions. The conclusion requires negligible advantage at every sufficiently large square dimension, including exclusion of distinguishers useful on a sparse unbounded sequence. The recent code-and-dual-code reduction uses an additional assumption that the selected target aims to remove.
formal:
Does the following implication hold?
\[
\operatorname{NCP}_2\notin\mathrm{BPP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\forall D\in\mathrm{PPT}\ \forall c>0\ \exists n_0\ge9\ \forall n\ge n_0:
\quad n\text{ a square}\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{Adv}_D(n)<n^{-c}.
\]
Here \(\operatorname{NCP}_2\) is the unrestricted binary Nearest Codeword decision problem defined below. The distinguisher receives either \((A,As+e)\) or \((A,u)\), with a uniform \(n^2\times n\) binary matrix, independent uniform secret and comparison vector, and independent noise bits of probability \(1/\sqrt n\). The conclusion requires negligible advantage at all sufficiently large square dimensions for every uniform classical probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher.
definitions:
The field \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) uses addition and multiplication modulo two. For a binary vector \(v\), its Hamming weight \(\operatorname{wt}(v)\) is the number of its one coordinates. An instance of \(\operatorname{NCP}_2\) is an explicitly given binary matrix \(G\in\mathbb F_2^{a\times b}\), a binary vector \(y\in\mathbb F_2^a\) and an integer \(t\) with \(0\le t\le a\), where \(a,b\ge1\). It is a YES instance exactly when some \(z\in\mathbb F_2^b\) has \(\operatorname{wt}(Gz-y)\le t\). The input lists the dimensions, entries and threshold with delimiters, using binary integers and row-major matrix entries. Invalid encodings are NO instances. There is no rank, balance, noise-distribution or closeness promise, and the task asks for one decision bit, not a codeword.

A language is in BPP if a single probabilistic Turing machine halts within a polynomial in the total binary input length on every input and every random tape, and answers correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. Its fair random bits are private; no advice or oracle is supplied. The premise means that no such machine decides this entire Nearest Codeword language.

For the average-case experiments let \(n=q^2\) with an integer \(q\ge3\). Independently draw all entries of \(A\), all bits of \(s\), and all bits of \(u\) uniformly. In the noisy experiment draw \(e_1,\ldots,e_{n^2}\) independently with \(\Pr[e_i=1]=1/q\), also independently of \(A,s,u\). The noisy vector is \(As+e\), computed over \(\mathbb F_2\); the other experiment uses \(u\). The distinguisher receives \(1^n\), the row-major entries of \(A\), and the corresponding vector with fixed delimiters. The sample count is exactly \(n^2\). It receives neither \(s\) nor \(e\), and cannot request extra samples. Square dimensions make the noise probability exactly rational.

A distinguisher \(D\in\mathrm{PPT}\) is one classical probabilistic Turing machine outputting a bit in worst-case polynomial time in the encoded input length, on every random tape. On these inputs that is equivalent to a polynomial in \(n\). Its description is independent of \(n\), and it has no advice, oracle or preprocessing depending on the particular random matrix. The advantage is
\[
\operatorname{Adv}_D(n)=\left|\Pr[D(1^n,A,As+e)=1]-\Pr[D(1^n,A,u)=1]\right|,
\]
where both probabilities include all experiment randomness and the independent internal randomness of \(D\).

The conclusion is eventual negligible advantage along the square dimensions: for each fixed distinguisher and positive exponent there is a threshold beyond which every square dimension satisfies the displayed upper bound. Its failure means that some fixed distinguisher and exponent have inverse-polynomial advantage at arbitrarily large square dimensions. The formulation uses this stronger length convention on 18 September 2026. The unrestricted decision premise, exact sample count and exact noise rate remain editorial specifications of the broader source direction, rather than a theorem stated verbatim there.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed implication. An affirmative proof must obtain eventual negligible advantage, including exclusion of a distinguisher that succeeds only on an unbounded subsequence of square dimensions. A sufficient route converts any such nonnegligible distinguisher into a BPP decider for the entire unrestricted Nearest Codeword language. A refutation must establish both the Nearest Codeword premise and a distinguisher violating the conclusion; an oracle separation or failure of a particular reduction is insufficient. An additional dual-code hardness assumption, a different sample/noise regime or only the exclusion of distinguishers successful at every sufficiently large length does not settle this target.

title: Noninteractive SZK versus SZK
summary: Statistical zero knowledge studies proofs whose verifier learns no statistically distinguishable information beyond the assertion being proved. The question is whether every such interactive proof can be replaced by a noninteractive proof with public randomness. The primary source expresses the same issue as a reduction between two promise problems on sampling circuits. The reduction must transform close or far pairs into distributions respectively close to or far from uniform. A deterministic polynomial-time reduction with the specified promises would establish NISZK equals SZK.
formal: Does NISZK equal SZK? Equivalently, does there exist a uniform deterministic polynomial-time reduction that maps every promised pair of sampling circuits X,Y to a sampling circuit Z, preserving the near/far promises specified below?
definitions: A sampling circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates, constants, a specified list of random input bits and an ordered list of output bits. Its description explicitly lists gates and wires in binary. Fresh independent uniform bits are supplied to all random inputs; the output distribution is the resulting distribution on bit strings. X and Y may have different numbers of random inputs but have the same output length. For finite distributions P,Q on the same set, \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|\). The source convention for Statistical Difference has YES instances with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(X,Y)<1/3\) and NO instances with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(X,Y)>2/3\). Inputs between these promises impose no correctness obligation. The reduction outputs one circuit Z with \(m\ge 3\) output bits. On every YES input require \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,U_{m})<1/m\); on every NO input require \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,U_{m})>1- 1/m\), where \(U_{m}\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{m}\). The reduction runs in a fixed polynomial of the combined encoded input length on every syntactically valid input, including inputs outside the promise; writing Z and all its input/output nodes counts in that time. It receives no advice or sampling oracle. These are the source’s Statistical Difference and Statistical Difference from Uniform promise problems. Their completeness under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions makes existence of this reduction equivalent to the original class equality. Thus the complete-problem formulation fixes the question without having to choose a new auxiliary-input or setup convention for protocols.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of a deterministic uniform polynomial-time many-one reduction satisfying both stated promises, or a Lean proof that such a reduction does not exist. The source’s complete-problem equivalence identifies these alternatives with equality or inequality of NISZK and SZK. Randomized reductions or computational zero knowledge concern different targets.

title: One-way functions in \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) from one-way functions
summary: A one-way function is easy to evaluate but resists inversion on a uniformly chosen input by every polynomial-size adversary. The question asks whether the existence of any such function guarantees one whose Boolean circuits have a single constant depth bound. The circuits must be generated deterministically in polynomial time, while inversion security is required against nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuits. Known theorems establish this implication under restricted computational assumptions, and a 2025 source still explicitly lists the general implication as open. A complete Lean proof must establish the implication or prove both that general one-way functions exist and that every eligible local family is insecure.
formal:
Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical one-way function computed by a polynomial-time uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) circuit family? With the definitions below, the proposition is
\[
\bigl[\exists f\;\mathrm{OWF}(f)\bigr]
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigl[\exists g\;\mathrm{OWF}(g)\land\mathrm{PUniformNC}^{0}(g)\bigr].
\]
Both sides require security against every nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit family. The conclusion asks for the existence of some such \(g\), with some constant depth and some polynomial bounds. These constants may depend on \(g\), but not on its input length or on an adversary. There is no additional assumption on the starting function's circuit depth, no requirement that \(f\) and \(g\) have the same input or output lengths, and no requirement of a black-box construction or an efficient compiler from descriptions of \(f\).
definitions:
A candidate function is a family \(f=(f_n)_{n\ge1}\), with a length function \(m_f:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb N\) and total maps
\[
f_n:\{0,1\}^{n}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m_f(n)}.
\]
The output length depends only on \(n\), and zero is an allowed length. Let \(\mathrm{PolyEval}(f)\) mean that there are a single deterministic machine \(M\) and integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\) and every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), the machine outputs exactly \(f_n(x)\) and halts within \(B(n+1)^k\) steps, with \(m_f(n)\le B(n+1)^k\). The machine is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with finitely many tapes, a fixed finite alphabet containing binary symbols, a separator and a blank, and one-cell head moves; each transition counts as one step. The input is the binary string on a read-only input tape with end markers, work tapes are initially blank, and output bits are written sequentially on an output tape. This fixes ordinary bit computation; the number of tapes, alphabet and program are fixed independently of \(n\). No advice, oracle or random coins are supplied to the evaluator.

A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph whose input nodes carry the input bits, whose constant nodes carry \(0\) or \(1\), and whose internal gates are binary AND, binary OR or unary NOT. Fan-out is unrestricted, and the same predecessor may occupy both input positions. Outputs are an ordered list of references to nodes, with repetitions allowed. Size is the number of nodes plus the number of output positions. Depth is the largest number of internal gates on a path from an input or constant node to an output. Circuit descriptions list the nodes in a topological order, with gate tags and predecessor indices, followed by the output indices; indices and list lengths are in binary with separators from a fixed finite alphabet. No gates for arbitrary functions or oracle evaluation are present.

For a candidate \(f\), an allowed inverter is any family \(A=(A_n)_{n\ge1}\) of Boolean circuits of this basis, together with integers \(r(n)\ge0\), such that
\[
A_n:\{0,1\}^{n+m_f(n)+r(n)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n},
\qquad
\exists C,c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1,
\quad\max\{\operatorname{size}(A_n),r(n)\}\le C(n+1)^c.
\]
No uniform procedure for producing \(A_n\) is required, and its depth is unrestricted. The input blocks are \(1^n\), a proposed function value, and \(r(n)\) independent fair random bits. Thus the security parameter is given in unary, the adversary may depend on the input length nonuniformly, and it is not restricted to shallow circuits. For independent uniform strings \(X\in\{0,1\}^{n}\) and \(R\in\{0,1\}^{r(n)}\), put
\[
s_{f,A}(n)=\Pr\!\left[
f_n\bigl(A_n(1^n,f_n(X),R)\bigr)=f_n(X)
\right].
\]
Success means finding any preimage of the specified length \(n\), not necessarily the sampled \(X\). The function itself is deterministic; the probability is only over \(X\) and the adversary's coins \(R\). The negligible-success requirement is
\[
\forall A\text{ allowed}\ \forall a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists N\ge2\ \forall n\ge N,
\qquad s_{f,A}(n)\le n^{-a}.
\]
The threshold \(N\) may depend on \(f,A,a\). Define \(\mathrm{OWF}(f)\) to mean \(\mathrm{PolyEval}(f)\) together with this requirement. Security holds at every sufficiently large length for each adversary and exponent, rather than merely on infinitely many lengths. There is no requirement of injectivity, length preservation, expansion, or any fixed ratio of output to input length.

The predicate \(\mathrm{PUniformNC}^{0}(g)\) means that there are a single deterministic circuit-generating Turing machine \(G\), integers \(B,k\ge1\), and an integer \(D\ge0\), such that for every \(n\ge1\), on input \(1^n\), the machine \(G\) outputs the full description of a circuit \(C_n\) in at most \(B(n+1)^k\) steps. That circuit has exactly \(n\) input bits, exactly \(m_g(n)\) outputs, size at most \(B(n+1)^k\), and depth at most \(D\), and satisfies \(C_n(x)=g_n(x)\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\). Generation uses the same deterministic bit-computation convention as above. The depth bound is a single constant for the entire family; in particular, every output depends on at most \(2^D\) input bits. The question places no bound on how many outputs a given input bit may influence. Circuit generation has no random setup, randomly chosen graph, public key or advice. The two existentially quantified functions may have different length functions and polynomial bounds.
answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed implication or of its logical negation, using exactly the evaluation, uniformity and nonuniform-security conventions above. A positive proof must establish the existence of a secure family with one constant depth bound from the sole assumption that a one-way function exists. A negative proof must establish both
\[
\exists f\;\mathrm{OWF}(f)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall g,\quad\mathrm{PUniformNC}^{0}(g)\Longrightarrow\neg\mathrm{OWF}(g).
\]
Equivalently, for every candidate \(g\) with such a uniform constant-depth implementation, it must establish an allowed polynomial-size inverter family \(A\) and an integer \(a\ge1\) with
\[
\forall N\ge2\ \exists n\ge N,\qquad s_{g,A}(n)>n^{-a},
\]
as well as the existence of an unrestricted one-way function. The inverter and exponent may depend on \(g\). A separation only relative to an oracle, an obstruction only to a selected kind of reduction, or failure of a particular local candidate does not prove this negation. A theorem under an additional computational assumption establishes only that conditional result.

title: Verifiable random functions from one-way functions alone
summary: A secret key evaluates a pseudorandom function and proves the value publicly. Every public key must permit at most one accepted value per input. The challenge input is chosen adaptively from an exponential-size domain. The challenge value is given without its proof. The target allows non-black-box constructions from arbitrary one-way functions.
formal: Does the existence of arbitrary one-way functions imply a standard-model verifiable random function on all \(\lambda\)-bit inputs with perfect correctness on honest evaluations, adaptive pseudorandomness and perfect uniqueness even for malformed public keys?
definitions:
The security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. Honest algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time machines. Security quantifies over nonuniform polynomial-size probabilistic circuits with polynomially many oracle queries. All message, instance and witness lengths in the experiment are polynomial in \(\lambda\). Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto). The model supplies no random oracle, trusted hardware or additional computational assumption.

Assume a uniform polynomial-time family \(f_\lambda:\{0,1\}^\lambda\to\{0,1\}^{\ell(\lambda)}\) with polynomially bounded output length. For uniform \(X\in\{0,1\}^\lambda\), every admissible adversary given \(\lambda\) and \(f_\lambda(X)\) has negligible probability of returning any \(\lambda\)-bit \(x'\) with \(f_\lambda(x')=f_\lambda(X)\). Collisions are allowed.

\(\operatorname{KeyGen}(1^\lambda)\) returns a public key pk and secret key sk. Deterministic Eval(sk,x) returns a \(\lambda\)-bit value for each x in \(\{0,1\}^\lambda\), and Prove(sk,x) returns a proof. Deterministic Verify(pk,x,y,pi) accepts or rejects. For every security parameter \(\lambda\ge1\), every pair \((pk,sk)\) that honest key generation can output, every \(x\in\{0,1\}^\lambda\), and every proof \(\pi\) that the honest prover can output on \((sk,x)\), require \[\operatorname{Verify}(pk,x,\operatorname{Eval}(sk,x),\pi)=1.\] This is the perfect provability condition in Definition 1 of Dodis and Yampolskiy. All sizes and runtimes are polynomial in \(\lambda\).

Perfect uniqueness requires that for every public-key string of the permitted polynomial length, every x, and any two pairs (y,pi),(y-prime,pi-prime) accepted by Verify, y=y-prime. A malformed key may reject everything. There is no requirement that the proof string itself be unique.

For pseudorandomness, an adversary receives an honest pk and adaptively queries an oracle returning (Eval(sk,x),Prove(sk,x)). It chooses a fresh challenge x-star not previously queried, receives either Eval(sk,x-star) or an independent uniform \(\lambda\)-bit string, and continues oracle queries excluding x-star. No proof for the challenge is supplied. Its distinguishing advantage must be negligible. The domain has \(2^\lambda\) inputs; weak security on randomly selected inputs is insufficient. Non-black-box techniques are allowed, and there is no setup beyond the individual generated key pair.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked construction with proofs of perfect honest correctness, perfect uniqueness and adaptive pseudorandomness from arbitrary one-way functions, or refute the unrestricted implication. A black-box separation alone does not rule out constructions using the one-way-function description.

title: Blind signatures from one-way functions alone
summary: A signer issues signatures without learning which messages are being signed. Blindness must survive interleaved sessions and malicious signer behavior. A user initiating q signing sessions must not obtain signatures on q+1 distinct messages. The selected game counts initiated sessions, including aborts. The target permits non-black-box methods but assumes no global random oracle or trusted setup.
formal: Does the existence of arbitrary one-way functions imply a classical plain-model blind-signature scheme with concurrent blindness and one-more unforgeability, allowing polynomially many interaction rounds and non-black-box constructions?
definitions:
The security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. Honest algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time machines. Security quantifies over nonuniform polynomial-size probabilistic circuits with polynomially many oracle queries. All message, instance and witness lengths in the experiment are polynomial in \(\lambda\). Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto). The model supplies no random oracle, trusted hardware or additional computational assumption.

Assume a uniform polynomial-time family \(f_\lambda:\{0,1\}^\lambda\to\{0,1\}^{\ell(\lambda)}\) with polynomially bounded output length. For uniform \(X\in\{0,1\}^\lambda\), every admissible adversary given \(\lambda\) and \(f_\lambda(X)\) has negligible probability of returning any \(\lambda\)-bit \(x'\) with \(f_\lambda(x')=f_\lambda(X)\). Collisions are allowed.

KeyGen generates a signer key pair (pk,sk). A polynomial-round interactive protocol between Signer(sk) and User(pk,m) gives the user a signature sigma or an abort symbol. Deterministic Verify(pk,m,sigma) checks signatures. Messages have polynomial length. Honest executions yield accepted signatures except with negligible probability. The scheme has no CRS or globally accessible oracle.

Blindness is tested against a malicious signer that chooses a public key and two equal-length messages m0,m1. A hidden uniform bit b assigns mb to one honest-user session and m(1-b) to another. The signer interleaves both sessions arbitrarily with any further polynomially many sessions on messages of its own choice. If both challenge users finish, it receives their final signatures ordered by message (m0 first, m1 second), without session labels; if either aborts it receives only the common failure notification instead of either signature. Together with its entire interaction view, this must give only negligible advantage in guessing b. Honest users verify signatures before reporting success; malformed public keys may lead to abort.

For one-more unforgeability a malicious user interacts with an honest signer under an honest public key in any polynomial number q of sessions, scheduled concurrently. It wins by outputting q+1 accepted message-signature pairs with pairwise distinct messages. Here q counts all sessions initiated, including aborted sessions; no stronger completed-session accounting is required. The win probability must be negligible for every polynomial-size adversary. Signer sessions use fresh random coins. This fixes the session-count convention explicitly. Signatures need not be unique, and no ideal-world universally composable security or extraction is demanded.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked construction and correctness, blindness and one-more-unforgeability reductions from arbitrary one-way functions, or refute the unrestricted implication. Black-box-only separations and constructions in a global random-oracle model do not settle the plain-model target.

title: PZK versus SZK
summary: Zero knowledge asks whether an efficient simulator can reproduce what any efficient verifier sees. Statistical simulation allows negligible total variation error, while perfect simulation requires exact agreement conditioned on not failing. The question compares the classes of promise problems admitting these two kinds of ordinary interactive proofs. All machines are uniform, simulators have strict polynomial runtime and receive only the common input. Known oracle separations and perfect-zero-knowledge results in other proof models leave this class equality unresolved in the checked sources.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{PZK}=\mathrm{SZK}\) for classical single-prover interactive proofs of promise problems in the precise input-only simulation model below? Both classes use uniform polynomial-time verifiers and simulators, negligible completeness and soundness errors, and zero knowledge against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier. Perfect simulation may output a failure symbol with probability at most \(1/2\); conditioned on success its distribution must be exactly correct. Statistical simulation permits negligible total variation distance.
definitions:
A promise problem is a pair \(L=(Y,N)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). An interactive proof has a single computationally unbounded honest prover \(P\) and a uniform probabilistic Turing verifier \(V\), both receiving the common input \(x\). They exchange binary messages over an ordinary interactive channel. The verifier uses at most polynomially many random bits, computational steps and communicated bits, with a fixed polynomial in \(|x|\); its bound holds on every random tape and against every prover. A message or interaction exceeding the verifier's prescribed length or turn limit can be rejected. The prover has arbitrary computation and private randomness, but sees only the input and communicated history, not the verifier's private random tape.

Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in \(n\). There must be one negligible error bound with honest acceptance probability at least \(1-\varepsilon(|x|)\) for every \(x\in Y\), and acceptance probability at most \(\varepsilon(|x|)\) for every \(x\in N\) and every possibly unbounded cheating prover strategy. Soundness thus concerns proofs, not arguments secure only against computationally bounded provers. No correctness or simulation condition is imposed outside the promise. Completeness is not required to be perfect.

A malicious verifier \(V^*\) is any fixed uniform probabilistic polynomial-time interactive Turing machine, with polynomial worst-case bounds on its computation, random bits and communication on every interaction. The honest prover has a specified behavior on every received history, including malformed messages or early halting. The view \(\operatorname{View}_{P,V^*}(x)\) is the resulting finite record of \(x\), the verifier's random bits and all exchanged messages with their order and delimiters. Its output and final state are determined by this record and its program. Random tapes can be padded to the verifier's fixed polynomial bound. This fixes one finite binary encoding of views; the special simulator failure symbol \(\bot\) is not a view.

The promise problem belongs to SZK if it has such a proof \((P,V)\) and, for every \(V^*\), a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulator \(S^*\) and a negligible function \(\mu_{V^*}\) such that for every \(x\in Y\),
\[
\operatorname{TV}\bigl(S^*(x),\operatorname{View}_{P,V^*}(x)\bigr)\le\mu_{V^*}(|x|).
\]
For distributions on finite binary records, \(\operatorname{TV}(D,E)=\tfrac12\sum_z|\Pr[D=z]-\Pr[E=z]|\); the sum may include records given zero probability by one distribution. Any simulator output not encoding a real view counts in that distance.

PZK uses the same requirements on the proof but replaces the last simulation condition by
\[
\Pr[S^*(x)=\bot]\le\tfrac12,\qquad
\mathcal L(S^*(x)\mid S^*(x)\ne\bot)=\mathcal L(\operatorname{View}_{P,V^*}(x))
\]
for every \(x\in Y\). Here \(\mathcal L\) denotes the probability distribution, and equality requires equality of each record's probability. Nonfailure has positive probability, so conditioning is defined.

Every simulator has a strict polynomial bound on every input and random tape, rather than an expected-time bound. Its polynomial and description may depend on the fixed verifier \(V^*\), but not on \(x\). It receives \(x\) alone, with no witness, prover interaction, nonuniform advice or separate auxiliary input. It may use the fixed verifier's description internally; no black-box simulation requirement is imposed. There is no common random string, oracle, computational assumption or multiprover resource. This retains the saved input-only convention; an auxiliary-input or expected-time variant is not substituted.

Class equality quantifies over all promise problems and permits the perfect proof system to differ completely from the statistical one. PZK is contained in SZK under these conventions: repeat a perfect simulator independently polynomially many times, retain the first nonfailure output and use any fixed record if all runs fail. The latter event can be made negligible while preserving a strict polynomial bound.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that every promise problem in the stated SZK class also belongs to the stated PZK class, or exhibit a promise problem in SZK and prove that it admits no PZK proof in this model. The positive direction need not be a uniform compiler from protocol descriptions. An oracle separation, a failure of one proposed compiler, a perfect-zero-knowledge PCP or multiprover protocol, or an honest-verifier-only result without a matching transformation does not resolve the unrelativized equality.

title: Polynomial-time computationally sound verification of \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\)
summary: The task is to check the exact number of satisfying assignments to a Boolean formula in polynomial time. An exponential-time honest prover supplies a short proof to a fully deterministic verifier. Even adversaries running in any polynomial in the honest prover’s time must almost never find a false counting claim that the verifier accepts. A 2025 theorem gives such verification for polynomial-space claims under strong hardness assumptions. This card asks whether the specified counting-verification system exists without those unproved assumptions.
formal: Do there exist deterministic uniform algorithms \(P,V\), integers \(C>c\ge1\), and a constant \(K\ge2\) giving the following plain-model argument system for exact \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\), without unproved hardness assumptions? On a Boolean formula \(\Phi\) encoded in \(N\) bits, \(P\) produces a proof of length at most \((N+1)^C\) in time \(T_P(N)=2^{K(N+1)^c}\). The verifier runs in time \(K(N+1)^C\) and outputs either the exact number of satisfying assignments or the rejection symbol \(\bot\). Completeness requires \(V(\Phi,P(\Phi))=\#\mathrm{SAT}(\Phi)\) on every valid formula. Soundness requires that every uniform randomized adversary running in any fixed polynomial in \(T_P(N)\) has only negligible probability, as a function of \(T_P(N)\), of generating a length-\(N\) formula and a proof on which \(V\) outputs an incorrect number. This card fixes the unconditional version of the source question; conditional constructions are recorded below.
definitions:
Fix a polynomial-time parsable binary encoding of formulas over AND, OR and NOT. An instance lists its \(n\) variables explicitly, so \(n\le N\), and its formula is a finite tree with leaves among those variables and Boolean constants. The value \(\#\mathrm{SAT}(\Phi)\) is the number of assignments in \(\{0,1\}^n\) on which the formula evaluates to one, including choices of any listed unused variables. The answer is written in binary and has at most \(n+1\) bits. Measuring resources in the full encoding length fixes the meaning of polynomial-size formulas and includes the cost of reading their descriptions.

The prover and verifier are deterministic multitape Turing machines with finite descriptions independent of input length. The proof is one finite binary string; there is no interaction, oracle, common reference string, advice, secret setup or verifier randomness. The verifier rejects malformed instances and overlong proofs. It halts within its stated bound on every input, reading at most one symbol beyond the permitted proof length to detect excess input. Increasing the fixed constant \(K\) absorbs encoding and rejection overhead. The honest prover must construct its proof in the stated exponential time; mere existence of a proof with no bound on its production is insufficient.

More explicitly, for every uniform probabilistic Turing machine \(A\) whose worst-case runtime on \(1^N\) is at most \(T_P(N)^a\) for some fixed \(a\ge1\), and for every integer \(d\ge1\), there is \(N_{A,d}\) such that, for every \(N\ge N_{A,d}\),
\[\Pr_{(\Phi,\pi)\leftarrow A(1^N)}\bigl[\Phi\text{ is valid},\ |\Phi|=N,\ V(\Phi,\pi)\notin\{\#\mathrm{SAT}(\Phi),\bot\}\bigr]\le T_P(N)^{-d}.\]
Probability is over independent fair random bits used by \(A\). Any output that is not a valid formula/proof pair is a failed attack. The adversary chooses both the formula and its proof, knows \(P,V\), and has no nonuniform advice or auxiliary input. The polynomial exponent \(a\) may be arbitrarily large and is not fixed by the protocol. Negligibility is measured in the honest prover's time, rather than merely inverse polynomial in the formula length. The constants \(c,C,K\) and the two machines must be fixed before quantifying over adversaries and accuracy exponents.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a system exists, including all completeness, uniformity, running-time and soundness requirements, or prove that no such system exists. A positive answer must be unconditional. A construction assuming a conjectured hard function is progress but does not settle this selected version. Randomized verification, interaction, a setup string, soundness only against polynomial-in-input-length adversaries, or an unbounded honest prover changes the question.

title: Efficient split-state non-malleable codes approaching capacity
summary: An encoding splits a message into two equally long shares. Each share may be changed by an arbitrary function unaware of the other share. The decoded result must be either the original message or statistically independent of it. Encoding and decoding must be uniform polynomial-time algorithms with negligible error. The rate must tend to one half when both shares count toward length.
formal: Do uniform polynomial-time two-share nonmalleable codes exist with k message bits, equal share length \(\ell(k)\), negligible statistical error in k, and rate \(k/(2\ell(k))\) tending to 1/2 as k tends to infinity, against all independent tampering functions on the two shares?
definitions:
For each positive integer \(k\), let \(S_k=\{0,1\}^{\ell(k)}\). The randomized encoder \(\operatorname{Enc}_k\) maps each \(k\)-bit message to a pair of shares \((L,R)\in S_k\times S_k\). The deterministic decoder \(\operatorname{Dec}_k\) maps every such pair into \(\{0,1\}^k\cup\{\bot\}\). The share length \(\ell(k)\) is polynomially bounded and computable in polynomial time. Both algorithms are uniform and run in polynomial time in \(k\) on every input and random tape. Honest decoding returns the message with probability one. The model provides no shared setup secret or computational hardness assumption.

There is one negligible function \(\eta\) such that for every \(k\) and every two deterministic maps \(f,g:S_k\to S_k\), there is a distribution \(D_{k,f,g}\) on \(\{0,1\}^k\cup\{\bot,\mathsf{same}\}\) with the following property for every message \(m\). Sample \((L,R)\) from \(\operatorname{Enc}_k(m)\). The total variation distance between \(\operatorname{Dec}_k(f(L),g(R))\) and the following simulated output is at most \(\eta(k)\). Draw \(d\) from \(D_{k,f,g}\), return \(m\) if \(d=\mathsf{same}\), and return \(d\) otherwise. The symbols \(\bot\) and \(\mathsf{same}\) are distinct and lie outside the message alphabet. The same distribution works for every \(m\) and need not be efficiently samplable. For every real \(c>0\), \(\eta(k)<k^{-c}\) for all sufficiently large \(k\).

Tampering maps may be computationally unbounded and know the public code but are fixed independently of the message and encoding randomness. Each sees only its own share; correlated choices of maps are covered by mixtures of deterministic pairs. The target is single-shot nonmalleability, not adaptive repeated tampering or leakage resilience. Rate counts both shares, and convergence to 1/2 is a single uniform family with \(\ell(k)=k+o(k)\), not a claim about an unbounded-time existential code.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked uniform code family with perfect correctness, the statistical simulation property and the limiting rate, or prove that no such efficient family exists. Computational nonmalleability, bitwise tampering or more than two shares does not answer this information-theoretic two-share question.

title: Unconditional zero knowledge for gap circuit complexity
summary: The input is a complete truth table promised to have either a small or a much larger minimum circuit. The selected question asks for some fixed gap admitting an unconditional computational zero-knowledge proof. The verifier is efficient, while soundness must hold even against an unbounded cheating prover. All promised inputs and all input lengths must satisfy the guarantees. Average-case protocols and the later one-way-function characterization do not establish this membership.
formal: Is there a fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\) for which \(\mathrm{Gap}_{\varepsilon}\mathrm{MCSP}\) admits a computational zero-knowledge interactive proof system without a computational hardness assumption? Given the length-\(N=2^n\) truth table of a Boolean function, the promise distinguishes circuit size at most \(N^\varepsilon\) from size greater than \(N^{1-\varepsilon}\). This card selects the MCSP branch of the original question and the gap family used by Hirahara and Nanashima; it does not claim equivalence with every MINKT or other gap variant.
definitions:
The common input is the full truth table \(x\) of a function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), with \(n\geq1\) and \(N=2^n\). Let \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)\) be its minimum Boolean circuit size. Fix the standard basis of binary AND and OR and unary NOT, with constant inputs available, arbitrary fan-out, one output, and size equal to the number of gates. Circuits are acyclic and compute every truth-table entry correctly.

A yes-instance satisfies \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)\leq N^\varepsilon\). A no-instance satisfies \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)>N^{1-\varepsilon}\). Inputs between these thresholds have no required decision outcome. The strict no-threshold follows the formal definition in the later source; the thresholds need not be integers. The constant \(\varepsilon\) is chosen once, not supplied per instance. The task has both low-complexity and high-complexity promised inputs at arbitrarily large lengths.

An interactive proof has an honest prover \(P\) and a randomized verifier \(V\). Total communication, rounds and verifier computation are polynomial in \(N\), the explicit truth-table length. No computational bound is imposed on the prover. On every yes-instance, the honest interaction accepts with probability at least \(2/3\). On every no-instance, every cheating prover, including an unbounded one, causes acceptance with probability at most \(1/3\). This is a proof system; soundness only against efficient provers would be an argument system.

Computational zero knowledge requires that for every randomized polynomial-time verifier \(V^*\), including one given arbitrary polynomial-length auxiliary information \(z\), there is a randomized polynomial-time simulator \(S_{V^*}\). Given only \(x,z\), it produces a distribution computationally indistinguishable from the entire view of \(V^*\) in the honest-prover interaction on \(x\). That view includes the common input, auxiliary information, verifier randomness, messages and final output. The simulator is not given a small circuit or other witness.

Indistinguishability is required on all yes-instances: every polynomial-size distinguishing circuit has only negligible advantage in \(N\), uniformly over these instances and polynomial-length auxiliary strings. Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in \(N\). The simulator and verifier use the ordinary polynomial-time convention of the later source. No setup, random oracle, trusted third party or hardness assumption is supplied.

The chosen circuit basis fixes a concrete representation. The existential constant-gap formulation tolerates constant-factor changes of standard finite bases by choosing a slightly wider gap and handling finitely many small lengths separately. It does not identify circuits with a shortest program: MINKT instead bounds the program length needed to print a string within a supplied time budget, and its gap parameters constitute a separate choice.

The target asks for one protocol meeting worst-case completeness, soundness and zero knowledge at every input length. A protocol that succeeds on most inputs from a particular distribution or only at infinitely many lengths is a weaker result.
answer_criterion: Give some fixed admissible gap constant and a protocol with proofs of polynomial verifier and simulator cost, completeness, soundness against all provers, and computational zero knowledge against arbitrary efficient auxiliary-input verifiers, without assuming one-way functions or another hardness premise. A negative answer must rule out the specified protocols for every constant in this selected gap family. Failure for that family would not by itself refute all alternatives in the original broader question.

title: Sublinear communication for perfectly secure two-party computation
summary: Two parties want to compute a Boolean circuit while keeping each input perfectly private. A trusted dealer can distribute correlated randomness before either input is supplied. The question asks whether polynomial setup and computation can give online communication sublinear in the circuit size, apart from the input-length cost. Such savings are known for layered circuits, while completely optimal communication can require exponential setup. The unresolved target covers arbitrary circuits with perfect passive privacy and shared outputs.
formal: Is there a uniform two-party protocol in the trusted correlated-randomness model that perfectly computes every Boolean circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) with polynomial setup and computation, and online communication \(O(n+g(s))\) for some function \(g(s)=o(s)\), where \(s\) is the circuit's supplied size? More precisely, seek fixed algorithms, constants \(K,q\ge1\), and \(g:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R_{\ge1}\) with \(\lim_{s\to\infty}g(s)/s=0\), such that every circuit and every pair of inputs satisfy the correctness and privacy conditions below; dealer computation, total setup length and both parties' computation are at most \(K(n+s+1)^q\), while at most \(K(n+g(s))\) bits are exchanged online. The circuit is arbitrary, without a layering or depth restriction. The additive input-length term fixes the source's sublinearity question in a form that also covers circuits of linear size.
definitions:
A circuit is an explicitly given finite directed acyclic graph with \(2n\) input vertices, Boolean constants, fan-in-two AND/OR gates, NOT gates, and one designated output. Fan-out is unrestricted. Let \(s\) count all vertices, including inputs and constants; in particular \(s\ge2n\). Gates and predecessors are encoded in topological order with binary indices. Both parties and the dealer know this public description. The inputs \(x_0,x_1\in\{0,1\}^n\) are private to their respective parties. The size in the bound is that of the supplied circuit; the protocol may optimize its computation, but cannot charge an artificially padded circuit to increase its communication allowance.

Before the parties receive their inputs, a trusted randomized dealer, given only \(C\), samples finite correlated strings \((r_0,r_1)\) and privately sends \(r_b\) to party \(b\). These strings may depend on \(C\) but not on either input. The dealer then takes no further part. Dealer randomness consists of independent fair bits; its computation and output length obey the polynomial bound on every run. Independent local random tapes can be included in these strings. After this phase the parties are deterministic machines on their input, setup string and message history. Their descriptions are fixed across all circuits and lengths, and their complete online runtimes obey the same polynomial bound. There is no other setup, oracle or computational hardness assumption.

The parties exchange binary messages and output private bits \(y_0,y_1\). Perfect correctness means
\[\Pr[y_0\mathbin\oplus y_1=C(x_0,x_1)]=1\]
for every input pair, where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The task uses the source's shared-output convention: neither party is required to learn the reconstructed answer. Perfect privacy against one passive corruption means that, for each \(b\) and each fixed \(C,x_b\), the distribution of party \(b\)'s entire view is identical for every choice of the other party's input. Its view includes \(r_b\), all sent and received messages and its output. A passive adversary follows the protocol and may inspect that entire view with unlimited computation; the parties do not collude. Privacy and correctness have zero error.

Online cost is the worst-case number of bits sent in both directions, over inputs and all dealer outcomes of positive probability. Message boundaries, control information and input-dependent stopping must be encoded in this communication; timing and silence are not free channels. There is no separate round bound beyond polynomial runtime. The dealer's private deliveries are excluded from online communication but included in the setup-length bound. For every family whose circuit size is polynomial in \(n\), the stated \(\operatorname{poly}(n+s)\) resource bound is polynomial in the input length, as required by the source. A single choice of algorithms, \(K,q,g\) must work for all such families, not only a fixed function or depth.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence, including perfect privacy, correctness, polynomial setup/computation and a uniform sublinear \(g\), or prove that no such protocol and resource bounds exist. A protocol for layered circuits only, a computationally secure construction, or a truth-table protocol using setup exponential in \(n\) does not settle this target. A negative answer must rule out all sublinear savings allowed above, rather than only exactly optimal or one-round online communication.

title: Quantum PCP conjecture with classical reductions
summary: A local Hamiltonian describes a quantum system through bounded-strength interactions on a fixed number of qubits at a time. The question asks whether distinguishing two constant-separated ranges of its average ground energy is as hard as every problem with a quantum witness verifier. The saved variant requires deterministic classical reductions, a stronger requirement than the original survey’s formulation allowing quantum reductions. All global quantum states are allowed, and neither growing locality nor a vanishing normalized gap meets the target. Known low-energy state complexity, interactive verification and restricted gap-amplification results leave the stated hardness question unresolved in the checked sources.
formal:
Do there exist fixed positive integers \(k,d\) and a rational constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\) for which the following promise problem \(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon}\) is QMA-hard under deterministic classical polynomial-time many-one reductions? An instance specifies \(n\geq1\) qubits, \(1\leq m\leq(n+1)^d\) local terms \(H_1,\ldots,H_m\), and rational thresholds \(0\leq a<b\leq1\) with \(b-a\geq\varepsilon\). Each term acts on at most \(k\) qubits, has rational real and imaginary matrix entries, and satisfies \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\). For the normalized Hamiltonian
\[H=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m H_i,\]
distinguish \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq a\) from \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\geq b\). The classical reduction requirement preserves the saved card’s variant; the cited survey’s standard formulation permits quantum reductions.
definitions:
A qubit has state space \(\mathbb C^2\), with basis \(|0\rangle=(1,0)\) and \(|1\rangle=(0,1)\). The \(n\)-qubit state space is \(\mathcal H_n=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n}\). A pure state is a vector of norm one; a general state is a positive semidefinite Hermitian operator \(\rho\) of trace one on that space. The adjoint \(M^*\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(M\) is Hermitian when \(M=M^*\). The order \(M\preceq N\) means that \(N-M\) is Hermitian and \(z^*(N-M)z\geq0\) for every complex vector \(z\). The symbol \(I\) denotes the identity on the relevant space.

A local term is specified by an increasing list of \(\ell\) distinct qubit indices, with \(0\leq\ell\leq\min(k,n)\), and the complete \(2^\ell\)-by-\(2^\ell\) matrix in lexicographic computational-basis order on these indices. It acts as that matrix on the listed tensor factors and as identity on all other factors. A zero-qubit matrix is a scalar multiple of the identity. The bounds \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\) concern the embedded operator, equivalently its supplied local matrix. Different terms may overlap and need not commute. Repeated terms are allowed and counted in \(m\). No spatial geometry, bound on the number of terms touching one qubit, or common zero-energy state is required.

The ground energy is
\[\lambda_{\min}(H)=\min_{\|\psi\|=1}\langle\psi,H\psi\rangle
=\min_{\rho\succeq0,\,\operatorname{tr}\rho=1}\operatorname{tr}(H\rho).\]
Both minima range over all global states, including entangled ones; no circuit preparation or classical description bound is imposed on a state. The promise gap \(b-a\) separates the two input cases. It is not a gap between the first and second eigenvalues of one Hamiltonian. The normalization and the per-term bound fix the energy scale, so \(0\leq\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq1\).

The input is an explicit finite bit string. To fix an encoding, for a natural number \(u\) let \(w(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(w(0)=0\), and write \(E(u)=1^{|w(u)|}0w(u)\). Encode an integer by a sign bit followed by \(E\) of its absolute value: sign 0 is nonnegative and sign 1 is negative, with sign 0 for zero. Encode a rational by its integer numerator and its positive denominator in lowest terms. A complex entry is its real rational part followed by its imaginary rational part. The instance consists of \(1^n0\), then \(E(m)\), then the rationals \(a,b\), then the \(m\) terms. A term consists of \(E(\ell)\), its \(\ell\) indices encoded by \(E\), and its matrix entries in row-major order. There are no trailing bits. The entire length \(N\) counts every numerator, denominator, index and matrix entry. Matrix precision is part of \(N\), not a unit-cost real input. Strings failing these syntactic conditions or any stated matrix or threshold condition are outside the promise, as are valid instances with \(a<\lambda_{\min}(H)<b\).

Here QMA is the following class of promise pairs \(\Pi=(Y,N_0)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). A verifier has one deterministic classical Turing machine that, given \(x\), outputs a quantum circuit \(V_x\) and its register sizes in time polynomial in \(|x|+1\). The circuit has polynomially many qubits and gates, with a designated witness register of \(w(|x|)\) qubits and all other qubits initialized to \(|0\rangle\). The function \(w\) is polynomial-time computable and polynomially bounded. The generator and all resource bounds are fixed for \(\Pi\), valid on all inputs, and have no advice or oracle. The witness may be any density operator on its register and need not have an efficient description.

Circuits use the fixed gate set consisting of the Hadamard gate
\[W=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\]
the phase gate \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), and controlled-NOT, which sends \(|u,v\rangle\) to \(|u,u\mathbin{\oplus}v\rangle\) for bits \(u,v\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates are specified by their names and qubit indices. At the end a designated output qubit is measured in the computational basis; outcome 1 is acceptance. Probabilities are given by the Born rule applied to the witness and zero ancillas after the circuit. For every \(x\in Y\), some witness is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in N_0\), every witness is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). There is no acceptance requirement outside \(Y\cup N_0\).

QMA-hardness under the required reductions means that for every such pair \(\Pi\), there is one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(R_\Pi\) that halts on every input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^r\) bit steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,r\), outputs a classical binary string, and satisfies
\[x\in Y\Rightarrow R_\Pi(x)\in(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon})_{\rm yes},\qquad
x\in N_0\Rightarrow R_\Pi(x)\in(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon})_{\rm no}.\]
Output writing is included in the time bound. On promised source inputs the output must obey every target condition, including the common locality and term-count bounds. Off the source promise no output guarantee is required, but the runtime bound still holds. The reduction may depend on \(\Pi\); \(k,d,\varepsilon\) must be chosen once before quantifying over \(\Pi\). Thus the order is \(\exists k,d,\varepsilon\;\forall\Pi\in\mathrm{QMA}\;\exists R_\Pi\). No random or quantum computation is allowed in \(R_\Pi\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the full stated existence of constants and classical QMA-hardness, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must prove the reduction guarantees and their uniform polynomial resource bounds for all QMA promise pairs with one fixed target triple \((k,d,\varepsilon)\). A negative answer must establish that for every allowed triple there is a QMA promise pair admitting no qualifying classical reduction to that target problem. The source pair may depend on the triple. A lower bound on one proposed reduction, a counterexample only to a particular construction, an oracle separation, or an algorithm for a restricted Hamiltonian family is not this negation. A proof allowing only quantum reductions does not by itself prove the saved classical-reduction variant; conversely, refuting the latter need not refute the weaker standard formulation. Constant-gap hardness with growing locality, a theorem solely about preparation depth of low-energy states, or an interactive verification theorem does not meet this answer criterion.
