The negative alternative means that every candidate algorithm fails termination or the error guarantee on at least one promised input and requested accuracy. The yes/no assertion quantifies over all requested accuracies; a fixed \(1/100\) error guarantee is not a replacement for it. A regularized formula without a finite stopping guarantee, polynomial-time hardness, or undecidability for an assisted, zero-error or memoryful capacity does not answer this question. Nor would undecidability of the exact predicate \(Q(\Phi)=0\) alone rule out additive approximation.

title: QMA versus \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\)
summary: QMA(2) receives two quantum witnesses that are promised unentangled across a specified division, whereas QMA receives one unrestricted quantum witness. Both use uniform polynomial-time quantum verification with constant completeness and soundness error. The question is whether the promise of unentanglement adds power for ordinary promise problems without an oracle. Known amplification and restricted-phase results do not resolve this comparison, and concatenating honest witnesses does not preserve soundness automatically. A September 2026 manuscript separates the classes relative to a unitary oracle while explicitly leaving their ordinary relationship unresolved.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)=\mathrm{QMA}\) for ordinary uniform promise problems without an oracle? A QMA(2) verifier receives two polynomial-length quantum witnesses that are promised to be unentangled across the two witness registers, even on a no-instance. A QMA verifier receives one arbitrary polynomial-length quantum witness. The easy inclusion \(\mathrm{QMA}\subseteq\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) follows by ignoring a second witness; the question is whether every QMA(2) promise problem is also in QMA under the definitions below.
definitions:
A promise problem is an ordered pair \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). There is no requirement on inputs outside their union. A verifier is specified by one deterministic classical Turing machine that, on a string \(x\) of length \(n\), outputs in time polynomial in \(n\) the description of a quantum circuit \(V_x\), its witness-register lengths and a designated output qubit. All register lengths and the number of gates are bounded by a polynomial depending on the verifier, not on \(x\). Apart from its witness registers, the circuit starts with ancillary qubits in state \(|0\rangle\). It uses the fixed gate set \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\), acting on specified qubits, where \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\] and \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\); \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The circuit accepts when its final computational-basis measurement of the output qubit is 1. Qubits are two-dimensional complex systems; an \(m\)-qubit pure state is a unit vector in \(\mathbb C^{2^m}\), with computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^m\}\). A mixed state is a positive semidefinite, trace-one complex matrix on this space. For witness density matrix \(\rho\), acceptance probability is \[\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_1V_x\bigl(\rho\otimes |0\rangle\langle0|^{\otimes a}\bigr)V_x^\dagger\right],\] where \(a\) is the number of ancillary qubits, \(V_x^\dagger\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(\Pi_1\) projects onto output-qubit value 1 and acts as identity on the other qubits. Positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\); \(\operatorname{Tr}\) is the sum of diagonal entries. Witnesses may depend arbitrarily on the whole input and need not be efficiently preparable. Circuit uniformity forbids advice depending only on input length, and neither model receives an oracle. The witness is sent once, before verification, with no further interaction. The stated finite universal gate set fixes an encoding; bounded-error classes permit the usual polynomial-overhead approximations of other effective universal gate sets. A different verifier and polynomial bound may be used for each promise problem.

The class \(\mathrm{QMA}\), quantum Merlin–Arthur, consists of the promise problems with such a verifier and one polynomial-length quantum witness register for which both conditions hold: for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\), some witness state is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\), every witness state is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). The quantifiers apply to arbitrary mixed states, not merely the honestly intended state. Pure witnesses suffice for completeness by linearity of acceptance probability.

For \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\), the verifier instead has two witness registers, each of length bounded by a polynomial in the input length. For every yes-input there must exist density matrices \(\rho\) and \(\sigma\) on the respective registers such that the product state \(\rho\otimes\sigma\) is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\). For every no-input and every pair \(\rho,\sigma\), the acceptance probability on \(\rho\otimes\sigma\) is at most \(1/3\). The two factors can each have arbitrary internal entanglement among their own qubits; the restriction concerns the division between the two registers. Equivalent soundness quantification allows every separable state \(\sum_jp_j\rho_j\otimes\sigma_j\), where \(p_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_jp_j=1\), because acceptance is linear. The two witnesses need not be identical. Both may depend on the whole input and may be coordinated before they are sent, but their joint state at receipt must satisfy the indicated separability restriction. After receipt, the verifier may perform arbitrary allowed joint gates and create entanglement. It is not required to test separability of an arbitrary incoming state; separability is a promise on the states against which soundness is required. Neither class restricts amplitudes to be nonnegative or witness states to have short classical descriptions. Equality means equality of all disjoint promise pairs admitted by the two definitions.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{QMA}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that some promise problem lies in QMA(2) but outside QMA. An equality proof must supply sound single-witness verification for every eligible two-witness problem; merely concatenating the intended honest witnesses is insufficient because the single-witness verifier must also resist entangled dishonest states. A separation must exclude every ordinary uniform polynomial-time QMA verifier for the same promise pair. A quantum- or classical-oracle separation, a result about a restricted-amplitude class, or a state-generation task does not alone settle this decision-class comparison.

title: Quantum entropy inequalities beyond strong subadditivity
summary: For a multipartite quantum state, the entropies of all subsystems form a vector subject to universal inequalities. Positivity and strong subadditivity give basic constraints on those vectors. This question asks whether additional inequalities are needed to describe the quantum entropy cone for four or more parties. The cited stabilizer-state analysis relates the problem to classical non-Shannon inequalities and to states violating the Ingleton inequality. New constraints or counterexamples would sharpen the mathematical description of how quantum information can be shared among several systems.
formal:
Is there an unconditional homogeneous linear inequality for finite-dimensional quantum subsystem entropies that does not follow from the standard von Neumann inequalities? Precisely, do there exist an integer \(n\ge4\), real coefficients \((c_J)_{\varnothing
e J\subseteq[n]}\), and a vector \(v\in\mathcal V_n\), as defined below, such that \[\sum_{\varnothing
e J\subseteq[n]}c_J S(ho_J)\ge0\] for every choice of finite local dimensions and every \(n\)-party density matrix \(ho\), while \[\sum_{\varnothing
e J\subseteq[n]}c_Jv_J<0?\] The same coefficients must work in every local dimension. The party count is any one finite \(n\ge4\); the target is not restricted to exactly four parties or to a special class of states.
definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Choose arbitrary positive integers \(d_1,\ldots,d_n\) and the Hilbert space \(\mathcal H=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mathbb C^{d_i}\), with its standard product basis. A density matrix is a Hermitian matrix \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\) that is positive semidefinite, meaning \(z^\dagger\rho z\ge0\) for every complex vector \(z\), and has trace one. Dagger denotes conjugate transpose and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. Arbitrary complex matrix entries and mixed states are allowed.

For a subset \(J\subseteq[n]\), the marginal \(\rho_J\) is obtained by tracing out its complement. In product-basis indices its entries are \[(\rho_J)_{a,b}=\sum_z\rho_{(a,z),(b,z)},\] where \(a,b\) index the factors in \(J\), \(z\) ranges over all basis indices of the complementary factors, and the tuples are placed in the original order of the parties. If \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_D\) are the eigenvalues of a density matrix, define its von Neumann entropy in bits by \(S=-\sum_{j=1}^D\lambda_j\log_2\lambda_j\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\). Define the empty-system entropy to be zero. The entropy vector \(s(\rho)\in\mathbb R^{2^n-1}\) has coordinates \(s(\rho)_J=S(\rho_J)\), indexed by the nonempty subsets.

The standard comparison cone \(\mathcal V_n\) consists of all real vectors \(v=(v_J)_{\varnothing\ne J\subseteq[n]}\), extended by \(v_\varnothing=0\), that satisfy \(v_J\ge0\) for every \(J\), and, for every pair of subsets \(A,B\subseteq[n]\), both \[v_A+v_B\ge v_{A\cap B}+v_{A\cup B}\qquad\text{(strong subadditivity)}\] and \[v_A+v_B\ge v_{A\setminus B}+v_{B\setminus A}\qquad\text{(weak monotonicity)}.\] Disjoint, overlapping, equal and empty subsets are all included. Thus familiar subadditivity and the Araki–Lieb inequalities are already among the consequences. Weak monotonicity follows from strong subadditivity after purifying a quantum state with an additional party; it is explicitly included here so it cannot be counted as a new inequality. Every actual quantum entropy vector lies in \(\mathcal V_n\), but a vector in this cone is only a list of real numbers and is not promised to come from a state.

An inequality is homogeneous linear if its left side is the displayed linear combination with constant coefficients and zero right side. It is unconditional if it holds for all states and dimensions, without extra entropy equalities, independence assumptions or a restriction to stabilizer, classical or holographic states. Not following from the standard inequalities means exactly that it fails at some vector of \(\mathcal V_n\), as required by the strict inequality in the target. This is semantic nonimplication; no choice of syntactic proof system is involved. Equivalently, since the closure of the set of quantum entropy vectors is a closed convex cone, the question asks whether this closure is strictly smaller than \(\mathcal V_n\) for at least one finite \(n\ge4\). Closure means approximation to arbitrary accuracy in the finite-dimensional real coordinate space; it is not exact realization by a single finite-dimensional state. No running-time or algorithmic discovery requirement is imposed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence, including validity for every finite-dimensional state and an exact vector witnessing nonimplication by the standard cone, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. The negative outcome must show that for every finite \(n\ge4\), every universally valid homogeneous linear entropy inequality is nonnegative on every vector in \(\mathcal V_n\). Equivalently it proves equality of the closed quantum entropy cone and \(\mathcal V_n\) for every such \(n\). A positive outcome needs only one party count, but a negative result for exactly four parties does not settle all larger counts. An inequality valid under additional constraints, a restriction to some states, or failure of exact realization of a boundary vector without excluding arbitrarily close realizations does not establish the requested separation. Numerical searches alone and approximate versions of the strict separation are insufficient.

title: Exponential repetition of two-player entangled games
summary: Two quantum players must win every copy of a fixed game repeated independently by the referee. They may use arbitrary finite-dimensional entanglement and joint local measurements across the copies. The target is exponential decay whenever the original optimal value is below one. The original paper establishes only polynomial decay, while game transformations give a different amplification guarantee. An August 2026 manuscript claims the full exponential theorem, but this review has not independently verified its proof.
formal: Does every finite two-player, one-round game \(G\) with entangled value \(\omega^{*}(G)<1\) admit a constant \(c_{G}>0\) such that \[\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})\leq \exp(-c_{G}n)\qquad\text{for every integer }n\geq1?\] The repetition uses the unchanged game and requires winning every coordinate. The 2016 paper proves convergence to zero at a polynomial rate; an August 2026 manuscript claims the exponential bound, with verification limits recorded below.
definitions:
A game is specified by finite nonempty question sets \(X,Y\), finite nonempty answer sets \(A,B\), a probability distribution \(\mu\) on \(X\times Y\), and a winning predicate \(V:X\times Y\times A\times B\to\{0,1\}\). The referee samples \((x,y)\) from \(\mu\), sends \(x\) only to Alice and \(y\) only to Bob, and accepts their answers \(a,b\) exactly when \(V(x,y,a,b)=1\). The two questions may be correlated, and some pairs may have probability zero.

Before receiving their questions, the players may share any finite-dimensional bipartite quantum state \(\rho\) on \(\mathcal H_{A}\otimes\mathcal H_{B}\). On question \(x\), Alice applies a measurement \(\{E^{x}_{a}:a\in A\}\); on question \(y\), Bob applies \(\{F^{y}_{b}:b\in B\}\). Each measurement is a family of positive semidefinite operators summing to the identity. Their conditional answer probability is
\[\Pr[a,b\mid x,y]=\operatorname{Tr}\!\bigl(\rho(E^{x}_{a}\otimes F^{y}_{b})\bigr).\]
They cannot communicate after receiving the questions. Shared randomness is permitted and can be incorporated into the shared state.

The entangled value \(\omega^{*}(G)\) is the supremum of the winning probability over all such finite-dimensional states and local measurements. The dimensions have no fixed upper bound, and a strategy attaining the supremum need not exist. This is the finite-dimensional tensor-product model, not the possibly larger commuting-operator or general nonsignaling model. No efficiency restriction is placed on a strategy.

In \(G^{\otimes n}\), the referee samples \(n\) independent pairs from \(\mu\), sends the complete tuple of Alice's questions to Alice and the complete tuple of Bob's questions to Bob, and receives answer tuples in \(A^{n}\) and \(B^{n}\). Acceptance requires \(V(x_{i},y_{i},a_{i},b_{i})=1\) for every coordinate \(i\).

Each player may use one joint local measurement depending on their entire tuple. Their shared state and its dimension may depend on \(n\). Thus independent sampling by the referee does not force independent play. Product strategies give the lower bound \(\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})\geq\omega^{*}(G)^{n}\); this is not the requested upper bound.

The constant \(c_{G}\) may depend on the entire fixed game, including its soundness gap \(1-\omega^{*}(G)\). It must be positive and independent of \(n\), the strategy and its dimension. No universal optimal exponent or algorithm for computing \(c_{G}\) is requested. A transformed game with added questions is a different game and cannot replace \(G\) in this statement.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal exponential upper bound in the stated strategy model, or exhibit one fixed finite game with value below one for which no positive \(c_{G}\) works. A sequence of different games with progressively slower exponential constants is not a counterexample. Polynomial decay, convergence to zero, exponential decay only for a special game family, or amplification after changing the game does not settle the conjecture.

title: Dihedral hidden subgroup problem in BQP
summary: The dihedral hidden subgroup problem presents a function that is constant on cosets of an unknown subgroup of a dihedral group. The task is to recover generators for that subgroup using quantum access to the function. The target is a uniform algorithm whose total running time is polynomial in the length of the group description and oracle values. Counting only a small number of oracle queries is insufficient if processing the resulting quantum information is expensive. An efficient solution would extend the reach of hidden-subgroup methods beyond the abelian setting and illuminate connections with lattice-related algorithmic problems.
formal: Does there exist one uniform quantum algorithm and integers \(C,c\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(N\ge2\), every integer \(\ell\ge1\), every subgroup \(H\le D_N\), and every function \(f:D_N\to\{0,1\}^{\ell}\) hiding \(H\) as defined below, the algorithm outputs a finite list generating exactly \(H\) with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(C(\lceil\log_2N\rceil+\ell+2)^c\) total operations? The only external quantum oracle is the reversible evaluation of \(f\). The bound is uniform over subgroup and hiding-function choices and includes both oracle calls and all other computation.
definitions:
Let \(\mathbb Z_N=\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\}\) with addition modulo \(N\). The dihedral group \(D_N=\mathbb Z_N\times\{0,1\}\) has multiplication \[(x,b)(y,d)=\bigl((x+(-1)^by)\bmod N,\ (b+d)\bmod2\bigr).\] Its identity is \((0,0)\). A subgroup is a subset containing the identity and closed under products and inverses. For \(g\in D_N\), the left coset \(gH\) is \(\{gh:h\in H\}\). The hiding promise is \[f(g)=f(g')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad gH=g'H.\] Thus each coset has one label and distinct cosets have different labels; no structure in the label bits is promised. The classical input is \(N\) in binary and the register width \(\ell\) in unary, fixing input size at the parameter scale \(\log N+\ell\) used in the inherited bound. With \(m=\lceil\log_2N\rceil\), an element is encoded by \(m\) bits for \(x\), followed by one bit for \(b\). Bit strings with \(x\ge N\) are invalid element encodings. The oracle acts on a group register and an \(\ell\)-bit register by \[U_f|g,z\rangle=|g,z\mathbin\oplus f(g)\rangle\] for valid \(g\), extended linearly to superpositions, and acts as identity on invalid group encodings. Here the XOR acts coordinatewise. Each invocation costs one operation; it is self-inverse. The algorithm has no classical truth table of \(f\), subgroup description, coset-state preparation oracle, subset-sum oracle or uncharged random-access-memory service. It may implement additional operations using the allowed gates and controller, with their full cost charged. Output is a classical finite list of valid encoded elements; success means that the smallest subgroup containing all listed elements is \(H\). The empty list generates the identity subgroup. Writing the list is charged, so its length is automatically bounded by the running time. The algorithm may fail with probability at most \(1/3\), but its running-time guarantee holds on every execution. Probability is over its measurements and internal randomness for each fixed legal \(N,\ell,H,f\). When \(\ell\) is polynomial in \(\log N\), as in the usual succinct oracle setting, the requested time is polynomial in \(\log N\).

The allowed elementary gates are \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), where \[H=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle.\] Here \(a,b\) are bits and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. A quantum register of \(r\) qubits has computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^r\}\); its pure state is a unit vector \(\sum_z\alpha_z|z\rangle\) with complex coefficients. Gates act by their specified unitary matrices on selected qubits and as identity elsewhere. A computational-basis measurement of a register has outcome probabilities given by the squared norms of its corresponding state components. All working qubits start at zero. Classical control is performed by one finite Turing program with no advice; each classical bit step, each elementary gate, and each measured or initialized qubit is charged. Fair random bits, if used, cost one step each. All executions halt within the displayed worst-case bound. This uniform circuit-and-control model charges total work, including input parsing, data preparation, classical postprocessing and output, rather than only circuit depth.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm with all stated guarantees, or of the logical negation ruling out every eligible uniform algorithm and polynomial total-work bound. An affirmative proof must establish exact subgroup-generation correctness with the specified probability for every legal hiding function. A negative proof must apply to the full model, not merely a particular sieve, measurement family or recently proposed procedure. Polynomial query complexity with superpolynomial postprocessing, a method requiring an additional oracle, or uncounted parallel work is insufficient. The target is a yes/no algorithm-existence statement; subgroup generators on each input must be exact, and numerical approximation of a group element is not an alternative answer.

title: Graph isomorphism in BQP
summary: Two graphs are isomorphic when a relabeling of vertices preserves every edge. This question asks whether a quantum algorithm can decide that equivalence in polynomial time for every pair of explicitly given graphs. The algorithm must include all processing costs and achieve bounded error, rather than merely extract a small amount of information from an oracle. Symmetry makes graph isomorphism a natural testing ground for quantum methods, but quantum access to related group structure is not itself a complete algorithm. A resolution would clarify whether quantum computation can efficiently handle this central classification problem.
formal: Does the ordinary graph-isomorphism decision problem belong to \(\mathrm{BQP}\), bounded-error quantum polynomial time? That is, do there exist one uniform quantum algorithm and integers \(C,c\ge1\) such that, for every pair of finite simple graphs given by their complete binary adjacency matrices, the algorithm decides whether a vertex bijection preserves adjacency, with error at most \(1/3\), using at most \(C(n+2)^c\) total elementary operations, where \(n\) is the larger vertex count? No distributional or structural promise is imposed on the graphs.
definitions:
For an integer \(r\ge0\), write \([r]=\{1,\ldots,r\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A finite simple graph on \([r]\) is an undirected graph with no loops or parallel edges. Its adjacency matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{r\times r}\) is symmetric with zero diagonal. Each input graph is encoded by its binary order with a self-delimiting length prefix, followed by all adjacency entries in row-major order; the two graph encodings are concatenated. A prefix can be encoded as \(1^t0\) followed by a \(t\)-bit binary order, using \(t\ge1\) and the usual minimal binary representation. Invalid encodings are rejected. Graphs of different orders are not isomorphic. If both have order \(r\), an isomorphism is a bijection \(\pi:[r]\to[r]\) such that \[A_{uv}=B_{\pi(u),\pi(v)}\qquad\text{for every }u,v\in[r].\] The two order-zero graphs are isomorphic. A yes-instance has at least one such bijection; a no-instance has none. The algorithm must accept every yes-instance with probability at least \(2/3\) and every no-instance with probability at most \(1/3\). Its probability is over its quantum measurement outcomes and any internal random bits, separately for each fixed input. It receives only the explicit classical input, with no witness, nonuniform advice, graph-orbit state, isomorphism oracle, promised rigidity, degree bound or typical-input assumption. Here GI denotes this ordinary permutation-based relation, not the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism in nonlocal-game theory. The running time is polynomial in the graph order and hence in the explicit input length; malformed encodings must be rejected in time polynomial in their actual length.

The allowed elementary gates are \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), where \[H=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle.\] Here \(a,b\) are bits and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. A quantum register of \(r\) qubits has computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^r\}\); its pure state is a unit vector \(\sum_z\alpha_z|z\rangle\) with complex coefficients. Gates act by their specified unitary matrices on selected qubits and as identity elsewhere. A computational-basis measurement of a register has outcome probabilities given by the squared norms of its corresponding state components. All working qubits start at zero. Classical control is performed by one finite Turing program with no advice; each classical bit step, each elementary gate, and each measured or initialized qubit is charged. Fair random bits, if used, cost one step each. All executions halt within the displayed worst-case bound. This uniform circuit-and-control model charges total work, including input parsing, data preparation, classical postprocessing and output, rather than only circuit depth.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that the specified language lies in BQP, including uniformity, bounded error on every input and polynomial total work, or a complete Lean-checked proof that it does not lie in BQP. A classical polynomial-time algorithm is a valid affirmative solution because it can be implemented within the quantum model with polynomial overhead. A negative proof must exclude all uniform bounded-error polynomial-time quantum algorithms, rather than only coset-state, Fourier-sampling or photonic-sampling methods. A necessary invariant that distinguishes only some nonisomorphic graphs, an efficient fixed relaxation, or uncharged preparation of a helpful state does not establish membership. The output is a proof of the yes/no complexity statement, not an approximate isomorphism score.

title: Bell nonlocality from finitely many copies of every entangled state
summary: Entanglement and Bell nonlocality are distinct properties of quantum states and measurement correlations. The question asks whether every entangled bipartite state becomes Bell-nonlocal after local filtering of some finite number of copies. The filter must succeed before measurement settings are selected, and no extra shared entangled state is provided. Single-copy counterexamples, auxiliary-state activation and four-party broadcast results address different resource models. A full answer would determine whether repeated copies of the state itself always make its entanglement observable through a conventional bipartite Bell violation.
formal: For every finite pair of local dimensions \(d_A,d_B\ge2\) and every entangled state \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb C^{d_A}\otimes\mathbb C^{d_B}\), do there exist a finite integer \(k\ge1\), local filters with strictly positive joint success probability, and finite families of local measurements for which the successfully filtered state obtained from \(\rho^{\otimes k}\) has Bell-nonlocal correlations? Both filters act before the measurement settings are chosen. No auxiliary shared entangled state is supplied. The number of copies, filters, output dimensions and measurement families may depend on \(\rho\).
definitions:
A density matrix is a Hermitian matrix \(X=X^\dagger\) with \(v^\dagger Xv\ge0\) for all complex vectors \(v\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}X=1\). Dagger is conjugate transpose and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. A bipartite state is separable if it is a finite convex combination of product density matrices; entangled means not separable. No purity, rational-entry or efficient-preparation promise is imposed. The \(k\) copies are independent copies of the same state. Regroup the tensor factors of \(\rho^{\otimes k}\) into Alice's \((\mathbb C^{d_A})^{\otimes k}\) and Bob's \((\mathbb C^{d_B})^{\otimes k}\); each party may act jointly on all of its own copies.

A successful local filter is specified by finitely many rectangular complex matrices \(A_j\) from Alice's input space to a finite output space \(\mathbb C^{r_A}\), with \(\sum_jA_j^\dagger A_j\le I\). It maps \(X\) to \(\mathcal F_A(X)=\sum_j A_jXA_j^\dagger\). Bob's filter \(\mathcal F_B\) is defined by matrices \(B_l\) and \(\sum_lB_l^\dagger B_l\le I\), with output \(\mathbb C^{r_B}\). Here \(S\le I\) means \(I-S\) is positive semidefinite. These are precisely finite-dimensional completely positive trace-nonincreasing maps. Their joint success probability and conditional output are \[q=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[(\mathcal F_A\otimes\mathcal F_B)(\rho^{\otimes k})\bigr]>0,\qquad \sigma=\frac{(\mathcal F_A\otimes\mathcal F_B)(\rho^{\otimes k})}{q}.\] No lower bound on \(q\) uniform over states or copy counts is required. The success flags may be compared before the measurement settings are chosen. The filters cannot depend on those settings. Local ancillary states are absorbed in the local maps; no entangled ancilla shared between the parties is permitted.

Let \(X,Y,O_A,O_B\) be finite nonempty sets of settings and outcomes. For each \(x\in X\), Alice's positive-operator-valued measurement is a family \((M_{\alpha|x})_{\alpha\in O_A}\) of positive semidefinite operators on \(\mathbb C^{r_A}\) summing to identity. Define Bob's \((N_{\beta|y})_{\beta\in O_B}\) similarly. The conditional correlation is \[p(\alpha,\beta\mid x,y)=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[\sigma(M_{\alpha|x}\otimes N_{\beta|y})\bigr].\] Measurement settings are independently selected after successful preparation; no communication is allowed after they are supplied. All outcomes are retained in this distribution, with no further postselection on outcomes or settings.

The correlation is Bell-local if there are a finite set \(L\), nonnegative weights \(w_\lambda\) summing to one, and normalized conditional probability distributions \(u_\lambda(\alpha\mid x)\), \(v_\lambda(\beta\mid y)\), such that \[p(\alpha,\beta\mid x,y)=\sum_{\lambda\in L}w_\lambda u_\lambda(\alpha\mid x)v_\lambda(\beta\mid y)\] for every setting and outcome. The weights cannot depend on \(x,y\). For finite settings and outcomes this includes all local hidden-variable models, since deterministic response tables have a finite convex hull. Bell-nonlocal means no such representation exists. Equivalently, the distribution violates some linear Bell inequality valid for all local distributions. The target permits every finite Bell scenario, not only two settings or the CHSH inequality. Public shared randomness may select local procedures, but cannot turn a convex combination of Bell-local correlations into a nonlocal one; existence can therefore be tested for fixed filters and measurements as above. There is no computation, sample or circuit-size bound on the chosen operations.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal finite-copy assertion, or of its logical negation: there is one finite-dimensional entangled state for which every finite \(k\), every allowed pair of filters with positive success probability, and every finite family of local measurements produces a Bell-local distribution. A positive proof need not bound \(k\), filter success probability or violation size uniformly over states. A one-copy local model, including a model surviving every one-copy filter, does not establish the negative all-copy assertion. Activation with a different auxiliary entangled state, a network with additional parties, or a test with quantum inputs does not establish the specified bipartite target. Bell violation and filter positivity are exact mathematical conditions; approximate numerical evidence alone is insufficient.

title: Maximum randomized-versus-quantum gap for total functions
summary: The question asks for the largest polynomial quantum query advantage over randomized algorithms on total Boolean functions. Both models must answer correctly with probability at least two thirds on every input. Only queries to input bits are counted, with other computation and workspace unrestricted. Known results put the optimal separation exponent between three and four. The target is to certify that exponent within one hundredth, without resolving finer logarithmic factors.
formal: Determine the optimal polynomial separation exponent \[\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}=\inf\bigl\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall\text{ nonconstant }f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\},\ R(f)\le C\,Q(f)^a\bigr\}.\] Here \(R(f)\) and \(Q(f)\) are randomized and quantum bit-query complexities with worst-case error at most \(1/3\). The constant \(C\) must be independent of both \(n\) and \(f\). The known range is \(3\le\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}\le4\). This card makes the source's maximum-gap question precise at the level of its polynomial exponent; logarithmic factors are not part of this numerical target.
definitions:
A total Boolean function assigns one output bit to every length-\(n\) bit string, with no promise restricting the inputs. Nonconstant means that both output values occur. A deterministic decision tree adaptively chooses an input coordinate, receives its bit, and ultimately outputs a bit. Its depth is the maximum number of queries on a root-to-leaf path. A randomized query algorithm is a probability distribution over deterministic trees of depth at most \(T\). It must output \(f(x)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for each fixed input \(x\). The least possible \(T\) is \(R(f)\); unlimited computation and storage between queries are free.

For an input \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), a quantum bit query is the unitary \(O_x|i,b,z\rangle=|i,b\mathbin{\oplus}x_i,z\rangle\), where \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(z\) is a work register, \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two, and the dummy coordinate has \(x_0=0\). A \(T\)-query algorithm starts in a fixed state, alternates at most \(T\) calls to this oracle with input-independent unitary operations on a finite-dimensional workspace, and finally measures a designated output bit. Arbitrary finite workspace and unitary matrices are allowed. Only oracle calls are charged; all other computation is free. Intermediate measurements and classical random choices can equivalently be included by storing their outcomes coherently. Algorithms may depend on the function and input length, but their operations cannot depend on the unknown input except through oracle calls. No uniform circuit-generation or time bound is imposed. Write \(Q(f)\) for the least integer \(T\) that achieves error at most \(1/3\) on every input in the domain of \(f\). The query bound is a worst-case bound, not an expected number of calls.

Both complexities are positive integers for nonconstant functions and at most \(n\). The infimum takes all real nonnegative exponents with a universal multiplicative bound. An exponent at the infimum need not itself admit such a bound: logarithmic factors may prevent attainment. Removing constant functions avoids zero-complexity conventions. The approximation tolerance for \(\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}\) concerns the exponent itself, not a relative approximation to a query count.
answer_criterion: Supply a real number \(a_*\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(|a_*-\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}|\le1/100\). A certified interval of width at most \(1/50\) suffices via its midpoint. It must control the universal upper bound and the existence of sufficiently large separations to certify this accuracy; merely improving one currently known bound does not suffice. The benchmark does not require resolving logarithmic factors or proving that the infimum exponent is attained.

title: Quantum query-to-communication lifting
summary: A lifting theorem would turn the quantum query complexity of a Boolean promise problem into the communication complexity of a composed two-party problem. The question asks for one gadget per input length that works for every partial outer function. Both complexity measures should agree up to common polylogarithmic factors. The communication model allows arbitrary prior entanglement and an unrestricted number of rounds. Known bounded-round, adversary and hybrid lifting results leave this general bounded-error transfer open in the checked 2026 source.
formal: Do there exist constants \(C\ge1\) and an integer \(k\ge0\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), there is a total nonconstant Boolean communication gadget \(g_n:\{0,1\}^{a_n}\times\{0,1\}^{b_n}\to\{0,1\}\), with finite positive integers \(a_n,b_n\), for which every partial Boolean function \(f:D\to\{0,1\}\), \(D\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), satisfies \[\frac{Q_{1/3}(f)}{C(\log_2n)^k}\ \le\ Q^*_{1/3}(f\circ g_n^n)\ \le\ C(\log_2n)^k Q_{1/3}(f)?\] Here \(Q_{1/3}\) is quantum query complexity and \(Q^*_{1/3}\) is two-party quantum communication complexity with unrestricted prior entanglement. Both have worst-case error at most \(1/3\). The gadget depends on \(n\), but not on \(D\) or \(f\), and the constants are common to the entire family.
definitions: For \(z\in D\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), a query applies \(O_z:|i,b,w\rangle\mapsto|i,b\mathbin{\oplus}z_i,w\rangle\), where \(i\in[n]\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), and \(w\) denotes an arbitrary finite workspace. A quantum query algorithm starts in an input-independent state, uses arbitrary input-independent local quantum operations and measurements between queries, and produces \(f(z)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every promised \(z\). \(Q_{1/3}(f)\) is the minimum worst-case number of calls to \(O_z\), counting all branches. Computation between queries is free; there is no uniformity or finite-gate-set restriction. A function constant on its promise, including an empty promise, has query complexity zero. For the composed communication problem Alice receives \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) with \(x_i\in\{0,1\}^{a_n}\), Bob receives \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)\) with \(y_i\in\{0,1\}^{b_n}\), and the promise is that \(z=(g_n(x_i,y_i))_{i=1}^n\) belongs to \(D\). Bob must output \(f(z)\). A protocol has arbitrary finite-dimensional local registers and any finite-dimensional shared initial state independent of the inputs, with no bound on its entanglement. It may exchange messages in both directions, perform arbitrary local quantum operations and measurements depending on its own input and local history, and use shared or private randomness. All communicated qubits in both directions count; a classical bit sent as a message costs one qubit. Local computation, local memory, and the shared initial state are free. \(Q^*_{1/3}\) is the minimum worst-case total communication over protocols whose error probability is at most \(1/3\) for every promised input pair. The number of rounds is unrestricted, subject to finite protocol length; communication cost includes every branch. Query algorithms and protocols may depend on the particular finite function and promise and need not be uniformly constructible. The gadget family is existential: no efficient method to print its truth table, input-length bound on \(a_n,b_n\), or fixed gadget independent of \(n\) is required. Its communication cost is nevertheless constrained by the universal two-sided inequality, which includes coordinate functions \(f(z)=z_i\). All logarithms in the inequality are base two.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence of this gadget family and common constants with both inequalities for all \(n,D,f\), or a complete Lean proof that no such family and constants exist. A theorem for a restricted class of outer functions, a fixed round bound, approximate polynomial degree instead of quantum query complexity, or a polynomial rather than polylogarithmic loss does not meet the stated affirmative target. The target is bounded-error lifting; a separate zero-error theorem is not also required.

title: Quantum versus classical nonuniform advice
summary: Quantum and classical advice supply information fixed for an entire input length to an efficient quantum computation. The selected advice must decide every binary input of that length correctly with bounded error, and can be arbitrarily hard to prepare. The question asks whether quantum advice increases the resulting ordinary class of total languages. A known simulation by PP with classical advice uses a different error and computation model, while successive oracle separations retain their black boxes. The latest standard classical-oracle separation does not resolve the ordinary equality, and fresh-copy advice remains distinct from untrusted per-instance witnesses.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}=\mathrm{BQP/poly}\) as classes of languages without an oracle? Explicitly, for every language decidable by a uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm supplied with a polynomial-size quantum advice state depending only on input length, does some uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm with polynomial-length classical advice decide the same language with error at most \(1/3\) on every input? The algorithm and polynomial advice bound may change. The reverse inclusion follows by encoding a classical advice string in the computational basis.
definitions: A language is a set \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\); here every binary string must be decided, with no promise excluding some inputs. For each \(n\ge0\), let \(m(n),a(n)\) be nonnegative integers bounded by a fixed polynomial. A single deterministic classical Turing machine, given an input string \(x\) of length \(n\), generates in polynomial time a quantum circuit \(U_x\) with an \(m(n)\)-qubit advice register, \(a(n)\) ancillary qubits initialized to \(|0\rangle\), polynomially many gates, and one designated output qubit. The generating machine has no advice and no oracle. It uses the fixed exact gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), with \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\mathbin\oplus c\rangle,\] where \(b,c\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The circuit outputs the computational-basis measurement of its output qubit. The quantum advice family is a sequence \((\rho_n)_{n\ge0}\) of density matrices on \(\mathbb C^{2^{m(n)}}\). A density matrix is positive semidefinite with trace one; positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho_nv\ge0\) for all vectors \(v\), and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. The probability of output 1 is \[\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_1U_x\bigl(\rho_n\otimes|0\rangle\langle0|^{\otimes a(n)}\bigr)U_x^\dagger\right],\] where \(\Pi_1\) projects onto output 1 and is identity on the remaining qubits, and dagger denotes conjugate transpose. The language belongs to \(\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}\) if some such generating machine, polynomial bounds and advice family satisfy output-1 probability at least \(2/3\) for every \(x\in L\) and at most \(1/3\) for every \(x\notin L\). The same fixed \(\rho_n\) must work for all \(2^n\) strings of length \(n\). A fresh copy of that state is supplied for each independent computation; no cloning or repeated reuse of a consumed copy is promised. Advice is trusted: the requirement concerns the selected family, not all possible advice states. There is no computability or efficient-preparation requirement on the family, and its preparation cost is not charged. The language belongs to \(\mathrm{BQP/poly}\) if the advice can instead be a binary string \(b_n\in\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\), supplied as the basis state \(|b_n\rangle\). Its length may have a different polynomial bound and the circuit may be different, but \(b_n\) still depends only on \(n\), need not be computable, and must work for every length-\(n\) input. Both classes use uniform quantum computation in addition to the explicitly allowed nonuniform advice. BQP abbreviates bounded-error quantum polynomial time; poly and qpoly indicate classical-bit and quantum-qubit advice of polynomial length.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP/poly}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that some language has quantum advice as defined but no eligible classical-advice algorithm and family. An affirmative proof need not produce the classical advice efficiently, but must establish one length-indexed family and a uniform algorithm that work for all inputs. A negative proof must rule out every polynomial advice length, every classical advice family and every uniform quantum algorithm. A separation of promise problems alone does not automatically meet this card’s retained total-language target. Oracle separations, a difficult-to-describe state, or an advantage for advice selected after seeing the input do not suffice.

title: Classical hardness of approximate Boson Sampling
summary: Boson Sampling records the occupations of indistinguishable photons after an ideal passive optical network. The selected question asks whether no uniform classical randomized algorithm can reproduce every such distribution to any requested total-variation error in time polynomial in the input size and inverse error. The distribution includes collisions and is defined by squared permanents with factorial normalization. Known hierarchy-collapse consequences and newer average-case results have explicit assumptions or use different error guarantees. An unconditional answer would establish or refute a fundamental classical limitation for a restricted quantum sampling experiment.
formal: Is the following classical sampling impossibility statement true? There is no single probabilistic classical Turing machine \(M\) and polynomial \(p\) such that, for every valid ideal Boson Sampling input \(B\) defined below and every integer \(k\ge2\), the machine \(M(B,1^k)\) outputs an occupation vector with law \(Q_{B,k}\), always halts in at most \(p(|B|+k)\) steps, and satisfies \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Q_{B,k},D_B)=\frac12\sum_{s\in\Omega_{m,n}}|Q_{B,k}(s)-D_B(s)|\le\frac1k?\] The target distribution is \[D_B(s)=\frac{|\operatorname{Per}(A_s)|^2}{\prod_{j=1}^{m}s_j!},\qquad A=\operatorname{GS}(B),\qquad \Omega_{m,n}=\{s\in\mathbb N_0^m:\sum_js_j=n\}.\] Thus the approximation must meet every requested error tolerance, in time polynomial in the explicit network description and the inverse tolerance. The claim is unconditional and concerns all valid inputs, rather than only typical random optical networks.
definitions:
There are \(n\ge1\) indistinguishable photons and \(m\ge n\) modes. A mode is one orthogonal single-particle state. Initially each of the first \(n\) modes contains one photon and every other mode is empty. The network is ideal passive linear optics: it preserves photon number and acts on the single-particle mode space by an \(m\times m\) unitary matrix \(U\). It has no loss, noise, distinguishability of photons, intermediate measurements, adaptive feed-forward or postselection. The output records the photon count in every mode. Collisions, meaning two or more photons in a mode, are included.

Only the first \(n\) columns of \(U\) matter for this input. Write these columns as \(A\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}\), so \(A^\dagger A=I_n\), where \(\dagger\) denotes conjugate transpose. Any such column isometry can be completed to a unitary, and the distribution below is independent of that completion. The input therefore specifies this part of the optical network rather than an exponentially large many-photon transition matrix.

Here is an explicit finite encoding of the matrix convention in the source's footnote19. The input \(B\) contains \(m,n\) and every entry of an \(m\times n\) complex matrix. Real and imaginary parts are signed dyadic rationals, each stored as an integer numerator and a nonnegative denominator exponent in unary: \(a/2^b\). All numerator bits, signs, exponents and matrix entries count toward \(|B|\). Dimensions and lists are explicitly delimited. A valid input satisfies \[\|B^\dagger B-I_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\frac12,\] where the operator norm is \(\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Cv\|_2\). This promise ensures that the columns are linearly independent. It is a convenient fixed conditioning threshold for the finite encoding, not a physical noise parameter. Define the represented ideal isometry by exact ordered Gram–Schmidt orthonormalization: for the columns \(b_j\) of \(B\), set \[v_j=b_j-\sum_{i<j}a_i(a_i^\dagger b_j),\qquad a_j=v_j/\sqrt{v_j^\dagger v_j},\] using the positive square root, and let \(A=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\). These equations define the ideal mathematical distribution exactly; they do not give the classical sampler a real-arithmetic oracle or make numerical computation free. Finer explicit dyadic approximations can represent arbitrary optical isometries to arbitrary precision. The encoding spells out the source's correction of a finite-precision matrix to an isometry; its chosen threshold does not impose a restriction on the number of photons or on network depth.

For \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_m)\in\Omega_{m,n}\), form the square \(n\times n\) matrix \(A_s\) by repeating row \(j\) of \(A\) exactly \(s_j\) times, in increasing row order. For an \(n\times n\) matrix \(C\), its permanent is \[\operatorname{Per}(C)=\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n C_{i,\pi(i)},\] where \(S_n\) is the set of permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The factorial convention is \(0!=1\). The bosonic transition rule gives the displayed \(D_B\); because \(A\) is an isometry, these nonnegative probabilities sum to one. The output lists all \(m\) occupation numbers in binary. No requirement to enumerate the whole distribution or to estimate each exponentially small probability is imposed.

The classical machine is a uniform multitape Turing machine with independent fair random bits. It receives the complete explicit finite input, has no advice, quantum operations or oracle, and its polynomial runtime bound holds for every input and every random tape. Correctness is required only on valid matrices. For each such input, its output must lie in \(\Omega_{m,n}\). The law \(Q_{B,k}\) averages over all its random bits; there is no separate high-probability event certifying closeness. Total variation compares this full output law with the target distribution. The polynomial and machine are fixed independently of \(m,n,B,k\).

The unary accuracy input \(1^k\) requests error at most \(1/k\). This gives the arbitrary-error convention \(\varepsilon>0\) with runtime polynomial in input length and \(1/\varepsilon\): choose \(k=\max\{2,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\}\). It does not require polynomial dependence on \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\). Every \(m\ge n\) is allowed, with its full matrix encoding charged; in particular the class includes the dilute, polynomially many-mode families used in the original hardness results. It does not claim that every individual network is hard. Easy subfamilies are compatible with the universal-sampler impossibility statement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the impossibility statement, or a complete Lean-checked refutation by a uniform classical probabilistic machine with one polynomial bound satisfying all input, output and accuracy quantifiers above. A positive answer must rule out every such machine without assuming a separation of complexity classes or an unproved permanent conjecture. A conditional polynomial-hierarchy consequence, hardness of computing an individual probability, an exact-sampling lower bound, a multiplicative-error result, a fixed numerical error guarantee, or experiments on finitely many networks do not settle this total-variation question. This is an exact yes/no question about arbitrarily requested sampling accuracy; the benchmark's numerical-value tolerance does not replace its quantified error requirement.

title: Black-box unitary synthesis
summary: The problem asks whether every quantum unitary can be implemented efficiently using an appropriately chosen Boolean oracle. One fixed circuit family must work for all unitaries, with the desired unitary encoded only in the oracle. The implementation must work on arbitrary inputs, including states entangled with an untouched reference. Both total computation and coherent oracle access must remain polynomial in the number of input qubits. Known exponential-time implementations and restricted-query lower bounds leave the general question unresolved.
formal: Is there one polynomial-time uniform family of polynomial-size quantum oracle circuits \(\{A_n\}_{n\ge1}\) such that, for every \(n\)-qubit unitary matrix \(U\), some Boolean function \(f_U:\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\to\{0,1\}\) makes the channel implemented by \(A_n^{f_U}\) approximate \(\rho\mapsto U\rho U^\dagger\) within diamond distance \(1/10\)? The oracle input length \(m(n)\), total number of qubits, number of ordinary gates, and number of oracle calls must all be bounded by one fixed polynomial in \(n\). The circuit family is chosen before \(U\); only the Boolean oracle may depend on \(U\). This is the fixed-constant-error version of black-box unitary synthesis.
definitions:
An \(n\)-qubit system has state space \(\mathbb C^{2^n}\). A unitary matrix satisfies \(U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=I\), where \(\dagger\) denotes conjugate transpose. A density matrix is a positive semidefinite matrix with trace one and describes a possibly mixed quantum state.

Each circuit receives an arbitrary \(n\)-qubit input, initializes all additional qubits to zero, and outputs a specified \(n\)-qubit register. Other registers are discarded, inducing a quantum channel \(\Phi_{A_n^{f_U}}\). The ordinary gate set is Hadamard \(H=2^{-1/2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), the phase gate \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), its inverse, and controlled NOT. Gates may act on any named wires. One oracle call applies \(|z,b\rangle\mapsto|z,b\mathbin{\oplus}f_U(z)\rangle\) to the address and answer registers, including on superpositions; \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. All calls use the same fixed Boolean function. Oracle inputs and answer registers count toward the qubit bound. The oracle's own computation is uncharged, but every ordinary gate and each oracle call counts toward circuit size. General adaptive quantum computation is allowed through its equivalent coherent circuit representation with polynomially many ancillas.

Uniformity means that a single deterministic Turing machine, on input \(1^n\), outputs the complete gate and wire list in time polynomial in \(n\). It receives no description of \(U\). The oracle function may be arbitrary, and no efficient procedure for computing it or deriving it from \(U\) is required. No additional quantum advice, input-dependent initial ancilla, postselection, or other oracle is available.

For channels with \(n\)-qubit input and output, define their diamond distance by \[D_\diamond(\Phi,\Psi)=\tfrac12\sup_{\rho}\|((\Phi-\Psi)\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(\rho)\|_1,\] where \(R\) is an untouched \(n\)-qubit reference register and the supremum ranges over density matrices on input and reference together. The trace norm is \(\|M\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{M^\dagger M}\). The desired inequality holds for every input, including one entangled with the reference. The constant \(1/10\) is the allowed channel-approximation error, not an acceptance-probability or heralded-success condition. Global phases of \(U\) are irrelevant to its channel.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a universal efficient oracle-circuit family exists, or a proof of its negation. A positive proof must supply the uniform circuit family and show the existence of a suitable Boolean oracle for every unitary while meeting all resource and diamond-distance bounds. A negative proof must rule out polynomially many sequential oracle calls with polynomial total computation. A lower bound restricted to one query, parallel queries, or a prescribed oracle encoding does not suffice.

title: Efficient approximation of the optimal dihedral measurement
summary: The selected question asks for efficient approximation of one explicitly defined optimal quantum measurement. Its input space contains several dihedral coset-state registers, and its outcomes are candidate hidden shifts plus a complementary outcome. The measurement is defined by the inverse square root of the sum of the ensemble states, with an explicit convention on its kernel. The required circuit must reproduce its outcome distribution uniformly on valid inputs to any requested inverse-polynomial accuracy. Known subset-sum connections constrain particular unitary implementations and do not establish hardness for every measurement circuit.
formal: Can the specific pretty good measurement \(\{E_0,\ldots,E_{N-1},E_{\bot}\}\) defined below be approximated by uniform polynomial-size quantum circuits to every requested inverse-polynomial accuracy? Precisely, does there exist one deterministic circuit generator and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every integer \(N\ge2\), number of copies \(k\ge1\), and precision parameter \(m\ge2\), it runs in time at most \(p(\lceil\log_2N\rceil+k+m)\) and produces a circuit with at most that many gates and ancilla qubits whose output distribution satisfies \[\sup_{\sigma}\frac12\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z_N\cup\{\bot\}}\left|\Pr[C_{N,k,m}(\sigma)=j]-\operatorname{Tr}(E_j\sigma)\right|\le\frac1m?\] The supremum ranges over all input density matrices on \((\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^N)^{\otimes k}\). The circuit receives one such state and returns one classical outcome. The selected target concerns this concrete measurement, without requiring a particular unitary realization or a Subset Sum algorithm.
definitions:
Write \(\mathbb Z_N=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}\), with addition modulo \(N\). For a hidden shift \(s\in\mathbb Z_N\) and \(x\in\mathbb Z_N\), let \[|c_x^{(s)}\rangle=\frac{|0,x\rangle+|1,x+s\rangle}{\sqrt2},\qquad \rho_s=\frac1N\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z_N}|c_x^{(s)}\rangle\langle c_x^{(s)}|.\] Thus \(\rho_s\) is the mixed state obtained by a uniform unknown coset offset. For \(k\) independent samples with the same shift, the state is \(\tau_s=\rho_s^{\otimes k}\) on \(\mathcal H_{N,k}=(\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^N)^{\otimes k}\). The discrimination ensemble assigns prior probability \(1/N\) to each shift \(s\). Both this prior and the average over coset offsets are part of the definition; neither \(s\) nor the offsets are supplied to the implementing circuit.

For this ensemble define \[G=\sum_{s\in\mathbb Z_N}\tau_s,\qquad E_s=G^{-1/2}\tau_sG^{-1/2},\qquad E_{\bot}=I-P_G.\] The inverse square root is the inverse on the support: if \(G=\sum_\lambda\lambda P_\lambda\) is its spectral decomposition, then \(G^{-1/2}=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda^{-1/2}P_\lambda\), with value zero on the kernel, and \(P_G=\sum_{\lambda>0}P_\lambda\). Every \(E_s\) is positive semidefinite and \(\sum_sE_s=P_G\). Adding \(E_{\bot}\) makes the sum the identity on the entire input space. A positive operator-valued measure is such a finite collection of positive semidefinite operators summing to identity; its outcome probabilities on state \(\sigma\) are \(\operatorname{Tr}(E_j\sigma)\). A density matrix is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one. Hermitian means \(\sigma=\sigma^\dagger\), with dagger conjugate transpose, and positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\sigma v\ge0\) for all vectors \(v\). The above expression, including its kernel convention, fully specifies the measurement even when \(G\) is singular. On each \(\tau_s\), outcome \(\bot\) has probability zero. The source associates that complementary outcome with the trivial hidden subgroup, but optimality is asserted for the uniform ensemble of order-two subgroups.

The classical generator receives \(N\) in binary and \(k,m\) in unary. This makes the error tolerance \(1/m\) and the polynomial dependence on its reciprocal explicit. The target does not demand polynomial dependence on \(\log m\). Each \(N\)-dimensional register is embedded in \(q=\lceil\log_2N\rceil\) qubits by the binary basis encodings of \(0,\ldots,N-1\); the input therefore uses \(k(q+1)\) qubits. No correctness condition is imposed on states outside that valid encoded subspace. The given state can be mixed, entangled across copies, and unrelated to an actual hidden shift; the error bound specifies the measurement on its whole valid input space. The circuit receives no further copies or a state-preparation oracle. It may consume the input, and no condition is imposed on the remaining quantum state after it outputs the label. In particular, this is a guarantee for classical outcome distributions, not for a prescribed post-measurement state or a particular coherent circuit extension.

Ancillas start in zero, and the circuit uses the fixed gates \[H=2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\quad \mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\oplus c\rangle.\] These act on the indicated wires and as identity elsewhere; \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two and \(i^2=-1\). A final computational-basis measurement produces a binary outcome label, with \(0,\ldots,N-1\) interpreted as shifts and every remaining label mapped to \(\bot\). Ordinary finite gates and classical bit operations have unit cost, so no arbitrary real matrix is supplied as one free gate. There is no nonuniform advice, extra oracle, postselection or unbounded repeat-until-success loop. The displayed half-sum is total variation distance between the actual and specified outcome distributions; it is the largest difference in probabilities of an event defined by a set of labels. The requirement is uniform in the input state and every finite \(N,k,m\), with one polynomial and generator for the whole family. It asks for a sample from the distribution, not an explicit list of its \(N+1\) probabilities.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the displayed uniform approximation family exists, including the circuit-generation and gate bounds and its total-variation guarantee, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such polynomially bounded family exists. A negative proof must cover all implementations of these outcome probabilities, not merely a prescribed subset-sum-basis unitary or a chosen extension to a larger Hilbert space. A different measurement with a good success probability for recovering the hidden shift does not by itself implement the specified POVM. Agreement only on the average success rate, or only on the coset ensemble without the uniform-input error guarantee, is insufficient for this precise implementation target. Exponential dependence on \(\log N\), \(k\), or the unary precision parameter does not meet the resource bound. This is a yes/no efficiency question with accuracy quantified in its definition, not a numerical output problem requiring only a fixed additive tolerance.

title: A finite quantum gate set with decision power strictly between P and BQP
summary: A finite quantum gate set determines which polynomial-size uniform circuits can be built from its operations. The question asks for a bounded-error decision class strictly larger than P and strictly smaller than BQP. The gates must also escape every common one-qubit conjugate of the Clifford group. The card fixes algebraic gates, computational-basis inputs and one final measured output bit to make the computational model precise. Known hardness results for sampling restricted circuits do not establish this stronger unconditional decision-class separation.
formal:
Does there exist a finite set \(G\) of constant-arity unitary quantum gates with algebraic complex matrix entries such that
\[
\mathrm{P}\subsetneq Q_G\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP},
\]
and \(G\) is not contained in any common one-qubit conjugate of the Clifford gates? The bounded-error decision class \(Q_G\), the circuit interface, and the conjugation exclusion are defined below. Both strict containments are unconditional parts of the assertion.
definitions:
A \(k\)-qubit gate is a \(2^k\)-by-\(2^k\) complex unitary matrix, for an integer \(k\ge1\). The set \(G\) is finite and independent of input length; its maximum arity is therefore a constant. Each matrix entry is algebraic over \(\mathbb Q\), and each gate can be specified exactly by its minimal polynomials and isolating data for the real and imaginary parts. These fixed descriptions are not input-dependent advice. Algebraicity is an explicit editorial finite-description convention.

A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) is in \(Q_G\) if one deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine, on each input \(x\), produces a polynomial-size circuit description \(C_x\) with polynomially many qubits, a computational-basis initial string \(b_x\), and one designated output qubit. Initialize the state to \(|b_x\rangle\). A gate from \(G\) may be applied to any ordered tuple of distinct qubits of the correct arity, with identity on all other qubits. There are no geometry or depth restrictions beyond the polynomial size bound. At the end, measure only the designated output qubit in the computational basis. Require
\[
x\in L\Longrightarrow\Pr[C_x\text{ outputs }1]\ge2/3,
\qquad
x\notin L\Longrightarrow\Pr[C_x\text{ outputs }1]\le1/3.
\]
The generator and polynomial bound may depend on \(L\) and \(G\), but not nonuniformly on input length. They count all classical bit operations. The generator may prepare additional \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\) qubits by specifying them in \(b_x\), but no other initial states. Wires may be named arbitrarily. Only gates listed in \(G\) are available: inverses, controlled variants, and arbitrary one-qubit gates are not free. Intermediate measurements, postselection, classically controlled quantum branches, quantum advice, and joint-output sampling followed by unrestricted classical postprocessing are not part of this interface. The final single-bit output convention makes the selected decision target precise.

Use the shared definition of [P](definitions.html#p-np). Define \(\mathrm{BQP}\) by the same uniform bounded-error circuit convention using the universal gates
\[
H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\quad
\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle.
\]
Classical preprocessing and basis preparation imply \(\mathrm{P}\subseteq Q_G\). Fixed algebraic gates are efficiently approximable, so \(Q_G\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\). The strictness requirements mean that some language in \(Q_G\) is not in \(\mathrm{P}\), and some language in \(\mathrm{BQP}\) is not in \(Q_G\). Merely failing to densely generate every unitary is insufficient, since encoded computation can still give full BQP power.

For the Clifford exclusion, let
\[
X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},
\]
and let \(\mathcal P_k=\{i^j P_1\otimes\cdots\otimes P_k:j\in\{0,1,2,3\},\ P_i\in\{I,X,Y,Z\}\}\) be the Pauli group. The Clifford group consists of the unitaries \(V\) satisfying \(V\mathcal P_kV^\dagger=\mathcal P_k\); global phase is immaterial. Require that there is no one-qubit unitary \(U\) such that, for every \(g\in G\) of arity \(k\),
\[
U^{\otimes k}g(U^\dagger)^{\otimes k}
\]
is Clifford. The same \(U\) must be tested for all gates, but it may be any complex unitary, not only an algebraic one. The condition is a structural exclusion, not an additional allowed operation.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of existence of a finite algebraic gate set satisfying both strict decision-class containments and the common-conjugate Clifford exclusion. Conditional sampling hardness, universality only after postselection, a separation for nonuniform circuits, or physical nonuniversality alone does not settle the statement. A positive proof must establish both strictness assertions in the specified uniform single-output model.

title: Parity versus \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) with shallow quantum preprocessing
summary: Parity is a basic function that small constant-depth classical circuits cannot approximate well on uniformly random inputs. This project asks whether a shallow quantum preprocessing stage can remove that limitation when its measured output is passed to a classical AC0 circuit. The conjecture concerns constant-depth quantum circuits with bounded-fan-in gates, followed by the specified classical postprocessing. Any approximation guarantee must account for both the random input and the randomness of quantum measurement. The single-output lower bound of Sun and Wang leaves parity correlation with arbitrary polynomial-size readout of all qubits unresolved.
formal: Does every polynomial-size constant-depth classical \(\mathrm{AC}^0\) circuit with polynomial-size constant-depth quantum preprocessing have asymptotically zero correlation with parity? Precisely, for every polynomial \(p\), constant \(d\in\mathbb N\), and sequence \((C_n,f_n)_{n\ge1}\) satisfying the model and bounds below, is \[\left|2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\ \sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{n+m(n)}}\Pr[C_n(x)=y]f_n(y)(-1)^{\sum_{i=1}^nx_i}\right|\longrightarrow0\quad(n\longrightarrow\infty)?\] Here \(m(n)\le p(n)\) zero-initialized ancillary qubits are allowed, both circuit stages have depth at most \(d\), and both have polynomial size bounded by \(p(n)\). There is no geometric locality, uniformity or clean-ancilla condition.
definitions:
For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), parity in the sign convention is \(\operatorname{Par}_n(x)=(-1)^{x_1+\cdots+x_n}\). The quantum circuit \(C_n\) begins in the computational-basis state \(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{m(n)}\rangle\). A qubit is a two-dimensional complex Hilbert space, and the full register has state space \((\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes(n+m(n))}\). A gate is any unitary on one or two qubits, acting as identity on the others. Unitary means \(U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=I\). Gates are arranged in layers, with disjoint supports in each layer. The number of layers is the quantum depth, at most \(d\); the total number of nonidentity gates is at most \(p(n)\). Any two wires may interact. The ancillary count is separately bounded by \(p(n)\), including ancillary wires that are only measured.

All output wires are measured once in the computational basis. If the product of the layers is \(U_n\), the resulting bit string \(y\) has probability \[\Pr[C_n(x)=y]=|\langle y|U_n|x,0^{m(n)}\rangle|^2.\] There are no intermediate measurements, adaptive gate choices or postselection. No ancillary wire has to return to zero, and garbage is allowed. The initial ancillas are zeros, not arbitrary input-dependent advice states. Gates may depend on \(n\) and may have arbitrary complex entries satisfying unitarity: this is the source's nonuniform circuit lower-bound model, not a uniform algorithm with free real-number input. Consequently no fixed finite gate alphabet or efficient gate-description requirement is imposed.

The classical postprocessor \(f_n:\{0,1\}^{n+m(n)}\to\{-1,1\}\) is a finite Boolean circuit of unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates and fan-in-one NOT gates, with constants permitted. Its underlying output bit \(b\) is interpreted as \((-1)^b\). Classical depth is the greatest number of gates on an input-to-output path and is at most \(d\). Its number of gates is at most \(p(n)\); repeated identical incoming wires can be omitted. Including wires in the size instead gives an equivalent polynomial-size family, since the vertex count is polynomial. There are no parity gates, arbitrary Boolean lookup-table gates, threshold gates or extra classical advice inputs. The entire classical circuit is allowed to depend nonuniformly on \(n\).

The two stages are composed once: measure the quantum output, then apply the deterministic classical circuit to that outcome. The correlation is the expectation of \(f_n(Y)\operatorname{Par}_n(X)\) when \(X\) is uniform on all \(n\)-bit strings and, conditional on \(X=x\), \(Y\) follows the Born probabilities above. There is no promise on the input Hamming weight. The average success probability at computing sign parity is \((1+\operatorname{Corr}_n)/2\). Correlation is signed; the displayed limit of its absolute value is equivalent to the source's limit \(\operatorname{Corr}_n\to0\). It also rules out a persistent advantage after negating the output.

The polynomial, depth and circuit sequence are fixed before taking the limit, but are otherwise arbitrary. Equivalently, for each such choice and every real \(\varepsilon>0\), there must be an \(N\) such that \(|\operatorname{Corr}_n|<\varepsilon\) for all \(n\ge N\). No particular rate of decay is requested. A refutation can consist of one polynomially bounded sequence and one \(\varepsilon>0\) with \(|\operatorname{Corr}_n|\ge\varepsilon\) at infinitely many input lengths; constant correlation at every length is sufficient but is not necessary for a negative answer.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified zero-correlation limit, or a complete Lean-checked refutation under the same gate, ancilla, depth, size and average-input conventions. A positive result must allow every polynomially bounded number of zero ancillas and every polynomial-size classical postprocessor. Ancilla-free preprocessing, linear-size classical circuits, geometric restrictions, uniform families, a finite restricted gate set or a worst-case statement about one input do not cover the whole conjecture. A negative result must supply a circuit sequence with a proved failure of convergence; search or sampling advantages for another task do not suffice. This is an exact asymptotic proposition, not a request to estimate a correlation at finitely many sizes.

title: Martin’s conjecture
summary: Turing-invariant functions send mutually computable reals to mutually computable outputs. Under determinacy and dependent choice, Martin’s conjecture predicts a rigid hierarchy for these operations when they are compared on Turing cones. Part I says every invariant function is constant in degree on a cone or computes its input on a cone. Part II says all operations above the identity are prewellordered, with the Turing jump increasing their ordinal rank by exactly one. Known uniform and order-preserving cases, choice-based counterexamples and conditional results for other output degrees leave the full stated conjecture unresolved in the checked sources.
formal: Assume \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\). Is the following conjunction true for all total Turing-invariant functions \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\)? Part I: every such \(f\) is constant in Turing degree on a cone or computes its input on a cone. Part II: the relation \(\leq_M\) of Turing reducibility on a cone prewellorders the set \(\mathcal F\) of all such functions above the identity on a cone, and for every \(f\in\mathcal F\), its pointwise Turing jump \(f'\) has rank exactly \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)+1\) in that same prewellorder. All functions, cones, ordinals and quantifiers are interpreted within the stated set-theoretic universe.
definitions:
Write \(\omega=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) and \(2^{\omega}=\{x:\omega\to\{0,1\}\}\). Such a real is identified with the subset \(\{n:x(n)=1\}\) of \(\omega\). Fix an acceptable effective enumeration \((\Phi_e)_{e\in\omega}\) of ordinary oracle Turing programs with natural-number inputs and outputs. The oracle answers membership queries in a real. Define \(x\leq_T y\) to mean that some index \(e\) satisfies \(\Phi_e^y(n)\downarrow=x(n)\) for every \(n\in\omega\), with no time bound. The single index computes the entire real, and may depend on \(x,y\). Define \(x\equiv_T y\) by mutual reducibility. A Turing degree is an equivalence class for \(\equiv_T\). The jump \(y'\) is the characteristic real of \(\{e:\Phi_e^y(e)\text{ halts}\}\). Any acceptable effective numbering gives the same induced operation on degrees.

A total function \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\) is Turing-invariant when \(\forall x,y:\ x\equiv_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\equiv_T f(y)\). No computability, measurability, Borel definability, order preservation or uniform production of reduction indices is required. The quantifiers concern functions on reals with this invariance property; no choice of a representative from every Turing degree is assumed.

For \(a\in2^{\omega}\), the cone with base \(a\) is \(C_a=\{x\in2^{\omega}:a\leq_T x\}\). Being constant in degree on a cone means
\[\exists a,b\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\equiv_T b.\]
Being above the identity on a cone means
\[\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ x\leq_T f(x).\]
The base may depend on \(f\). Constancy is equality of degrees, not literal equality of output reals. A cone requirement holds for every real in that cone, not merely infinitely many reals or a set of full ordinary Lebesgue measure.

For invariant \(f,g\), define
\[f\leq_M g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\leq_T g(x).\]
The base may depend on both functions; no single base must work for all comparisons. Set \(f\equiv_M g\) when both \(f\leq_M g\) and \(g\leq_M f\). Let \(\mathrm{id}(x)=x\) and \(\mathcal F=\{f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}: f\text{ is Turing-invariant and }\mathrm{id}\leq_M f\}\). The prewellorder clause means that \(\leq_M\) is reflexive, transitive and total on \(\mathcal F\), and that the induced order on the set \(\mathcal F/{\equiv_M}\) is a well-order: every nonempty subset of that quotient has a least member. Its strict order is \([g]<[f]\) when \(g\leq_M f\) and \(f\not\leq_M g\). When this clause holds, \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)\) is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly below \([f]\), with its least class having rank zero. The pointwise jump is \(f'(x)=(f(x))'\). The \(+1\) in Part II is ordinal successor, and the rank is computed in the full quotient above the identity, not a selected definable subclass.

The background \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. Full dependent choice \(\mathsf{DC}\) asserts that for every nonempty set \(S\), every relation \(R\subseteq S\times S\) with \(\forall s\in S\;\exists t\in S:\ sRt\), and every \(s_0\in S\), there is a sequence \((s_n)_{n\in\omega}\) starting at \(s_0\) with \(s_nRs_{n+1}\) for all \(n\). The axiom of determinacy \(\mathsf{AD}\) asserts that for every set \(W\subseteq\omega^{\omega}\), the following perfect-information game is determined. Players I and II alternate choosing natural numbers, with I moving at even-numbered stages starting at zero; I wins exactly when the resulting sequence belongs to \(W\). A strategy assigns a next move to every finite history at that player’s turn, and is winning if every infinite play compatible with it is won by that player. Determined means that one player has such a winning strategy. No regularity condition is imposed on \(W\). These are internal set-theoretic axioms; the full axiom of choice is not added to them.
