answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of both parts of the conjunction under \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\), or a refutation of at least one part under that same background. A refutation of Part I must establish the existence of an invariant function that is neither constant in degree on any cone nor above the identity on any cone. A refutation of Part II must establish failure of the stated full prewellorder or, when that prewellorder exists, failure of the exact jump-successor clause. A result only for uniformly invariant, Borel, regressive or order-preserving functions does not prove the full conjunction. Counterexamples obtained with the full axiom of choice do not refute the stated determinacy version. The Lean formalization must represent the set-theoretic background faithfully, for example through an internal set universe and its satisfaction relation, with all reals and functions interpreted there; importing ambient choice into that universe and deriving a contradiction with determinacy is not a proof of this target. No unproved classification or uniformity principle may be substituted for a required part.

title: Busy Beaver \(\mathrm{BB}(6)\)
summary: \(\mathrm{BB}(6)=S(6)\) is the maximum number of steps taken by a halting six-state binary Turing machine from the blank tape. The required answer supplies one complete transition table and Lean-checked proofs of its halting and universal runtime maximality. That proved-halting machine’s runtime names the exact integer without requiring a decimal expansion, closed form or execution trace. The five-state value is established, while six-state machines already exhibit enormous halting runtimes and unresolved arithmetic behavior. The September 2026 project pages still report the value as unknown; lower bounds, heuristics and a shrinking holdout list do not certify the requested maximum.
formal:
Determine the exact six-state binary Busy Beaver runtime \(\mathrm{BB}(6)=S(6)\) by giving a concrete machine \(M_*\in\mathcal M_6\) and proving
\[M_*\text{ halts on the blank tape},\qquad
\forall M\in\mathcal M_6:\ M\text{ halts on the blank tape}\ \Longrightarrow\ T(M)\le T(M_*).\]
Here \(\mathcal M_6\) is the finite class of deterministic six-nonhalting-state, two-symbol Turing machines defined below, and \(T(M)\) is the number of transitions through the first entry into the separate halting state. The complete transition table of \(M_*\), together with proofs of its halting and universal maximality, specifies the answer exactly as \(S(6)=T(M_*)\).
definitions:
Machine. Fix the nonhalting states \(Q=\{A,B,C,D,E,F\}\), one additional halting state \(Z\notin Q\), and the tape alphabet \(\{0,1\}\). A machine is a total transition function
\[\delta:Q\times\{0,1\}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}\times\{-1,+1\}\times(Q\cup\{Z\}).\]
Thus its description has exactly twelve entries. The three outputs specify the symbol to write, a move of exactly one cell left or right, and the next state, respectively. There are no stationary moves, extra tapes or transitions out of \(Z\). Unreachable states and entries are allowed. Different tables need not have different behavior; no symmetry reduction is imposed on the quantified class \(\mathcal M_6\).

Execution. The tape is indexed by all integers. A configuration consists of a state \(q\), a head position \(h\in\mathbb Z\), and a tape function \(\tau:\mathbb Z\to\{0,1\}\). At time zero, \(q=A\), \(h=0\), and \(\tau(i)=0\) for every integer \(i\). If \(q\ne Z\) and \(\delta(q,\tau(h))=(b,d,q')\), one transition replaces \(\tau(h)\) by \(b\), leaves every other tape cell unchanged, replaces the head position by \(h+d\), and enters \(q'\). Execution stops immediately on entering \(Z\); that final write-and-move transition is included in the count. Each transition costs one step, irrespective of head position or time elapsed. There is no external input, randomness or resource limit.

Halting time and maximum. A machine halts if its unique execution first enters \(Z\) at some positive integer time. Only for such a machine, \(T(M)\) denotes this least time. Let \(\mathcal H_6\subseteq\mathcal M_6\) be the halting machines. Define
\[S(6)=\max\{T(M):M\in\mathcal H_6\}.\]
There are \(28^{12}\) tables in \(\mathcal M_6\), since each entry has \(2\cdot2\cdot7\) choices. The halting subset is nonempty, since a table can send \((A,0)\) directly to \(Z\). Hence the maximum exists as a finite positive integer. No value of \(T\) on a nonhalting machine is used in the statement or the submitted certificate.

Answer representation. The runtime of a specified, proved-halting table defines an exact integer through a terminating step-counting computation, even when actually evaluating it is infeasible. The accepted answer need not separately evaluate that computation. In this card, \(\mathrm{BB}\) always means the runtime maximum \(S\), not the distinct extremal function \(\Sigma\) that maximizes the number of ones on the final tape.

Notation in the context. For positive integer \(k\), \(2\uparrow\uparrow k\) is a tower of \(k\) twos, equivalently \(2\uparrow\uparrow1=2\) and \(2\uparrow\uparrow(k+1)=2^{(2\uparrow\uparrow k)}\). Three arrows mean iteration of this tower operation: \(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow1=2\) and \(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow(k+1)=2\uparrow\uparrow(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow k)\).
answer_criterion:
Supply the complete twelve-entry transition table of a particular \(M_*\in\mathcal M_6\), with complete mathematically correct proofs checked in Lean that it halts from the stated blank initial configuration and that every halting \(M\in\mathcal M_6\) has \(T(M)\le T(M_*)\). These two proofs must establish the exact equality \(\mathrm{BB}(6)=T(M_*)\). This is the exact witness criterion, superseding the default numerical tolerance for this card only.

The witness runtime is an accepted exact finite description of the integer. A simple closed form, decimal expansion, separately evaluated integer literal or full execution trace is not required. A candidate machine without both proofs, an estimated runtime, a one-sided bound, a list of undecided machines or a restatement of the defining maximum is insufficient. Any reduction to representative transition tables must itself be justified as covering the full stated class. A result for a different alphabet, state count, tape convention or final-tape score does not settle this target.

title: Rigidity of the Turing degrees
summary: Turing degrees identify oracle sets that compute one another, and their order compares relative computational power. The question asks whether every bijection of all degrees that preserves and reflects this order fixes every degree. The target allows arbitrary set-theoretic automorphisms and requires a complete Lean proof of rigidity or of a nontrivial global automorphism. Known jump, cone, representation and local-structure results impose substantial restrictions without settling the entire order. Cooper’s historical full-solution claim remains explicitly separated from verified partial results, and the card records uncertain status because its construction was reported as unverified.
formal:
Let \(D_T=\mathcal P(\mathbb N)/{\equiv_T}\) be the set of all Turing degrees, ordered by Turing reducibility. Is this order rigid? The exact assertion is
\[\forall\pi:D_T\to D_T,\quad \Bigl[\pi\text{ is bijective}\ \land\ \forall a,b\in D_T\,\bigl(a\le_T b\iff\pi(a)\le_T\pi(b)\bigr)\Bigr]\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall a\in D_T\,\pi(a)=a.\]
The domain is the full quotient of all subsets of the standard natural numbers. The quantifier over \(\pi\) ranges over arbitrary functions on this quotient in ordinary classical set theory, with ZFC as the set-theoretic background.
definitions:
Write \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), \(\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\) for its full power set, and \(\chi_A:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}\) for a set's characteristic function. A deterministic oracle Turing machine is a finite program with ordinary unbounded work tapes and an additional operation that receives \(\chi_B(k)\) when it asks whether \(k\) belongs to the oracle set \(B\). Each terminating computation takes finitely many steps and makes finitely many queries; no uniform bound on their number, time or space is imposed. Natural inputs and queries have the usual finite binary encodings. Any fixed effective enumeration \((\Phi_e)_{e\in\mathbb N}\) of all such programs gives
\[A\le_T B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists e\in\mathbb N\ \forall n\in\mathbb N,\ \Phi_e^B(n)\text{ halts with output }\chi_A(n).\]
The same index must work on every input, but may depend on \(A,B\). Programs contain no additional oracle, infinite advice or noncomputable constants. All subsets are eligible oracle sets, including noncomputable ones.

Define \(A\equiv_T B\) by \(A\le_T B\) and \(B\le_T A\). A degree \([A]\) is the equivalence class of \(A\), and \([A]\le_T[B]\) means \(A\le_T B\); this is independent of the representatives. Equality of degrees is mutual reducibility, not equality of their representatives. The set \(D_T\) includes every degree, not just degrees containing computably enumerable sets, arithmetical degrees, or degrees below a selected bound. A set is computably enumerable if a program with no oracle lists exactly its members, with arbitrary repetition and delay allowed.

An order automorphism is a total injective and surjective map \(\pi:D_T\to D_T\) that preserves and reflects every reducibility comparison. It need not be computable, definable, continuous or induced by a prescribed operation on sets. A representation \(F:\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\to\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\), if used to specify it, must satisfy \([F(A)]=\pi([A])\) for every \(A\); the representation itself need not be bijective. The order language has only equality and \(\le_T\). Jump preservation is a known consequence of this order structure, not an extra assumption in the target.

For the dated context, \(\mathbf 0=[\varnothing]\). The join \([A]\vee[B]\) is \([A\oplus B]\), where \(A\oplus B=\{2n:n\in A\}\cup\{2n+1:n\in B\}\). Set \(A'=\{e:\Phi_e^A(e)\text{ halts}\}\); the Turing jump is \([A]'=[A']\), and \(\mathbf 0''=(\mathbf 0')'\). These degrees are independent of the chosen effective machine enumeration. The upper cone with base \(b\) is \(\{a:b\le_T a\}\). Its complement includes both degrees below \(b\) and degrees incomparable with \(b\).

The assertion concerns the degree order built from the full power set in the ambient universe, not a selected countable model's internally computed degrees. The continuum hypothesis and determinacy are not hypotheses of the target. There are no finite input sizes, efficiency bounds or numerical approximation parameters in this structural question.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed universal assertion or its exact negation. A positive answer must apply to every set-theoretic order automorphism of the entire \(D_T\). A negative answer must prove
\[\exists\pi:D_T\to D_T\ \exists a\in D_T,\quad\pi\text{ is bijective},\quad \forall b,c\in D_T\,\bigl(b\le_Tc\iff\pi(b)\le_T\pi(c)\bigr),\quad\pi(a)\ne a.\]
An existence proof is sufficient; no computable formula for the automorphism is required. A construction on representatives must establish that it descends to this full quotient and has all the stated properties. Proving rigidity only on a proper substructure or for a restricted family of maps does not meet the criterion. Nor does a non-surjective order embedding or a permutation of representatives that fixes every degree. Both answer directions retain the stated classical background without an unproved extra hypothesis; relative consistency or independence alone does not assert either of these two mathematical conclusions. All supporting formalized definitions and theorems needed for the chosen direction must be included or supplied by verified Lean libraries.

title: Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness versus Martin-Löf randomness
summary: Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies make computable fair bets while adaptively querying previously unseen coordinates of an infinite binary sequence. The problem asks whether defeating every such strategy implies passing every uniform effective null test for fair-coin measure. Strategies may be partial and may omit coordinates forever, but they cannot borrow, revisit observed bits or inspect them through an oracle. Liu and Meng construct a measure supported on sequences failing one fixed Martin-Löf test. Almost every sequence under that measure defeats every computable nonmonotonic bettor, so the two randomness classes differ.
formal:
Is every Kolmogorov–Loveland random infinite binary sequence Martin-Löf random for the fair-coin product measure? In the precise model below, determine whether
\[\forall X\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N},\qquad
\operatorname{KLR}(X)\Longrightarrow\operatorname{MLR}(X).\]
The reverse implication is known, so this is equivalently equality of the two randomness classes. Betting strategies may choose fresh coordinates adaptively, need not visit every coordinate, and are ordinary partial computable procedures without an oracle.
definitions:
Space and measure. Let \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Cantor space \(2^{\mathbb N}=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) consists of all functions \(X:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}\), including noncomputable ones. Let \(2^{<\mathbb N}\) be the finite binary strings. For a string \(\sigma\), its length is \(|\sigma|\), and its cylinder is
\[[\sigma]=\{X:\ X(i)=\sigma(i)\text{ for all }i<|\sigma|\}.\]
The fair-coin product probability measure \(\mu\) makes coordinates independent and assigns \(\mu([\sigma])=2^{-|\sigma|}\). No bias, alternative measure or oracle relativization is involved.

Martin-Löf tests. A uniformly effectively open family is specified by one ordinary Turing program enumerating a set \(W\subseteq\mathbb N_{\ge1}\times2^{<\mathbb N}\). Put
\[U_k=\bigcup_{(k,\sigma)\in W}[\sigma].\]
It is a Martin-Löf test when \(\mu(U_k)\le2^{-k}\) for every \(k\ge1\). This condition concerns the measure of the union, not the sum of cylinder measures when cylinders overlap. Repetitions in an enumeration are harmless, no disjointness or prefix-free presentation is required, and levels need not be nested. The measure bound is a mathematical condition on a test; the enumerating program is not required to certify it or compute the exact measure. Define
\[\operatorname{MLR}(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{for every Martin-Löf test }(U_k)_{k\ge1},\quad X\notin\bigcap_{k\ge1}U_k.\]
Uniform enumeration across all levels is mandatory.

Histories and betting procedures. A history is a finite ordered list
\[h=((j_0,a_0),\ldots,(j_{s-1},a_{s-1}))\]
with distinct \(j_i\in\mathbb N\) and \(a_i\in\{0,1\}\). It records precisely the coordinates already queried and their observed values, in query order. A strategy is a deterministic partial computable function \(S\) which, on such a history, either fails to return an action or returns
\[S(h)=(j,q),\qquad j\notin\{j_0,\ldots,j_{s-1}\},\quad q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,2].\]
Every returned action on a valid history must meet these conditions. Computability means a finite Turing-machine program operating on an effective finite encoding of this list, natural coordinates, and rational numerator/positive-denominator pairs. These encodings carry no resource bound. The program receives only the history; it cannot inspect any further bit of \(X\) before choosing its action, use an oracle, or use an uncomputable real parameter. Internal deterministic work and previously computed data can be recovered from the history and program. The equivalent history of observed bit values alone suffices when the query coordinates are reconstructed by rerunning that same strategy.

Run and capital. Start at empty history with capital \(C_0^S(X)=1\). If \(S(h_s)=(j_s,q_s)\) returns, reveal \(a_s=X(j_s)\), append \((j_s,a_s)\), and update
\[C_{s+1}^S(X)=\begin{cases}
C_s^S(X)q_s,&a_s=0,\\
C_s^S(X)(2-q_s),&a_s=1.
\end{cases}\]
The two possible multipliers average to one, so the bet is fair on a fresh unbiased bit. Capital is always nonnegative, with no borrowing or outside deposits; zero capital remains zero. The choice \(q_s=1\) reads a bit without risking capital. Coordinates may be arbitrarily large and need not increase. They cannot repeat, including after a zero wager. There is no requirement to query every coordinate even on an infinite run.

If the next computation diverges or returns no action, the run has no further completed bets and earns no further capital. Computation time itself does not increase capital. There are no time or space bounds. Let \(D_S(X)\subseteq\mathbb N\) be the finite or infinite initial segment of completed-bet counts, including zero. The strategy succeeds precisely when
\[\forall K\in\mathbb N\ \exists s\in D_S(X):\quad C_s^S(X)>K.\]
This is unbounded supremum of capital, not a requirement that capital converge to infinity, grow at a computable rate, or exceed a single fixed threshold.

Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness. Let \(\mathcal S\) be the class of all strategies just specified. Define
\[\operatorname{KLR}(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall S\in\mathcal S\ \exists K\in\mathbb N\ \forall s\in D_S(X):\quad C_s^S(X)\le K.\]
The bound may depend on both \(S\) and \(X\), and no algorithm producing those bounds is required. Rational stakes and unit initial capital give the standard notion. Replacing partial computability by total computability gives the same randomness class, but requiring every coordinate to be visited is a separate condition and is not imposed here.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication or its negation, with these exact measure, effectiveness and betting conventions.

A positive answer must hold for every infinite binary sequence and every uniformly effective Martin-Löf test. Equivalently, prove that for each \(X\) failing some Martin-Löf test there exists an admissible computable strategy with unbounded capital on \(X\). That existential strategy may depend on \(X\); it must still be a finite oracle-free program. A uniform conversion of tests to a finite universal family of strategies is not an additional requirement.

A negative answer must prove the existence of one sequence \(X\) and one Martin-Löf test \((U_k)_{k\ge1}\) such that
\[X\in\bigcap_{k\ge1}U_k\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall S\in\mathcal S\ \exists K\in\mathbb N\ \forall s\in D_S(X):\ C_s^S(X)\le K.\]
The same sequence must satisfy every test level and defeat every allowed strategy. A nonconstructive existence proof qualifies; an algorithm computing the bits of \(X\) is not required. Different sequences for different levels or strategies, a separation for fixed query orders, a generalized betting game, or a frequency-only stochasticity result does not settle the full target. Finite simulations or a one-sided known implication are insufficient.

title: Computability of the Mandelbrot set
summary: The Mandelbrot set consists of complex parameters whose quadratic iteration starting at zero remains bounded. The question asks for one ordinary program that approximates the entire set to every requested accuracy. Its output must be a finite set of dyadic points with a proved Hausdorff error bound, and no running-time bound is imposed. Known positive results depend on a hyperbolicity conjecture, including the checked 2025 application to escape problems. The selected unconditional approximation question differs from exact real membership, computing area and producing images without certified error.
formal:
Is the Mandelbrot set a computable compact subset of the plane?

Precisely, does there exist a single deterministic Turing machine \(A\) such that for every integer \(k\ge0\), \(A(k)\) halts and outputs a finite nonempty set \(S_k\) of points with dyadic rational coordinates satisfying
\[
d_H(S_k,M)\le 2^{-k},
\]
where
\[
M=\{c\in\mathbb C:\ (z_j(c))_{j\ge0}\text{ is bounded}\},\qquad
z_0(c)=0,\quad z_{j+1}(c)=z_j(c)^2+c?
\]
The assertion is unconditional and places no complexity bound on \(A\).
definitions:
Identify \(\mathbb C\) with \(\mathbb R^2\) and use the Euclidean norm \(|\cdot|\). Boundedness of the orbit means that there exists a finite real \(R\ge0\), depending on \(c\), such that \(|z_j(c)|\le R\) for every integer \(j\ge0\). For this family, equivalently,
\[
M=\{c:\ \forall j\ge0,\ |z_j(c)|\le2\}.
\]
The set \(M\) is nonempty, closed and contained in the closed disk of radius two, hence compact.

A dyadic rational is an integer divided by a nonnegative integer power of two, encoded by signed binary integers for numerator and exponent. The output \(S_k\) is an explicit finite list of pairs of such numbers; repetitions may be removed. No bound on the list length is imposed. The accuracy input \(k\) has its ordinary finite binary encoding.

For two nonempty compact subsets \(X,Y\) of the plane, their Hausdorff distance is
\[
d_H(X,Y)=\max\left\{
\sup_{x\in X}\inf_{y\in Y}|x-y|,
\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}|x-y|
\right\}.
\]
Thus every reported point must be within the stated accuracy of \(M\), and every point of \(M\) must be within that accuracy of a reported point. A close picture on a selected finite grid without a proved global error guarantee is insufficient.

The machine is an ordinary algorithm operating on finite strings. It receives only \(k\); it has no oracle for complex numbers, set membership, the halting problem or a dynamical conjecture. One finite program must work at every precision, rather than a separately chosen program or advice string for each \(k\).

This is the standard computable-analysis notion for a fixed compact set. Equivalently, its distance function
\[
\operatorname{dist}(q,M)=\inf_{c\in M}|q-c|
\]
must be uniformly computable: a machine, given any rational point \(q\in\mathbb Q^2\) and \(k\ge0\), returns a rational number within \(2^{-k}\) of this distance. The equivalence uses the fixed compact bound on \(M\). The question does not ask for a total exact membership decision on arbitrary real inputs, for a polynomial running time, for the area of \(M\), or for its boundary alone.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of \(A\) with the stated all-precision Hausdorff guarantee. A positive answer must prove both termination and the approximation bound for every \(k\). A negative answer must rule out all ordinary Turing programs with this behavior. An implication from an additional unproved conjecture or an undecidability result for exact real membership does not settle the assertion. This is a binary computability question: a fixed numerical tolerance such as \(1/100\) does not replace the requirement to handle every \(2^{-k}\).

title: Reversal of Hindman’s theorem to the \(\omega\)-jump
summary: Hindman’s theorem finds an infinite set whose nonempty finite sums of distinct elements all have one color. This card asks whether that theorem forces every set’s complete sequence of finite Turing jumps over the weak base theory RCA0. The question concerns a formal implication between theories, not whether Hindman’s theorem is true in ordinary mathematics. A July 2026 result limits what one arithmetic coloring can force a solution to compute but explicitly leaves the full implication undecided. A complete Lean-checked proof must establish the stated formal derivation or its nonexistence, for example through a verified separating model.
formal:
Does the following formal provability statement hold?
\[
\mathrm{RCA}_0+\mathrm{HT}\ \vdash\
\forall X\,\exists Y\,
\bigl[Y_0=X\ \wedge\ \forall j\,(Y_{j+1}=Y_j')\bigr].
\]
Here \(\mathrm{HT}\) is Hindman's theorem for every finite coloring of the positive integers and all nonempty finite sums of distinct members of one infinite set. The conclusion says that every set has its coded \(\omega\)-jump. Equivalently, does full Hindman's theorem imply \(\mathrm{ACA}_0^+\) over \(\mathrm{RCA}_0\)?
definitions:
Use classical two-sorted first-order logic, with number variables, set-of-number variables, equality, membership, \(0\), successor \(S\), addition and multiplication. Set equality is extensional. Models may have nonstandard numbers, and their set sort need not contain every subset of their number domain. Thus the logical semantics is Henkin semantics, not full second-order semantics.

The number axioms are Robinson arithmetic: \(Sx\ne0\), \(Sx=Sy\Rightarrow x=y\), \(x\ne0\Rightarrow\exists y\,x=Sy\), \(x+0=x\), \(x+Sy=S(x+y)\), \(x\cdot0=0\), and \(x\cdot Sy=x\cdot y+x\). Write \(1=S0\), define \(x<y\) by \(\exists z\,x+S(z)=y\), and define \(x\le y\) by \(x<y\) or \(x=y\).

A bounded arithmetic formula has only number quantifiers bounded by number terms; set membership and free set parameters are allowed, but quantified set variables are not. A \(\Sigma^0_1\) formula consists of a finite block of existential number quantifiers followed by a bounded formula; a \(\Pi^0_1\) formula uses a universal block instead. The base theory \(\mathrm{RCA}_0\) adds the universal closures of the following schemes, allowing number and set parameters. For every \(\Sigma^0_1\) formula \(\varphi(n)\), it includes
\[
[\varphi(0)\wedge\forall n(\varphi(n)\Rightarrow\varphi(Sn))]
\Rightarrow\forall n\,\varphi(n).
\]
For every \(\Sigma^0_1\) formula \(\varphi(n)\) and \(\Pi^0_1\) formula \(\psi(n)\), it includes
\[
[\forall n(\varphi(n)\leftrightarrow\psi(n))]
\Rightarrow\exists Z\,\forall n\,[n\in Z\leftrightarrow\varphi(n)],
\]
where \(Z\) is not free in either defining formula. This is \(\Delta^0_1\) comprehension.

Functions and finite sequences are represented by their usual arithmetic codes. Fix the pairing \(\langle j,e\rangle=(j+e)(j+e+1)/2+e\), whose division is exact, and a standard effective coding of finite sequences and oracle Turing computations. All statements about a coded finite computation or sequence are interpreted inside the theory. In particular, finite lengths and color counts range over its number sort, rather than only over externally standard integers.

In \(\mathrm{HT}\), quantify over every number \(k\ge1\) and every set coding the graph of a total function \(c:\mathbb N_{>0}\to\{0,\ldots,k-1\}\). There must exist a set \(H\subseteq\mathbb N_{>0}\) and a number \(i<k\) such that \(\forall b\,\exists h>b\,(h\in H)\) and
\[
c(h_0+\cdots+h_{r-1})=i
\]
for every coded strictly increasing finite sequence \(h_0<\cdots<h_{r-1}\) from \(H\) with \(r\ge1\). There is no fixed bound on \(r\), no repeated summand and no extra separation condition on the binary supports of the integers in \(H\).

Fix a standard enumeration of oracle Turing machines. For a set \(A\), the notation \(A'\) denotes the halting set
\[
\{e:\text{the }e\text{-th machine with oracle }A\text{ halts on input }e\}.
\]
The assertion \(B=A'\) is the arithmetic formula saying that membership of \(e\) in \(B\) is equivalent to existence of a coded finite halting computation using the answers supplied by \(A\). It does not assume that the jump set already exists in the model. For a single set \(Y\), define its sections by \(Y_j=\{e:\langle j,e\rangle\in Y\}\). The target requires one such \(Y\) simultaneously recording every finite jump iterate, beginning with \(Y_0=X\). The theory \(\mathrm{ACA}_0^+\) is \(\mathrm{RCA}_0\) plus this closure axiom.

The symbol \(\vdash\) means existence of a finite formal derivation in a sound and complete classical two-sorted first-order proof calculus using the stated axioms and schemes. Equivalent standard encodings of syntax and computation do not alter the question. This is an exact provability proposition, with no bound on proof length or computational resources.
answer_criterion:
Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that a finite formal derivation of the displayed closure axiom exists from \(\mathrm{RCA}_0+\mathrm{HT}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such derivation exists. For the latter, a fully verified Henkin model of \(\mathrm{RCA}_0+\mathrm{HT}\) omitting the coded \(\omega\)-jump of some set suffices, together with the soundness argument. A model with standard natural numbers is sufficient but is not required.

Proving the closure axiom in the ambient logic of Lean without verifying the restriction to the stated object theory does not prove this reversal. Neither the known \(\mathrm{ACA}_0\) lower bound, the known \(\mathrm{ACA}_0^+\) upper bound, nor a claim about one computable coloring decides it. A negative answer need not establish equivalence with \(\mathrm{ACA}_0\); any valid separation from the displayed closure axiom settles the question.

title: Unconditional coding theorem for randomized Kolmogorov complexity
summary: An efficient sampler assigns a probability to each string it can produce. The question asks whether every such string has a short randomized description close to its information content. One fixed description must reconstruct the string in polynomial time with probability at least two thirds using private random bits. The guarantee must cover the whole sampler support, while the encoder that finds a description may be inefficient. Known conditional, average-case and public-randomness coding results do not establish the stated unconditional theorem.
formal:
Is the following coding statement true without a computational hardness or derandomization assumption?
\[
\forall D\in\mathrm{PSamp}\ \exists c,d\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\forall n\ge2\ \forall x\in\operatorname{supp}(D_n):
\quad
\mathrm{rK}^{(n+2)^d}(x)
\le
\left\lceil\log_2\frac1{D_n(x)}\right\rceil
+c\left\lceil\log_2(n+2)\right\rceil .
\]
Here \(D=\{D_n\}_{n\ge2}\) ranges over uniformly polynomial-time samplable distributions on \(n\)-bit strings, and \(\mathrm{rK}^t\) uses private random bits and success probability at least \(2/3\), as defined below. The constants \(c,d\) may depend on the fixed sampler but must work for every length and every string in its support.

The target is existence of short polynomial-time randomized descriptions. No efficient algorithm for finding a description from \(x\) is required.
definitions:
Fix one standard efficiently universal probabilistic Turing machine \(U\), with a binary program, a one-way tape of independent fair random bits and an output tape. Its simulation of any fixed machine has polynomial time overhead and a constant program-description overhead. The program receives no input string, length, advice, shared random tape or oracle for the sampler's distribution.

For \(t\in\mathbb N\), define
\[
\mathrm{rK}^{t}(x)=
\min\left\{
 |p|:
 \Pr_{r\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{t}}
 [U(p;r)\text{ halts within }t\text{ steps with output exactly }x]
 \ge\frac23
\right\}.
\]
A computation uses at most \(t\) random bits in \(t\) steps; unused bits are ignored. Failure to halt in time or outputting another string is failure. The minimum is \(+\infty\) if there is no such program. The same program \(p\) must succeed for the indicated fraction of random tapes. It may depend on \(D,n,x\), but it is chosen before the random tape. A description can encode the length and a sampler description within its counted program bits.

Membership \(D\in\mathrm{PSamp}\) means that there is one deterministic algorithm \(S\), a polynomially bounded, polynomial-time computable integer function \(a(n)\), and a polynomial time bound, such that for every \(n\ge2\) and every \(r\in\{0,1\}^{a(n)}\), the computation \(S(1^n,r)\) outputs exactly \(n\) bits within that bound. The law of \(S(1^n,R)\) for uniform \(R\) is \(D_n\). Thus \(D_n(x)\) is an exact rational probability and \(\operatorname{supp}(D_n)=\{x:D_n(x)>0\}\). The sampler is uniform and has no length-dependent advice.

The expression \(\log_2(1/D_n(x))\) is the information content, in bits, of the particular string. The inequality is pointwise on the entire support, including very unlikely strings. It is not only an expected-length bound or a guarantee outside a small exceptional set. There is one polynomial decoding-time exponent and one logarithmic-overhead constant for the whole sampler family.

For comparison, probabilistic complexity \(\mathrm{pK}^{t}(x)\) permits the short deterministic program to be chosen after seeing public random bits: its quantifiers have the form \(\Pr_r[\exists p\text{ short}:U(p;r)=x]\ge2/3\). That is a different measure from the single-program private-randomness measure in the question. Likewise, an efficient coding theorem would additionally require an efficient encoder that finds a short description; this card does not impose that requirement.

No assumption about one-way functions, average-case hardness or circuit lower bounds is part of the statement. The fixed universal-machine convention is harmless for this existential polynomial-time and logarithmic-overhead target, since the constants and exponent may change.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed universal coding statement. An affirmative answer must cover every uniformly polynomial-time sampler and every supported string with the stated quantifier order. A negative answer must establish a sampler family for which no pair of constants \(c,d\) works. A conditional result, a coding theorem only for public-randomness complexity, an expected-length bound, or a theorem allowing exceptional strings does not suffice. This is a binary question; numerical \(1/100\) tolerance does not relax the coding inequality or its universal quantifiers.

title: Mortality of \(2\times 2\) integer matrix semigroups
summary: A finite list of two-by-two integer matrices generates all nonempty products with arbitrary order and repetition. The question asks whether a terminating algorithm can decide if any such product is the zero matrix. Matrix entries and the number of generators are unrestricted. NP-hardness is known, while decidability results for restricted determinants do not cover the general case. Resolving the question would locate a basic computability boundary for products of small matrices.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that, for every finite list \(A_{1},\ldots ,A_{m}\) of \(2\times 2\) integer matrices, halts and correctly decides whether there exist \(\ell\ge 1\) and indices \(i_{1},\ldots ,i_{\ell}\in \{1,\ldots ,m\}\) with \(A_{i_{1}} A_{i_{2}} \cdots  A_{i_{\ell}}=0_{2}\)?
definitions: The input explicitly gives \(m\ge 0\) and all four entries of each \(A_{i}\) as signed binary integers. Entries have no magnitude or sign restriction, and m is part of the input, not a fixed constant. Products use ordinary exact integer matrix multiplication: \((AB)_{r,s}=\sum _{t=1}^{2} A_{r,t}B_{t,s}\). The target \(0_{2}\) is the matrix with all four entries zero. The product length \(\ell\) is finite but unbounded, and generator indices may repeat in any order. Only listed generators can be used; inverses are not supplied automatically. The empty product is excluded, and an empty list is a NO instance. The semigroup generated by the list is the set of all such nonempty products, so mortality means membership of \(0_{2}\) in that set. The machine must return YES exactly for mortal lists and NO otherwise, terminating on both kinds. No running-time or memory bound is imposed beyond finite termination; there is no oracle, numerical tolerance or real-arithmetic primitive.
answer_criterion: A positive answer gives a uniform decision algorithm with proofs of correctness and termination on every finite input list. A negative answer proves that the stated decision problem is undecidable. A procedure that only certifies particular zero products, a bounded-length decision algorithm, or a lower bound against polynomial time does not settle the target.

title: Hartmanis–Stearns conjecture
summary: The question concerns a fixed machine that prints all digits of a real number with bounded delay between outputs. Every rational number permits this because its expansion is eventually periodic. The conjecture says that any irrational number generated this quickly must be transcendental. It quantifies over unrestricted deterministic multitape machines, beyond the restricted automata covered by known partial results. A proof would connect the arithmetic nature of numbers to a stringent computation bound and rule out linear-time integer multiplication.
formal: For every integer \(b\ge 2\) and every real \(x\in[0,1)\), if a deterministic multitape Turing machine generates the base-b digits of x in order with a constant bound on the time between successive digits, must x be rational or transcendental?
definitions: Write \(x=\sum _{n\ge 1}d_{n} b^{- n}\), where \(d_{n}\in \{0,\ldots ,b- 1\}\), using the unique expansion that is not eventually all \(b-1\). A terminating expansion continues with zeros. Rational means \(x=p/q\) for integers p,q with \(q\ne 0\). Algebraic means \(P(x)=0\) for a nonzero polynomial P with integer coefficients; transcendental means not algebraic. A machine has a finite control, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of two-way infinite work tapes, each with one head and initially blank. Each transition reads the symbols under the heads, writes at those cells, changes state and moves each head at most one cell. It may also append one digit to a separate write-only output stream; written digits are irrevocable. It starts with no input and no advice or oracle and runs indefinitely. There must be a constant \(C\ge 1\) such that its first digit appears by step C and, writing \(t_{n}\) for the step at which \(d_{n}\) appears, \(1\le t_{n+1}- t_{n}\le C\) for every \(n\ge 1\). The finite machine and C may depend on the fixed x and b, but not on n. This is the constant-delay, or real-time, convention used by this card. Restricting to [0,1) only removes an integer part, which does not change rationality or transcendence.
answer_criterion: Prove the implication for all bases, numbers and machines just defined, or refute it by exhibiting an algebraic irrational x, a base b and a machine with proofs of correct infinite digit generation and a uniform constant delay. A computation of any finite prefix, a slower digit algorithm or a theorem restricted to finite automata does not settle the statement.

title: Reversible simulation in polynomial time and linear space
summary: The question asks whether every deterministic computation can be compiled into a reversible one with polynomial time overhead and only a constant-factor space increase. The simulator preserves the input and exact output, clears auxiliary storage and retains nontermination on divergent inputs. Time and space are compared on the same input, and input, output and history storage all count. Known general simulations attain the two desired efficiencies separately or with a tradeoff, while catalytic-space results use a different resource model. A complete answer must prove or refute one computable compiler meeting all of these guarantees simultaneously.
formal:
Does there exist one computable compiler \(\mathcal C\) that maps every deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) to a reversible multitape machine \(R=\mathcal C(M)\) with the following simultaneous guarantees? For every \(M\), there are a constant \(c_M\ge1\) and an integer \(d_M\ge1\) such that, on every input \(x\) on which \(M\) halts, \(R\) halts with exactly the output pair \((x,M(x))\), clears its auxiliary tapes, and satisfies
\[S_R(x)\le c_M S_M(x),\qquad T_R(x)\le c_M T_M(x)^{d_M}.\]
On every input on which \(M\) does not halt, \(R\) must also fail to halt. The same \(R\) must meet both bounds on every halting input. This is the previously selected polynomial-time, linear-space version of the source's broader simulation tradeoff question.
definitions:
Each machine has a finite transition table, finitely many states, a finite tape alphabet containing 0, 1, a blank and delimiters, and a fixed finite number of two-way tapes with one head per tape. A transition reads the scanned symbols, writes symbols and moves each head by at most one cell. Tapes are indexed by integers, and all heads initially sit at a designated origin. The machine description lists these finite objects explicitly in a fixed effectively decodable binary syntax. Alphabet size, tape count and states may depend on the fixed machine but not on its input. There are no oracle, advice, random or external-storage tapes.

Initially the binary input \(x\), with fixed delimiters, occupies consecutive cells of one tape; all other cells are blank. A halting run has a finite designated binary output \(M(x)\), with delimiters on an output tape. A transition is a partial deterministic function on full configurations; a configuration with no next transition is terminal. The full configuration includes the state, every tape's contents and every head position. A simulator must implement the stated terminal-output convention on its intended input runs.

A machine is reversible if its partial one-step map is injective on its entire configuration space: whenever transitions from configurations \(u\) and \(v\) produce the same configuration, \(u=v\). Thus no step may merge two different predecessor configurations. This property concerns the finite machine's full transition semantics, not just the particular run from a blank workspace. Halting states have no outgoing step; injectivity does not require every configuration to have a predecessor. Reversibility is logical reversibility of a classical machine, not a physical energy model or a quantum operation.

For a halting run, \(S_M(x)\) is the number of distinct tape cells initially occupied or visited during the entire run, summed over all tapes, with a minimum of 1. A cell still counts if it is later erased. Input, output, delimiter, history and work cells all count. Let
\[T_M(x)=\max\{1,|x|,\text{number of transitions before halting}\}.\]
Define \(S_R,T_R\) in exactly the same way. This is a per-input resource comparison, not a comparison of unrelated worst-case inputs of a given length. Finite control is part of the fixed machine description, while every tape cell used at run time is included. No additional initially full catalytic tape is supplied for free.

At termination, the simulator has two designated output tracks or tapes containing the original \(x\) and \(M(x)\), with the fixed delimiters, and all auxiliary tape contents are blank. Retaining \(x\) is essential: different inputs can yield the same \(M(x)\), but a reversible computation cannot merge their histories into an identical final configuration. The output pair is required exactly; leaving a computation-history string as garbage is not accepted. The simulator need only preserve the partial function in this input-preserving sense, rather than reproduce each intermediate configuration of \(M\).

The compiler is a single total deterministic computable function on valid machine descriptions; its compilation time is unrestricted. It outputs a finite reversible machine description, with no dependence on the later input \(x\). Neither the compiler nor the simulator is given the eventual halting time or space use as an extra input. The constants \(c_M,d_M\) may depend on \(M\), but are fixed before quantifying over all \(x\). No halting-time or resource bound is required on divergent runs beyond preservation of nontermination. A simulator chosen separately for every individual input would not satisfy the compiler requirement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of this compiler. A positive answer must establish total computability of compilation, reversibility of every output machine on its full configuration space, preservation of the partial function and nontermination behavior, clean input-preserving output, and the two simultaneous per-input resource bounds. A negative answer must prove that no compiler can satisfy these requirements for all machines and inputs; failure of one known construction does not suffice. Separate simulators achieving the time and space bounds independently do not settle the conjunction. A lower bound only for reversible pebble games, an oracle-relative simulation model or circuits does not refute unrestricted reversible multitape simulation. The resource requirements are exact asymptotic claims, without additive numerical tolerance.

title: Superpolynomial Extended Frege lower bounds
summary: Extended Frege is a classical propositional proof system that can introduce reusable names for previously specified formulas. The question asks whether no single polynomial bounds the shortest proof of every tautology by its statement length. The target counts the full encoded proof and allows arbitrary depth and reuse of earlier lines. Its negation would give short proofs for every tautology without necessarily making them easy to find. Recent conditional, algebraic and intuitionistic results do not supply the unrestricted classical lower bound.
formal: Is classical Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every pair of integers \(C\ge1,c\ge1\), does there exist a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) such that every Extended Frege proof \(\pi\) of \(\varphi\) has binary encoding length \(|\pi|>C(|\varphi|+2)^c\)? The formula and proof encodings and the fixed proof rules are specified below.
definitions:
A propositional formula is a finite syntax tree built from variables \(v_i\), indexed by \(i\in\mathbb N\), unary negation and binary material implication. Its Boolean value under an assignment \(v_i\mapsto\{0,1\}\) is defined recursively, with \(A	o B\) false exactly when A is true and B is false. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. Let code(a), for \(a\ge0\), be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, with \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)floor+1\). Encode \(v_i\) as 00 followed by code(i), \(
eg A\) as 01 followed by the encoding of A, and \(A	o B\) as 10 followed by the encodings of A and B. This prefix syntax contains the whole formula tree, not a circuit or a program generating it; \(|\varphi|\) is its bit length. Fix the three classical Frege axiom schemes \(A	o(B	o A)\), \((A	o(B	o C))	o((A	o B)	o(A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o
eg A)	o(A	o B)\). An instance substitutes arbitrary formulas for A, B and C consistently. Modus ponens infers B from two earlier lines A and \(A	o B\). An extension introduction adds two consecutive lines \(e	o	heta\) and \(	heta	o e\), where e is a variable absent from the target formula, theta and every line before this pair. The defining formula theta may use variables of the target and previously introduced extension variables, so definitions are acyclic. Freshness is checked before the pair, not between its two lines. There are no unproved hypotheses. A proof is a finite nonempty list of lines justified by these axiom schemes, modus ponens or such an extension pair; its last line is exactly the target formula and contains no extension variables. Earlier lines can be cited any number of times. There is no depth bound, tree-like proof restriction or restriction on the sizes of intermediate formulas. For a complete proof encoding, first write code(m) for its number of lines, and then encode each line with a two-bit tag, its metadata and its entire formula in the prefix syntax above. Tag 00 stores the axiom-scheme number 1, 2 or 3 with code; tag 01 stores with code the two earlier, one-based line indices for modus ponens, in the order A then A implies B; tag 10 stores with code the index of the fresh extension variable and must be followed immediately by a tag-11 line giving the reverse implication for the same definition. Tag 11 has no metadata and is valid only as that second line of an extension pair. The first extension formula uniquely determines theta, and both implication formulas are fully written and counted. Missing or trailing bits and invalid justifications are rejected. The proof length counts all bits, including the line count, formulas, variable indices, rule tags and inference references. This is a fixed polynomial-time checkable presentation of classical EF, polynomially equivalent to the usual finite Frege bases with extension. EF is complete, so every tautology has some finite proof; the issue is a common polynomial bound. The chosen binary encoding and paired extension rule fix presentation details without changing polynomial boundedness. The hard formula may depend on C and c; no polynomial-time procedure generating a hard family is imposed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed lower-bound assertion or its logical negation. The affirmative answer must, for every polynomial bound \(C(n+2)^c\), establish a tautology whose every valid EF proof exceeds that bound. The negative answer must establish fixed integers C,c for which every tautology has some valid EF proof of length at most \(C(|\varphi|+2)^c\); it need not give a polynomial-time proof-search algorithm. A bound for one search procedure, for bounded-depth or ordinary Frege, for a different logic, or for an algebraic encoding without a valid polynomial-size propositional translation does not settle this target.

title: Existence of p-optimal proof systems
summary: Does one propositional proof system efficiently translate proofs from every other efficiently checkable system? The translation must preserve the proved formula and run in time polynomial in the given proof length. Each simulated system may have its own translator and polynomial. This is stronger than comparing proof lengths alone, and different from requiring short proofs of every tautology. The 2026 oracle and jump-operator results leave the ordinary, oracle-free existence question open.
formal: Does there exist a Cook–Reckhow proof system P for propositional tautologies such that, for every Cook–Reckhow proof system Q for the same tautologies, there is a deterministic polynomial-time translation \(t_{Q}\) satisfying \(P(t_{Q}(\pi ))=Q(\pi )\) for every finite binary proof string \(\pi\)?
definitions: Fix an explicit binary syntax for Boolean formulas built from indexed variables, AND, OR and NOT. A tautology evaluates to true under every assignment to its variables; TAUT is the set of encodings of such formulas. A Cook–Reckhow proof system is a total function \(P:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\mathrm{TAUT}\), computed by one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in its input length, whose range is all of TAUT. A string \(\pi\) proves formula F when \(P(\pi )=F\). Soundness requires every output to be a tautology; completeness requires every tautology to occur as an output. There is no polynomial upper bound on the shortest proof of every formula. In this total-function presentation, strings that would be malformed proofs in a conventional calculus may instead produce a fixed tautology such as \(x_{1}\lor \neg x_{1}\). A simulation translation is total and satisfies the equality on all strings, preserving the exact output formula. Its program, polynomial exponent and constants may depend on Q and P, but not on \(\pi\). The order is \(\exists P \forall Q \exists t_{Q} \forall \pi\). No algorithm taking an arbitrary program for Q and producing its translator is required. Neither advice, randomization nor an oracle is allowed in the systems or translations. Polynomial translation time also bounds the translated proof length polynomially in \(|\pi |\).
answer_criterion: Prove that one sound and complete polynomial-time proof system admits the required polynomial-time translations from every other such system, or prove that for every candidate P some sound and complete Q has no such translation. A proof-length comparison without an efficient translation proves only ordinary optimality. Refuting a particular named proof system’s p-optimality does not exclude all systems.

title: Frege versus Extended Frege
summary: Extended Frege permits named definitions that share intermediate formulas within an otherwise ordinary propositional proof. The question asks whether every such proof has an ordinary Frege proof of the same conclusion with only polynomially larger total encoded size. The statement fixes the formula syntax, inference rules, freshness conditions and binary accounting while allowing unrestricted depth and reuse of proof lines. Known finite-consistency characterizations, fixed-parameter combinatorial upper bounds and restricted algebraic simulations do not settle this universal comparison. A complete Lean proof must establish either one universal polynomial size bound or its logical negation, without imposing a polynomial-time procedure for finding translated proofs.
formal:
Does ordinary Frege polynomially simulate Extended Frege in proof size? For the two fixed systems and binary size convention below, determine whether
\[\exists C,k\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \forall\varphi\ \forall\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{EFProof}(\pi,\varphi)\Rightarrow\exists\rho\,[\operatorname{FProof}(\rho,\varphi)\land |\rho|\le C(|\pi|+2)^{k}]\bigr).\]
Here \(\varphi\) ranges over all finite propositional formulas in the ordinary variables, and \(\pi,\rho\) range over finite binary strings. The constants are independent of the formula and of both proofs. This asks for existence of short Frege proofs of the same conclusions; it does not require a polynomial-time algorithm that finds them. Equivalently, for every tautology \(\varphi\), is its minimum Frege proof size \(s_{\mathrm F}(\varphi)\) bounded by one fixed polynomial in its minimum Extended Frege proof size \(s_{\mathrm{EF}}(\varphi)\)?
definitions:
Formulas are finite ordered syntax trees generated by ordinary variables \(x_i\), temporary extension variables \(e_i\), negation \(\neg A\), and material implication \(A\to B\), with \(i\in\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,\ldots\}\). Ordinary formulas contain no \(e_i\). A Boolean assignment gives each variable a value in \(\{0,1\}\); negation reverses this value and implication is false exactly when its antecedent is true and consequent false. A tautology is an ordinary formula true under every assignment to its ordinary variables. Every syntactic occurrence is written separately: a formula is a tree, not a circuit with shared subformulas.

The fixed Frege calculus has precisely these three axiom schemes:
\[A\to(B\to A),\qquad (A\to(B\to C))\to((A\to B)\to(A\to C)),\qquad (\neg B\to\neg A)\to(A\to B).\]
Each occurrence of a scheme uses a consistent substitution of formulas for its metavariables \(A,B,C\). The only inference rule is modus ponens, deriving \(B\) from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\to B\). A Frege proof is a nonempty finite sequence of ordinary formulas, each justified by an axiom instance or modus ponens, with the last formula its conclusion. There are no hypotheses, extension axioms or separate rules that substitute into an already derived line. Any earlier line may be reused arbitrarily often. Auxiliary ordinary variables not occurring in the conclusion are permitted.

Extended Frege uses the same schemes and modus ponens, and additionally permits a consecutive pair of extension lines \(e_i\to\theta\) and \(\theta\to e_i\). At this introduction, \(e_i\) has not occurred in any earlier line and does not occur in \(\theta\) or in the final conclusion. The formula \(\theta\) may contain any ordinary variables and extension variables from completed earlier pairs, but no other extension variables. Both lines are written explicitly. After the pair, \(e_i\) may occur in later axiom instances, modus-ponens lines and definitions. Every extension variable in any line must be introduced this way; the final conclusion contains none. Definitions are thus acyclic, and cannot assert arbitrary assumptions about the ordinary variables. There is no bound on formula depth, proof depth, number of extensions, or reuse of earlier lines. No tree-like restriction is imposed on the proof sequence.

Use the following fixed prefix-free binary encoding. For an integer \(t\ge0\), let \(b(t)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\), where concatenation is intended. A formula uses tag 00 followed by \(E(i)\) for \(x_i\), tag 01 followed by \(E(i)\) for \(e_i\), tag 10 followed by the child encoding for negation, and tag 11 followed by the antecedent and consequent encodings for implication. A proof of \(m\ge1\) lines starts with \(E(m)\). Each line then consists of a three-bit justification tag and its entire formula encoding. Tags 000, 001 and 010 specify the first, second and third axiom schemes, respectively; the written formula must be an instance of the specified scheme. Tag 011 specifies modus ponens and is followed, after the formula, by \(E(a)E(b)\): for line number \(j\), the indices satisfy \(1\le a,b<j\), line \(a\) is \(A\), and line \(b\) is exactly \(A\to B\) where the current formula is \(B\). Tags 100 and 101 specify the first and second lines of an extension pair. They must occur consecutively with exactly the two formulas and freshness conditions above; no additional data are implicit. The other tags and all malformed encodings are invalid. Frege permits only the first four tags and no extension variables. The size \(|\pi|\) is the bit length of this entire string, including every formula occurrence, variable index, line count and inference reference.

The predicates in the question mean validity under these syntactic rules with the specified final formula, not mere semantic validity of an unverified proof string. The displayed finite calculus is a standard complete classical Frege presentation; the explicit pair convention, auxiliary-variable convention and binary annotations fix ordinary polynomially equivalent presentations of the source systems. In particular, the bit cost is not merely the number of inference steps. The minimum sizes are defined for tautologies, all of which have finite Frege proofs. A size simulation alone is the target; the stronger notion of p-simulation additionally requires a polynomial-time proof translation.
answer_criterion:
Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation for the fixed systems and encoding. A positive answer must establish one pair of constants \(C,k\ge1\) that works for every valid Extended Frege proof and supplies the existence of a Frege proof of exactly the same ordinary conclusion with the required size. A negative answer must establish
\[\forall C,k\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \exists\varphi,\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{EFProof}(\pi,\varphi)\land\forall\rho\,[\operatorname{FProof}(\rho,\varphi)\Rightarrow |\rho|>C(|\pi|+2)^k]\bigr).\]
The formula and Extended Frege proof may depend on \(C,k\); no additional uniform construction of a separating family is imposed. All validity, size and quantifier claims must be justified in Lean. Conditional comparisons, a particular expensive expansion, restricted proof systems, a quasipolynomial simulation, or a polynomial-time proof-search lower bound alone do not meet this criterion. This is a binary asymptotic proof-size comparison, so the numerical 1/100 tolerance does not replace its polynomial bound.

title: Weak automatability of Resolution
summary: The input is a CNF formula and a proof-length budget written in unary. The algorithm must distinguish satisfiable formulas from those having a short general Resolution refutation. The proof is not supplied, and the algorithm need not produce a Resolution proof. Unsatisfiable formulas whose shortest refutations exceed the budget can receive either answer. Known hardness for finding Resolution proofs does not settle this weaker recognition problem.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, running in time polynomial in \(|F|+s\), that on input a CNF formula \(F\) and a unary proof budget \(1^{s}\) distinguishes the following two promised cases: \(F\) is satisfiable, or \(F\) has a Resolution refutation with at most \(s\) clauses?
definitions:
A CNF formula is an explicit conjunction of clauses over finitely many Boolean variables. Each clause is a disjunction of literals, where a literal is a variable or its negation. Let \(|F|\) be its ordinary binary encoding length, including literal indices and clause boundaries. Variables may be renamed consecutively in polynomial time.

A Resolution derivation is a finite sequence of clauses. Each line is an input clause of \(F\), or follows from two earlier lines by
\[\frac{A\lor x\qquad B\lor\neg x}{A\lor B},\]
where neither \(A\) nor \(B\) contains the pivot variable \(x\). Repeated literals are identified. A refutation ends in the empty clause, which is false under every assignment. Its length is the number of clauses in the sequence. Earlier lines may be reused: this is general directed-acyclic-graph Resolution, with no tree-like or regularity restriction.

The integer \(s\geq1\) is encoded in unary, so the input length is proportional to \(|F|+s\). The short refutation is promised to exist but is not given to the algorithm. Counting total proof symbols instead of clauses changes this polynomial-time question only by polynomial factors, since every clause uses variables of \(F\).

One fixed uniform deterministic algorithm must halt within a fixed polynomial bound on every input. It must output SAT whenever \(F\) is satisfiable, and UNSAT whenever \(F\) has a refutation of length at most \(s\). These cases are disjoint by soundness of Resolution. If \(F\) is unsatisfiable but all its Resolution refutations have length greater than \(s\), either output is allowed. Malformed encodings can be rejected immediately.

No satisfying assignment or refutation has to be output. In particular, the task does not ask whether a refutation of length at most \(s\) exists on every input: an UNSAT output is allowed even when all Resolution refutations are longer. This promise distinction is the decision formulation of weak automatability, corresponding to allowing efficiently checkable proofs in another fixed proof system instead of insisting on Resolution output.
answer_criterion: Construct the stated deterministic polynomial-time separator, or prove that no such separator exists. If a lower bound assumes a complexity separation, that separation must also be proved to settle the negative answer. Hardness of finding a Resolution refutation, estimating its minimum length, or solving unrestricted SAT does not establish hardness of this particular promise separator without a reduction that respects its two promised cases.

title: Superpolynomial \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\)-Frege lower bounds
summary: Modular Frege proofs can reason with shallow Boolean formulas containing gates that count true inputs modulo a fixed prime. The problem asks for one polynomial-time constructible DNF tautology family per prime that requires superpolynomial total proof size at every fixed logical line depth. The statement fixes a complete finite classical calculus, the modular recurrence axioms, all encodings and the distinction between formula depth and unrestricted derivation depth. Ordinary bounded-depth lower bounds and recent parity-resolution or restricted algebraic results do not establish this stronger modular-Frege target. A complete Lean proof must supply genuine tautologies and all construction and lower-bound guarantees, or prove the logical negation of the specified family-existence claim.
formal:
For every prime integer \(p\), does there exist a single polynomial-time constructible family of DNF tautologies \((\tau_{p,n})_{n\ge1}\) of length polynomially related to \(n\), such that its proofs in the fixed modular Frege calculus below exceed every polynomial size bound at every fixed line depth? Precisely, require for each \(p\) a finite deterministic machine \(M_p\) and integers \(C_p,k_p\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), on input \(1^n\) the machine outputs a DNF \(\tau_{p,n}\) within \(C_p(n+2)^{k_p}\) bit steps, this formula is a tautology, and
\[n\le |\tau_{p,n}|\le C_p(n+2)^{k_p}.\]
The required lower bound is
\[\forall d,r,N\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \exists n\ge N\ \forall\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{Proof}_{p,d}(\pi,\tau_{p,n})\Rightarrow |\pi|>n^r\bigr).\]
The machine and the family may depend on \(p\) but not on \(d,r,N\); the witness \(n\) may depend on all three. No effective procedure producing \(M_p\) from \(p\) is required. The family consists of genuine tautologies, not formulas whose lack of short proofs might be due to falsity. The lower bound is infinitely often, not necessarily eventually for every \(n\).
definitions:
Fix a prime \(p\ge2\). Formulas are finite ordered syntax trees built from constants \(0,1\), variables \(x_i\) for \(i\in\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), unary \(\neg\), binary \(\land,\lor\), and gates \(\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}(A_1,\ldots,A_t)\) for \(0\le j<p\) and any finite arity \(t\ge0\). Under an assignment of Boolean values to the variables, the usual connectives have their ordinary truth tables, and a modular gate is true exactly when the number of its true arguments is congruent to \(j\) modulo \(p\). A tautology is true under every assignment. A literal is a variable or its negation. A DNF is a finite disjunction of finite conjunctions of literals, written as a binary formula with any parenthesization; an empty conjunction is \(1\), an empty disjunction is \(0\), and a singleton conjunction or disjunction is its sole member. Target DNFs contain no modular gates.

The notation \(A\Rightarrow B\) is an abbreviation for \(\neg A\lor B\), and \(A\Leftrightarrow B\) abbreviates \((A\Rightarrow B)\land(B\Rightarrow A)\). Both are expanded fully before checking syntax, depth or size. Fix the following finite ordinary Frege axiom schemes, in the order displayed:
\[\begin{gathered}
 A\Rightarrow(B\Rightarrow A),\\
 (A\Rightarrow(B\Rightarrow C))\Rightarrow((A\Rightarrow B)\Rightarrow(A\Rightarrow C)),\\
 (\neg B\Rightarrow\neg A)\Rightarrow(A\Rightarrow B),\\
 (A\land B)\Rightarrow A,\qquad (A\land B)\Rightarrow B,\\
 A\Rightarrow(B\Rightarrow(A\land B)),\\
 A\Rightarrow(A\lor B),\qquad B\Rightarrow(A\lor B),\\
 (A\Rightarrow C)\Rightarrow((B\Rightarrow C)\Rightarrow((A\lor B)\Rightarrow C)),\\
 1,\qquad \neg0.
\end{gathered}\]
The metavariables \(A,B,C\) may be replaced consistently by arbitrary formulas of the full modular language. The sole inference rule is modus ponens: from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\Rightarrow B\), infer \(B\). There are no hypotheses. Besides these eleven schemes, allow the modular axioms
\[\operatorname{MOD}_{p,0}(),\qquad \neg\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}()\quad(1\le j<p),\]
and every instance of
\[\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}(\Gamma,A)\Leftrightarrow
 \bigl((\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}(\Gamma)\land\neg A)\lor
 (\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j-1}(\Gamma)\land A)\bigr),\]
where \(\Gamma\) is any finite ordered list of formulas, including the empty list, and \(j-1\) is reduced modulo \(p\) to \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\). These are the modular schemes of the cited source, attached to the specified finite complete classical Frege basis. An axiom line must match its indicated scheme syntactically after expansion, using the same substituted formula at each occurrence of a metavariable. A proof is a nonempty finite sequence of axiom or modus-ponens lines ending with the claimed formula. Earlier lines may be reused without restriction. There are no extension-variable definition axioms, no separate substitution rule for previously derived lines, and no restrictions of regularity or tree shape.

Define the logical depth \(\delta\) of constants and variables to be zero. Negation has depth \(1+\delta(A)\), and a modular gate has depth \(1+\max(0,\delta(A_1),\ldots,\delta(A_t))\). For a conjunction, flatten its maximal connected subtree of conjunction nodes and collect the boundary subformulas whose roots are not conjunctions; its depth is one plus the maximum depth of those subformulas. Use the same rule for disjunctions. Flattening does not cross a negation, modular gate or different Boolean connective. It defines the depth measure only: the actual binary syntax tree is still written and counted in full. A depth-at-most-\(d\) proof must have \(\delta\le d\) for every line, including instantiated axioms and the conclusion. This bounds individual formulas, not the length of an inference path in the proof graph. Such paths and the total number of lines are unrestricted.

All sizes are bits in a fixed prefix encoding. For \(t\ge0\), let \(b(t)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and let \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\), using concatenation. Formula tags 000 and 001 encode constants \(0\) and \(1\); 010 followed by \(E(i)\) encodes \(x_i\); 011 followed by the child encodes negation; 100 and 101 followed by both child encodings encode conjunction and disjunction. Tag 110 followed by \(E(j)E(t)\) and all \(t\) ordered child encodings represents \(\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}\). Tag 111 is invalid. The prime is fixed by the system, not supplied as an oracle. A proof starts with \(E(m)\), its positive number of lines. Each line contains \(E(q)\) followed by its complete formula encoding. Rule labels \(q=1,\ldots,11\) refer to the ordinary schemes in their displayed order; labels 12, 13 and 14 refer respectively to the empty-zero-residue, empty-nonzero-residue and recursive modular schemes. Label 15 denotes modus ponens and is followed, after the formula, by \(E(a)E(b)\): on line \(j\), require \(1\le a,b<j\), line \(a=A\) and line \(b=A\Rightarrow B\), with the current line exactly \(B\). Other rule labels and malformed strings are invalid. The length \(|\pi|\) includes every variable index, gate, repeated formula occurrence, line count and inference reference. Formula length uses the same formula encoding. Nothing is given by a compressed circuit, advice or a program for generating a larger proof.

The predicate \(\operatorname{Proof}_{p,d}(\pi,\tau)\) means validity under all these rules, conclusion \(\tau\), and line depth at most \(d\). Construction time for the target family is measured on a standard deterministic Turing machine with a fixed finite number of tapes and a finite alphabet containing input/output bits and blank. A transition reads and writes at most one cell per tape and moves each head by at most one cell; all transitions and output writes count. Each \(M_p\) is one finite program, with no oracle or length-dependent advice. Its constants \(C_p,k_p\) may depend on that program and the fixed prime. The formula-size lower bound \(|\tau_{p,n}|\ge n\) and polynomial upper bound make size in \(n\) polynomially comparable with size in the conclusion. Quantifying over positive integer exponents \(r\) is equivalent to exceeding every polynomial bound, including bounds with arbitrary fixed multiplicative constants.
answer_criterion: Supply the stated families, their construction machines and bounds, together with a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that all outputs are DNF tautologies and that the displayed lower-bound quantifiers hold for every prime and every fixed line depth. Alternatively, give a complete Lean proof of the logical negation: some prime \(p\) has no family satisfying all the stated requirements. Equivalently, for that prime, every polynomial-time constructible DNF tautology family of the prescribed length scale has some fixed depth \(d\), exponent \(r\) and threshold \(N\) for which every \(n\ge N\) admits a valid depth-\(d\) proof of size at most \(n^r\). A negative answer does not require an efficient proof-finding algorithm. Unproved tautologicity, one fixed polynomial lower bound, a bound only at restricted derivation depth, or a result for only one prime does not establish the full positive claim. All assumptions, construction bounds, depth and size conventions must match the card. This binary asymptotic claim retains its polynomial precision; the numerical 1/100 tolerance is not a replacement for a proof-size lower bound.

title: Separating levels of bounded arithmetic
summary: The question asks whether two positive levels of Buss’s bounded-arithmetic hierarchy prove different sentences. Each level has the same basic arithmetic axioms but permits induction for a different class of bounded formulas. A solution may choose any two distinct positive levels and must prove an unconditional difference in their deductive strength. The full axiom list, formula grammar and induction scheme specify the theories without relying on an unstated standard model. Recent conditional separations do not provide the unconditional nonprovability witness required here.
formal:
Are there integers \(i>j\ge1\) and a closed first-order arithmetic sentence \(\theta\) such that
\[T_2^i\vdash\theta\qquad\text{and}\qquad T_2^j\nvdash\theta?\]
The theory \(T_2^r\) is BASIC together with induction for every \(\Sigma_r^b\) formula in the language defined below. The question asks for a separation as sets of provable sentences, with no assumed separation of computational complexity classes and no additional oracle symbols. One pair of levels is enough; it need not be fixed in advance, and proving strictness at every pair is not required.
definitions:
Use classical first-order logic with equality and the one-sorted language \(L=\{0,1,+,\cdot,H,\ell,\#,\le\}\). Here \(H\) and \(\ell\) are unary, \(+\), \(\cdot\), \(\#\) are binary, and \(\le\) is a binary predicate. Terms are the finite expressions formed from variables, these constants and these function symbols. Atomic formulas are equalities or inequalities between terms. The logical operations are negation, conjunction, disjunction and first-order universal/existential quantification; implication and equivalence abbreviate their usual Boolean expansions. The successor notation \(Sx\) abbreviates \(x+1\), \(2\) abbreviates \(1+1\), and \(2x\) means \(2\cdot x\).

The intended standard structure has domain \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), its usual addition, multiplication and order, \(H(x)=\lfloor x/2\rfloor\), \(\ell(0)=0\), \(\ell(x)=\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor+1\) for \(x>0\), and \(x\#y=2^{\ell(x)\ell(y)}\). This interpretation explains the symbols; the theory's nonlogical axioms are exactly the following finite BASIC list and the specified induction scheme, rather than all sentences true in this standard structure. Every free variable in the following displays is universally quantified.

The order and successor axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
a\le b\ \to\ a\le b+1,\qquad a\ne a+1,\qquad 0\le a,\\
(a\le b\land a\ne b)\ \to\ a+1\le b,\qquad a\ne0\ \to\ 2a\ne0,\\
a\le b\lor b\le a,\qquad (a\le b\land b\le a)\ \to\ a=b,\\
(a\le b\land b\le c)\ \to\ a\le c,\qquad a\le a+b,\\
(a\le b\land a\ne b)\ \to\ (2a+1\le2b\land 2a+1\ne2b).
\end{gathered}\]
The addition and multiplication axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
a+b=b+a,\qquad a+0=a,\qquad a+(b+1)=(a+b)+1,\\
(a+b)+c=a+(b+c),\qquad a+b\le a+c\ \to\ b\le c,\\
a\cdot0=0,\qquad a\cdot(b+1)=a\cdot b+a,\qquad a\cdot b=b\cdot a,\\
a\cdot(b+c)=(a\cdot b)+(a\cdot c),\\
1\le a\ \to\ ((a\cdot b\le a\cdot c)\leftrightarrow(b\le c)).
\end{gathered}\]
The length, halving and smash axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
\ell(0)=0,\qquad \ell(1)=1,\qquad a\le b\ \to\ \ell(a)\le\ell(b),\\
a\ne0\ \to\ (\ell(2a)=\ell(a)+1\land\ell(2a+1)=\ell(a)+1),\\
\ell(a\#b)=\ell(a)\cdot\ell(b)+1,\qquad 0\#a=1,\\
a\ne0\ \to\ (1\#(2a)=2(1\#a)\land1\#(2a+1)=2(1\#a)),\\
a\#b=b\#a,\qquad \ell(a)=\ell(b)\ \to\ a\#c=b\#c,\\
\ell(a)=\ell(b)+\ell(c)\ \to\ a\#d=(b\#d)\cdot(c\#d),\\
a\ne0\ \to\ \ell(a)=\ell(H(a))+1,\\
a=H(b)\ \leftrightarrow\ (2a=b\lor2a+1=b).
\end{gathered}\]
These are the 32 axioms in Krajíček's Definition 5.2.1, regrouped by operation, with \(H\) and \(\ell\) replacing the printed halving and length notation. No sequence function or oracle predicate is added.

For a term \(t\) not containing \(y\), write \(\exists y\le t\,\psi\) for \(\exists y(y\le t\land\psi)\), and \(\forall y\le t\,\psi\) for \(\forall y(y\le t\to\psi)\). These are bounded quantifiers. They are sharply bounded when the bound is explicitly \(\ell(t)\). The bound may contain other free variables. Let \(\Sigma_0^b=\Pi_0^b\) be all formulas built from atomic formulas using Boolean operations and only sharply bounded quantifiers. Recursively, \(\Sigma_{r+1}^b,\Pi_{r+1}^b\) are the smallest pair of classes satisfying: both contain \(\Sigma_r^b\cup\Pi_r^b\); both are closed under conjunction, disjunction and both sharply bounded quantifiers; \(\Sigma_{r+1}^b\) is closed under bounded existential quantification; \(\Pi_{r+1}^b\) is closed under bounded universal quantification; and negation sends either class into the other. These are the full formula classes, allowing sharply bounded quantifiers inside as well as outside the other quantifiers, rather than only a strict prenex fragment.

For a set \(T\) of closed axioms, \(T\vdash\theta\) means that the closed sentence \(\theta\) has a finite proof in classical first-order logic with equality from those axioms. Equivalently, every nonempty \(L\)-structure satisfying all axioms of \(T\) satisfies \(\theta\). This equivalence is first-order completeness; structures in this characterization are not restricted to the standard natural numbers. There is no bound on proof length. Equality of theories here means equality of their deductive closures in the same language.

For each integer \(r\ge1\), \(T_2^r\) has the displayed BASIC axioms and, for each \(\varphi(x,\vec a)\in\Sigma_r^b\), the universal closure over all parameter variables \(\vec a\) of
\[\bigl(\varphi(0,\vec a)\land\forall x(\varphi(x,\vec a)\to\varphi(x+1,\vec a))\bigr)\ \to\ \forall x\,\varphi(x,\vec a).\]
Parameters are allowed and are not required to be numerals. There are no induction axioms for formulas outside the specified class unless they are consequences of these axioms. Since the formula classes are nested, \(T_2^j\subseteq T_2^i\) in deductive strength when \(j<i\). A positive answer therefore gives a strict inclusion. The separating sentence may have unrestricted first-order quantifiers; no complexity or syntactic bound on that witness sentence is part of the target.

The indices, finite formulas and finite proofs in the question range over ordinary standard mathematical objects. The nonprovability claim is external: it means that no finite proof from the weaker theory exists, rather than asking the weaker theory itself to prove its inability. A countermodel for the weaker theory and the sentence is an equivalent way to certify that nonprovability. A positive answer must be unconditional in the usual mathematical metatheory; adding an unproved complexity assumption changes the requested statement.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existential separation. A positive answer must establish one pair of standard integers \(i>j\ge1\), a closed sentence provable in \(T_2^i\), and its nonprovability in \(T_2^j\); the latter can equivalently be proved by a model of \(T_2^j\) falsifying the sentence. A negative answer must establish equality of the deductive closures for every pair \(i>j\ge1\). A difference between axiom lists, a lower bound on the shortest proof of a still-provable sentence, a relativized separation, or a separation conditional on an unproved complexity conjecture does not settle this target.

title: Superpolynomial \(\mathrm{Res}(\oplus)\) lower bounds
summary: Resolution over parities extends ordinary resolution by allowing disjunctions of linear equations modulo two. The question asks whether unsatisfiable CNF formulas can require more proof lines than every universal polynomial bound in their input size. Proofs may reuse earlier lines without any restriction on depth, width, regularity or space.
