Use the [De Morgan circuit basis](definitions.html#boolean-circuits) with \(n\) input variables, free constants 0 and 1, and one designated output. A supplied circuit has size \(s\), the number of its operation gates. An input, constant or gate may serve as the output. Depth, fan-out and the growth of \(s\) with \(n\) are unrestricted. The polynomial overhead exponent \(d\) is fixed across all these sizes.

For an assignment \(a\in\{0,1\}^n\), evaluate gates in topological order using ordinary Boolean operations. Satisfiability means that at least one such assignment gives output 1. The algorithm returns exactly this yes/no answer; it need not count or enumerate satisfying assignments. All declared input nodes are explicitly listed and included in \(n\), even if some are unused.

Use the [self-delimiting integer code](definitions.html#sat-encoding). List the codes of \(n,s\), then \(n\) input-node markers, and then the \(s\) gates in a topological order. Number the constants 0 and 1 first, the inputs next and the gates last. Each gate has a two-bit type tag and coded predecessor indices, all smaller than its own index. Finish with the coded output-node index, with no trailing data. Invalid encodings are outside the domain. The total length \(N\) is \(O((n+s)\log(n+s+2))\); the polynomial factor pays for processing the entire explicit description.

The algorithm is one classical deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, no advice, no oracle and no random bits. All input processing, intermediate bit computation and output are charged. The constants, function and program are chosen before the input: the quantifier order is \(\exists(A,d,K,g)\;\forall C\), subject to the displayed limit on \(g\). In particular, \(g\) depends only on \(n\), and \(d\) cannot grow with circuit size or an accuracy parameter. The limit means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\), there is an integer \(N\) such that \(g(n)\le\varepsilon n\) for every \(n\ge N\). Thus one fixed saving \(2^{(1-\delta)n}\) for a constant \(0<\delta<1\) does not by itself meet this target.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must supply a single deterministic algorithm, prove exact decision correctness on every encoded circuit, and prove the full charged running-time bound with fixed \(d,K\) and \(g(n)/n\to0\). A negative answer must unconditionally rule out every such algorithm and bound; a lower bound conditional on another conjecture establishes only that conditional statement.

An algorithm restricted to linear-size circuits, bounded depth, formulas or a fixed clause width does not establish this universal target. A running time subexponential only in \(N\) or \(n+s\), or a fixed positive saving in the coefficient of \(n\), also does not suffice. This is a genuine existence question, not a numerical request to approximate an infimum running-time exponent.

title: Online matrix–vector multiplication conjecture
summary: A fixed Boolean matrix is given first, followed by a sequence of Boolean vectors. The algorithm must return each Boolean product before it sees the next vector. The question asks for a fixed polynomial saving over cubic total time, including preprocessing, with a constant probability that every answer is correct. Known speedups, free-computation cell-probe bounds and faster structured-matrix queries do not resolve the unrestricted word-RAM target. A complete Lean-checked resolution would either refute or prove a central hypothesis behind dynamic-problem lower bounds.
formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), a constant \(K>0\), an integer word-size constant \(B\ge3\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\) with the following property? For every integer \(n\ge2\), every Boolean matrix \(M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\), and every sequence \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\{0,1\}^n\) supplied online, the algorithm outputs each \(Mv_t\) before receiving \(v_{t+1}\), and outputs \(Mv_n\) at the end, using at most
\[
 K n^{3-\varepsilon}
\]
word-RAM instructions in total on every execution, including preprocessing of \(M\), with probability at least \(2/3\) that all \(n\) output vectors are correct? Products are over the Boolean semiring:
\[
 (Mv_t)_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(M_{ij}\wedge(v_t)_j\bigr).
\]
The OMv conjecture asserts a negative answer.
definitions:
The input initially supplies \(n\) and all \(n^2\) entries of the fixed matrix \(M\), in row-major order. After the algorithm's initial preprocessing, vectors arrive one at a time in the order \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\). Each vector is an arbitrary length-\(n\) bit string. The next vector is unavailable until the algorithm has finished returning the current vector's complete answer. The algorithm may preserve its computed state and earlier vectors, but cannot postpone an output to use future inputs. There is no per-query time bound beyond the total bound and these deadlines.

Both the matrix bit string and each input vector are explicitly packed into consecutive words with known zero padding. An output vector contains its \(n\) bits in coordinate order; an explicit array with one Boolean value per word is an allowed canonical output representation. Returning an implicit circuit, a pointer to uncomputed answers, a count of nonzero entries or just one queried coordinate is insufficient. All input access and output writes are charged. The matrix never changes. The operations \(\wedge\) and \(\vee\) mean Boolean AND and OR; this is neither arithmetic multiplication over the reals nor multiplication over the field of two elements.

The computation is a sequential word RAM with
\[
 w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil
\]
bits per word and one fixed finite program for all \(n\). Memory cells, registers and addresses are word-sized. Unit-cost instructions are reads, writes, copies, comparisons, branches, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) positions return zero. Multiword computations cost their component instructions. An independent uniform random \(w\)-bit word can be generated in one instruction. This permits deterministic algorithms as a special case. There are no quantum instructions, nonuniform advice, free precomputed tables or input-dependent oracles. Unused memory initially contains zero.

All instructions are counted, including construction of auxiliary tables, allocation or initialization performed by the program, preprocessing before the first vector, work between vectors, generation of random words, copying and output. There is no separate allowance for an arbitrary polynomial preprocessing phase. Space has no additional sublinear or near-linear restriction, but every address must fit in a word and writing any used state costs instructions. Only the currently supplied input is made available by the online interface; it supplies no information about a future vector.

For the success guarantee, the matrix and complete vector sequence are fixed independently of the algorithm's randomness. The probability is over the program's random words, and the successful event requires every bit of every output to be correct. A separate success probability of \(2/3\) for each individual query is not the specified joint guarantee. The time bound holds for every random execution, including erroneous executions. Every output deadline and eventual termination must likewise be met on every execution.

The constants \(\varepsilon,K,B\) and the program are chosen once, independently of the input dimension and contents. Any fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) suffices. A merely logarithmic or subpolynomial improvement in total time is not a fixed exponent saving. No restriction to combinatorial algorithms is imposed: every algorithm implementable by the specified word-RAM instructions is allowed.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the stated algorithm exists, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm and constants exist.

A positive answer must establish the fixed exponent saving after charging preprocessing and all input/output work, the online deadlines, and joint success for every fixed input. It refutes the OMv conjecture in this model. A negative answer must exclude every admissible uniform randomized program, every fixed word-size constant and every positive exponent saving. It proves the conjecture in this model and cannot assume the conjecture itself or another unproved hardness hypothesis.

An algorithm for structured matrices, an offline matrix product, a query bound after uncharged preprocessing, or a cell-probe bound with free computation does not meet the target without a proved extension. Neither does a speedup of the form \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\), which supplies no fixed positive saving in the exponent.

title: Truly subquadratic exact edit distance
summary: Can exact edit distance between two length-n binary strings be computed in truly subquadratic time? Each insertion, deletion and substitution costs one, and the algorithm must always return the exact minimum. The requested deterministic worst-case bound has a fixed positive saving in the exponent of n. Known reductions rule out such an algorithm if SETH is true, but that hypothesis remains unproved. The 2026 approximation improvement has different accuracy and randomness guarantees.
formal: For the binary alphabet \(\Sigma=\{0,1\}\), do there exist constants \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), \(C>0\) and one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm \(A\) such that for every \(n\ge1\) and every \(x,y\in\Sigma^n\), the algorithm outputs the exact unit-cost edit distance \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\) in at most \(C(n+1)^{2-\varepsilon}\) operations?
definitions: An edit inserts one symbol, deletes one symbol, or substitutes one symbol by the other; each operation costs 1. \(ED(x,y)\) is the minimum total number of edits transforming the entire string x into the entire string y. Equal symbols can be retained at cost 0. The output is this integer, not necessarily a sequence of edits. Both strings have length n and are provided explicitly, one symbol per word. The word-RAM has \(w=\operatorname{ceil}(4 \log _{2}(n+2))\) bits per word, zero-initialized addressable memory of w-bit words, and a fixed finite program independent of n. One operation reads or writes one addressed word, branches or compares words, or applies unsigned addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer division by a nonzero word with rounding down, a bitwise Boolean operation, or a logical shift by fewer than w positions. Constants are fixed by the program, and words cannot hold arbitrarily large integers in one step. The running time includes every memory access and arithmetic operation; no oracle, advice or input-dependent precomputed table is supplied. All preprocessing is charged. The time guarantee is worst-case over inputs, with no random coins or probability of error. The constant exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) cannot tend to zero with n. The chosen binary alphabet is an explicit specialization of the imported phrase “a fixed finite alphabet”, supported by Bringmann–Künnemann’s binary-alphabet formulation; a unary alphabet would make the equal-length problem trivial.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution supplies one algorithm with a proof of exact correctness for every binary input pair and a worst-case \(O(n^{2- \varepsilon})\) bound for some fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) in the specified model. A negative resolution rules out every such deterministic algorithm and every fixed positive exponent saving. A lower bound conditional on an unproved hypothesis is not an unconditional negative resolution. Faster approximation, special-case performance and logarithmic-factor savings do not meet the target.

title: Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis
summary: Bichromatic Orthogonal Vectors asks whether two explicit lists contain binary vectors with disjoint supports. The retained hypothesis says that every proposed fixed saving over quadratic time fails at some fixed logarithmic-dimension constant. It concerns uniform randomized word-RAM algorithms with all preprocessing charged, worst-case running time and bounded error on every input. A complete Lean refutation must provide one positive exponent saving valid for every dimension constant, although its individual programs and time constants may depend on that constant. Known deterministic and randomized dimension-dependent savings, average-case improvements and restricted-model lower bounds leave this full hypothesis unresolved.
formal:
Is it true that
\[\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1)\ \exists c\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\ \text{no allowed algorithm solves bichromatic Orthogonal Vectors in }O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\text{ time}\]
for all integers \(n\ge2\) on two lists of \(n\) vectors in \(\{0,1\}^{d}\), where \(d=\lceil c\log_2n\rceil\)? An allowed algorithm is a uniform randomized classical word-RAM program in the model below. Its running-time bound is worst-case over both inputs and random choices, and its answer must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. The dimension constant \(c\) may depend on the proposed exponent saving \(\varepsilon\), but is fixed as \(n\) grows.
definitions:
Decision problem. For \(n\ge2\), the input consists of ordered lists \(A=(a^{(1)},\ldots,a^{(n)})\) and \(B=(b^{(1)},\ldots,b^{(n)})\) of binary vectors of common dimension \(d=\lceil c\log_2n\rceil\). Repeated vectors, zero vectors and overlap between the lists are allowed. Output YES exactly when
\[\exists r,s\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:\quad\sum_{j=1}^{d}a^{(r)}_j b^{(s)}_j=0.\]
The sum is an ordinary nonnegative integer sum. Equivalently, the two supports are disjoint. Orthogonality modulo two is a different predicate. The selected pair must come from opposite lists, but the task only asks for a decision bit, not for a witness. There is no promise on Hamming weights, intersections, number of solutions or input distribution.

Words and encoding. A machine fixes an integer \(\lambda\ge2\) and uses unsigned words of
\[w=\lambda\lceil\log_2(n+d+2)\rceil\]
bits. Input headers supply \(n,d\), followed by the two lists in order. Each vector occupies \(\lceil d/w\rceil\) consecutive words, with its coordinates packed from least to most significant bit and unused final bits zero. Thus for fixed \(c\) one vector occupies a constant number of words as \(n\) grows. The input is explicit, not supplied by a membership or inner-product oracle. Changing between ordinary explicit bit arrays and this packing costs at most a logarithmic factor; the stated acceptance bound itself uses the packed model.

Instruction set and cost. The program is finite and independent of \(n\). It has word registers and random-access memory addressed by single words. One step may read or write a constant number of addressed words; perform addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\); perform unsigned integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor; apply bitwise AND, OR, XOR or NOT; shift logically left or right; compare words; or branch using a comparison. Shifts discard overflow and give zero when their shift count is at least \(w\). A fresh uniform random \(w\)-bit word costs one step and is independent of all previous random words. A compound operation on several words must be built from these instructions and charged accordingly. There is no unit-cost arbitrary-precision arithmetic, real arithmetic, vector instruction of input-dependent width, or additional oracle.

Uniformity, memory and preprocessing. Outside the explicit input, memory initially contains only zeros. Programs may contain fixed finite constants, but receive no advice, precomputed tables or extra data depending on \(n\). Any such tables must be produced during the charged computation. The program and \(\lambda\) may depend on the fixed \(c\) and \(\varepsilon\), as may constants in the running-time bound; none may vary with \(n\). Single-word addressing bounds available memory by \(2^w\) words. Reading input, constructing tables, preprocessing either list, generating randomness and producing the answer are all charged. There is no separate free preprocessing phase.

Time and error. To solve the problem, the program must halt with a decision bit on every allowed input and random execution. For each fixed input, over its independent internal random words, the bit must equal the predicate above with probability at least \(2/3\). Either type of error is allowed within this bound. The claim \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) means that there exist a real \(K>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge2\) such that every input of every size \(n\ge n_0\), and every sequence of random choices, takes at most \(K n^{2-\varepsilon}\) steps. An expected-time or average-input bound is not itself this worst-case guarantee. Deterministic programs are included by ignoring the random instruction.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this lower-bound proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must cover every allowed uniform randomized program in the specified instruction model, with the quantifier order \(\forall\varepsilon\,\exists c\) and the per-input success requirement. A proof conditional on an unproved version of the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis is evidence for the conjecture, not an unconditional resolution.

A refutation must establish
\[\exists\varepsilon\in(0,1)\ \forall c\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists A_c,\lambda_c,K_c,n_{0,c}:\quad A_c\text{ meets the stated time and correctness conditions}.\]
The same positive saving \(\varepsilon\) must work for every fixed \(c\). The programs, word-size constants, multiplicative constants and asymptotic thresholds may depend on \(c\). Each \(A_c\) must be uniform in \(n\); no additional uniform algorithm taking \(c\) as input is demanded. A deterministic family would also refute the randomized hypothesis.

An exponent saving \(\varepsilon_c>0\) that shrinks with \(c\), a bound for a fixed small dimension, logarithmic improvements over quadratic time, success only on random instances, or a lower bound restricted to monotone circuits, formulas or branching programs does not settle the full proposition. A fast online query bound with separate preprocessing must satisfy the total charged offline time before it qualifies. This is an asymptotic yes-or-no claim, with no additive numerical approximation tolerance.

title: Algebraic k-Clique Hypothesis
summary: For each fixed clique size, the task is to decide whether an arbitrary graph contains that many pairwise adjacent vertices. The hypothesis compares the leading coefficient of the optimal randomized time exponent with one third of the true matrix-multiplication exponent. The graph algorithm uses logarithmic-size words, and its time bound must hold on every random tape. The graph size tends to infinity first, while the clique size is fixed; the outer limit then considers growing clique sizes. A complete Lean-checked proof or refutation must address that full asymptotic comparison, rather than only logarithmic savings or one fixed clique size.
formal:
For each fixed integer \(k\ge3\), let \(\tau(k)\) be the infimum worst-case time exponent for uniform classical randomized algorithms deciding whether an \(n\)-vertex graph contains a \(k\)-clique, in the word-RAM model defined below. Let \(\omega\) be the arithmetic matrix-multiplication exponent over \(\mathbb C\). Is
\[
 \liminf_{k\to\infty}\frac{\tau(k)}{k}=\frac{\omega}{3}?
\]
The input size \(n\) tends to infinity with \(k\) fixed when defining \(\tau(k)\); only afterwards does \(k\) grow in the displayed limit inferior.
definitions:
A graph is simple and undirected, with vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(n\ge k\), and an explicitly given symmetric Boolean adjacency matrix with zero diagonal. Its \(n^2\) entries are stored in row order, one per word, together with \(n\). A \(k\)-clique is a set of \(k\) distinct vertices with all pairs adjacent. The algorithm outputs a YES or NO bit; it is not asked to list or count cliques.

For fixed \(k\), call a real \(a\ge0\) admissible if there exist a finite uniform randomized program, an integer word-size constant \(B\ge3\), real \(C>0\) and integer \(N\ge k\), such that for every graph on \(n\ge N\) vertices every execution takes at most \(Cn^a\) instructions and the answer is correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The program must also terminate and meet the same probability guarantee on each valid smaller input. Constants and program may depend on \(k\) and \(a\), but not on \(n\) or the graph. Define
\[
 \tau(k)=\inf\{a\ge0:a\text{ is admissible for }k\}.
\]
Exhaustive enumeration makes this set nonempty. Its infimum need not itself be achieved. There is no requirement for an efficient compiler taking \(k\) to its program; uniformity here means one program handling every \(n\) for each fixed \(k\).

At size \(n\), words contain \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits. One instruction may read or write a word at a word-sized address, copy a word, perform addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\), divide two unsigned words with nonzero divisor and return quotient or remainder, apply a bitwise Boolean operation, shift a word, compare two unsigned words, or branch. Logical shifts discard bits beyond the word; a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. A fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit word may also be obtained in one instruction. All other memory is initially zero, and every preprocessing operation is charged. No nonuniform advice, free table depending on \(n\), arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic or external oracle is allowed. The constant \(B\) may be chosen with the algorithm so that its polynomially many addressed cells fit in a word. The time bound holds on every random tape, not only in expectation, while success probability is over that tape on each fixed graph.

To define \(\omega\), for each integer \(N\ge1\) let \(M(N)\) be the smallest number of binary addition, subtraction and multiplication gates in an arithmetic circuit over \(\mathbb C\) that computes every entry of the product of two formal \(N\)-by-\(N\) matrices. The \(2N^2\) entries of those matrices are independent indeterminates. Circuits may share intermediate results and use arbitrary complex constants, but not division or branching; they must compute the required polynomial identities exactly. Put
\[
 \omega=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \exists N_0\ \forall N\ge N_0,
                       \ M(N)\le CN^a\}.
\]
This is the characteristic-zero arithmetic exponent, not a particular currently published numerical upper bound. The complex constants used to define it are not free constants or arithmetic oracles supplied to the word-RAM graph algorithm.

For a real sequence \(u_k\), its limit inferior is \(\sup_K\inf_{k\ge K}u_k\). Thus the question concerns the leading coefficient of clique size in the optimal exponent. The standard matrix-multiplication benchmark gives the upper asymptotic coefficient \(\omega/3\); the hypothesis asserts the matching lower coefficient. The inherited leading-exponent formulation does not separately assert the precise optimum for each small fixed \(k\). Nor does it invoke an informal restriction to algorithms described as combinatorial: all classical algorithms in the specified machine model are included.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed equality or a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation, with exactly the models and order of limits defined above.

In view of the matrix-multiplication upper benchmark, an affirmative result must establish that for every real \(\delta>0\) there is \(K\) such that \(\tau(k)\ge(\omega/3-\delta)k\) for every integer \(k\ge K\). A negative result can establish one fixed positive saving \(\delta\) for arbitrarily large clique sizes, with proved algorithms and resource bounds, so that the limit inferior is strictly smaller than \(\omega/3\).

An improvement confined to a single fixed \(k\), logarithmic factors in \(n\), or an additive \(o(k)\) saving in the exponent does not by itself refute this formulation. Beating an outdated numerical upper bound on \(\omega\) is also insufficient. Lower bounds only for a restricted algorithm family, or only conditional on an additional unproved hypothesis, do not prove the unrestricted proposition. This is an exact yes-or-no hypothesis about exponents; numerical accuracy within \(1/100\) is not a substitute for the equality or its negation.

title: Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis
summary: Min-plus convolution returns the minimum sum of two array entries for each possible sum of their indices. The input arrays contain polynomially bounded integers and need not be monotone. The question asks for a fixed improvement in the quadratic running-time exponent. Bounded-error randomization is allowed and every output entry must be correct simultaneously. Faster algorithms for monotone instances do not settle this unrestricted fine-grained barrier.
formal: Does there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm computes the min-plus convolution of any two length-\(n\) integer arrays with entries in \([-n^{a},n^{a}]\) in \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) worst-case time?
definitions: For \(n\ge2\), input arrays \(A=(a_{0},\ldots,a_{n-1})\) and \(B=(b_{0},\ldots,b_{n-1})\) are explicitly listed. Output all \(2n-1\) integers \(c_{k}=\min\{a_{i}+b_{j}:0\le i,j<n,\ i+j=k\}\), for \(0\le k\le2n-2\). Inputs need not be sorted or monotone. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) is common to all fixed magnitude exponents \(a\); the program, word-size constant and hidden time constant may depend on \(a\). Signed entries and exact output sums use a constant number of words.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) permits the stated family of uniform algorithms for every fixed magnitude exponent \(a\), with worst-case time and whole-output success guarantees, or prove the logical negation in Lean. In the negation, every proposed saving \(\varepsilon\) fails for at least one fixed \(a\), allowing all permitted algorithms and their constants. Neither a conditional hardness implication nor a theorem for monotone inputs proves that negation.

title: Randomized APSP hypothesis for polynomial integer weights
summary: All-pairs shortest paths asks for the exact distance between every ordered pair of vertices in a directed graph. The graph has polynomially bounded signed integer edge weights and no negative-weight cycle. The hypothesis says that for every fixed improvement over the cubic exponent, some polynomial weight bound rules out every randomized algorithm with that running time. The 2026 deterministic \(O(n^{2.9995})\) algorithm refutes this hypothesis. The same algorithm satisfies the stated reduction to 3SUM using zero oracle calls.
formal: Is the following hypothesis true? \[\forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1]\ \exists c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:\ \neg\mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon).\] Here \(\mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon)\) means that a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm computes the entire exact distance matrix of every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with integer edge weights in \([-n^c,n^c]\) and no negative-weight cycle, succeeds with probability at least \(2/3\) on each input, and has worst-case time \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) over all inputs and coin sequences. The word model and the quantifiers hidden in this definition are specified below. The weight exponent \(c\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\). This makes explicit the weaker quantifier order stated in the 2026 source; the 2018 source's phrase about sufficiently large \(c\) did not specify that dependence.
definitions:
For fixed integers \(n\ge2\) and \(c\ge1\), the vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input is \(n\) and an \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix in vertex order, with a presence flag for each ordered pair and, for each present edge, a signed integer weight \(w(u,v)\) satisfying \(|w(u,v)|\le n^c\). There is at most one edge per ordered pair; self-loops are allowed. Missing edges are indicated by their flags. The graph is promised to have no directed cycle with negative total weight. Negative edges, zero-weight cycles and ties between shortest paths are allowed. For vertices \(u,v\), let \(d_G(u,v)\) be the minimum total weight of a finite directed walk from \(u\) to \(v\), or a separate unreachable symbol \(+\infty\) if there is no such walk. The empty walk has weight zero. Under the promise every reachable minimum is attained, \(d_G(u,u)=0\), and each finite distance has absolute value at most \((n-1)n^c\). The output consists of these \(n^2\) exact integers or unreachable flags in vertex-pair order; listing all path vertices is not required.

The machine is a word RAM with one fixed finite program. For a fixed integer \(a\ge c+4\), its word length on \(n\)-vertex inputs is \(b(n)=\lceil a\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Each memory address and memory cell is one word. The input is one word for n followed in row-major order by two words for each matrix entry: its zero-or-one presence flag and its signed weight, with zero in the weight word when the flag is zero. The output uses the same row-major order and two words per entry: a zero-or-one finite-distance flag and its signed distance, with zero in the second word for unreachable pairs. Signed integers use two's-complement encoding; distances fit in a constant number of words. Word load, store, copy, comparison, conditional branch, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts, and addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b(n)}\) each cost one step. Unsigned quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one step. Division by zero is invalid; shifts by at least \(b(n)\) positions return zero. Algorithms may use several words for larger quantities, charging all operations. All accessed addresses must fit in a word. Work memory initially contains zero, and no input-dependent precomputed tables, advice or oracle are supplied. All preprocessing, table construction, memory operations and output writing count toward the time bound. One random instruction yields one fresh independent fair bit in one step. The input graph is fixed before the coins are drawn. Deterministic programs are included by ignoring random bits.

Precisely, \(\mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon)\) asserts the existence of a finite program \(A\), an integer word-size factor \(a\ge c+4\), and an integer constant \(C\ge1\), such that for every integer \(n\ge2\) and every promised graph, every run halts within \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) steps, and with probability at least \(2/3\) its entire output matrix equals \((d_G(u,v))_{u,v\in[n]}\). Correctness is joint for the matrix, rather than a separate bound for each entry. The program, \(a\) and \(C\) may depend on the fixed \(c\) and \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(n\) or the input graph. There is no requirement to classify or detect inputs that violate the promise. The exponent in the time bound concerns the number \(n\) of vertices; the input has \(\Theta(n^2)\) words and \(O(n^2\log n)\) bits for each fixed \(c,a\). Rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\) capture every possible fixed positive exponent saving.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed hypothesis, or of its full logical negation \[\exists\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1]\ \forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:\ \mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon).\] A refutation must therefore establish one common positive exponent saving for every fixed polynomial weight bound; programs and runtime constants may depend on \(c\). A proof of the hypothesis must rule out all uniform randomized algorithms in the specified model for a suitable \(c\) at each saving \(\varepsilon\). A deterministic-only lower bound, a barrier for a particular algorithm or reduction technique, or a truly subcubic algorithm only for one restricted weight regime does not settle the statement. Neither do approximate distances, random input distributions, single-source bounds, distributed round bounds or extra accurate predictions. A subpolynomial-factor improvement over cubic time alone is insufficient. This yes/no target concerns exact APSP algorithms; an unproved APSP hypothesis cannot be assumed as the proof of itself.

title: Hitting Set conjecture
summary: Two lists contain subsets of a logarithmic-size universe. The task is to find whether one supplied set in the first list intersects every set in the second. The conjecture rules out a single fixed polynomial improvement over quadratic time across all constant multiples of logarithmic dimension. The selected model permits randomization with bounded error and counts all word-RAM computation. Its existential–universal structure makes it useful for graph-radius and quantified-ordering lower bounds.
formal:
Is the randomized Hitting Set conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(c\ge1\) such that no uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm decides the following problem in worst-case time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\)? The input is two lists \(A,B\), each of \(n\) subsets of \([d]\), where \(n\ge2\) and \(d=\lceil c\log_2 n\rceil\). Decide whether
\[\exists a\in A\ \forall b\in B:\quad a\cap b\ne\varnothing.\]
The chosen set must be one of the supplied sets in \(A\). This is the source's fine-grained two-list problem, not the general optimization problem of selecting a small hitting set from the universe.
definitions:
Write \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). Sets are supplied explicitly as \(d\)-bit incidence vectors; lists may contain repetitions and empty sets. Equivalently, the answer is yes if some vector \(a\in A\) has integer inner product \(\sum_{j=1}^d a_j b_j>0\) with every \(b\in B\). The coordinate sum is over integers, not modulo two. The dimension constant \(c\) is fixed independently of input size.

Use a word RAM with word length
\[
w=\max\!\left\{\lceil4\log_2(n+2)\rceil,\ \lceil\log_2(2nd+n+d+8)\rceil\right\}.
\]
The second term ensures that the full explicit input and its headers fit in the address universe even for small \(n\) and a large fixed dimension constant \(c\). For every fixed \(c\), it is eventually dominated by the first term, so this finite-input correction leaves the stated asymptotic time hypothesis unchanged. Incidence vectors are packed into consecutive words, with unused bits zero. A machine has a finite program independent of \(n\), word-addressed memory, and unit-cost word reads/writes, copies, comparisons, branches, arithmetic addition/subtraction/multiplication modulo \(2^w\), quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero; division by zero may return zero. A uniformly random independent \(w\)-bit word is available at unit cost. Memory initially contains only the instance; any further preprocessing or lookup-table construction is charged. There are no oracles, advice or unit-cost operations on arbitrarily long integers.

A bounded-error algorithm must output the correct yes/no answer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid input. Its runtime bound applies to every random tape and every input, not only in expectation. For fixed \(\varepsilon,c\), a forbidden algorithm would have constants \(K,n_0\) such that it takes at most \(Kn^{2-\varepsilon}\) instructions for every \(n\ge n_0\); the constants and program may depend on \(c,\varepsilon\). Finite smaller instances must also be decided correctly within finite time.

The order \(\forall\varepsilon\,\exists c\) is essential. Refutation requires one \(\varepsilon>0\) such that for every fixed \(c\) there is an algorithm with that same exponent saving; it does not require the same program or multiplicative constant for all \(c\). Conversely, a faster algorithm at one small dimension constant does not refute the conjecture. Choosing integral \(c\) is harmless because extra zero coordinates pad smaller dimensions.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the conjecture or its negation in the stated bounded-error word-RAM model. A refutation must supply a common positive exponent saving across all fixed dimension constants. A proof conditional on another unproved hypothesis is not a proof of this conjecture. A lower bound only for deterministic algorithms, a restricted instruction set, or an isolated value of \(c\) does not suffice.

title: P versus BPP
summary: P contains total decision languages with a deterministic polynomial-time decider, while BPP allows fair random bits and error at most one third separately on every input. The randomized machine must obey one polynomial time bound on every random tape, and the deterministic decider must work correctly at every input length. The question is whether these classes are equal, allowing a different deterministic algorithm and a different polynomial exponent for each language. Nonuniform simulation and equality under strong circuit-hardness assumptions are established results, while recent insensitivity bounds retain additional hypotheses. A current preprint claims a full separation, but this review has not independently validated its proof and therefore retains uncertain status.
formal:
Does \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{BPP}\)? Equivalently, is the following statement true?
\[\forall L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \Longrightarrow\ L\in\mathrm{P}.\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPP}\) requires one randomized polynomial-time machine whose probability of a correct answer is at least \(2/3\) separately on every input, including both members and nonmembers of \(L\). The proposed deterministic machine must decide the same total language correctly on every input in polynomial time.
definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings; its membership bit is \(\mathbf1_L(x)\in\{0,1\}\). Put \(n=|x|\), allowing \(n=0\). Computation uses finite multitape Turing-machine programs over fixed finite tape alphabets. Each ordinary tape transition costs one step. A randomized transition may read at most one fresh independent unbiased bit. There is no oracle, advice, quantum operation, input distribution or promise excluding some inputs.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that there exist one randomized program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that, with \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\), both of the following hold for every \(x\):
\[\begin{gathered}
 R(x)\text{ halts within }p(n)\text{ steps on every random tape and outputs a bit},\\
 \Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.
\end{gathered}\]
The probability is only over the internal fair bits. An exact finite interpretation is to supply a uniformly distributed string \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\), ignoring its unused suffix. The probability condition is then the integer inequality
\[3\bigl|\{z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ \ge\ 2\cdot 2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over both the input and every random tape, rather than an expectation. The error bound is pointwise: success on almost all inputs of a length does not suffice. The same constants apply at every length; an input-dependent exponent is not polynomial time in this definition.

Use the shared definition of [P](definitions.html#p-np). The deterministic program and its fixed time bound may depend on the language and its randomized decider, but not on the particular input or length. All input access, arithmetic and output count in the [bit model](definitions.html#bit-model).

The requested deterministic computation may use a different algorithm and a different polynomial exponent. The target does not require an effective compiler taking descriptions of randomized machines to deterministic ones. It asks for existence of a polynomial-time deterministic decider for each language in the class. Deterministic programs are also randomized programs that ignore their coins, so \(\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) holds directly. Sampling a distribution, returning a valid witness, and answering only promised inputs are different tasks from deciding this total membership bit.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated inclusion, or of its logical negation
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \land\ L\notin\mathrm{P}.\]
A positive proof must establish existence, correctness and a uniform polynomial time bound for a deterministic decider of every language satisfying the randomized definition. A negative proof must give one fixed language with a single randomized decider meeting the full pointwise error and worst-case polynomial time guarantees, and prove that no deterministic program with any fixed polynomial time bound decides that language.

A result conditional on an unproved hardness assumption, a nonuniform circuit simulation, an oracle separation, a promise-problem separation, or a simulation valid only at some lengths does not settle the target. A lower bound for one simulation rule or one generator family does not exclude every deterministic decider. The probability threshold is exact; this is a yes/no question with no numerical approximation tolerance.

title: L versus BPL
summary: L contains languages decided by one deterministic machine using logarithmic work space, while BPL permits fresh fair random bits and bounded error. Random bits are read once unless stored in counted memory, and the randomized machine obeys uniform logarithmic-space and polynomial-time bounds on every run. The question asks whether every BPL language has a deterministic logarithmic-space decider that is correct on every input. The best general simulation reviewed here uses more than logarithmic space, and recent weighted-generator and regular-program results retain distinct guarantees or restrictions. A solution requires a complete Lean proof of the inclusion or a single total language separating the two classes under the stated uniform model.
formal:
Is \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{BPL}\)? Equivalently, is it true that
\[\forall S\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad S\in\mathrm{BPL}\ \Longrightarrow\ S\in\mathrm{L}?\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPL}\) consists of total decision languages recognized with two-sided error at most \(1/3\) by one uniform randomized machine using logarithmic work space and polynomial time on every input and every random tape. The target is a uniform deterministic logarithmic-work-space decider for each such language.
definitions:
A language \(S\) is a set of finite binary strings; put \(n=|x|\), including \(n=0\). A machine has a finite program, one two-way read-only input tape bounded by endmarkers, and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. The input head cannot move outside the endmarkers. Work tapes are semi-infinite; their heads move by at most one cell per step. Space is the sum of the numbers of distinct work-tape cells visited, including blank cells. The read-only input and finite control are excluded from this count; all stored counters, arithmetic operands, history and auxiliary data are included. Acceptance or rejection is a halting control state, not an additional readable output tape.

A randomized transition can obtain at most one fresh independent fair bit. Past bits cannot be revisited unless retained in counted work space. There is no random-tape address, free clock, oracle, advice, or additional uncounted storage. A deterministic machine has the same tape model and no coin transitions. One ordinary machine transition costs one time step.

Membership \(S\in\mathrm{BPL}\) means that there exist one randomized program \(R\) and positive integers \(K,C,d\) such that for every input \(x\) and every realization of its random choices, \(R\) visits at most
\[K\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\]
work cells and halts with a bit in at most \(T(n)=C(n+2)^d\) steps. In addition, for every \(x\),
\[\Pr[R(x)=\mathbf 1_S(x)]\ge 2/3.\]
The probability is only over internal coins. Exactly, supply a uniform string \(u\in\{0,1\}^{T(n)}\), consuming one bit whenever requested and ignoring the unused suffix; the success requirement is
\[3\bigl|\{u\in\{0,1\}^{T(n)}:R(x;u)=\mathbf1_S(x)\}\bigr|\ge 2\cdot2^{T(n)}.\]
This finite counting formula defines the probability; it is not an extra operation available to the machine. The space and time bounds hold on every random string, not merely in expectation. Success is required separately on every member and nonmember, not only for a typical input distribution. No promise excludes inputs with intermediate acceptance probability: a valid decider for \(S\) must meet the appropriate bound on every binary string.

Membership \(S\in\mathrm{L}\) means that there exist one deterministic program \(D\) and a positive integer \(K'\) such that for every \(x\), \(D\) halts with \(\mathbf1_S(x)\) and visits at most \(K'\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) work cells. In this bounded-input-head model there are only polynomially many configurations at a fixed input length. A halting deterministic run cannot repeat a configuration, so a separate polynomial time guarantee follows. The program and its constants may depend on \(S\), but not on the particular input or its length.

The deterministic machine may have a different space constant, time exponent and computation from the randomized decider. Uniformity means a single finite program serves all input lengths, without length-dependent advice. Deterministic machines are a special case of randomized machines, so \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq\mathrm{BPL}\). The question asks for the reverse inclusion of languages; it does not prescribe a pseudorandom-generator construction or a compiler transforming arbitrary machine descriptions.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the inclusion in the statement, or of its logical negation
\[\exists S\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad S\in\mathrm{BPL}\ \land\ S\notin\mathrm{L}.\]
A positive proof must establish a uniform deterministic decider with one logarithmic work-space bound for every language satisfying the full randomized definition. A negative proof must establish one fixed total language with a valid bounded-error randomized decider and exclude every deterministic decider with every constant logarithmic space bound for that language.

Extra polylogarithmic space, a rereadable uncounted random tape, advice, an oracle, a promise-problem separation, or correctness only at selected lengths does not meet this target. A failed generator construction or a lower bound for a restricted family of simulations does not rule out all deterministic deciders. Unproved hardness assumptions yield conditional results only. This is a yes/no class-comparison question with an exact probability threshold, not a numerical approximation target.

title: Optimal explicit pseudorandom generators for read-once branching programs
summary: An ordered read-once branching program reads each input bit in order while retaining one of a bounded number of states, with arbitrary merging transitions allowed. The question asks for one ordinary uniform-seed generator family that simultaneously approximates the acceptance probability of every such program. Seed length and worst-case workspace must be linear in the logarithms of length and width plus the error parameter, with a uniform polynomial-in-length,width,inverse-error time bound. Recent weighted generators, permutation-program PRGs and width-three hitting sets retain guarantees or hypotheses different from this unrestricted target. A solution requires a complete Lean proof constructing the uniform family with all resource and error bounds, or ruling out every such program and universal constants.
formal:
Does there exist one deterministic finite-program algorithm \(A\) and absolute integers \(C,D\ge1\) with the following property? For every \(n,w\ge2\) and \(p\ge1\), all integers, the algorithm specifies an integer seed length \(s=s(n,w,p)\ge0\) and a function
\[G_{n,w,p}:\{0,1\}^{s}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n}\]
with \(s\le Cq\), where \(q=\lceil\log _2 n\rceil+\lceil\log _2 w\rceil+p\), such that every length-\(n\), width-at-most-\(w\) ordered binary read-once branching program \(B\) satisfies
\[\left|\Pr_{u\sim U_s}[B(G_{n,w,p}(u))=1]-\Pr_{z\sim U_n}[B(z)=1]\right|\le 2^{-p}?\]
Here \(U_k\) is the uniform distribution on the \(2^k\) binary strings of length \(k\). Require \(A\) to compute both \(s(n,w,p)\) and any requested bit \(G_{n,w,p}(u)_i\), \(1\le i\le n\), in at most \(Dq\) work bits and \((nw2^p)^D\) steps per call, in the model below. The same algorithm, constants and generator family must work for every parameter triple and every permitted program.
definitions:
A length-\(n\), width-at-most-\(w\) ordered binary read-once branching program consists of nonempty finite layers \(V_0,\ldots,V_n\), each of size at most \(w\), a start state in \(V_0\), an accepting subset of \(V_n\), and functions \(\delta_{i,b}:V_{i-1}\to V_i\) for \(1\le i\le n\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\). On input \(z\), the state is updated by \(\delta_{i,z_i}\) at step \(i\); \(B(z)=1\) exactly when the final state is accepting. The bit order is \(z_1,\ldots,z_n\). Transitions may merge states, including two equally labeled edges from distinct states; no regularity or permutation promise is imposed. The transition tables, start state and accepting subset are arbitrary finite, possibly nonuniform data. The generator receives none of them.

The algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and a mode flag. In the seed-length mode its input is \((n,w,p)\) and its output is \(s(n,w,p)\) in binary. In the bit mode its input is \((n,w,p,u,i)\) and it outputs exactly one bit before halting. Integer parameters use canonical binary notation with separators; the seed is its full binary string, with leading zeroes retained. Inputs occupy read-only tapes whose heads are bounded by endmarkers. There is a fixed finite number of initially blank, semi-infinite work tapes over \(\{0,1,\square\}\), with heads moving by at most one cell per transition. Each distinct work-tape cell visited is charged two work bits, including blank cells. This fixed encoding of tape symbols only fixes a constant in the space bound. All counters, arithmetic, stored history and preprocessing are charged; output is write-only and cannot serve as storage. There is no advice, oracle, external clock or other uncounted memory. Each transition costs one time step. The required bounds hold on every valid call, for every seed and requested index. Only the requested bit must be output in bit mode; there is no requirement to store the whole length-\(n\) string.

Probabilities are exact uniform finite averages. In particular, a seed always has weight \(2^{-s}\), even if several seeds produce the same string; signed weights and externally assigned coefficients are not permitted. The parameter \(p\) controls additive error, not failure probability of a randomized construction: \(A\) itself is deterministic. With \(\varepsilon=2^{-p}\), the target is \(O(\log n+\log w+\log(1/\varepsilon))\) seed length and work space. Ceiling conventions change only constants. Arbitrary \(0<\varepsilon<1\) can be covered by a dyadic tolerance no larger than \(\varepsilon\). No compression requirement \(s<n\) is imposed in parameter regimes where the displayed allowance is already at least \(n\).
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existential proposition above or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify a single finite program and universal constants, formalize its seed-length and bit computations, establish the stated worst-case resource bounds, and prove the additive-error inequality for every permitted program and every parameter triple. A negative proof must rule out every such uniform program and choice of constants; a limitation of one construction, one analysis or one restricted generator class is insufficient. The theorem must use the stated ordinary uniform-seed distribution and arbitrary merging transitions. A result solely for weighted generators, hitting sets or a restricted branching-program subclass does not meet this target.

title: AM versus NP
summary: Arthur–Merlin protocols let a prover choose a polynomial-length reply after seeing the verifier’s public random challenge. The question asks whether every language with such a protocol also has ordinary NP certificates. The verifier must be uniform and polynomial time, with completeness and soundness on every input. Graph nonisomorphism would acquire static polynomially checkable certificates if the equality holds, but is not assumed complete for the whole question. Known conditional derandomization and weaker recent simulations leave the unconditional class comparison open.
formal:
Does \(\mathrm{AM}=\mathrm{NP}\)? Equivalently, does every language having an Arthur–Merlin protocol admit polynomial-length certificates checked deterministically in polynomial time?

For a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), an Arthur–Merlin protocol is specified by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and polynomially bounded lengths \(p(n),q(n)\). Arthur draws a uniform public string \(r\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\); after seeing \(x\) and \(r\), Merlin may choose a reply \(y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}\). With \(n=|x|\), require
\[x\in L\Longrightarrow\Pr_r[\exists y:\ V(x,r,y)=1]\ge\tfrac23,\]
\[x\notin L\Longrightarrow\Pr_r[\exists y:\ V(x,r,y)=1]\le\tfrac13.\]
Must there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(W\) and a polynomially bounded length \(s(n)\) such that, for every binary string \(x\),
\[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{s(|x|)}:\ W(x,z)=1?\]
The resulting verifier and its polynomial bounds may depend on \(L\), but must work uniformly at all input lengths.
definitions:
Languages are subsets of the finite binary strings. Every input string is either a yes-instance in the language or a no-instance outside it; the target is an equality of ordinary language classes. There is no omitted promise domain. Input size \(n\) is the full bit length of \(x\), and the empty input is allowed.

Use classical uniform multitape Turing machines with finite descriptions. A polynomial time bound means \(C(n+1)^a\) steps for some fixed constants \(C\ge1\) and integer \(a\ge0\). In a verifier taking several strings, time is polynomial in their total encoded length; the stated polynomial message bounds make this polynomial in \(n\) on protocol inputs. The verifier terminates on every such tuple, including misleading messages. It has no advice depending on the input length, oracle or quantum operation. All communication consists of ordinary binary strings.

The functions \(p,q,s:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) are computable in polynomial time and bounded by fixed polynomials. They may be taken to be integer-coefficient polynomial bounds, with unused bits ignored. Messages have the indicated exact lengths. Permitting shorter messages with a length encoding and padding gives the same class. Malformed messages are rejected according to the chosen verifier; they cannot provide an extra form of communication or uncounted computation.

The protocol has two messages: Arthur’s random challenge followed by Merlin’s reply. Arthur samples \(p(n)\) independent fair bits, so each challenge has probability \(2^{-p(n)}\). All of these bits are public before Merlin replies. The verifier’s final computation \(V(x,r,y)\) is deterministic; there is no additional hidden random tape. A zero-length challenge or reply is permitted. The polynomial defining each length is fixed for the protocol, not chosen separately for individual inputs.

Merlin is computationally unbounded. He knows the entire input and challenge and may choose a different reply for every pair \((x,r)\). Thus the existential quantifier over \(y\) is inside the probability over \(r\). Completeness says that on each yes-instance an accepting reply exists for at least two thirds of the challenges. Soundness says that on each no-instance an accepting reply exists for at most one third of them, even with an unbounded dishonest prover. Randomizing Merlin’s reply cannot increase the set of challenges for which some accepting reply exists.

These two probability conditions define \(\mathrm{AM}\). They are per-input guarantees. Neither the inputs nor Merlin’s strategy are averaged over an external distribution. The soundness bound is information-theoretic: it is not limited to efficient cheating provers. The fixed gap between two thirds and one third is part of the chosen standard definition; ordinary amplification yields equivalent constant-gap conventions. Perfect completeness is not an added requirement of this card.

The class \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages with a verifier \(W\) and certificate length \(s\) satisfying the displayed exact equivalence. On yes-instances at least one certificate is accepted, and on no-instances every certificate is rejected. The verifier is deterministic and has no random challenge. The certificate itself need not be found in polynomial time. A proof of AM containment in NP must establish existence of these certificates and their efficient verification, not efficient deterministic decision or witness generation.

The inclusion \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{AM}\) is immediate by letting the AM verifier ignore its challenge. Thus equality asks for the converse inclusion. A positive answer must cover every AM language. A negative answer must exhibit, or prove the existence of, an AM language that has no polynomially bounded deterministic certificate system. Failure of one proposed verifier, one circuit family or one polynomial exponent does not establish such a separation.

The quantifier order is \(\forall L\in\mathrm{AM}\;\exists W\;\exists s\;\forall x\), with a fixed polynomial running-time bound for each \(W\). There is no common required exponent for all languages. Equality of language classes does not additionally require a computable compiler from protocol descriptions to NP verifiers, although a proved general transformation would suffice. A certificate system whose exponent changes with the individual input is not polynomially bounded in this sense.

The related class \(\mathrm{MA}\) reverses the message order: Merlin supplies a certificate before Arthur’s fresh random choices. Moving \(\exists y\) outside the probability changes the condition and must not be done here. Standard results identify AM with constant-round interactive proofs, but the explicit two-message public-coin definition above is the target model. Protocols with an input-dependent polynomial number of rounds are not the target.

A promise problem consists of disjoint sets \(Y,N\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), with no correctness requirement outside \(Y\cup N\). The notation \(\mathrm{prAM}\) refers to the analogous promise-protocol class. A claim that every promise-AM problem has a separating NP language is stronger than the ordinary language inclusion asked here and is not assumed equivalent. This distinction matters for the neighboring targeted-generator question TCS-1135 and for several recent derandomization theorems.

Graph nonisomorphism is an example consequence, not a completeness reformulation. A finite simple undirected graph has no loops or parallel edges; two such graphs are isomorphic if some bijection between their vertex sets preserves adjacency. Graph nonisomorphism asks whether no such bijection exists, for explicitly encoded graph pairs. An NP certificate for nonisomorphism would be a polynomial-length binary witness of that negative assertion checked in polynomial time. Since graph nonisomorphism has an AM protocol, AM equality with NP would supply such certificates. Solving only that graph problem would not establish the full class equality without an additional proved completeness reduction.

For the conditional progress cited below, \(\mathrm{NE}=\bigcup_{c\ge1}\mathrm{NTIME}(2^{cn})\) and \(\mathrm{coNE}\) is its complement class. A single-valued nondeterministic Boolean circuit has ordinary input bits, auxiliary choice bits, and two outputs: a flag and a value bit. For every input some choice must set the flag to one, and every choice with flag one must give the correct value of the function. Choices with flag zero are ignored. Circuit size counts gates in a fixed fan-in-two AND/OR and unary NOT basis, together with auxiliary input bits. Circuits may vary nonuniformly with the input length. An exponential lower bound means that some \(\alpha>0\) requires size at least \(2^{\alpha n}\) for every sufficiently large length \(n\). This hardness hypothesis belongs to the cited conditional result and is not a premise of the question.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that \(\mathrm{AM}\subseteq\mathrm{NP}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that some language lies in \(\mathrm{AM}\setminus\mathrm{NP}\), with the specified verifier, message-order, uniformity and probability conventions. Equality must supply the existence of polynomial-length certificates and deterministic polynomial-time verification for every AM language on every input. It need not supply a deterministic decision algorithm or an efficient way to find the certificates. A separation must rule out every NP verifier and polynomial certificate bound for the chosen language. Conditional collapses, oracle results, simulations with advice, average-input correctness, larger time bounds and a certificate system only for graph nonisomorphism do not settle the unconditional class comparison. The default numerical approximation tolerance does not apply to this exact proposition.

title: Unconditional subexponential simulation of BPP
summary: BPP contains decision problems solved efficiently using random bits with bounded error on every input. The question asks whether all of them have exact deterministic simulations in the class SUBEXP. Here SUBEXP requires a simulation in time two to the n-to-epsilon power for every fixed positive epsilon. The simulator may depend on the chosen exponent, but it must work on every input without advice or assumptions. Known general brute-force simulations take larger exponential time, while stronger derandomization theorems rely on unproved hardness.
formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{SUBEXP}\) unconditionally? Here the subexponential class is the intersection
\[\mathrm{SUBEXP}=\bigcap_{k\ge1}\mathrm{DTIME}\!\left(2^{n^{1/k}}\right).\]
Thus, for every language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) decidable with two-sided bounded error in randomized polynomial time, and for every integer \(k\ge1\), must there exist a deterministic algorithm deciding \(L\) on every input in time \(O(2^{n^{1/k}})\)? The algorithm and the constant in its time bound may depend on \(L,k\). The target selects the subexponential question in the source's Open Problem 3.4; its separate quasipolynomial-time question is stronger.
definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings. An algorithm decides \(L\) if it halts and outputs one exactly on inputs in \(L\), and zero on all other inputs. Use uniform multitape Turing machines with finite descriptions independent of input length. One transition costs one time unit. A randomized machine may additionally request independent unbiased bits, at unit cost per bit. It has no advice, oracle or preprocessing that depends on input length without being computed by the machine.

Membership in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) means that there are such a randomized machine \(M\) and constants \(a,C\ge1\) with worst-case runtime at most \(C(n+1)^a\) on every length-\(n\) input and every random tape, and with
\[x\in L\Rightarrow\Pr[M(x)=1]\ge2/3,\qquad x\notin L\Rightarrow\Pr[M(x)=1]\le1/3.\]
This is a class of total decision problems. The acceptance-probability gap holds on every input; it is not a promise that an external user must supply.

The notation \(L\in\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^{1/k}})\) means that a deterministic machine decides \(L\) and has worst-case runtime at most \(C_k\lceil2^{n^{1/k}}\rceil\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), for some fixed \(C_k\). All finitely many smaller inputs must also be decided correctly and with termination. Requiring every integer \(k\) is equivalent to requiring time \(O(2^{n^\varepsilon})\) for every fixed real \(\varepsilon>0\). The machine is allowed to change with the exponent; an effective compiler taking \(M,k\) and producing the simulator is not an additional requirement.

This definition of SUBEXP is the source's intersection of subpower-exponential time classes. A single \(2^{o(n)}\)-time bound, such as \(2^{n/\log n}\), need not meet it. Likewise, correctness only on most inputs, or on infinitely many input lengths, is insufficient. The simulator must decide the same language exactly on all strings.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the inclusion or its negation. A positive proof must cover every BPP language and every fixed exponent \(1/k\), without a hardness assumption, oracle or advice. A negative proof must establish a language in BPP that is outside one of the deterministic time classes in the displayed intersection. A conditional simulation, a simulation for a particular randomized problem, or a heuristic correct on almost all inputs does not settle the question.

title: Pseudorandom generators from hitting-set generators
summary: A hitting-set generator produces strings that intersect every sufficiently dense set accepted by a polynomial-size Boolean circuit. A pseudorandom generator must instead approximate every such circuit’s acceptance probability when its seed is chosen uniformly. The selected cryptographic question asks whether the existence of the first kind of uniform polynomial-time generator entails the existence of the second, with negligible security bounds and any nontrivial stretch. The generators may have different parameters, and the known seed-extending result for logarithmic-depth circuits does not establish the unrestricted implication. A complete Lean proof must decide this existence implication, clarifying the relationship between two basic forms of computational randomness.
formal:
Does the existence of a polynomial-time hitting-set generator secure against all polynomial-size Boolean circuits imply the existence of a polynomial-time pseudorandom generator secure against all such circuits, in the cryptographic regime defined below? In symbols, decide
\[
\bigl(\exists H\;\operatorname{HSG}(H)\bigr)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigl(\exists G\;\operatorname{PRG}(G)\bigr).
\]
Both generators must be uniform, have a seed shorter than their output, and meet their respective security conditions with negligible error. Their seed lengths, negligible functions and polynomial running-time bounds may differ. This is an implication between existence statements; it does not require an algorithm that compiles a given hitting-set generator into a pseudorandom generator.
definitions:
For an integer \(m\ge 0\), let \(U_m\) denote the uniform distribution on the \(2^m\) binary strings of length \(m\). Output lengths are integers \(N\ge 2\). An admissible generator family \(F=(F_N)_{N\ge 2}\) has a seed-length function \(s:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to\mathbb N\) with \(1\le s(N)<N\) and maps \(F_N:\{0,1\}^{s(N)}\to\{0,1\}^{N}\). One deterministic multitape Turing machine computes \(s(N)\) from \(1^N\), and another computes \(F_N(z)\) from \((1^N,z)\) for every seed \(z\). Here \(1^N\) is the unary encoding of \(N\). There are constants \(A,b\ge 1\), depending only on the family, such that each computation takes at most \(A(N+1)^b\) steps. In particular, time is polynomial in the output length. A machine has finite control, one read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes with a fixed finite alphabet. In one step each head reads and may move by at most one cell, each work head may write one symbol, and at most one output bit may be appended. All tapes start at their first cell and are indexed by nonnegative integers; a left move at zero stays at zero. The generator input is the literal string \(1^N\#z\), and the seed-length output is the binary encoding of \(s(N)\). The machine programs and tape counts are independent of \(N\). These machines receive no advice, oracle or randomness. The output need not contain the seed, and different seeds may have the same output.

A test at length \(N\) is an arbitrary deterministic Boolean circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^{N}\to\{0,1\}\), with AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates of fan-in one, constant gates, unrestricted fan-out and unrestricted depth. Its size is its number of gates, excluding the input nodes. There is no uniformity requirement on tests at different lengths. Security against polynomial-size circuits means the quantifier \(\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge 1}\) followed by a threshold length that may depend on \(c\), and then a guarantee for every circuit of size at most \(N^c\) at every larger length.

Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in \(N\). The functions here take values in \((0,1]\) for \(N\ge2\). No computability assumption is imposed on a security-bound function.

For an admissible family \(H\) with seed length \(s\), the property \(\operatorname{HSG}(H)\) means that there exists a negligible function \(\varepsilon\) such that
\[
\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge 1}\ \exists N_c\ge 2\ \forall N\ge N_c\ \forall C\text{ of size at most }N^c,
\]
\[
\Pr_{x\sim U_N}[C(x)=1]\ge\varepsilon(N)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{s(N)}\; C(H_N(z))=1.
\]
The hit is an existence guarantee; it need not occur with any specified fraction of seeds.

For an admissible family \(G\) with its own seed length \(t\), the property \(\operatorname{PRG}(G)\) means that there exists a negligible function \(\eta\) such that
\[
\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge 1}\ \exists M_c\ge 2\ \forall N\ge M_c\ \forall C\text{ of size at most }N^c,
\]
\[
\left|\Pr_{z\sim U_{t(N)}}[C(G_N(z))=1]
-\Pr_{x\sim U_N}[C(x)=1]\right|\le\eta(N).
\]
Thus generated outputs are sampled by a uniform seed, with multiplicity when seeds collide. The same generator and the same negligible function must serve every circuit-size exponent. In the implication, all generator, seed-length, time-bound and security-bound witnesses are existentially quantified separately on the two sides.
answer_criterion: An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the stated existence implication or of its negation. A positive answer must establish the existence of a generator satisfying the full PRG definition whenever a generator satisfying the HSG definition exists. A negative answer must establish that an HSG as defined exists while no PRG as defined exists, in the stated ordinary model. A theorem restricted to a smaller test class, additional hardness assumptions, infinitely many lengths, or the impossibility of a particular conversion method does not decide this implication.

title: Explicit near-optimal vertex expanders
summary: The goal is to construct arbitrarily large regular graphs by a deterministic polynomial-time procedure. Every sufficiently small set must have almost the largest possible number of distinct neighbors outside itself. The survey asks for at least d−2−δ external neighbors per vertex of each sufficiently small set. Explicit two-sided lossless constructions achieve (1−ε)d neighbors when the degree is sufficiently large as a function of ε. Their parameter bounds leave the survey’s additive loss of 2+δ open.
formal: Is the following proposition true? For every rational \(\delta>0\), there exists an integer \(d_0\ge3\) such that, for every integer \(d\ge d_0\), there exist a rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\), real \(K>0\), integer \(a\ge1\), and one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\) which, for every integer \(j\ge1\) supplied in unary, outputs a finite simple undirected \(d\)-regular graph \(G_j\) within \(K(j+1)^a\) bit operations, with strictly increasing vertex counts \(n_j=|V(G_j)|\), and such that \[|\Gamma_{G_j}(S)\setminus S|\ \ge\ (d-2-\delta)|S|\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V(G_j)\text{ with }1\le |S|\le\eta n_j?\]
definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph has no loops or multiple edges. It is \(d\)-regular if each vertex has exactly \(d\) distinct neighbors. Its labeled vertex set is \([n_j]=\{1,\ldots,n_j\}\). For \(S\subseteq[n_j]\), define
\[
\Gamma_{G_j}(S)=\{v\in[n_j]:\ \exists u\in S,\ \{u,v\}\in E(G_j)\}.
\]
The left side in the target counts distinct neighbors outside \(S\), not edges leaving \(S\), not neighbors counted with multiplicity, and not neighbors inside \(S\). The cutoff \(\eta n_j\) is a real number; the condition is imposed on every integer set size satisfying the displayed inequality. Empty sets impose no requirement. The same positive \(\eta\) works for the entire family at the fixed values of \(\delta,d\).

The output of \(A\) is \(n_j\) in binary followed by an explicit list of the edges, each an unordered pair of distinct binary vertex labels, with delimiters. Isolated vertices would still be specified by \(n_j\), although none occur for \(d\ge3\). Reading the unary index, all computation and every output bit count in the bound. The machine has a finite program, no random bits, advice, oracle or uncharged preprocessing. It must work on every \(1^j\), not merely on infinitely many selected indices. The integers \(n_j\) must increase strictly, so the construction gives arbitrarily large graphs; an allowed family need not contain every admissible vertex count.

The degree threshold \(d_0\) may depend on \(\delta\). After \(d\) is fixed, the machine \(A\) and constants \(\eta,K,a\) may depend on both \(\delta,d\), but not on \(j\) or \(S\). No algorithm uniform in \(\delta,d\) is required. The construction requirement is the survey's mild explicitness convention, polynomial time in the family index, with full output charged. It does not additionally require computing one neighbor in time polynomial in \(\log n_j\). Restricting positive \(\delta\) and the small-set fraction to rationals loses no expansion guarantee: a smaller positive rational tolerance or fraction can be chosen when needed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the entire proposition, including the explicit algorithm families, their cost bounds and the expansion inequality for all indicated sets, or a complete Lean proof of its negation. Random existence alone is insufficient. A construction with a relative loss tending to zero as degree grows does not meet this additive-loss target without a proof of the displayed bound with the stated quantifier order. A result for one degree or a one-sided bipartite expansion promise does not by itself establish the proposition.

title: Two-source extraction at log n plus constant entropy
summary: Two arbitrary independent distributions on n-bit strings each have min-entropy at least log base two of n plus one fixed additive constant. The question asks for one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that turns one string from each source into a bit with bias at most one hundredth. The same program and time bound must work at every length without an extra seed, advice or descriptions of the distributions. Li’s checked theorem achieves a constant multiple of log n entropy, while his source explicitly leaves the additive threshold as a further question. Matching that threshold efficiently would sharpen a central randomness-extraction result and have consequences for explicit Ramsey graphs.
formal:
Does there exist an integer \(C\ge0\) and one uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) defining functions
\[
E_n:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\longrightarrow\{0,1\}\qquad(n\ge1)
\]
such that, for every \(n\) and every two independent probability distributions \(X,Y\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\) with
\[
H_\infty(X),H_\infty(Y)\ge\log_2 n+C,
\]
we have
\[
\left|\Pr[E_n(X,Y)=1]-\frac12\right|\le\frac1{100}?
\]
The algorithm receives only \(n\) and the two strings. The same additive constant, finite program and polynomial running-time bound must work for all lengths and all eligible distributions.
definitions:
Write \(S_n=\{0,1\}^n\) for all binary strings of length \(n\). A probability distribution on this finite set is any function \(p:S_n\to[0,1]\) with real values and \(\sum_xp(x)=1\). Its min-entropy is
\[
H_\infty(p)=-\log_2\!\left(\max_{x\in S_n}p(x)\right).
\]
Thus the required entropy condition means \(p(x)\le 1/(2^C n)\) for every string \(x\). Distributions need not be uniform on their support, rational, computable or efficiently samplable. Independence means that the joint distribution is \(\Pr[X=x,Y=y]=p(x)q(y)\). The output probability in the question is the finite sum
\[
\Pr[E_n(X,Y)=1]=\sum_{x,y\in S_n}p(x)q(y)\,\mathbf1_{\{E_n(x,y)=1\}}.
\]
The indicator is one when its subscripted condition holds and zero otherwise. For a single output bit, the displayed bias is its statistical distance from the uniform bit, where statistical distance between distributions \(r,s\) on a finite set is \(\frac12\sum_z|r(z)-s(z)|\). There is no conditioning on either source in this guarantee.

Computation uses a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and fixed finite tape alphabet. Its read-only input is \(1^n\#x\#y\), where \(|x|=|y|=n\), and its work tapes initially contain blanks. One transition reads and writes at most one symbol on each tape and moves each tape head by at most one cell, costing one step. There are no random coins, oracle calls, auxiliary seed, advice or length-dependent precomputed tables. The machine must halt and output exactly one bit on every such input. There must be integers \(K,d\ge1\) such that this takes at most \(K(n+1)^d\) transitions for all \(n,x,y\), including inputs at lengths with no eligible sources. The input contains no distribution description or samples other than \(x,y\); \(C,K,d\) and the machine are fixed existential choices, independent of both distributions and of \(n\). Let \(\mathcal A\) be the class of all machines meeting this total polynomial-time evaluation condition, and write \(E^A_n\) for the function computed by a member \(A\).

Only the probability bound concerns the random choice of the two input strings; the evaluator itself is deterministic. When \(\log_2n+C>n\), no eligible distribution exists, so the extraction requirement at that length is vacuous.
