Using a nonnegative integer for the existential additive constant fixes a harmless convention: any fixed real constant can be increased to such an integer. The task has one output bit and fixed error \(1/100\); it does not demand arbitrarily small error, more output bits or resilience to tampering.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence proposition, including one finite machine, its uniform polynomial-time bound and the probability guarantee for all eligible distributions. Alternatively, give a complete Lean proof of its logical negation: for every integer \(C\ge0\) and every \(A\in\mathcal A\), there exist \(n\ge1\) and distributions \(p,q\) on \(S_n\), each having min-entropy at least \(\log_2n+C\), for which
\[
\left|\sum_{x,y\in S_n}p(x)q(y)\mathbf1_{\{E^A_n(x,y)=1\}}-\frac12\right|>\frac1{100}.
\]
In this negation the length and distributions may depend on the machine and additive constant. A construction requiring \(c\log_2n\) entropy for an unspecified constant \(c>1\), nonuniform existence alone, or a conditional implication does not establish the displayed unconditional target.

title: Seeded extraction with constant total entropy loss
summary: A seeded extractor combines an arbitrary weak random source with a short independent uniform seed. This question asks for logarithmic seed length and an output losing at most a constant number of the combined available entropy bits. The statistical error is fixed at one hundredth for every source meeting the min-entropy bound. The entire family must be evaluated by one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, including any preprocessing. Nonconstructive existence and recent faster constant-fraction extractors leave this specific combination of parameters unsettled in the checked sources.
formal:
Do there exist an explicit family of ordinary seeded extractors and absolute constants \(C,\Delta\in\mathbb N\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge2\) and \(0\le k\le n\), the family supplies a function
\[\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}:\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{d(n,k)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m(n,k)}\]
with
\[d(n,k)\le C\lceil\log_2 n\rceil,\qquad 0\le k+d(n,k)-m(n,k)\le\Delta,\]
and, for every distribution \(X\) on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) with min-entropy at least \(k\),
\[\operatorname{TV}\bigl(\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}(X,U_{d(n,k)}),U_{m(n,k)}\bigr)\le1/100?\]
The seed is uniform and independent of \(X\). Explicitness means uniform deterministic evaluation in time polynomial in \(n\), with the same algorithm and polynomial for all \(n,k\). This is the constant-total-entropy-loss question in Vadhan's Open Problem 6.41.
definitions:
All lengths \(n,k,d,m\) are integers measured in bits, with \(d,m\ge0\), and logarithms have base two. For a finite random variable \(X\),
\[H_{\infty}(X)=-\log_2\max_x\Pr[X=x].\]
Thus the source promise is \(\Pr[X=x]\le2^{-k}\) for every \(n\)-bit string \(x\). The source may have arbitrary dependencies between its coordinates and need not be samplable by an efficient algorithm. The extractor receives a sample string, not a description of its distribution. \(U_t\) denotes the uniform distribution on all \(t\)-bit strings, including the unique empty string when \(t=0\). For distributions \(P,Q\) on the same finite set,
\[\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|.\]
The condition is statistical and quantifies over every promised source, with no computational restriction on a test of the output.

A family is explicit if there are two fixed deterministic multitape Turing machines and integers \(K,q\ge1\): a parameter machine on \((1^n,k)\), with \(k\) in binary, outputs \(d(n,k),m(n,k)\) in binary; an evaluation machine on \((1^n,k,x,y)\) outputs the entire \(m(n,k)\)-bit string. Both halt within \(K(n+1)^q\) steps on all valid inputs. All preprocessing and output writing are counted. There is no advice, oracle, randomized construction or length-dependent table supplied for free. The machines, \(C,\Delta,K,q\) are chosen before \(n,k\) and before the source distribution.

Total entropy loss means \(k+d-m\): it counts the source's guaranteed entropy together with all perfect seed bits consumed. This ordinary extractor requirement concerns the output distribution alone. It does not require that the output remain uniform when the seed is separately disclosed. A strong extractor, whose output is uniform jointly with a disclosed seed, may be converted to an ordinary one by including its seed in the total output, but those seed bits must then be counted in \(m\). The convention \(m\le k+d\) is harmless output truncation for this error level. Integer entropy thresholds suffice for the stated additive-constant target; rounding down a real threshold changes the loss by less than one bit.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed uniform construction claim. A positive answer must specify the algorithms and universal constants and prove the extraction guarantee, logarithmic seed bound, constant total loss and polynomial evaluation time throughout the parameter domain. A negative answer must rule out every such uniform family. An existence proof without efficient evaluation, a loss growing with \(n\) or \(k\), or an output bound that ignores consumed seed entropy does not meet the criterion.

title: Subpolynomial-seed pseudorandom generators for \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[2]\)
summary: The question asks for pseudorandom bits that fool constant-depth circuits built from AND, OR and parity gates. For each fixed depth, one generator family must work against every circuit with at most as many computation gates as output bits. The difference in acceptance probabilities must be at most one quarter for every permitted circuit. The seed length must eventually be smaller than every positive power of the output length. Uniform generation may take time polynomial in the number of seeds, and known restricted-circuit or larger-field results do not meet the whole target.
formal:
For every fixed integer \(k\ge1\), is there an unconditional, mildly explicit generator family
\[
G_{k,m}:\{0,1\}^{d_k(m)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m}\qquad(m\ge1)
\]
whose integer seed length satisfies \(d_k(m)=m^{o(1)}\), and which fools every depth-at-most-\(k\), size-at-most-\(m\) \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[2]\) circuit on \(m\) input bits with error at most \(1/4\)?

Precisely, for every such circuit \(C\),
\[
\left|\Pr_{s\sim U_{d_k(m)}}[C(G_{k,m}(s))=1]
-\Pr_{x\sim U_m}[C(x)=1]\right|\le1/4.
\]
The generator for a given \(k,m\) must work simultaneously for all the indicated circuits and cannot depend on \(C\). “Mildly explicit” means uniform deterministic evaluation in time polynomial in \(m\) and \(2^{d_k(m)}\), with the polynomial permitted to depend on \(k\).
definitions:
A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one output bit. Input nodes carry literals \(x_i\), their negations \(\neg x_i\), or constants \(0,1\), for \(1\le i\le m\). Every computation node is an AND, OR or parity gate with arbitrarily many predecessors. AND is one exactly when all its input bits are one; OR is one exactly when at least one is one; parity is the sum of its inputs modulo two. For no predecessors, AND is one and OR and parity are zero. Fan-out is unrestricted. Gates may be used at any depth, and parity gates may feed other parity gates or either Boolean gate type.

Size counts computation nodes only. Input literals and constants are free input nodes. Depth is the maximum number of computation nodes along a directed path from an input to the output; a literal or constant output has depth zero. There is no restriction on wires beyond a finite circuit description, and no requirement that the testing circuit descriptions be generated uniformly over lengths. Negations are available at inputs as in the source definition. Allowing complemented parity outputs or internal NOT gates gives the same all-fixed-depth target after routine constant changes in resources, but the formal statement uses the specified basis.

For an integer \(\ell\ge0\), \(U_\ell\) is the uniform distribution on all \(\ell\)-bit strings; \(U_0\) is concentrated on the empty string. Randomness consists only of the uniformly chosen seed. The generator is a deterministic map, may have collisions and outputs exactly \(m\) bits. The two probabilities use independent draws from the stated uniform domains.

For each fixed \(k\), a single function \(d_k:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb N_{\ge0}\) must satisfy
\[
\forall a>0\ \exists M_{k,a}\ \forall m\ge M_{k,a}:\ d_k(m)\le m^a.
\]
This defines the subpolynomial seed requirement. It does not ask merely for one fixed sublinear power, nor permit choosing a different generator family separately for each \(a\).

Uniform mild explicitness requires deterministic algorithms for computing \(d_k(m)\) and evaluating \(G_{k,m}(s)\). There are constants \(A_k\ge1,b_k\ge1\) such that on input \(1^m\) the first algorithm outputs the binary encoding of \(d_k(m)\), and on input \((1^m,s)\), with \(|s|=d_k(m)\), the second outputs \(G_{k,m}(s)\), each within
\[
A_k\bigl(m+2^{d_k(m)}+1\bigr)^{b_k}
\]
steps. Use the ordinary uniform deterministic multitape Turing model: finitely many tapes and finite alphabets, initially blank work tapes, and one-cell head moves per transition. Input access and output writing are charged. There is no advice, random construction, oracle, unbounded unit-cost arithmetic or assumed computational hardness. The programs and constants may depend on the fixed \(k\); no efficient procedure producing them from \(k\) is required. A fully explicit polynomial-in-\(m\) evaluation algorithm also qualifies, but is not required.

The size parameter is the source's number of computation gates and is set equal to the output length. The requested error bound is the absolute difference of acceptance probabilities, with no averaging over circuits. It must hold at every positive \(m\); only the seed-length estimate is asymptotic.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked construction or a proof that the asserted family cannot exist. A positive answer must prove the uniform evaluation bound, the subpolynomial seed condition and the \(1/4\) fooling guarantee for every fixed depth and every circuit in the stated class. A construction using a hardness assumption, treating only one depth, restricting the locations or number of parity gates, or providing only a fixed sublinear seed exponent does not suffice. This is an existence question with its own exact error threshold; numerical \(1/100\) answer tolerance does not replace the \(1/4\) pseudorandomness condition.

title: FPT versus \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)
summary: A k-clique is a set of k graph vertices joined by every possible edge. The question asks for one exact deterministic algorithm whose input-size exponent is constant while a computable multiplier absorbs all dependence on k. Polynomial time separately for each fixed k does not establish that uniform bound. Clique completeness makes the question equivalent to FPT equalling W[1]. Conditional lower bounds and recent fixed-k or approximation results explain the conjecture’s significance without deciding it.
formal: Does there exist one deterministic algorithm A, a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and an integer \(c\ge0\), such that A decides whether G contains a k-clique and uses at most \(f(k)(N+2)^c\) steps for every encoded pair (G,k) of total bit length N? The exponent c is independent of both k and G. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\) under parameterized many-one reductions?
definitions: A graph G is finite, simple and undirected, with vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), including n=0. A k-clique is a subset of exactly k vertices with an edge between each pair of distinct vertices. The empty subset is a 0-clique; no k-clique exists when k>n. For a fixed binary encoding, write \(1^n0\), then the n by n adjacency matrix in row order, then the ordinary binary representation of the nonnegative integer k (0 is written as 0, and otherwise there are no leading zeroes). A valid matrix is symmetric with zero diagonal, and the entire remaining suffix is the representation of k. N counts all bits, including k. A rejects any malformed string in time polynomial in its bit length. The bound in the statement applies to every valid pair, including k>n. The parameter is k alone; there is no promise on density, degree, clique number or any other graph property. A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input and initially blank work tapes; each transition reads or writes only at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The runtime includes parsing, input access and all internal work. Correctness is exact, and no advice, randomness, oracle or quantum operations are supplied. The same A, f and c work for every pair; f must be computable by a machine that halts on every nonnegative integer input, but its growth and the time needed to compute it have no prescribed bound. Constant multiplicative overhead can be absorbed into f. Using full input length rather than n gives the usual FPT question: for k at most n the two lengths are polynomially related, and k>n is rejected after parsing. Use [FPT and FPT many-one reductions](definitions.html#parameterized). Here the parameter is the requested clique size \(k\). The languages reducible to this parameterized Clique problem form \(\mathrm{W}[1]\). Hence an FPT algorithm for Clique is equivalent to \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the single algorithm, computable multiplier and constant exponent in the statement, or prove their joint nonexistence. In the affirmative case, prove correctness and the uniform worst-case bound on all pairs, together with the malformed-input convention. In the negative case, exclude every such algorithm, computable f and exponent c; a conditional lower bound, a bound for a restricted algorithm model, or failure at one proposed multiplier and exponent does not settle this target. An algorithm whose polynomial exponent depends on k also does not satisfy the displayed quantifiers.

title: Exponential Time Hypothesis
summary: ETH asks whether the optimal deterministic exponential rate for 3-SAT is strictly positive. The exponential parameter is the number of distinct variables, while polynomial factors account for the complete encoded input. One positive rate must obstruct every algorithm, and refutation permits different algorithms for arbitrarily small positive rates. The fixed-width SAT algorithm released in October refutes ETH. Mazor and Pass give an elementary proof using bounded-occurrence counting and sparsification.
formal: Is \(s_3>0\) in the deterministic bit model defined below? Equivalently, does there exist one real \(c>0\) such that no 3-SAT decider A has a runtime bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{c n(F)}(N(F)+1)^d\) on every valid 3-CNF formula F for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The same positive c must exclude all such algorithms. This is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis.
definitions:
Use the shared [bounded-width CNF encoding and rate \(s_q\)](definitions.html#sat-encoding). The exponential term uses the number of distinct variables \(n(F)\). The polynomial factor uses the full input length \(N(F)\), including every repeated clause. The decider may depend on the fixed width \(q\).

This card specializes q to 3. Its negation, \(s_3=0\), means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a 3-SAT decider \(A_\varepsilon\) with fixed constants \(C_\varepsilon,d_\varepsilon\) satisfying \(t_{A_\varepsilon}(F)\le C_\varepsilon 2^{\varepsilon n(F)}(N(F)+1)^{d_\varepsilon}\) on every valid formula. The machine and constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\). This statement does not require one machine with a single subexponential runtime bound, nor a computable map from \(\varepsilon\) to a machine.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(s_3>0\) or of \(s_3=0\) for the explicitly defined rate. A positive answer requires a positive constant excluding every valid deterministic decider at that exponential rate, with any polynomial input factor. A negative answer must establish arbitrarily small attainable positive exponents with the stated quantifiers. A fixed improved positive exponent, a bound for a restricted algorithm class, or a conditional lower bound does not settle this question. No numerical estimate of \(s_3\) is requested: the target is its strict positivity.

title: Set Cover conjecture
summary: Set Cover asks whether a few supplied sets can cover a given universe. The conjecture concerns exact algorithms when each available set has a fixed maximum size. It says that no constant improvement over exponential base two works across all such size bounds. The target allows bounded-error randomization and polynomial factors that depend on the fixed bound. Recent results show that a major conjecture about tensor rank would refute SCC, but neither side is settled unconditionally.
formal:
Is the Set Cover conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist a fixed integer \(d\ge1\) such that no uniform randomized bounded-error algorithm solves \(\le d\)-Set Cover on an \(n\)-element universe in worst-case time
\[O\!\left((2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\right)\]
for any fixed exponent \(r\)? An instance supplies a family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^{[n]}\) with \(|S|\le d\) for every \(S\in\mathcal F\), and an integer \(t\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\). The task is to decide whether some subfamily \(\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal F\) of at most \(t\) sets satisfies \(\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal H}S=[n]\). Sets chosen for the cover may overlap. The randomized interpretation is explicit in the later primary sources.
definitions:
Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\). Each set is represented by its sorted list of distinct element indices in binary; the family is an explicitly supplied list without duplicate sets. Empty sets and an empty family are allowed. Write \(m=|\mathcal F|\). For fixed \(d\),
\[m\le\sum_{j=0}^{\min(d,n)}\binom nj\le(n+1)^d,\]
so the entire valid input has length polynomial in \(n\), with its degree allowed to depend on \(d\). The threshold can be capped at \(n\), since any cover contains a subcover of at most \(n\) sets. The question counts the universe size, not the number of available sets or selected sets, in the exponential part of the time bound.

Use a uniform random-access machine with finite program, binary words of length \(w=\lceil4(n+\log_2(m+2)+1)\rceil\), and word-addressed memory. This allows the usual exponential-size dynamic-programming tables while keeping each word polynomially many bits long. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copies, branches, comparisons, addition/subtraction/multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer division with remainder by a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts, and obtaining a uniformly random independent word. Shifts by at least \(w\) and division by zero may return zero. Initially memory holds only the input and otherwise zeroes. Every table construction and preprocessing operation is counted. The machine has no oracle or nonuniform advice, and no operation acts on an exponentially long bit string as one word. Charging polynomial bit cost for scalar word operations only alters the allowed polynomial factor.

A randomized algorithm must return the correct decision with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid input and halt within its asserted time bound on every random tape. The bound means that for a fixed \(d,\varepsilon\), there are constants \(K,r,n_0\) for which runtime is at most \(K(2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\) whenever \(n\ge n_0\). All finite smaller valid instances must also be correctly decided. These constants and the program may depend on \(d,\varepsilon\), but not on \(n,\mathcal F,t\).

The negation is a single \(\varepsilon>0\) that works for every fixed \(d\), allowing a different algorithm and polynomial factor for each \(d\). An improved base for one particular set-size bound does not refute the conjecture. The decision version used here and the source's minimum-cover optimization version have the same exponential base: searching thresholds and recovering a cover uses only polynomially many calls for fixed \(d\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the conjecture or its negation in the stated randomized computational model. A refutation must give a uniform positive improvement of the exponential base across every fixed maximum set size. Proving a lower bound assuming SETH or another conjecture, restricting to deterministic algorithms, improving one bounded-size case, or counting only arithmetic operations on unbounded-size objects does not settle this target.

title: Strictness of the W-hierarchy
summary: The W-hierarchy groups parameterized decision problems by reductions to exact-weight satisfiability for restricted Boolean circuits. The question asks whether each positive level is strictly contained in the next. The circuit depth is fixed for each target problem, and reductions may spend arbitrary computable time in the parameter times a fixed polynomial in input length. Independent Set and Dominating Set illustrate the first two levels, whose known completeness does not itself separate them. A solution must prove all adjacent separations or prove equality at one particular adjacent pair; oracle-based evidence is insufficient.
formal:
Is the \(W\)-hierarchy strict at every positive level?
\[
\forall\,t\in\mathbb N_{\ge1},\qquad
W[t]\subsetneq W[t+1].
\]
The classes use uniform deterministic fixed-parameter many-one reductions and exact-weight satisfiability of bounded-depth Boolean circuits, as defined below. Equivalently, for every \(t\ge1\), is there a parameterized decision problem in \(W[t+1]\) that does not belong to \(W[t]\)?
definitions:
A parameterized decision problem is a set \(P\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\times\mathbb N\). An input is a finite binary string \(x\) together with a nonnegative integer \(k\), its parameter. The input length \(L\) includes both \(x\) and the binary encoding of \(k\), with delimiters. Membership is an exact yes/no question.

Use [FPT many-one reductions](definitions.html#parameterized) in the deterministic [bit model](definitions.html#bit-model). Both the input and output parameters belong to the encoded pairs. Time includes writing the target instance.

A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with at least one input node and a designated output node of outdegree zero. Nodes of indegree zero are distinct Boolean input variables. Each other node is either a NOT gate of indegree one or an AND or OR gate of indegree at least two, with the usual Boolean semantics. Gates have unrestricted fan-out. A gate is large if its indegree exceeds two. The depth of the circuit is the maximum number of edges on a path from an input node to the designated output. Its weft is the maximum number of large gates on such a path. Unused input nodes are allowed and still count among the input variables.

For an explicit encoding, order all \(N\) nodes topologically, put the \(n\) input nodes first, and give the integers \(n,N\) and the output-node index, followed by each remaining gate's type, indegree and list of distinct predecessor indices. Predecessors must have smaller indices. Encode each integer \(u\ge0\) by \(1^{h}0w\), where \(w\) is the binary representation of \(u+1\) and \(h=|w|\); encode gate types NOT, AND, OR by integers \(1,2,3\). All listed integers use this code, and there are no trailing bits. Invalid encodings are no-instances in the circuit problems below.

For fixed integers \(t,d\ge1\), let \(\operatorname{WCS}_{t,d}\) be the parameterized problem consisting of pairs \((C,k)\) where \(C\) is an encoded circuit of weft at most \(t\) and depth at most \(d\), and some assignment to its input nodes has exactly \(k\) ones and makes its output one. The parameter is \(k\) alone. Circuits exceeding either structural bound, or having fewer than \(k\) input nodes, are no-instances.

Define
\[
W[t]=\{P:\ \exists\,d\ge1\text{ such that }P
\text{ has a fixed-parameter many-one reduction to }
\operatorname{WCS}_{t,d}\}.
\]
The integer \(d\) may depend on the problem \(P\) and level \(t\), but it is a fixed constant independent of the input and its parameter. The reduction may also depend on \(P,t,d\). This quantifier does not allow depth growing as a function of \(k\).

The inclusions \(W[t]\subseteq W[t+1]\) follow directly from the weft bounds. Strict inclusion means that at least one problem belongs to the larger class and not the smaller one. The formal target quantifies over all fixed positive integers \(t\); it does not require an algorithm that constructs witnesses from \(t\).

Separating \(\mathrm{FPT}\) from \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) would leave the requested adjacent-level separations to be proved.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that \(W[t]\subsetneq W[t+1]\) for every integer \(t\ge1\), with the classes and reductions above; or supply a complete Lean-checked refutation, proving \(W[t]=W[t+1]\) for at least one particular \(t\ge1\). A proof for just finitely many strict inclusions does not establish the universal positive answer. Completeness or hardness for one of these classes, an oracle-relative separation, or a separation conditional on an unproved hypothesis does not settle the target. No claim about collapse of all other levels is required for a negative answer.

title: Polynomial kernel for Edge Multiway Cut
summary: Edge Multiway Cut removes a small number of edges so that no two designated terminals remain connected. The question asks whether polynomial-time preprocessing can reduce any instance to an equivalent instance of size polynomial in the deletion budget alone. The number of terminals is unrestricted, and the size exponent must not depend on it. Randomized preprocessing is allowed with a per-instance equivalence guarantee of at least two thirds. Known fixed-terminal kernels and quasipolynomial-size kernels leave the unrestricted polynomial-size target open in the checked sources.
formal:
Does undirected Edge Multiway Cut, parameterized only by the allowed number \(k\) of edge deletions, admit a randomized polynomial kernel? Specifically, do there exist a uniform randomized algorithm \(R\) and positive integers \(C,a,b\) such that for every explicitly encoded instance \(I=(G,T,k)\) of length \(N\), on every random tape \(R\) halts within \(C(N+1)^a\) steps and outputs a well-formed instance \(I'=(G',T',k')\) of the same problem with
\[|I'|\le C(k+1)^b,\qquad k'\le C(k+1)^b,\]
and
\[\Pr_R[I\text{ is a yes-instance}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ I'\text{ is a yes-instance}]\ge2/3?\]
A yes-instance has a set of at most \(k\) edges whose removal leaves no connected component containing two terminals. The number of terminals is unbounded and is not an extra parameter. The constants, including the exponent \(b\), must be independent of \(|T|\).
definitions:
An input graph is a finite undirected unweighted loopless multigraph \(G=(V,E)\). Vertices are labeled \(1,\ldots,n\); edges are an explicitly listed sequence of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Parallel edges are distinct listed objects, each costing one deletion. The terminal set \(T\subseteq V\) consists of distinct designated vertices. The budget \(k\ge0\) is an integer in binary. Encode \(n\) in unary, the edge-list length and endpoints in a self-delimiting binary format, the terminal set as an \(n\)-bit membership vector, and \(k\) in self-delimiting binary. The total encoding length \(N\) includes every listed edge, vertex and terminal and the budget. The output uses the same format; succinct circuits, binary edge multiplicities and binary weights are not allowed.

A cut is a subset \(F\subseteq E\) of edge identities with \(|F|\le k\). The graph \(G-F\) retains every vertex and terminal. It must contain no path between any two distinct terminals. Terminals cannot be deleted, and terminal labels carry no further pairing data: every terminal must be separated from every other. Disconnected graphs, empty graphs, zero budgets and fewer than two terminals are included. The kernel need only preserve the decision answer, not the optimum cut value or every terminal-partition cut. It may relabel vertices and change the terminal set and budget.

The multigraph convention permits the contractions used in kernelization. It does not change polynomial-kernel existence relative to explicit simple graphs: replacing every edge by its own two-edge path through a fresh nonterminal gives a simple graph of polynomial encoding size with the same minimum number of edge deletions needed to separate terminals. Either part of such a path can be deleted at unit cost, while deleting both never helps beyond deleting one.

Use a uniform multitape probabilistic Turing machine with independent fair random bits and one transition per time unit, charging for writing the output. There is no advice, oracle or separately provided preprocessing. Runtime, output-format and size guarantees hold on every random tape. The probability of preserving equivalence is at least \(2/3\) for each fixed input, with two-sided error permitted. This explicitly fixes the saved card's allowance of randomized preprocessing; deterministic or one-sided-error polynomial kernels also qualify. The failure probability is not averaged over a distribution of graphs.

A polynomial kernel has size bounded solely by a fixed polynomial in \(k\), even when the original graph and terminal set are much larger. A bound such as \(k^{|T|+1}\) does not satisfy this condition, since its exponent changes with the input. A size bound \(k^{\log^{O(1)}k}\) is quasipolynomial and is likewise insufficient. Both bounds use the full encoding length, not just the number of vertices while ignoring labels, edges or weights.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the randomized polynomial-kernel claim. A positive proof must provide the preprocessing algorithm and verify the all-tape polynomial runtime, output size and parameter bounds, and per-instance equivalence probability for arbitrary terminal sets. A negative proof must rule out every algorithm in this model. A kernel for a fixed number of terminals, a reduction to a different decision language, quasipolynomial preprocessing or output size, or a conditional exclusion relying on an unproved complexity assumption does not by itself settle the stated unconditional claim.

title: Polynomial compression versus polynomial kernelization
summary: A polynomial compression replaces an instance by a short string for a possibly different decision language. A polynomial kernel must instead return a short equivalent instance of the original parameterized problem. The selected question asks for an NP-complete unary source language with deterministic polynomial compression but a conditional obstruction to polynomial kernels. The obstruction must show that any such kernel would put every NP language in coNP with polynomial advice. The compression is unconditional, its target language is unrestricted, and the original informal naturalness requirement is replaced by the precise source class.
formal: Does there exist a fixed parameterized language \(Q\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\times\mathbb N\) such that its unary-parameter encoding \(\widetilde Q\) is NP-complete and \[\operatorname{PC}(Q)\ \land\ \bigl(\operatorname{PK}(Q)\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\bigr)?\] Here \(\operatorname{PC}\) means deterministic polynomial compression to an arbitrary fixed language, and \(\operatorname{PK}\) means deterministic polynomial kernelization back to \(Q\), with the exact definitions below. Thus the requested compression is unconditional, while its separation from kernels uses the explicitly stated hypothesis \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\).
definitions:
The parameter \(k\) is a nonnegative integer supplied in unary. Encode a pair \((x,k)\) by
\[
\langle x,k\rangle=1^{|x|}0\,x\,1^k,
\qquad
\widetilde Q=\{\langle x,k\rangle:(x,k)\in Q\}.
\]
The prefix determines the end of the binary string \(x\); the remaining symbols must all be one. Strings that fail this syntax are outside \(\widetilde Q\). Input length is \(2|x|+k+1\), equivalent within fixed constants to \(|x|+k+1\).

The property \(\operatorname{PC}(Q)\) holds when there exist a fixed language \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a constant \(C\ge1\), and integers \(a,b\ge1\), such that for every binary string \(x\) and every \(k\ge0\), \(A\) on \(\langle x,k\rangle\) halts within \(C(|x|+k+2)^a\) bit steps and outputs a binary string \(y\) satisfying
\[
|y|\le C(k+1)^b,\qquad
(x,k)\in Q\ \longleftrightarrow\ y\in R.
\]
The target language \(R\) is fixed across all inputs and parameters. No decidability or NP-membership condition is imposed on \(R\). The compressor has no membership oracle for \(R\); it only computes the string. The machine, exponents and constants may depend on the selected \(Q\) and compression scheme, never on \(x,k\).

The property \(\operatorname{PK}(Q)\) holds when there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(B\), a constant \(D\ge1\), and integers \(c,d\ge1\), such that, for every \((x,k)\), \(B\) outputs an encoded pair \(\langle x',k'\rangle\) within \(D(|x|+k+2)^c\) bit steps, with
\[
|x'|+k'\le D(k+1)^d,\qquad
(x,k)\in Q\ \longleftrightarrow\ (x',k')\in Q.
\]
The output language is the same \(Q\), and the bound includes the new parameter in unary. In both definitions all input reading, computation and output writing count. Algorithms have finite fixed programs, no advice, no oracle and no randomness. They must be correct on every valid pair, without a promise on \(x\) beyond the language membership being decided.

For completeness, a binary language \(L\) is in NP if there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and a polynomial bound \(p\) such that
\[
x\in L\ \longleftrightarrow\
\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}\ V(x,z)=1.
\]
The notation \(\{0,1\}^{\le r}\) denotes all binary strings of length at most \(r\). A language \(L\) is in \(\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\) if there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(W\), a polynomial bound \(p\), and a sequence of advice strings \((\alpha_n)_{n\ge0}\) with \(|\alpha_n|\le p(n)\), such that
\[
x\in L\ \longleftrightarrow\
\forall z\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}
\ W(x,\alpha_{|x|},z)=1.
\]
Advice may depend on input length but not on the particular input, and need not be computable. It belongs only to this comparison class, not to the compression or kernel algorithms. Each language may have its own verifier, polynomial and advice sequence. The inclusion \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\) means every NP language belongs to that advice class.

A language is NP-complete when it belongs to NP and every NP language reduces to it by one deterministic polynomial-time many-one map preserving membership. This is ordinary polynomial-time completeness of the unary-encoded language \(\widetilde Q\), not parameterized hardness of \(Q\).

The main proposition quantifies over a single fixed \(Q\), with an unconditional compression scheme and the displayed implication for every possible polynomial kernel. It does not require proving the hypothesis that NP is not contained in the advice class. It also does not assert unconditional nonexistence of a kernel. The informal adjective “natural” is not a further uncheckable requirement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify the language and encoding, prove NP-completeness of its unary form, establish an unconditional deterministic compression with all size and running-time guarantees, and prove that any deterministic polynomial kernel would imply the displayed complexity-class inclusion. Absence of a known kernel, a randomized compression alone, or an output language merely not known to belong to NP does not establish the proposition. The lower-bound implication must be proved; the assumed noninclusion itself need not be proved.

title: General Formula-SAT with a fixed exponential saving
summary: The input is any explicit Boolean formula tree, and the task is to decide exactly whether some assignment satisfies it. The time target is 2^((1-epsilon)n) times a fixed polynomial in the full formula length, for some fixed positive epsilon. One uniform deterministic algorithm must work for all sizes, depths and variable-occurrence patterns. Known faster algorithms for restricted-size formulas do not provide this full guarantee, and a positive answer would refute deterministic SETH. A complete Lean-checked proof or unconditional refutation is required; the precise saving is an editorial specification of the source’s qualitative question.
formal:
Do there exist a rational constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), constants \(K\ge1\), an integer \(d\ge1\), and one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\) such that every explicitly given Boolean formula \(F\) over AND, OR and NOT is correctly decided for satisfiability in at most
\[
K\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}\bigl(N(F)+1\bigr)^d
\]
Turing-machine bit steps? Here \(n(F)\) is the number of distinct variables occurring in \(F\), \(N(F)\) is its full binary encoding length, and no restriction is placed on its size or depth. The same algorithm, positive saving and constants must work for every formula.
definitions:
Use the explicit [SAT formula tree](definitions.html#sat), with binary AND and OR, unary NOT and constants 0 and 1. All declared variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) must occur, and \(n=0\) is permitted. The input permits repeated occurrences, arbitrary depth and arbitrary negations. Every occurrence is written in full.

The output is one bit indicating whether an assignment makes the root true. A formula with no variables has its ordinary Boolean constant value.

Use the [self-delimiting integer code](definitions.html#sat-encoding). Begin with \(\operatorname{code}(n)\), then traverse the tree in preorder. Each node has a three-bit tag specifying constant zero, constant one, variable, NOT, AND or OR. A variable tag is followed by \(\operatorname{code}(i)\), \(1\le i\le n\); other tags determine their arity and have no extra payload. There must be exactly one complete tree, no unused tags or trailing bits, and all declared variables must occur. The full length of this encoding is \(N(F)\). This includes every copy of a repeated subexpression. A succinct generator, truth-table oracle or circuit with shared gates is not an alternative input encoding.

The algorithm is one fixed finite deterministic multitape Turing machine with a read-only input tape, finitely many initially blank work tapes and finite tape alphabets. One transition reads or writes only the cells under its heads and moves each head by at most one cell; its cost is one bit step up to a fixed machine-dependent factor. It halts on every input, rejects malformed encodings in polynomial time in their length and returns the exact satisfiability answer for every valid formula. Parsing, input access, preprocessing and internal computation are included in the runtime. There is no advice, randomness, oracle, quantum computation or unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers. No separate workspace restriction is imposed.

The quantifier order is \(\exists(\varepsilon,K,d,A)\,\forall F\). In particular, neither the exponent saving nor the polynomial exponent may deteriorate with formula size, depth, variable-occurrence count or a chosen size bound. The target includes formulas of every polynomial size as well as larger explicit formulas; their input length remains charged through the displayed factor. For a fixed polynomial relation \(N\le n^q\), any polynomial overhead is absorbed into a smaller fixed exponential saving for sufficiently large \(n\), but no separate size-dependent algorithm is substituted for the single program demanded here.

Exhaustive evaluation gives a bound \(2^n\operatorname{poly}(N)\). The question asks to replace its exponential base by some fixed smaller value. A bound \(2^{n-n^\alpha}\operatorname{poly}(N)\), \(0<\alpha<1\), or a polynomial-factor improvement over \(2^n\) does not meet the target: its saving divided by \(n\) tends to zero. No particular numerical saving is prescribed. Restricting \(\varepsilon\) to rational values in \((0,1)\) preserves existence of a positive fixed saving.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must supply an exact deterministic decision algorithm and a fixed positive saving valid for every allowed formula, with all input and computation costs counted. A negative proof must rule out all algorithms and constants in the proposition unconditionally; a lower bound assuming SETH, ETH or another unproved hardness hypothesis is only a conditional result.

Results restricted to fixed clause width, bounded variable occurrences, linear-size or subcubic-size formulas do not establish the universal positive answer. A counting algorithm could establish it only if it satisfies the full stated size, time and machine requirements. There is no additive numerical tolerance or minimum required saving of one hundredth.

title: Single-exponential Directed Feedback Vertex Set
summary: A directed feedback vertex set meets every directed cycle by deleting its vertices. The question asks for an exact deterministic algorithm with a fixed exponential base in the allowed number of deletions. The remaining dependence on graph size must be polynomial with an exponent independent of the deletion budget. Known fixed-parameter algorithms retain a factorial-scale parameter cost, including the checked SOSA 2025 improvement. This card targets arbitrary digraphs, while the survey’s planar restriction and structural-parameter results remain distinct.
formal: Do there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm and constants \(A,c>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\), which decide Directed Feedback Vertex Set on every \(n\)-vertex directed graph and deletion budget \(0\le k\le n\) within \(A\,2^{ck}(n+1)^d\) bit-computation steps? The answer must be YES exactly when deleting at most \(k\) vertices makes the graph acyclic. The exponential dependence is solely on the solution-size budget, and the polynomial exponent is independent of \(k\).
definitions: The input digraph is \(D=([n],E)\), \(n\ge1\), with \(E\subseteq[n]\times[n]\). Self-loops and opposite arcs are allowed; repeated copies of an arc are not represented and have no effect. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices \(v_1,\ldots,v_t\), \(t\ge1\), with arcs \((v_j,v_{j+1})\) for \(j<t\) and \((v_t,v_1)\). Thus self-loops are cycles of length one, and opposite arcs give a cycle of length two. For \(S\subseteq[n]\), the remaining graph is the induced digraph \(D[[n]\setminus S]\). A feedback vertex set is a set \(S\) for which this remaining digraph contains no directed cycle. Its cost is the cardinality \(|S|\); no vertex weights are present. There are no promises of planarity, bounded degree, bounded treewidth, a supplied solution or bounds on cycle length. Use a deterministic multitape Turing machine with one finite program for all \(n,k,D\), no advice and no random bits. A valid input consists of the prefix \(1^n0\), followed by the \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row-major order, followed by exactly \(\ell=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits encoding \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) in most-significant-bit-first binary. The machine must halt and return the correct decision on every valid input. Each Turing-machine transition costs one step, including all input processing and preprocessing. No running-time condition on malformed strings is part of the target. The fixed encoding has length polynomial in \(n\), so ordinary polynomial-time changes of explicit graph encoding only alter the permitted polynomial factor. The quantified constants \(A,c,d\) are independent of \(n,k,D\). The target is worst-case exact decision, including NO instances; it requires neither an optimal deletion set nor enumeration of all solutions.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction of the specified deterministic algorithm with its correctness and \(A2^{ck}(n+1)^d\) worst-case bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm and constants exist. A \(2^{O(k\log k)}n^{O(1)}\) algorithm, an exponent depending on \(k\) in the polynomial input-size factor, an approximation, or a result for restricted graph classes is insufficient for the affirmative answer. A lower bound conditional on an additional unproved hypothesis establishes only that conditional version of the negative statement.

title: Exact recognition of bounded clique-width
summary: Clique-width measures how many reusable vertex labels are needed to build a graph with four specified operations. Even a complete graph of arbitrary size needs only two labels. The question asks whether graphs of width at most k can be recognized in polynomial time for every fixed k. The polynomial exponent may depend on k, so known NP-completeness when k is input does not settle it. Small thresholds are understood, while approximate or supplied decompositions do not give exact recognition at every threshold.
formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 1\), do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A_{k}\) and constants \(C_{k},c_{k}\ge 1\) such that \(A_{k}\) decides whether \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\) for every finite simple undirected graph G in at most \(C_{k}(N+1)^{c_{k}}\) steps, where N is the bit length of G’s adjacency-matrix encoding?
definitions: A k-expression is a finite expression building a labeled graph using labels from \(\{1,\ldots ,k\}\). It can create one isolated vertex with a chosen label; take the disjoint union of two previously constructed labeled graphs; add all edges between the vertices labeled i and those labeled j for distinct i,j; or change every label i to j. Edge insertion leaves existing edges in place without duplicating them. Relabeling changes no edges. The two operands of a disjoint union may both be arbitrary expressions, so this is ordinary clique-width, not linear clique-width. For a nonempty graph \(G, \operatorname{cw}(G)\) is the least k for which some k-expression produces a graph isomorphic to G after labels are erased. Set \(\operatorname{cw}(\varnothing )=0\). The input contains \(n\ge 0\) and the \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-diagonal \(0/1\) adjacency matrix for the graph on \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). It contains no construction expression or promise about its width. \(A_{k}\) outputs YES exactly when \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\) and NO otherwise, always halting with the stated worst-case bit bound. The quantifier order is \(\forall k \exists A_{k},C_{k},c_{k} \forall G: k\) is fixed for each machine, and the polynomial exponent may depend on it. Each \(A_{k}\) is a single finite program with no advice depending on graph size; the statement imposes no effective map from k to its program and no uniform exponent.
answer_criterion: Prove polynomial-time exact recognition for every fixed threshold k in the model stated, or prove that for at least one fixed k the language \(\{G:\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\}\) has no deterministic polynomial-time decider. An expression with more than k labels does not establish a YES answer; failure of one construction does not establish NO. Variable-k NP-hardness, or fixed-k hardness under an unproved assumption, does not alone unconditionally refute this proposition.

title: Chromatic number in \(2^{n}\) time and polynomial space
summary: The chromatic number is the minimum number of colors needed so that adjacent vertices receive different colors. The question asks for one deterministic algorithm computing it on every graph in base-two exponential time up to polynomial factors. The same algorithm must use only polynomially many bits of working memory. Known algorithms separately achieve base-two time with exponential memory or polynomial memory with a larger time base. Recent randomized algorithms for each fixed color count and improved exponential-space bounds do not meet the complete target.
formal:
Is there one uniform deterministic algorithm that computes the chromatic number of every \(n\)-vertex finite simple undirected graph in time \(O^{*}(2^n)\) and polynomial space?

Precisely, do there exist a deterministic machine \(A\) and fixed integers \(K\ge1,c,d\ge0\) such that, for every such graph \(G\), the machine outputs \(\chi(G)\), halts after at most
\[
K\,2^n(n+1)^c
\]
transitions, and uses at most
\[
K(n+1)^d
\]
work-tape cells throughout its computation? The graph encoding and computation model are defined below. Both bounds must hold for the same algorithm on the same input.
definitions:
The input graph has vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge0\), and an edge set consisting of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops, parallel edges, weights or promises about the graph class. The input consists of \(1^n0\), followed by one adjacency bit for each pair \((i,j)\) with \(1\le i<j\le n\), in lexicographic order. Thus it has \(n+1+\binom n2\) bits. There are no trailing bits.

A proper \(q\)-coloring is a map \(h:[n]\to[q]\) such that \(h(i)\ne h(j)\) whenever \(\{i,j\}\) is an edge. The chromatic number is the least integer \(q\ge0\) for which such a map exists. In particular, \(\chi(G)=0\) for the empty graph and \(1\le\chi(G)\le n\) for a nonempty graph. The output is the ordinary binary encoding of this integer, using the string \(0\) for zero. A coloring itself is not required as output.

The computation model is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and finitely many tapes over fixed finite alphabets. It has a read-only input tape, initially blank work tapes and a write-only output tape. Heads start at cell zero; a transition reads or writes only the cells under the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. Tapes have nonnegative cell indices, with left moves at zero staying there. The time bound counts all transitions, including parsing, input access, arithmetic and output writing. Work space counts the total number of work-tape cells visited; the finite alphabets make this equivalent to bits up to a constant factor. The output tape is append-only and cannot serve as extra readable memory. The read-only input has polynomial length and does not affect the polynomial-space requirement.

There is no random source, advice depending on input length, oracle, unbounded-integer unit-cost operation or uncharged preprocessing. Malformed encodings must be rejected in time polynomial in their length. Constants and the machine are fixed once for all graphs and all \(n\). The bounds are worst-case bounds, not expected or average-case guarantees.

The notation \(O^{*}(2^n)\) suppresses only a factor polynomial in \(n\). A factor \(2^{o(n)}\) is not automatically permitted: for example, \(2^{n+\sqrt n}\) does not meet the displayed bound. A smaller exponential base does qualify if the same algorithm uses polynomial space.

The task is to determine the unrestricted chromatic number, so the number of colors may grow with \(n\). Separate algorithms for every fixed color count, with resources or advice depending on that count, do not by themselves give the required uniform bound. A procedure outputting a rational approximation to \(\chi(G)\) with proved absolute error at most \(1/100\) also yields an exact integer output by rounding; if it meets the stated resource bounds, this conversion incurs only polynomial overhead.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proofs of exact correctness, the \(K2^n(n+1)^c\) time bound and the \(K(n+1)^d\) space bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such machine exists. Correctness must cover every finite simple graph, including inputs whose chromatic number grows with their size. A fixed-color algorithm, a randomized algorithm with possible error, an exponential-space construction, or a result conditional on an unproved hypothesis does not meet the target. The question asks for the existence of an algorithm with simultaneous resource bounds; approximate experimental running times or sampled graph tests are insufficient.

title: Unique Games Conjecture
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
summary: A Unique Games instance consists of explicitly listed vertices and permutation constraints between pairs of labels. UGC asks for NP-hardness of distinguishing almost completely satisfiable instances from those with arbitrarily small optimum value. The alphabet and deterministic reduction may depend on the fixed gap parameters, but must be independent of the growing input formula. A complete Lean proof must establish the full reduction statement or its negation over every alphabet and polynomial-time candidate reduction. The September 2026 perfect-completeness 4-to-1 claim and the known half-completeness Unique Games theorem do not establish this near-one-completeness permutation-constraint conjecture.
formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every pair of rational constants \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\) with \(\varepsilon+\delta<1\), there exists an integer \(q\ge2\) such that it is NP-hard to distinguish the following two classes of explicitly listed Unique Games instances over the alphabet \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\):
\[\text{YES: }\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\varepsilon,\qquad \text{NO: }\operatorname{val}(G)\le\delta.\]
NP-hardness here means a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3SAT with the completeness and soundness guarantees defined below. The alphabet size and the reduction may depend on the two constants but must be fixed before the input size grows. The target is this hardness proposition itself, without assuming \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\).
definitions:
Instance and value. An instance has a finite vertex set \(V=[n]\) with \(n\ge2\), an ordered nonempty list of \(m\ge1\) directed edges \((u_j,v_j)\) with distinct endpoints in \(V\), and a permutation \(\pi_j:[q]\to[q]\) for each edge index \(j\in[m]\). Repeated directed edges, including repeated constraints or different constraints on the same ordered pair, are allowed and counted separately. There is no restriction on degree, expansion, connectedness or bipartiteness, and isolated vertices are allowed. A permutation is a bijection: each label occurs exactly once among its \(q\) images. A labeling is one map \(\ell:V\to[q]\), with no probabilistic or quantum strategy. Edge \(j\) is satisfied when \(\pi_j(\ell(u_j))=\ell(v_j)\). Define
\[\operatorname{val}(G)=\max_{\ell:V\to[q]}\frac{|\{j\in[m]:\pi_j(\ell(u_j))=\ell(v_j)\}|}{m}.\]
The finite maximum is attained and lies in \([0,1]\). All edge occurrences have equal weight. Reversing an edge would require using the inverse permutation; its stored direction fixes the equation used here. The two promised classes are disjoint because \(\delta<1-\varepsilon\). Instances with \(\delta<\operatorname{val}(G)<1-\varepsilon\) are outside the promise.

Explicit encoding. Vertex labels and all integers are written in binary with length prefixes. Concretely, a nonnegative integer \(z\) may be encoded by \(1^b0\) followed by the \(b\)-bit binary expansion of \(z+1\), where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(z+1)\rfloor+1\). A game encoding lists \(q,n,m\), all \(n\) vertex labels in order, and for each edge its two endpoints followed by the entire table \(\pi_j(1),\ldots,\pi_j(q)\). Tables are not circuits or oracles representing longer objects. Input and output lengths count every listed bit. This convention fixes a finite-string model; polynomially interconvertible standard explicit encodings give the same hardness question.

Reduction and source problem. A 3CNF formula \(\varphi\) is an explicitly listed conjunction of clauses, each an ordered disjunction of three literals, where a literal is a Boolean variable \(x_i\) or its negation. Repeated literals are allowed. List the variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_s\) and the clauses, recording literal signs as bits and indices and list lengths with the integer encoding above. The empty conjunction is allowed and is true. A satisfying assignment is a map from these variables to \(\{0,1\}\) making every clause true. Let \(|\varphi|\) be the full bit length of this encoding. For fixed \(\varepsilon,\delta,q\), the required reduction is a single deterministic Turing-machine program \(F\) for which some constants \(C\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\) bound its time by \(C(|\varphi|+1)^k\) on every valid formula. Time includes writing the output. On each such formula it must output one valid game \(G=F(\varphi)\) over exactly \([q]\), satisfying
\[\varphi\text{ satisfiable}\Rightarrow\operatorname{val}(F(\varphi))\ge1-\varepsilon,\qquad
\varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}\Rightarrow\operatorname{val}(F(\varphi))\le\delta.\]
Thus both kinds of formulas map into the promise. A multi-tape deterministic Turing machine with a fixed finite alphabet and a fixed finite number of tapes suffices as the computation model; each transition reads and writes one symbol per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. No advice, randomness or oracle is allowed. Behavior on malformed formula strings is immaterial. Since 3SAT is NP-complete, this reduction is the meaning of NP-hardness used here; no decision algorithm for the game is part of the requested reduction.

Parameter quantifiers. The order is \(\forall(\varepsilon,\delta)\ \exists q\ \exists F,C,k\ \forall\varphi\). The machine, alphabet, time exponent and constant may depend on the fixed gap parameters, but not on the formula. The parameters are not growing input variables, and no common polynomial exponent or effective procedure selecting reductions for all parameters is additionally required. Restricting the gap parameters to positive rationals loses none of the usual real-parameter conjecture: smaller rational errors give the required inclusions of the real-parameter YES and NO classes. The usual one-error formulation is equivalent by taking the smaller of the two errors.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the entire quantified hardness proposition, including the deterministic reductions, polynomial output/time bounds, valid permutation constraints, and both implications for every formula, or prove its logical negation. A negative answer must identify fixed rational \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\) with \(\varepsilon+\delta<1\) such that no alphabet \(q\ge2\) admits the required reduction. Equivalently, for each \(q\) and every deterministic polynomial-time candidate program, some valid 3CNF formula has an invalid output or violates its applicable YES/NO guarantee. This is a statement about all reductions, not just a failed construction or a particular alphabet. No unproved complexity assumption may replace the requested conclusion. A polynomial-time distinguishing algorithm alone does not logically refute the NP-hardness proposition without an appropriate separation such as \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Hardness with completeness bounded away from one, perfect satisfiability testing, a restricted graph class, or a result for many-to-one constraints does not by itself settle this target.

title: Constant-factor approximation for Densest k-Subgraph
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
summary: Densest k-Subgraph asks which exactly k vertices contain the most internal edges. The target is one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that always returns a k-set within one universal constant of optimum. The card fixes explicit graph encoding, bit cost, output cardinality and a guarantee on every input. ETH already excludes this guarantee conditionally, while ordinary NP-hardness of even a 1.001 approximation remains absent in the inspected 2026 source. Recent continuous-optimization and at-least-k density results address different guarantees and do not resolve this target.
formal:
Does Densest \(k\)-Subgraph have a deterministic polynomial-time constant-factor approximation on all explicitly given finite simple undirected unweighted graphs?

For \(n\ge1\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). If \(G=([n],E)\) and \(1\le k\le n\), define
\[e_G(S)=|\{\{u,v\}\in E:u,v\in S\}|,\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=\max_{\substack{T\subseteq[n]\\|T|=k}}e_G(T).\]
The proposition is that there exist one real constant \(C\ge1\), positive integer constants \(D,d\), and one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\) such that, on every encoded input of length \(L\), \(A\) halts within \(D(L+1)^d\) bit steps, and on every valid \((G,k)\) it outputs an explicitly represented set \(S\subseteq[n]\) satisfying
\[|S|=k\qquad\text{and}\qquad C\,e_G(S)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(G,k).\]
The same algorithm, constants and polynomial clock must work for all \(n,G,k\).
definitions:
The graph has exactly the labelled vertices \([n]\), including isolated vertices. Each edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices, with no repetitions, loops, weights or directions. Its input is \(U(n)U(k)\) followed by the \(n(n-1)/2\) adjacency bits in lexicographic order of pairs \((u,v)\) with \(u<v\). Here \(U(a)=1^\ell0b\), where \(b\) is the canonical binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(a\), \(\ell=|b|\), and zero uses \(b=0\). The code must have precisely the indicated number of adjacency bits, with \(n\ge1\) and \(1\le k\le n\). Invalid encodings may be rejected; the clock applies to them too. This dense explicit encoding is polynomially equivalent to an explicit vertex-and-edge list. A succinct circuit or edge oracle is not an input representation for this card.

The output is an \(n\)-bit indicator vector. A one at position \(i\) means vertex \(i\) belongs to \(S\), and exactly \(k\) bits must be one. The objective counts each internal edge once. The maximum exists because the family of \(k\)-subsets is finite and nonempty. An estimate of the optimum without an accompanying vertex set does not satisfy the output requirement.

Running time counts ordinary bounded-symbol Turing-machine steps, including reading input, arithmetic and writing all output bits. The machine has one fixed finite program and a fixed finite number of tapes. The constants cannot depend on graph size, \(k\), edge density or any promise about the input. No advice, randomness, quantum operations or uncharged oracle is supplied. A running time whose polynomial exponent increases with \(k\) does not meet the clock.

The approximation is purely multiplicative and holds on every valid input, with no additive loss, input-distribution exception or probability of failure. When \(\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=0\), the inequality is automatic but the output must still be a valid \(k\)-set. This includes \(k=1\), edgeless graphs and \(n=1\). The case \(k=n\) is included. The quantifier over \(C\) could equivalently use a positive integer, since rounding an admissible real factor upward preserves the guarantee.

Exactly \(k\) vertices is part of the target. On these feasible sets, maximizing internal edge count, average degree \(2e_G(S)/k\), or edges per vertex \(e_G(S)/k\) gives the same approximation ratio. If the number of selected vertices is allowed to vary, these objectives are no longer interchangeable. A guarantee for at least \(k\) vertices, a special graph class, a planted input distribution or a randomized algorithm is a different statement.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this proposition or of its full logical negation. A positive answer must specify one deterministic algorithm and universal constants, prove the global polynomial clock, and prove both exact output cardinality and the approximation inequality on every valid graph and parameter. A negative answer must exclude every such constant-factor polynomial-time algorithm. Equivalently, for every deterministic polynomial-time machine that always outputs a valid \(k\)-set and every fixed \(C\ge1\), some valid input must satisfy \(C e_G(A(G,k))<\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)\). A lower bound conditional on an unproved complexity hypothesis, or a limitation of a specified relaxation or algorithm family, does not by itself prove the full negation.
