title: Constant additive error for one-dimensional bin packing
summary: The input explicitly lists rational item sizes, and each item must be assigned whole to a unit-capacity bin. The question asks for a polynomial-time algorithm using at most a fixed constant more bins than the optimal integral packing. Randomization is allowed, but every output must be feasible and the quality guarantee must hold with probability at least two thirds on every input. All computation uses counted bit operations, and repeated items are listed rather than encoded by compressed multiplicities. The sharper question asks whether one extra bin always suffices with the same success guarantee.
formal:
Do there exist an integer \(C\ge0\), a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), and absolute integers \(K,d\ge1\) such that every explicitly listed one-dimensional bin-packing instance \(I\), of binary input length \(N\), satisfies all three conditions below?

Every execution of \(A(I)\) takes at most \(K(N+1)^d\) bit operations and outputs a feasible packing into bins of capacity one; and, writing \(B_A(I)\) for its number of nonempty bins,
\[
\Pr[B_A(I)\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)+C]\ge\frac23.
\]
The constants do not depend on the number of items, their sizes or precision, the number of distinct sizes, or the optimum. The entire input is available before any packing decisions are made.

The sharper one-extra-bin question fixes \(C=1\) in the same model. Such a guarantee would also settle the constant-additive question. A guarantee with a larger constant would leave the one-extra-bin question open.
definitions:
An instance is a finite list \(I=(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\), with \(n\ge1\) and rational sizes \(0<s_i\le1\). Write each size as \(s_i=a_i/b_i\), where \(1\le a_i\le b_i\) are positive integers given in canonical binary. The numerator and denominator need not be relatively prime. A fixed unambiguous encoding includes \(n\) and every pair \((a_i,b_i)\); \(N\) is its full bit length, including boundaries. Repeated items are separate entries. Binary multiplicities, an oracle, a circuit or a program generating a larger item list are not alternative input encodings. Malformed strings may be rejected in polynomial time.

A packing assigns each item to exactly one bin, without splitting or discarding any item. It is output as a list \(b(1),\ldots,b(n)\) of labels in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Its nonempty-bin count is \(B=|\{b(i):1\le i\le n\}|\); unused labels do not count. It is feasible if
\[
\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\qquad
\sum_{i:b(i)=j}s_i\le1.
\]
All these inequalities use the exact rational input values. Define \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) as the minimum of \(B\) over all feasible assignments. A singleton bin for each item is feasible, so \(1\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le n\).

The algorithm is a single classical multitape Turing machine that may read independent fair random bits. Reading random bits, reading the input, arithmetic on binary integers and rationals, preprocessing and writing every output label count toward bit time. The polynomial time bound must hold on every random tape for every valid input. Feasibility must also hold on every tape. Only the additive-quality bound is probabilistic, and its probability must be at least \(2/3\) separately for every fixed input, not merely on average over an input distribution. On unsuccessful tapes the algorithm may use more than \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)+C\) bins, but must still produce a feasible assignment.

The algorithm is offline and can inspect all sizes before assigning any item. Bins all have exactly capacity one; there is no augmentation of capacity, additional cardinality constraint, packing order requirement, restriction on the number of item types or lower bound on item size beyond positivity. It cannot call an optimum oracle or use uncharged instance-dependent advice. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as a special case.

The additive constant \(C\) is existentially chosen once for all instances. The question does not require \(C=1\), a prescribed value of \(C\), or finding the smallest possible constant. The benchmark \(\operatorname{OPT}\) is the integral packing optimum, not the value of a fractional relaxation. This is an exact algorithm-existence proposition; the numerical tolerance for a separate value-estimation problem does not alter the displayed approximation guarantee.
answer_criterion:
Supply \(A,C,K,d\) and complete Lean-checked proofs of worst-case bit time, feasibility on every random tape and the per-input probability bound. Alternatively, supply a complete Lean-checked proof that no choices of a uniform randomized algorithm and such absolute constants meet these conditions.

An additive loss growing with the instance or optimum, a fixed multiplicative approximation ratio, increased bin capacity, a guarantee only for a restricted family, or an existential fractional integrality-gap bound without the required algorithm does not settle the question. Impossibility of one rounding method is not impossibility of all algorithms. A negative answer restricted to deterministic algorithms would not exclude the permitted randomized algorithms. The benchmark scores the existence of some absolute constant. The one-extra-bin guarantee is recorded as a stronger milestone.

title: Breaking factor two for precedence-constrained makespan
summary: Precedence constraints require some jobs to finish before others start. Jobs run without interruption on identical parallel machines. The question asks for a polynomial-time approximation uniformly better than factor two. The improvement must be a fixed positive constant independent of the machine count. Unit-job and fixed-machine special cases do not cover this full model.
formal: Do there exist a fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and one uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm that, for every instance of nonpreemptive precedence-constrained scheduling on identical parallel machines, outputs a feasible schedule \(S\) with \[C_{\max}(S)\le(2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}?\] Processing times are positive binary-encoded integers, the precedence graph is arbitrary and acyclic, and the number of machines is part of the input. The constant \(\varepsilon\) cannot depend on the instance. No complexity assumption is imposed.
definitions:
For context, let \(\mathcal R\) be the real factors achieved by a uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm on every valid instance, and let \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}=\inf\mathcal R\). 

Instance. There are jobs \(J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\), positive integer processing times \(p_j\), a positive integer machine count \(m\), and a directed acyclic graph \(D=(J,F)\). An arc \((i,j)\in F\) requires job \(i\) to finish before job \(j\) starts. Every arc is a requirement; its transitive consequences also hold. There is no promise on the shape or depth of the directed acyclic graph, and the machine count is not fixed in advance. Every job may run on every machine, and every machine takes exactly \(p_j\) units of time to process job \(j\).

Schedule and feasibility. A schedule specifies for each job a machine \(a_j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and a nonnegative start time \(s_j\). The job occupies precisely the half-open interval \([s_j,s_j+p_j)\) on that machine. Intervals on the same machine must be pairwise disjoint, and
\[s_j\ge s_i+p_i\quad\text{for every }(i,j)\in F.\]
Execution is continuous and uninterrupted: no job may be split, preempted or migrated. Finishing one job and starting another at the same instant is allowed. All jobs are available initially subject to their precedences. There are no release dates, deadlines, communication delays, setup times, machine eligibility restrictions or other resource constraints. The schedule uses the same number of unit-speed machines as the optimum; extra machines or speed are not allowed.

Objective. The makespan is the latest completion time,
\[C_{\max}(S)=\max_{j\in J}(s_j+p_j),\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{S\text{ feasible}}C_{\max}(S).\]
This is elapsed time from zero, not the sum or average of completion times. The optimum is positive and at most \(W=\sum_j p_j\). It is unchanged if start times are restricted to nonnegative integers: for any feasible schedule, retain its machine assignments and within-machine job orders and start each job as early as those orders and the precedences allow. Positive integer durations give an acyclic augmented order and integral earliest starts without increasing the makespan. Thus an optimal integer schedule exists. Having more than \(n\) machines offers no advantage, although the full encoded value of \(m\) is counted in the input length.

Encoding. For an integer \(i\ge0\), let \(\ell\) be the bit length of \(i+1\) and set \(U(i)=1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(i+1)\), with exactly \(\ell\) bits in the last part. Encode an instance as \(U(n)U(m)U(p_1)\cdots U(p_n)\) followed by the \(n^2\) adjacency bits of \(D\) in row-major order. Valid inputs have the stated positivity and acyclicity properties. Encode an output schedule as the list \(U(a_1)U(s_1)\cdots U(a_n)U(s_n)\), with integer starts. These are explicit binary data, not succinct circuits or value oracles. All output bits and arithmetic costs count.

Algorithms and ratios. Computation uses a finite deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite alphabet, no advice, oracle or random bits. Polynomial time is measured in the full bit length \(N\), including all durations and the machine count, not in the numeric sum of processing times. Invalid encodings may be rejected. Each algorithm defining membership in \(\mathcal R\) must halt within its fixed polynomial bound on all valid inputs and always output a feasible schedule. Its factor \(r\) must hold simultaneously for every job count, machine count, positive duration vector and precedence graph. The program and polynomial may depend on the fixed factor \(r\), but cannot be chosen separately for each instance size. No accuracy parameter is supplied to that program in this definition.

The infimum. Graham’s polynomial-time list-scheduling guarantee implies \(2\in\mathcal R\), while feasibility forces all ratios to be at least one. Hence \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le2\). The real infimum is defined even if no algorithm attains it. In particular, proving \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le u\) may establish algorithms with ratios arbitrarily close to \(u\) from above; it need not exhibit an algorithm with ratio exactly \(u\).
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that some fixed improvement \(\varepsilon>0\) over factor two is attainable by one deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm on every allowed precedence instance, or refute this for every fixed improvement.

title: Optimal competitive ratio of online bin packing
summary: Items of sizes at most one arrive without future information. Each item must be placed permanently into a unit bin. The ratio compares the number of used bins with an offline optimum. A single additive constant is allowed for all inputs. The benchmark requires certified absolute accuracy 1/100 for the optimal asymptotic ratio.
formal: Determine \(R_{\mathrm{BP}}\), the infimum asymptotic competitive ratio of deterministic online bin packing.
definitions:
An input \(\sigma\) is a finite sequence of real item sizes in \((0,1]\), arriving one by one. The policy knows only the revealed prefix and its own assignments. It must assign each item irrevocably to a unit-capacity bin on arrival. It cannot split items or move them later. The sequence length is unknown, and computation is unrestricted.

Let \(A(\sigma)\) be the number of nonempty bins used by a deterministic policy and \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)\) the minimum for an offline packing. Both are zero on the empty sequence. Use the [asymptotic competitive ratio](definitions.html#online): \(R_{\mathrm{BP}}\) is the infimum of \(r\ge1\) for which a single policy \(A\) and a constant \(b\ge0\) satisfy \(A(\sigma)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)+b\) on every sequence. The same \(b\) applies to every input length and choice of sizes.
answer_criterion: Supply a real number a and a complete Lean-checked proof that its absolute distance from the defined optimal ratio is at most 1/100. Certified upper and lower bounds with gap at most 1/50 qualify via their midpoint. To certify an upper endpoint \(U\), for each \(\eta>0\) it suffices to give one policy and one additive constant working at ratio \(U+\eta\) on every input. To certify a lower endpoint \(L\), for every \(1\le r<L\), every eligible policy and every additive constant \(b\ge0\), prove that some input violates the bound with \(r,b\).

title: Polynomial-time constant approximation for the General Scheduling Problem
summary: Jobs have release times and may be preempted on one machine. Each job has its own nondecreasing completion-cost function. Costs are explicitly encoded by rational step-function breakpoints. The input horizon may be exponentially large in its binary encoding. The target is a uniform constant factor in polynomial bit complexity.
formal: For the explicitly encoded General Scheduling Problem below, is there a deterministic polynomial-time approximation with a universal constant factor?
definitions: An instance has n jobs, positive integer processing requirements \(p_j\) and nonnegative integer release times \(r_j\) in binary. Time is divided into unit slots \([t,t+1)\); a job may occupy arbitrary slots at integer \(t\ge r_j\), at most one job per slot, until \(p_j\) slots have been allocated. Completion time \(C_j\) is one plus the last occupied slot. Let \(H=\max_j r_j+\sum_j p_j\); schedules are required to finish by H. Each cost function \(f_j:\{0,\ldots,H\}\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) is supplied by a list of integer breakpoints and rational values, encoded in binary, constant between consecutive breakpoints and nondecreasing. Minimize \(\sum_j f_j(C_j)\). This is an explicit discrete-time, piecewise-constant input variant; each job may be preempted between slots at no cost. Output is a list of intervals assigned to jobs, not an H-slot expansion. Running time and output length must be polynomial in total binary input length N, even if H is exponential in N. The guarantee is \(\operatorname{cost}\le c\operatorname{OPT}\) for one absolute finite c, including cost zero when \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated proposition or its negation, for precisely the specified model. A negative answer must rule out every admissible algorithm under the assumptions in the question. A lower bound that needs an additional complexity hypothesis settles the card only if that hypothesis is also proved. A quasipolynomial running time or polynomial dependence on numeric H is not the requested bound.

title: Optimal prophet-secretary constant
summary: Independent values come from known distributions. Their arrival order is uniform and independent of the samples. The policy observes both identity and value before accepting or rejecting. Only one value can be selected and past rejections cannot be recalled. The benchmark is the expected maximum and the target is the optimal universal factor.
formal: Determine the optimal prophet-secretary constant \(\alpha_{\mathrm{PS}}\) for independent nonnegative values arriving in a uniformly random order, with each value’s identity revealed on arrival.
definitions:
For \(n\ge1\), let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be independent nonnegative real random variables with known Borel laws and \(0<\mathbb E[\max_i X_i]<\infty\). An independent uniform permutation reveals the pairs \((i,X_i)\) sequentially. A policy knows \(n\) and all the laws. It may accept one value irrevocably, receiving zero if it accepts none. Choices must be measurable functions of the observed history and independent private randomness. Computation is unrestricted, and the laws may have atoms.

For an instance \(I\), write \(v(I)\) for the supremum expected reward over these policies. Then \(\alpha_{\mathrm{PS}}=\inf_I v(I)/\mathbb E[\max_i X_i]\), over all permitted \(n\) and laws. The supremum need not be attained.
answer_criterion: Supply a real number a and a complete Lean-checked proof that its absolute distance from the defined optimal ratio is at most 1/100. Certified upper and lower bounds with gap at most 1/50 qualify via their midpoint. To certify a lower endpoint \(L\), for every instance and every \(\eta>0\) show that an allowed policy achieves expected reward at least \((L-\eta)\mathbb E[\max_i X_i]\). To certify an upper endpoint \(U\), for every \(\eta>0\) show that some instance limits every allowed policy to expected reward at most \((U+\eta)\mathbb E[\max_i X_i]\). Each policy may use the known laws.

title: Average-case NP hardness from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
summary: The premise P != NP only states a worst-case separation between efficient decision and verification. The conclusion asks for one fixed NP language and one strict polynomial-time sampler whose generated inputs defeat every deterministic exact decider under a positive-moment runtime bound. The ensemble parameter is supplied to the decider, while correctness is required even on inputs outside the sampler’s support. Known reduction barriers concern restricted proof methods, and recent description-complexity results retain specialized hardness premises or different average-case conventions. A solution requires a complete Lean proof of the implication from the stated premise alone or of its full negation in the ordinary uniform model.
formal:
Is the following implication true in the ordinary uniform Turing-machine model?
\[\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists L\in\mathrm{NP}\ \exists S\in\mathrm{PSamp}\ :\ (L,D^S)\notin\mathrm{AvgP}.
\]
Here \(S\) is one exact polynomial-time sampler, \(D^S=(D^S_n)_{n\ge1}\) its output distribution ensemble, and \(\mathrm{AvgP}\) means deterministic, always-correct computation with the positive-moment runtime bound below. Thus the conclusion requires one fixed language and one fixed feasible sampling procedure for which no exact deterministic decider has average polynomial running time. No additional hardness or derandomization hypothesis may be assumed.
definitions:
All algorithms have one fixed finite program, use ordinary multitape Turing machines with finite tape alphabets and unit-cost transitions, and receive explicit binary strings. There is no oracle or nonuniform advice. Randomized machines obtain independent fair coin bits; reading input, generating coins, computing intermediate data and writing output all take time.

A language is a set \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\). It belongs to \(\mathrm{P}\) if one deterministic machine decides membership on every input \(x\) within \(a(|x|+1)^d\) steps for fixed positive integers \(a,d\). It belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and fixed positive integers \(a,d\) such that \(x\in L\) exactly when some binary certificate \(y\) of length at most \(a(|x|+1)^d\) satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). The verifier is total and polynomial time in its full input length. The premise concerns these total decision classes.

A sampler \(S\in\mathrm{PSamp}\) is one randomized machine which, on unary input \(1^n\), \(n\ge1\), halts on every random tape within \(q(n)=a(n+1)^d\) steps, for fixed positive integers \(a,d\) depending on \(S\). It outputs a finite binary string of length at most \(q(n)\), possibly the empty string. Put \(D^S_n(x)=\Pr[S(1^n)=x]\). Sampling is exact, not an approximation, and its time bound holds for every coin sequence. The parameter \(n\) need not equal the sampled string length. These probabilities form a finite distribution: one may regard the random tape as \(q(n)\) fair bits, with unused bits ignored.

An exact decider \(A\) for \(L\) is one deterministic machine that, on the explicitly separated pair \((1^n,x)\), halts and returns \(1\) exactly when \(x\in L\), for every \(n\ge1\) and every binary string \(x\), including strings of zero probability under \(D^S_n\). It cannot answer 'unknown'. Let \(T_A(1^n,x)\) be its number of transitions, charged at least one step. There is no worst-case polynomial-time requirement on this decider. By definition,
\[(L,D^S)\in\mathrm{AvgP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists A\ \exists\eta>0\ \exists C>0\ \exists k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1:
\sum_x D^S_n(x)T_A(1^n,x)^{\eta}\le C(n+1)^k,
\]
where \(A\) must be an exact decider and \(\eta,C\) are real constants. The sum is over the finite support of \(D^S_n\). The algorithm and constants may depend on \(L,S\) but not on \(n\). Nonmembership means that for every such \(A,\eta,C,k\), some \(n\ge1\) violates the inequality. It is not necessary to violate it at every sufficiently large length.

This is the positive-moment convention for average polynomial time. It allows \(\eta\ne1\); the definition is not a bound on expected runtime itself and does not permit incorrect membership answers. The existentially selected sampler is part of the distributional problem, not input to the decider, which may have its fixed description built into its program.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed implication or its logical negation, under the stated uniform models and quantifiers. An affirmative result must, from \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone, establish a fixed \(L\in\mathrm{NP}\) and a fixed exact strict-polynomial-time sampler for which every deterministic exact decider fails every positive-moment polynomial bound. The sampler and language cannot depend on the decider being challenged. A negative result must prove \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) together with \((L,D^S)\in\mathrm{AvgP}\) for every permitted \(L,S\); an oracle separation or a barrier for one reduction method is not that negation. A complete proof of the implication may use the premise without separately proving it. Partial improvements, an additional unproved hardness assumption, or a failure of one particular algorithm do not establish the target.

title: Planted clique conjecture
summary: A detector receives one random graph and must tell whether a uniformly chosen set of exactly k vertices was made into a clique. The selected conjecture excludes a uniform randomized polynomial-time detector with balanced success at least two thirds at all sufficiently large sizes when k is a fixed power below the square-root scale. The input, all sources of randomness, the complete bit-time clock and the precise order of quantifiers are specified. Known recovery algorithms reach the square-root scale, while sum-of-squares integrality gaps and other method restrictions do not exclude every detector. Conditional distinguishing results and newer inference reductions remain evidence about the hypothesis, with differing planting conventions and guarantees identified explicitly.
formal: Is the following hardness statement true? For every fixed real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), with \(k_n=\lfloor n^{1/2-\varepsilon}\rfloor\), there is no uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) for which \[\Pr[\widehat b=b]\geq\frac23\] in the balanced one-graph experiment below for every sufficiently large integer \(n\).
definitions:
For \(n\geq2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The null distribution \(N_n\) is the distribution of a simple undirected labeled graph on \([n]\) in which each unordered pair of distinct vertices is an edge independently with probability \(1/2\). For \(0\leq k\leq n\), the planted distribution \(P_{n,k}\) chooses \(S\) uniformly among all \(k\)-element subsets of \([n]\), includes every edge inside \(S\), and chooses each other edge independently with probability \(1/2\). There are no loops. The planted set has exactly \(k\) vertices; it is not formed by independently including each vertex.

In the experiment, first choose a fair bit \(b\). If \(b=0\), sample \(G\sim N_n\); if \(b=1\), sample \(G\sim P_{n,k_n}\). Give \(A\) only \((n,k_n,G)\), and let \(\widehat b\in\{0,1\}\) be its output. All randomness of the sampling and of \(A\) is independent. Success is averaged over \(b\), the graph, the planted set when present and the algorithm’s random bits. Writing \(s_A(n,\varepsilon)\) for this probability, \[s_A(n,\varepsilon)=\tfrac12\big(\Pr_{G\sim N_n,A}[A(n,k_n,G)=0]+\Pr_{G\sim P_{n,k_n},A}[A(n,k_n,G)=1]\big).\] This is not a separate \(2/3\) guarantee on each individual graph or on each of the two distributions. The algorithm receives one sampled graph, without the label \(b\), the set \(S\), sample access to the unknown distribution or other side information.

For \(u\geq0\), define \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^a0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(a\) bits and no leading zeroes. The input is \(1^n0\operatorname{code}(k)\), followed by the full \(n^2\) adjacency matrix in row order, with no trailing bits. A valid input has \(n\geq2\), \(0\leq k\leq n\), a symmetric matrix and zero diagonal; let \(L\) be its full bit length. An allowed algorithm is one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and tape alphabet, using fresh independent fair bits and no oracle or advice. For some integers \(C,c\geq1\), on every input and every random-bit sequence it outputs one bit within \(C(L+1)^c\) transitions. Malformed encodings return 0 within this bound. Input processing, bit arithmetic and any additional graphs generated by the algorithm count toward time. On valid inputs \(L=\Theta(n^2)\), so polynomial time in \(L\) and in \(n\) are equivalent.

For each fixed \(\varepsilon\), the forbidden guarantee is \(\exists A,C,c,N\ \forall n\geq N:\ s_A(n,\varepsilon)\geq2/3\), with the global clock condition just specified. The program and constants may depend on this fixed \(\varepsilon\), but cannot change with \(n\); \(\varepsilon\) is not supplied as an oracle or an infinite advice string. The supplied integer \(k_n\) removes any need to compute a real power to construct the input. The conjecture therefore says that every allowed algorithm has success below \(2/3\) for arbitrarily large \(n\), for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). It does not assert that its success tends to \(1/2\).
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of this hardness proposition or its logical negation. To refute it, give some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), one allowed polynomial-time algorithm and a proof that its balanced success is at least \(2/3\) for every sufficiently large \(n\). To prove it, exclude every such algorithm for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). Success only on infinitely many sizes does not satisfy the refutation target. A limitation on sum-of-squares relaxations, local searches or another restricted model does not establish hardness against all allowed machines. A recovery result must imply the stated detection guarantee; a change of planting distribution or a conditional theorem must not be treated as an unconditional resolution of this exact experiment.

title: Computational threshold for tensor PCA
summary: The card asks whether every efficient classical algorithm fails to recover constant correlation with a hidden spherical direction below a specified tensor-PCA signal scale. Its observation is one fully listed tensor with independent ordered Gaussian noise, fixed finite-precision rounding and no extra information. The statement precisely separates failure on arbitrarily large dimensions from the eventual-success counterexample needed to refute it. Recent low-degree, power-iteration, multiple-observation and threshold-refinement results retain model or resource restrictions. A Lean resolution must handle the full uniform bit model and its exact spherical recovery probability, preserving all normalization and precision choices.
formal: Is the following computational impossibility statement true? For every fixed integer \(k\ge3\), rational \(0<\varepsilon<(k-2)/4\), and rational \(0<c<1\), no uniform randomized polynomial-time classical algorithm can, for all sufficiently large \(n\), recover a vector with absolute correlation at least \(c\) with a uniformly random hidden unit direction from the single rounded tensor observation \[Y=\lambda_n v^{\otimes k}+Z,\qquad \lambda_n=n^{k/4-\varepsilon},\qquad v\sim\operatorname{Unif}(S^{n-1}),\] where all \(n^k\) ordered entries of \(Z\) are independent \(N(0,1)\) variables. Recovery must succeed with probability at least \(2/3\), averaged over the hidden direction, noise and algorithm coins. Rounding, output normalization and the uniform bit-cost model are defined below. The fixed power saving \(n^\varepsilon\) and the spherical prior are parts of the existing target, not replaced by a threshold for one algorithm family.
definitions:
\(S^{n-1}=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\sum_i v_i^2=1\}\), with its rotation-invariant probability measure. A tensor is an array indexed by all ordered tuples \((i_1,\ldots,i_k)\in[n]^k\), including repeated indices. Its rank-one signal has entry \(\lambda_n v_{i_1}\cdots v_{i_k}\). The Gaussian noise entries, the direction and learner coins are independent. In particular the noise is not symmetrized: entries indexed by different permutations remain independent. The learner has exactly one tensor observation, with no labeled coordinates, informative starting vector, auxiliary graph or additional independent noise samples. The fixed constants \(k,\varepsilon,c\) are known to its program, but \(v\) and \(Z\) are hidden.

For \(n\ge2\), put \[b_n=\lceil10k\log_2 n\rceil,\qquad Q_b(x)=2^{-b}\left\lfloor2^b\max\{-2^b,\min\{x,2^b\}\}\right\rfloor.\] The actual input is \(n\) and the complete list \((Q_{b_n}(Y_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}))_{[n]^k}\) in lexicographic tuple order. Each entry is encoded by its signed integer numerator with the common denominator \(2^{b_n}\); the numerator has at most \(2b_n+2\) bits. The clipping interval and rounding direction are fixed, not chosen adaptively by the algorithm. The exact real tensor exists only in the sampling experiment; the machine receives no oracle for its discarded digits. The input length is \(O(n^k\log n)\) at fixed \(k\). This is the previously adopted explicit finite-precision version of the Gaussian question, not a theorem asserting equivalence to every exact-real formulation.

An allowed algorithm is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with independent fair random bits. There exist constants \(B,a\ge1\), possibly depending on the fixed triple, such that it terminates within \(Bn^a\) bit operations on every encoded input of this dimension and every random tape. Reading, storage operations, arithmetic, writing the output and its rational encodings are included. The single program and polynomial work for all \(n\), with no advice depending on dimension. Since \(k\) is fixed, this is polynomial in the complete input length. There are no exact-real or quantum operations.

The output is a list of \(n\) rational coordinates \(w_i\), each a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator. A malformed vector or \(w=0\) fails. Otherwise interpret \(u=w/\|w\|_2\), where \(\langle w,v\rangle=\sum_i w_i v_i\) and \(\|w\|_2=(\sum_i w_i^2)^{1/2}\). The success event is the mathematically defined inequality \[|\langle w,v\rangle|\ge c\|w\|_2.\] The learner need not compute that event, since it does not know the planted direction. Absolute correlation permits a global sign flip, including the inherent even-order ambiguity. The output need not encode the irrational normalized vector exactly; its rational representative determines the direction.

Write \(p_A(n;k,\varepsilon,c)\) for the probability of this event in the specified experiment. The target is \[\forall(k,\varepsilon,c)\ \forall A\text{ of polynomial bit cost}\ \forall N\ge2\ \exists n\ge N:\quad p_A(n;k,\varepsilon,c)<2/3.\] Thus the conjecture rules out eventual success on all dimensions; it does not claim that every algorithm fails at every large dimension, or that its success probability must tend to zero. Conversely, a refutation needs one fixed triple and one machine with eventual success at least \(2/3\). The range of \(\varepsilon\) ensures \(\lambda_n/\sqrt n=n^{(k-2)/4-\varepsilon}\to\infty\), placing the signal above the usual statistical scale in the unrounded model.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the full quantified impossibility statement, or a Lean-verified counterexample consisting of one fixed triple, a single algorithm, polynomial worst-case bit/output bounds and an \(N\) for which \(p_A(n)\ge2/3\) for every \(n\ge N\). A lower bound against low-degree estimators, one iterative method, or a different prior is not the universal statement. Detection and recovery must not be interchanged without a proved reduction. Any normalization, symmetrization, multiple-sample or precision transfer must be justified in the same success and resource model. A conditional hardness reduction is partial progress until its premise is proved. Logarithmic threshold improvements or a constant-prefactor improvement at \(n^{k/4}\) do not supply the fixed exponent saving. The desired output quality is a fixed absolute correlation, not coordinatewise numerical recovery.

title: Computational Kesten–Stigum threshold
summary: A sparse stochastic block model hides a fixed number of equally likely community labels in a random graph. The question asks whether any fixed assortative parameters below the Kesten–Stigum threshold allow polynomial-time recovery with a constant expected advantage over chance. The algorithm receives one graph, and success is measured after the best permutation of the community names. Information can survive below the threshold, but known computational barriers retain conjectural or restricted-estimator assumptions. Recent algorithms with a growing number of communities do not supply the fixed-parameter example required here.
formal:
Do there exist a fixed integer \(q\ge5\), fixed rational numbers \(a>b>0\), a fixed real \(\delta>0\), and one uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) such that
\[(a-b)^2<q\bigl(a+(q-1)b\bigr)\]
and, for every sufficiently large integer \(n\), the symmetric stochastic block model defined below satisfies
\[\mathbb E\bigl[\operatorname{ov}(A(G),\sigma)\bigr]\ge\frac1q+\delta?\]
All model parameters and the algorithm are chosen once, independently of \(n\). The expectation is over the planted labels, the graph and the algorithm's random bits.
definitions:
For \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), draw the hidden labels \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n\) independently and uniformly from \([q]\). Conditional on these labels, independently include each unordered pair \(\{i,j\}\), \(i\ne j\), as an edge with probability \(a/n\) when \(\sigma_i=\sigma_j\), and with probability \(b/n\) otherwise. The graph is simple and undirected. Take integer \(n\ge\max\{1,\lceil a\rceil\}\), so these probabilities are valid. Groups have equal prior probabilities; their sizes are not conditioned to be exactly equal.

The input to \(A\) is this single graph on the named vertices \([n]\), encoded by its explicit binary adjacency matrix together with \(n\). The constants \(q,a,b\) are known to the algorithm and may be incorporated into its finite description. No hidden labels, correlated side information or auxiliary sample graphs are supplied. On every graph input and every random tape, the algorithm halts within \(K(n+1)^k\) ordinary Turing-machine bit steps for some fixed constants \(K,k\), and outputs a vector \(\widehat\sigma\in[q]^n\). Randomness consists of independent unbiased bits. Uniform means one finite program for all input lengths, with no length-dependent advice. The program, runtime constants and recovery advantage may depend on the chosen \(q,a,b\), but not on \(n\).

For label vectors \(u,v\in[q]^n\), set
\[\operatorname{ov}(u,v)=\max_{\pi\in S_q}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{u_i=\pi(v_i)\},\]
where \(S_q\) is the finite set of all permutations of \([q]\) and the indicator is one exactly when its condition holds. Relabelling communities does not change their quality. Output labels may be unused. The maximum is part of the mathematical performance measure; the algorithm does not know \(\sigma\) and is not asked to compute this maximum. The chance baseline \(1/q\) is the limiting baseline for fixed \(q\), not a claim that the finite-sample expectation of a maximized random overlap equals exactly \(1/q\).

Write
\[d=\frac{a+(q-1)b}{q},\qquad \theta=\frac{a-b}{a+(q-1)b}.\]
Here \(d\) is the limiting expected degree; the finite graph has expected degree \((1-1/n)d\). The Kesten–Stigum threshold is \(d\theta^2=1\), and the required strict inequality is \(d\theta^2<1\). The case \(a>b\) is assortative: edges are more likely within a group. The card asks for a fixed positive expected recovery advantage for all \(n\ge n_0\), for one finite \(n_0\); it does not replace that requirement by a probability tending to one, a statement only on a subsequence, or a community count growing with \(n\). There is no separate promise of information-theoretic recoverability: a successful algorithmic example would itself prove it.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the exact existential proposition. A positive answer must give one fixed eligible \(q,a,b,\delta,A\), a uniform worst-case polynomial runtime bound, and a finite \(n_0\) for which the expected-overlap inequality holds for every eligible \(n\ge n_0\). A negative answer must exclude every such choice: for every eligible fixed parameter triple, uniform polynomial-time randomized algorithm and positive \(\delta\), and every proposed \(n_0\), some eligible \(n\ge n_0\) must violate that expected-overlap inequality. Information-theoretic recovery with unlimited computation, conditional computational hardness, lower bounds for a restricted estimator class, and results with growing \(q\) do not settle the proposition. This is exact yes/no acceptance, with no numerical tolerance applied to the threshold or the quantifiers.

title: Polynomial-time refutation of random 3-SAT at constant density
summary: A random 3-SAT formula at sufficiently large constant clause density is almost surely unsatisfiable. The question asks for one polynomial-time randomized refuter that recognizes almost all such formulas while never rejecting a satisfiable formula. The density, algorithm and time bound must be fixed independently of the number of variables. Gap refutation, planted detection and lower bounds for particular proof systems do not settle this exact-sound unrestricted target. An accepted answer proves existence or impossibility with the full quantifiers in Lean.
formal:
Do there exist an integer \(C\geq6\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) such that \(A\) never outputs \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) on any satisfiable \(3\)-CNF formula, and
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr_{F\sim R_3(n,Cn),\,\rho}
 [A(F;\rho)=\mathrm{UNSAT}]=1?
\]
The distribution \(R_3\), exact soundness, and worst-case time bound are defined below. The constant \(C\), machine and its time polynomial must be fixed before \(n\); the probability includes the algorithm’s independent random bits \(\rho\).
definitions:
A Boolean variable takes values in \(\{0,1\}\). A literal is a variable or its negation, a clause is a disjunction of literals, and a CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses. General inputs are explicitly listed \(3\)-CNF formulas, with at most three literals in each clause; repeated clauses, repeated literals and empty clauses are allowed. The empty clause is false. The number \(n\) of named variables and the list length are encoded in binary, followed by binary indices and sign bits with delimiters. Valid indices lie in \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\); unused variables are allowed. Let \(N\) be the complete encoded length. Malformed encodings receive \(\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\) in polynomial time.

For \(n\geq3\), the random distribution \(R_3(n,m)\) is an ordered list of \(m\) independent clauses sampled with replacement. For each clause choose a uniformly random three-element subset of \([n]\), and independently negate each selected variable with probability \(1/2\). Write its three variables in index order. Thus each random clause has three distinct variables, duplicate clauses may occur, and signs in all clauses are independent. This fixed-size distribution is not a planted distribution or a distribution conditioned on unsatisfiability.

The algorithm always outputs either \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) or \(\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\). Exact soundness means that for every satisfiable input formula \(F\) and every sequence \(\rho\) of its random bits, \(A(F;\rho)=\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\). On an unsatisfiable formula it may also return \(\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\); the required frequency of success applies only to the stated random distribution. Even on exceptional input formulas or random choices there is no allowed false assertion of unsatisfiability.

Use a uniform randomized multitape Turing machine with independent fair bits and no advice or external oracle. There must be integers \(K,d\geq1\) such that every computation takes at most \(K(N+1)^d\) bit operations on every input and every random-bit sequence, including adversarial formulas. Reading random bits and producing the answer are charged, so only polynomially many bits may be used. This is a worst-case bound, not an expected-time bound on random formulas. Deterministic machines are included.

The probability limit requires that for every real \(\eta>0\) there is an integer \(n_0\) such that for every integer \(n\geq\max\{3,n_0\}\), the probability of \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) is at least \(1-\eta\). The rate of convergence need not be supplied as an algorithm. The density \(C\) is an absolute constant, not a function tending to infinity with \(n\). Choosing integer \(C\geq6\) loses no successful smaller constant-density regime: on a denser input the algorithm can run a lower-density refuter on the appropriate clause prefix, whose distribution is exactly the lower-density model. Unsatisfiability of a prefix implies unsatisfiability of the full formula, preserving soundness.

No named proof system or explicit derivation format is imposed. The output \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) must be justified by the proven soundness of the algorithm; the machine need not print a resolution or sum-of-squares proof. Existence of short unsatisfiability certificates without an efficient way of finding them does not meet this definition.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must supply one constant \(C\), one uniform algorithm, its worst-case polynomial time bound, exact soundness for every satisfiable input and every random-bit sequence, and the success limit for \(R_3(n,Cn)\).

A negative answer must rule out every such constant and every such algorithm. Equivalently, for every proposed sound polynomial-time \(A\) and every integer \(C\geq6\), there must be some \(\eta>0\) such that failure probability is at least \(\eta\) for arbitrarily large \(n\). Showing failure for a single algorithm, proof system or finite set of inputs is insufficient. A conditional theorem under an unproved complexity assumption is partial progress on this unconditional target. Algorithms requiring a growing clause density, allowing erroneous refutations on rare satisfiable inputs, or merely distinguishing a planted distribution do not satisfy the criterion.

title: Polynomial smoothed complexity of FLIP for Max-Cut
summary: Does FLIP for Max-Cut have polynomial expected path length on every graph under independent bounded-density edge weights? Each step moves just one vertex and must strictly increase the cut weight. The expectation controls the longest path after the weights are sampled, including all starting cuts and improving choices. Polynomial bounds for sparse graph families and a general high-probability bound do not finish this target. The known smoothed superpolynomial example permits three-vertex moves, while its single-vertex analogue is unperturbed.
formal: Are there absolute constants \(C,a,b>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every simple undirected graph G on n vertices, every \(\varphi \ge 1/2\) and every collection of independent edge-weight distributions supported on \([- 1,1]\) with probability densities bounded by \(\varphi\), the expected length of the longest strictly improving single-vertex-flip path is at most \(C(n+1)^{a}(1+\varphi )^{b}\)?
definitions: The graph and one Lebesgue-measurable density \(f_{e}\) for each edge are chosen adversarially before the random weights. Each \(f_{e}\) is nonnegative, integrates to 1 on \([- 1,1]\), and is at most \(\varphi\) almost everywhere; weights \(w_{e}\) are sampled independently once from these densities and then held fixed. They may be negative and need not be identically distributed. A cut is a subset \(S\subseteq V\), with value \(W_w(S)=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E,\;|\{u,v\}\cap S|=1}w_{\{u,v\}}\). A legal step replaces S by \(S\triangle \{v\}\) for one vertex v, and requires a strictly larger cut value. Define \(L(G,w)\) as the largest number of steps in any such path, maximized over all starting cuts and all choices of improving vertices after w is known; set \(L=0\) if there is no step. There are finitely many cuts and strict improvement prevents revisiting one, so \(L\le 2^{n}- 1\) and its expectation is well-defined. The expectation is over w alone, with the maximum over paths inside it. The resource counted is improving steps, not the bit cost of exact real arithmetic or of sampling distributions. The target concerns all graphs and all allowed densities with one common polynomial. A run ends at a single-flip local maximum, which need not maximize cut value globally.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal polynomial bound on \(E_{w}[L(G,w)]\), or prove its logical negation by exhibiting admissible families that exceed every such polynomial. A bound for selected graph classes or for one favorable pivot rule does not establish the proposition. A rare long path or an unperturbed worst-case instance alone does not refute an expected bound under these density constraints.

title: Asymptotically optimal algorithms for random three-dimensional assignment
summary: An instance contains independent exponential costs for all triples of three equal-sized label sets. A feasible axial assignment uses every label exactly once. The question asks for one polynomial-time algorithm whose relative error vanishes with high probability. The cited efficient bound has a subpolynomial approximation factor and does not establish this guarantee. A resolution would clarify whether random higher-dimensional assignment admits algorithmic asymptotic optimality.
formal: Is there a uniform polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) and a deterministic sequence \(\eta_n\ge0\) with \(\eta_n\to0\) such that, for an \(n\times n\times n\) array of independent mean-one exponential costs, \(A\) returns permutations \(\pi,\sigma\in S_n\) satisfying \[\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n C_{i,\pi(i),\sigma(i)}\le(1+\eta_n)\operatorname{OPT}(C)\right]\longrightarrow1?\] The dimension is exactly three and the assignment is axial, as defined below.
definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(S_n\) for its permutations. The \(n^3\) input coordinates \(C_{ijk}\) are mutually independent with \(\Pr[C_{ijk}>t]=e^{-t}\) for \(t\ge0\). A feasible assignment is the set of \(n\) triples \((i,\pi(i),\sigma(i))\); each label in each coordinate position occurs once. Define \(\operatorname{OPT}(C)=\min_{\pi,\sigma\in S_n}\sum_i C_{i,\pi(i),\sigma(i)}\). It is positive with probability one. The question concerns approximation to the realized optimum of the same array, not to its expectation.

The array is explicitly accessible in random-access memory, with each real entry read at unit cost. Use exact real arithmetic with addition, subtraction, multiplication, nonzero division and comparison, ordinary indexing and fair random bits, each at unit cost. No unit-cost operation exposes infinitely many bits of an input real. A finite program must run in at most \(Cn^c\) operations on every nonnegative input and every random tape, for some absolute constants \(C,c\). Polynomial time in \(n\) is also polynomial in the array length \(n^3\). The algorithm always returns two permutations; its approximation guarantee is only probabilistic. This explicitly chosen arithmetic model does not claim a bit-complexity result for finitely rounded costs.

Probability is jointly over the independent input array and any internal coins, taken independently. No success guarantee is required for each individual array. The same algorithm works for all \(n\); \(\eta_n\) is independent of the realized costs and no particular convergence rate is prescribed. Thus a scheme giving a separate algorithm for every fixed accuracy does not by itself state the required single polynomial-time, vanishing-relative-error guarantee.

The planar three-dimensional assignment problem imposes one chosen entry on each axis-parallel line and selects \(n^2\) entries. That is a different feasible set. This card instead imposes one entry in each coordinate plane and selects \(n\) entries.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked affirmative proof supplying the algorithm, polynomial bound, vanishing error sequence and probability limit, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists in the stated model. Bounding the optimum's expected value, giving a constant approximation factor, or obtaining an \(n^{o(1)}\) factor does not suffice for a factor tending to one. A runtime or quality guarantee confined to the planar variant does not answer this axial question.

title: Polynomial-time exact optimization of random asymmetric TSP
summary: Each directed edge receives an independent uniform real cost. The task is to return an exactly cheapest Hamiltonian tour. The desired runtime is a fixed polynomial with probability tending to one, with zero-error output. The checked 2026 revision proves a quasi-polynomial bound and keeps the exact polynomial question distinct. This tests whether random instances permit efficient exact optimization despite worst-case hardness.
formal: Does there exist a uniform algorithm \(A\) and absolute constants \(C,c>0\) such that, for the complete directed graph on \([n]\), with mutually independent costs \(w_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\) for \(i\ne j\), the probability that \(A\) returns an exactly minimum-cost directed Hamiltonian cycle within \(Cn^c\) arithmetic operations tends to one as \(n\to\infty\)? The algorithm must be correct whenever it terminates and terminate almost surely on this input distribution.
definitions:
For \(n\ge2\), the graph has every ordered edge \((i,j)\) with distinct endpoints. Opposite directions receive independent costs; no metric or triangle inequality is promised. A directed Hamiltonian cycle is a cyclic ordering \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) of all vertices, of cost \(\sum_{t=1}^n w_{v_t,v_{t+1}}\), where \(v_{n+1}=v_1\). Cyclic rotations represent the same tour. The optimum is the minimum of these finitely many sums. The output is a tour, not a rounded estimate of its value.

The explicit real-valued edge array is the input. Use a uniform real RAM with exact addition, subtraction, multiplication, nonzero division, comparisons, register accesses, ordinary indexing and optional fair random bits at unit cost. There is no unit-cost binary-digit extraction from a real. Exactness therefore means correctness of comparisons and of the chosen tour in this arithmetic model, rather than a claim about storing a continuously distributed input in finitely many bits.

Let \(T_A(w,\rho)\) be the operation count, allowing infinity for a nonterminating run, where \(\rho\) is an internal random tape independent of \(w\). Require zero-error output: every terminating run on an eligible edge array returns an optimum tour. Require \(\Pr[T_A<\infty]=1\) under the product input-and-coin law for each \(n\), and \(\Pr[T_A\le Cn^c]\to1\). Deterministic algorithms are included. Slow exceptional runs are allowed; a bound on expected runtime is not imposed. These conventions make the imported high-probability exact-computation question explicit.

The algorithm need not use branch and bound or any particular relaxation. The assignment relaxation permits several directed cycles instead of a single cycle; solving that relaxed problem exactly is not the same task. Likewise, an asymptotically negligible additive tour-cost error does not establish exact optimality.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated algorithmic existence and probability limit, or its logical negation in the specified arithmetic model. The proof must establish exact output correctness and one fixed polynomial runtime threshold holding with probability tending to one. A quasi-polynomial bound, approximate tours, or polynomial behavior only under a discrete small-integer cost distribution does not suffice. A lower bound for a particular branch-and-bound implementation does not refute the existence of all algorithms allowed here.

title: Average-case optimality of standard Shellsort
summary: Standard Shellsort repeatedly insertion sorts positions separated by fixed gaps. The gap list may depend on array length but is chosen before seeing the input. Du and Wan prove that a fixed sequence of gaps achieves an average of O(n log n) key comparisons on uniform random permutations. They first analyze a distribution of gap lists and then average over random inputs to prove existence of a fixed list for each length. The resulting algorithm uses the usual insertion-sort pass for each gap.
formal: Does there exist a choice, for every \(n\ge2\), of a finite deterministic increment list \(h^{(n)}=(h_1,\ldots,h_p)\), with \(1\le h_i<n\) and \(h_p=1\), such that standard Shellsort with these increments uses at most \(Cn\log n\) key comparisons on average over a uniformly random permutation of \([n]\), for one absolute constant \(C\)? The list may depend on \(n\) but not on the input permutation.
definitions:
The array has positions \(0,\ldots,n-1\) and contains distinct keys of ranks \(1,\ldots,n\). At a pass with increment \(h\), split positions into residue classes modulo \(h\). In each residue class, process entries from left to right by ordinary insertion sort: compare the key being inserted with preceding keys, shift larger keys one position right in that subsequence, and stop at the first preceding key no larger than it or at the beginning. Count every actual comparison between two keys, including the final unsuccessful comparison when it occurs. Index and loop-bound tests are not key comparisons.

Passes execute in the prescribed order. The terminal increment one guarantees sorting for every input. The definition permits any fixed list of valid increments, not an input-dependent choice or randomized compare-exchange pattern. No monotone-decreasing restriction is silently added to the imported question. A sequence with redundant passes still pays for all their comparisons.

Let \(C(h,\pi)\) be the total number of key comparisons on permutation \(\pi\). The requested bound is \(n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}C(h^{(n)},\pi)\le Cn\log n\) for all sufficiently large \(n\); changing the logarithm base changes only the constant. This is a comparison-count existence question, with increments prescribed independently for each size. It imposes no separate bound on computing or describing those increments, and does not claim an overall RAM-time bound that includes generating them.

The input distribution is uniform over all rank permutations, not a random gap list or independent continuous key magnitudes with ties. Average-case success here is a bound on work: standard Shellsort still sorts every permutation exactly.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such a family of increment lists exists and has the stated uniform expectation bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation. A randomized modification of Shellsort, a bound on a restricted input distribution, or empirical comparison counts do not settle this deterministic-increment question. A lower bound for a single proposed sequence does not exclude all families.

title: Asymptotic random-order ratio of Best Fit bin packing
summary: An adversary fixes item sizes and a uniformly random permutation determines their arrival. Best Fit places each item into the fullest bin that can hold it. The target is its worst expected ratio in the limit of large optimal bin count. The checked 2024 bounds leave a substantial gap between 1.144 and a value just below 1.5. Determining the ratio measures how much random arrival order improves this widely used heuristic.
formal: Determine the asymptotic random-order ratio \[R_{\mathrm{BF}}=\lim_{M\to\infty}\sup_{I:\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge M}\frac{\mathbb E_{\pi}[\mathrm{BF}(I^\pi)]}{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}\] of the Best Fit bin-packing algorithm. Benchmark acceptance requires absolute error at most \(1/100\) in this dimensionless constant; exact determination also qualifies.
definitions:
An instance \(I=(s_1,\ldots,s_N)\) is any finite nonempty labelled list of real item sizes in \((0,1]\). A bin has capacity one. A packing assigns every item to a bin with total assigned size at most one, and \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is the minimum number of nonempty bins over all packings. There is no bound on the number of distinct sizes or a positive lower bound on the smallest size.

Best Fit starts with no bins. For an arriving item of size \(s\), among all existing bins of load at most \(1-s\), it selects one of maximum load and puts the item there. It opens a new bin only if none can accommodate the item. Equal-load ties are broken by the bin's creation order, earliest first. Items are never moved afterward. \(\mathrm{BF}(I^\pi)\) is the final bin count when labels arrive in the order specified by \(\pi\), uniformly distributed over all \(N!\) permutations. Repeated sizes still have distinct labels. The only randomness is this permutation; the adversary fixes the entire list before it is sampled.

For every positive integer \(M\), the supremum ranges over lists of arbitrary length whose optimal bin count is at least \(M\). These tail suprema are nonincreasing and bounded, so the displayed limit is well defined. Equivalently it is the limsup, as \(m\to\infty\), of the largest expected ratio among instances with optimum exactly \(m\). It is not the supremum over all finite optimum sizes: that latter absolute random-order ratio can differ. Nor is it the ratio of two expectations over independently sampled item sizes. Expectations here condition on a fixed adversarial multiset, whose optimum is deterministic.

The scientific target is the asymptotic constant, with vanishing additive effects measured relative to the optimal bin count. The numerical benchmark tolerance is an acceptance rule for that constant, not a multiplicative relaxation of the packing algorithm or a proof of an exact conjectured value.
answer_criterion: Supply a mathematically specified real number \(a\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|a-R_{\mathrm{BF}}|\le1/100\). A proved interval of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies by its midpoint, and an exact value qualifies. Write \(r(I)=\mathbb E_\pi[\mathrm{BF}(I^\pi)]/\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). An upper bound \(U\) must cover every sufficiently large optimum: for every \(\eta>0\) there is an \(M\) such that \(r(I)\le U+\eta\) whenever \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge M\). For a lower bound \(L\), for every \(\eta>0\) and integer \(M\ge1\) it suffices to exhibit a list with \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge M\) and \(r(I)\ge L-\eta\). Experiments, a distribution-specific ratio, an absolute-ratio example with bounded optimum, or a certified interval wider than the stated tolerance are insufficient.

title: Rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics with \(\Delta +2\) colours
summary: The question concerns a local Markov chain that recolours one vertex uniformly from its currently available colours. It asks for one polynomial mixing bound for every graph and every palette with at least two more colours than the maximum degree. The stationary law is uniform on all proper labelled colourings and the bound must hold from the worst initial colouring. Known general-graph and recent near-threshold results retain larger palette slack, structural assumptions or parameter-dependent qualifications. Resolving the uniform additive-threshold conjecture would clarify the power of elementary local sampling for constrained spin systems.
formal: Are there absolute constants \(C,c>0\) such that for every finite simple undirected graph \(G\) with \(n\ge1\) vertices and maximum degree \(\Delta\), and every integer \(q\ge\Delta+2\), the single-vertex heat-bath Glauber chain on proper labelled \(q\)-colourings satisfies \[t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le Cn^c?\] The constants must be independent of the graph, its degree and the number of colours. This retains the previously selected degree-uniform polynomial target; the time unit is one vertex update, not a sweep or a bit operation.
definitions:
Let \(V(G)=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E(G)\) be a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops or parallel edges. Set \(N_G(v)=\{u:\{u,v\}\in E(G)\}\) and \(\Delta=\max_v|N_G(v)|\). The state space is \[\Omega_{G,q}=\{\sigma:[n]\to[q]:\sigma(u)\ne\sigma(v)\text{ for every }\{u,v\}\in E(G)\},\] where \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\). Colours are labelled and may be unused. There is no constraint on colour-class sizes, and no prescribed partial colouring or vertex-specific list. The state space is nonempty for the stated colour range.

At each discrete step, choose \(v\) uniformly from \([n]\). Given the current state \(\sigma\), form the available set \[A_\sigma(v)=[q]\setminus\{\sigma(u):u\in N_G(v)\}.\] Choose a colour uniformly from \(A_\sigma(v)\), assign it to \(v\), and leave every other vertex unchanged. The set has at least \(q-\Delta\ge2\) elements and includes the current colour; staying in the same colouring is allowed. The choices at successive steps are made from these conditional distributions. Let \(P\) be the resulting finite stochastic matrix and let \(P^t(\sigma,\tau)\) be its \(t\)-step transition probabilities, with \(P^0\) the identity matrix. The chain is reversible with respect to \(\pi(\sigma)=1/|\Omega_{G,q}|\), the uniform law on all proper labelled colourings. In this range it is irreducible and has self-loops, so that this stationary law is approached from every state.

Use [worst-start total variation mixing time](definitions.html#probability-distance) at tolerance \(1/4\), over every proper initial colouring. Denote it by \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\). The chain is ergodic in the stated range.

A step updates one vertex. No factor of \(n\) is absorbed into the time unit, and uniform sampling from a potentially large colour set is part of the mathematical transition rule. Thus the statement concerns the convergence rate of a specified chain, not an implementation bound polynomial only in \(n\) for operations on \(\log q\)-bit colour names. If a graph is encoded for formalization, use its explicit vertex and edge lists and the binary integer \(q\); no succinct graph representation is intended.

The bound is simultaneous for all finite degrees and all \(q\ge\Delta+2\), including \(q\) unbounded as a function of \(n\). A theorem of the form \(C_{\Delta,q}n^{c_{\Delta,q}}\) for each fixed pair of parameters does not automatically meet it. No girth, treewidth, chordality, planarity, expansion or random-graph assumption is imposed. Girth is the shortest cycle length, with infinity for a forest. A fixed multiplicative slack \(q\ge(1+\delta)\Delta\), with \(\delta>0\), does not cover \(q=\Delta+2\) uniformly as \(\Delta\) increases.

The heat-bath convention differs from proposing a uniformly random colour from all \([q]\) and rejecting a conflict, often also called Glauber or Metropolis dynamics. In the heat-bath chain, every proposed colour is available; in the latter chain, unsuccessful proposals contribute further holding probability. Flip dynamics can recolour an entire two-colour component and is a third chain. Related results must retain their update convention and comparison costs. The present question fixes the heat-bath chain exactly.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed uniform polynomial bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its failure. An affirmative proof must supply absolute \(C,c\) working for every graph, degree, colour count and initial proper colouring in the definition. A negative answer must show that for every proposed \(C,c\) there are eligible \(n,G,q\) with \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)>Cn^c\); one slow instance does not refute every polynomial. Polynomial mixing only for each fixed degree with an uncontrolled exponent, larger multiplicative palette slack, restricted graphs, a different dynamics, or an unspecified faster sampler is not the required bound. This is an exact asymptotic proposition about the specified chain, not a request to approximate a finite mixing time to the numerical benchmark tolerance.

title: Polynomial mixing of critical three-dimensional Ising dynamics
summary: This question concerns local heat-bath sampling of the Ising model at the critical point of the infinite cubic lattice. The finite system is a three-dimensional box with free boundaries and zero external field. It asks whether every initial spin configuration becomes close to equilibrium after polynomially many individual updates. The critical inverse temperature is specified by the infinite-volume magnetization threshold, without relying on a numerical estimate. Known critical results in other dimensions and at the regular-tree threshold do not settle this three-dimensional lattice problem.
formal:
For the zero-field nearest-neighbor ferromagnetic Ising model on the three-dimensional box \(V_L=\{1,\ldots,L\}^{3}\) with free boundary conditions, at the infinite-lattice critical inverse temperature \(\beta_c(\mathbb Z^3)\) defined below, is the worst-initial-state total-variation mixing time of random-site heat-bath dynamics polynomial in \(L\)? Precisely, do there exist constants \(C,a>0\) such that
\[\forall L\in\mathbb N,\ L\ge1,\qquad t_{\mathrm{mix}}(L,1/4)\le C(L+1)^a?\]
Time is counted in individual site-update attempts. The critical parameter is fixed independently of \(L\), and the target is the exact critical point, not a subcritical parameter approaching it at an unspecified rate.
definitions:
Let \(E_L\) contain each unordered pair of vertices of \(V_L\) at lattice distance \(\|u-v\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{3}|u_i-v_i|=1\), once. A configuration is \(\sigma\in\Omega_L=\{-1,+1\}^{V_L}\). At inverse temperature \(\beta\ge0\), the Gibbs probability is
\[\pi_{L,\beta}(\sigma)=Z_{L,\beta}^{-1}\exp\!\left(\beta\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E_L}\sigma_u\sigma_v\right),\]
where \(Z_{L,\beta}\) is the sum of the displayed weight over all configurations. Each interaction strength is one, there is no external magnetic field, and free boundary means there are no interactions with vertices outside \(V_L\). Boundary vertices inside the box are updated just like other vertices.

To specify the critical inverse temperature without a numerical approximation, let \(B_R=\{-R,\ldots,R\}^{3}\subset\mathbb Z^3\), for integers \(R\ge1\). Define \(\mu^+_{R,\beta}\) on spins in \(B_R\) by fixing all neighboring exterior spins to \(+1\): its weight is proportional to
\[\exp\!\left(\beta\left[\sum_{\substack{\{u,v\}\subset B_R\\\|u-v\|_1=1}}\sigma_u\sigma_v+\sum_{\substack{u\in B_R,\ v\notin B_R\\\|u-v\|_1=1}}\sigma_u\right]\right).\]
Internal unordered edges and crossing edges are each counted once. Set
\[m_+(\beta)=\inf_{R\ge1}\mathbb E_{\mu^+_{R,\beta}}[\sigma_0],\qquad\beta_c(\mathbb Z^3)=\inf\{\beta\ge0:m_+(\beta)>0\}.\]
The monotone limit of finite-volume plus-boundary magnetizations gives this standard infinite-lattice critical value, which is finite and positive. Plus boundaries are used only in defining the infinite-volume threshold; the finite chain being tested has free boundaries.

In one discrete step, choose a vertex \(v\) uniformly from the \(L^3\) sites, independently of previous choices. With \(h_v(\sigma)=\sum_{u:\{u,v\}\in E_L}\sigma_u\), redraw its spin as \(+1\) with probability
\[\frac{\exp(\beta h_v(\sigma))}{\exp(\beta h_v(\sigma))+\exp(-\beta h_v(\sigma))},\]
and as \(-1\) otherwise, leaving all other spins unchanged. Choosing its existing value still counts as one step. Set \(\beta=\beta_c(\mathbb Z^3)\) and denote the resulting transition matrix by \(P_L\). This finite chain is irreducible and aperiodic and has stationary measure \(\pi_L=\pi_{L,\beta_c}\).

Use [worst-start total variation mixing time](definitions.html#probability-distance) at tolerance \(1/4\) for \(P_L\) with law \(\pi_L\), from every initial spin configuration. One step is one site update. A continuous-time clock of rate one per site has a different normalization. The target concerns the defined transition law with its exact probabilities.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the polynomial mixing bound or its negation for this exact model. A positive proof must establish finite constants independent of \(L\), with the critical parameter, free boundaries, update rule, worst initial state and distance threshold specified here. A negative proof must show that no fixed polynomial bounds this sequence of mixing times. Results at a tree threshold, in another lattice dimension, below criticality, with different boundaries or from a restricted initialization do not meet the criterion.

title: Kannan–Tetali–Vempala conjecture
summary: The lazy switch chain samples binary matrices while preserving every row and column sum. Each attempted move chooses a two-by-two rectangle and may exchange its two checkerboard patterns. The target is polynomial convergence to the uniform distribution for every feasible choice of margins and every starting matrix. Fu, Qin and Wang’s July 2026 preprint states an explicit bound meeting this target and supplies a Lean formalization. The card records that claimed resolution with uncertain status because its proof and formalization were not independently verified here.
formal: Do universal constants \(K,c>0\) exist such that, for all \(r,s\ge 1\) and all nonnegative integer margins \(a\in \mathbb{N} ^{r},b\in \mathbb{N} ^{s}\) with a nonempty realization set \(\Omega (a,b)\), the lazy switch chain below satisfies \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le K(r+s)^{c}\)?
definitions: For integers \(r,s\ge1\), let \(a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{r}\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{s}\). The promised nonempty set \(\Omega(a,b)\) consists of binary matrices \(M\in\{0,1\}^{r\times s}\) with row sums \(a_i\) and column sums \(b_j\). At each attempted transition independently, stay with probability \(1/2\). Otherwise choose an unordered pair of distinct rows uniformly and an unordered pair of distinct columns uniformly and independently. If their rectangle has either alternating pattern \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) or \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), replace it by the other; otherwise stay. If \(r<2\) or \(s<2\), the state space is a singleton and the chain stays. Let \(P\) be the transition matrix and \(\pi\) the uniform distribution on \(\Omega(a,b)\). For an integer \(t\ge0\), define \(d(t)=\max_{M\in\Omega(a,b)}\frac12\sum_{N\in\Omega(a,b)}|P^t(M,N)-1/|\Omega(a,b)||\). Let \(t_{\rm mix}(1/4)=\min\{t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:d(t)\le1/4\}\), or \(+\infty\) if this set is empty. Time counts attempted transitions, including holds. The polynomial bound must use the same constants for every dimension and feasible pair of margins, without density, regularity or balance assumptions. This is a mathematical mixing-time question, with no requirement on bit complexity or implementation of a sampler.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that universal constants \(K,c>0\) bound the specified worst-case mixing time by \(K(r+s)^c\) for every nonempty binary-margin state space, or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every such pair of constants there are feasible dimensions and margins violating that bound. The theorem must concern the exact lazy chain and every starting matrix defined here.

title: Cutoff for bounded-degree transitive expanders
summary: Expander graphs are sparse graphs on which random walks mix rapidly. This question asks whether vertex symmetry forces a sharp transition to equilibrium in every bounded-degree expander sequence. The model uses a lazy walk, a uniformly positive spectral gap and graph sizes tending to infinity. Cutoff requires the mixing times at any two fixed total-variation accuracy levels to become asymptotically equal. The checked Ramanujan theorem covers a special spectral regime, while the 2025 source retains the general conjecture.
formal:
Does every sequence of bounded-degree vertex-transitive expander graphs exhibit total-variation cutoff for lazy simple random walk? More precisely, consider any sequence \((G_k)_{k\ge1}\) of finite connected undirected simple graphs, with \(N_k=|V(G_k)|\to\infty\). Assume each \(G_k\) is vertex-transitive, that there is a fixed integer \(D\ge3\) with \(3\le d_k\le D\) for its vertex degree \(d_k\), and that the lazy-walk spectral gaps satisfy \(\gamma_k\ge\delta\) for some constant \(\delta>0\) independent of \(k\). Must
\[\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1/2),\qquad\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{t_k(\varepsilon)}{t_k(1-\varepsilon)}=1?\]
The transition rule and worst-start mixing times \(t_k\) are defined below. The constants \(D\) and \(\delta\) may depend on the sequence. No quantitative cutoff window or common leading constant for different sequences is demanded.
definitions:
A simple graph has no loops or parallel edges. Vertex-transitive means that for any vertices \(x,y\) there is a bijection of the vertex set preserving adjacency in both directions and mapping \(x\) to \(y\). Consequently all its vertices have the same degree \(d_k\). The graph sequence is deterministic and need not come from a particular construction or a random-graph model.

One lazy-walk step stays at the current vertex with probability \(1/2\), and otherwise chooses a neighbor uniformly and moves there. Its transition matrix is
\[P_k(x,y)=\begin{cases}1/2&y=x,\\1/(2d_k)&\{x,y\}\in E(G_k),\\0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]
The stationary probability is \(\pi_k(y)=1/N_k\). List the real eigenvalues in decreasing order as \(1=\lambda_{1,k}>\lambda_{2,k}\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_{N_k,k}\ge0\), and set \(\gamma_k=1-\lambda_{2,k}\). A uniformly positive lower bound on \(\gamma_k\), together with bounded degree, is the expander assumption used here. Laziness includes bipartite graphs without periodicity problems.

At an integer time \(t\ge0\), let
\[d_k(t)=\max_{x\in V(G_k)}\frac12\sum_{y\in V(G_k)}\left|P_k^t(x,y)-\frac1{N_k}\right|,\qquad t_k(\eta)=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:d_k(t)\le\eta\}\quad(0<\eta<1).\]
The maximum is over every starting vertex. Times count discrete lazy steps, including steps that stay put. For a fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), the denominator \(t_k(1-\varepsilon)\) is positive for all sufficiently large \(k\); the limit uses this eventual tail. The displayed ratio condition defines total-variation cutoff. It asks that the transition between distance near one and distance near zero occupy a vanishing fraction of the mixing time.

The source first states the question with one fixed degree. Allowing degree to vary in a fixed finite range is equivalent at the level of this universal conjecture: each degree occurring infinitely often gives a fixed-degree subsequence. Neither degrees growing without bound nor expansion constants tending to zero are admitted.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that every sequence satisfying the hypotheses has the displayed cutoff property, or a Lean-checked refutation. A negative answer must establish a sequence satisfying every hypothesis for which the ratio limit fails for at least one fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\). A single finite graph cannot refute an asymptotic cutoff statement. Logarithmic mixing-time bounds alone, cutoff in a different distance, or a result only for a special class of expanders do not meet the criterion.

title: Stationary-start cover-time lower bound
summary: Start a finite reversible chain in its stationary distribution. Count transitions until every state has been seen. The proposed lower bound equals the complete-graph walk value. Self-loops and periodic chains are included. The exact inequality is stronger than a leading-order asymptotic bound.
formal: For every finite irreducible reversible discrete-time Markov chain on \(n\ge2\) states started in stationarity, does its cover time \(C\) satisfy \[\mathbb E_\pi[C]\ge(n-1)\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\frac1j\,?\]
definitions:
The transition matrix \(P\) has nonnegative real entries and each row sums to one. Irreducibility means that for every \(i,j\) there is \(t\ge0\) with \((P^t)_{ij}>0\). Its unique stationary distribution \(\pi\) has positive entries and satisfies \(\pi P=\pi\). Reversibility requires \(\pi_i P_{ij}=\pi_j P_{ji}\). Self-loops and periodic chains are allowed.

Draw \(X_0\sim\pi\) and evolve using \(P\). The cover time \(C=\min\{t\ge0:\{X_0,\ldots,X_t\}=\{1,\ldots,n\}\}\) counts transitions. The initial state counts as visited at time zero, and the expectation includes the choice of \(X_0\). The bound is required at each finite \(n\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated proposition or its negation for the specified model.

title: A single hard-core uniqueness threshold on the square lattice
summary: Occupied lattice vertices may not be adjacent. Activity weights configurations by the number of occupied sites. Infinite-volume laws are specified through all finite conditional distributions. The chosen question asks for one threshold separating uniqueness and coexistence. It leaves behavior exactly at the threshold and its numerical value outside this card.
formal: Is there a finite \(\lambda_c>0\) such that the hard-core model on \(\mathbb Z^2\) has a unique Gibbs measure for every \(0<\lambda<\lambda_c\) and more than one for every \(\lambda>\lambda_c\)?
definitions:
Join vertices of \(\mathbb Z^2\) at Manhattan distance one. A configuration \(\eta\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z^2}\) is admissible if adjacent vertices are never both occupied. Given a finite \(\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^2\) and an admissible exterior configuration \(\tau\), assign each compatible interior configuration \(\xi\) probability \(\lambda^{\sum_{v\in\Lambda}\xi(v)}/Z_{\Lambda,\tau}\), where the normalizing factor sums these weights. Incompatible configurations have probability zero.

A Gibbs measure is supported on admissible configurations and has these conditional laws almost surely for every finite \(\Lambda\). Uniqueness and multiplicity range over all Gibbs measures, including measures without translation invariance. The question leaves behavior at \(\lambda=\lambda_c\) open and asks only for existence of the threshold.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated proposition or its negation for the specified model. A numerical estimate of a candidate transition point, or separated small-activity and large-activity theorems, does not establish the single-threshold statement.

title: Polynomial mixing of the self-avoiding-walk pivot chain
