summary: A self-avoiding lattice walk never visits the same vertex twice. A pivot step rotates or reflects a suffix and rejects self-intersecting proposals. The question asks whether this chain reaches its uniform stationary distribution in polynomially many attempted pivots. The mixing guarantee is from every starting walk. Fast implementation of one pivot does not itself prove a mixing bound.
formal: Do there exist constants \(C>0\) and \(a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that \[t_{\mathrm{pivot}}(n)\le Cn^a\qquad\text{for every integer }n\ge1?\] The chain below acts on rooted \(n\)-step self-avoiding walks in the square lattice, uses the five specified pivot symmetries, and counts every attempted pivot including rejection. Mixing means total-variation distance at most \(1/4\) from the uniform law, from every starting walk.
definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge1\), the finite state space \(\Omega_n\) consists of sequences \(\omega=(\omega_0,\ldots,\omega_n)\) in \(\mathbb Z^2\) such that \(\omega_0=(0,0)\), \(\|\omega_{i+1}-\omega_i\|_1=1\) for \(0\le i<n\), and \(\omega_i\ne\omega_j\) whenever \(i\ne j\). Here \(\|(x,y)\|_1=|x|+|y|\). Walks are ordered, rooted at the origin and not identified under rotation, reflection or reversal. There is no confining box or additional energy weight. Let \(\pi_n\) give equal probability \(1/|\Omega_n|\) to each walk.

In one step independently choose \(k\) uniformly from \(\{0,\ldots,n\}\) and \(S\) uniformly from these five maps:
\[(x,y)\mapsto(y,-x),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(-y,x),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(-x,y).\]
These are the three nontrivial quarter-turn rotations and the two coordinate-axis reflections in Example B.5. Propose
\[\omega'_i=\begin{cases}\omega_i&i\le k,\\\omega_k+S(\omega_i-\omega_k)&i>k.\end{cases}\]
If the proposal belongs to \(\Omega_n\), accept it; otherwise keep \(\omega\). In either case the time increases by one. Fresh choices are independent at subsequent steps. In particular \(k=n\) always leaves the walk unchanged. Denote this transition matrix by \(P_n\).

The proposal maps occur with the same probabilities as their inverses, so the chain is reversible for \(\pi_n\). The irreducibility established in the source, together with the positive holding probability, gives a unique stationary law and convergence to it. Write \(t_{\mathrm{pivot}}(n)\) for the [worst-start total variation mixing time](definitions.html#probability-distance) of \(P_n\) at tolerance \(1/4\), over every walk in \(\Omega_n\).

The clock counts proposals rather than CPU operations or accepted pivots. Testing whether a proposed walk intersects itself is part of implementing a transition, but its computational cost is not multiplied into this mathematical mixing time. The textbook’s instruction to repeat after rejection is interpreted as proceeding to the next proposal with the old state retained, as explicitly specified in Clisby’s standard pivot dynamics. Discarding all rejected attempts from the clock would define a different chain and is not the convention here.
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that the worst-start mixing time of the specified pivot chain is bounded by one polynomial in the walk length, or prove that every such bound fails. Count rejected pivots as steps when establishing either result.

title: Weakly negatively regressive sampling of matroid bases
summary: The problem asks for efficient sampling of a matroid basis with any prescribed rational point of the base polytope as its exact marginal vector. The output law must satisfy weak negative regression for every increasing function of all coordinates except one. The chosen model uses an independence oracle and a uniform exact sampler with expected polynomial bit complexity. This dependence property implies favorable submodular expectations and supports known concentration guarantees. A reported gap in an older general-matroid claim remains acknowledged in the 2026 literature, while newer special-case rounding results do not settle this target.
formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm which, for every finite matroid \(M\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) given by an independence oracle and every rational point \(p\) of its base polytope, samples a basis \(B\) with exact marginals
\[\Pr[i\in B]=p_i\quad(i\in[n])\]
and a weakly negatively regressive output distribution, in expected time polynomial in \(n\) and the binary encoding length of \(p\)?

Here weak negative regression (WNR) requires, simultaneously for every \(i\in[n]\) and every increasing function \(f:2^{[n]\setminus\{i\}}\to\mathbb R\),
\[\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{\{i\in B\}} f(B\setminus\{i\})]\le p_i\,\mathbb E[f(B\setminus\{i\})].\]
The algorithm receives no objective function \(f\). One output law must satisfy all these inequalities.

This card selects WNR, the weakest of the three alternative dependence requirements in the source question. Negative association or negative regression would also suffice by implying WNR. The independence-oracle, rational-input and exact expected-time sampling conventions below make the source's efficiency question precise; they are explicit editorial conventions.
definitions:
A matroid \(M=([n],\mathcal I)\), with \(n\ge1\), consists of a nonempty family \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^{[n]}\) of independent sets. If \(A\in\mathcal I\) and \(A'\subseteq A\), then \(A'\in\mathcal I\). If \(A,D\in\mathcal I\) and \(|A|<|D|\), some \(e\in D\setminus A\) has \(A\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). A basis is an inclusion-maximal member of \(\mathcal I\); all bases have the same cardinality. Let \(\mathcal B(M)\) be their family, including the singleton family containing the empty set for a rank-zero matroid.

The base polytope is
\[P_B(M)=\left\{\sum_{B\in\mathcal B(M)}\lambda_B\mathbf 1_B:\lambda_B\ge0,\ \sum_B\lambda_B=1\right\},\]
where \(\mathbf 1_B\in\{0,1\}^n\) is the incidence vector. This is the convex hull of bases, as specified by the source's maximal-independent-set convention. It is distinct from the convex hull of all independent sets.

An oracle query supplies an \(n\)-bit incidence vector for a set \(A\) and receives the exact bit indicating whether \(A\in\mathcal I\). The oracle is fixed throughout a run and is promised to describe a matroid. The input gives \(n\) in binary and \(p_i=a_i/b_i\), with binary integers \(0\le a_i\le b_i\) and \(b_i\ge1\). Let \(L\) be their total encoding length. The promise is \(p\in P_B(M)\); membership testing is not an additional required output. A convex decomposition of \(p\), an explicit list of bases and a sampling oracle are not supplied.

Use a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with this independence oracle and independent fair random bits. All ordinary bit operations, random-bit generation, oracle-query preparation and output writing count toward time; obtaining the answer to a completed oracle query costs one additional step. There must be fixed constants \(C,d\) such that expected total work is at most \(C(n+L+1)^d\) on every promised input and every matroid oracle. These constants and the machine are independent of the instance. No arbitrary real-arithmetic operations or nonuniform advice are available.

The machine must halt with probability one, and every terminating run must output the incidence vector of a basis. Its probability law over outputs must have the exact stated marginals and satisfy WNR without an additive tolerance. There is no failure output or exceptional probability on which feasibility or the distributional guarantees may fail. Expected time permits exact sampling with rational probabilities whose denominators are not powers of two. Independent invocations use fresh random bits; a joint coupling across different inputs is not required.

Increasing means \(f(A)\le f(D)\) whenever \(A\subseteq D\). The domain is finite, so each real-valued \(f\) has finite expectation. For \(0<p_i<1\), the displayed WNR inequality is equivalent to
\[\mathbb E[f(B\setminus\{i\})\mid i\in B]\le\mathbb E[f(B\setminus\{i\})\mid i\notin B].\]
For \(p_i=0\) or \(p_i=1\), the unconditional inequality is automatically an equality and does not invoke undefined conditional probabilities. WNR concerns all increasing functions of the remaining coordinates, not just pairwise covariances or linear functions.

For context, a set function \(F:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) is submodular when \(F(A)+F(D)\ge F(A\cup D)+F(A\cap D)\) for all sets \(A,D\). Submodular dominance at marginals \(p\) means \(\mathbb E[F(B)]\ge\mathbb E[F(R_p)]\) for every such \(F\), where \(R_p\) includes each element independently with probability \(p_i\). This consequence of WNR is not a substitute for the stronger specified distributional target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence statement in the declared oracle and bit-computation model. A positive answer must establish one uniform sampler, exact feasibility and marginals, all WNR inequalities, almost-sure termination and the expected polynomial resource bound for every promised input. A negative answer must prove that no such sampler exists; it need not show that a WNR law is nonexistent for any individual input. A theorem that only supplies a distribution nonconstructively, approximate marginals, pairwise negative correlation, submodular dominance, or a sampler for a restricted class of matroids does not by itself meet the full criterion.

title: Exact uniform spanning-tree sampling in linear time
summary: The input is any connected unweighted graph. Every spanning tree must have exactly the same output probability. The desired expected runtime is linear in the number of edges. Almost-linear exact sampling is known, but does not meet strict linear time. The card charges all preprocessing and permits no statistical approximation.
formal: Is there a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every connected simple unweighted undirected graph G with m edges, outputs an exactly uniform spanning tree in expected \(O(m)\) total time?
definitions:
The graph has n≥1 labelled vertices and is supplied by adjacency lists with every undirected edge represented at both endpoints. For n=1 the algorithm returns the empty tree in O(1) time; the asymptotic bound is O(m+1). A spanning tree is an acyclic connected subset of n−1 input edges. Let T(G) be the finite set of all such subsets. Exact uniformity means that for every H∈T(G), the output probability equals 1/|T(G)|.

Use a uniform word RAM with word width \(w=\Theta(\log(n+2))\) large enough for graph addresses. Use the [integer word instructions](definitions.html#ram) at width \(w\). A fresh independent uniform word costs one step. Unbounded exact real arithmetic is unavailable. The algorithm terminates almost surely, always returns a valid spanning tree, and has expected cost at most C(m+1) on each fixed input, for one absolute C. Reading or transforming the graph, preprocessing, random-number generation and writing all tree edges are charged. Rejection sampling is allowed and its work is counted. There is no total-variation tolerance, failure symbol or conditioning on successful runs in the output specification. Weighted graphs are outside this card’s target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked sampler with proofs of exact uniformity, almost-sure termination and the expected linear bound, or a complete impossibility proof in this model. An almost-linear m^(1+o(1)) runtime is insufficient. A distribution within small total variation distance is also insufficient, even if its computational bound is linear.

title: Deterministic approximation scheme for graph cover times
summary: The cover time is the expected number of random-walk steps needed to visit every vertex. This card asks for a deterministic approximation scheme from any specified starting vertex of an arbitrary connected graph. For each fixed relative accuracy, the runtime must be polynomial in graph size. The original source asks for approximation, so the imported demand for exact output has been corrected. Known constant-factor and restricted-family results do not provide the full all-graph guarantee stated here.
formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time approximation scheme for the expected cover time of simple random walk from a specified starting vertex of an arbitrary finite connected undirected simple graph? Specifically, does there exist one deterministic algorithm \(A\) such that, for every integer \(q\ge2\), there are constants \(C_q,a_q>0\) for which every allowed \(n\)-vertex input \((G,v,q)\) is processed within \(C_q(n+1)^{a_q}\) bit operations and the output rational number \(\widehat C\ge0\) satisfies
\[\left|\widehat C-C(G,v)\right|\le\frac{C(G,v)}q?\]
Here \(C(G,v)\) is defined below. The runtime is polynomial in graph size for every fixed accuracy \(1/q\); its exponent may depend on \(q\). This restores the relative-approximation question actually stated by Aldous and Fill, rather than the unsupported exact-output wording in the imported draft.
definitions:
The input graph has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(n\ge1\), and no loops, parallel edges or edge weights. It is promised connected. Its encoding consists of \(n\) in unary followed by its \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix, a binary starting label \(v\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and the integer accuracy parameter \(q\ge2\) in binary, with standard self-delimiting integer fields. All graph families and degrees are allowed; in particular there is no bounded-degree or rapid-mixing promise.

For \(n\ge2\), let \((X_t)_{t\ge0}\) be the discrete-time walk with \(X_0=v\). At each step it independently chooses a uniformly random neighbor of its current vertex. It has no added holding probability. Define
\[\tau_{\mathrm{cov}}=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:\{X_0,\ldots,X_t\}=V(G)\},\qquad C(G,v)=\mathbb E_v[\tau_{\mathrm{cov}}].\]
The initial vertex is already visited at time zero, and time counts edge traversals. There is no requirement to return to \(v\) after the last new vertex is visited. For \(n=1\), put \(C(G,v)=0\). Connectedness guarantees finite expectation. The quantity \(\max_v C(G,v)\), often called the graph’s cover time, is related but is not substituted for the supplied-start expectation.

The algorithm is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine, with no random bits, advice or sampling oracle. Input processing, rational arithmetic and output writing count toward the runtime. Its output is a pair of binary integers representing a nonnegative rational with positive denominator. The required inequality holds for every input, not merely with high probability. When \(n=1\), it requires output zero.

The integer \(q\) represents reciprocal relative accuracy. This discretization covers any fixed requested \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) by taking \(q\ge\max\{2,1/\varepsilon\}\). The constants \(C_q,a_q\) are independent of the graph and the starting vertex. No polynomial dependence on \(q\) is demanded; that would be the stronger fully polynomial scheme. Nor is an exact numerator and denominator for the unknown expectation demanded.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that an algorithm with the displayed correctness and runtime guarantees exists, or a Lean-checked proof of the negation of that existence statement. A positive answer must work at arbitrarily fine fixed relative accuracy on every allowed graph and starting vertex. A constant-factor estimate, a randomized approximation, a theorem restricted to trees or a promise on hitting times, and a procedure that computes only the worst-start maximum do not establish the stated scheme. An exponential-time exact formula by itself does not establish the polynomial-time guarantee.

title: FPRAS for counting perfect matchings
summary: A perfect matching pairs every vertex of a graph with exactly one neighbor. The question asks for one randomized algorithm giving arbitrarily accurate relative estimates of their number on every finite unweighted simple graph. Its worst-case running time must be polynomial in the full input length and inverse accuracy, with success probability at least three quarters for each input. Bipartite perfect matchings and all matchings have approximation schemes, but the checked 2026 dense-graph and permanent results retain restrictions absent from this target. A complete Lean proof must establish such a uniform scheme with exact zero behavior or prove that no scheme meeting all requirements exists.
formal:
Does there exist one uniform probabilistic algorithm \(A\) and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, for every finite undirected simple graph \(G\) and every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), \(A(G,\varepsilon)\) halts on every random tape within
\[C\bigl(N+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+1\bigr)^{k}\]
Turing-machine steps and outputs a nonnegative rational \(\widehat Z\) satisfying
\[\Pr\bigl[(1-\varepsilon)Z(G)\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon)Z(G)\bigr]\ge\frac34?\]
Here \(Z(G)\) is the number of perfect matchings, \(N\) is the complete input bit length defined below, and, whenever \(Z(G)=0\), every run must output zero. This is the existence question for a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme on general unweighted graphs.
definitions:
For every integer \(n\ge0\), a graph has labeled vertex set \([n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and an arbitrary subset of the unordered pairs of distinct vertices as its edges. It has no loops, parallel edges or weights. A matching is a subset of edges with pairwise disjoint endpoints; it is perfect when every vertex is incident to exactly one of its edges. Each such edge set is counted once, regardless of order or orientation. Thus \(Z(G)\in\mathbb N\), an odd-order graph has count zero, and the empty graph has count one, from its empty matching. The domain includes disconnected graphs, isolated vertices, odd cycles and arbitrarily large degrees, with no bipartiteness, density, planarity, expansion, or existence promise.

Use the following explicit finite encoding. The graph is encoded by \(1^{n}0\) followed by one adjacency bit for each pair \(0\le i<j<n\), in lexicographic order. This includes the full vertex set even when there are no edges and is polynomially equivalent to an explicit vertex-and-edge list. Write \(\varepsilon=r/s\) in lowest terms with integers \(0<r<s\). Let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary expansion of a nonnegative integer, with \(b(0)=0\), and let \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Append \(E(r)E(s)\) to the graph encoding. The total length is \(N\); the numerical value of \(1/\varepsilon\), not just the length of its encoding, may enter the time bound. The output has the form \(E(u)E(v)\) with integers \(u\ge0,v\ge1\), meaning \(\widehat Z=u/v\); reduction to lowest terms is not required.

An algorithm is one finite multitape probabilistic Turing-machine program with a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes over fixed finite alphabets, and an output tape. Each ordinary transition and each newly requested independent fair bit costs one step. Its probability space is the infinite product of fair bits, and the clock bound must hold on every tape for every valid input. Reading, arithmetic, storage operations and writing the whole rational output are all charged. There is no advice, oracle, nonuniform dependence on the graph or accuracy, or unit-cost operation on unbounded integers. No guarantee is needed on malformed inputs. The same \(A,C,k\) must work for all graphs and all valid accuracies; success is per input and is not an average over a graph distribution.

The estimate has relative multiplicative error. In particular, an additive error guarantee on the raw count or on its logarithm is a different condition. Requiring deterministic zero output when no perfect matching exists is a harmless normalization of the usual FPRAS question because perfect-matching existence on general graphs is deterministically decidable in polynomial time. The probability \(3/4\) is fixed, and no random output is required to be an actual matching. This card asks whether the approximation algorithm exists; it does not ask for the numerical value of a fixed graph’s count at the catalogue’s default absolute tolerance.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition above or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a finite uniform algorithm and constants \(C,k\), and prove its every-random-tape clock, output encoding, exact zero behavior and per-input relative-error probability for every graph and rational accuracy. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm and every such polynomial bound; it need not consist of a single finite counterexample graph. Failure or slow mixing of a particular algorithm family does not prove that negation. A conditional impossibility theorem is only a conditional result unless its hypothesis is also proved. Exact exponential-time counting, constant-factor approximation without arbitrary requested accuracy, algorithms only for bipartite or dense graphs, and approximation of the total number of all matchings do not meet the target.

title: FP versus #P
summary: The question asks whether every polynomially verifiable witness count can be evaluated exactly in deterministic polynomial time. Witnesses are binary strings of a fixed polynomial length, and different witnesses retain their multiplicities. The exact count is output in binary, so even an exponentially large value needs only polynomially many output bits. An affirmative answer would imply P = NP, but efficient existence testing or relative approximation does not establish exact counting. A resolution would settle the basic computational boundary for counting satisfiability, permanents and all other functions in #P.
formal:
Is every function in \(\#\mathrm{P}\) computable exactly in deterministic polynomial time? With the numerical function convention defined below, the proposition is
\[\#\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N},\]
equivalently \(\#\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\). Each function may have its own fixed machine and polynomial running-time bound. The output is the exact nonnegative integer in binary.
definitions:
Write \(\{0,1\}^*\) for all finite binary strings, including the empty string, and \(|x|\) for their bit length. Natural numbers include zero. A polynomial witness bound is a fixed polynomial \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) with nonnegative integer coefficients; allowing any polynomial-time computable, polynomially bounded integer length gives the same class by unique zero padding. A verifier \(V(x,y)\) is a fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine returning a bit on every pair of strings within polynomially many bit steps in \(|x|+|y|\). The class \(\#\mathrm{P}\) consists of the total functions
\[f_{V,p}(x)=\left|\left\{y\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1\right\}\right|.\]
Each distinct witness string is counted once. If several witnesses describe the same combinatorial object, their multiplicity is retained. The witness length is exactly the displayed length; shorter witnesses are not additionally counted. Equivalently, these functions count accepting paths of polynomial-time nondeterministic machines with binary choices and an explicit machine convention preserving path counts.

The class \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\) consists of total functions from binary strings to nonnegative integers for which some deterministic multitape Turing machine outputs the canonical binary representation on every input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) bit steps. Here \(C,d\) are fixed positive integers, the representation of zero is the single bit 0, and positive outputs have no leading zeros. All computation and output writing are charged. Machines have finite programs, no advice and no oracle. No error probability or approximation is allowed. The constants and program may depend on the function but never on the input. There is no requirement of a common exponent or a uniform compiler taking arbitrary verifiers as input.

Every \(\#\mathrm{P}\) value is at most \(2^{p(|x|)}\), so its binary representation has at most \(p(|x|)+1\) bits. The question does not request output in unary, listing all witnesses, or a time bound polynomial in the value of the count. Conversely, if a numerical function has a polynomial-time exact algorithm, choose a polynomial \(q\) longer than its output bit bound and accept a \(q(|x|)\)-bit witness precisely when its numerical value is smaller than \(f(x)\). Exactly \(f(x)\) witnesses are accepted. Thus \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\subseteq\#\mathrm{P}\), which justifies writing equality rather than only the displayed inclusion. The source writes FP for this numerical interpretation of polynomial-time string functions.

For the comparisons below, \(\mathrm{P}\) is the class of languages decided by deterministic machines in polynomial time, and \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages of the form \(\{x:f_{V,p}(x)>0\}\). Use the shared definition of [PSPACE](definitions.html#space). A polynomial-time Turing reduction to a numerical function may make adaptively chosen exact queries, charging query writing and answer processing, while receiving the binary answer from its oracle. Counting completeness mentioned below uses this convention unless a stronger count-preserving reduction is stated.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(\#\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\), or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must supply existence of an exact uniform polynomial-time machine for every fixed verifier and witness bound; it suffices to solve an appropriately proved counting-complete problem exactly in polynomial time. A negative proof must establish a \(\#\mathrm{P}\) function admitting no such machine. A conditional separation assuming \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), a lower bound for one restricted algorithm, or an efficient relative approximation does not by itself settle the unconditional proposition. Computing only whether the count is zero is also insufficient.

title: Deterministic FPTAS for the nonnegative permanent
summary: The permanent of a nonnegative matrix sums the weights of all perfect matchings in its bipartite support graph. The question asks for one deterministic algorithm approximating this value to any requested relative accuracy on every nonnegative rational matrix. Its running time must be polynomial in the full binary input length and inverse accuracy, with a fixed exponent and exact output zero when the permanent is zero. Randomized approximation is established, while checked 2026 deterministic results have dimension-dependent error factors or fixed density and weight restrictions. A complete Lean proof must establish the unrestricted deterministic scheme or prove that none meets the stated guarantees.
formal:
Does there exist one finite deterministic algorithm \(D\) and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), every explicitly encoded matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}^{n\times n}\), and every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), \(D(A,\varepsilon)\) halts within
\[C\bigl(N+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+1\bigr)^{k}\]
Turing-machine steps and returns a nonnegative rational \(z\) satisfying
\[(1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{per}(A)\le z\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{per}(A)?\]
Here \(N\) is the full binary input length, and the permanent is defined below. The guarantee must hold on every input without randomness.
definitions:
Let \([n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and let \(S_{n}\) be the set of bijections from \([n]\) to itself. For a nonnegative rational matrix define
\[\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\pi\in S_{n}}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}A_{i,\pi(i)}.\]
Zero entries, zero rows, reducible matrices and arbitrarily large or small positive rational entries are permitted. There is no density, expansion, degree, rank, stochastic-scaling, or positive-entry lower-bound promise. This is the usual unsigned permutation sum, not the determinant or the hafnian. For a zero–one matrix it counts perfect matchings in the bipartite graph having one vertex for each row and each column, with an edge exactly where the entry is one. For a weighted matrix, each matching contributes the product of its edge weights.

For an integer \(t\ge0\), let \(b(t)\) be its ordinary binary expansion, with \(b(0)=0\), and set \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Encode \(n\) as \(E(n)\), then encode all \(n^{2}\) entries in row-major order. Each entry is a reduced pair \(u/v\), with integers \(u\ge0,v\ge1\), encoded by \(E(u)E(v)\). Encode \(\varepsilon=r/s\) in lowest terms, \(0<r<s\), by appending \(E(r)E(s)\). The length of this complete string is \(N\). It is not a succinct circuit or oracle description of a larger matrix. Output \(E(p)E(q)\), with \(p\ge0,q\ge1\), represents \(z=p/q\); the output need not be reduced.

Computation uses one finite deterministic multitape Turing machine, a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes over fixed finite alphabets and an output tape. Each transition costs one step, including all arithmetic, reading, writing, storage and output costs. There are no random bits, advice strings, oracles or unit-cost exact-real operations. The machine and the two clock constants are independent of the dimension, entries and requested accuracy. The exponent is fixed independently of \(\varepsilon\); polynomial dependence on the numerical value of \(1/\varepsilon\) is permitted in addition to dependence on its encoding length. No guarantee is required on malformed inputs.

The approximation is relative to the permanent itself, not additive relative to \(n!\), a matrix norm, or a rescaled quantity. Nonnegativity makes the permanent positive precisely when the positive-entry bipartite support graph has a perfect matching. Thus the zero case is deterministically recognizable in polynomial time, and the displayed inequality requires \(z=0\) exactly in that case. Arbitrarily small positive permanents must still receive the same relative guarantee. This is a genuine algorithm-existence question, not a numerical-value target at the catalogue’s absolute \(1/100\) tolerance.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify the finite deterministic machine and constants \(C,k\), and prove termination, the full bit-cost bound, the rational output and both inequalities for every valid nonnegative rational matrix and every valid accuracy. A negative answer must rule out every such machine and clock, rather than just one approximation formula or family of algorithms. A conditional lower bound remains conditional unless its hypothesis is also proved. A randomized FPRAS, a scheme restricted to positive dense matrices, a fixed dimension-dependent approximation factor, or running time \(n^{h(1/\varepsilon)}\) with an unbounded accuracy-dependent exponent does not qualify. Exact #P-hardness alone is not a negative answer: an exponentially small requested error may legitimately require exponential time under an FPTAS clock.
references: https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~sinclair/perm2.pdf | https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.02933v2 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26599v1 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28031v2 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31061v1 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10516v1 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04079v1

title: FP = #P from \(\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{NP}\)
summary: The question asks whether P = NP forces exact polynomial-time computation of every #P witness count. Each counting function has its own uniform deterministic machine, and its exact value must be output in binary. Finding one witness or approximating an exponential count to inverse-polynomial relative accuracy does not give its exact value. The literal negative answer would require P = NP together with a counting function outside numerical FP. A 2026 preprint claims the implication, but a directly checked internal defect prevents this review from accepting it as a resolution.
formal:
Does the following implication hold for ordinary uniform Turing computation?
\[\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\#\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}.\]
The conclusion means exact deterministic polynomial-time computation of every polynomially verifiable witness count, output as a binary nonnegative integer. Since \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\subseteq\#\mathrm{P}\) holds unconditionally, the conclusion is also written \(\#\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\).
definitions:
All language inputs are finite binary strings, of bit length \(n=|x|\). A deterministic polynomial-time machine has a finite program and halts on every input within \(C(n+1)^d\) steps of a multitape Turing machine, for fixed positive integers \(C,d\). Each tape read, write and head move is charged; writing an output is part of the bound. There is no advice, randomness or oracle. The program and constants may depend on the fixed problem, but not on the input. A language belongs to \(\mathrm{P}\) when such a machine outputs its exact membership bit.

For a fixed polynomial \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) with nonnegative integer coefficients and a deterministic verifier \(V(x,y)\) running in time polynomial in \(|x|+|y|\), put
\[W_{V,p}(x)=\{y\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1\},\qquad f_{V,p}(x)=|W_{V,p}(x)|.\]
The class \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages \(\{x:W_{V,p}(x)\ne\varnothing\}\). The class \(\#\mathrm{P}\) consists of the total numerical functions \(f_{V,p}\). The verifier is required to halt on every pair of binary strings. Witnesses have exactly the specified length; each distinct witness string contributes one, even when several describe the same object. The hypothesis \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) asserts equality of these language classes, with a separate polynomial-time decider permitted for each language.

The class \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\) consists of total functions from binary strings to \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) computed by deterministic polynomial-time machines under the same bit-cost convention. The output is the exact binary integer, with 0 represented by a single zero and no leading zeros for positive integers. Every \(\#\mathrm{P}\) function satisfies \(f_{V,p}(x)\leq2^{p(n)}\), so polynomially many output bits suffice. Conversely, a polynomial-time numerical function is in \(\#\mathrm{P}\): choose a fixed polynomial witness length longer than its output bound, regard witnesses as binary integers, and accept exactly those smaller than its value. This explains the numerical FP equality convention in the source.

In the conclusion the quantifiers are \(\forall V,p\ \exists M,C,d\ \forall x\): one exact counting program for every fixed witness-counting function. No common exponent or effective transformation from arbitrary existence deciders to counting machines is required. The proposition is an implication about these unrelativized classes. It does not assert that P = NP actually holds, introduce access to a SAT oracle, or restrict the algorithms to a specified proof technique.

The logical negation of the target is \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) together with \(\#\mathrm{P}\not\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\). In particular, a proof of \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) would prove the implication through its false antecedent, not refute it. Here and below exact computation differs from relative approximation: an approximation \(a\) with parameter \(0<\varepsilon<1\) need only satisfy \(|a-f(x)|\leq\varepsilon f(x)\), which forces \(a=0\) when the count is zero.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed implication, or of its logical negation. A direct affirmative proof may assume \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) and derive an exact deterministic polynomial-time counting machine for every fixed verifier; a proof of \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) also settles the literal implication affirmatively. A negative answer must establish both \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) and a \(\#\mathrm{P}\) function outside numerical FP. An oracle-relative counterexample, a limitation of one proposed reduction, or an error in a claimed affirmative proof does not establish that negation. Approximation, finding a single witness and time polynomial in the numerical count do not meet the exact-computation conclusion.

title: Deterministic relative counting for DNF
summary: A DNF formula describes a union of sets of Boolean assignments, one set for each conjunction. The question asks for deterministic relative approximation of the number of assignments in that union. One uniform algorithm must run in time polynomial in the explicit formula size and reciprocal error. The estimate must count assignments once despite overlapping terms and must be exactly zero for an unsatisfiable formula. Randomized schemes and deterministic algorithms for restricted formulas leave the general fully polynomial target unresolved in the checked sources.
formal:
Is there a deterministic fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for the number of satisfying assignments of an arbitrary explicitly given DNF formula? In the precise reciprocal-integer accuracy convention used here, do there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\) and positive integers \(C,a\) such that for every DNF formula \(\varphi\) of encoding length \(N\) over its declared \(n\) variables, and every integer \(q\ge2\), the algorithm outputs a nonnegative rational number \(\widehat Z\) with
\[|\widehat Z-Z(\varphi)|\le Z(\varphi)/q,\qquad Z(\varphi)=|\{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}:\varphi(x)=1\}|,\]
and halts within \(C(N+q+1)^a\) steps? The guarantee must hold on every input without randomness, advice or an oracle. There is no bound on term width or on the number of occurrences of a variable other than the explicit input length.
definitions:
A literal is a declared variable \(x_i\), \(1\le i\le n\), or its negation. A term is a finite conjunction of literals; a DNF formula is a finite disjunction of terms. All literal occurrences and all terms are listed explicitly. Empty conjunctions evaluate to true and the empty disjunction evaluates to false. Repeated literals or terms are allowed, and a term containing both signs of one variable is false. A variable assignment specifies every declared variable, including unused ones; every satisfying assignment is counted once regardless of how many terms it satisfies.

Use an explicit encoding consisting of \(1^n\), a self-delimiting binary term count, and for each term its self-delimiting literal count followed by variable indices in binary and one sign bit per literal. Thus the declared variable set is part of the input, \(n\le N\), and arbitrary circuits or compressed representations of an exponentially larger DNF are excluded. Valid formulas with \(n=0\) are included and are evaluated on the unique empty assignment. Malformed encodings may be rejected in polynomial time and are not counted as instances of the formula problem.

The accuracy parameter \(q\) is given in binary. Computation uses a fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine; one transition costs one step, and writing the output is counted. Represent \(\widehat Z\) by a binary nonnegative numerator and positive denominator. They need not be in lowest terms. The constants in the running-time bound are independent of the formula, its width, its variable occurrence counts and \(q\). All preprocessing is included.

The target is relative error \(1/q\). This is the usual fully polynomial accuracy convention: an arbitrary requested \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) can be met by taking \(q=\max\{2,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\}\), with the time to read that request also counted. The runtime is polynomial in the reciprocal accuracy, not merely its bit length. If \(Z=0\), the output must equal zero exactly. If \(Z>0\), it must lie between \((1-1/q)Z\) and \((1+1/q)Z\). Additive error \(2^n/q\) is a different and potentially much weaker guarantee when satisfying assignments are rare. The algorithm is allowed to output a rational estimate; exact integer counting is not required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence or nonexistence of this deterministic approximation scheme. A positive answer must specify the algorithm and prove its relative-error and fully polynomial-time guarantees for all formulas and all \(q\ge2\), including zero counts. A negative answer must rule out every such uniform deterministic scheme. Randomized high-probability estimates, an additive-error approximation alone, quasipolynomial runtime, or polynomial algorithms restricted to bounded-width or bounded-occurrence formulas do not settle the full target.

title: Output-polynomial hypergraph transversal enumeration
summary: A transversal meets every edge of a hypergraph and is minimal if removing any selected vertex destroys that property. The required algorithm lists all such sets exactly once and detects when enumeration is finished. Its total time must be polynomial in the combined input and complete output length. The output may be exponentially large, and no separate bound on delay is requested. A 2026 lower bound excludes a particular practical algorithm while leaving the existence of a general output-polynomial algorithm open.
formal: Do a deterministic Turing algorithm \(A\) and constants \(C,c>0\) exist such that, for every explicitly given finite hypergraph \(H\), \(A\) outputs every inclusion-minimal transversal exactly once and terminates within \(C(N(H)+N_{\mathrm{out}}(H)+1)^c\) bit steps? Here \(N(H)\) and \(N_{\mathrm{out}}(H)\) are the encoded input and total output lengths.
definitions: \(H=([n],E), n\ge 0\), is supplied as the explicit vertex list and a finite list of edges \(e\subseteq [n]\), each edge an increasing list of binary vertex identifiers. Repeated edges have no effect. \(N(H)\) is the bit length of this input including delimiters. A transversal is a set \(T\subseteq [n]\) intersecting every \(e\in E\); it is inclusion-minimal when no proper subset has this property. Output each such T as an increasing list of its binary vertex identifiers with a delimiter, in arbitrary order; no duplicate, nonminimal or incomplete output is allowed. \(N_{\mathrm{out}}(H)\) is the sum of the bit lengths of these records, counting one delimiter even for \(T=\varnothing\). If E is empty, the unique minimal transversal is \(\varnothing\). If E contains \(\varnothing\), there is no transversal and \(N_{\mathrm{out}}=0\). Time includes all computation, output and termination detection. The polynomial and algorithm are independent of n, E, edge size and output size; there is no separate delay or workspace bound, advice, oracle or randomization. Use the [explicit encoding convention](definitions.html#encoding).
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of a single algorithm meeting the total output-polynomial bound, including completeness, uniqueness and termination on every finite hypergraph, or a Lean proof that none exists. The target imposes no polynomial-delay or polynomial-space bound. A lower bound for one enumeration algorithm does not establish nonexistence of all algorithms.

title: Output-polynomial vertex enumeration
summary: The input describes a bounded rational polyhedron by linear inequalities in variable dimension. The task is to list every distinct extreme point exactly once and then halt. The requested total time is polynomial in the combined binary lengths of the input and the required vertex list. Degeneracy, exponentially many bases per vertex and infeasible arrangement intersections obstruct straightforward enumeration strategies. An accepted answer proves existence or impossibility of the full uniform algorithm in Lean.
formal:
Do there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every rational matrix \(M\) and rational vector \(b\) for which
\[
P=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Mx\leq b\}
\]
is bounded, \(A\) lists every vertex of \(P\) exactly once and halts in at most \(p(N+S)\) bit operations? Here \(N\) is the complete binary input length and \(S\) is the length of the required exact vertex list in the canonical encoding below. The dimension \(d\) is part of the input. Empty, lower-dimensional and degenerate polytopes are included.
definitions:
The input consists of integers \(m,d\geq1\), an explicitly listed matrix \(M\in\mathbb Q^{m\times d}\) and vector \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\). The inequality \(Mx\leq b\) is coordinatewise. Every rational is represented by a signed integer numerator and a positive denominator in binary, in lowest terms, with no leading zeros; zero has numerator zero and denominator one. Fixed delimiters separate dimensions, entries and rows. The input length \(N\) includes all these symbols. Dimensions are unbounded, and no rank, sparsity, integrality or conditioning restriction is imposed.

A polyhedron is a set described by finitely many closed linear inequalities. The promise here is that it is bounded: there exists a finite real number \(B\) such that \(\|x\|_2\leq B\) for every \(x\in P\). An empty set satisfies this promise. The number \(B\) is neither supplied nor assumed to have a given value. A bounded polyhedron is called a polytope. Redundant inequalities, repeated inequalities and a non-full-dimensional affine hull are allowed; no nondegeneracy or general-position promise is made.

A vertex is an extreme point. A vector \(v\in P\) is a vertex if, for all \(x,y\in P\), the equality \(v=(x+y)/2\) implies \(x=y=v\). Every vertex of a rational polyhedron is rational. The output must contain the coordinate vector of each distinct vertex, exactly once, in arbitrary order, with all \(d\) coordinates in the same reduced rational encoding. It ends with a fixed end marker. An empty polytope produces only that marker. A singleton produces its unique point even if its affine dimension is zero.

Define \(S\) as the sum of the canonical lengths of the distinct required coordinate vectors, including fixed separators and the end marker. Permuting the list does not change its length. Extra padding, duplicate vectors, alternative descriptions of the same vertex and extraneous certificates do not enlarge \(S\). At a vertex, a full-rank selection of active equations determines its coordinates; Cramer’s rule bounds their binary lengths by a polynomial in \(N\). Thus every individual output has polynomial length even though the number of outputs can be exponential.

Use a deterministic multitape Turing machine with bit-operation cost, no advice and no oracle. The same finite program and the same polynomial \(p\) must work for every input satisfying the boundedness promise. Arithmetic precision, preprocessing, writing all coordinates, duplicate handling and the final termination signal are charged. The bound is on total time from start to termination. No polynomial-delay, incremental-polynomial-time or input-polynomial-working-space requirement is added. The algorithm may use space up to its total time bound. Its behavior outside the boundedness promise is immaterial; malformed encodings can be rejected.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such an algorithm and polynomial exist, or a proof in Lean of their nonexistence. A positive proof must establish exactness of every rational output, completeness, absence of duplicates, termination and one uniform \(p(N+S)\) bit bound for all bounded rational input polyhedra, including the empty and lower-dimensional cases.

A negative proof must rule out every correct uniform deterministic enumerator with every polynomial total input-plus-output bound. It is not enough to exhibit an input on which a particular pivot rule or intermediate-representation algorithm is slow. A conditional hardness theorem under an unproved complexity assumption is partial progress on this unconditional existence question. Approximate vertices, a fixed dimension, bounded branch-width, nondegeneracy, or enumeration measured against all bases or all arrangement intersections does not meet the full criterion.

title: Incremental polynomial-time binary-matroid circuit enumeration
summary: A circuit of a binary matroid is a nonempty inclusion-minimal linearly dependent set of matrix columns. The question asks to enumerate all circuits exactly once in incremental polynomial time using memory polynomial only in the matrix input length. The running time for the first k circuits may be polynomial in k, but the memory bound must remain independent of the number already output. Incremental enumeration is known with large saturation storage, while polynomial-space regularization assumes that this memory problem has already been solved. A positive answer would expose all minimal binary dependencies efficiently without storing an exponentially large circuit history.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, for every explicitly given binary matrix \(A\in\mathbb F_2^{r\times m}\), enumerates all circuits of its column matroid exactly once in incremental polynomial time while using space polynomial only in the input length? Equivalently, does binary-matroid circuit enumeration belong to \(\mathrm{IncP}^{\mathrm{poly}}\) under the source’s conventions? The target permits any fixed polynomial exponent in the number of outputs; retaining the known quadratic incremental exponent is a stronger variant distinguished in the later source.
definitions:
The field \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) has addition and multiplication modulo two. The input matrix has nonnegative dimensions \(r,m\), represented by unary dimension headers followed by its \(rm\) entries in row order. Its encoded length \(L\) is of order \(r+m+rm+1\), including isolated zero columns and zero-dimensional cases. Malformed encodings are rejected in polynomial time. Column indices are distinct ground-set elements, even if their vectors coincide.

The column matroid has ground set \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). A subset is independent exactly when its columns are linearly independent over \(\mathbb F_2\). A circuit is a nonempty inclusion-minimal dependent subset: \(C\subseteq[m]\) is a circuit if \(\operatorname{rank}(A_C)<|C|\) and every proper subset of \(C\) is independent. Equivalently over this field, the columns in \(C\) sum to zero and no nonempty proper subset has zero sum. A zero column gives a singleton circuit; two equal nonzero columns give a two-element circuit. A circuit is not required to have globally minimum cardinality.

The output for each circuit is its \(m\)-bit characteristic vector. Every circuit must occur once, no other set may be output, the order is unrestricted, and enumeration must halt. Let \(N(A)\) be the number of circuits, which can be exponential in \(L\). If there are no circuits, the algorithm must halt in polynomial time. The output stream is write-only and cannot be read back as free external memory. Registers or buffers retaining previously emitted vectors count toward working space.

Use the source’s deterministic random-access machine convention: finite programs, integer registers, basic arithmetic consisting of addition, subtraction and multiplication, with arithmetic cost proportional to operand bit lengths and unit-cost register access and other basic instructions. Working space counts the bits in all stored integers, including retained outputs and register addresses needed to access them. Output uses designated registers; its polynomial-length encoding may be charged explicitly without changing the class. There is no advice or randomness. The matrix is read-only input and contributes polynomially many bits even if copied into memory.

Incremental polynomial time means that there are fixed positive integers \(C,a,b\) such that, on every valid \(A\) and for every \(1\leq k\leq N(A)\), the time from the start through the \(k\)-th distinct output is at most \(C(L+1)^b(k+1)^a\). Preprocessing is included. Total time through termination is at most \(C(L+1)^b(N(A)+1)^a\), enlarging constants or exponents if necessary. Polynomial working space means that fixed positive integers \(D,c\) bound space at every moment by \(D(L+1)^c\), independently of \(k\) and \(N(A)\). All constants are uniform over matrices and dimensions. These are class-membership bounds, not a prescribed delay exponent or an order requirement.

The cited original circuit-enumeration algorithm also accepts a matroid through an independence oracle. On the promise that the matroid is binary, that representation and an explicit binary matrix are interchangeable with polynomial overhead: greedily find a basis \(B\), make its columns unit vectors, and for every \(e\notin B\) set its coordinate at \(b\in B\) to one exactly when \((B\setminus\{b\})\cup\{e\}\) is independent. In a binary matroid these are the unique fundamental-circuit coordinates and give a representing matrix with at most \(m\) rows. This uses polynomially many queries and polynomial space. Conversely, Gaussian elimination simulates independence queries from a matrix. Oracle queries are exact, and writing their \(m\)-bit sets is charged; the equivalence uses the binary promise and does not apply to arbitrary matroids.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such an algorithm exists, or that no such algorithm exists. A positive proof must establish completeness, absence of duplicate outputs, termination, one uniform incremental polynomial bound and one simultaneous polynomial working-space bound for every binary matrix. A negative proof must rule out all algorithms meeting these bounds, not merely show that the known saturation algorithm stores exponentially many circuits. Polynomial total time without the prefix guarantees, unrestricted output-sized memory, enumeration with repeated circuits, or bounds only for graphic matroids do not settle the target. A conditional lower bound under an unproved complexity assumption is partial progress on this unconditional question.

title: Edge-exchange Gray codes for directed spanning trees
summary: The root is fixed before listing directed spanning trees. Every listed tree must orient all paths away from that root. Successive trees delete one arc and insert one arc. The endpoints of the full list need not be adjacent. This directed statement would imply the related undirected pivot-exchange statement.
formal: For every finite loopless simple directed graph and root r admitting an out-arborescence, do all spanning out-arborescences admit an arc-exchange listing?
definitions: A directed graph has a finite nonempty vertex set V and arcs (u,v) with u≠v, at most one arc for each ordered pair; opposite arcs may both occur. The root r∈V is fixed. An out-arborescence is an arc set of size |V|−1 in which r has indegree zero, every other vertex has indegree one, and every vertex is reachable from r along chosen arcs. The graph is promised to contain at least one such set. A listing contains every such arc set exactly once, and consecutive sets differ by deleting one arc and inserting one other arc. There is no last-to-first requirement and no bound on computation. The one-vertex case has the single empty arborescence.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal listing proposition or a counterexample and nonexistence proof.

title: Exact counting of linear extensions below base two
summary: A linear extension orders all labeled elements of a poset while respecting every precedence constraint. The question asks for an exact deterministic counting algorithm with a fixed exponential base below two. Inputs are arbitrary finite posets, with no promise on dimension or other structural parameters. An August 2026 preprint answers this target, and its complete proof and supporting finite tests received the recorded review. The card is archived as resolved by a checked preprint, without claiming peer review or Lean formalization.
formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\), constants \(K>0\) and \(1<c<2\), and an integer \(n_0\), such that, for every \(n\ge n_0\) and every partial order \(P\) on \([n]\), \(A\) outputs the exact number \(e(P)\) of linear extensions using at most \(Kc^n\) bit-cost random-access steps? It must also terminate correctly on every smaller valid input. There is no restriction on the width, height, dimension, sparsity or a graph parameter of \(P\).
definitions:
For \(n\ge0\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A partial order \(\le_P\) is a reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive binary relation on \([n]\). The input consists of binary \(n\) and its explicit \(n\times n\) Boolean relation matrix in row-major order. A list of comparable pairs or a Hasse diagram can be converted to this representation in polynomial time. Invalid matrices may be rejected in polynomial time; the time bound ranges over valid posets.

A linear extension is a permutation \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) of the distinct labels such that \(x\le_P y\) and \(x\ne y\) imply that \(x\) precedes \(y\). The integer \(e(P)\) counts these permutations. Elements with identical comparabilities remain distinct. The empty poset has one linear extension, and \(1\le e(P)\le n!\) for every finite poset. The required algorithm outputs this exact integer in binary; a sample, relative approximation or count modulo one prime is insufficient.

Use a uniform deterministic random-access machine with finite binary-string registers. Reading and writing a register charges for its address and data bits. Comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and elementary integer arithmetic charge for all operand and output bits using standard polynomial bit-cost arithmetic algorithms. No arithmetic on arbitrarily large integers is a unit-cost operation. Time includes reading the input and writing the output, and is worst-case over all \(n\)-element input posets. There is no additional polynomial-space requirement. This makes the source's exponential-time convention explicit; the reviewed construction uses polynomial-bit addresses and counters and polynomial work per state.

The constants \(K,c,n_0\) and the finite algorithm are fixed before the input is chosen. A bound \(O(b^n n^d)\) with fixed \(b<2\) and \(d\) answers the question: any fixed \(c\) between \(\max\{1,b\}\) and two absorbs the polynomial factor for sufficiently large \(n\). A \(2^{n-o(n)}\) bound does not suffice. The task asks for existence of a strict constant-base improvement, not determination of the optimal base. The second question in the same source passage, about treewidth of the Hasse diagram, is distinct.
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked affirmative answer must specify one algorithm and prove exact correctness and termination for every finite input poset, together with the uniform worst-case bound for fixed \(c<2\) in the stated model. A negative answer must prove the full negation of this existence claim. This is an algorithm-existence proposition requiring exact output; numerical benchmark tolerance does not replace exact counting by approximation. A citation or finite collection of tests is not a substitute for the Lean theorem.

title: Hadwiger’s conjecture
summary: Hadwiger’s conjecture says that a finite graph needing at least t colors always contains a complete graph on t vertices as a minor. Such a minor consists of disjoint nonempty connected vertex sets with an edge between every pair of sets. There are no parity requirements, restrictions on the sizes of these sets, or algorithmic running-time requirements. The conjecture would extend the Four-Color Theorem to an exact relation between coloring and clique minors in all finite graphs. A solution must prove the full assertion or certify a finite counterexample in Lean; the recent coloring improvement and the disproof for odd minors do not settle this target.
formal: Is the following proposition true? For every integer \(n\ge1\), every simple undirected graph \(G\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and every integer \(t\ge1\), if \(\chi(G)\ge t\), then \(G\) contains \(K_t\) as an ordinary graph minor. Equivalently, \(h(G)\ge\chi(G)\) for every such graph, where \(h\) is the Hadwiger number defined below.
definitions: The edge set of \(G\) is any set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices in \([n]\); there are no loops or parallel edges. For an integer \(r\ge1\), a proper \(r\)-coloring is a map \(c:[n]\to\{1,\ldots,r\}\) such that \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). The chromatic number \(\chi(G)\) is the least such \(r\); it exists and lies between \(1\) and \(n\). The graph \(K_t\) has \(t\) vertices and every possible edge. A \(K_t\) minor in \(G\) means that there are \(t\) pairwise disjoint nonempty vertex sets \(B_1,\ldots,B_t\) with both of the following properties: for every \(i\), any two vertices of \(B_i\) are joined by a finite path of edges of \(G\) whose vertices all lie in \(B_i\); and for every \(i<j\), some edge of \(G\) has one endpoint in \(B_i\) and one in \(B_j\). A singleton is connected. The branch sets may have any sizes, need not cover all vertices, and have no restrictions on extra internal edges or on parity. This is equivalent to obtaining \(K_t\) by vertex deletions, edge deletions and edge contractions, discarding loops and merging parallel edges after contraction. It is neither an induced-minor nor an odd-minor requirement. The Hadwiger number \(h(G)\) is the largest \(t\) admitting these branch sets, so \(1\le h(G)\le n\). For \(t\ge2\), the proposition equivalently says that absence of a \(K_t\) minor implies a proper \((t-1)\)-coloring; the \(t=1\) assertion holds automatically for a nonempty graph. Relabeling vertices has no effect. The quantifiers impose no connectedness, degree, order or other restriction on \(G\), and no running-time bound on finding a coloring or a minor.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition for all finite nonempty simple undirected graphs and all integers \(t\ge1\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: existence of a finite graph \(G\) and integer \(t\ge1\) with \(\chi(G)\ge t\) and no \(t\) branch sets satisfying the definition. A counterexample must certify both the chromatic lower bound and absence of the ordinary clique minor. A proof of \(h(G)\ge\chi(G)\) for every graph is an equivalent positive answer. No efficient algorithm is required. A constant-factor or asymptotic coloring bound, a finite list of established values of \(t\), a restricted graph class, or a counterexample only to the odd-minor variant does not cover the target.

title: Erdős–Hajnal conjecture
summary: The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture predicts a polynomial-size clique or independent set whenever a graph excludes one fixed induced pattern. The positive exponent may depend on that entire forbidden pattern but must work for every size and every permitted host graph. An accepted answer proves this universal assertion or refutes it for one fixed forbidden graph with a complete Lean-checked proof. General bounds and recent special-case results still fall short of the universal guarantee recorded by the checked primary literature. A revised historical full-solution claim remains unverified here, so the card distinguishes that uncertainty from the precise mathematical target.
formal: For each integer \(h\ge 2\) and each undirected simple graph \(H\) on \([h]\), is there a real constant \(c_H>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every undirected simple graph \(G\) on \([n]\) containing no induced copy of \(H\), \[\max\{\alpha(G),\omega(G)\}\ge n^{c_H}?\] The exponent is chosen after the entire forbidden graph \(H\) and before the host graph \(G\); the assertion must hold for all such \(H\).
definitions: Write \([m]=\{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}\). A simple undirected graph on \([m]\) is a symmetric irreflexive adjacency relation on this set; it has no loops or multiple edges. An induced copy of \(H\) in \(G\) is an injection \(f:[h]\to[n]\) such that \(u\) and \(v\) are adjacent in \(H\) if and only if \(f(u)\) and \(f(v)\) are adjacent in \(G\), for every distinct \(u,v\in[h]\). Both edges and nonedges must be preserved. A clique is a vertex subset in which every distinct pair is adjacent, and an independent or stable set is one in which every distinct pair is nonadjacent. The integers \(\omega(G)\) and \(\alpha(G)\) are their respective maximum cardinalities; a homogeneous set in this card means a clique or an independent set. The right side \(n^{c_H}\) is an ordinary positive-real power, and the integer on the left is compared as a real number. The constant \(c_H\) may depend on all of \(H\), but not on \(G\) or \(n\). There is no additional degree, density, dimension or algorithmic promise. All positive host sizes, including \(n<h\), are included. This is an existence statement, with no required algorithm for computing \(c_H\) or finding the homogeneous set. A hereditary graph class is closed under isomorphism and induced subgraphs; a proper such class omits some finite graph.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer proves existence of a positive exponent for every finite forbidden graph and the homogeneous-set guarantee for every permitted host graph. A negative answer proves that there is one fixed graph \(H\) with \(|V(H)|\ge2\) such that, for every real \(c>0\), some positive integer \(n\) and some \(H\)-free graph \(G\) on \([n]\) satisfy \(\max\{\alpha(G),\omega(G)\}<n^c\). The witness host graph may depend on \(c\), but the forbidden graph must be the same for all \(c\). Failure of one proposed exponent or verification of finitely many host sizes does not establish this negation. No numerical approximation to an optimal exponent is being requested.
references: https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~asuk/erdos_hajnal.pdf | https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.10147 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.15333 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15032 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06258 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28551 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.08303 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09049 | https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.3876

title: Tutte’s 5-flow conjecture
summary: Tutte’s 5-flow conjecture asks whether every finite bridgeless graph can carry a nonzero integer circulation with edge magnitudes at most four. One orientation and one assignment of values must make the incoming and outgoing totals agree at every vertex. Parallel edges, disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are included, and no efficient construction is required. The assertion would sharpen the universal 6-flow theorem and improve a quantitative guarantee for packing sets that meet all directed cuts. A complete Lean proof must establish universal existence or certify a bridgeless counterexample; special graph classes, vector flows and reconfiguration results do not settle that question.
formal: Does every finite loopless bridgeless undirected multigraph \(G=(V,E)\) admit an orientation \(D\) of all its edges and a function \(f:E\to\{1,2,3,4\}\) such that, at every vertex \(v\in V\), \[\sum_{e\in E:\,\operatorname{head}_D(e)=v}f(e)=\sum_{e\in E:\,\operatorname{tail}_D(e)=v}f(e)\] as an equality of integers?
definitions: A finite loopless undirected multigraph has a finite vertex set \(V\) and a finite set \(E\) of distinct edge identities, each assigned an unordered pair of two distinct vertices. Multiple edges with the same pair of endpoints are allowed and counted separately in every sum. Two vertices lie in the same connected component when a finite sequence of incident edges joins them; a vertex is joined to itself by the empty sequence. A bridge is an edge whose deletion, with the vertex set retained, increases the number of connected components. Bridgeless means that no edge has this property. Disconnected graphs, isolated vertices and the graph with no vertices are allowed. An orientation chooses, for each edge, one endpoint as its tail and the other as its head. The orientation and all values are chosen together for the whole graph; conservation must hold at all vertices simultaneously. Empty sums equal zero. For an integer \(k\ge2\), a nowhere-zero \(k\)-flow in this convention has the same conservation law and values in \(\{1,\ldots,k-1\}\). Thus a 5-flow uses four possible positive integer values; it may use any subset of them. Equivalently, after fixing an arbitrary reference orientation, signed integer values \(z(e)\) with \(1\le|z(e)|\le4\) may be used: a negative value is represented by reversing that edge and taking its absolute value. Values are scalar integers, not vectors, and conservation is exact, not merely a congruence. There are no sources, sinks, externally prescribed demands, capacities, embedding, degree restrictions or construction-time requirements. The proposition is universal over finite graphs, with the orientation and values allowed to depend on the graph.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this universal existence proposition, or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: there exists a finite loopless bridgeless undirected multigraph \(G\) such that for every orientation \(D\) and every assignment \(f:E(G)\to\{1,2,3,4\}\), at least one vertex violates the integer conservation equality. A negative answer must prove both the graph hypotheses and the nonexistence of every permitted flow; failure of one orientation, one search method or a finite collection of trial assignments is insufficient unless it establishes that universal nonexistence. A positive answer must cover every size and all allowed parallel edges and components. A 6-flow, an assertion only for graphs with an additional restriction, or a statement conditional on an unproved conjecture does not settle this target. An alternative formulation can qualify only with a Lean-checked implication establishing the exact proposition or its negation. No efficient procedure for constructing the witness is required.

title: Erdős girth conjecture
summary: The girth conjecture asks for dense graphs with every short cycle forbidden. For each fixed k, the target is \(\Omega (n^{1+1/k})\) edges and girth at least \(2k+2\). The lower bound must hold for every sufficiently large n, with constants depending on k. The known cases are \(k=1,2,3,5\), as still recorded in July 2026. A resolution would sharpen fundamental lower bounds for routing and graph spanners.
formal: For every integer \(k\ge 1\), do there exist constants \(c_{k}>0\) and \(N_{k}\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge N_{k}\), some simple undirected graph G on exactly n vertices has at least \(c_{k} n^{1+1/k}\) edges and contains no cycle of length less than \(2k+2\)? Equivalently, is \(M_{2k+2}(n)=\Omega _{k}(n^{1+1/k})\) for every fixed k, where \(M_{s}(n)\) is the maximum number of edges in an n-vertex graph with no cycle shorter than s?
definitions: A simple undirected graph consists of a finite vertex set and a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices; loops and repeated edges are not allowed. A cycle of length \(\ell\ge 3\) has \(\ell\) distinct vertices and the edges joining them cyclically. The girth is the length of the shortest cycle, and is +∞ for a forest. Thus “girth at least \(2k+2\)” forbids every cycle of lengths \(3,\ldots ,2k+1\), including non-induced cycles. \(M_{s}(n)\) is a maximum over all such graphs on the vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\); connectedness, regularity and efficient construction are not required. The quantifier order is \(\forall k \exists c_{k},N_{k} \forall n\ge N_{k} \exists G\). Constants may depend on k, but not on n; k remains fixed as n tends to infinity. The target is the stated constant-factor asymptotic density, not merely \(n^{1+1/k- o(1)}\), nor a claim for an arbitrarily sparse subsequence of n. This at-least-girth convention reproduces the source’s definition.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed existence claim for every fixed integer k, or refute it for at least one fixed k. Refutation means that no positive \(c_{k}\) and threshold \(N_{k}\) work at that k; a construction for only selected k or a smaller exponent does not settle the universal conjecture.

title: Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture
summary: The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture asks whether excluding any fixed induced tree makes chromatic number bounded at each fixed clique bound. The host is an arbitrary finite simple undirected graph, and the bound may depend on the tree and clique bound but not on host size. An accepted answer requires a complete Lean proof, or one fixed tree and clique bound supporting graphs of unbounded chromatic number. Path-induced copies, fractional colouring and subpolynomial size-dependent bounds are distinct from the selected ordinary-colouring statement. The conjecture would identify forests as the precise single forbidden-pattern boundary for this form of hereditary graph colouring.
formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every finite nonempty tree \(T\) and every integer \(r\ge1\), there exists an integer \(B\ge0\) such that every finite simple undirected graph \(G\) satisfies
\[\bigl(\omega(G)\le r\ \land\ G\text{ has no induced copy of }T\bigr)
\ \Longrightarrow\ \chi(G)\le B.\]
The quantifier order is \(\forall T\,\forall r\,\exists B\,\forall G\). The bound may depend on the entire tree \(T\) and on \(r\), but must be independent of the number of vertices and every other parameter of \(G\). No rate of growth or computational requirement on \(B\) is prescribed.
definitions:
Graphs and trees. A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) consists of a finite vertex set and a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops or multiple edges. A path has distinct vertices, with adjacent consecutive vertices; a cycle has at least three distinct vertices with consecutive and last-to-first adjacency. A tree is a nonempty connected graph containing no cycle. Connected means that each pair of vertices is joined by a path. The one-vertex tree is allowed. Host graphs need not be connected and may have no vertices. Equivalently, one may quantify over graphs with vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) for every integer \(n\ge0\), with \([0]=\varnothing\); labels have no mathematical significance.

Induced exclusion. For \(S\subseteq V(G)\), the graph \(G[S]\) has vertex set \(S\) and exactly the edges of \(G\) with both ends in \(S\). An induced copy of \(T\) is an injective map \(\varphi:V(T)\to V(G)\) such that for all distinct \(u,v\in V(T)\),
\[\{u,v\}\in E(T)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\{\varphi(u),\varphi(v)\}\in E(G).\]
A graph is \(T\)-free when no such map exists. The requirement preserves nonedges as well as edges. It is different from excluding an ordinary subgraph, a minor or a subdivision of \(T\). Edges from the image to vertices outside it are unrestricted.

Clique and chromatic numbers. A clique is a vertex subset whose distinct vertices are pairwise adjacent. Its maximum possible size is \(\omega(G)\). A proper \(k\)-colouring is a map \(c:V(G)\to[k]\) with \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). The least nonnegative integer \(k\) admitting such a map is \(\chi(G)\). Thus both parameters are zero for the empty graph, and every nonempty edgeless graph has both equal to one. The bound \(\omega(G)\le r\) is equivalent to excluding a clique on \(r+1\) vertices. Colour classes are independent sets, meaning subsets with no adjacent pair. Colouring here is ordinary vertex colouring, without lists, weights, fractional assignments or edge orientations.

Scope of the bound. Both the tree and the clique bound are fixed before the host graph varies. There is no maximum-degree, girth, geometric-representation, size or other promise on the host. The integer \(B=B(T,r)\) may grow arbitrarily quickly with its two allowed parameters. The target asks for existence of a finite bound, not its minimum value, a polynomial in \(r\), a computable function, or a procedure finding a colouring. There is consequently no input encoding, algorithmic running time or random-error parameter in the proposition.

Equivalent terminology. A class of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs. The \(T\)-free graphs form such a class. Saying it is \(\chi\)-bounded means that there is a function \(f_T:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that \(\chi(G)\le f_T(\omega(G))\) for every graph in the class. The conjecture asserts this for every nonempty tree; there is no requirement that the same function work for all trees. A negative answer means there are one fixed tree \(T\) and one fixed integer \(r\ge1\) for which chromatic numbers of the permitted hosts have no finite upper bound.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition or its negation. A positive answer must establish a finite \(B(T,r)\) for every permitted pair and prove the bound for every finite host graph. A nonconstructive existence proof is sufficient; neither a sharp formula nor an efficient colouring algorithm is required.

A negative answer must specify a single finite tree \(T\) and a single integer \(r\ge1\) and prove
\[\forall k\ge1\ \exists G:\quad G\text{ is finite and }T\text{-free},\qquad
\omega(G)\le r,\qquad\chi(G)\ge k.\]
Equivalently, supply such a family \((G_k)_{k\ge1}\) with verified unbounded chromatic number. Changing the excluded tree or clique bound as \(k\) grows does not refute the proposition. One finite example can invalidate a proposed numerical bound but cannot rule out a larger bound.

Bounds depending on host size, special tree families, additional host promises, path-induced copies, or a different colouring parameter do not resolve the full statement. Nor does disproving only a polynomial or computable strengthening refute the unrestricted finite-bound target.

title: Vertex reconstruction conjecture
summary: The vertex reconstruction conjecture asks whether every finite simple graph with at least three vertices is determined by all its one-vertex-deleted views. The views forget vertex labels but retain the multiplicity of repeated isomorphism classes. Even the edge count and degree multiset can be recovered, while the full arrangement of edges is the unresolved target in current specialist sources. Finite computational checks and a theorem for interval graphs provide partial results. A new theorem on sufficiently dense graphs uses edge deletions, and the conjecture for vertex deletions remains open.
formal: For every integer \(n\ge 3\) and every pair of finite simple undirected graphs G,H on n vertices, does equality \(D(G)=D(H)\) of their vertex decks imply that G and H are isomorphic?
definitions: A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a finite vertex set V and an edge set E consisting of unordered two-element subsets of V; there are no loops or parallel edges. An isomorphism from G to H is a bijection \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(\{u,v\}\) is an edge of G if and only if \(\{f(u),f(v)\}\) is an edge of H. Write \([G]\) for its isomorphism class. For \(v\in V(G), G- v\) is the induced graph on \(V(G)\setminus \{v\}\): remove v and exactly the edges incident with v. Define \(D(G)\) to be the multiset \(\{[G- v]:v\in V(G)\}\), with one entry for every deleted vertex. Thus \(D(G)=D(H)\) means that for each isomorphism class K of graphs on \(n- 1\) vertices, the number of vertices v with \([G- v]=K\) equals the corresponding number for H. Each entry forgets all original vertex labels, including the identity of the deleted vertex; repeated isomorphism classes retain their multiplicities.
