All graphs, including disconnected graphs and graphs with isolated vertices, are included. The question is a structural uniqueness statement and imposes no running-time requirement on an algorithm.
answer_criterion: Prove that equal vertex decks imply isomorphism for every \(n\ge 3\), or refute the conjecture by exhibiting two nonisomorphic finite simple undirected graphs with \(n\ge 3\) and identical decks, with proofs of those properties.

title: List edge-coloring conjecture
summary: A proper edge coloring assigns different colors to edges that share an endpoint. In list edge coloring, each edge must choose its color from its own finite set of allowed colors. The conjecture asks whether giving every edge as many choices as the ordinary chromatic index always suffices, even with arbitrary list overlaps and parallel edges. It holds for bipartite multigraphs, and a general asymptotic theorem leaves only a vanishing relative gap. Exact equality for every finite loopless multigraph would show that local availability restrictions never impose an additional per-edge palette requirement.
formal: For every finite loopless multigraph G and every assignment L of finite sets of colors to its edges with \(|L(e)|\ge \chi ' (G)\) for every edge e, does there exist a proper edge coloring c with \(c(e)\in L(e)\) for every e? Equivalently, is \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)=\chi ' (G)\) for every such G?
definitions: A finite loopless multigraph consists of finite sets V and E and a map \(\partial\) assigning to each edge \(e\in E a\) two-element subset \(\partial e\subseteq V\). Distinct edges may have the same endpoints and are still distinct objects. Two distinct edges are adjacent if their endpoint sets intersect. A proper edge coloring assigns different colors to any two adjacent edges. For an integer \(k\ge 0\) let \([k]=\{1,\ldots ,k\}\), with [0] empty; \(\chi ' (G)\), the chromatic index, is the least k admitting a proper map \(E\to [k]\). A list assignment is a function \(e\mapsto L(e)\) where each \(L(e)\) is a finite subset of the positive integers, used only as distinct color names. Lists may differ, overlap arbitrarily and have an arbitrarily large finite union. The list chromatic index \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)\) is the least \(k\ge 0\) such that every assignment with \(|L(e)|\ge k\) admits a proper edge coloring from those lists. Both indices are zero when E is empty and are at most |E| otherwise; hence these minima exist. Requiring lists of exactly k colors is equivalent, since larger lists can be restricted to k colors. Any finite collection of abstract colors can be renamed by distinct positive integers without changing feasibility. Isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and arbitrary parallel-edge multiplicities are allowed. The maximum degree \(\Delta\) counts edges incident with a vertex, including parallel copies separately, and is zero for an empty vertex set. The target concerns existence, with no required algorithm, running time or bound on color-name bit lengths.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated universal list-colorability assertion, or refute it. A finite counterexample can specify a multigraph with ordinary chromatic index k and lists of k colors on every edge, together with a proof that no proper coloring from those lists exists. Equality only up to a vanishing relative error, a result for a restricted graph class, or successful coloring of selected list assignments does not resolve the universal claim.

title: Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture
summary: The Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture asks how short a directed cycle must exist when every vertex has many outgoing neighbors. For n vertices and minimum outdegree at least r, it predicts a cycle of length at most the ceiling of n divided by r. The graph may contain opposite arcs, which form a two-cycle, but has no loops or repeated arcs. The target is an exact theorem for every graph and degree threshold, with no extra regularity or indegree assumption. Sharp examples and many partial results are known, while the recent rainbow and regular-digraph results do not resolve the general statement.
formal:
For every integer \(n\ge2\), every integer \(r\) with \(1\le r\le n-1\), and every simple loopless digraph \(D=(V,A)\) on \(n\) vertices, does
\[\bigl(\forall v\in V:\ d_D^+(v)\ge r\bigr)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\bigl(\exists\text{ a directed cycle of length }\ell\le\lceil n/r\rceil\bigr)\]
hold? Opposite arcs are allowed, and a pair of opposite arcs counts as a directed cycle of length two. The bound is exact, for every permitted pair \((n,r)\), with no additive error.
definitions:
A simple loopless digraph consists of a finite set \(V\), with \(|V|=n\), and an arc set
\[A\subseteq\{(u,v)\in V\times V:u\ne v\}.\]
There is at most one copy of each ordered pair; both \((u,v)\) and \((v,u)\) may occur. Relabeling the vertices by \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) changes no requirement. The out-neighborhood and outdegree of a vertex are
\[N_D^+(v)=\{w\in V:(v,w)\in A\},\qquad d_D^+(v)=|N_D^+(v)|.\]
The minimum outdegree is \(\delta^+(D)=\min_{v\in V}d_D^+(v)\). Every vertex must meet the lower bound; an average-degree bound or a condition on only some vertices is not the hypothesis.

A directed cycle of length \(\ell\) is a sequence of pairwise distinct vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_{\ell-1}\), where \(2\le\ell\le n\), such that \((v_i,v_{i+1})\in A\) for \(0\le i<\ell-1\) and \((v_{\ell-1},v_0)\in A\). It need not be induced: additional arcs among these vertices are allowed. Length counts arcs, equivalently the number of distinct vertices on the cycle. The closing return to \(v_0\) is not counted as an additional vertex. A repeated-vertex closed walk is not the cycle witness specified here.

The directed girth \(g(D)\) is the minimum length of a directed cycle, with value \(+\infty\) if there is none. Under the positive minimum-outdegree hypothesis it is finite. The ceiling is the least integer at least the real quotient \(n/r\); equivalently, \(\lceil n/r\rceil=\lfloor(n+r-1)/r\rfloor\) for the positive integers used here. Thus the target can also be written
\[g(D)\le\lceil n/r\rceil,\quad\text{or equivalently}\quad n\ge r(g(D)-1)+1.\]
It does not assert \(g(D)\le n/r\) without rounding.

No lower bound on indegree is imposed. In particular, a graph need not be regular, strongly connected, vertex-transitive, planar or randomly generated. An oriented graph is the restricted case with no opposite pair of arcs. The target includes oriented graphs and all the other simple loopless digraphs above. This is a finite extremal existence statement, with no construction, search-algorithm, encoding or computational resource requirement.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must cover all integers \(n,r\) in the stated ranges and all eligible digraphs, producing a cycle with the exact ceiling bound. A negative answer may specify finite \(n,r\) and a finite arc set, but must prove in Lean both the minimum-outdegree condition and the absence of every directed cycle of lengths \(2,\ldots,\lceil n/r\rceil\). A proof of the full logical negation without an explicitly listed counterexample also qualifies. An asymptotic estimate, an additive-constant relaxation, a special degree value, or an extra regularity, indegree or forbidden-subgraph hypothesis settles only a restricted statement.

title: Seese’s conjecture
summary: Seese’s conjecture concerns arbitrary classes of finite simple undirected graphs. Its premise is an algorithm deciding whether some graph in the class satisfies any input monadic second-order sentence over vertices and vertex sets. Its conclusion is one finite clique-width bound holding for all graphs in that class. The algorithm and bound may depend on the class, and parity predicates or edge-set quantifiers are excluded from the premise. A complete Lean-checked solution must prove the universal implication or verify a class with decidable satisfiability and unbounded clique-width.
formal:
For every isomorphism-closed class \(\mathcal C\) of finite simple undirected graphs, does
\[
\operatorname{Sat}_{\mathrm{MSO}_1}(\mathcal C)\ \text{decidable}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists k\ge1\ \forall G\in\mathcal C,\quad\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k
\]
hold?

The language \(\operatorname{Sat}_{\mathrm{MSO}_1}(\mathcal C)\) contains exactly the encoded vertex-set monadic second-order sentences satisfied by at least one graph in \(\mathcal C\). The bound \(k\) may depend on the whole class but must hold for every graph in it.
definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a finite vertex set and an edge set consisting of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops, multiple edges, labels or additional relations in the logical vocabulary. The empty graph is allowed. A graph class \(\mathcal C\) contains only such graphs and is closed under isomorphism: renaming vertices does not change membership. It may be empty, finite or infinite, and no hereditary, degree, minor or forbidden-subgraph restriction is imposed. Equivalently, classes can be viewed as arbitrary collections of finite graph isomorphism types.

The logic \(\mathrm{MSO}_1\) has individual variables \(x,y,\ldots\) and vertex-set variables \(X,Y,\ldots\). Its atomic formulas are \(x=y\), \(E(x,y)\) and \(x\in X\). Formulas are finite expressions built from these atoms using Boolean connectives and existential or universal quantification over either sort. Set equality, when used, is shorthand for equality of membership at every vertex. A sentence has no free variables. On a finite graph, individual quantifiers range over \(V\) and set quantifiers over all subsets of \(V\), with the ordinary truth conditions. There is no vertex order, arithmetic relation, edge-set quantifier, cardinality predicate or modular counting extension.

Fix an effective, uniquely parsed finite-string encoding of this syntax, with binary variable indices and symbols for the finitely many logical operations. Define
\[
\operatorname{Sat}_{\mathrm{MSO}_1}(\mathcal C)
=\{\operatorname{enc}(\varphi):
\varphi\text{ is an }\mathrm{MSO}_1\text{ sentence and }
\exists G\in\mathcal C\ (G\models\varphi)\}.
\]
Decidable means that some deterministic Turing machine halts on every string, rejects malformed encodings and answers membership in this language correctly. That machine may depend on \(\mathcal C\); its only input is the sentence encoding. The class is not supplied as another input or as an oracle, and no running-time bound is imposed. No effective presentation of the class is assumed separately from this decidability premise. By negation of sentences, the premise is equivalent to decidability of the theory consisting of sentences true in every graph of \(\mathcal C\). It is not the model-checking problem in which a particular finite graph is also supplied.

For a positive integer \(k\), a \(k\)-expression is a finite term constructing a graph with temporary vertex labels in \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\). Its permitted operations are creation of a single vertex with any one label; disjoint union of two previously constructed labelled graphs; relabelling every vertex with label \(i\) to label \(j\); and, for distinct labels \(i,j\), adding every missing edge between a vertex labelled \(i\) and a vertex labelled \(j\). Vertices and existing edges are never deleted. Repeated edge additions have no further effect. The labels are forgotten in the final graph and are not extra relations available to the logic.

For a nonempty graph \(G\), the clique-width \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\) is the minimum positive \(k\) for which a \(k\)-expression yields a graph isomorphic to \(G\). Set \(\operatorname{cw}(\varnothing)=0\). Every finite graph has finite clique-width, but bounded clique-width of a class requires a single \(k\) independent of its members and their orders. For the empty class the conclusion is vacuous.

The quantifier order is: for every class, if some class-specific sentence decider exists, then some class-specific finite width bound exists. The proposition does not demand one decider for all classes, a method to extract \(k\) from machine code, or an algorithm producing clique-width expressions. It is an exact universal implication, not a request for a numerical estimate of a width.
answer_criterion:
Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of the implication for every stated graph class. Alternatively, specify one isomorphism-closed class \(\mathcal C\), a total sentence-deciding machine, and complete Lean-checked proofs of its correctness and of
\[
\forall k\ge1\ \exists G\in\mathcal C,\qquad\operatorname{cw}(G)>k.
\]
A single finite graph cannot refute a class-wide boundedness claim. Decidability for a restricted set of sentences, model checking on a given graph, a theorem with parity or edge-set quantification in the premise, or a result for only specially restricted graph classes does not establish the full target.

title: Excluded-grid treewidth exponent
summary: The Grid-Minor Theorem forces a large square grid minor when treewidth is sufficiently large. The extremal threshold is measured against the side length of that grid. The card asks for the polynomial growth exponent of this threshold to absolute accuracy 0.01. A grid of side length r has r squared vertices, so the parameter convention matters. Logarithmic factors and the exact threshold function are not part of this numerical target.
formal: Determine the excluded-grid exponent \(x_{\mathrm{grid}}\) to absolute error at most \(1/100\). For each integer \(r\ge2\), let \[f(r)=\min\{t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:\forall G,\ \operatorname{tw}(G)\ge t\Longrightarrow Q_r\text{ is a minor of }G\},\] where \(G\) ranges over finite simple undirected graphs and \(Q_r\) is the \(r\)-by-\(r\) square grid. Define \[x_{\mathrm{grid}}=\inf\{a\ge0:f(r)=O(r^a)\}.\] The precise asymptotic quantifiers, treewidth and ordinary graph-minor model are given below. The parameter \(r\) is grid side length, not its \(r^2\) vertices. Logarithmic factors are outside the requested precision.
definitions:
Graphs and grids. A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a finite vertex set and an edge set consisting of unordered pairs of distinct vertices; there are no loops or parallel edges. The vertex set of \(Q_r\) is \(\{1,\ldots,r\}^2\), and two vertices \((i,j)\) and \((i',j')\) are adjacent exactly when
\[|i-i'|+|j-j'|=1.\]
Thus \(r\) counts the side length, while the grid has \(r^2\) vertices. Host graphs may be disconnected and have arbitrary order, degree and genus.

Minor containment. A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if there are nonempty vertex subsets \((B_v)_{v\in V(H)}\) of \(V(G)\) such that they are pairwise disjoint, each induced graph \(G[B_v]\) is connected, and for every edge \(uv\in E(H)\) an edge of \(G\) joins \(B_u\) to \(B_v\). These subsets are called branch sets. Extra edges inside or between branch sets are allowed. Equivalently, one may delete vertices and edges and contract edges, then remove loops and merge parallel edges. This is ordinary minor containment, with no prescribed roots, induced-subgraph condition or topological-minor requirement.

Treewidth. A tree decomposition of \(G\) consists of a finite nonempty tree \(T\) and bags \(X_t\subseteq V(G)\) for its nodes such that every vertex lies in a bag, both endpoints of every edge lie together in a bag, and for each vertex the nodes whose bags contain it form a nonempty connected subtree of \(T\). A tree is a connected acyclic undirected graph. The decomposition width is \(\max_{t\in V(T)}|X_t|-1\). The treewidth \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\) is the minimum width over all such decompositions. In particular, the empty graph has treewidth \(-1\) under this convention and has no effect on thresholds \(t\ge0\).

Extremal threshold. The qualitative Grid-Minor Theorem ensures that the defining set of thresholds is nonempty. Since treewidth is integer valued,
\[f(r)=1+\max\{\operatorname{tw}(G):G\text{ is a finite simple undirected graph with no }Q_r\text{ minor}\}.\]
This maximum exists: its set of integer values is nonempty and bounded above by the qualitative theorem. It is a maximum of widths, not a bound on the number of vertices of a grid-excluding graph. Arbitrarily large trees, for example, do not contain \(Q_r\) for \(r\ge2\).

Exponent convention. Define \[x_{\mathrm{grid}}=\inf\{a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}:\exists C>0\ \exists r_0\ge2\ \forall r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge r_0},\ f(r)\le Cr^a\}.\] The known polynomial Grid-Minor Theorem makes this set nonempty; the cited ninth-power bound with polylogarithmic overhead gives \(x_{\mathrm{grid}}\le9\), and the quadratic-logarithmic lower bound gives \(x_{\mathrm{grid}}\ge2\). The exponent is equivalently the limit superior of \(\log f(r)/\log r\); no ordinary limit or attainment of the infimum is assumed. In particular, exponent two permits a growing logarithmic factor and does not assert \(f(r)=O(r^2)\). Constants may depend on a chosen positive slack in the exponent, but not on the grid side length or host graph. This is a structural existence exponent, not a running-time exponent for finding a grid.
answer_criterion: Supply \(a\) and prove \(|a-x_{\mathrm{grid}}|\le1/100\) in Lean. The growth parameter in both bounds is the side length \(r\) of the grid minor. A [certified enclosing interval](definitions.html#numerical-answers) of width at most \(1/50\) also suffices via its midpoint.

title: Lovász conjecture
summary: A graph is vertex-transitive when an adjacency-preserving permutation can send any vertex to any other vertex. The Lovász conjecture asks whether every finite nonempty connected vertex-transitive simple undirected graph has a path that visits each vertex exactly once. The path need not return to its starting vertex, and the statement includes graphs outside the Cayley-graph setting without requiring an efficient path-finding algorithm. A resolution would decide whether connectedness and vertex symmetry alone force a spanning path, beyond known long-cycle guarantees and restricted Hamiltonicity results. A complete Lean answer must prove the path exists for every graph in the stated class or prove that one graph in the class has no such path.
formal:
Does every finite nonempty connected vertex-transitive simple undirected graph have a Hamiltonian path? With the definitions below, prove or refute
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall E\subseteq\binom{[n]}2\quad
\bigl(\operatorname{Connected}([n],E)\land
\operatorname{VertexTransitive}([n],E)\bigr)
\Longrightarrow
\exists p\in S_n\ \forall i\in[n-1]\quad
\{p(i),p(i+1)\}\in E.
\]
There is no restriction on the number of vertices, degree, automorphism group or representation as a Cayley graph. The required spanning object is a path; its endpoints need not be adjacent. This is an existence assertion without a computational time bound or a requirement to find the path efficiently.
definitions:
Let \(\mathbb N_{\ge1}=\{1,2,\ldots\}\), and write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A finite nonempty simple undirected graph is a pair \(G=([n],E)\), where \(n\ge1\) and \(E\) is a set of two-element subsets of \([n]\). Vertices \(u,v\) are adjacent when \(\{u,v\}\in E\). Thus there are no loops, parallel edges, orientations or weights. Using labeled vertices loses no generality because every finite graph is isomorphic to one on \([n]\). A finite representation consists of \(n\) and the \(\binom n2\) adjacency bits in lexicographic order of unordered pairs; no algorithmic constraint depends on this representation.

The graph is connected if for every \(u,v\in[n]\) there are an integer \(m\ge0\) and vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_m\in[n]\) such that \(v_0=u\), \(v_m=v\), and \(\{v_{j-1},v_j\}\in E\) for every \(1\le j\le m\). A sequence of length zero is permitted when \(u=v\).

Write \(S_n\) for the set of all bijections \([n]\to[n]\). An automorphism of \(G\) is a bijection \(\sigma\in S_n\) with
\[
\forall x,y\in[n]\quad
\bigl(\{x,y\}\in E\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \{\sigma(x),\sigma(y)\}\in E\bigr).
\]
The graph is vertex-transitive if for every ordered pair \(u,v\in[n]\) there exists an automorphism \(\sigma\) with \(\sigma(u)=v\). The automorphism may depend on the pair. Equal vertex degrees alone are not the condition.

A Hamiltonian path is a permutation \(p\in S_n\) such that consecutive vertices in \(p(1),\ldots,p(n)\) are adjacent. Bijection ensures that every vertex occurs exactly once. For \(n=1\), the adjacency requirement ranges over the empty set \([0]\), so the single vertex is a Hamiltonian path. No closing edge from \(p(n)\) to \(p(1)\) is required. A cycle discussed in the context is a cyclic sequence of at least three distinct vertices with edges between consecutive vertices and from the last back to the first; its length is its number of vertices. Such a cycle is Hamiltonian only if it contains every vertex.

For the restricted results mentioned below, a Cayley graph has the elements of a finite group as its vertices and joins \(g\) to \(gs\) for elements \(s\) of a fixed inverse-closed set of nonidentity group elements. A connected Cayley graph is an example of a connected vertex-transitive graph, but the conjecture includes all graphs satisfying the stated symmetry condition. A directed graph instead has ordered edges; results about paths or cycles required to follow those directions concern a different class of objects.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the formal assertion, or of its full logical negation, using the finite graph and permutation definitions above.

A positive answer must show that for every \(n\ge1\) and every connected vertex-transitive graph \(([n],E)\), some permutation has all its consecutive pairs in \(E\). It may establish existence without providing a uniformly efficient construction.

A negative answer must establish
\[
\exists n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists E\subseteq\binom{[n]}2\quad
\operatorname{Connected}([n],E)\ \land\
\operatorname{VertexTransitive}([n],E)\ \land\
\forall p\in S_n\ \exists i\in[n-1]\quad
\{p(i),p(i+1)\}\notin E.
\]
This requires one finite graph satisfying both hypotheses and a proof that every ordering of its vertices fails to be a Hamiltonian path. Existence of the counterexample can itself be proved; an efficient search procedure is not an additional requirement. An arbitrarily long nonspanning path, a spanning result for one subclass, or a counterexample to a directed or cyclic variant does not establish either required conclusion. The target is exact, so numerical \(1/100\) approximation does not relax it.

title: Graph isomorphism in polynomial time
summary: Graph isomorphism asks whether two finite simple graphs agree after a bijective relabeling of their vertices. The target is a single deterministic algorithm that answers correctly on every explicitly encoded pair in polynomial time. A proposed relabeling is easy to verify, while ruling out all relabelings can require substantially more structure. The checked general upper bound is quasipolynomial, and efficient algorithms for restricted graph classes do not establish the unrestricted polynomial bound. A resolution would settle a central structural comparison problem whose position between P and NP-completeness remains unresolved.
formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic Turing machine M and fixed positive integers C,k such that on every binary input x, M halts within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions and accepts exactly when x encodes two isomorphic finite simple undirected graphs? Equivalently, is the language \(\mathrm{GI}\) defined below in deterministic polynomial time?
definitions: For \(n\ge 0\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]\) empty. A finite simple undirected graph G on \([n]\) has an adjacency matrix \(A_G\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) that is symmetric with zero diagonal. Its vertices are labeled; its edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Encode a pair G,H by \(1^n0\), followed by the full row-major matrix of G, followed by \(1^m0\) and the full row-major matrix of H. The total binary length is \(N=n^2+m^2+n+m+2\). Extra trailing bits, missing entries, or nonsymmetric or nonzero-diagonal matrices make an encoding malformed. Graphs G,H are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if there is a bijection \(\pi:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(A_G(i,j)=A_H(\pi(i),\pi(j))\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\). If \(n\ne m\), no such bijection exists; the two empty graphs are isomorphic. All valid graph pairs are in the domain, without degree, connectivity, automorphism, sparsity or random-input promises. Computation receives the entire binary string, rather than an oracle or succinctly generated adjacency matrix. The computation model is one uniform classical multitape Turing machine with a finite program, finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. In one transition each tape head moves at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including input access and internal computation. Polynomial time means a bound \(C(N+1)^k\) for fixed positive integers C,k, independent of the input and of the graph sizes. There is no advice, prover, witness supplied with the input, graph-isomorphism oracle or uncounted preprocessing. The machine is deterministic and must always answer correctly. The language \(\mathrm{GI}\) contains exactly the valid encodings with \(G\cong H\); malformed encodings are rejected. Use the shared definition of [P](definitions.html#p-np). Ordinary vertex-permutation isomorphism is the equivalence relation in the target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the specified language \(\mathrm{GI}\) belongs to P, or that \(\mathrm{GI}\notin\mathrm{P}\). A positive answer must establish one deterministic machine, fixed polynomial bounds and correctness on every input, including rejection of malformed strings. A negative answer must exclude every such polynomial-time machine; a lower bound for only one algorithm, invariant or representation does not suffice. No isomorphism witness or canonical representative must be output: the target is decision.

title: Deterministic linear-time minimum spanning tree
summary: The problem asks for an exact minimum spanning tree of every connected simple undirected graph with arbitrary real edge weights. The target is one uniform deterministic sequential algorithm whose worst-case total running time is linear in the explicitly listed vertices and edges. The weight keys are opaque and ties may be broken by the input edge indices. Khanna, Putterman and Song prove that linearly many deterministic weight comparisons suffice in the worst case. The Pettie–Ramachandran uniform algorithm converts this bound into linear total running time.
formal: Does there exist one uniform deterministic comparison-RAM algorithm that, for every finite connected simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with arbitrary real weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), outputs a minimum spanning tree in \(O(n+m)\) worst-case total time, where \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\)? The graph is explicitly listed, and weights are opaque keys that may only be copied and compared. The machine, output and quantifier conventions are fixed below; the bound counts all computation, not only weight comparisons.
definitions:
Instance and objective. Let \(n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\), \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E\) be a set of distinct unordered pairs of distinct vertices, with \(G=(V,E)\) connected. Write \(m=|E|\) and \(N=n+m+2\). Each \(e\in E\) has a weight \(w(e)\in\mathbb R\), with no integrality, magnitude, distinctness or sign promise. A spanning tree is a set \(T\subseteq E\) for which \((V,T)\) is connected and has no cycle; necessarily \(|T|=n-1\). Its weight is the finite real sum \(W(T)=\sum_{e\in T}w(e)\). A minimum spanning tree satisfies
\[\forall T'\subseteq E\text{ that is a spanning tree}:\quad W(T)\le W(T').\]
Connectedness ensures a spanning tree exists, and the finite collection of trees has a minimum. For \(n=1\), the graph has no edges and the required output is the empty tree. Equal or negative edge weights are allowed, and any minimizing tree is accepted. The algorithm need not output the numerical sum.

Explicit input and output. Input records give \(n,m\), the list of vertex labels, and an ordered list of \(m\) edge records. Edge \(j\), for \(1\le j\le m\), has endpoints \(1\le u_j<v_j\le n\) and a handle for its opaque weight key. Pairs are not repeated, but their list order is arbitrary. The index \(j\) is the edge's distinct identifier. The input occupies \(\Theta(n+m)\) constant-size records. It is a full graph description rather than a circuit or oracle generating a larger graph. A weight key is supplied as an abstract atom, not a finite precision approximation or a binary expansion of its real value. The output lists exactly \(n-1\) distinct valid edge identifiers forming a minimum tree, in any order. No behavior is required on malformed or disconnected inputs.

Weight access. A weight handle can be stored, copied or retrieved in constant time. An instruction given two such handles returns their exact three-way real comparison: less, equal or greater. That instruction costs one operation independently of the real numbers. These are the only observations of weight values available to the algorithm. Weight handles identify their edge records; their numerical identifiers encode no information about the values. The program cannot inspect a weight's bits, add or subtract weights, multiply them, convert them to integers, hash their numerical representations, or compare arithmetic expressions involving weights. Copying a handle does not manufacture a new numerical key. The sum \(W(T)\) defines mathematical correctness, not an allowed machine instruction.

Nonweight machine operations. The algorithm fixes an integer \(b\ge2\), and for input parameter \(N\) uses unsigned words of
\[\ell=b\lceil\log_2N\rceil\]
bits for vertex labels, edge identifiers, counters and memory addresses. A word represents an integer from zero to \(2^\ell-1\). The machine has a fixed finite program, a constant number of registers and random-access work memory addressed by one word, initially zero; weight-key storage can equivalently keep the corresponding input handles. The input is read-only, and output is a sequential list of words. Each instruction touches a constant number of words or handles. Reading, writing, copying, comparing nonweight words and conditional branching cost one operation. Addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^\ell\), integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor, and bitwise AND/OR/XOR/NOT are also unit-cost. Logical shifts by fewer than \(\ell\) positions discard bits outside the word and fill with zeros; a shift by at least \(\ell\) returns zero. Larger integer calculations require multiple words and their operations are charged. The program may use \(\ell\) as the machine word length. Word arithmetic is not arithmetic on the represented real weights.

Uniformity and time. There is no random input, random instruction, input-size advice, free preprocessing table or external computational oracle. The same finite program and word constant are used on every instance and edge-list order. All initialization it performs, comparisons, ordinary computation, generated tables and writing every output identifier count. Let \(T_A(G,w)\) be the number of these operations, with the edge-list representation understood as part of the input. The algorithm must halt with a correct tree on every valid instance. The time requirement is
\[\exists C>0\ \exists N_0\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall(G,w)\text{ with }n+m\ge N_0:\quad T_A(G,w)\le C(n+m).\]
The constants are independent of the graph, weights, density and representation order. This is deterministic worst-case sequential time. It is not an expectation over random graphs or over random choices, and an unbounded slowly growing extra factor does not count as linear.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic program and fixed word constant and prove termination, spanning-tree feasibility, exact minimum total weight and the displayed total-time bound for every connected simple graph and all real weight assignments. The proof must cover repeated and negative weights and the single-vertex case. If it uses decision trees or lookup tables, all work needed to produce and use them must be included.

A negative answer must rule out every correct deterministic program in the specified comparison-RAM model. Equivalently, for every word constant and every program that halts with a minimum tree on every valid input, prove that for each \(C>0\) and each \(N_0\) there is a valid instance and edge-list order with \(n+m\ge N_0\) on which the time exceeds \(C(n+m)\). A lower bound for one particular algorithm, one data structure, or a stricter pointer-only model does not establish this negation. A conditional lower bound must identify its unproved assumption and is not an unconditional resolution.

Expected-linear randomized algorithms, deterministic integer-weight algorithms that inspect weight bits, restricted graph classes and a linear number of comparisons with superlinear control overhead do not alone meet the target. Optimality relative to an unknown decision-tree complexity must include a linear bound on that complexity and the necessary implementation overhead to establish an affirmative answer. This card requires an exact minimum tree and an actual linear bound, with no numerical approximation tolerance.

title: Almost-linear-time exact maximum matching in general graphs
summary: Maximum-cardinality matching selects as many pairwise vertex-disjoint edges as possible in an arbitrary finite simple undirected graph. The target is one uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that constructs an optimum matching with probability at least two thirds on every input. It must halt almost surely, always return a valid matching when it halts, and have expected time within every fixed positive exponent slack above the full explicit input size. A complete Lean proof must establish the algorithm and all these guarantees or rule out every permitted randomized program with this expected-time behavior. Known almost-linear bipartite algorithms, approximation schemes and catalytic-space results do not settle the general exact target, and the older Glauber-dynamics claim has an acknowledged error.
formal:
Does there exist one uniform randomized sequential word-RAM algorithm that, on every explicitly represented finite simple undirected graph \(G\), terminates almost surely, always outputs a valid matching when it terminates, and outputs a maximum-cardinality matching with probability at least \(2/3\), with expected running time
\[(n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}?\]
Here \(n=|V(G)|\), \(m=|E(G)|\), and the precise machine, input, probability and asymptotic conventions are below. In particular, the same program must meet every positive exponent slack; an algorithm chosen separately for each fixed slack is not the stated target.
definitions:
Graph and optimum. Let \(n\in\mathbb N_{\ge0}\), \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E\) be a set of distinct unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Disconnected graphs, isolated vertices, odd cycles, the empty graph and the edgeless graph are included. Put \(m=|E|\) and \(N=n+m+2\). A matching is a subset \(M\subseteq E\) such that no vertex belongs to two selected edges. Its cardinality is \(|M|\), and
\[\nu(G)=\max\{|M|:M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\}.\]
The empty matching is allowed, so this finite maximum exists on every input. The problem is unweighted. The algorithm must return the selected edges, not only the number \(\nu(G)\), a fractional solution, or a certificate that a perfect matching exists. Any maximum matching is acceptable.

Explicit representation. Use an edge list with headers \(n,m\), the vertex list \(1,\ldots,n\), and then \(m\) indexed pairs \((u_j,v_j)\) with \(1\le u_j<v_j\le n\) and no repeated pair. Edge indices are \(j=1,\ldots,m\); their order is arbitrary. Each integer occupies one machine word, so the entire input has \(2+n+2m\) words. Isolated vertices count in \(n\). The graph is a full list, not a succinct circuit or query oracle. The output consists of its cardinality \(t\) and a list of \(t\) distinct valid edge indices, in any order. Ordinary explicit adjacency lists can be converted to this form in \(O(n+m)\) word operations, preserving the target time scale. No guarantee is required on malformed inputs.

Machine. The algorithm fixes an integer \(b\ge2\) and, on inputs of size parameter \(N\), uses words of exactly
\[w=b\lceil\log_2N\rceil\]
bits. A word represents an unsigned integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). The machine has a fixed finite program, a constant number of word registers and random-access work memory addressed by one word, initially all zero. The input is read-only and the output is a sequential list of words. Each instruction operates on a constant number of words. Reading or writing an addressed word, copying, comparing, branching, bitwise AND/OR/XOR/NOT, and arithmetic addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\) cost one operation. Integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor also cost one operation. A left or right shift by fewer than \(w\) positions discards bits outside the word and fills with zeros; a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Larger exact integers use multiple words, and their processing is charged. A random instruction supplies one fresh uniform \(w\)-bit word, independent of all previous random words. There are no exact-real primitives, oracle calls, nonuniform advice, or precomputed tables supplied at no cost. The program may use \(w\) as the machine word length. Preprocessing, input access, initialization it performs and writing every output word are included in time.

Randomness and correctness. For a fixed valid input, the probability space is the infinite sequence of independent uniform random words used by the machine. Let \(T_A(G,R)\) count its operations, with value \(+\infty\) on a nonterminating execution. For every input, termination must have probability one. On every terminating execution, including those outside the success event, the output indices must represent a matching. On each input separately,
\[\Pr_R[\text{the output matching has cardinality }\nu(G)]\ge2/3.\]
The output may be suboptimal on other executions, but it must remain feasible. No distribution over input graphs is assumed, and success is not merely an expectation bound on matching size. A single program is used for every graph and edge-list order.

Almost-linear expected time. The expectation is over the algorithm's random words, with the input fixed. The notation in the question means that this same algorithm and word constant satisfy
\[\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists C_\varepsilon>0\ \exists N_\varepsilon\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall G\text{ with }N\ge N_\varepsilon:\quad \mathbb E_R[T_A(G,R)]\le C_\varepsilon N^{1+\varepsilon}.\]
Constants and the threshold may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and on the fixed algorithm, but not on the graph, its density, its edge order or its random choices. The slack \(\varepsilon\) is not an input selecting a different program. This is a worst-case-over-inputs bound on expected time, not a bound on every individual random execution. The claim covers sparse and dense graphs simultaneously and allows subpolynomial overhead beyond polylogarithmic factors.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence statement or its logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify a uniform finite program and a fixed word constant, prove almost-sure termination and feasibility on every terminating execution, prove per-input success probability at least \(2/3\), and establish the displayed expected-time bound for every positive exponent slack. All preprocessing, arithmetic and explicit output costs must fit that proof. A deterministic exact algorithm meeting the time bound is also a positive answer.

A negative answer must rule out all algorithms in the allowed randomized model. Equivalently, for every fixed word constant and program satisfying the termination, feasibility and success requirements, prove that there is some \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, for every \(C>0\) and every size threshold \(N_0\), there is a valid graph encoding with \(N\ge N_0\) and \(\mathbb E[T_A]>C N^{1+\varepsilon}\). The exponent slack may depend on the program. A conditional running-time lower bound must name its unproved assumptions and does not alone establish this unconditional negation.

Algorithms only for bipartite graphs, a near-linear maximal matching, a fixed-accuracy approximation, the optimum size without an output matching, and average performance on random input graphs do not meet the full target. Bounds for pointer machines, parallel rounds, catalytic space or restricted algorithmic techniques must not be substituted for the permitted word-RAM expected time. No additive numerical tolerance applies to either exact optimality or the asymptotic exponent.

title: Near-linear-time short cycle decomposition
summary: The input is a finite undirected unweighted graph given explicitly. Partition its edges into simple cycles and a small uncovered remainder; cycles may meet at vertices but cannot share an edge. The target is a uniform near-linear-time algorithm with only fixed polylogarithmic factors in its running time, cycle length, and remainder divided by the vertex count. Randomized algorithms are allowed with probability at least two thirds that the entire decomposition is valid, while every execution obeys the time bound. Known almost-linear-time constructions do not automatically meet this stronger running-time requirement.
formal:
Can short cycle decomposition be computed in near-linear time with only polylogarithmic losses in cycle length and the number of uncovered edges?

Precisely, put \(h(n)=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). Do there exist one uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(C,a,b,c,q\), with \(q\ge2\), such that the following holds for every finite simple undirected unweighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(n\ge1\), and \(m=|E|\)?

On the explicit input defined below, using words of \(q h(n)\) bits, every execution of \(A\) halts within
\[
C(n+m)h(n)^a
\]
operations. With probability at least \(2/3\), it outputs simple cycles \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_t\) and an edge set \(R\) satisfying
\[
E=R\;\dot\cup\; E(Q_1)\;\dot\cup\;\cdots\;\dot\cup\; E(Q_t),
\qquad
|R|\le C n h(n)^c,
\qquad
|E(Q_i)|\le C h(n)^b\quad(1\le i\le t)?
\]
Here \(\dot\cup\) denotes disjoint union: no edge may appear in two output pieces. Distinct cycles may share vertices. All constants, logarithmic exponents, and the program are chosen before the input graph.
definitions:
The graph has no loops or parallel edges. Disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed. The input gives \(n,m\) and an array of \(m\) distinct unordered pairs of different vertex labels, with each pair written in increasing order. These array positions identify the edges; their order is arbitrary. Input entries are binary integers stored in machine words. The algorithm must handle every valid such representation. The additive \(n\) in the time bound includes the cost of processing the vertex set, even when \(m<n\).

A simple cycle is a cyclic list \((v_0,\ldots,v_{\ell-1})\) of \(\ell\ge3\) distinct vertices such that every consecutive pair, including \(\{v_{\ell-1},v_0\}\), is an input edge. Its length is its number \(\ell\) of edges. Each output cycle is written explicitly as this vertex list. The remainder \(R\) is written as a list of input edge indices. The number \(t\) of cycles may be zero. The displayed partition covers every input edge exactly once; the remainder has no additional structural requirement. Every listed cycle must use only edges of the original graph, without adding shortcut edges, contracting vertices, or reusing an edge in multiple cycles.

The word RAM is a sequential random-access machine with one finite program independent of \(n\). Its word length is \(w=q h(n)\) bits. It has a fixed finite number of registers and a word-addressed memory with \(2^w\) cells. Each register and memory cell holds a word-sized unsigned integer; addresses occupy one word, and work memory is initially zero. Reading or writing one word, copying, comparison, conditional branching, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts by fewer than \(w\) positions each cost one operation. Addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, also cost one operation. Shifts discard bits outside the word. Fresh independent unbiased random bits are available at unit cost per bit. Input access, workspace operations, and writing every output word count toward running time. There is no oracle, nonuniform advice, unbounded-precision arithmetic, or free graph preprocessing.

Probability is over the algorithm's independent random bits for a fixed input. The entire output must simultaneously satisfy all the stated conditions with probability at least \(2/3\). On other runs it may report failure or produce an invalid output, but the same worst-case time bound still applies. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as a special case.

In this card, a polylogarithmic factor means at most a fixed power of \(h(n)\), up to a fixed multiplier. The three exponents may differ but cannot grow with \(n\). Near-linear time means the displayed \((n+m)\)-times-polylogarithmic bound, rather than a bound allowing an arbitrary subpolynomial factor.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence statement above or its logical negation. A positive result must specify one uniform algorithm and fixed constants, prove the running-time bound on every random tape, and establish the joint success probability for every valid input graph. A negative result must rule out every choice of program and fixed constants in this model; an explicitly conditional lower bound alone does not establish the unconditional negation.

Existence of the decomposition without the required construction time is insufficient. An almost-linear-time result, or a near-linear algorithm whose cycle length or uncovered-edge bound has an arbitrary \(n^{o(1)}\) loss, qualifies only if its actual bounds meet the fixed logarithmic powers required here. This is a binary algorithm-existence target, not a request to approximate a running-time exponent numerically.

title: Deterministic Exact Matching
summary: Exact Matching asks whether a red/blue graph has a perfect matching with exactly the requested number of red edges. The target is one deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm for all simple undirected graphs. Knowing only the minimum and maximum red counts does not determine which intermediate counts are attainable. The recent faster general algorithm remains randomized, while a separate claimed deterministic result is restricted to bipartite graphs. A complete Lean-checked solution must establish membership in P or prove its unconditional negation.
formal:
Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A\), a real constant \(K>0\) and an integer \(d\ge1\) such that, for every explicitly given finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with an even number \(n\ge0\) of vertices, every red-edge subset \(R\subseteq E\), and every integer \(0\le k\le n/2\), the machine halts within \(K(N+1)^d\) steps and outputs YES exactly when
\[
 \exists M\subseteq E:\qquad
 \bigl(\forall v\in V,\ |\{e\in M:v\in e\}|=1\bigr)
 \quad\text{and}\quad |M\cap R|=k?
\]
Here \(N\) is the input bit length under the explicit encoding below. No bipartition is promised.
definitions:
Vertices are labelled \(1,\ldots,n\), and an edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices. Loops and parallel edges are excluded. Every edge is either red, meaning it belongs to \(R\), or blue, meaning it belongs to \(E\setminus R\). The graph, all its edges and their colours are given explicitly, not through an oracle or a succinct circuit. One fixed encoding uses a length-prefixed binary header and a list of adjacency records, one for each vertex including isolated vertices, with neighbour labels and colour bits; each undirected edge has consistent entries at both endpoints. The integer \(k\) is in binary. The encoding contains all \(n\) vertex records, so its length is at least \(n\); a binary header alone does not describe exponentially many unlisted vertices.

A matching is a subset of edges no two of which share a vertex. It is perfect if every vertex belongs to one of its edges, equivalently the degree condition in the formula. Every perfect matching then has \(n/2\) edges. The requested count is exactly \(k\) red edges, rather than at least \(k\), at most \(k\) or a count congruent to \(k\) modulo an integer. On the empty graph, the empty matching is perfect and the allowed input \(k=0\) has answer YES.

The machine is one uniform finite classical multitape Turing program; all bit operations, reading, auxiliary computation and output count toward its running time. It has no random bits, nonuniform advice or external oracle. The same \(A,K,d\) must work on every input size, colour pattern and allowed \(k\), with no error. Malformed encodings, odd vertex counts and out-of-range values of \(k\) can be rejected as invalid inputs in polynomial time. The graph may be disconnected, nonplanar and nonbipartite, with arbitrary degrees.

The required output is a decision bit; computing the number of matchings is not requested. Polynomial time means membership of this explicitly encoded decision language in the class \(\mathrm{P}\). Only sequential polynomial time is sought; a polylogarithmic-depth parallel algorithm is not required. The statement is unconditional: no computational hardness or derandomization assumption is supplied.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the stated deterministic algorithm and common polynomial bound exist, or a complete Lean-checked proof that this decision language does not belong to \(\mathrm{P}\).

A positive answer must cover both YES and NO instances on all finite simple graphs. A randomized polynomial-time procedure, nonuniform circuit family, special graph class, exact-parity test or algorithm with a small red-count or matching-size error does not by itself suffice. A conditional lower bound or a barrier to one algebraic approach is not an unconditional negative answer. No numerical approximation tolerance applies.

title: Exact directed maximum flow in \(O((m+n) \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time
summary: An exact maximum flow routes the largest possible integral amount between two terminals while obeying every arc capacity and intermediate conservation law. For each fixed polynomial bound on capacities, the question asks for one algorithm whose time is input size times a single fixed power of a logarithm. The specified randomized word-RAM must respect that total time on every execution and return a complete optimal flow with probability at least two thirds on each valid input. A complete Lean proof must supply the algorithm and both guarantees or rule out all such algorithms for some fixed capacity exponent. The checked exact almost-linear algorithms and undirected approximation results do not establish this fixed-polylogarithmic exact directed-flow target.
formal:
For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm \(A_a\), integers \(B_a\ge a+3\), \(k_a\ge0\) and \(C_a\ge1\) with the following property? On every explicitly represented directed graph \(G\) with \(n\ge2\) vertices, \(m\) arcs, distinct terminals \(s,t\), and integer arc capacities
\[0\le u_e\le n^a,\]
the algorithm uses words of \(w=B_a\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, halts on every random execution within
\[C_a(m+n)\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil^{k_a}\]
word operations, and outputs an exact integral maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow with probability at least \(2/3\)?
The output must give a flow value on every original arc. The algorithm, constants and logarithmic exponent may depend on \(a\), but not on the graph, its capacities, its terminal choices or its input ordering. The complete graph, flow and machine conventions are specified below.
definitions:
Graph and representation. The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). An ordered arc list \((e_1,\ldots,e_m)\) consists of distinct ordered pairs \(e_j=(x_j,y_j)\in[n]^2\) with \(x_j\ne y_j\), so \(0\le m\le n(n-1)\). Opposite arcs may both occur and have independent capacities; parallel copies of the same ordered pair and loops are excluded. The graph may be disconnected and may contain isolated vertices and zero-capacity arcs. The terminals \(s,t\in[n]\) are distinct. The input is an array of machine words containing the header \((n,m,s,t)\), the list \(1,\ldots,n\) of vertices, and the triples \((x_j,y_j,u_{e_j})\) in the given arc order. Correctness and time bounds hold for every ordering. Capacities and labels are unsigned integers, each in one word. The explicit vertex list fixes the \(m+n\) convention even when \(m=0\). There is no succinct representation, adjacency oracle or precomputed index.

Feasible flow and optimum. A flow is a list \(f=(f_{e_1},\ldots,f_{e_m})\) of integers with \(0\le f_e\le u_e\) on every arc and
\[\sum_{e=(x,v)}f_e=\sum_{e=(v,y)}f_e\qquad\text{for every }v\in[n]\setminus\{s,t\}.\]
Each sum ranges over the arcs actually present. Its value is the net flow leaving the source,
\[\operatorname{val}(f)=\sum_{e=(s,y)}f_e-\sum_{e=(x,s)}f_e.\]
Incoming arcs at \(s\), outgoing arcs at \(t\), and circulations are allowed. Conservation implies that this equals the net flow entering \(t\). Define \(F(G,u,s,t)\) as the largest value among the feasible integral flows. The set of such flows is finite and nonempty because the all-zero list is feasible, so the maximum is attained and nonnegative. Also \(F\le(n-1)n^a\). The usual integral-flow theorem identifies this optimum with the real-valued maximum flow for integral capacities. A successful output is the list of exactly \(m\) integers in original arc order that forms a feasible flow with value \(F\). No prescribed tie-breaking between different optimal flows is required. If \(m=0\), the empty list is the correct output.

Machine model. Put \(L_n=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), so each word contains \(w=B_aL_n\) bits. A word stores an integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). The random-access machine has a fixed finite program, a fixed finite set of registers and word-addressed memory; input words occupy the initial array and other memory is initially zero. Each executed instruction costs one operation. Allowed instructions are word reads and writes, moves, conditional branches, comparisons, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned integer division with a nonzero divisor. A logical shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. A memory address must fit in one word. Input, output and all memory used must fit within the address space, with \(B_a\) chosen as part of the algorithm's fixed constants. Arithmetic on more than one word must be implemented using these operations and charged accordingly. Exact real arithmetic is not a unit-cost instruction.

Randomness and resources. A random-word instruction returns a fresh independent uniform element of \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\) at cost one; equivalently its bits are independent fair bits. The success probability is over this sequence for each fixed valid input. A run outside the successful event may return a failure marker or an incorrect result, but must obey the same time bound. All graph preprocessing, memory accesses, random generation and writing of output words are charged. The bound is on the total running time of every run of this one static computation, not merely on expected time or on typical executions. An amortized analysis of internal operations is permitted if it establishes this total bound. There are no oracles, quantum operations, input-dependent advice or free preprocessing. Behavior outside the stated input promises is unrestricted.

Uniformity and quantifiers. For each fixed \(a\), one finite program works for all \(n,m,G,u,s,t\); it cannot contain a table or different advice indexed by \(n\). The quantifier order is
\[\forall a\ge1\ \exists A_a,B_a,k_a,C_a\ \forall(G,u,s,t).\]
The selected target does not additionally require an effective procedure that constructs \(A_a\) from \(a\), a common logarithmic exponent for all \(a\), or a bound polynomial in \(a\). For each fixed \(a\), however, \(k_a\) is a single integer independent of input size. The explicit running-time expression is precisely the meaning of the title's \(O((m+n)\operatorname{polylog}n)\).
answer_criterion: Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the existence proposition or its logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish, for each fixed capacity exponent \(a\), one program and fixed constants satisfying both the every-run time bound and the per-input success probability, including exact integral feasibility and optimality of all output arc values. A deterministic algorithm with that bound also qualifies. A negative proof must establish a fixed \(a\ge1\) for which every uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm in this model having any such fixed-polylogarithmic worst-case bound has some valid instance with success probability strictly below \(2/3\). A lower bound for one flow framework, an oracle-only algorithm, or a conditional conjecture does not prove that universal negation. A \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximate flow, the optimum value alone, an algorithm for a restricted graph class, or a bound of \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) without the required fixed logarithmic overhead is insufficient. The algorithmic exact-flow requirement is retained; numerical benchmark tolerance does not replace its output specification.

title: Almost-linear triangle detection
summary: The input is an explicit undirected graph, and the output says whether three distinct vertices are pairwise adjacent. One fixed randomized program must work on every graph and every adjacency-list order. Every execution must take almost linear time in the number of vertices plus edges, with success probability at least two thirds on every input. The local-sketching argument overestimates the probability that the two relevant neighbors land in the same prefix class. The published bounds reviewed leave the all-density almost-linear target open.
formal: Does one uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm exist that, for every finite simple undirected graph with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges given by explicit adjacency lists, returns whether a triangle exists with probability at least \(2/3\), while every execution takes at most \((n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}\) word instructions? The running-time guarantee must cover all graph densities, all valid adjacency-list orders and every random tape.
definitions:
Let \(n\ge0\), \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E\) be a set of unordered pairs of distinct elements of \(V\). Set \(m=|E|\). There are no loops or multiple edges. A triangle is a set \(\{u,v,z\}\) of three distinct vertices for which all three pairs are edges. The output is YES exactly when such a set exists, and NO otherwise; the algorithm need not output a witness or list triangles.

The input supplies \(n,m\), an array of \(n+1\) list offsets, and a contiguous array of \(2m\) vertex labels. The segment for vertex \(v\) contains precisely its neighbors, in an arbitrary order. Each undirected edge occurs once in each endpoint's list. Validity of this representation is promised. Vertex labels, counts and offsets occupy single words. Thus the input occupies \(O(n+m+1)\) words. Disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed; graphs with fewer than three vertices are legitimate NO-instances.

The word length is
\[
 w=\left\lceil4\log_2(n+2)\right\rceil.
\]
Memory consists of addressable \(w\)-bit words; addresses are unsigned words. Input is initially stored in its specified arrays, and other memory is initially zero. A fixed finite program may read or write one addressed word, copy a word, compare unsigned words, branch, perform bitwise Boolean operations, shift logically, add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\), or take the integer quotient and remainder of unsigned division by a nonzero word, at unit cost per instruction. A shift by at least \(w\) positions returns zero. It may also obtain one independent uniform \(w\)-bit random word in one instruction. Longer integers and algebraic operations must be implemented using these instructions. There is no unit-cost arbitrary-precision arithmetic, matrix-product oracle, input-dependent advice or free precomputed table. All input access and preprocessing count toward time. The fixed word length permits the explicit graph representation at every \(n\).

Precisely, set \(S=n+m+2\). The algorithm must halt on every valid graph and every random tape. For every real \(\varepsilon>0\), there must be an integer \(S_\varepsilon\) such that, on every valid input with \(S\ge S_\varepsilon\), every execution uses at most \(S^{1+\varepsilon}\) instructions. The same program works for every \(\varepsilon\); it does not receive \(\varepsilon\) as input. This convention absorbs fixed multiplicative constants and defines the displayed almost-linear bound. Thresholds may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and the program, but not on the graph, its list order or the random tape.

For each fixed input separately, the probability over internal random words of a correct YES/NO output must be at least \(2/3\). There is no average-case input distribution, degree bound, forbidden-subgraph promise, triangle-count promise or restriction to combinatorial methods. Algebraic algorithms are allowed with their actual implementation cost. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as a special case.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked construction and proof of an algorithm satisfying the exact uniformity, word model, all-input time and per-input probability guarantees; or give a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists in this model.

A bound with any fixed exponent greater than one is insufficient. A quadratic bound in \(n\) alone need not be almost linear on sparse inputs. Restricted graph classes, counting or listing results, average-case guarantees, and conditional lower bounds do not settle the target by themselves. An expected-time or high-probability-time result needs a proved conversion to the stated all-tapes bound and success guarantee. A separate program for each exponent slack requires a justified uniform combination. The negation of this target need not supply one common positive exponent gap against every algorithm. No numerical approximation tolerance applies to the decision.

title: Linear-time directed shortest paths with nonnegative real weights
summary: The task is to compute every exact distance from one source in a directed graph with nonnegative real arc lengths. The requested running time is linear in the number of vertices and arcs. A uniform deterministic machine may compare, add and subtract real values but cannot inspect their encodings. All memory access, control, preprocessing and output instructions count toward the bound. The latest expected-time speedup for undirected graphs leaves the deterministic linear-time problem on directed graphs open.
formal: Do there exist an integer word-size constant \(B\ge3\), an absolute constant \(K>0\), and one uniform deterministic comparison-addition RAM algorithm that, on every explicitly given simple directed graph with \(n\ge2\) vertices and \(m\) arcs of arbitrary nonnegative real lengths, and every specified source vertex, outputs all exact source distances within \(K(n+m)\) instructions? The model below charges control, memory access, preprocessing and output as well as operations on real values.
definitions:
The graph has vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), no loops and at most one arc for each ordered pair of distinct vertices; opposite arcs are allowed. Input consists of \(n,m\), a source \(s\in[n]\), and an arbitrary-order explicit list of all arcs, each with its two integer endpoints and one exact real length \(w_e\ge0\). There is no bound on real magnitudes or rationality. Zero lengths, zero-length cycles, disconnected graphs and vertices unreachable from the source are allowed.

A directed walk from \(s\) to \(v\) follows arcs in their given directions and has length equal to the sum of their lengths. The empty walk has length zero. For a reachable vertex, its distance is the minimum of these lengths; nonnegative weights allow repeated vertices to be removed without increasing length, so a minimum is attained by a simple path, or by the empty path when \(v=s\). An unreachable vertex has distance \(+\infty\). The output is an array indexed by \([n]\), containing each exact finite distance or a distinct infinity marker. No sorted order of distances is requested, and an unevaluated implicit distance expression is not the output.

The machine has integer control words of \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits and separately typed exact-real cells. Integer addresses must fit a word. An instruction can read or write one cell, copy a value, compare values of the same type and branch. Integer instructions also include Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and quotient or remainder by a nonzero word. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Multiword computations pay for their constituent instructions.

Real instructions are copying, comparison, addition and subtraction, each of unit cost. Finitely many rational program constants are allowed. There is no real multiplication or division, rounding, floor, access to digits or bits, or conversion of an input-dependent real value to an integer. Real values cannot serve as addresses. Integer instructions cannot inspect real encodings. The saved subtraction convention can be represented with pairs of sums and comparisons of such pairs; it does not supply multiplication or encoding access. The infinity output is a separate tag and is not treated as a real operand.

One finite program and the constants \(B,K\) work for all \(n,m,s\), graphs and real inputs. There are no random bits, advice strings, precomputed input-dependent tables or free oracles. Every executed instruction counts, including graph preprocessing, initialization of working storage, control and address arithmetic, and writing the \(n\) outputs. Table construction is charged. Time is worst-case over all inputs, and includes every operation needed to choose the next real comparison or sum; bounding only the number of real arithmetic operations is insufficient. The algorithm must halt correctly on every allowed input. The linear bound is uniform over real edge values and graph density.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of a program and constants with the stated all-input bound, or prove its logical negation in exactly this model. A one-sided improvement above linear time, a result only for undirected graphs or integer weights, or a bound that excludes control and preprocessing time does not suffice. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion unless the condition is also proved.

title: Deterministic almost-linear vertex connectivity
summary: Vertex connectivity is the smallest number of vertices whose deletion disconnects a graph or leaves at most one vertex. The input is an explicit unweighted undirected graph, including all isolated vertices. The task is to output the exact value and an attaining set in deterministic almost-linear worst-case time. Randomized almost-linear time is known, while the reviewed deterministic bound retains a connectivity factor. A complete Lean-checked answer must cover every connectivity value with the same algorithm and time bound.
formal:
Do there exist one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm \(A\), a real constant \(K>0\), an integer word-size constant \(d\ge4\), and a function \(h:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to[1,\infty)\) satisfying
\[
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\log h(N)}{\log N}=0
\]
such that, for every explicitly given simple unweighted undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge2\), \(m=|E|\) and \(N=n+m\), the algorithm uses at most \(KNh(N)\) instructions and outputs both
\[
 \kappa(G)=\min\bigl\{|S|:S\subseteq V,
 G[V\setminus S]\text{ is disconnected or }|V\setminus S|\le1\bigr\}
\]
and a set \(S\) attaining this minimum?

The machine has word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) and the operations and charged costs below. No randomness is allowed.
definitions:
An edge is an unordered pair of distinct labelled vertices. Loops, parallel edges, edge weights and vertex weights are absent. The input explicitly lists all \(n\) vertices, including isolated ones, and the \(m\) edges as pairs of endpoint labels, with length headers. It occupies \(\Theta(n+m)\) words; a small binary header cannot stand for an unlisted exponentially large set of vertices. Edge order is arbitrary.

The induced graph \(G[V\setminus S]\) deletes every vertex of \(S\) and all its incident edges. A graph with at least two vertices is disconnected when some two of them have no path between them. The separate at-most-one-vertex clause defines the degenerate endpoint. In particular, \(\kappa(G)=0\) for an initially disconnected graph and \(\kappa(K_n)=n-1\) for a complete graph. There is always an attaining set. The requested output lists its vertices explicitly without repetitions, together with its integer size. Any minimum set is allowed; no canonical choice is prescribed.

This is global vertex connectivity: no distinguished source or sink is part of the input. The measure counts deleted vertices, not deleted edges. Every graph is allowed, including disconnected, dense and complete graphs, with connectivity possibly growing linearly in \(n\). A fixed-parameter running time whose hidden coefficient depends on \(\kappa(G)\) does not automatically give the stated uniform bound.

The uniform sequential word RAM is a fixed finite program with unsigned \(w\)-bit words, word-sized addresses and no advice, external oracle or free lookup table. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copies, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Computation involving multiple words pays for each constituent instruction. All initialization, input access, preprocessing, constructed tables, auxiliary computation and output writes are charged. Both correctness and the instruction bound hold on every input, without random choices or error.

The function \(h\) depends only on \(N\), not on the graph or its connectivity, and is only a bound rather than an oracle supplied to the program. The same algorithm has running time \(N^{1+o(1)}\): for every real \(\eta>0\), it runs in \(O(N^{1+\eta})\) for all sufficiently large \(N\), with the constant and threshold allowed to depend on \(\eta\). A different program for each fixed \(\eta\) is not the one-program assertion here. No separate space bound is imposed beyond the stated machine and charged time.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the stated algorithm, constants and bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof of their logical nonexistence in this model.

A positive answer must compute the exact value and an attaining vertex set on every allowed graph within the common worst-case time bound. A randomized algorithm, an approximation, a result for bounded connectivity or a conditional lower bound does not decide the full proposition. No numerical approximation tolerance applies to this algorithm-existence target.

title: Polynomial-time computation of planar treewidth
summary: Can one polynomial-time algorithm compute the exact treewidth of every planar graph? Treewidth measures how small the largest bag can be in a tree decomposition, counting its size minus one. The input graph can have arbitrarily large treewidth. A related parameter, branchwidth, can be computed exactly on planar graphs and gives an approximation to treewidth. The running time for obtaining the exact value on all planar graphs remains open.
formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that computes the exact treewidth of every finite planar graph?

Precisely, do there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that \(M\) halts on every binary input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions and, for every finite simple planar graph \(G\) in the encoding below,
\[
M(\operatorname{enc}(G))=\operatorname{bin}_{\pm}(\operatorname{tw}(G))?
\]
The output is the exact integer treewidth in the specified signed binary encoding. Graph size and treewidth are unrestricted; the polynomial is fixed independently of both. No planar embedding, tree decomposition or bound on treewidth is supplied with the graph.

This is the polynomial-time existence question stated in §4.6 of the 2016 seminar report. It asks for an exact algorithm, not an optimal numerical running-time exponent. A negative answer is the full negation of that existence assertion, not merely an NP-hardness theorem conditional on a separate complexity-class separation.
definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph is \(G=(V,E)\), with \(V=[n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) for an integer \(n\ge0\), and \(E\) a set of two-element subsets of \(V\). Loops and parallel edges are absent; isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and the empty graph are allowed. Graphs are unweighted. A path is a sequence of distinct vertices with consecutive vertices joined by edges. A cycle is a closed sequence of at least three edges visiting no vertex twice except its starting and ending vertex. A nonempty finite tree is a finite simple connected graph with no cycle; it has a unique path between each pair of its vertices.

A graph is planar if its vertices can be mapped injectively to points of \(\mathbb R^2\), and each edge can be represented by a continuous injective curve \([0,1]\to\mathbb R^2\) whose endpoints are the points of its two vertices, such that no interior point of a curve is a vertex point and distinct edge curves intersect only at common endpoint vertices. The existence of such a drawing is a promise on the input graph; its curves and coordinates are not part of the input. The algorithm is not required to output a drawing.

A tree decomposition is a nonempty finite tree \(T\) with a bag \(B_t\subseteq V\) at each node \(t\in V(T)\), satisfying
\[
\bigcup_{t\in V(T)} B_t=V,
\qquad
\forall\{u,v\}\in E\ \exists t\in V(T):\{u,v\}\subseteq B_t,
\]
and the connectedness condition: for every \(v\in V\), the set \(\{t\in V(T):v\in B_t\}\) induces a connected subtree of \(T\). Equivalently, every node on the unique path between two bags containing \(v\) also has \(v\) in its bag. Empty bags are allowed. The width of this decomposition is \(\max_{t\in V(T)}|B_t|-1\), and
\[
\operatorname{tw}(G)=
\min_{(T,(B_t))\text{ a tree decomposition of }G}
\left(\max_{t\in V(T)}|B_t|-1\right).
\]
The one-node tree with bag \(V\) is a decomposition, so the minimum exists. For the empty graph this convention gives \(-1\); for any nonempty graph it is an integer between \(0\) and \(n-1\). The convention on the single empty graph does not affect polynomial-time solvability.

Encode \(G\) as the bitstring \(1^n0\) followed by exactly \(n(n-1)/2\) bits. These final bits list the indicators of \(\{i,j\}\in E\) in lexicographic order of pairs \((i,j)\) with \(0\le i<j<n\). Thus the encoding length is
\[
L(G)=n+1+\frac{n(n-1)}2.
\]
The empty graph is encoded by the single bit 0. The unary prefix includes every vertex, even if isolated. This explicit adjacency encoding and the ordinary explicit adjacency-list encoding are polynomially interconvertible, so the chosen representation does not alter the polynomial-time question.

The output encoding \(\operatorname{bin}_{\pm}(z)\) for an integer \(z\) is one sign bit, 0 for a nonnegative integer and 1 for a negative integer, followed by the usual base-two representation of \(|z|\), with no leading zero except that zero has magnitude string 0. Negative zero is forbidden. For example, the output for the empty graph's treewidth is the sign bit 1 followed by the magnitude bit 1. Exact numerical equality is part of the algorithm's task; it is not an additional demand for an exact-value benchmark answer.

A deterministic multitape Turing machine has one finite program, a finite tape alphabet, a read-only binary input tape, finitely many work tapes initially blank, and a binary output tape. A transition inspects or changes only the scanned symbol on each tape and moves each head by at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including reading the graph, arithmetic, preprocessing and writing the answer. There is no oracle, random tape, advice depending on input length, unbounded-word unit-cost arithmetic or free preprocessing. The polynomial clock is worst case and applies to every bitstring, including malformed encodings and encodings of nonplanar graphs. On those inputs, correctness and the output format are unrestricted. Imposing this total clock does not change the promised polynomial-time question, because a candidate machine with fixed bounds can be stopped at its own polynomial clock.

An algorithm returning only the exact minimum width suffices; an optimal tree decomposition need not be printed. Conversely, any polynomial-time algorithm producing an optimal decomposition would also answer this question. Fixed-parameter algorithms whose dependence on treewidth is superpolynomial do not give the required single polynomial bound when treewidth is unrestricted.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the exact algorithm-existence proposition, or its full logical negation, using the definitions and encoding above.

A positive answer must specify a finite deterministic machine and fixed polynomial bound, prove the total clock, and prove that its output is the exact treewidth for every encoded planar graph. It must cover all sizes, components and treewidth values, without an embedding or decomposition in the input.

A negative answer must prove that for every finite deterministic machine \(M\) and every pair of integers \(C,k\ge1\), at least one of the following holds:
\[
\exists x\in\{0,1\}^{*}:\quad
M(x)\text{ does not halt within }C(|x|+1)^k\text{ transitions},
\]
or
\[
\exists G\text{ finite, simple and planar}:\quad
M(\operatorname{enc}(G))\text{ fails to halt with output }
\operatorname{bin}_{\pm}(\operatorname{tw}(G)).
\]
Failure includes a malformed output, an incorrect integer or nontermination. The graph or failing input may depend on the machine and its proposed bound. Refuting one particular algorithm is insufficient.

An NP-hardness proof together with a proof of \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) would give a negative answer; NP-hardness alone is not the negation of polynomial-time solvability.
