definitions: Use a deterministic uniform word RAM with word width \(w=\Theta(\log(n+2))\) large enough to address the stated space and with no nonuniform advice. Use the [integer word instructions](definitions.html#ram) at width \(w\). The vertex set [n] is fixed, graphs are simple and undirected, and updates insert an absent edge or delete a present edge. The graph starts empty and all outputs must be correct for every legal update sequence. Intermediate graphs may be nonplanar. A graph is planar when its vertices and edges can be drawn in the plane so that edges meet only at common endpoints. After every update a query must return the exact Boolean planarity value; neither an embedding nor an obstruction is requested. Require initialization O(n log^c(n+2)), space O((n+m)log^c(n+2)) words for current edge count m, O(log^c(n+2)) time for every individual update, and O(1) time for every query, for one absolute c. Rejected insertions or a promise that the graph stays planar are not allowed. The structure must reclaim unused edge storage within the stated space bound.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proof of the specified correctness and resource guarantees, or prove that this precise target is impossible. A lower bound under an additional complexity hypothesis settles the negative answer only together with a proof of that hypothesis.

title: Fast constant-factor fully dynamic edit distance
summary: Two strings change through insertions, deletions and substitutions at arbitrary positions. The goal is a constant-factor estimate of their current edit distance after each update. The selected data structure allows polynomial initialization and requires polylogarithmic expected amortized updates and constant-time queries. The cited result obtains subpolynomial factors and times, which are weaker guarantees. The question asks whether general sequence similarity can be maintained at the cost of elementary dynamic operations.
formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(A\ge1\) and a randomized fully dynamic data structure that maintains two strings of length at most \(N\), after polynomial preprocessing and in polynomial space, under arbitrary single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions, with expected amortized update time \((\log(2+N))^{O(1)}\) and constant query time, returning \(D\) with \(\operatorname{ED}(X,Y)\le D\le A\operatorname{ED}(X,Y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) at each specified query against an oblivious update sequence?
definitions:
Fix a maximum length \(N\ge2\) and alphabet \(\Sigma=[N]\), with symbols occupying \(O(\log N)\) bits. Both strings may be empty. An update identifies one string and a current position, then inserts one symbol into a gap, deletes one existing symbol, or replaces one symbol. Only valid updates keeping both lengths at most \(N\) are required. Edit distance is the minimum number of unit-cost insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming one entire string into the other.

Preprocessing receives \(N\) and the two initial strings, each as an array with one symbol per word and an explicit length. Use a word RAM with word width \(w=\Theta(\log N)\) large enough to address the allowed polynomial storage. Use the [integer word instructions](definitions.html#ram) at width \(w\). A fresh independent uniform word costs one step. The data structure has a uniform finite program. For some absolute exponent \(c\), preprocessing and storage are at most \(N^c\). For every fixed finite legal sequence of \(t\) updates, the expected total update cost, excluding preprocessing, is at most \(C t(\log(2+N))^c\). Expectation is over the data structure's internal randomness.

The entire sequence of updates and query times is chosen independently of that randomness and of answers; this is the oblivious-adversary convention. At each fixed query time, the approximation inequalities hold with probability at least \(2/3\). The statement does not require one probability event covering infinitely many queries or robustness to answer-dependent updates. The returned value is a numerical estimate only, not an alignment or edit script. Multiplicative approximation forces \(D=0\) when the strings agree.

The factor \(A\) is independent of maximum length, alphabet and the update history. Neither an \(N^{o(1)}\) factor nor \(N^{o(1)}\) update time implies the requested constant and polylogarithmic bounds. The alphabet and error/adversary conventions above make the imported editorial strengthening explicit.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked construction and proof of all stated space, initialization, update, query and approximation guarantees, or a Lean-checked refutation in this model. Bounds for substitutions only, small-distance promises, static strings, or subpolynomial rather than polylogarithmic update time are insufficient. A lower bound relying on an additional complexity hypothesis settles the negative answer only if that hypothesis is also proved.

title: Worst-case logarithmic dynamic planar convex hulls
summary: Maintain an arbitrary changing set of exact points in the plane, starting from the empty set. Insertions and deletions may occur in any order, and a query asks for one point farthest in a supplied direction. The target is deterministic logarithmic worst-case time for each operation and linear total space. Known optimal amortized bounds and recent practical implementations do not provide that per-operation guarantee. The answer must be a complete Lean-checked construction or unconditional refutation in the specified real-arithmetic model.
formal: Does there exist one uniform deterministic data structure and an absolute constant \(K\ge1\) that maintain a finite set \(P\subset\mathbb R^2\), initially empty, with the following guarantees on every finite valid online sequence? Each point insertion, point deletion and extreme-point query takes at most \(K\log_2(n+2)\) worst-case real-RAM steps, where \(n\) is the larger set size immediately before and after that operation. The stored representation uses at most \(K(1+|P|)\) cells. Given any \(u\in\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}\), an extreme-point query returns a point \(p\in P\) maximizing \(\langle u,p\rangle\), or an empty marker if \(P=\varnothing\).
definitions:
Insert receives the two exact real coordinates of a point not currently in \(P\), adds it and returns a stable handle. Delete receives a valid handle for a currently present point and removes that point; the handle then becomes invalid. A previously deleted coordinate pair may be inserted again with a new handle. A handle is only a reference to an item, not an encoding of free auxiliary information. Each live handle must remain usable until its item is deleted, including across internal restructuring.

For \(u=(u_x,u_y)\) and \(p=(p_x,p_y)\), the objective is \(\langle u,p\rangle=u_xp_x+u_yp_y\). Any maximizing point is acceptable, chosen deterministically by the algorithm. All finite sets are allowed: no general-position, distinct-x-coordinate, noncollinearity, convex-position or bounded-coordinate promise is made. Updates may occur in arbitrary order. A query returns only one point or an empty marker, not a cyclic list of the entire convex hull, its edges, or all changes caused by an update.

Use an algebraic real RAM with a fixed finite program. A cell stores an exact real scalar, a pointer or a constant-size control value. Copying a cell, reading or writing an addressed cell, following or changing a pointer, comparison, branching, exact real addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by a nonzero value each cost one step. Allocating or releasing a constant-size record also costs one step. The program contains only fixed rational numerical constants and uses ordinary discrete address bookkeeping; a real coordinate is not an address encoding. No floor, bit extraction from a real, arbitrary-precision packing primitive, unbounded parallel operation, randomness, advice or oracle is supplied. There is no charge for coordinate bit length: these are exact real-arithmetic costs, not rational-input bit complexity.

All stored points, handles, indexes, auxiliary records and retained historical information count toward space. All comparisons, rebuilding, initialization and query work count toward time. Initialization on the empty set takes constant time and space. Between operations at most \(K(1+|P|)\) cells are retained; during an operation at most \(K(1+n)\) cells, including its workspace, are used, after enlarging the same universal constant if necessary. The client holds input coordinates and handles but supplies no uncharged index or preprocessing. Deleted data may be retained only within the current space bound.

The algorithm must finish each operation and return its answer before seeing the next. It has no advance knowledge of the sequence length, future operations, maximum eventual set size or coordinate values. The one program and constant \(K\) work for every sequence and every direction. Both time and space are measured against current size; an occasional expensive update cannot be paid for by averaging over other operations. Reading two input coordinates or returning one stored point takes constant work.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must establish exact answers, linear total storage and a logarithmic bound for every individual insertion, deletion and query, with all rebuilding and workspace charged. A negative proof must rule out all data structures in the stated model unconditionally; a conditional lower bound is only a conditional result.

Logarithmic amortized updates, expected bounds, ordered or one-sided update restrictions, and data structures requiring superlinear storage do not meet the full target. An argument that explicitly reporting a changed hull can have linear output size does not refute this one-point query interface.

title: Polynomial-sample worst-case trace reconstruction
summary: A deletion trace removes each bit independently and hides the removed positions. Repeated traces all come from the same unknown binary string. The question asks whether polynomially many traces suffice for exact worst-case reconstruction. The deletion probability is any fixed constant strictly between zero and one. Only the number of traces is bounded; reconstruction time is unrestricted.
formal: For every fixed real deletion probability \(\delta\in(0,1)\), do there exist constants \(C_\delta>0\) and \(a_\delta\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that \[N_\delta(n)\le C_\delta n^{a_\delta}\qquad\text{for every }n\ge2?\] Here \(N_\delta(n)\), defined below, is the number of independent deletion traces needed to reconstruct every unknown \(n\)-bit string exactly with success probability at least \(2/3\). Processing is unrestricted, and the length and deletion probability are known. Constants may depend on fixed \(\delta\).
definitions:
Observation space. Fix \(n\in\mathbb N\) with \(n\ge2\), and a real \(\delta\in(0,1)\). An arbitrary fixed string \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\) is unknown. A deletion trace independently keeps each input bit with probability \(p=1-\delta\) and concatenates the surviving bits in their original order. The output lies in the finite set
\[\mathcal Y_n=\bigcup_{k=0}^{n}\{0,1\}^k,\]
where \(\{0,1\}^0\) consists of the empty string. The length of each received trace is observable. Its original retained indices and deletion mask are not supplied. There are no substitutions, insertions, reversals, cyclic shifts or alignment labels.

Trace law. For \(y\in\{0,1\}^k\), let \(e_x(y)\) be the number of increasing index tuples \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n\) with \(x_{i_j}=y_j\) for all \(j\). Define \(e_x(\varnothing)=1\). The trace distribution is
\[\mu_{x,\delta}(y)=e_x(y)(1-\delta)^k\delta^{n-k}.\]
Different deletion masks producing the same observed string all contribute to this probability. For example, for \(x=00\), the one-bit trace \(0\) has probability \(2(1-\delta)\delta\). All \(m\) observations use independent masks on the same original \(x\), so their joint distribution is \(\mu_{x,\delta}^{\otimes m}\).

Estimators. A randomized estimator for fixed \(n,\delta,m\) is a stochastic kernel \(K\) assigning every observed tuple \(\mathbf y\in\mathcal Y_n^m\) a probability distribution on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Thus \(K(\mathbf y,z)\ge0\) and \(\sum_zK(\mathbf y,z)=1\). The kernel may depend on \(n,\delta,m\), but not on the unknown string. It describes all permitted internal randomization; a deterministic estimator assigns probability one to a single output. Its success probability on \(x\) is
\[s_{x,\delta}(K)=\sum_{\mathbf y\in\mathcal Y_n^m}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mu_{x,\delta}(y_j)\right)K(\mathbf y,x).\]
The output must equal the whole original string, with its original linear order. Small edit distance, a list containing the string, or recovery of only some coordinates does not count as success. There is no prior distribution on \(x\); the success inequality must hold separately for every string.

Sample complexity. With \(\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), set
\[N_\delta(n)=\min\left\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\exists K\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^n,\ s_{x,\delta}(K)\ge\frac23\right\}.\]
For \(m=0\), the observation tuple is empty and the product is one. The minimum is finite: a single trace has length \(n\) with probability \((1-\delta)^n>0\), and any such trace equals \(x\). Consequently the probability of receiving at least one complete trace tends to one with the number of independent samples. The cost is the fixed total number of traces, including empty or repeated traces, not their total bit length. Allowing a procedure to use at most \(m\) traces gives the same convention by ignoring unused samples; a bound only on the expected number of observations is not the definition.

Information-theoretic scope. There is no limit on running time, storage, description length or processing between observations, and no computability or uniformity restriction on the kernel family. The real deletion probability is a known mathematical parameter, so no finite encoding or estimation of \(\delta\) is required. These conventions make the question purely statistical. The input string has no codebook, sparsity, separation, random-generation or other promise. The asymptotic limit varies \(n\) while keeping \(\delta\) fixed; a simultaneous guarantee for \(\delta\) depending on \(n\), or uniform constants as \(\delta\) approaches an endpoint, is not required.
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that for each fixed deletion probability the worst-case trace count for exact reconstruction at success probability \(2/3\) is polynomial in the string length. A refutation requires one fixed deletion probability for which no polynomial bound suffices.

title: Constant-factor edit-distance approximation in \(O(n\operatorname{polylog} n)\) time
summary: Edit distance is the minimum number of unit-cost insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming one string into another. The question asks for one randomized algorithm with a universal constant approximation factor and only a fixed polylogarithmic overhead beyond linear input length. Its runtime must hold on every execution and its probability of a correct multiplicative estimate must be at least two thirds separately on every pair. Known fixed-slack constant-factor algorithms and earlier subpolynomial or additive approximations do not meet all these requirements simultaneously. The target remains distinct from the two retained questions about arbitrarily accurate estimates at slower stated runtimes.
formal:
Do there exist absolute real constants \(C\geq1\), \(K>0\), \(d\geq0\), an integer word-size constant \(B\geq3\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\) such that for every integer \(n\geq1\) and all explicitly given \(x,y\in\{0,1,\ldots,n^2+1\}^n\), every execution uses at most
\[Kn\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^d\]
word-RAM instructions and its integer output \(D\) satisfies
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq D\leq C\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\bigr]\geq\frac23?\]
The constants and program are chosen once for all input lengths and all pairs. The distance is unit-cost Levenshtein distance; the probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness on that fixed pair.
definitions:
Write \(\Sigma_n=\{0,1,\ldots,n^2+1\}\). The input is \(n\geq1\) followed by two arrays of \(n\) symbols from \(\Sigma_n\), stored in consecutive memory cells with one symbol per word. Binary strings and strings over any fixed alphabet are included after relabeling. The arrays are explicitly present; there is no compressed representation, access oracle, preprocessed database or promised input distribution.

The distance \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions that transform \(x\) into \(y\). Inserted and substituted symbols belong to \(\Sigma_n\), and intermediate strings may have any finite length. Each operation has cost one; leaving an equal symbol unchanged has cost zero. No transpositions, block moves, variable symbol weights or affine gap penalties are allowed. A substitution costs one, not two. The optimum is an integer between zero and \(n\).

The word length is \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, with one fixed integer \(B\geq3\) for the algorithm. A word represents an unsigned integer from \(0\) to \(2^w-1\); memory addresses are words and all cells outside the given input are initially zero. The machine has a fixed finite instruction sequence and fixed integer constants, independent of \(n,x,y\). The unit-cost instructions are random-access reads or writes of one word, comparisons, conditional branches, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero word divisor. Shifts fill with zeros and discard overflow; a shift amount at least \(w\) gives zero. Address calculations obey the same costs. Larger integers occupy several words and require several charged instructions. No arbitrary-precision arithmetic, advice, oracle or quantum instruction is available.

One fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit random word costs one instruction; its individual bits are independent fair bits, and different draws are independent. All preprocessing, memory operations, random draws and output writing count toward the bound. The output is an integer in signed binary notation. Only its value is requested, not a sequence of edits. Every execution must terminate within the stated bound, including those that produce an incorrect estimate. An incorrect execution may return an integer outside the interval. The success guarantee is separate for every pair, not an average over an input distribution.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C,K,d,B,A\;\forall n,x,y\), followed by the displayed probability and all-execution time requirements. Neither the approximation factor nor the logarithmic exponent may grow with \(n\). There is no promise that the distance is large or positive. In particular, when \(x=y\), successful output must be zero. There is no additive error. The shorthand \(O(n\operatorname{polylog}n)\) refers exactly to one bound of the displayed form with fixed \(K,d\), not to \(n^{1+\eta}\) for each fixed \(\eta>0\) or to an arbitrary \(n^{1+o(1)}\) overhead.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of one algorithm and fixed constants meeting both requirements on all input pairs, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must rule out every finite approximation constant, every fixed logarithmic exponent and every permitted randomized algorithm and word-size constant; failure at one chosen factor or for deterministic algorithms alone is insufficient. A conditional lower bound gives only a conditional conclusion unless its hypothesis is also proved. An \(n^{1+\eta}\)-time algorithm for a fixed positive \(\eta\), an approximation factor growing with input length, an additive-error guarantee, an expected-time bound alone, or a theorem only for distant pairs does not settle the question. A large but fixed approximation constant is acceptable. This is an existence question, with no additional numerical approximation tolerance on its answer.

title: Constant-factor approximation of the smallest grammar
summary: The input is any explicit string over an integer alphabet that may grow with its length. The algorithm must output an acyclic grammar whose unique expansion is that string. Grammar size counts all symbols on production right-hand sides, and the target is one universal constant times the optimum. The algorithm must be deterministic and polynomial in the full input bit length; known small-factor hardness does not rule out every constant. A complete Lean-checked proof or unconditional refutation is required, with any conditional hardness result clearly distinguished.
formal:
Do there exist absolute constants \(C\ge1\), \(K\ge1\), an integer \(d\ge1\), and one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\) and explicitly supplied string \(s\in\{1,\ldots,n\}^n\), the algorithm outputs an acyclic grammar \(G\) generating exactly \(s\), with
\[
|G|\le C\,g^*(s),
\]
in at most \(K(L(s)+1)^d\) Turing-machine bit steps? Here \(|G|\) is the total number of terminal and nonterminal occurrences on all right-hand sides, \(g^*(s)\) is the minimum such size among grammars generating \(s\), and \(L(s)\) is the explicit binary input length.
definitions:
A permitted grammar consists of ordered nonterminals \(X_1,\ldots,X_r\), one production \(X_j\to\alpha_j\) per nonterminal, and start nonterminal \(X_r\). Each \(\alpha_j\) is a finite nonempty sequence whose entries are terminals from \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) or references to \(X_i\) with \(i<j\). Every nonterminal is reachable from the start. The order makes the dependency graph acyclic, and each variable has exactly one expansion into terminals. The expansion of \(X_r\) must equal \(s\), symbol for symbol. There are no alternatives, cycles, empty productions, reversal instructions, iteration instructions or extra generated strings. Right-hand sides may have arbitrary positive length; they need not be binary concatenations.

The size is \(|G|=\sum_{j=1}^r|\alpha_j|\). Every occurrence of a terminal or a referenced nonterminal contributes one unit, even when the same entry occurs repeatedly. This counts neither just the number of productions nor the binary description length. A repeated block written many times on a right-hand side is charged for each occurrence; a run-length exponent is not a substitute. The optimum \(g^*(s)\) ranges over all permitted grammars, independently of the algorithm. It exists and satisfies \(1\le g^*(s)\le n\), since one production containing \(s\) is permitted. Ordering the acyclic dependencies and removing unreachable rules does not change the optimal value.

For definiteness, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), \(a\ge0\), consist of \(1^b0\) followed by the \(b\)-bit binary representation of \(a+1\), where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). The input is \(\operatorname{code}(n)\), followed by the \(n\) symbols, each in \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Its full length is \(L(s)\). The alphabet is not required to have a fixed size, and symbols not used by \(s\) are allowed in the ambient alphabet.

The output explicitly lists \(r\), then for each production its right-hand-side length and all its entries. Lengths and identifiers use the same self-delimiting code, and each entry has a one-bit terminal/nonterminal tag. The start is \(X_r\). Writing this entire binary output counts toward runtime. The approximation inequality still uses the stated symbol-occurrence size, not the number of output bits.

The computational model is a fixed finite deterministic multitape Turing machine with finite tape alphabets, read-only binary input, initially blank work tapes and a binary output tape. Each step reads or writes the cells under its heads and moves each head at most one cell. All parsing, preprocessing, computation and output writing are charged. There is no advice, oracle, randomness, quantum computation or unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers. No separate workspace bound is imposed. Malformed inputs may be rejected in polynomial time.

The quantifier order is \(\exists(C,K,d,A)\,\forall n\,\forall s\). The approximation factor and runtime exponent cannot depend on string length, alphabet size, repetition pattern or optimum grammar size. The task is to produce a grammar, not only estimate its minimum size. Exact optimization and approximation arbitrarily close to one are stronger targets than required here.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must construct one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm and prove its grammar is valid and within one fixed factor of the optimum for every allowed string. A negative proof must rule out every fixed constant factor and polynomial-time algorithm unconditionally. A theorem under \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) or another unproved hypothesis must be identified as conditional and does not alone prove the logical negation.

Hardness of exact optimization, a PTAS, or some small approximation constants does not refute all constant factors. An empirical bound, a guarantee only for a restricted string family, or a lower bound for one particular compressor does not decide the proposition. A proof in a different grammar-size convention must justify its transfer to the convention stated here.

title: Breaking two for sum-of-pairs multiple sequence alignment
summary: The inputs are an arbitrary number of sequences and a metric cost table. An alignment inserts gaps while preserving each sequence. Its objective sums costs over every pair of rows and every column. The question asks for a polynomial-time approximation below two by a fixed constant. An improvement shrinking with the number of sequences does not meet the target.
formal: Does there exist a rational constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that returns a \((2-\varepsilon)\)-approximation for minimum sum-of-pairs alignment of any number of strings under an input metric substitution-and-gap cost?
definitions: An instance gives \(k\ge2\) explicit strings over a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), and a table \(d:(\Sigma\cup\{-\})^2\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) encoded by binary numerators and denominators. The distinguished gap symbol \(-\) is not an input-string symbol. Promise \(d(a,b)=d(b,a)\), \(d(a,b)=0\) exactly when \(a=b\), and the triangle inequality for all alphabet and gap symbols. An alignment is a \(k\)-row array of equal-length strings over \(\Sigma\cup\{-\}\) such that erasing gaps from each row returns its input string, and no column consists entirely of gaps. The cost is \(\sum_{1\le i<j\le k}\sum_c d(A_{i,c},A_{j,c})\). The minimum is over all such alignments. Empty input strings are allowed, and the all-empty instance has the empty alignment and zero optimum. The output is an explicit feasible alignment with cost at most \((2-\varepsilon)\) times optimum. Time is measured on a deterministic finite-tape Turing machine in the total bit length of the explicit strings and metric table. The constant, finite program and polynomial are independent of \(k\), the alphabet, lengths and costs. The metric promise is part of the input domain; the algorithm must halt within one fixed polynomial on all input strings, with output correctness required on well-formed promised instances. Ordinary length-delimited encodings list all alphabet symbols, all strings, and all metric-table entries; empty strings still have explicit list entries. If \(N\) is the total number of input symbols, every feasible alignment has at most \(N\) columns because each column contains at least one non-gap symbol. Hence the feasible set is finite and nonempty, and the stated minimum is attained. A zero optimum requires a zero-cost output. Gap costs are charged separately per column and pair; no additional gap-opening or run-length penalty is present.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of one rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), one uniform deterministic algorithm and one polynomial bit-time bound that always return a feasible alignment of cost at most \((2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\) for every promised instance, including zero-optimum cases. Alternatively prove in Lean that no such choices exist. The improvement and polynomial must be independent of the number of strings, alphabet, lengths and rational metric entries; a fixed-number-of-strings guarantee or a conditional lower bound alone does not decide the full proposition.

title: Truly subquadratic \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation of edit distance
summary: Unit-cost edit distance counts insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to transform one string into another. The question asks whether every fixed positive relative tolerance permits a randomized approximation with a positive fixed saving from the quadratic time exponent. Both the algorithm and the exponent saving may depend on the tolerance but must work on every explicitly stored pair with the stated per-input success probability. A second milestone asks for almost-linear time, including on pairs of unequal length. The October 2026 construction meets both time bounds.
formal:
For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), do there exist real constants \(\delta_\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), \(K_\varepsilon>0\) and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_\varepsilon\) such that, for every integer \(n\geq1\) and every pair of length-\(n\) strings \(x,y\), every execution uses at most \(K_\varepsilon(n+2)^{2-\delta_\varepsilon}\) word-RAM instructions and its integer output \(D\) satisfies
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq D\leq(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\bigr]\geq\frac23?\]
The distance is unit-cost Levenshtein distance, the alphabet and computational model are specified below, and probability is over independent internal random bits for each fixed input pair.

The stronger almost-linear milestone asks for the same approximation and per-input success probability on strings of arbitrary lengths with total \(N=|x|+|y|\ge2\) over \(\{0,\ldots,N^2+1\}\). For each fixed accuracy a single algorithm must run in \(N^{1+o(1)}\) worst-case time. This also gives the truly subquadratic guarantee on equal-length inputs.
definitions:
The input consists of \(n\geq1\) and two explicit arrays \(x,y\in\Sigma_n^n\), where \(\Sigma_n=\{0,1,\ldots,n^2+1\}\). Each symbol occupies one word. The arrays and length are stored in consecutive input cells. Binary and any fixed alphabet are included, after relabeling the symbols. No compressed representation, access oracle, prior preprocessing or input distribution is supplied.

The distance \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\) is the minimum number of edits in a sequence transforming \(x\) into \(y\), where one edit inserts one symbol of \(\Sigma_n\), deletes one symbol, or substitutes one symbol for another. Each costs one, and an equal-symbol match costs zero. Intermediate strings may have different lengths. There are no block edits, transpositions, symbol weights or affine gap penalties. In particular, a substitution costs one rather than an insertion plus a deletion. The minimum is an integer between zero and \(n\).

For each fixed accuracy, the algorithm may choose a fixed integer \(B_\varepsilon\geq3\) and uses words of
\[w=B_\varepsilon\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\]
bits. Words represent unsigned integers modulo \(2^w\); memory is addressed by words, and all non-input cells start at zero. The program is a finite list of instructions and integer constants independent of \(n,x,y\). One instruction can read or write one word, compare words, branch, perform a bitwise Boolean operation, shift a word, add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\), or compute an integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor. Shifts discard overflow and fill with zeros; a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Address arithmetic has the same cost. Larger integers require several words and several charged instructions. A fresh independent fair random bit costs one instruction. All preprocessing, random draws and output writing are charged; no arbitrary-precision, oracle, advice or quantum instruction is available. The bound in the statement holds on every random-bit sequence, including executions with an incorrect answer, and forces termination.

The output is an integer written in signed binary notation. A successful execution must satisfy the displayed interval; a failed execution may output an integer outside it. Only the estimate is required, not a sequence of edits. Success must hold separately on every input pair, including identical strings and pairs at distance one. No additive error term is allowed.

The accuracy \(\varepsilon\) is fixed before choosing the algorithm, the word-size constant, the exponent saving and the runtime constant. They may all depend on \(\varepsilon\), but never on \(n\) or the strings. Thus the order is \(\forall\varepsilon\;\exists A_\varepsilon,B_\varepsilon,\delta_\varepsilon,K_\varepsilon\;\forall n,x,y\). No one positive exponent saving must work for all accuracies. The accuracy is not a varying input to a common algorithm, and no effective procedure generating these algorithms, or bound polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\), is required. The term truly subquadratic means the positive saving \(\delta_\varepsilon\) remains fixed as \(n\) grows; savings such as a fixed power of \(\log n\) do not suffice.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the full existence statement for every fixed rational accuracy, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must prove that for some fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), no permitted randomized algorithm and word-size constant achieve the per-input multiplicative guarantee with any positive fixed exponent saving and any fixed runtime constant. A deterministic lower bound alone does not rule out the stated randomized algorithms. A conditional lower bound settles only the corresponding conditional claim unless its hypothesis is also proved. One fixed coarse approximation factor, a bound with only a subpolynomial saving from quadratic time, an expected-time guarantee alone, or a theorem for restricted input pairs is insufficient. This is an algorithm-existence target with the stated relative accuracy, not a numerical target with a separate additive tolerance. The two running-time milestones are tracked on one card. The benchmark scores the truly subquadratic guarantee.

title: Factor-two approximation for shortest common superstring
summary: A common superstring contains every input string as a contiguous substring. The objective is its total number of symbols. The question asks for a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm within factor two of optimum. The input alphabet and every string are explicit. The target permits any algorithm and is separate from analyzing one greedy heuristic.
formal: Does there exist one uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm that, given any explicit finite list of strings over an explicitly given finite alphabet, outputs a common superstring of length at most twice the minimum possible length? All occurrences are forward contiguous substrings. The input, zero-optimum convention and full bit-cost model are defined below. The algorithm need not use the maximum-overlap greedy rule.
definitions:
For context, let \(\mathcal R\) be the set of ratios achievable by the deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithms defined below, and let \(\rho_{\mathrm{SCS}}=\inf\mathcal R\). 

An instance is an integer \(\sigma\ge1\) and a finite list of finite strings \(s_1,\ldots,s_k\) over \(\Sigma=\{1,\ldots,\sigma\}\), where \(k\ge0\). Encode \(\sigma,k\), the length of each string and each symbol in binary with self-delimiting integer fields. For definiteness, encode \(z\ge0\) by a unary prefix giving the bit length of \(z+1\), a zero delimiter, then the binary expansion of \(z+1\). The list contains every symbol explicitly; neither grammar compression nor an oracle representation is allowed. Let \(L\) be the total number of input bits.

A feasible output is an explicit string \(w\in\Sigma^*\) such that, for each \(i\), there are strings \(u_i,v_i\) with \(w=u_i s_i v_i\). Occurrences are ordinary forward contiguous substrings; reversal, reverse complementation, subsequences and cyclic wraparound are not allowed. The objective \(|w|\) counts symbols, not bits. Define \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) as the minimum feasible length. Concatenating the input strings proves feasibility and finiteness. Empty and repeated input strings are allowed. If the list is empty or every member is empty, the optimum is zero, and every finite-factor algorithm must return the empty string. Strings contained in other input strings may be removed by preprocessing, but that work is charged.

An admissible algorithm is one finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program. For its chosen ratio \(r\), some constants \(K>0\) and integer \(d\ge1\) bound its total steps by \(K(L+1)^d\) on every encoded input. It rejects malformed encodings within that bound. On valid inputs it always outputs a feasible string satisfying the claimed ratio. Reading, preprocessing, integer and symbol operations and writing the complete output all count as bit steps. The program has no advice, randomness or free oracle. Its program and polynomial may depend on \(r\), but not on input size or on the instance.

The infimum is over ratios achievable with one such global guarantee. It need not itself be achievable by a single algorithm. Known constant-factor algorithms make the set nonempty, so \(\rho_{\mathrm{SCS}}\) is finite and at least one. A lower bound on this infimum concerns all deterministic polynomial-time algorithms; a bad input for one particular heuristic is insufficient. No separation assumption such as \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) is built into this existence question. In particular, an algorithmic or hardness claim conditional on an assumption yields only a conditional bound unless that assumption is also proved.
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that a uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm always outputs a superstring at most twice optimal in length, or rule out every such algorithm on the specified list encoding.

title: Text-to-pattern Hamming distances below the square-root barrier
summary: The input is an explicit text and pattern over a polynomial-size integer alphabet. The output contains the exact number of mismatches at every alignment, in order. The target improves the square-root dependence on pattern length by one fixed positive exponent. Randomness may affect running time but must never produce an incorrect terminating answer. Acceptance requires a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation in the stated uniform word-RAM model.
formal:
Do there exist absolute constants \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), \(K>0\), an integer \(B\ge8\), and one uniform classical Las Vegas word-RAM algorithm \(A\) such that, for all integers \(n\ge2\), \(1\le m\le n\), every text \(T\in\{0,\ldots,n^2-1\}^{n}\) and pattern \(P\in\{0,\ldots,n^2-1\}^{m}\), it outputs every exact distance
\[
 h_i=|\{j\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}:T[i+j]\ne P[j]\}|
 \quad (i=0,\ldots,n-m)
\]
and satisfies
\[
 \mathbb E[\operatorname{time}_A(T,P)]
 \le Knm^{1/2-\varepsilon}?
\]
The expectation is over internal randomness for each fixed input. The word length is \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), and correctness is required on every terminating execution.
definitions:
The text and pattern are explicit arrays with one integer symbol per word. Hamming distance between equal-length strings counts unequal coordinates; only substitutions matter, and there are no insertions, deletions, wildcards or symbol weights. Alignment \(i\) compares the entire pattern to the consecutive length-\(m\) substring of the text starting at zero-based position \(i\). Every permitted alignment is included, even if its distance is large.

The output is the array \((h_0,\ldots,h_{n-m})\), in increasing alignment order, with one integer in \(\{0,\ldots,m\}\) per word. It is not enough to identify zero distances, report only alignments below a threshold, return one best alignment or approximate the distances. No text index or auxiliary preprocessing is supplied for free. Both strings may be accessed throughout the computation, and the time includes reading, initialization, preprocessing, all intermediate work and output writes.

The sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program. Allowed unit-cost instructions are word reads and writes, copying, comparison, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor, and generation of an independent uniformly random \(w\)-bit word. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Values and addresses fit in words, and multiword operations are charged by their constituent instructions. There are no arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic operations, advice, external oracles or free size-dependent lookup tables. Workspace is limited by this address model but has no separate linear-space requirement.

Las Vegas means that every execution which terminates has the correct entire output, and termination occurs with probability one on every fixed valid input. The expected instruction count has the displayed bound; no worst-case cap on every random tape is required. A Monte Carlo algorithm with a small chance of incorrect output is not sufficient. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as a special case. There is no restriction to methods described informally as combinatorial; algebraic computation and fast matrix multiplication are permitted if implemented in the stated model and charged for their actual instructions.

The same \(\varepsilon,K,B\) and program work for all lengths and strings. The saving is chosen once and may be arbitrarily small but positive. It may not tend to zero with the input size, depend on the ratio of the two lengths, or apply only to a selected length regime. The target has no additional hidden logarithmic factor in \(n\); all costs must fit the explicit bound. Restricting to a fixed-size alphabet changes the problem because it enables faster special-case algorithms.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish exact Las Vegas correctness, almost-sure termination and the uniform expected bound for some fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), over the full input domain.

Removing logarithmic factors while retaining \(m^{1/2}\), a saving that vanishes with input size, approximate distances, or a faster algorithm on a constant alphabet does not meet this target. Conditional hardness under a matrix-multiplication or arithmetic conjecture establishes only a conditional conclusion. A restriction to combinatorial algorithms cannot refute existence in the unrestricted RAM class. No minimum saving such as \(1/100\) is imposed.

title: Almost-quadratic unweighted tree edit distance
summary: The inputs are two explicit rooted ordered trees with integer vertex labels. Unit-cost edits insert, delete or relabel individual vertices while preserving the order of surviving children. The target is the exact edit distance in almost-quadratic worst-case time using one deterministic program. Recent static and derandomization results improve the cubic bound but do not reach this target. A complete Lean-checked answer must prove or refute the proposition with the stated edit convention and quantifiers.
formal:
Is there one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\), an integer word-size constant \(B\ge8\), a constant \(K>0\), and a function \(g:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to[1,\infty)\) satisfying
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log g(n)}{\log n}=0,
\]
such that, for every two nonempty rooted ordered labelled trees with a total of \(n\ge2\) vertices, \(A\) outputs their exact unit-cost tree edit distance using at most
\[
 Kn^2g(n)
\]
word-RAM instructions in the worst case? Each vertex label is an integer in \(\{0,\ldots,n^2-1\}\), both trees are explicitly supplied, and the word length is \(B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\).
definitions:
A rooted ordered tree has one designated root and a left-to-right order on the children of every vertex. It is supplied by explicitly listed vertex labels and ordered child lists. The parameter \(n\) is the sum of the numbers of ordinary vertices in the two input trees, not a bound on each tree separately. Vertex identifiers, labels and pointers each fit in one word. No balance, degree, depth, leaf-count, similarity or constant-alphabet promise is imposed.

To specify root edits without ambiguity, attach a permanent unlabelled super-root above each input root. It contributes no vertex to \(n\), cannot be edited, and is preserved in the final object. An intermediate object is an ordered forest of ordinary vertices below this super-root, possibly empty. Each of the following operations costs one:

1. Delete an ordinary vertex, replacing it in its parent's ordered child list by its own children in their existing order.
2. Insert one new labelled vertex as a child of an existing vertex or the super-root, placing beneath it a consecutive block of that parent's children. The block may be empty, in which case a leaf is inserted in a specified position.
3. Change the label of one ordinary vertex to another label from the input alphabet.

Insertion is the inverse of deletion. Deleting a vertex does not delete its descendants as a single operation. Moving or reordering a subtree is not a unit-cost operation. Intermediate ordinary labels belong to \(\{0,\ldots,n^2-1\}\). The final forest below the super-root must be a single rooted ordered labelled tree isomorphic to the second input, preserving all labels and sibling orders. Ordinary vertex identifiers themselves need not be preserved.

The distance \(\operatorname{TED}(T_1,T_2)\) is the minimum length of such an edit sequence. It is an integer between zero and \(n\): deleting every ordinary vertex and then inserting the target tree is always permitted. The output is this integer alone. No edit script, intermediate forest, alignment or approximate value is requested. This is a static computation on one pair of input trees, with no index or preprocessed dynamic state provided for free.

The algorithm is one finite sequential word-RAM program independent of the input size and trees. Unit-cost instructions are word reads and writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. All addresses and values fit in words; multiword computation pays for its constituent instructions. Every initialization, preprocessing step, table construction, arithmetic operation and output write is charged. There are no random instructions, advice, external oracles or free tables depending on size. There is no additional space restriction beyond this model and the charged running time.

The function \(g\) describes a subpolynomial overhead, not advice available to the program. Equivalently, the same algorithm has, for every fixed real \(\eta>0\), constants \(K_\eta,n_\eta\) such that its running time is at most \(K_\eta n^{2+\eta}\) whenever \(n\ge n_\eta\). A collection of unrelated algorithms, each with one chosen positive exponent slack, does not by itself establish this one-program assertion. The guarantee must hold on every valid input; it is not an average-case or expected-time bound.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must provide one uniform deterministic program and prove that it returns the exact edit distance and satisfies the stated worst-case \(n^{2+o(1)}\) guarantee over all input trees.

A fixed exponent above two, merely subcubic time, an approximation, a small-distance promise, a restriction to paths or bounded-depth trees, or a dynamic amortized bound does not suffice. A lower bound relying on an additional complexity assumption settles the negative answer only together with a proof of that assumption. A conditional barrier for weighted costs or combinatorial dynamic algorithms is not an unconditional refutation of this unweighted static proposition. No additive numerical tolerance is applied.

title: Linear-time LZ77 pattern matching
summary: A text is supplied as literal and copy phrases, and the pattern is an explicit string. Copies may overlap themselves, so the decoded text can be much longer than the input representation. The question asks for exact deterministic occurrence detection in time and working space linear in the phrase count plus pattern length. The machine allows integer division, and all preprocessing is charged. Linear-time algorithms are known when the compressed text is supplied as a grammar. Conversion from LZ77 can increase the representation size.
formal: For every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), do there exist constants \(K\ge1\), an integer \(B\ge c+8\), and one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\) with the following property? Given any valid \(z\)-phrase LZ77 representation of a text \(T\) of length \(N\ge1\), and an explicit nonempty pattern \(P\) of length \(m\), with symbols in \(\{1,\ldots,(z+m)^c\}\), the algorithm decides whether \(P\) occurs contiguously in \(T\) using at most \(K(z+m)\) word-RAM instructions and \(K(z+m)\) working words. Self-referential copy phrases are allowed, the word size is \(w=B\lceil\log_2(N+m+2)\rceil\), and all preprocessing is included.
definitions:
The input contains \(z,N,m\), an array of \(z\ge1\) phrase descriptors, and the \(m\ge1\) pattern symbols. Each descriptor occupies three words: a type tag and two integer fields. A literal descriptor \((\mathrm{literal},a,0)\) appends the single symbol \(a\). A copy descriptor \((\mathrm{copy},s,\ell)\) has \(\ell\ge1\). If the next text position is \(p\), it requires \(1\le s<p\) and appends \(\ell\) symbols sequentially, setting \(T[p+j]=T[s+j]\) for \(j=0,\ldots,\ell-1\). The source position is always earlier than the destination, so it may refer to a symbol generated earlier in this same phrase. The copied interval need not end before \(p\). After all phrases the length is exactly \(N\). All literal and pattern symbols belong to the displayed alphabet. These conditions are input promises; no greedy or minimum-size parse is promised. In particular, \(z\le N\).

The required output is one bit, equal to one exactly when some \(i\) with \(1\le i\le N-m+1\) satisfies \(T[i+j]=P[j+1]\) for every \(0\le j<m\). If \(m>N\), it is zero. Occurrences may cross any phrase boundaries or lie inside an overlapping copy. The algorithm need not report positions or enumerate occurrences.

Use a sequential random-access machine with one fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed cells. A word stores an unsigned \(w\)-bit integer. Unit-cost operations are a read or write, comparison, branch, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and logical shifts; shifts by at least \(w\) give zero. Addresses fit in a word. Division is expressly allowed. There is no randomness, advice, oracle, quantum operation or unit-cost operation on an unbounded integer. Multiword calculations must be performed with charged word instructions.

The supplied compressed representation and explicit pattern are read-only input arrays. Working space counts every other word retained by the algorithm, including copies, tables, indexes and intermediate representations. Time counts reading the input and building any auxiliary representation. There is no separately supplied uncompressed text, grammar, text-access oracle or precomputed index. The larger word size reflects positions in the potentially very long decoded text, not permission to perform uncharged decompression.

The quantifier order is \(\forall c\,\exists(K,B,A)\,\forall(T\text{ represented by its supplied parse},P)\). The finite program and constants may depend on the fixed alphabet exponent \(c\), but not on \(N,z,m\), the phrase contents or the pattern. They must satisfy the bounds on every valid input.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of this existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must implement the decision procedure uniformly in the specified word RAM and prove its correctness, worst-case time and working-space bounds for every permitted parse and pattern. A negative answer must rule out the stated algorithms in this model; a conditional lower bound is only a conditional result.

Time linear in the decoded length \(N\), or in the size of a supplied or newly constructed grammar that can exceed \(z\), does not meet the target. Neither does an uncharged preprocessing phase. A lower bound for a model lacking integer division does not refute this proposition.

title: Fully functional suffix trees in BWT-run-linear total space
summary: A binary text with a sentinel determines a suffix tree and a run count in its Burrows–Wheeler transform. The target stores the entire specified navigation and direct-access interface in space proportional to that run count. Every query must be exact and take polylogarithmic worst-case time after deterministic polynomial-time construction. The space budget includes the text representation and any access oracle, which distinguishes the target from recent partial-interface results. A complete Lean-checked answer must establish or refute all of these guarantees simultaneously.
formal:
Do there exist constants \(C,K>0\), integers \(c\ge0\), \(p\ge1\), \(B\ge8\), and one uniform deterministic static data structure such that, for every \(n\ge2\) and every explicitly given text
\[
T\in\{0,1\}^{n-1}\#,
\]
it constructs a representation of the compact suffix tree in at most \(Kn^p\) word-RAM instructions, retains at most \(Cr\) words, and answers each operation specified below exactly in at most
\[
K\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^c
\]
worst-case instructions, while the retained representation together with all temporary query work uses at most \(Cr\) words? Here \(r\) is the number of runs in the Burrows–Wheeler transform of \(T\), including its unique sentinel, and the word length is \(B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). All constants and programs are chosen once, independently of the text and its length.
definitions:
Text positions and suffix ranks are zero-based. The alphabet is ordered \(\#<0<1\); the sentinel \(\#\) occurs only at position \(n-1\). For \(0\le i<n\), the suffix beginning at \(i\) is \(T[i]\cdots T[n-1]\). The suffix array \(\operatorname{SA}[j]\) is the starting position of the suffix of lexicographic rank \(j\), and \(\operatorname{ISA}[i]\) is the unique rank \(j\) with \(\operatorname{SA}[j]=i\). Define
\[
\operatorname{BWT}[j]=T[(\operatorname{SA}[j]-1)\bmod n].
\]
The residue lies in \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\). A run is a maximal nonempty interval of equal symbols in this BWT array; \(r\) is its number of runs. The sentinel is counted in both \(n\) and \(r\).

The suffix trie contains the paths spelling all \(n\) suffixes, with the empty string at its root. Contract maximal paths whose intermediate vertices have just one child, concatenating their edge labels. The resulting compact suffix tree retains the root, branching vertices and leaves. Every edge has a nonempty string label. A node's path label is the concatenation of edge labels from the root to that node. Leaves are ordered by suffix rank. Every node is represented externally by the pair \([l,h]\) of smallest and largest ranks among its descendant leaves. These intervals uniquely identify explicit nodes; an interior point of an edge is not an additional queryable node. In particular, the root is \([0,n-1]\) and leaf rank \(j\) is \([j,j]\).

The complete required interface consists of the following operations. Node arguments are valid node intervals of the indexed text; ranks and positions lie in \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\).

- Return the root, or return the leaf of a supplied suffix rank.
- Given a node, return its parent, its lexicographically first child, or its next sibling in its parent's child order. Children are ordered by the first symbols of their edge labels. Return a distinguished marker \(\bot\) when the requested parent, child or sibling does not exist; in particular the root has no parent or sibling.
- Given a node and a symbol \(a\in\{\#,0,1\}\), return its child whose edge label begins with \(a\), or \(\bot\) if there is no such child.
- Given any node, return its tree depth, the number of edges from the root, or its string depth, the number of symbols in its path label. Both root depths are zero. A leaf for suffix position \(i\) has string depth \(n-i\).
- Given two nodes, return their lowest common ancestor, namely their common ancestor of maximum tree depth. A node is its own ancestor.
- Given a nonroot internal node with path label \(aU\), return its suffix link: the explicit node whose path label is \(U\). This node exists in this suffix tree; \(U\) may be empty, in which case the answer is the root. No suffix-link query on a leaf or on the root is required.
- Given \(j\), return \(\operatorname{SA}[j]\); given \(i\), return \(\operatorname{ISA}[i]\) or \(T[i]\).

Every query returns only a constant number of words. Arbitrary valid node intervals can be supplied directly; handles are not required to originate from a preceding traversal. Every operation must work after construction with no access to an uncounted input copy or external text-access service. All retained text, suffix samples, lookup tables, oracle implementations and internally retained handles count toward the space bound. Temporary query memory, including registers, also counts. Externally supplied arguments and the constant-size returned result may be excluded. Construction starts from the explicitly supplied text, one symbol per word, and may use additional temporary memory; construction instructions and initialization are charged to its polynomial time bound. That temporary memory is discarded before queries begin.

The machine is a sequential word RAM with a fixed finite program and the stated word length. Unit-cost instructions are word reads and writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Values and addresses fit in words, and multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. There is no randomness, nonuniform advice, uncharged preprocessing, free size-dependent table or input-dependent oracle. A static query starts without input-dependent private state outside the counted representation. The bounds hold for every text and every valid query, without amortization over a query sequence.

The binary alphabet and this explicitly enumerated interface are the retained editorial specialization of the broader suffix-tree question. “Fully functional” here means exactly these operations; no unlisted operation is silently required.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must provide the uniform construction and all query algorithms, prove their exact behavior, and prove the simultaneous polynomial construction, run-linear total space and polylogarithmic worst-case query bounds.

A structure supporting only pattern counting, occurrence reporting or a proper subset of the required interface is insufficient. Space charged in addition to a separately stored text or access oracle does not establish the total-space target unless that additional representation is also included in the proved \(Cr\) bound. An extra logarithmic space factor does not meet the target. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion. There is no additive numerical tolerance on this existence question.

title: Existence of complete EFX allocations for additive valuations
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
summary: The problem asks whether every instance with at least four agents and nonnegative additive values admits a complete EFX allocation of indivisible goods. Complete means that each good is assigned to exactly one agent, with empty bundles allowed. For every potentially envious agent i and other bundle \(A_{j}\), removing any good that i values positively must leave a bundle worth at most i’s own bundle. The statement permits zero values and fixes the positive-good EFX convention, without requiring payments or an efficient algorithm. Universal existence would establish this fairness guarantee despite the inability to divide individual goods.
formal: For all integers \(n\ge4\) and \(m\ge0\), and every matrix \((v_{ig})_{i\in[n],g\in[m]}\) of nonnegative real values, does there exist a complete allocation \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) such that \(\sum_{h\in A_i}v_{ih}\ge\sum_{h\in A_j\setminus\{g\}}v_{ih}\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\) and every \(g\in A_j\) satisfying \(v_{ig}>0\)?
definitions: For an integer \(k\ge0\), write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). There are \(n\) agents and \(m\) indivisible goods. The finite nonnegative real number \(v_{ig}\) is agent \(i\)'s value for good \(g\); her value for a bundle \(S\subseteq[m]\) is \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\). A complete allocation is an ordered partition \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) into pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is \([m]\); empty bundles are allowed and every good is allocated exactly once. Envy-freeness up to any positively valued good (EFX) means that, for all agents \(i,j\) and all \(g\in A_j\) with \(v_{ig}>0\), one has \(v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})\). Both the positivity test and the comparison use agent \(i\)'s valuation. If all goods in \(A_j\) have value zero for \(i\), there is no inequality for that pair. Values need not be rational or strictly positive. No payments, chores, discarded goods, randomized allocations, or efficiency requirement are present. This uses the positive-good convention of Definition 5 in the cited survey; the stronger per-allocation condition EFX-zero also tests goods with value zero.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence for every valuation matrix in the stated domain, or prove its negation in Lean: there are finite \(n\ge4\), \(m\ge0\), and nonnegative additive valuations for which every complete partition violates at least one of the stated EFX inequalities. The target is existence, with no algorithmic, efficiency or stronger fairness requirement.

title: Constant-factor universally truthful auctions for submodular bidders
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
summary: The auction allocates indivisible items to bidders with private normalized monotone submodular bundle valuations. The question asks for a constant expected-welfare approximation with universal truthfulness and polynomial communication in bidders, items and per-value bit precision. Local computation is unrestricted, but every query description, price, reply, allocation and payment must fit the bit bound. A complete Lean proof must establish the fixed-random-tape incentive inequality and all-profile welfare guarantee, or rule out every protocol in this full class. Value-query impossibility, graph eligibility results, growing approximation factors and budget-feasible procurement do not settle the selected target.
formal:
Does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge1\) and one uniform randomized combinatorial-auction mechanism with polynomial worst-case communication which is universally truthful and, for every number \(n\ge1\) of bidders, number \(m\ge1\) of items, public precision bound \(B\ge1\), and admissible normalized monotone submodular valuation profile \(v\), satisfies
\[\mathbb E_r\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(S_i(v;r))\right]
\ \ge\ \frac{\operatorname{OPT}(v)}{C}?\]
The constant is independent of \(n,m,B\). The expectation is over report-independent mechanism randomness. For each fixed random realization the allocation and payment rule must satisfy the dominant-strategy inequality below. Communication is measured in bits, with unlimited terminating local computation and arbitrary interactive messages, including demand queries.
definitions:
Items and types. Let \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Bidder \(i\) privately holds the entire function \(v_i:2^{[m]}\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). It is normalized, monotone and submodular: for all subsets \(S,T\subseteq[m]\),
\[v_i(\varnothing)=0,\qquad S\subseteq T\Longrightarrow v_i(S)\le v_i(T),\]
\[v_i(S)+v_i(T)\ge v_i(S\cup T)+v_i(S\cap T).\]
The public integer \(B\ge1\) bounds each value separately: every value admits a representation \(p/q\) with integers \(0\le p<2^B\), \(1\le q<2^B\). Write \(\mathcal V_{m,B}\) for this domain. Different bidders may have completely different functions in the domain. Their full tables have \(2^m\) entries each and are private local inputs, not publicly supplied data. There is no oracle promise, common valuation, eligibility graph, prior distribution, budget or succinct representation requirement on the types. The domain of an alternative reported valuation is also \(\mathcal V_{m,B}\), with the same public parameters.

Outcomes and utilities. A feasible allocation is \(a:[m]\to\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\), with zero meaning unallocated. Bidder \(i\) receives \(S_i=\{j:a(j)=i\}\); bundles are pairwise disjoint and no item is split. Each bidder has a finite rational payment \(p_i\in\mathbb Q\), with positive sign meaning money paid to the auctioneer. Its utility is \(v_i(S_i)-p_i\). No individual-rationality, budget-balance or transfer-sign condition is added. For a true profile \(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\), define
\[W_v(a)=\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(S_i),\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(v)=\max_{a:[m]\to\{0,\ldots,n\}}W_v(a).\]
The finite maximum exists. Welfare measures bidder values only; it excludes payments and auctioneer revenue. Zero valuations and zero optimum are allowed. All bidders are evaluated using their true values at the final allocation.

Communication model. The auctioneer and bidders run a common uniform protocol on distributed reported types. Local algorithms are ordinary finite programs, with unrestricted computation on their private tables; all local computations and protocol executions must terminate. The auctioneer initially knows only \(n,m,B\). A public blackboard holds the transcript; each transmitted bit counts once. The next speaker and the decision to halt are determined by the public transcript, public parameters and fixed random tape. Private computation time and silent delays are not messages or additional information channels. The output allocation and all payments are written to the transcript and count toward its length. Any use of private channels can instead be specified with sender and recipient information and charged in the transcript.

Rational values, prices and payments are communicated exactly as finite binary numerator/positive-denominator pairs, with a sign bit when needed and self-delimiting integer encodings. For example, for \(z\ge0\), use \(1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(z+1)\), where \(\ell\) is the bit length of \(z+1\). Subsets can be transmitted by their \(m\)-bit incidence vectors. Every query description, price, reply, routing description and final output is charged. A value query specifies a bidder and a bundle and receives its value. A demand query specifies rational item prices \((\pi_j)_{j\in[m]}\) and receives a bundle maximizing \(v_i(S)-\sum_{j\in S}\pi_j\). Any deterministic tie rule needed to define the mechanism is part of the protocol. Solving that finite optimization locally has no time charge, but sending its prices and answer does. These are examples of allowed messages, not an exhaustive query restriction.

Polynomial communication and randomness. There must exist constants \(K>0\) and \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that the total number of transmitted bits is at most \(K(n+m+B+1)^d\) for every valid reported profile and every realization of the mechanism’s random bits. This is worst-case communication, not expected communication and not merely a query count. Randomness is a public tape of independent fair bits, independent of all types and reports; its use and local computation are uncharged, although execution still terminates. The uniform protocol describes how those bits are used. Fixing the tape \(r\) defines a deterministic allocation and payment rule \((S(v;r),p(v;r))\).

Universal truthfulness. For every public parameter triple, every fixed \(r\), bidder \(i\), true and alternative reported types \(v_i,w_i\in\mathcal V_{m,B}\), and other reported profile \(b_{-i}\in\mathcal V_{m,B}^{n-1}\), require
\[v_i(S_i(v_i,b_{-i};r))-p_i(v_i,b_{-i};r)
\ \ge\ v_i(S_i(w_i,b_{-i};r))-p_i(w_i,b_{-i};r).\]
Both sides use the same true valuation and random tape. The protocol implements this direct-report outcome rule without transmitting the full reported tables. There is no averaging in the incentive condition; averaging is used only in the welfare guarantee. No assumption that other bidders are honest, no prior over their values, and no weakening to Bayesian or truthful-in-expectation incentives is permitted.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its negation. A positive answer must specify the uniform protocol, payment rule and randomization, a fixed approximation constant and a fixed polynomial communication bound. Prove feasibility, termination, all-bit accounting, the incentive inequality for every fixed random tape, and the expected welfare bound for every admissible profile.

A negative answer must rule out every fixed constant and every protocol in the full model, including arbitrary interactive messages, demand queries and unlimited local computation. Failure of one mechanism or one prescribed approximation constant does not refute existence of another. A lower bound restricted to value queries, deterministic mechanisms, a particular family of allocation rules, or polynomial local time alone is insufficient.

Truthfulness in expectation alone, approximate incentives, a factor growing with \(m\), an uncharged exponential price description, or a constant guarantee with extra valuation promises does not meet the target. Conditional impossibility results must keep their hypotheses explicit and do not by themselves refute this unconditional communication claim. The target is expected welfare; a stronger high-probability guarantee is welcome but not required.

title: Constant-factor truthful-in-expectation scheduling
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
summary: Machines report their private processing times for the jobs. A truthful-in-expectation mechanism makes honest reporting optimal for expected utility. The question asks whether expected makespan can stay within a universal constant of the offline optimum. The constant must be independent of the number of machines and jobs. Payments and correlated randomness are allowed, with no computation restriction.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(K\ge1\) such that, for every machine count \(m\ge2\), some family of truthful-in-expectation mechanisms handles every finite job count \(n\ge1\) and every finite nonnegative real processing-time matrix \(t\) with \[\mathbb E[C(M_{m,n}(t),t)]\le K\operatorname{OPT}(t)?\] Here \(C(\sigma,t)\) is the makespan of assignment \(\sigma\), as defined below. The factor is independent of \(m,n,t\); arbitrary correlated random assignments and payments are allowed, and computation is unrestricted.
definitions:
\[R(m)=\inf_{M\in\mathcal M_m}\ \sup_{\substack{n\ge1,\ t\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{m\times n}\\\operatorname{OPT}(t)>0}}
\frac{\mathbb E[C(M_{m,n}(t),t)]}{\operatorname{OPT}(t)}.\]
Here \(\mathcal M_m\) consists of the families satisfying the incentive and zero-optimum conditions below. 

Jobs, machines and private costs. Write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\). There are \(m\ge2\) machines and \(n\ge1\) indivisible jobs. Machine \(i\) has a private type \(t_i=(t_{i1},\ldots,t_{in})\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n\). Executing a set \(S\subseteq[n]\) costs it \(\sum_{j\in S}t_{ij}\). All entries are finite; zero is allowed. The times on different machines and jobs have no promised relation. Every job is assigned exactly once, and all jobs assigned to one machine are executed sequentially. There are no release times, precedences, eligibility restrictions, migration, preemption or interactions between different jobs' costs.

Direct mechanisms. Reports have the same domain as types. For each report matrix \(b\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{m\times n}\), a mechanism specifies numbers
\[q_\sigma(b)\ge0\quad(\sigma:[n]\to[m]),\qquad\sum_\sigma q_\sigma(b)=1,\]
and a finite real expected payment \(p_i(b)\in\mathbb R\) to each machine. Thus the outcome at each fixed report is a distribution on the finite set of \(m^n\) assignments. Define the marginal assignment probability
\[x_{ij}(b)=\sum_{\sigma:\sigma(j)=i}q_\sigma(b).\]
The numbers \(q_\sigma(b)\) may be arbitrary reals, and assignments of different jobs need not be independent. Payments can be deterministic amounts \(p_i(b)\): allowing random payments with finite expectations makes no difference to the risk-neutral utility or objective here. Positive payments are received by the machine. No individual rationality, budget balance, sign restriction, transfer bound, anonymity or task-independence condition is imposed.

Truthfulness in expectation. For every machine \(i\), true type \(t_i\), alternative report \(b_i\), and fixed reports \(b_{-i}\) of all other machines, require
\[p_i(t_i,b_{-i})-\sum_{j=1}^n t_{ij}x_{ij}(t_i,b_{-i})
\ \ge\ p_i(b_i,b_{-i})-\sum_{j=1}^n t_{ij}x_{ij}(b_i,b_{-i}).\]
This is the dominant-strategy condition for expected payment minus true processing cost. Only one agent's report changes in this comparison. There is no prior distribution on types, expectation over other players' reports, or assumption that those reports are honest. The expectation is over the mechanism's own allocation randomness. Truthfulness of each deterministic rule obtained by fixing a random seed is not required.

Performance. When the report matrix equals the true matrix \(t\), an assignment has makespan
\[C(\sigma,t)=\max_{i\in[m]}\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}t_{ij},\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(t)=\min_{\sigma:[n]\to[m]}C(\sigma,t).\]
The expectation in the formal statement is the finite sum \(\sum_\sigma q_\sigma(t)C(\sigma,t)\). It is the expected maximum load, not the maximum of the expected loads. Payments do not enter the makespan. The optimum uses the same machines and jobs with full knowledge of the true processing times. For every \(t\) with \(\operatorname{OPT}(t)=0\), an admissible mechanism must have expected makespan zero; division by zero is omitted from the displayed supremum. All positive-optimum instances and all job counts are included, with no additive error term.

Optimization over mechanisms. For a fixed \(m\), a family \(M=(M_{m,n})_{n\ge1}\) belongs to \(\mathcal M_m\) precisely when each member has the stated domain and satisfies truthfulness and the zero-optimum condition at every report profile. Its supremum ratio may be infinite. The infimum is finite because a truthful minimum-total-cost allocation has ratio at most \(m\), so \(1\le R(m)\le m\). A single family must meet its ratio simultaneously for every \(n\) and \(t\); it cannot be chosen after the true instance is known. Different job counts and machine counts may have different rules, and no uniform finite program, computability, representation or time bound is required. The selected problem is an incentive-theoretic extremum over mathematical rules on real reports. A bit encoding or efficient sampling requirement would change that class.

Attainment and asymptotics. The infimum need not be attained. To establish \(R(m)\le u\), it is enough to have admissible families with ratios at most \(u+\varepsilon\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\). The constants in the requested asymptotic comparison must be independent of \(m\), \(n\), and all processing times. The finite distribution on assignments at each individual report must not be confused with a report-independent finite or countable distribution over entire deterministic truthful mechanisms; the latter is an additional restriction.
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one finite approximation factor works for every machine count through truthful-in-expectation mechanisms satisfying the stated bound on expected makespan. A refutation must rule out every finite universal factor.

title: Constant-factor truthful subadditive combinatorial auctions
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
summary: Bidders may value bundles subadditively without any prior distribution. The mechanism accesses valuations through exact demand and value queries. Allocated bundles cannot overlap. Truthful reporting must maximize each bidder’s expected quasilinear utility. A single positive welfare factor must hold independently of the number of items.
formal: Is there a polynomial-time, polynomial-demand-query truthful-in-expectation mechanism with a universal constant welfare approximation for arbitrary subadditive bidders?
definitions:
There are m distinct indivisible items M=[m] and n buyers. A valuation v:2^M→R_≥0 is normalized by v(∅)=0, monotone under set inclusion, and subadditive: v(S∪T)≤v(S)+v(T) for all S,T⊆M. A feasible allocation gives pairwise disjoint item subsets S_i to the buyers; unsold items are allowed. Welfare is ∑_i v_i(S_i), and OPT(v) is its maximum over feasible allocations. In this oracle variant all valuation values are nonnegative rationals of at most L bits each; the full valuation table is not supplied. For any subset S a value query returns v_i(S). For nonnegative rational item prices p, a demand query returns a bundle maximizing v_i(S)−∑_{j∈S}p_j, choosing the lexicographically least characteristic vector among maximizers. The answer includes the bundle’s value. Query inputs and all payments must have polynomial bit length in n+m+L. A reported type is any valuation in this same domain, and its oracle answers are those of that valuation; arbitrary inconsistent transcripts are not a separate strategy type.

The randomized mechanism outputs disjoint bundles X_i and rational payments P_i. For every true v_i, alternative reported valuation v_i′, and other reports v_−i, require E[v_i(X_i(v_i,v_−i))−P_i(v_i,v_−i)]≥E[v_i(X_i(v_i′,v_−i))−P_i(v_i′,v_−i)]. Also require nonnegative expected utility when reporting truthfully and no positive transfers (P_i≥0 for every outcome). Feasibility is required in every outcome. For every valuation profile, E[∑_i v_i(X_i)]≥α OPT(v) for one absolute α>0.
