Runtime, number of queries and output length are polynomial in n+m+L in the worst case over coins, excluding the oracle’s internal computation but including writing prices and reading answers. No prior distributions are provided.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the proposition or its negation for the stated model. The proposition has no complexity assumption. A hardness implication supplies a negative answer only together with a proof of its premise. Universal truthfulness is stronger than required; guarantees for only submodular valuations do not cover this domain.

title: Black-box conversion to dominant-strategy truthfulness without expected-welfare loss
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
summary: Independent finite type distributions are explicitly known. The original allocation algorithm is accessible only through oracle calls. Feasibility can be certified only for allocations actually returned by the oracle. The transformed mechanism must be truthful for each fixed vector of other reports. Expected welfare must match or exceed the original algorithm with no additive loss.
formal: For the finite rational single-parameter model below, is there a polynomial-query black-box transformation to dominant-strategy truthfulness in expectation that loses no expected welfare?
definitions:
There are n agents. Agent i has a finite publicly listed support V_i⊆Q_≥0 with publicly listed positive rational probabilities F_i summing to one; values are independent. All supports and probabilities have total bit length L. Reports are restricted to these supports. A deterministic oracle A accepts any profile in ∏_i V_i and returns an allocation x∈[0,1]^n∩Q^n with each coordinate encoded in at most B bits, where B is supplied. There is an arbitrary unknown feasible set X⊆[0,1]^n containing every oracle output; no downward closure, membership oracle or explicit description is supplied.

A simulator on an actual reported profile may make adaptive queries to A at other profiles and must output one allocation returned by one of its queries, with no permutation or coordinate modification unless that modified vector is itself an observed output. It also returns rational payments. It may sample from the listed priors with fresh private coins, but has no stored exponential advice or free preprocessing. All work, queried input lengths and payment output lengths have expected polynomial cost in n+L+B, on every profile, and the expected number of oracle queries is polynomial in those parameters. Oracle evaluation itself is charged one call plus reading its answer.

For every i, v_i,v_i′∈V_i and v_−i∈∏_{j≠i}V_j, require E[v_i x_i(v_i,v_−i)−p_i(v_i,v_−i)]≥E[v_i x_i(v_i′,v_−i)−p_i(v_i′,v_−i)], with expectations over simulator randomness only. Payments must be integrable; no individual-rationality or no-subsidy requirement is imposed in this variant. Require E_{v∼∏F_i,coins}[∑_i v_i x_i(v)]≥E_{v∼∏F_i}[∑_i v_i A_i(v)] exactly, without ε loss. One uniform transformation must work for every such prior and oracle.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the proposition or its negation for the stated model. Bayesian truthfulness, preservation only up to an additive loss, or impossibility only for MIDR transformations does not settle this stated variant.

title: Universal maximin-share approximation for additive goods
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
summary: Each agent’s maximin share is the best value they can secure by partitioning the goods and receiving a least-valued bundle. The target is the largest fraction of those personal shares that can always be met simultaneously for nonnegative additive valuations. It ranges over all finite numbers of agents and indivisible goods, with equal entitlements and no sharing. Two November results show that the guaranteed share approaches one for large numbers of agents. The worst case over all market sizes, including small markets, still determines the requested constant.
formal: Determine the universal maximin-share approximation constant for additive indivisible goods, \[\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}=\sup\bigl\{\alpha\in[0,1]:\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall m\ge0\ \forall v\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{n\times m}\ \exists(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\in\Pi_n([m])\ \forall i\in[n],\ v_i(A_i)\ge\alpha\,\mu_i(v)\bigr\}.\] Here \(n,m\) range over integers, \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\), and \(\mu_i(v)=\max_{(P_1,\ldots,P_n)\in\Pi_n([m])}\min_{j\in[n]}v_i(P_j)\). The benchmark asks for this one dimensionless constant with absolute error at most \(1/100\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof of the error bound.
definitions: Write \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). The set \(\Pi_n([m])\) consists of ordered \(n\)-tuples of pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is all of \([m]\); empty bundles are allowed. Each item belongs to exactly one agent, with no splitting, sharing, disposal, payments or externalities. Each entry \(v_{ig}\) is an arbitrary finite nonnegative real value, and values of bundles are additive. Every agent has the same entitlement; the number of agents determining each maximin share is the original \(n\). The partition maximizing \(\mu_i(v)\) is chosen separately for each agent using that agent’s valuations. Its maximum exists because there are finitely many partitions. If \(\mu_i(v)=0\), the corresponding approximation requirement is simply \(v_i(A_i)\ge0\); no ratio with a zero denominator is taken. Valuations need not be identical, normalized, strictly positive or drawn from a finite value set. The allocation may depend on the entire instance. No runtime bound, incentive condition, randomness model or finite encoding of the real entries is imposed, because the target concerns mathematical existence rather than efficient computation. The supremum is well-defined in \([0,1]\), since the feasible set contains zero. The question covers all finite agent and item counts simultaneously, rather than the best guarantee for any one fixed \(n\).
answer_criterion: Supply a real number \(a\), or an unambiguous mathematical specification of one, and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(|a-\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}|\le1/100\), using exactly the universal domain and maximin-share definition above. A proved interval \([L,U]\) containing \(\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}\) with \(U-L\le1/50\) qualifies via its midpoint. One-sided guarantees, counterexamples without a matching sufficiently close lower bound, empirical searches, or results only for a fixed number of agents do not meet the criterion. Determination of the exact supremum is welcome but not required; the submitted approximation need not itself be a universally attainable allocation ratio. The existing gap between \(7/9\) and \(39/40\) is wider than the permitted interval.
references: https://tcsopenproblems.com/problem/4 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04977v2 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.10423v1 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13056v2 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33051v1 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33052v1

title: Polynomial query complexity of exact envy-free cake cutting
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
summary: The cake is a continuous interval whose value may differ arbitrarily between agents. The task is to allocate all of it exactly without any agent preferring another agent’s piece. Preferences are learned only through exact value and cut queries, and disconnected pieces are allowed. One deterministic protocol must use polynomially many queries on every profile, although computation between queries is unrestricted. Aziz gives a deterministic protocol using O(n⁷ log n) queries, with an improved O(n⁶ log n) bound in Appendix H.
formal:
Do there exist absolute integers \(C,d\ge1\) and one uniform deterministic Robertson–Webb protocol which, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every profile of \(n\) nonatomic additive cake valuations, makes at most \(Cn^d\) queries and produces a partition \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) of the entire cake satisfying
\[
 \mu_i(A_i)\ge\mu_i(A_j)\qquad\text{for every }1\le i,j\le n?
\]
Every allocated piece may be a finite union of intervals. The allocation must be complete and exactly envy-free on every profile and for every valid choice of cut-query responses.
definitions:
The cake is \([0,1]\). Agent \(i\)'s valuation \(\mu_i\) is an arbitrary nonatomic Borel probability measure: it is nonnegative and countably additive, \(\mu_i([0,1])=1\), and \(\mu_i(\{x\})=0\) for every point \(x\). A piece is a finite union of intervals, with endpoints assigned consistently to make the pieces disjoint. Endpoints have zero value for every agent. Measures need not have densities, and there is no bound on density, number of breakpoints or description complexity. No distribution over profiles is assumed.

The protocol receives \(n\) and accesses valuations only through these exact oracles:

\(\operatorname{Eval}(i,x,y)\), for known marks \(0\le x\le y\le1\), returns \(\mu_i([x,y])\).

\(\operatorname{Cut}(i,x,\alpha)\), for a known mark \(x\) and a requested real value \(0\le\alpha\le\mu_i([x,1])\), returns some \(y\in[x,1]\) such that \(\mu_i([x,y])=\alpha\). This returned coordinate becomes a known mark. Initially only \(0\) and \(1\) are known. Nonatomicity guarantees existence of an answer. If an interval has zero value, a cut may have several valid positions; every such response must preserve the guarantee. The protocol must issue only valid queries.

Each evaluation or cut call counts as one query. The protocol may combine interval values by additivity and use previously learned values without paying again. It may query one agent at a mark obtained from another. The final allocation must use endpoints among the known marks; arbitrary newly guessed endpoints are not available as free cuts.

Uniformity means one finite program for all \(n\). Between queries it may use integer computation, store and copy exact real answers, perform real addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by a nonzero number, and compare real numbers exactly. Its program has rational real constants and may perform arbitrary finite loops and finite searches. Only the number of oracle calls is bounded; no time, memory or bit-precision bound is imposed on this local computation. It must nevertheless terminate after finitely many operations on every allowed execution. This specifies a query model with exact real arithmetic, not a Turing computation of the digits of arbitrary valuation reals.

The output lists, for each agent, finitely many intervals with known endpoints. Their union covers \([0,1]\), and no interior point belongs to two agents' pieces. Shared boundary points are assigned to one incident piece. Empty pieces are allowed, but no positive-length residue may be discarded, even if all agents value it at zero.

Envy-freeness compares all pieces using the evaluating agent's own measure. It requires every displayed inequality exactly, with no additive or multiplicative fairness error. It does not require a connected piece per agent or impose any incentive-compatibility condition. The query bound is worst-case over both valuation profiles and valid oracle responses. There is no randomization or favorable-profile exception.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked construction of one protocol and constants satisfying the statement, with proofs of query validity, termination, complete allocation, exact envy-freeness and the uniform polynomial query bound; or give a complete Lean-checked refutation of this existence claim in the specified model.

A protocol with an arbitrary finite bound depending on \(n\), a polynomial average-case or approximate-fairness guarantee, or a protocol leaving cake unallocated is insufficient. A lower bound for one particular procedure does not rule out all polynomial-query protocols. This is an existence question about an exact fairness property and an asymptotic resource bound, so numerical approximation of envy does not meet the answer criterion.

title: Constant price of stability for undirected network design
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
summary: Each player chooses a path joining its own pair of terminals. Users of an edge split that edge’s cost equally. A stable profile permits no profitable unilateral path change. The comparison uses the cheapest stable profile and the socially cheapest network. The proposed constant must work for arbitrary terminal pairs and player counts.
formal: Is the price of stability of undirected equal-cost-sharing network design games bounded by a universal constant?
definitions: An instance is a finite undirected graph with nonnegative real edge costs c_e and k≥1 players, each with connected terminal pair (s_i,t_i). Player i chooses a simple s_i-to-t_i path (the empty path is allowed if its terminals coincide). For path profile P, let n_e be the number of chosen paths using e. Player i pays ∑_{e∈P_i} c_e/n_e. A pure Nash equilibrium is a profile at which no single player can reduce its own payment by switching to any other feasible path, with the shares recomputed after the deviation. Social cost C(P)=∑_{e:n_e>0}c_e counts every used edge once. OPT is the minimum social cost over all path profiles, equivalently the minimum-cost subgraph connecting all terminal pairs. The assertion is ∃C<∞ such that every instance has a pure Nash profile P with C(P)≤C OPT. This inequality includes OPT=0. It does not require every equilibrium to be cheap or an efficient algorithm for finding one; terminal pairs need not share a common source.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the proposition or its negation for the stated model. A bound growing with k or a theorem restricted to common-source instances is insufficient.

title: Pure positional Nash equilibria in reachability games
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
summary: Every player in a finite deterministic turn-based game wants to visit their own target set at least once. The question asks for a Nash equilibrium in which each player always makes the same choice at the same vertex. A player testing a unilateral improvement may remember the entire play history while all other players keep their original choices. Equilibrium is required from one designated start, targets need not be absorbing, and neither a particular winning vector nor randomized strategies are allowed. A complete Lean-checked solution must prove universal existence or verify a counterexample; the 2026 randomized theorem leaves this pure all-reachability target open.
formal:
Does every finite deterministic turn-based multiplayer game with a designated initial vertex and a reachability objective for each player admit a pure positional Nash equilibrium?

The equilibrium is evaluated from that one initial vertex. A unilateral deviating strategy may depend on the complete finite history, even though every strategy in the proposed equilibrium must depend only on the current vertex.
definitions:
Fix any integer \(k\ge1\). An arena consists of a nonempty finite vertex set \(V\), a directed edge relation \(E\subseteq V\times V\), a partition \(V=V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_k\), and an initial vertex \(v_0\in V\). Empty parts are allowed. Every vertex has at least one outgoing edge; self-loops are allowed. At a vertex in \(V_i\), player \(i\) chooses the next vertex along one outgoing edge. All players observe the full history. There are no simultaneous moves, random transitions or hidden information.

Player \(i\) has any target set \(T_i\subseteq V\), which may be empty or overlap other targets. Targets are not required to be absorbing: play may leave a target after reaching it. An infinite play \(\rho=v_0v_1v_2\cdots\) follows edges of \(E\). Its payoff to player \(i\) is
\[
u_i(\rho)=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if }v_t\in T_i\text{ for some integer }t\ge0,\\
0,&\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
Thus a visit at time zero counts, and visiting a target once suffices forever. No player has a safety, recurrence or parity objective.

A pure strategy for player \(i\) assigns a legal successor to each finite path whose last vertex lies in \(V_i\). It can use the entire path and has no memory or computability restriction. A pure positional strategy is a function \(\sigma_i:V_i\to V\) satisfying \((v,\sigma_i(v))\in E\) for every \(v\in V_i\); at every occurrence of that vertex it makes the same choice.

A profile \(\sigma=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_k)\) determines one infinite play \(\operatorname{Out}(v_0,\sigma)\). It is a Nash equilibrium from \(v_0\) when, for every player \(i\) and every pure history-dependent strategy \(\tau_i\),
\[
u_i\bigl(\operatorname{Out}(v_0,\sigma)\bigr)
\ge
u_i\bigl(\operatorname{Out}(v_0,\sigma_{-i},\tau_i)\bigr).
\]
Here \((\sigma_{-i},\tau_i)\) replaces only player \(i\)'s strategy; every other player keeps the originally specified strategy, including at vertices not reached by the original play. A player already winning cannot improve. A losing player must have no unilateral way to reach its target.

The question quantifies over all finite arenas, all target sets, all player counts and every designated start, and asks for the existence of a positional profile for each such instance. The profile may depend on the start. It need not be an equilibrium from every vertex simultaneously or following every history, and no particular payoff vector is prescribed. No running-time bound or algorithm to find the profile is required. Randomized positional profiles do not meet the pure-strategy requirement. Allowing randomized deviations with expected binary payoffs would give the same equilibrium condition against a fixed pure profile: a positive probability of reaching a target entails a finite legal reaching history that can be followed by a pure deviation.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every instance in the stated class has such a pure positional equilibrium, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A refutation may provide one finite arena, target sets and initial vertex together with a proof that every pure positional profile has a profitable unilateral deviation.

A counterexample using other objective types, stochastic transitions, a required payoff vector, or equilibrium simultaneously from every vertex does not settle this proposition. Existence of randomized memoryless profiles or pure profiles with memory does not prove it. Positive results restricted to absorbing targets do not cover the full target.

title: Randomized metric distortion in social choice
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
summary: What is the smallest universal expected metric distortion achievable from full voter rankings? The voting rule selects a lottery without seeing the distances that produced those rankings. The former value-two conjecture is false, with a general lower bound around 2.11264. A preprint dated 8 September 2026 states an upper bound of 2.13713, leaving a nonzero gap. The Lean benchmark accepts a certified determination with absolute error at most 0.01 throughout the stated numerical domain.
formal: Determine \(D^\star\), the infimum worst-case distortion of a randomized voting rule that sees every voter’s full ranking of the candidates. Evaluate a rule by the expected total distance from voters to the selected candidate. The same rule must handle every finite election.
definitions:
An election \(E\) consists of disjoint nonempty finite labeled sets of voters \(V\) and candidates \(C\), and a strict total order \(\succ_v\) on \(C\) for each voter. A pseudometric \(d\) on \(V\cup C\) is consistent when \(a\succ_v b\) implies \(d(v,a)\le d(v,b)\). Distinct points can coincide, and distance ties can be ranked either way. Write \(\operatorname{SC}_d(a)=\sum_{v\in V}d(v,a)\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}_d=\min_{a\in C}\operatorname{SC}_d(a)\).

A rule \(f\) maps the full labeled rankings to a lottery on \(C\). It has access only to these rankings, may use arbitrary real probabilities and has unrestricted computation. The class includes rules without anonymity, neutrality or incentive-compatibility assumptions. For \(D\ge1\), a rule achieves distortion at most \(D\) when, for every election and every consistent pseudometric,
\[\sum_{a\in C}f(E)_a\operatorname{SC}_d(a)\le D\operatorname{OPT}_d.\]
This requires zero expected cost whenever the optimum is zero. Define \(\operatorname{Dist}(f)\) as the infimum of all such \(D\), with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\), and \(D^\star=\inf_f\operatorname{Dist}(f)\). The expectation is over the selected candidate. Using average distance divides both sides by the same positive number of voters.
answer_criterion: Supply a real number \(a\) and a Lean proof of \(|a-D^\star|\le1/100\). For example, prove \(\ell\le D^\star\le u\) for explicit endpoints with \(u-\ell\le1/50\), and take \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). A proof of the exact value also suffices. The tolerance belongs to the benchmark’s answer criterion.

title: Matrix multiplication exponent two
summary: Matrix multiplication computes all entries of the product of two input matrices. The card asks whether every exponent strictly above two is achievable by exact complex arithmetic circuits. The circuit model allows nonuniform constants and charges arithmetic gates. This does not require a quadratic-size family attaining the endpoint exponent. OpenAI gives the matching lower bound and determines the complex matrix multiplication exponent as 9/4.
formal: Does the matrix multiplication exponent over \(\mathbb C\) equal two? Precisely, writing \(s(n)\) for the minimum arithmetic gate count of an exact circuit multiplying two \(n\times n\) complex matrices, is it true that \[\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists C_\varepsilon>0\ \forall n\in\mathbb N_{\ge2},\qquad s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{2+\varepsilon}?\] The circuit family and its constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\); an \(O(n^2)\) bound is not required.
definitions: For each integer \(n\ge2\), the inputs are the \(2n^2\) independent complex variables \(a_{ij},b_{ij}\), with \(1\le i,j\le n\). The required \(n^2\) outputs are the polynomials \(c_{ij}=\sum_{t=1}^n a_{it}b_{tj}\). Use an [arithmetic circuit](definitions.html#arithmetic-circuits) over \(\mathbb C\), with input variables, arbitrary field constants, and binary addition, subtraction and multiplication gates. Multiple uses of a previously computed value are allowed. Each ordered output position \((i,j)\) designates a node whose polynomial is exactly \(c_{ij}\), so one circuit must be correct on every pair of complex matrices. Circuit topology and constants may depend on n, but not on the matrix entries. Size is the number of arithmetic gates, including gates operating on constants; source nodes and output designations have zero cost. No division, comparison, branching, randomness, approximation or test of the input values is permitted. This is a nonuniform algebraic model: a separate finite circuit may be chosen for each n, with no required algorithm generating the circuits or their constants. Scalar arithmetic is exact, and costs of representing complex numbers in bits are outside the model. The number of gates differs only by a constant factor from the source’s binary-circuit wire measure, and allowing an explicit subtraction gate also changes size by at most a constant factor; neither changes the exponent. Define s(n) as the least size among correct circuits. This minimum exists because the elementary multiplication formula gives a circuit, and sizes are nonnegative integers. The n squared output polynomials are distinct and none is a source polynomial, so each needs a distinct arithmetic gate and \(s(n)\ge n^2\). The elementary upper bound \(s(n)\le2n^3\) makes the exponent set nonempty and gives \(2\le\omega\le3\). The infimum need not be attained. Specifically, \(\omega\le u\) means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a real \(C_\varepsilon>0\) such that \(s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{u+\varepsilon}\) for every integer n at least two. A lower bound \(\omega\ge\ell\) means that for every real \(\tau<\ell\) and C>0 there is an integer n at least two with \(s(n)>Cn^\tau\). These quantified bounds do not demand a circuit family attaining the endpoint exponent or a pointwise lower bound at that endpoint. The binary target is \(\omega=2\), with the positive-slack convention just stated.
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that for each \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an upper bound \(C_\varepsilon n^{2+\varepsilon}\) on the specified arithmetic-circuit size over \(\mathbb C\), or show that some positive \(\varepsilon\) admits no such bound.

title: Logarithmic exponent of integer multiplication
summary: The inputs are two binary integers and the output is their exact product. Time counts elementary transitions of one fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine. The requested exponent is the infimum of attainable powers of the logarithmic overhead beyond linear time. OpenAI gives an unconditional upper bound of one half on this logarithmic exponent. Its matching lower bound assumes Weak ETH for 3-SAT, leaving the unconditional estimate to within 0.01 open.
formal:
For a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) that exactly multiplies every pair of \(n\)-bit nonnegative binary integers, let \(t_M(n)\) be its worst-case transition count. Determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the logarithmic-overhead exponent
\[
\alpha_{\mathrm{mult}}=\inf\left\{a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}:\exists M\ \exists C>0\ \exists n_0\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge n_0,\quad t_M(n)\le Cn\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^a\right\}.
\]
The machine model and quantifiers are specified below. The linear factor \(n\) accounts for the bit scale of the input and output; the requested number describes the power of the logarithmic overhead. The output is the exact product, explicitly written in \(2n\) bits. The exponent lies in \([0,1]\); attaining its infimum is not required.
definitions:
For every integer \(n\ge 1\) the input consists of two length-n binary strings encoding integers a,b with \(0\le a,b<2^{n}\); leading zeroes are allowed. The required output is the ordinary binary representation of ab, padded to length 2n. The machine has a fixed finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes with one head per tape. Input strings and end markers occupy designated tapes initially, other tapes are blank, and the output must be written explicitly on a designated output tape. In one transition the machine reads and writes at most one cell per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. The cost is the number of transitions, including access, data movement and output. The same machine must halt correctly for every n and every input pair; its tape count and alphabet cannot grow with n. For a fixed correct machine M, let \(t_{M}(n)\) be its maximum running time over the \(2^{2n}\) pairs of n-bit strings. Bounds concern these fixed-machine functions as n tends to infinity. A fresh hardcoded machine for each n is not allowed. No random access, unit-cost arithmetic on arbitrarily long integers, advice, oracle or quantum operations are part of the model. Changing the padded output convention to ordinary unpadded binary changes the cost by only \(O(n)\).

The infimum ranges over logarithmic powers attainable as upper bounds by correct machines in this model. For each candidate exponent \(a\), the machine \(M\), multiplicative constant \(C\) and threshold \(n_0\) may depend on \(a\), but not on the input length or input values. One fixed machine must meet each asserted bound at every sufficiently large length and remain correct at all lengths. It is not permissible to minimize separately over a different hardcoded program for each \(n\).

The explicit output requires \(\Omega(n)\) transitions. The known \(O(n\log n)\) algorithm makes the defining set nonempty and gives \(0\le\alpha_{\mathrm{mult}}\le1\). This definition neither assumes an ordinary growth limit nor requires one machine to attain the infimum. Exponent zero does not by itself assert a linear-time algorithm: it allows separate upper bounds with arbitrarily small positive powers of \(\log n\). Multiplicative constants and iterated-logarithmic factors are not part of the requested numerical accuracy.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguously specified real number \(b\) and a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(|b-\alpha_{\mathrm{mult}}|\le1/100\), in the stated uniform deterministic multitape model. A certified enclosing interval of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies via its midpoint; both endpoints must be justified. An exact value also qualifies. Upper bounds must respect the order of quantifiers: each machine is fixed across all input lengths. A lower bound must cover every correct machine in the model. A lower bound on the infimum does not require an attained optimal time or an eventual matching lower bound at every input length. The answer concerns the logarithmic exponent after the linear factor \(n\), not a polynomial exponent of \(n\), a matching full running-time function, or a rounded estimate without a proved error bound.

title: Derandomizing polynomial identity testing
summary: An arithmetic circuit may compute the zero polynomial even when cancellation is difficult to see from its graph. The question asks for an exact deterministic polynomial-time test given the entire circuit over binary-encoded integer constants. Circuits may reuse intermediate results, have arbitrary depth and compute polynomials of exponential degree. Randomized polynomial-time tests are known, while removing their randomness would have major circuit lower-bound consequences. Recent deterministic results for restricted circuit shapes do not provide the requested algorithm for all explicit circuits.
formal: Is polynomial identity testing for explicitly represented arithmetic circuits over the integers in deterministic polynomial time? More precisely, do a deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) exist such that, on every valid circuit encoding of bit length \(N\), \(A\) decides whether the output is the zero formal polynomial and halts within \(C(N+2)^k\) steps?
definitions: An arithmetic circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output. Each input node is either one of the explicitly listed variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) or a signed integer constant given in binary. Each internal gate has two ordered predecessors and computes addition, subtraction or multiplication over \(\mathbb Z\). Intermediate results may be used by several later gates; the graph need not be a formula. A topological list of all nodes, their labels, predecessor indices and the output index is supplied, with the full variable list and all bits of every constant included in the input length \(N\). Repeated use of a variable or predecessor is allowed. Gates compute in the commutative polynomial ring \(\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), and the zero polynomial means that every coefficient is exactly zero. No division, exponentiation, comparison, oracle or approximate-arithmetic gate is present. There is no depth restriction, multilinearity promise or bound on the number of nonzero monomials. No separate polynomial bound on total degree is promised: repeated multiplication can give a degree exponential in the circuit description length. The algorithm has access to the complete graph and labels, not only an oracle for evaluations. Its running time counts bit-level Turing-machine operations, including all work on constants and any integers it computes; unbounded-size integer operations are not free. Correctness is exact on every valid encoding, with no randomness or advice. Malformed encodings are rejected within the same polynomial bound. One fixed machine and one fixed polynomial bound must work for all numbers of variables, circuits, degrees and integer constants.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm exists, or prove that no such algorithm exists in the stated bit model. A positive answer requires a uniform algorithm correct for every allowed circuit, including those of exponential degree. A negative answer must exclude every deterministic machine with any fixed polynomial time bound; a lower bound for one procedure does not suffice. Results only for formulas, restricted depth, bounded-read circuits, sparse polynomials or a restricted degree regime do not resolve the full target. An evaluation-only lower bound without the explicit circuit-description promise also does not refute it. Numerical agreement at sampled inputs does not establish a formal identity.

title: Deterministic polynomial-time factorization over finite fields
summary: The input is a densely written polynomial over a finite field whose polynomial-basis representation is supplied. The requested output is every monic irreducible factor, its multiplicity, and the original leading scalar. One deterministic algorithm must run in time polynomial in the degree and the logarithm of the field size for all valid inputs. Randomized methods, special decoding instances, averages over primes and characteristic-dependent bounds do not provide that guarantee. A complete Lean-checked proof must establish both universal correctness and the uniform bit-time bound, or prove their impossibility.
formal:
Does there exist one deterministic Turing algorithm \(A\) and absolute integers \(K,d\ge1\) such that, for every valid explicit field representation \(\mathbb F_q=\mathbb F_p[t]/(h(t))\) and every dense polynomial \(f\in\mathbb F_q[x]\) of degree \(n\ge1\), the algorithm outputs the complete irreducible factorization of \(f\) in at most
\[
K\bigl(n+\lceil\log_2q\rceil+1\bigr)^d
\]
bit operations?

The input includes the prime \(p\), the supplied monic irreducible field modulus \(h\), and every coefficient of \(f\). The algorithm and the constants are independent of \(n,p,h\) and \(f\), and no unproved number-theoretic assumption is allowed.
definitions:
Let \(p\ge2\) be a prime, let \(e\ge1\), and let \(h(t)\in\mathbb F_p[t]\) be a monic irreducible polynomial of degree \(e\). The field \(\mathbb F_p\) is the integers modulo \(p\), and \(\mathbb F_q=\mathbb F_p[t]/(h(t))\), where \(q=p^e\), is the field of residue classes modulo \(h\). Its elements are represented uniquely by polynomials of degree less than \(e\), with each coefficient in \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\). Addition and multiplication mean polynomial addition and multiplication followed by reduction modulo \(p\) and \(h\).

The input writes \(p,e,n\) in binary, all coefficients of \(h\), and all \(n+1\) coefficients of \(f(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n a_jx^j\), with \(a_n\ne0\). Each field coefficient uses its full \(e\)-tuple of residues, each residue occupying \(\lceil\log_2p\rceil\) bits. Integer and array boundaries use a fixed unambiguous encoding. In particular, the polynomial is dense: zero coefficients are present, and neither a circuit nor an evaluation oracle substitutes for the coefficient list. The field representation is also part of the counted input, rather than fixed advice. Primality of \(p\) and irreducibility and degree of \(h\) are promises; constructing \(h\) from \(p,e\) is not an additional output task. No correctness condition is imposed on malformed or unpromised inputs.

A nonconstant polynomial \(g\in\mathbb F_q[x]\) is irreducible if it cannot be written as the product of two polynomials of positive degree over this same field. Monic means that its leading coefficient is one. A complete factorization consists of a nonzero field element \(u\), a list of pairwise distinct monic irreducible polynomials \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\) of positive degree, and positive binary integers \(m_1,\ldots,m_r\), satisfying the exact polynomial identity
\[
f=u\prod_{i=1}^r g_i^{m_i}.
\]
All factors are written as dense coefficient lists in the supplied field representation. The order of factors is irrelevant. Multiplicities are required, including for repeated factors in positive characteristic; there is no square-free or separability promise. Merely deciding irreducibility, returning a proper factor, or finding roots when they exist is not the specified output.

Time is worst-case deterministic bit time on a standard multitape Turing machine. Reading, arithmetic, conversions, preprocessing and writing the factorization all count. The full input length is polynomially related to \(n+\lceil\log_2q\rceil+1\), so the displayed bound is equivalent to a single polynomial bound in that length. It is not polynomial dependence on the numerical value of \(p\) or \(q\). There is no random tape, oracle, uncharged field operation or family of field-specific algorithms. Extension degree and characteristic may both grow with the input.

The target is an existence proposition about an exact symbolic factorization algorithm. Absolute numerical approximation does not replace the polynomial identity or irreducibility conditions.
answer_criterion:
Supply an algorithm and a complete Lean-checked proof that it terminates with the specified complete factorization on every valid input and obeys one bound of the displayed form. Alternatively, supply a complete Lean-checked proof that no deterministic algorithm with any such absolute polynomial bound exists.

An expected-time randomized algorithm, an average over inputs or primes, polynomial dependence on the field cardinality or characteristic, a restriction on degree or Galois group, or a bound conditional on an unproved hypothesis does not settle this proposition. The failure of a particular method is not a proof of the negative answer.

title: Word problem for one-relation monoids
summary: An ordinary one-relation monoid identifies words using one fixed reversible literal replacement rule in arbitrary surrounding contexts. The question asks whether a single algorithm can decide equality of any two words when the alphabet and defining relation are also supplied. Empty words and length-changing relations are allowed, and the algorithm must halt on unequal pairs as well as equal ones. Recent undecidability results for inverse monoids, submonoid membership and equations with unknowns concern different or broader problems. A resolution would locate a central decidability boundary for equality under minimal finite algebraic presentations.
formal: Is the uniform word problem for ordinary one-relation monoids decidable? Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which, given any finite alphabet \(A\) and four finite words \(u,v,s,t\in A^*\), always halts and decides whether \(s\) and \(t\) represent the same element of the monoid \(\langle A\mid u=v\rangle\)? The presentation and the word pair are all parts of the input; no running-time bound is prescribed.
definitions:
The free monoid \(A^*\) consists of all finite literal strings over \(A\), including the empty word \(\varepsilon\), with concatenation as multiplication and \(\varepsilon\) as identity. The monoid \(\langle A\mid u=v\rangle\) is the quotient \(A^*/{\equiv}\), where \(\equiv\) is the least equivalence relation containing \(u\equiv v\) and satisfying \(p\equiv q\Rightarrow xpy\equiv xqy\) for all words \(x,y\). Equivalently, \(s\equiv t\) if and only if some finite sequence \(s=w_0,w_1,\ldots,w_k=t\) exists in which every adjacent pair is \((xuy,xvy)\) or \((xvy,xuy)\) for some \(x,y\in A^*\). A zero-step sequence is allowed.

The four words are fully supplied literal strings, not variables to be instantiated by unknown strings. The two relation sides and the tested words may be empty. Replacing an empty side means inserting the other side at a gap in the current finite word. The relation may have equal sides and may preserve or change length. The alphabet itself may be empty, in which case every word is empty. There are no inverse symbols with automatic cancellation, group axioms, cancellation laws or commutativity laws beyond consequences of the single stated monoid relation.

The input explicitly gives an integer alphabet size \(a\ge0\), identifies \(A\) with \(\{1,\ldots,a\}\), and lists all four words with binary letter indices and lengths. This is finite ordinary string input, with malformed encodings rejectable. One ordinary deterministic program must give exact YES/NO answers for all valid presentations and all pairs, terminating on both answers. It receives no oracle, nonuniform advice, random coins or unbounded precomputed data for a presentation. No numerical approximation arises. This is uniform decidability across presentations; a separate non-effectively chosen algorithm for each fixed presentation has different quantifiers.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that the displayed language of presentation-and-word-pair instances is decidable by a total computable function, or a proof of its undecidability. A positive proof must formalize finite words, the single-relation contextual congruence, finite encoding and a uniform algorithm whose termination and both correctness directions hold for all allowed empty and nonempty inputs. A negative reduction must stay inside ordinary one-relation monoids and preserve equality in both directions. A single fixed one-relation monoid with undecidable word problem suffices for a negative answer but is stronger than necessary to refute uniform decidability. A semidecision procedure that halts only on equal words, an unproved termination claim, an exponential derivation-length lower bound, or a negative theorem for inverse monoids, submonoid membership or equations with unknowns does not by itself settle the target. No Lean resolution is asserted by this review.

title: Sum-of-square-roots problem
summary: The input describes a signed integer combination of square roots of positive integers using binary encodings. The question is whether one deterministic algorithm can decide exactly whether its value is nonnegative in polynomial time. All input magnitudes count toward the bit length, and zero or extremely small values are included. The original separation-bound question, equality testing, unary inputs and nonuniform circuit results provide related context without settling this target. A complete Lean proof must establish the uniform algorithm and its bound or prove that no such algorithm exists.
formal:
Does the sum-of-square-roots decision problem belong to deterministic polynomial time? An instance explicitly gives an integer \(n\ge1\), signed integers \(c_1,\ldots,c_n\), and positive integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\), all in binary. The required answer is whether
\[
E(c,a)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_i\sqrt{a_i}\ \ge0,
\]
where each square root is the nonnegative real square root. There is no promise that \(E\ne0\), that the radicands are distinct or square-free, or that their magnitudes are polynomial in \(n\). The target is one uniform deterministic algorithm with a polynomial bound in the total input bit length. This selects the standard algorithmic question explicitly stated in the newer sources; the original TOPP entry principally asks for tight separation bounds, a related quantitative question distinguished below.
definitions:
For \(a>0\), \(\sqrt a\) denotes the unique real \(r\ge0\) with \(r^2=a\). Coefficients may be positive, negative or zero, and repeated terms are permitted. The comparison is exact: when \(E=0\) the answer is yes, however close a nonzero \(E\) is to zero. No approximate value of \(E\), promise of a numerical gap or factorization of the radicands is supplied.

Fix the following binary encoding. For an integer \(r\ge0\), let \(\ell\) be the bit length of \(r+1\); its code is \(\ell\) one-bits, one zero-bit and the \(\ell\)-bit binary expansion of \(r+1\). A signed integer \(c\) is encoded by the code of \(2c\) if \(c\ge0\), and of \(-2c-1\) otherwise. A valid instance is the code for \(n\ge1\), followed by the signed code for \(c_i\) and the code for \(a_i\ge1\), for each \(i=1,\ldots,n\) in order, with no trailing bits. Write \(L\) for the full encoded length. Define the language \(Q\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) to consist exactly of valid encodings for which \(E(c,a)\ge0\); every malformed string is outside \(Q\).

Computation uses a deterministic multitape Turing machine with finite control, one read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes. Its fixed alphabet is \(\{0,1,\#,\square\}\), with \(\square\) blank. Tapes have nonnegative integer cell indices, all heads start at zero, and the input tape holds the input bits followed by blanks. One transition reads all scanned symbols, updates the state, writes at most one symbol on each work tape and moves each head by at most one cell; a left move at zero stays at zero. Two halting states output zero and one. Each transition costs one, including all parsing and arithmetic work. The program and number of tapes are independent of the instance. There is no advice, randomness, oracle, exact-real register or unit-cost square-root instruction.

The statement \(Q\in\mathrm{P}\) means
\[
\exists M\ \exists C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists d\in\mathbb N_{\ge0}\
\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*}:
\]
the single machine \(M\) halts within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) transitions and outputs one exactly when \(x\in Q\). Thus the clock holds on every binary input, and all binary magnitudes contribute to the measured length. No running-time dependence exponential in \(n\), in the largest radicand or in its bit length is hidden in the polynomial constants.
answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(Q\in\mathrm{P}\), or that \(Q\notin\mathrm{P}\), for the stated encoding and machine model. A positive answer must provide the one finite machine and polynomial constants and prove termination, the uniform time bound and both correctness directions on all inputs. A negative answer must show that for every such machine \(M\) and every \(C\ge1,d\ge0\), some binary input either is not answered within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) transitions or is answered incorrectly.

A proof for equality testing alone, unary inputs, a fixed number of terms, inputs separated from zero by a promised gap, or a unit-cost real-arithmetic model does not meet the criterion. Nor does a lower bound against a particular numerical procedure prove the negative answer. This is an unconditional yes/no complexity question: a conditional separation of complexity classes or a merely conditional algorithm does not decide it.

title: Polynomial-time finite-group isomorphism in the Cayley-table model
summary: Two finite groups are isomorphic when one bijection of their elements preserves every product. The input supplies both complete multiplication tables, and the target is deterministic polynomial-time decision in their explicit bit length. The algorithm must cover all finite groups without additional structural information. Qiao and Zhang’s November 2026 manuscript gives a deterministic algorithm that computes the coset of all isomorphisms in time polynomial in the group order. Its emptiness decides the question, and the explicit tables can be checked for valid group operations in polynomial time.
formal:
Is isomorphism of finite groups given by their complete multiplication tables decidable in deterministic polynomial time?

Precisely, do there exist one uniform deterministic machine \(A\) and integers \(C,c\ge1\) such that, on every binary input of length \(N\), \(A\) halts within \(C(N+1)^c\) steps and outputs YES exactly when the input encodes two finite groups \(G,H\) and there is a bijection \(\varphi:G\to H\) satisfying
\[
\forall x,y\in G,\qquad
\varphi(x\cdot_G y)=\varphi(x)\cdot_H\varphi(y)?
\]
The constants and program are independent of the orders and structure of both groups.
definitions:
A table of order \(n\ge1\) is a function \(T:[n]\times[n]\to[n]\), given by listing every one of its \(n^2\) entries. It defines a group precisely when the following three conditions hold:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\forall x,y,z\in[n],\quad T(T(x,y),z)=T(x,T(y,z));\\
&\exists e\in[n]\ \forall x\in[n],\quad T(e,x)=x=T(x,e);\\
&\forall x\in[n]\ \exists y\in[n],\quad T(x,y)=e=T(y,x).
\end{aligned}
\]
The identity \(e\) in the inverse condition is the same identity supplied by the second condition. All entries already belong to \([n]\), so closure is part of the table definition. Commutativity is not required. A group of order one is allowed; an empty group is not.

The input contains tables \(T_G\) and \(T_H\) of orders \(n\) and \(m\), respectively. If \(n\ne m\), they cannot be isomorphic. When \(n=m\), an isomorphism uses one bijection on elements in all three positions of the multiplication equation. Independent permutations of table rows, columns and entries are not the definition of the predicate. The labels \(1,\ldots,n\) have no mathematical significance, and the identity need not have label one.

Encode a table by \(1^n0\), followed by its \(n^2\) entries in row-major order, each in exactly \(\ell_n=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits, using ordinary most-significant-bit-first binary. Each entry must be in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Concatenate exactly two such encodings, with no trailing bits. The input bit length is
\[
N=n+m+2+n^2\ell_n+m^2\ell_m.
\]
Malformed encodings, entries outside the indicated range and tables failing any group axiom are NO instances. Group axioms can be checked in polynomial time, so this total-language convention does not add a new algorithmic obstacle to the promised-group version.

The output is only the decision bit. An explicit isomorphism, a canonical table and generators of an automorphism group are not required. There is no restriction to abelian, solvable, nilpotent or prime-power-order groups, and no distinguished subgroups, generators or decompositions are supplied.

The machine is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, a fixed finite number of tapes and fixed finite tape alphabets. Its input tape is read-only; work tapes begin blank. Each transition accesses only the cells under the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. Parsing, checking the group axioms, accessing table entries, computing auxiliary data and returning the answer all count. There is no randomness, advice, oracle or free preprocessing.

Polynomial time is measured in the full explicit bit length \(N\). For equal-order groups this is polynomially equivalent to polynomial time in \(n\), since the table already has \(n^2\) entries. It is not polynomial time in \(\log n\), the length needed merely to name the group order. An input consisting only of generators, a presentation, matrices, permutations or oracle access to multiplication would define a different representation model.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked construction of \(A,C,c\), proving exact correctness and the polynomial worst-case bound on all encoded pairs and invalid strings; or supply a complete Lean-checked proof that no such deterministic polynomial-time decider exists. A lower bound for bounded-depth circuits or a restricted algorithmic method is not a lower bound for this entire machine class. An algorithm for only a proper family of groups, an average-case guarantee, a quasipolynomial bound or an unverified claimed general algorithm does not settle the target.

title: Linear-size circuits for integer multiplication
summary: The input consists of two unsigned binary integers of the same width. The circuit must output every bit of their exact product on every input. The question is whether a constant times the input width always suffices in AND, OR and NOT gates. Known near-linear constructions and a conditional lower bound leave the unrestricted linear-size question unresolved in the checked sources. A complete Lean-checked proof of the circuit-family existence claim or its unconditional negation is required.
formal: Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_0\), some Boolean circuit with at most \(Cn\) gates computes the exact product of every pair of unsigned \(n\)-bit integers, outputting all \(2n\) product bits? The gates are binary AND and OR and unary NOT; fan-out and depth are unrestricted, and the circuit family need not be uniform.
definitions:
The \(2n\) inputs are bits \(a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1},b_0,\ldots,b_{n-1}\), representing
\[
a=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_i2^i,\qquad b=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}b_i2^i.
\]
The ordered output bits \(c_0,\ldots,c_{2n-1}\) must satisfy
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{2n-1}c_j2^j=ab
\]
on every input, including inputs with leading zeros. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph whose internal gates apply the stated Boolean operations. Constant sources 0 and 1 are available. Size counts operation gates, excluding input nodes, constant sources and output wires. Wires may copy a bit to arbitrarily many gates or outputs without an additional charge. There is no randomness, approximation or restriction on depth.

Let \(\operatorname{Mult}_n:\{0,1\}^{2n}\to\{0,1\}^{2n}\) be the multiplication function just defined. Its minimum gate count is \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(\operatorname{Mult}_n)\), using the shared [DM convention](definitions.html#boolean-circuits). The proposition is \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(\operatorname{Mult}_n)=O(n)\). The same \(C\) bounds all sufficiently large widths, but each width may use a different circuit, with no requirement to compute the family’s descriptions. A machine instruction multiplying entire words is not one Boolean gate. Any other fixed functionally complete bounded-fan-in Boolean basis changes this linear-size question only by constant factors.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must establish one constant \(C\), a threshold \(n_0\), and the existence of correct circuits at every \(n\ge n_0\). It need not give a uniform algorithm constructing their descriptions.

A negative proof must establish
\[
\forall C>0\;\forall n_0\ge1\;\exists n\ge n_0:\ \operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(\operatorname{Mult}_n)>Cn.
\]
It may give a stronger asymptotic lower bound, but such a stronger bound at every sufficiently large length is not required. A fixed linear lower bound, a bound only for restricted depth or wiring, or the failure of one multiplication construction does not settle the target. A conditional lower bound proves only its conditional statement.

title: Tensor decomposition at Kruskal’s uniqueness threshold
summary: A third-order tensor is represented as a sum of outer products of three families of vectors. Kruskal’s condition guarantees uniqueness when the three Kruskal ranks sum to at least twice the number of components plus two. The historical question asks for polynomial-time recovery throughout that entire regime, with the number of components allowed to grow. A September 2026 preprint gives such recovery in an exact real algebraic model that permits univariate root finding. After checking its proof and scope, this exact-recovery card is archived as resolved, while the separate questions about noisy data and finite-precision computation are not claimed solved.
formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized algorithm that, for every real third-order tensor having a decomposition satisfying Kruskal’s condition, recovers its rank decomposition in polynomial time in the exact algebraic model specified below? More precisely, are there constants \(C,c>0\) and one finite program whose cost is at most \(C(N+1)^c\) on every run and whose probability of outputting a correct decomposition is at least \(2/3\) on every promised input, where \(N=n_1n_2n_3\) is the number of input entries? The number of components and all Kruskal ranks may grow with the dimensions and are not supplied to the program.
definitions:
An input consists of positive integers \(n_1,n_2,n_3\) in binary and the explicitly listed real entries of an array \(T\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times n_2\times n_3}\), held in exact real registers. It is promised that, for some integer \(R\ge2\), there exist nonzero vectors \(a_j\in\mathbb R^{n_1}\), \(b_j\in\mathbb R^{n_2}\), \(c_j\in\mathbb R^{n_3}\), \(1\le j\le R\), such that \(T_{uvw}=\sum_{j=1}^{R}(a_j)_u(b_j)_v(c_j)_w\). Write \(A=[a_1|\cdots|a_R]\), and likewise \(B,C\). The Kruskal rank \(k_A\) is the largest integer \(k\in\{0,\ldots,R\}\) for which every choice of \(k\) distinct columns of \(A\) is linearly independent over \(\mathbb R\); the empty choice is independent. The promise is \(k_A+k_B+k_C\ge2R+2\). No hidden vectors, rank values, decomposition certificate, conditioning bound or generic-position assumption beyond this promise are provided.

Tensor rank is the minimum number of nonzero rank-one terms in any such sum over \(\mathbb R\). Kruskal’s theorem states that the promised \(R\) is the tensor rank and that its decomposition is unique up to reordering and componentwise nonzero rescaling. A valid output is \(R\) and three explicitly listed real factor matrices giving exactly \(T\). Permuting their columns together, or multiplying the three columns of component \(j\) by nonzero scalars whose product is \(1\), gives an equivalent output. Exact equality of all tensor entries is required; an approximation or a decomposition with more terms is not the specified output.

The computational model is an exact algebraic random-access machine with real registers and finite binary control. Copying, reading or writing a real register, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero real, and comparison of two reals each cost one operation. The only built-in real constants are \(0\) and \(1\). Integer arithmetic and control use ordinary binary bit operations, which also count. The model additionally has a real-root operation: given an explicitly listed coefficient vector \((u_0,\ldots,u_m)\) of a nonzero univariate polynomial, it returns all distinct real roots in increasing order, at cost \(m+1\); the coefficient-list construction and output storage count separately. This degree-cost convention is equivalent for polynomial-time existence to charging any fixed polynomial in the degree. An identically zero polynomial, or a division by zero, must be detected and handled without an undefined operation.

Each random instruction draws one independent real uniformly from \([0,1]\), at unit cost. Probability is taken over the product of these draws; the total running-time bound must hold on every run, including exceptional draws, on which the program may return failure. The finite program is independent of dimensions and input entries and has no advice, arbitrary input-dependent constants, multivariate-system oracle, floor operation or transcendental primitive. All reads, output writes, root calls and integer work are charged. The guarantee is a worst-case input bound with bounded failure probability, not an average over input tensors. This is an algebraic operation bound: it does not assert a bit-complexity or numerical-conditioning guarantee for approximations to the real entries.
answer_criterion: The historical benchmark asks for a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of an algorithm with the stated polynomial cost and success guarantee for every promised tensor, or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm exists in this precise model. A bound whose exponent depends on \(R\) or on a Kruskal rank does not establish a uniform polynomial bound. This record is archived after checking an affirmative algebraic-model result; the editorial verification does not itself supply a Lean formalization.

title: Exact Kronecker-polytope membership in polynomial time
summary: The input consists of three integer partitions of the same size, written as binary lists whose length may grow. The task is to decide exact membership of their normalized triple in the Kronecker polytope. Equivalently, the three lists must occur as spectra of the reduced matrices of some unit complex three-dimensional array. The desired algorithm is deterministic and polynomial in the full bit length, including arbitrarily close boundary cases. A complete Lean-checked complexity proof must go beyond known certificates and algorithms whose time depends polynomially on inverse approximation error.
formal:
Does there exist a deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm which, given three partitions \(\lambda,\mu,\nu\) of the same positive integer \(k\), each as a list of \(n\) nonnegative binary integers, decides whether
\[
\left(\frac{\lambda}{k},\frac{\mu}{k},\frac{\nu}{k}\right)\in\Delta_n,
\]
where \(\Delta_n\) is the Kronecker polytope defined below? The dimension \(n\) is part of the input, and membership is exact, including points on the boundary.
definitions:
A partition in this representation is a list \(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n\ge0\) of integers with \(\sum_i\lambda_i=k\). Trailing zeros are allowed. The lists \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) obey the same conditions and have the same sum. Division by \(k\) is coordinatewise. All entries and list lengths use binary encoding with fixed length delimiters; the complete lists are given explicitly. Let \(N\) be the total input bit length. In particular the number of parts grows with the input, while \(k\) may be exponentially large relative to its bit length.

Here is a self-contained spectral definition of \(\Delta_n\). For an array \(z=(z_{abc})_{a,b,c=1}^n\in\mathbb C^{n\times n\times n}\) satisfying \(\sum_{a,b,c}|z_{abc}|^2=1\), form three \(n\times n\) matrices
\[
R^{(1)}_{aa'}=\sum_{b,c}z_{abc}\overline{z_{a'bc}},\quad
R^{(2)}_{bb'}=\sum_{a,c}z_{abc}\overline{z_{ab'c}},\quad
R^{(3)}_{cc'}=\sum_{a,b}z_{abc}\overline{z_{abc'}}.
\]
The bar denotes complex conjugation. These matrices are Hermitian positive semidefinite and have trace 1. Write \(\operatorname{spec}_{\downarrow}(R)\) for the length-\(n\) list of real eigenvalues, with multiplicity, in nonincreasing order. Define
\[
\Delta_n=\left\{
\bigl(\operatorname{spec}_{\downarrow}(R^{(1)}),
\operatorname{spec}_{\downarrow}(R^{(2)}),
\operatorname{spec}_{\downarrow}(R^{(3)})\bigr):
z\in\mathbb C^{n\times n\times n},\ \sum_{a,b,c}|z_{abc}|^2=1
\right\}.
\]
This is the usual rational convex Kronecker polytope. The spectral definition is equivalent to the representation-theoretic definition in the source and specifies the question without requiring a representation-theory oracle. The tensor \(z\) is existentially quantified in the definition; it is not part of the input, need not have rational coordinates and need not be output by the algorithm.

The target algorithm is one deterministic multi-tape Turing machine \(A\) with constants \(K>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\), which halts on every valid input within \(K(N+1)^d\) steps and returns the exact membership bit. There is no advice, randomness, supplied list of facets, or oracle. All integer and rational arithmetic has its actual bit cost. No positive distance from the boundary is promised and no additive tolerance is allowed. A different precomputed algorithm for each fixed \(n\) is insufficient.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that this exact membership language is in deterministic polynomial time, or a proof that it is not. A positive answer must establish the full variable-dimension bit bound and exact correctness on boundary points. An approximate tensor-scaling result polynomial in inverse error, a nondeterministic certificate bound, or a fixed-dimension polytope computation does not suffice.

title: Polynomial-time computation of addition-chain length
summary: An addition chain starts at one and repeatedly forms a new integer by adding two earlier entries. Its shortest length is the fewest such additions needed to reach a specified positive target. The target is given in binary, and the requested algorithm must output the exact optimum in time polynomial in that bit length. This is a question about computing the minimum count, without additionally requiring an optimal chain as output. Known short chains, restricted families, heuristics and hardness for multiple targets do not establish the requested general deterministic algorithm or its impossibility.
formal: Do there exist constants \(K>0\), \(a\in\mathbb N\) and one deterministic multitape Turing machine that, on every positive integer \(n\) supplied in binary, outputs the exact shortest addition-chain length \(\ell(n)\) in binary within \(K(b+1)^a\) steps, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1\) is the input length?
definitions:
An addition chain for \(n\ge1\) is a finite strictly increasing sequence of positive integers
\[
1=a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_r=n
\]
such that for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\) there exist indices \(j,k\in\{0,\ldots,i-1\}\) with \(a_i=a_j+a_k\). The two indices may coincide, and an earlier entry may be reused any number of times. The length is the number \(r\) of additions, not the number \(r+1\) of entries. Define \(\ell(n)\) as the minimum such length; in particular, \(\ell(1)=0\). The only initially available number is \(1\). Subtraction, division, multiplication of chain entries and additional initial constants are not chain operations. The sum need not use the immediately preceding entry.

The machine receives just the ordinary binary expansion of \(n\), with no leading zeros. Its output is the ordinary binary expansion of the integer \(\ell(n)\), with \(0\) written as a single zero bit. The same finite program and constants must work for all valid inputs. The program has the usual unrestricted finite alphabet and binary work tapes of a multitape Turing machine, but all work, input reads and output writing count in its worst-case step bound. It has no advice, oracle, random bits or uncharged preprocessing. Invalid input strings must be rejected within the same bound with \(b\) interpreted as their string length. No addition chain or auxiliary number-theoretic data are supplied.

The requested machine may use any deterministic computation to find the length; the restrictions on chain operations define the quantity being optimized, rather than restricting the machine's internal calculations. The output is only the optimal length, not a chain attaining it. The input is a single binary target, not a list of targets and not a unary string of length \(n\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of an algorithm and fixed polynomial bound satisfying the exact-output task for every \(n\ge1\), or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm exists. Exact integer output is part of this computational existence question, not an extra accuracy restriction on a numerical-value benchmark. A fast approximation, a heuristic, polynomial time in \(n\) instead of its bit length, or a result for special targets does not meet the stated guarantee. Hardness for a single target under an additional hypothesis settles the negative answer only with a proof of that hypothesis. Hardness for several prescribed targets addresses a different input problem.

title: VP versus VNP
summary: The permanent sums one product of matrix variables for each permutation of the columns. The question is whether exact division-free arithmetic circuits over the complex numbers compute these polynomials with one polynomial size bound for all matrix dimensions. Theorem 1.1 of Anthropic’s November 2026 paper gives a superpolynomial circuit lower bound for the permanent over the complex numbers. The circuits can use arbitrary constants, reuse gates and have unrestricted depth. The result separates VP from VNP in the arithmetic model.
formal:
Over the complex field \(\mathbb C\), do there exist integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), some arithmetic circuit with at most \(B(n+1)^k\) operation gates computes the permanent polynomial
\[\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i,\sigma(i)}\ \in\mathbb C[x_{ij}:1\le i,j\le n]?\]
Circuits are division-free, have binary addition, subtraction and multiplication gates, allow arbitrary complex constants and unrestricted reuse, and compute exact formal polynomials. No uniform construction of the circuits is required. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\), with the classes defined below? The usual conjecture is that the answer is no.
definitions:
Polynomial and parameter. For \(n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(S_n\) be the set of bijections from \([n]\) to itself. The matrix \(X=(x_{ij})_{i,j\in[n]}\) consists of \(n^2\) independent commuting indeterminates. The displayed sum has one product for each permutation; each product chooses one variable in each row and column. Its total degree is \(n\). The growing parameter in the size bound is the matrix dimension \(n\), not the number of monomials or the magnitude of a numerical input. The number of input variables is \(N=n^2\).

Circuit model. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a distinguished output node. Each input node carries either one of the indeterminates or one exact constant from \(\mathbb C\). Each other node has two ordered incoming wires and a label \(+\), \(-\) or \(\times\); the same preceding node may feed both incoming wires. A node is evaluated in the commutative polynomial ring by applying its operation to the polynomials at its two predecessors. An input node itself may be the output. The circuit's size \(s(D)\) is the number of operation nodes; input nodes are not counted. A computed value may feed arbitrarily many subsequent nodes at no additional gate cost. Cancellations are allowed. Neither depth nor the degrees of intermediate polynomials are restricted. All constants are freely selected as part of the finite circuit and may depend on \(n\); their numerical bit lengths, descriptions or computability are not charged. Each arithmetic operation costs one gate. This is an arithmetic circuit measure, not a Turing-machine bit-time model. Input constants supply no operation other than their fixed field value: there are no bit-extraction, comparison, branching, oracle or division gates. Approximation and limits of circuits are also outside this model.

Exact computation and families. A circuit computes \(f\) when its output equals \(f\) as an element of the polynomial ring, meaning that every monomial has the same coefficient. Agreement at a selected finite set of matrices is not the correctness definition. Let \(c_{\mathbb C}(f)\) be the minimum size of such a circuit for \(f\). Every polynomial has a finite circuit, so this minimum is a nonnegative integer. In the main question the quantifier order is
\[\exists B,k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists D_n:\quad s(D_n)\le B(n+1)^k,\quad D_n\text{ computes }\operatorname{perm}_n.\]
The constants \(B,k\) are shared across all matrix dimensions. The circuits themselves may be unrelated from one dimension to the next: no machine, advice-generation procedure or polynomial-time algorithm for producing them is part of the assertion. Restricting constants to integers or rationals, or asking for a uniform family, would change this selected model.

Complexity classes. A sequence \(a(n)\) of nonnegative integers is polynomially bounded if some integers \(B,k\ge1\) satisfy \(a(n)\le B(n+1)^k\) for every \(n\ge1\). A polynomial family is a sequence \((m(n),f_n)_{n\ge1}\) with \(m(n)\ge0\) and \(f_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}]\); both \(m(n)\) and the total degree of \(f_n\) must be polynomially bounded. Total degree is the largest sum of exponents of a monomial with nonzero coefficient; for this boundedness condition give the zero polynomial degree zero. The family lies in \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\) if \(c_{\mathbb C}(f_n)\) is polynomially bounded as well, using the circuit model above. These are bounds on the resulting polynomials, not extra syntactic degree bounds at circuit gates.

Such a family lies in \(\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\) if there are a polynomially bounded witness length \(w(n)\in\mathbb N\) and a family
\[g_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)},y_1,\ldots,y_{w(n)}]\]
in \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\), with combined variable counts and total degrees polynomially bounded in \(n\), such that
\[f_n(x)=\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}^{w(n)}}g_n(x,a).\]
Each Boolean witness is embedded into \(\mathbb C^{w(n)}\) using the field elements zero and one; the sum is a finite algebraic sum over exactly those witnesses, not an existential quantifier and not a sum over all complex tuples. If \(w(n)=0\), there is one empty witness, so \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\subseteq\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\). No uniformity is imposed on these families or their circuit constants. Class equality means equality of these collections of polynomial families.
answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish common integers \(B,k\ge1\) and an appropriate finite circuit for every \(n\), with exact polynomial identity and the size bound in this model. A uniform construction is sufficient but is not required. A negative answer must prove
\[\forall B,k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists n\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\quad c_{\mathbb C}(\operatorname{perm}_n)>B(n+1)^k.\]
Equivalently, the violating dimension can be required to exceed any specified lower threshold, since finitely many exceptions can be absorbed into the coefficient \(B\). The lower bound must cover every finite circuit with arbitrary complex constants, cancellations and reuse. A result proved via the class-equality formulation must include the equivalence to this concrete permanent target. A fixed polynomial lower bound, even superlinear in \(n^2\), is insufficient to prove the negation. Lower bounds confined to formulas, monotone circuits, fixed depth, or superpolynomial determinantal complexity do not by themselves establish the required general-circuit separation. A numerical approximation scheme, a border-limit construction, or a result only over another field does not supply the exact circuits quantified here.

title: Superpolynomial arithmetic formula lower bounds
summary: The question asks whether the permanent requires arithmetic expression trees larger than every fixed polynomial bound. The trees compute formal polynomials over the complex numbers using addition and multiplication with arbitrary constants and unrestricted cancellations. The permanent is the particular polynomial family fixed by this question. Anthropic’s November 2026 lower bound applies to every arithmetic circuit for this family over the complex numbers. An expression tree is such a circuit, so its size must also grow faster than any fixed polynomial bound.
formal:
Is the permanent family outside polynomial-size arithmetic formulas over \(\mathbb C\)? Precisely, is the following assertion true?
\[
\forall K,C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\
\forall F,\qquad
\llbracket F\rrbracket=\operatorname{Perm}_n
\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{size}(F)>K n^C,
\]
where \(F\) ranges over the arithmetic formulas defined below and
\[
\operatorname{Perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i,\sigma(i)}
\in\mathbb C[x_{ij}:i,j\in[n]]?
\]
This card fixes the standard complex-field \(\mathrm{VNP}\)-versus-formula interpretation of the source’s broadly phrased explicit lower-bound challenge. By the permanent’s completeness under polynomially bounded projections, this asks whether some family in \(\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\) lacks polynomial-size formulas; it does not impose a separate uniform construction condition on the family of small formulas being ruled out. The source’s Open Problem 8 does not itself name a field or a particular hard family, so this precise choice is an explicit editorial specification.

Superpolynomial means that no single polynomial bound works for all dimensions. It does not demand one particular exponential rate or an eventually pointwise lower bound exceeding every polynomial. There are \(n^2\) input variables; \(n\) in the displayed size bound is the matrix dimension.
definitions:
For each integer \(n\ge1\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let \(S_n\) be the set of all permutations of \([n]\), and let \(X=(x_{ij})_{i,j\in[n]}\) be a matrix of distinct commuting indeterminates. The permanent is the displayed sum with coefficient one on every permutation monomial. Equality of outputs is equality of formal polynomials, including all coefficients; there is no numerical input distribution, approximation error or promise on matrix entries.

An arithmetic formula is a finite rooted ordered binary tree. Each leaf is labelled by one variable \(x_{ij}\) or one constant in \(\mathbb C\); each internal vertex is labelled \(+\) or \(\times\). Its output \(\llbracket F\rrbracket\) is defined recursively by the corresponding operations in the polynomial ring. Every vertex other than the root has exactly one parent. Reusing an expression requires another copy of its subtree. A sum or product with more than two operands must be expanded into binary operations and its full tree is counted.

The size is the total number of vertices, including every occurrence of each constant and variable. Thus a leaf has size one and a binary node with subformulas \(A,B\) has size \(1+\operatorname{size}(A)+\operatorname{size}(B)\). This is one plus the edge count used by the original survey, an equivalent convention for polynomial boundedness. Arbitrary negative and nonreal constants are allowed; subtraction can be expressed using a constant \(-1\) and the permitted operations. There is no division gate, exponentiation gate, Boolean operation, test, conditional branch or determinant gate.

Constants have unit size regardless of their magnitude, algebraic degree, computability or description length. The finite tree and its constants may depend arbitrarily on \(n\); no algorithm for generating them and no finite binary encoding of arbitrary complex constants is required. A formula is a finite mathematical object with complex labels, not a bit-cost algorithm for evaluating a numerical matrix. There is no restriction on depth, cancellation, intermediate degree, repeated variables, monotonicity or homogeneity of intermediate polynomials. The output permanent is multilinear, but its subformulas need not be multilinear.

Define
\[
L_{\mathrm{perm}}(n)=\min\{\operatorname{size}(F):\llbracket F\rrbracket=\operatorname{Perm}_n\}.
\]
A finite formula exists by expanding the defining sum, so this integer minimum is well defined. The assertion is \(\forall K,C\ge1\ \exists n\ge1:\ L_{\mathrm{perm}}(n)>K n^C\). All finite initial exceptions to a prospective polynomial upper bound can be absorbed by increasing \(K\). Replacing \(n\) by the variable count \(n^2\) in the phrase polynomial size gives the same class of bounds.

For clarity, the class interpretation uses the following nonuniform algebraic definitions. A polynomial family \((f_t)_{t\ge1}\), with \(f_t\in\mathbb C[z_1,\ldots,z_{v(t)}]\), is in \(\mathrm{VF}_{\mathbb C}\) if its variable counts, degrees and formula sizes are bounded by fixed polynomials in \(t\). It is in \(\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\) if its variable count is polynomially bounded and there is a polynomially bounded witness count \(w(t)\) and a family \(g_t(z,y)\) of polynomial degree and polynomial-size arithmetic circuits such that
\[
f_t(z)=\sum_{b\in\{0,1\}^{w(t)}}g_t(z,b).
\]
Here a circuit uses the same inputs and binary operations as a formula, but may share intermediate results in a finite directed acyclic graph.
