All bounds in these class definitions use constants independent of \(t\), while circuits and constants may depend on \(t\). The zero polynomial may be assigned degree zero for these bounds. A polynomially bounded projection substitutes variables or field constants into a member of another family whose index is polynomially bounded in \(t\). The direct permanent assertion is the acceptance target; these definitions explain its class-theoretic scope without adding an algorithmic requirement.
answer_criterion:
Supply a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed assertion or its full negation for the specified formula model.

A positive answer must prove failure of every polynomial upper bound, with the quantifier order \(\forall K,C\ \exists n\ \forall F\) in the statement. A proof for another family suffices only if its implications for this exact target are also proved. One fixed polynomial lower bound, even with a larger exponent than all currently cited bounds, does not establish the assertion.

A negative answer must prove
\[
\exists K,C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \forall n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\
\exists F:\quad
\llbracket F\rrbracket=\operatorname{Perm}_n
\ \land\ \operatorname{size}(F)\le K n^C.
\]
The same constants work for every dimension; individual formulas and complex constants may vary with the dimension. A uniform construction is sufficient if it meets the size guarantee, but is not an additional obligation.

A lower bound only for fixed depth, monotone formulas, multilinear subformulas, bounded coefficients, or noncommuting variables does not by itself cover the formulas in this card. A polynomial-size circuit permitting shared intermediate results does not by itself provide the required formula upper bound. The numerical \(1/100\) tolerance does not change this asymptotic class-separation question.

title: Permanent versus determinant
summary: The permanent sums permutation products without the signs used by the determinant. The question asks whether its representation as a determinant of affine-linear forms can be bounded in dimension by any polynomial in the original matrix size. The affine entries may use arbitrary complex coefficients. Polynomial-size determinants have division-free polynomial-size arithmetic circuits. Anthropic’s circuit lower bound for the permanent therefore rules out every polynomial bound on the dimension of an exact affine determinant representation.
formal: Over \(\mathbb C\), is the determinantal complexity of the permanent not bounded above by any polynomial? Precisely, writing \(d_n=\operatorname{dc}_{\mathbb C}(\operatorname{perm}_n)\) as defined below, is it true that for every triple of integers \(B,k,N\ge1\) there is an integer \(n\ge N\) with \(d_n>B(n+1)^k\)? The matrices in the definition are unrestricted exact affine-linear representations over \(\mathbb C\).
definitions: For an integer \(n\ge1\), let \(X=(x_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}\) consist of \(n^2\) algebraically independent commuting variables over \(\mathbb C\). Let \(S_n\) be the set of all permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and set \(\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n x_{i,\sigma(i)}\). For any \(m\times m\) matrix \(M\) over a commutative ring, \(\det(M)=\sum_{\pi\in S_m}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{a=1}^m M_{a,\pi(a)}\), where \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)=(-1)^{|\{(a,b):a<b,\ \pi(a)>\pi(b)\}|}\). Define \(d_n\) to be the least integer \(m\ge1\) for which there exist constant matrices \(A_0,A_{ij}\in\mathbb C^{m\times m}\), one \(A_{ij}\) for each input variable, such that \[\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\det\!\left(A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}A_{ij}\right)\] as an identity in \(\mathbb C[x_{ij}:1\le i,j\le n]\). Thus every entry is a constant plus an arbitrary complex linear combination of all input variables. Equality means equality of every coefficient, equivalently equality for every complex assignment, not just Boolean assignments. Finite representations exist, so the minimum is defined; for example the known bound \(d_n\le2^n-1\) suffices. The resource is the matrix dimension \(m\), not its number of entries, coefficient bit lengths or time to find the matrices. Constants can be arbitrary complex numbers, independently for each \(n\), with no computability or uniform construction requirement. Variables may be reused in any number of entries. No symmetry, sparsity, rank condition on \(A_0\), sign restriction, read-once property or restriction on cancellation is imposed. A limit of determinants is not an exact representation unless some permitted matrix already has determinant equal to the permanent. Since every \(d_n\) is finite, the formal assertion is equivalent to nonexistence of integers \(B,k\ge1\) satisfying \(d_n\le B(n+1)^k\) for all \(n\ge1\): finitely many exceptions to an upper bound can be absorbed into \(B\). The stated lower-bound quantifiers require arbitrarily large violating indices for every proposed polynomial, not eventual domination of that polynomial at every sufficiently large index.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the quantified lower-bound proposition, or of its logical negation: there exist integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that for every \(n\ge1\) there exist an integer \(1\le m\le B(n+1)^k\) and complex matrices \(A_0,A_{ij}\) satisfying the exact polynomial identity above. A negative answer may prove existence of this nonuniform family without an algorithm to generate its constants. A positive answer must exclude all allowed affine-linear matrices for the relevant \(n,m\), including those that break the permanent’s symmetries. A fixed-degree polynomial lower bound, a bound restricted to real coefficients or a restricted matrix class, or a lower bound for a different polynomial does not prove the proposition. A polynomial-size limiting representation alone does not refute this exact target.

title: VP versus VBP over the complex numbers
summary: VP versus VBP asks whether every polynomial-degree family with small arithmetic circuits also has small algebraic branching programs over the complex numbers. The branching programs compute exact sums of affine-label products along paths, with all coefficients and variable occurrences included in the algebraic size. Both models are nonuniform and allow arbitrary complex constants, with no imposed symmetry, width or multilinearity restriction. OpenAI constructs a family of state sums on binary trees with polynomial-size circuits. The family requires superpolynomial algebraic branching programs even over the complex numbers.
formal: Is \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\)? More explicitly, let \((m_n,f_n)_{n\ge1}\) be any family with integers \(m_n\ge0\) and commutative polynomials \(f_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m_n}]\). Suppose that some positive integer \(a\) satisfies \[m_n\le(n+2)^a,\qquad \deg f_n\le(n+2)^a,\qquad c(f_n)\le(n+2)^a\quad\text{for all }n\ge1,\] where \(c\) is minimum arithmetic-circuit size in the model below. Must there exist a positive integer \(b\), depending on the whole family, such that \[\operatorname{abp}(f_n)\le(n+2)^b\quad\text{for all }n\ge1?\] Computation is exact and nonuniform over the complex field, and the competing branching programs are unrestricted.
definitions:
A polynomial is a finite complex linear combination of commutative monomials in the listed variables. Its total degree is the maximum sum of exponents among nonzero monomials, with degree zero assigned to the zero polynomial. An arithmetic circuit is a finite acyclic graph with one designated output. Input gates are labelled by one listed variable or one arbitrary complex constant. Every other gate has two ordered input ports and is labelled by addition or multiplication in the polynomial ring; both ports may refer to the same predecessor, and any predecessor may be reused. There are no division gates. Size is the number of gates plus the number of wires, counting each input port’s wire separately; constant and variable input gates each have unit cost. Intermediate degrees are not separately bounded: the degree hypothesis is on the output polynomial after cancellations. The minimum of this size among circuits computing \(f\) is \(c(f)\).

An algebraic branching program (ABP) is a finite directed acyclic multigraph with distinct designated vertices \(s,t\), no edges entering \(s\), and no edges leaving \(t\). Each edge \(e\) is labelled by an affine form \(\lambda_e=\alpha_{e,0}+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\alpha_{e,j}x_j\), with arbitrary complex coefficients. It computes \(\sum_{\pi:s\leadsto t}\prod_{e\in\pi}\lambda_e\), where distinct paths include their edge choices and an empty sum is zero. Its size is \[|V|+|E|+\sum_{e\in E}\left(\mathbf1_{\alpha_{e,0}\ne0}+2\bigl|\{j\in[m]:\alpha_{e,j}\ne0\}\bigr|\right).\] Here \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), including the empty set if \(m=0\), and \(\mathbf1_P\) is one when \(P\) holds and zero otherwise. Thus every nonzero scalar coefficient and its variable occurrence are charged; labels are not arbitrary polynomial oracles. There is no width, layering, variable-order, read-once, syntactic multilinearity, symmetry, homogeneity or monotonicity requirement. The minimum size computing \(f\) is \(\operatorname{abp}(f)\).

Both minima concern formal polynomial identities, not agreement on finitely many inputs or convergence of coefficients. Sizes count algebraic objects and field elements, not bits encoding complex numbers; coefficients need not have bounded or computable bit descriptions. No algorithm generating a family’s circuits, programs or constants is required. Every polynomial has finite representations in both models. Positive integer exponents in \((n+2)^a\) absorb multiplicative constants and finitely many initial values of any polynomial bound. The families meeting the circuit hypotheses define \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\); polynomially many variables and a polynomial ABP bound define \(\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\). ABP size already bounds output degree, and ABPs have polynomial-size circuit simulations, so only the displayed converse inclusion is at issue.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed inclusion or its negation, with the specified field, polynomial identities, resource accounting and quantifiers. A positive proof establishes a polynomial ABP bound for every family satisfying the circuit and degree hypotheses; it need not produce an efficient uniform converter. A negative proof establishes one family \((m_n,f_n)\) and one fixed positive integer \(a\) satisfying all three circuit-side bounds, but such that \[\forall b\ge1\ \forall N\ge1\ \exists n\ge N,\quad \operatorname{abp}(f_n)>(n+2)^b.\] The lower bound must cover every permitted ABP over \(\mathbb C\), including arbitrary constants, reuse of variables and cancellations. There is no required effective generator for a separating family. A lower bound in a restricted ABP model, a family of exponential output degree, or a border-complexity separation does not meet this criterion.

title: Polynomial-size arithmetic formulas for the determinant
summary: The symbolic determinant has n² commuting input variables for an n-by-n matrix. The question asks whether its exact polynomial can be expressed by arithmetic trees of size bounded by one fixed polynomial in n. Every occurrence of a variable, constant or copied subexpression is charged, while arbitrary fixed complex constants and cancellations are allowed. OpenAI gives a superpolynomial lower bound for the determinant even when formulas may approximate its homogeneous component in the border-complexity sense. The bound also applies to every exact formula over the complex numbers.
formal:
Do there exist positive integers \(K,C\) such that for every integer \(n\ge1\) there is an arithmetic formula \(F_n\) over \(\mathbb C\) satisfying
\[\operatorname{size}(F_n)\le K n^C,\qquad \llbracket F_n\rrbracket=\operatorname{Det}_n(X),\]
where \(\llbracket F_n\rrbracket\) is its output as a formal commutative polynomial and
\[\operatorname{Det}_n(X)=\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i,\pi(i)}?\]
The formula is a binary expression tree with arbitrary complex constants and addition, subtraction and multiplication. Computations may use cancellations, but intermediate expressions cannot be shared. The same constants \(K,C\) must work for all dimensions.
definitions:
Polynomial and parameters. The matrix \(X=(x_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}\) has \(n^2\) distinct commuting indeterminates as its entries. The positive integer \(n\) is the matrix dimension, not the number of variables. The set \(S_n\) consists of all permutations of \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Define \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)=(-1)^{\operatorname{inv}(\pi)}\), where \(\operatorname{inv}(\pi)\) counts pairs \(i<j\) with \(\pi(i)>\pi(j)\). All calculations take place in the polynomial ring \(\mathbb C[x_{11},\ldots,x_{nn}]\). In particular \(\operatorname{Det}_1=x_{11}\); no invertibility or numerical-entry promise is imposed.

Formula syntax and evaluation. A formula is a finite rooted binary tree with ordered children. A leaf is labelled by one input variable or one constant in \(\mathbb C\). Each internal node is labelled \(+\), \(-\) or \(\times\) and computes the corresponding operation on the two child polynomials; subtraction uses left child minus right child. The root’s polynomial is denoted \(\llbracket F\rrbracket\). Every node other than the root has exactly one parent. Repeated uses of an expression therefore require separate copies of its entire subtree. No powers, determinants, summations or other compound expressions are primitive gates: any such shorthand in a proposed family must expand to allowed binary nodes.

Size. Every node counts once, including each occurrence of a variable or constant. Equivalently, a leaf has size one and a node with children \(A,B\) has size \(1+\operatorname{size}(A)+\operatorname{size}(B)\). Distinct leaves carrying the same value count separately. Define
\[L_{\det}(n)=\min\{\operatorname{size}(F):\llbracket F\rrbracket=\operatorname{Det}_n\}.\]
The set is nonempty by the finite permutation expansion, so this positive-integer minimum exists. The question is whether \(L_{\det}(n)\) is bounded by one fixed polynomial in \(n\). Allowing real constants in a size bound rather than positive integer \(K,C\) would give the same polynomial-boundedness claim.

Constants and nonuniformity. Each constant leaf has unit size regardless of its magnitude, algebraic degree or description length. Constants and the tree may depend arbitrarily on \(n\), and complex constants need not be computable or rational. They cannot depend on the values later substituted for input variables. There is no algorithmic or efficiency requirement for generating the family, and no bit-cost bound on its representation: the resource is algebraic tree size. The field \(\mathbb C\) is fixed throughout; the target is not a simultaneous assertion for all fields.

Exact unrestricted computation. The equality at the root is an exact polynomial identity, coefficient by coefficient. Approximation of coefficients, a limit of formulas or correct evaluation only on a restricted input set does not meet it. Division, inverses, comparisons, branching, input-dependent constants and additional input variables are not allowed. There is no restriction on depth, homogeneity, signs or coefficient magnitudes. Intermediate polynomials may have powers or monomials absent from the determinant, provided they cancel in the final identity. A polynomial is multilinear if every variable has exponent at most one in every monomial. The output determinant is multilinear, but the formula is not required to be multilinear at intermediate nodes.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its negation. For a positive answer, prove the existence of allowed formula trees for every dimension, their exact determinant identity, and one common polynomial size bound. A uniform construction is welcome but is not required by this nonuniform target. Count all copied subtrees and constant occurrences.

A negative answer must prove
\[\forall K,C\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists n\ge1:\ L_{\det}(n)>K n^C.\]
It must cover arbitrary complex constants and all unrestricted intermediate computations permitted above. Equivalently, for every \(K,C,N\ge1\), there must be some \(n\ge N\) violating that polynomial bound; finitely many exceptional dimensions can always be absorbed into its constant. It is not necessary to prove that every sufficiently large dimension violates every given polynomial, a stronger eventual-growth claim.

A fixed-power lower bound, such as \(\Omega(n^3)\), leaves larger polynomial bounds possible. Lower bounds only for multilinear, homogeneous, symmetric, monotone, bounded-depth, bounded-coefficient or noncommutative computations do not refute the stated unrestricted commutative claim. An exact identity using a small circuit with shared intermediate results is not yet a small formula, and a large size for one particular determinant expansion is not a lower bound for all formulas. A proof conditional on an unresolved separation must keep that assumption explicit and does not settle this unconditional question.

title: Shub–Smale \(\tau\)-conjecture
summary: A straight-line program constructs an integer polynomial using only one, a variable, addition, subtraction and multiplication. The conjecture asks for one fixed polynomial bound on the number of distinct integer roots in terms of the shortest program length. All operations constructing constants count, shared registers are allowed, and the zero polynomial is excluded. A short program can already create exponential degree or exponentially many distinct real roots, so neither supplies the desired integer-root bound. The conjecture has major conditional consequences in algebraic computation and proof complexity, while finite censuses and bounds in other complexity measures leave its universal claim unsettled.
formal: Does there exist an integer \(C\geq1\), independent of the polynomial, such that every nonzero \(f\in\mathbb Z[x]\) satisfies \[z_{\mathbb Z}(f)\leq(1+\tau(f))^C,\] where \(z_{\mathbb Z}(f)\) is the number of distinct integer roots and \(\tau(f)\) is the minimum number of additions, subtractions and multiplications needed to construct \(f\) from only \(1\) and \(x\)?
definitions:
The ring \(\mathbb Z[x]\) consists of formal univariate polynomials with integer coefficients. A straight-line program of length \(s\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) starts with registers \(g_0=1\) and \(g_1=x\). For each \(i=2,\ldots,s+1\), it chooses \(j_i,k_i<i\) and one operation from \(\{+,-,\times\}\), and sets \(g_i=g_{j_i}\mathbin{\circ_i}g_{k_i}\). Operands may coincide, and an earlier register may be used arbitrarily many times. One register is designated as output. The program computes \(f\) if this output equals \(f\) as a formal polynomial. Define \(\tau(f)\) to be the least possible \(s\) among such programs. Every integer polynomial can be constructed in finitely many operations, so this minimum exists. When \(s=0\), only \(1\) or \(x\) can be output.

Every new arithmetic register costs one operation, including operations used to build integer constants. In particular \(2\), \(0\) and \(-1\) are not additional free inputs. There is no division, primitive exponentiation, comparison, conditional branch or access to a supplied coefficient list. The finite program may be chosen separately for each polynomial; there is no uniformity requirement on these choices. Intermediate degrees, coefficient sizes and integer magnitudes are unrestricted. Cost measures arithmetic operations, not the number of bits in coefficients, a formula without shared registers or the bit length of the program encoding.

For \(f\ne0\), define \(z_{\mathbb Z}(f)=|\{a\in\mathbb Z:f(a)=0\}|\), counting negative roots, zero and positive roots once each, regardless of multiplicity. This cardinality is finite because a nonzero univariate polynomial has at most its degree many roots; a nonzero constant has no roots. The zero polynomial is excluded. The exponent \(C\) must be one constant for all \(f\), without dependence on degree, coefficients, root sizes or the choice of an optimal program. The question asks only for a bound, not for an efficient root-counting or root-finding algorithm.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the universal bound or its logical negation, \(\forall C\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}\ \exists f\in\mathbb Z[x]\setminus\{0\}:z_{\mathbb Z}(f)>(1+\tau(f))^C\). A positive answer may use any one absolute exponent; a negative answer must exclude all such exponents. No computable rule for choosing the counterexample polynomials is required. A counterexample to just one proposed exponent, bounds for a restricted program class, multiplicity counts, or results only about real or complex roots do not settle this full target. Conditional consequences of the conjecture are not proofs of it.

title: Explicit three-dimensional tensors of superlinear rank
summary: A three-way tensor is a cubic array, and its ordinary rank is the fewest rank-one arrays whose sum equals it. The selected branch asks for rational entries written by one deterministic algorithm in polynomial time in the dimension. Rank is measured over the complex numbers, and its ratio to the side length must tend to infinity. The tensor for multiplying two square matrices of side m has local dimension m² and ordinary complex rank at least m to the power 9/4. Padding this zero-one tensor to each requested side length n gives an explicit family of rank at least a constant times n to the power 9/8.
formal: Do there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a real constant \(K>0\) and an integer \(a\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), on input \(1^n\) it outputs all entries of a rational tensor \(T_n\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n\times n}\) within \(K(n+1)^a\) bit operations, and \[\forall B\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists N\ge1\ \forall n\ge N:\quad \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}(T_n)\ge Bn?\] Here rank is ordinary tensor rank over the complex numbers. Thus the required ratio \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}(T_n)/n\) tends to infinity, with no prescribed rate.
definitions:
A tensor \(T\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n\times n}\) is the array \((T_{ijk})_{1\le i,j,k\le n}\), regarded as an element of \(\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n\) through the usual inclusion of the rationals into the complex numbers. Its ordinary rank is the smallest integer \(r\ge0\) for which there are vectors \(u^{(s)},v^{(s)},w^{(s)}\in\mathbb C^n\), for \(1\le s\le r\), satisfying
\[
T_{ijk}=\sum_{s=1}^{r}u^{(s)}_i\,v^{(s)}_j\,w^{(s)}_k
\quad\text{for every }1\le i,j,k\le n.
\]
An empty sum is the zero tensor. The factors in a rank decomposition may be arbitrary complex vectors, although the constructed tensor entries are rational. No symmetry is required. The target is not matrix rank of an array rearrangement, slice rank, border rank, or an asymptotic tensor-power rank.

The machine outputs the \(n^3\) entries in lexicographic order of \((i,j,k)\). Each entry is an explicitly written signed binary integer numerator and positive binary integer denominator, with delimiters. All bits are charged, so their total length and each individual entry's bit length are polynomially bounded in \(n\). A symbolic power, root-of-unity description, unevaluated arithmetic expression or arbitrary real constant is not a rational-entry output under this convention. All input reading, integer arithmetic, preprocessing and output writing count. The finite program and \(K,a\) are independent of \(n\); there is no advice, oracle, randomness or uncharged preprocessing.

The algorithm is required on every positive integer dimension, and the rank guarantee holds for all sufficiently large dimensions for each \(B\). The integer threshold \(N\) may depend on \(B\) and the fixed family; it is not required to be computed. No rank decomposition, rank value or lower-bound certificate is an output requirement for \(A\); the rank-growth guarantee must instead be established by the submitted proof. Explicitness here means polynomial time in the dimension to write the whole tensor, not a separate polylogarithmic-time entry-query requirement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence of such a finite construction algorithm, its uniform polynomial bit-cost bound and the entire eventual superlinear rank guarantee, or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm exists. An existence proof without the construction cost, a fixed constant multiple of the dimension, growth only along an unspecified subsequence, or a conditional lower bound alone does not meet this target. Any growth rate tending to infinity in the displayed normalized rank suffices; a fixed positive power improvement is not required.

title: Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture
summary: A three-factor tensor can be decomposed into elementary products, and its rank is the least number of those products. The question asks whether every concise complex tensor of equal factor dimension has asymptotic rank exactly that dimension when corresponding factors of many copies are grouped. The dimension and tensor stay fixed during the limit, and no tightness, symmetry, computability or uniform convergence promise is imposed. The tensor for multiplying two 2-by-2 matrices is a concise complex tensor with factor dimension four. OpenAI computes its asymptotic rank as two to the power 9/4, which exceeds four.
formal:
Work over the complex field \(\mathbb C\). Is the following general cubic formulation of the asymptotic rank conjecture true?
\[\forall n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall T\in\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n:\quad \bigl(\operatorname{rank}F_1(T)=\operatorname{rank}F_2(T)=\operatorname{rank}F_3(T)=n\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \widetilde R(T)=n,\]
where \(F_i(T)\) are the three matrix flattenings and
\[\widetilde R(T)=\lim_{k\to\infty}R(T^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}=\inf_{k\ge1}R(T^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}?\]
Here \(R\) is exact tensor rank, and \(\boxtimes\) groups corresponding factors of tensor products. The tensor \(T\) and its dimension \(n\) are fixed while \(k\) tends to infinity. The quantifier covers all complex tensors satisfying the flattening condition; no additional symmetry, support or computational promise is imposed.
definitions:
Tensors and flattenings. For a positive integer \(d\), let \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and let \(e_1,\ldots,e_d\) be the standard basis of \(\mathbb C^d\). A tensor \(T\) in three factors of dimensions \(a,b,c\) is the coefficient array \((t_{ij\ell})_{(i,j,\ell)\in[a]\times[b]\times[c]}\), interpreted as \(\sum_{i,j,\ell}t_{ij\ell}e_i\otimes e_j\otimes e_\ell\). For the cubic format \(a=b=c=n\), define three \(n\)-by-\(n^2\) matrices by
\[(F_1(T))_{i,(j,\ell)}=t_{ij\ell},\qquad(F_2(T))_{j,(i,\ell)}=t_{ij\ell},\qquad(F_3(T))_{\ell,(i,j)}=t_{ij\ell}.\]
Pairs are ordered lexicographically; the ordering does not affect matrix rank. Matrix rank is the dimension of the column span over \(\mathbb C\). A tensor is concise in this format when all three matrix ranks are \(n\). This excludes zero tensors and tensors that effectively use a smaller subspace in some factor. For \(n=1\), it just means a nonzero scalar.

Exact rank. For any positive dimensions \(a,b,c\), define
\[R(S)=\min\left\{r\in\mathbb N:\ S=\sum_{s=1}^{r}u_s\otimes v_s\otimes w_s,\quad u_s\in\mathbb C^a,\ v_s\in\mathbb C^b,\ w_s\in\mathbb C^c\right\}.\]
The empty sum is zero. A pure tensor has coefficients \((u_i v_j w_\ell)\); equality in a decomposition is exact coefficientwise equality. Finite decompositions always exist, so the minimum is well-defined. The three vectors in a summand are independent choices: there is no symmetric-rank restriction. Their complex entries are unrestricted, including noncomputable numbers; the question does not ask for a finite input encoding or an algorithm to find the decomposition.

Grouped powers. For \(k\ge1\), the tensor \(T^{\boxtimes k}\) has exactly three factors, each with coordinates indexed by \([n]^k\), and hence each of dimension \(n^k\). Its entries are
\[(T^{\boxtimes k})_{(i_1,\ldots,i_k),(j_1,\ldots,j_k),(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_k)}=\prod_{h=1}^{k}t_{i_h j_h\ell_h}.\]
Its rank is taken after this grouping. A vector in a rank decomposition may be any element of \(\mathbb C^{n^k}\); it need not itself split into \(k\) vectors of dimension \(n\). Thus ranks of grouped powers need not equal \(R(T)^k\).

Asymptotic value. Tensoring decompositions gives
\[R(T^{\boxtimes(k+\ell)})\le R(T^{\boxtimes k})R(T^{\boxtimes\ell}).\]
For a concise tensor the elementary flattening lower bound and a slice decomposition give
\[n^k\le R(T^{\boxtimes k})\le n^{2k}.\]
Subadditivity of the logarithms therefore proves existence of the positive real limit in the question and its equality with the displayed infimum. In particular \(n\le\widetilde R(T)\le n^2\). The proposed equality is equivalently
\[\forall n\ \forall T\text{ concise}\ \forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists K\ge1\ \forall k\ge K:\quad R(T^{\boxtimes k})\le(n+\varepsilon)^k.\]
Here \(K\) may depend on \(n,T,\varepsilon\), with no uniform or effective rate required. The actual decompositions may depend on \(k\) as well. Neither attainment of the infimum at a finite power nor rank \(n^k\) for any finite power is asserted.

Related ranks. Border rank of \(S\) is the least integer \(r\) such that \(S\) is a Euclidean limit of tensors of exact rank at most \(r\) in its fixed complex coefficient space. The defining ranks in this card are exact ranks. A finite-power border-rank result or a finite-power exact-rank lower bound must be connected to the quantified asymptotic statement before it can settle this question.
answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the proposition or its logical negation, including the stated limit convention. An affirmative proof must cover every positive dimension and every concise complex tensor, with arbitrarily small positive \(\varepsilon\) in the equivalent power bound. A negative proof must establish the existence of a positive integer \(n\), a concise \(T\) in the specified cubic format, and a real \(\eta>0\) such that
\[\forall k\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\quad R(T^{\boxtimes k})\ge(n+\eta)^k.\]
This is equivalent to a counterexample with \(\widetilde R(T)>n\); no explicitness or computability condition is added to the counterexample. A large rank at one power is insufficient. A result only for a restricted class of tensors, only over another field, or conditional on an unproved complexity assumption does not settle the universal complex-field target. This is an exact yes/no conjecture, so a fixed additive tolerance such as \(1/100\) does not replace the equality.

title: \(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb R}\) versus \(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\)
summary: The BSS model computes exactly with arbitrary real inputs using unit-cost arithmetic and comparisons. Each machine has one fixed finite program and finitely many fixed real constants for all input dimensions. The question asks whether polynomial-time verification with real witnesses always yields polynomial-time deterministic decision. Real polynomial feasibility is complete for the nondeterministic class, while Boolean-input PosSLP results concern different restrictions. A complete answer must prove equality or separation in the full model; a claimed separation was withdrawn in July 2026.
formal:
Is
\[\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb R}=\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\]
in the unit-cost Blum–Shub–Smale model over the ordered real field, with arbitrary real inputs and arbitrary finitely many fixed real machine constants? Equivalently, does every set of finite real tuples with polynomial-length real witnesses checkable in polynomial BSS time have a deterministic polynomial-time BSS decider? The decider and its finite constants may depend on the set, but must be fixed for all input lengths.
definitions:
The input domain is the disjoint union \(\mathbb R^{*}=\bigsqcup_{n\ge0}\mathbb R^{n}\). An input is a tuple \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\); its size is its dimension \(n\), independent of the magnitudes, precision or computability of its coordinates. Length is supplied as part of the input convention. Distinct tuple lengths remain distinct even when trailing coordinates are zero.

A deterministic BSS machine has a finite control graph and real registers, initially containing the input and zeros elsewhere, with a fixed finite set of real constants including 0 and 1. Constants may be transcendental or uncomputable; there is no requirement for finite binary descriptions of their values. The same program and constants serve all inputs and all dimensions. Each arithmetic instruction adds, subtracts, multiplies or divides two stored reals, or loads a fixed machine constant; a division is allowed only with nonzero denominator. A branch tests equality to zero or order relative to zero, exactly. Copies, control steps and register shifts each have unit cost, as do arithmetic operations and tests. Accepting and rejecting states output the bits 1 and 0.

For a concrete standard register convention, use a doubly infinite sequence of real registers with finite support at every finite time. Ordinary arithmetic, copy and test instructions refer to finitely many fixed register offsets in the program. A shift moves the sequence one position left or right, giving access to arbitrary input coordinates over time. Initially register 0 holds \(n\), registers 1 through \(n\) hold the input, and the others hold zero. The verifier input similarly records the two lengths and the two tuples in adjacent registers. This is the ordinary shift-register presentation of BSS computation, polynomially equivalent to the source's restricted copy-address presentation. Division by zero is treated as rejection, so a proposed decider must still meet correctness and totality on every input. There is no primitive floor, digit extraction, transcendental-function evaluation, square root, oracle or random instruction. An arithmetic step costs one even when its value would need arbitrarily many bits in a discrete representation.

For \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^{*}\), membership in \(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb R}\) means that there exist one such deterministic machine \(M\) and constants \(C,d\in\mathbb N\), with \(C\ge1\), such that, for every \(n\ge0\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), it halts within \(C(n+1)^d\) steps and accepts exactly when \(x\in L\).

Membership in \(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\) means that there are one deterministic BSS verifier \(V\) and fixed polynomial bounds \(p,q:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that \(V(x,y)\) halts within \(q(n)\) steps for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and every real tuple \(y\) of length at most \(p(n)\), and
\[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists m\le p(n)\;\exists y\in\mathbb R^m:\ V(x,y)=1.\]
The time bound depends on \(n\), not on the coordinate values; polynomial bounds may be written as \(C(n+1)^d\). A padded fixed witness length gives the same class. No-instance inputs must be rejected for every permitted witness. The witness contains arbitrary exact reals, not just rationals or finite strings. The verifier's constants and polynomial bounds may depend on \(L\), but not on \(x\), \(n\) or the witness. Equality of classes quantifies over every such \(L\), with no promise on input coordinates.

The notation \(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb R}^{0}\) restricts the machine constants to 0 and 1. The Boolean part of a class restricts its input tuples to coordinates in \(\{0,1\}\); write it as \(\mathrm{BP}(\cdot)\). These are different restrictions from the full target. In particular, \(\exists\mathbb R=\mathrm{BP}(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}^{0})\) concerns finitely encoded problems, while this card retains all real tuples and arbitrary fixed real constants. Neither finite-precision computation nor bit-cost arithmetic is the model being compared.

For the cited discrete comparison, PosSLP asks whether a finite arithmetic straight-line program, starting from 0 and 1 and using addition, subtraction and multiplication, outputs a positive integer. Such a program is an explicitly listed acyclic sequence of operations on earlier values. \(\mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{PosSLP}}\) is ordinary polynomial-time Turing computation with a unit-cost yes/no oracle for this language; \(/\mathrm{poly}\) permits an additional polynomial-length advice string depending only on input length. The counting hierarchy is the union of the levels \(\mathrm C_0\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{P}\) and \(\mathrm C_{k+1}\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{PP}^{\mathrm C_k\mathrm{P}}\), where PP uses a strict majority of the computation paths of a polynomial-time nondeterministic binary machine.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete proof checked in Lean of the stated class equality or its negation in this precise full BSS model. A positive answer must establish a uniform polynomial-time BSS decider for every language having the defined verifier, allowing a different fixed program and finite constants for each language. A negative answer must establish some \(L\in\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\setminus\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb R}\), ruling out every polynomial-time deterministic BSS decider even with arbitrary finite real constants. A result only for constant-free machines, only for Boolean inputs, with extra oracle operations, or under an unproved complexity assumption does not alone prove the full unconditional target. All decisions are exact; numerical approximation tolerance does not apply.

title: Superpolynomial noncommutative circuit lower bounds
summary: The target is some polynomial-degree family with rational coefficients and ordered noncommuting variables. One deterministic polynomial-time algorithm must compute any requested word coefficient exactly. Take the permanent with factors in each monomial placed in row order. Its word coefficients are zero or one and can be recognized by checking row order and column distinctness. Making variables commute converts any small circuit for this family into a small circuit for the ordinary permanent, which Anthropic’s theorem rules out.
formal:
Does there exist a family
\[
f_n\in\mathbb Q\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\rangle\qquad(n\ge2)
\]
of polynomial degree with uniformly polynomial-time computable word coefficients, such that
\[
\forall k\ge1\ \forall N\ge2\ \exists n\ge N:
\operatorname{NC}_{\mathbb C}(f_n)>n^k?
\]
Here \(k,N,n\) are integers and \(\operatorname{NC}_{\mathbb C}\) is minimum size among unrestricted noncommutative arithmetic circuits with arbitrary complex constants. The family can be chosen freely subject to the explicitness and degree requirements below; it is not required to be a particular permanent or determinant family.
definitions:
The free associative algebra \(\mathbb C\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\rangle\) consists of finite complex linear combinations of words in the symbols \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). Addition adds the coefficients of equal words. Multiplication concatenates words and distributes over sums; it is associative. Scalars commute with every word, but variable symbols do not commute. The empty word has value 1. Thus \(x_1x_2\) and \(x_2x_1\) are different monomials, and polynomial equality is exact equality of every word coefficient. This is not a problem about functions on scalar inputs or on matrices of one fixed dimension.

A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one output. Input gates are variable symbols or arbitrary complex constants. An internal gate adds or multiplies two predecessor values. Each multiplication gate specifies a left and a right input; the same predecessor may occur in both positions. The size is the total number of gates, including inputs. There are no division gates, tests, approximation operations or limits. Fan-out, reuse of intermediate values and depth are unrestricted. Each scalar costs one input gate without a description-length restriction. Intermediate polynomials can have arbitrarily large degree and need not be homogeneous. \(\operatorname{NC}_{\mathbb C}(f)\) is the minimum size of any such circuit whose formal output is \(f\), with rational coefficients embedded in \(\mathbb C\).

Polynomial degree and uniform explicitness mean that there are fixed integers \(a,b\ge1\), a fixed real \(K>0\), and one deterministic multi-tape Turing machine \(M\) with the following properties. Every nonzero \(f_n\) has degree at most \(n^a\), where degree is the largest length of a word with nonzero coefficient; the zero polynomial is allowed. Given \(1^n\) and any explicitly listed word \(w\) of length \(\ell\) over \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(M\) outputs the exact coefficient \([w]f_n\) in at most
\[
K\bigl(n+(\ell+1)\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\bigr)^b
\]
Turing steps. Word symbols are written as fixed-width binary indices. The output is a reduced fraction \(p/q\) with binary integers \(p\), \(q>0\), and \(\gcd(|p|,q)=1\); zero is \(0/1\). Words of length greater than \(n^a\) have coefficient zero. The empty word is included. The bound includes writing the output and thus also limits coefficient bit lengths. No advice depending on \(n\) is supplied to \(M\).

The explicitness requirement prevents choosing arbitrary hard coefficient tables by counting. It concerns an algorithm to compute any one coefficient, not an algorithm to list all coefficients or a small arithmetic circuit for the full polynomial. Conversely, the circuits being ruled out are nonuniform and may use complex constants even though the target family has efficiently computable rational coefficients. The lower-bound quantifiers mean absence of every polynomial family-size upper bound, witnessed at arbitrarily large indices; they do not require an eventual lower bound at every index.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of this existence statement or its logical negation. A positive answer must define the family and its coefficient algorithm, prove the degree and uniform running-time bounds, and exclude every polynomial circuit-size upper bound in the stated unrestricted model. A negative answer must prove that every family meeting these requirements has a polynomial-size noncommutative circuit family over \(\mathbb C\). An exponential formula or branching-program lower bound does not suffice. Nor does a circuit lower bound for bounded depth, homogeneity, restricted syntactic degree, or a fixed polynomial exponent.

title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
summary: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals asks whether an arbitrary integer-coefficient polynomial has a zero consisting of exact rational numbers. The target requires one deterministic algorithm that always halts and decides this for every number of variables, degree and coefficient size. There is no efficiency requirement, and merely enumerating rational solutions does not decide instances with no solution. Undecidability over integers, universal definitions and results with extra height predicates have different logical or arithmetic scope. Recent advances over rings of integers preserve that distinction, and the checked sources do not settle the rational-solvability question.
formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) that, on every input encoding a polynomial \(f\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\ldots,X_m]\) with \(m\geq1\), halts and outputs YES exactly when \[\exists(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m\quad f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0,\] and outputs NO otherwise? The number of variables, degree and coefficients are unrestricted finite input data, and there is no time or space efficiency requirement.
definitions:
The field \(\mathbb Q\) consists of exact fractions \(a/b\), with \(a\in\mathbb Z\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), identifying fractions of the same value; addition and multiplication are the usual exact field operations. A polynomial input describes \(f=\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_j\prod_{i=1}^{m}X_i^{e_{ji}}\), with \(r\geq0\), \(a_j\in\mathbb Z\) and \(e_{ji}\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Repeated monomials and zero coefficients are allowed. The empty sum is the zero polynomial and \(X_i^0=1\), including when evaluating at zero. Constants are represented with all exponents zero. A rational zero is any tuple in \(\mathbb Q^m\) giving exact value zero; there is no bound on its numerators or denominators and no integrality restriction.

Use the following explicit effective binary encoding. For \(u\geq0\), let \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(b\) bits and no leading zeroes. Encode an integer \(a\) by a sign bit followed by \(\operatorname{code}(|a|)\), with 0 denoting a nonnegative integer and 1 a negative integer; negative zero is invalid. A complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(m)\operatorname{code}(r)\), followed for each \(j=1,\ldots,r\) by the signed code of \(a_j\) and \(\operatorname{code}(e_{j1}),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(e_{jm})\), with no trailing bits. Require \(m\geq1\). The machine halts and outputs NO on every malformed encoding.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program with a finite tape alphabet, ordinary discrete transitions and unbounded work tapes, without advice or an oracle. On every input it must halt after finitely many transitions; its running time need not satisfy a polynomial, elementary or other prescribed bound. Its program is independent of \(m,r\), all degrees and all coefficients. The input supplies only the polynomial, without additional height-comparison predicates or a promise of solvability. The question concerns decision of existence; a YES output need not itself contain a rational tuple.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify one effective algorithm and prove termination and exact correctness on every polynomial in the stated domain, together with rejection of invalid input. A negative answer must prove that no such total correct Turing machine exists. Recognizing only polynomials that have a rational zero, excluding polynomial-time algorithms, or proving undecidability for equations with integer-constrained unknowns or added predicates does not establish the required negation. Any conditional result must be identified as conditional and does not alone settle this unconditional question.

title: Integer factorization in randomized polynomial time
summary: Integer factorization recovers the ordered primes and positive multiplicities whose product is a given positive integer. The question asks for one classical randomized algorithm taking polynomial time in the number of input bits on every random sequence. Its full factor list must be correct with probability at least two thirds separately on every positive input. Efficient primality testing and verification do not resolve the task of finding the factors. Google’s Cogentic manuscript gives an unconditional subexponential expected running time for complete classical factorization, leaving polynomial time in the number of input bits open.
formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,c\ge0\) and one uniform classical randomized algorithm A such that, for every positive integer N in binary, A outputs the complete prime factorization of N with probability at least \(2/3\), and for every random-bit sequence halts within \(C(n+1)^c\) bit steps, where \(n=\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor+1\)? The same A, C and c must work for all N.
definitions: The input is the ordinary base-two representation of N, with no leading zeroes; its length n counts bits, not the numerical value of N. The one-character string 1 represents N=1. The empty string and all strings beginning with 0 are invalid and must be rejected on every random-bit sequence within the same polynomial bound in their length. For \(N\ge2\), the unique correct factorization is the finite list \((p_1,e_1),\ldots,(p_r,e_r)\), where \(p_1<\cdots<p_r\) are primes, each \(e_i\) is a positive integer, and \(N=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}\). A prime is an integer at least 2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. The correct list for N=1 is empty. To fix a binary output format, encode a nonnegative integer a by \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary representation of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). A successful output is 1 followed by code(r) and then code(p_i), code(e_i) for i in increasing order, with no other bits; the single bit 0 is the failure or invalid-input symbol. A is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with one finite program, a fixed finite number of tapes and fixed finite alphabets. It has a read-only input tape and initially blank work and output tapes; a transition accesses only cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. It may request one new independent fair bit at a transition. The probability space is \(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) with independent uniform coordinates, and the probability guarantee is separate for every fixed input N. The runtime is the total transition count, including all input access, random-bit requests, arithmetic and output writing. Every random-bit sequence obeys the clock; thus only finitely many random bits affect each run. A malformed factor list, an incorrect list and the failure symbol all count as failure on a positive input. The algorithm receives no promise that N is semiprime or belongs to a particular distribution, no advice or precomputed factors, no order-finding or factoring oracle, and no quantum or unit-cost operations on unbounded integers. The task is full factorization, not merely deciding whether N is prime.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one algorithm and constants satisfy the all-input success guarantee and the all-random-sequences polynomial clock, or prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. A negative proof must exclude arbitrary uniform classical randomized algorithms with arbitrary fixed polynomial exponents; excluding deterministic algorithms alone does not suffice. For the affirmative answer, correctness includes every prime base, multiplicity, ordering and product in the complete output. A heuristic complexity estimate, a guarantee for sampled or restricted inputs, or a quantum algorithm does not meet the stated classical worst-case target.

title: Prime-field discrete logarithms in randomized polynomial time
summary: Given a prime p, a generator g and a nonzero residue h, the task is to recover the unique exponent x between zero and p minus two with g to the x congruent to h modulo p. The question asks whether one classical randomized algorithm can do this in polynomial time in the full binary input length on every promised input. All preprocessing is charged, and the running-time bound must hold for every random sequence while success is at least two thirds separately on each instance. This would invert a basic arithmetic operation used in finite-field cryptography and match a known quantum capability. Google’s Cogentic algorithm improves the bound for extension fields of small characteristic, leaving the question about prime fields of unbounded characteristic open.
formal: Does there exist one uniform classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\), and integers \(C,c\ge1\), such that \(A\) halts within \(C(L+1)^c\) steps on every binary input of length \(L\) and every sequence of its random bits, and has the following correctness property? For every prime \(p\), every generator \(g\) of the multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^{\times}\), and every \(h\in\mathbb F_p^{\times}\), given the binary encoding of \((p,g,h)\) specified below, it outputs the unique integer \(x\in\{0,\ldots,p-2\}\) satisfying \(g^x\equiv h\pmod p\) with probability at least \(2/3\).
definitions: The field \(\mathbb F_p\) consists of residues \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\) with addition and multiplication modulo the prime \(p\). Its multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^{\times}\) is \(\{1,\ldots,p-1\}\) with multiplication modulo \(p\). The promise that \(g\) is a generator means that \(g^0,g^1,\ldots,g^{p-2}\), reduced modulo \(p\), list these \(p-1\) residues without repetition; hence the requested exponent exists and is unique. Each input integer is represented by its ordinary base-two expansion \(\operatorname{bin}(a)\), without leading zeros and with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\). Writing \(\ell(a)=|\operatorname{bin}(a)|\), set \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^{\ell(a)}0\operatorname{bin}(a)\). The complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(p)\operatorname{code}(g)\operatorname{code}(h)\), with \(p\) prime and \(1\le g,h<p\). Its length \(L=2(\ell(p)+\ell(g)+\ell(h))+3\) is \(\Theta(\log_2 p)\) on promised inputs. A successful output is exactly \(\operatorname{bin}(x)\); any different output or a designated failure symbol is unsuccessful. For \(p=2\), the sole promised pair is \(g=h=1\) and the answer is \(x=0\). The machine has a fixed finite program, fixed finite alphabets, a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes and an output tape; each transition costs one step, and any random transition reads one fresh independent fair bit. The time bound includes input processing, bit arithmetic, random-bit generation, output and all preprocessing. The same \(A,C,c\) work for every input, with no advice, oracle, precomputed table or supplied factorization of \(p-1\). Arbitrary classical computations on the concrete binary residues are permitted, not just generic group operations. Malformed encodings may be rejected as failure; on well-formed triples outside the mathematical promise, only the global time bound is required. The success guarantee is separately for each promised triple, over the machine’s coins, not over a distribution of primes or targets. The question concerns the multiplicative group of a prime field; additive groups, extension fields and elliptic-curve groups are different models.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of \(A,C,c\) with both the all-input, all-random-sequence time bound and the per-promised-input success guarantee, or a Lean-checked proof that no such triple exists. Equivalently, a negative answer must prove that every machine obeying some global polynomial clock has a promised input on which its probability of outputting the required exponent is less than \(2/3\). Failure of a particular algorithm, an average-case conjecture for a selected prime distribution, or a lower bound restricted to generic group operations does not establish this negation. A quantum algorithm, success only for selected prime families, or a bound polynomial in \(p\) rather than its bit length does not meet the positive target.

title: Polynomial-time, polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
summary: The shortest vector problem asks for a nonzero integer combination of a rational lattice basis with minimum Euclidean length. This card asks whether one uniform classical randomized algorithm can approximate that length within some fixed power of the rank on every basis. It must return a nonzero vector on every run, achieve the length bound with probability at least two thirds per input, and count all input, arithmetic and output bits in a polynomial clock. Known general upper guarantees, conditional hardness at smaller factors and basis-dependent approximation expressions do not settle this target. The September 2026 review retains the distinctions between search and decision, classical and quantum computation, and current theorems and withdrawn claims.
formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\), a real constant \(K>0\), an integer \(k\geq1\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\) such that for every pair of integers \(d\geq n\geq1\) and every explicitly encoded \(B\in\mathbb Q^{d\times n}\) with linearly independent columns, every run halts in at most \(K(N+1)^k\) bit operations and returns a nonzero \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), with
\[\Pr\!\left[\|Bz\|_2\leq n^C\lambda_1(L(B))\right]\geq\frac23?\]
The input length \(N\) includes all matrix entries. The lattice is \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), and \(\lambda_1\) is its shortest nonzero Euclidean length. Randomness consists of independent fair bits on that fixed input. The program and all constants are chosen once, before any input.
definitions:
The input contains \(d,n\) and all \(dn\) rational entries in row-major order. To fix a binary encoding, let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(t\), using the one-bit string \(0\) for zero, and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Dimensions use \(E(d),E(n)\). A rational number is encoded by a sign bit followed by \(E(|a|)E(q)\), where it equals \(a/q\), \(q>0\), and \(\gcd(|a|,q)=1\); zero has positive sign and denominator one. There are exactly \(dn\) entries and no trailing bits. Valid inputs satisfy \(d\geq n\geq1\) and column independence over \(\mathbb Q\). The total number of encoded bits is \(N\). The polynomial clock applies on every binary input; behavior and output on malformed or dependent-basis inputs are otherwise unrestricted.

The Euclidean norm of \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}\). The lattice consists of all integer combinations of the columns, with its usual embedding in \(\mathbb R^d\). Independence makes \(z\mapsto Bz\) injective and makes \(L(B)\) discrete in its real span. Thus
\[\lambda_1(L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2>0\]
is attained. No uniqueness of the shortest vector up to sign is assumed. The algorithm returns the coefficient vector: its \(n\) signed integer coordinates use a sign bit and \(E\) of the absolute value, with positive sign for zero. It must return a valid nonzero vector on every run on a valid input. An unsuccessful run may exceed the norm bound, but may not output zero, fail to halt or omit the vector. The squared norm can equivalently be used in the displayed guarantee with squared factor \(n^{2C}\).

Use one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a finite description independent of all input parameters. Its tapes have a fixed finite alphabet encoding bits. Each transition can read and write only a fixed number of cells and move each head by at most one cell. An additional instruction obtains one fresh independent fair bit at unit cost. This describes ordinary uniform classical bit computation, with no advice, oracle, quantum operations, uncharged preprocessing or unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers. All reading, writing, arithmetic, memory manipulation and random-bit generation count toward the bound. The output uses the integer encoding specified above, and every bit written is charged.

For a given valid input, randomness is the product measure of independent uniform bits on an infinite random tape; the polynomial clock ensures that only finitely many are read. The success event is the displayed norm inequality, separately for every input. All runs, including those outside that event, must return a valid nonzero integer vector within the same clock. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as the special case that uses no random bits. Expected polynomial time alone is not the stated requirement.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C,K,k,A\;\forall d,n,B\), with both the probability guarantee and the all-run clock imposed after choosing the input. In particular, \(C\) may be large but must be fixed. The factor is \(n^C\), determined by lattice rank; it is not a polynomial in the ambient dimension, the coefficient magnitude or the input bit length. In rank one it is exactly one. There is no input-distribution, shortest-vector uniqueness, ideal-lattice, conditioning, modular or basis-quality promise. The problem concerns arbitrary finite rational bases, including ones with very large coefficients.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of one algorithm and constants meeting every requirement, or of the logical negation of that existence statement. A negative answer must rule out every fixed exponent \(C>0\) and every permitted randomized polynomial-time algorithm, rather than only a deterministic algorithm or a selected small approximation factor. A positive answer must establish the actual nonzero-vector output, success on each basis and all-run bit clock, including coefficient and output lengths. A conditional complexity lower bound gives only a conditional conclusion unless its assumption is proved. A gap-decision certificate, a factor depending without a rank bound on the input basis, a uniqueness-promised result, an oracle-call bound excluding subroutine time, or a quantum algorithm alone does not settle this classical search target. No additional numerical tolerance weakens this exact existence proposition.

title: Vinogradov’s least quadratic nonresidue conjecture
summary: A quadratic nonresidue is a nonzero residue that is not a square modulo the prime. Vinogradov’s conjecture says that the least positive one eventually lies below every fixed positive power of the prime. The threshold may depend on the exponent, but the bound must cover every sufficiently large odd prime. Conditional logarithmic-square estimates and almost-all-prime results do not establish this unconditional statement. A refutation would require one fixed positive exponent and arbitrarily large primes violating its bound.
formal:
For an odd prime \(p\), let \(n(p)\) be the least positive quadratic nonresidue modulo \(p\), defined below. Is it true, unconditionally, that
\[\forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists P_\varepsilon\in\mathbb N\ \forall p\ge P_\varepsilon\text{ odd prime},\qquad n(p)\le p^{\varepsilon}?\]
Equivalently, is \(n(p)=p^{o(1)}\) as \(p\) tends to infinity through the odd primes? The threshold may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on the prime. No unproved analytic hypothesis is assumed.
definitions:
For integers \(a,b\) and a positive integer \(p\), the congruence \(a\equiv b\pmod p\) means that \(p\) divides \(a-b\). An integer \(a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\) if there exists \(x\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\) with \(x^2\equiv a\pmod p\); otherwise it is a quadratic nonresidue. Define
\[n(p)=\min\{a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}:\forall x\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\},\ x^2\not\equiv a\pmod p\}.\]
For an odd prime, exactly half of its nonzero residue classes are squares, so the set is nonempty. Representatives are ordered as ordinary positive integers; this is not the least absolute value among positive and negative representatives. Multiples of \(p\) are not counted as nonresidues.

The domain is all odd primes, not composite moduli, almost all primes, or one prescribed congruence class. The prime \(2\) is omitted because every nonzero residue modulo \(2\) is a square. Real powers have the convention \(p^\varepsilon=\exp(\varepsilon\log p)\), where \(\log\) is the natural logarithm.

The statement can equivalently be expressed using only integer powers:
\[\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists P_k\in\mathbb N\ \forall p\ge P_k\text{ odd prime},\qquad n(p)^k\le p.\]
Likewise, the subpolynomial notation means \(\lim_{p\to\infty,\ p\ \mathrm{prime}}\log n(p)/\log p=0\). The source writes \(n(p)=O_\varepsilon(p^\varepsilon)\); since its claim quantifies over every positive exponent, the implicit constant can be absorbed by using a smaller exponent and increasing the threshold. The unit-leading-constant formulation above is therefore equivalent. The conjecture asks for existence of the thresholds, without an extra requirement to compute them effectively.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal statement, or a Lean-checked refutation. A refutation must establish a fixed \(\varepsilon_0>0\) and arbitrarily large odd primes \(p\) with \(n(p)>p^{\varepsilon_0}\). A finite numerical exception cannot refute an eventual bound. A result for almost all primes, a bound with one fixed positive exponent, or a theorem assuming GRH or Elliott–Halberstam is insufficient without also proving the necessary hypothesis.

title: Exact Euclidean SVP in BQP
summary: Can a quantum computer find an exactly shortest nonzero lattice vector in time polynomial in the encoded basis length? The output must be a classical integer combination of the basis, with success probability at least two thirds on every valid input. Randomized NP-hardness would make such an algorithm a major quantum complexity result, but is not a quantum impossibility proof. August 2026 exact-SVP preprints claim faster exponential algorithms with additional memory details. The disputed dihedral-coset proposal has an approximate-SVP consequence and does not settle this exact target.
formal: Do there exist a uniform quantum algorithm and a polynomial \(p\) with the following guarantee? Given an integer matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{m\times d}\) with \(m\ge d\ge1\) and linearly independent columns, the algorithm outputs a nonzero \(z\in\mathbb Z^d\) satisfying \[\|Bz\|_2=\min_{y\in\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{0\}}\|By\|_2\] with probability at least \(2/3\). Every execution must take at most \(p(N)\) elementary steps, where \(N\) is the full binary length of the dimensions and all matrix entries.
definitions:
The lattice is \(\Lambda(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^d\}\). Its rank is \(d\), its ambient dimension is \(m\), and its first minimum \(\lambda_1(\Lambda(B))\) is the Euclidean norm of a shortest nonzero vector. Full column rank guarantees a positive, attained minimum. The output gives the coefficient vector \(z\) in signed binary. Every vector attaining the minimum qualifies, including when there is a tie.

Use the [uniform quantum circuit model](definitions.html#quantum). On \(1^N\) a classical polynomial-time machine generates a circuit with an \(N\)-bit input register, zero-initialized ancillas, gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\) and computational-basis measurement. Classical decoding, circuit size, qubit count, input processing and output writing all have polynomial bounds in \(N\). The success guarantee applies separately to each valid basis. Malformed inputs and rank-deficient matrices can be rejected classically. For rational bases, clearing denominators scales all lengths by the same factor and increases the encoding length only polynomially.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of the algorithm with the stated worst-case polynomial cost and exact-search success on every valid basis, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Classical NP-hardness alone does not establish the negative answer for quantum computation. A polynomial-factor approximation, an algorithm for a promised special family, or an exponential-time speedup does not establish the positive answer.
