title: Deterministic polynomial-time construction of a prime of a given bit length
summary: Given a requested bit length in unary, the task is to output the ordinary binary expansion of a prime with exactly that many bits. The question asks whether one fixed deterministic algorithm can do this for every length at least two in polynomial bit time. Primality testing is efficiently possible, while deterministic construction of a suitable candidate remains a central explicit-construction problem. Polynomial-time pseudodeterministic generation is known for infinitely many lengths, but that algorithm still uses randomness and does not meet the all-length deterministic requirement. A complete Lean answer must prove the existence of the required algorithm or prove that every deterministic program and polynomial bound fail at some requested length.
formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that constructs a prime of every requested bit length in polynomial bit time?

The input is the unary string \(1^n\), for any integer \(n\ge2\). The output must be the binary expansion of some prime \(p\) satisfying
\[
2^{n-1}\le p<2^n.
\]
The prime may be any one in this interval; no particular choice, such as the smallest prime, is prescribed.

With the finite machine model and output predicate below, the precise assertion is
\[
\exists A\ \exists C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ 
\forall n\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\quad
\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\ 
\bigl(
\operatorname{HaltWithin}(A,1^n,y,Cn^k)
\land \operatorname{PrimeOutput}(n,y)
\bigr).
\]
One fixed deterministic program and one polynomial bound must work for every requested length. This retains the source's unary-input prime-construction question and makes its bit-computation convention explicit.
definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge2\), the unary string \(1^n\) consists of exactly \(n\) consecutive copies of the symbol one. Its length, rather than the binary length of the integer \(n\), is the input size. Valid inputs are precisely these strings; other input strings impose no requirements.

A positive integer \(p\) is prime when \(p\ge2\) and every positive integer dividing \(p\) is either one or \(p\) itself. A binary output string \(y=y_0y_1\cdots y_{n-1}\) of length \(n\), with \(y_0=1\), represents
\[
\operatorname{val}(y)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}y_i2^{n-1-i}.
\]
Here each symbol \(y_i\) is identified with the integer zero or one. The predicate \(\operatorname{PrimeOutput}(n,y)\) means that \(y\) has exactly this length, its first bit is one, and \(\operatorname{val}(y)\) is prime. No leading zeros, additional bits, compressed description or separate certificate form part of the output. This predicate is equivalent to requiring the ordinary binary expansion of a prime in the displayed interval.

An algorithm \(A\) is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with one read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes, and a binary output stream. Its finite control, finite tape alphabets and number of tapes are fixed independently of the input. Tape cells have nonnegative integer addresses. Initially all heads are at cell zero, work tapes are blank, the input tape contains the input followed by blanks, and the output is empty. Each transition reads the symbols under the heads, changes the finite control, writes at most one symbol on each work tape, moves each head left, right or not at all by at most one cell, and appends at most one bit to the output. A move left from cell zero leaves the head there. The transition rule is a finite deterministic table, defined on every nonhalting state and tuple of scanned symbols, and a designated halt state ends the computation.

One transition costs one bit-computation step. All computation, preprocessing, reading and writing count, including production of all \(n\) output bits. There are no random bits, quantum operations, oracle calls, input-dependent advice or unbounded integers with unit-cost operations. The finite program may contain fixed constants, but receives no additional information depending on \(n\).

The predicate \(\operatorname{HaltWithin}(A,x,y,T)\) means that the computation on input \(x\) reaches its halt state after at most \(T\) transitions and has produced exactly the finite output string \(y\). Requiring positive integer constants \(C,k\) expresses ordinary polynomial time: increasing them covers any fixed polynomial bound. Both constants and the whole finite program precede the universal quantifier over \(n\). The assertion is unconditional; an unproved hypothesis about primes or computational hardness is not an additional assumption.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence assertion or of its full logical negation.

A positive answer must supply one finite deterministic program \(A\) and positive integers \(C,k\), and prove for every \(n\ge2\) that it halts on \(1^n\) within \(Cn^k\) bit steps and outputs exactly the binary expansion of an \(n\)-bit prime. The output prime need not be the first prime in its interval.

A negative answer must prove
\[
\forall A\ \forall C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\quad
\exists n\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\quad
\neg\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\ 
\bigl(
\operatorname{HaltWithin}(A,1^n,y,Cn^k)
\land \operatorname{PrimeOutput}(n,y)
\bigr).
\]
Thus each proposed deterministic program and polynomial bound must fail at some length, which may depend on both. Failure includes running longer than the bound, never halting, or producing an invalid prime output. This does not assert that some bit length contains no prime.

A randomized or pseudodeterministic construction, success only at infinitely many lengths, or a bound that is polynomial in the numerical value of the output instead of its bit length does not establish the positive assertion. A conditional result establishes the target only if its additional hypothesis is also proved. A lower bound for one search procedure does not establish the unrestricted negative assertion. This is an exact algorithm-existence question, so numerical \(1/100\) approximation is not a substitute for the required proof.

title: Deterministic NP-hardness reductions for Euclidean SVP
summary: Euclidean SVP asks whether a lattice contains a nonzero vector within an explicitly given radius. The source asks for a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction proving NP-hardness and explicitly allows the exact decision version. This formulation fixes rational full-rank bases, rational squared radii, binary encodings and a uniform bit-cost machine, without an extra approximation gap or complexity assumption. Wan’s 2026 preprint states a matching positive result, and an independent September conference paper recognizes its deterministic polynomial-time hardness range. The recorded proof-chain review supports resolution of the original exact target, while keeping its limits and the preprint status explicit.
formal:
Is the exact decision version of the Euclidean shortest vector problem NP-hard under a uniform deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction?

An instance consists of a positive integer \(n\), a nonsingular rational matrix \(B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), and a positive rational squared-radius threshold \(b\), all explicitly encoded in binary as specified below. Its lattice and Euclidean minimum are
\[
L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^{n}\},\qquad
\lambda_{1}(L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^{n}\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_{2},
\qquad \|x\|_{2}=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{2}\right)^{1/2}.
\]
The answer is YES if \(\lambda_{1}(L(B))^{2}\le b\), and NO if \(\lambda_{1}(L(B))^{2}>b\). Thus the geometric radius is \(\sqrt{b}\), represented exactly by its rational square.

Precisely, does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(M\) and integers \(a,k\ge1\) such that, on every encoded 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\), it outputs a valid instance \((B_{\varphi},b_{\varphi})\) within \(a(|\varphi|+1)^{k}\) steps and
\[
\varphi\text{ is satisfiable}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists z\in\mathbb Z^{n_{\varphi}}\setminus\{0\}\quad
\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\varphi}}(B_{\varphi}z)_{i}^{2}\le b_{\varphi}?
\]
The same machine and constants must work for every input length. It must have the same time bound on malformed input strings, mapping them to valid NO instances.

This is the exact endpoint \(\gamma=1\) expressly allowed by the source's request for hardness of exact or approximate GapSVP under a deterministic Karp reduction. No approximation factor greater than one is required; a valid stronger gap reduction would also settle this endpoint.
definitions:
A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of exactly three literals; a literal is a Boolean variable or its negation. Variables have positive integer labels, and labels or literals may repeat. An assignment maps the finitely many labels occurring in the formula to \(\{0,1\}\); a positive literal is true when its variable is one, and a negative literal when its variable is zero. A clause is true if at least one literal is true, and the formula is true if every clause is true. The conjunction of zero clauses is true.

Fix the finite input alphabet \(\Sigma=\{0,1,+,-,(,),\texttt{,}\}\). A literal is a sign followed by the usual binary representation of a positive integer, without leading zeros. A clause consists of an opening parenthesis, three such literals separated by commas, and a closing parenthesis. An encoded formula is a concatenation of zero or more clauses; no whitespace is used. The empty string encodes the empty conjunction. All other strings over \(\Sigma\) are malformed. Let \(\mathrm{SAT}_{3}(s)\) mean that \(s\) is a well-formed formula with a satisfying assignment, and let this predicate be false for malformed strings. The input length \(|s|\) is the number of symbols in this encoding; integer labels are represented explicitly, not by unit-cost integers or a separate count of unused variables.

For lattice output, an integer is represented by a sign and its binary magnitude, without leading zeros; zero has the representation \(+0\). A rational is represented by a numerator and a strictly positive denominator in lowest terms, separated by \(\texttt{/}\); its zero numerator is therefore paired with denominator one. The output is the binary dimension \(n\ge1\), followed by the \(n^{2}\) entries of \(B\) in row-major order, followed by \(b\), with consecutive fields separated by \(\texttt{;}\). The dimension has no leading zeros. The numerator uses the signed integer encoding, and denominators use unsigned positive binary encoding. The complete output contains exactly the indicated number of fields. Validity requires \(\det B\ne0\) and \(b>0\). This provides a finite exact representation of every allowed rational full-rank basis and squared-radius threshold; the reduction must print the whole representation.

The rational basis vectors are the columns of \(B\), and their integer span defines \(L(B)\). Nonsingularity ensures that \(Bz\ne0\) exactly when \(z\ne0\), and that the lattice has a positive attained minimum. The input basis need not be reduced, orthogonal, triangular, or short. There is no uniqueness promise for a shortest vector and no restriction on the determinant, entries, or dimension beyond their explicit encoding and the reduction's polynomial output bound. The norm is the ordinary Euclidean norm of the specified coordinates. All comparisons in the decision predicate use the rational number \(b\) and squared rational coordinates; no rounding or unit-cost real arithmetic is allowed. Storing a rational square permits an irrational geometric radius, such as the square root of an integer, without any ambiguity.

A deterministic machine is an ordinary multitape Turing machine with a finite control, a fixed finite tape alphabet containing the encoding symbols, a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes, and an output tape. Every transition reads and writes at most one symbol per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. The initial state, blank symbol and initial head positions are fixed in its finite description. Input inspection, arithmetic on binary integers and fractions, and writing every output symbol count toward runtime. There are no random bits, advice strings, nondeterministic choices, oracle calls, quantum operations, or unit-cost operations on arbitrarily large numbers. The resource bound is worst-case total running time on every string. In particular, the output dimension and total bit length are automatically polynomially bounded in input length. Polynomial exponents and leading constants may depend on the single chosen machine, but not on the input length or formula.

A Karp reduction is a many-one reduction: the machine produces one instance, whose one YES/NO answer decides the original membership question. It does not make adaptive queries to a shortest-vector oracle and need not compute a shortest vector or a satisfying assignment. Using the fixed NP-complete source language \(\mathrm{SAT}_{3}\) is equivalent to NP-hardness under this reduction type. Use the shared definition of [NP](definitions.html#p-np). NP-hardness is the unconditional reduction assertion; the target does not assume \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), an exponential-time hypothesis, or a circuit lower bound.

For completeness, the source defines \(\gamma\)-GapSVP, for \(\gamma\ge1\), by the promise that either \(\lambda_{1}(L(B))\le r\) or \(\lambda_{1}(L(B))>\gamma r\). In this card's encoding \(r=\sqrt{b}\), so these conditions become \(\lambda_{1}(L(B))^{2}\le b\) and \(\lambda_{1}(L(B))^{2}>\gamma^{2}b\). At \(\gamma=1\), every valid instance meets exactly one of the two conditions, so the selected problem is an ordinary decision problem with no missing interval. The word Gap in the source's name distinguishes decision from search and does not itself impose a gap larger than one. The card keeps the source's Euclidean norm and exact endpoint. Storing the squared radius is an explicit finite-encoding convention, polynomial-time equivalent for rational-basis exact SVP to a rational-radius encoding; it does not impose a stronger approximation theorem or a numerical tolerance.
answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence assertion in the formal statement or of its logical negation.

For a finite deterministic machine description \(M\), positive integers \(a,k\), and a string \(s\in\Sigma^{*}\), define \(\mathrm{Good}(M,a,k,s)\) to mean that the run halts within \(a(|s|+1)^{k}\) steps, prints exactly one valid encoded rational full-rank lattice instance \((B,b)\), and satisfies
\[
\mathrm{SAT}_{3}(s)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists z\in\mathbb Z^{n}\setminus\{0\}\quad
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Bz)_{i}^{2}\le b.
\]
Thus the affirmative theorem is
\[
\exists M\;\exists a,k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\;\forall s\in\Sigma^{*},
\quad\mathrm{Good}(M,a,k,s).
\]
A positive solution must prove deterministic uniform construction, the total bit-cost runtime bound, output validity, and both the satisfiable and unsatisfiable cases, for all strings. No separate assumption about \(\mathrm{P}\), \(\mathrm{NP}\), randomness, or cryptographic hardness is allowed.

The negative theorem is the full negation
\[
\forall M\;\forall a,k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\;\exists s\in\Sigma^{*},
\quad\neg\mathrm{Good}(M,a,k,s).
\]
It must rule out every deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction in the stated model, allowing the failed input to depend on the machine and its proposed time bound. A failure of one construction, an oracle separation, or a limitation on a special reduction framework does not establish this negation. A randomized reduction, a nonuniform family, a deterministic superpolynomial-time reduction, hardness only in a different norm, or a conditional hardness theorem does not establish the positive assertion. There is no numerical tolerance on the exact YES/NO equivalence or the polynomial-time guarantee.

title: Exact Euclidean SVP in single-exponential time and polynomial space
summary: An input basis generates a lattice by taking all integer combinations of its rational columns. The algorithm must output coordinates of an exactly shortest nonzero Euclidean lattice vector, with success probability at least two thirds. One uniform algorithm must use single-exponential time in the lattice rank and polynomial working space in the full input length simultaneously. Both resource bounds include preprocessing, arithmetic precision and unsuccessful random executions. A complete Lean-checked proof must establish those guarantees or their impossibility; exponential storage, approximation and heuristic memory savings do not meet the target.
formal:
Do there exist one randomized classical algorithm \(A\) and absolute integers \(C,d\ge1\) such that, for every rational lattice basis \(B\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) with linearly independent columns and total binary encoding length \(N\), the algorithm finds an exact shortest nonzero vector of \(\Lambda(B)\) with probability at least \(2/3\), while using simultaneously at most
\[
2^{Cn}N^d\quad\text{bit operations}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
N^d\quad\text{bits of working space}?
\]
Both bounds must hold on every random tape. The exponent parameter \(n\) is lattice rank, and every \(m\ge n\ge1\) and every valid coefficient encoding are included.
definitions:
The input explicitly gives \(m,n\) and every entry of \(B\), in column or row order fixed by the encoding. A rational entry is a signed binary numerator divided by a positive binary denominator, using canonical integer encodings and unambiguous boundaries. Reduction to lowest terms is not required. The bit length \(N\) includes all entries and dimension data; the input is not a generating circuit or an oracle. Full column rank and \(m\ge n\ge1\) are promises. No behavior on unpromised inputs is required for the target.

The rank-\(n\) lattice is
\[
\Lambda(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^m.
\]
The columns are linearly independent over the rationals, equivalently over the reals, so \(Bz\ne0\) for every nonzero integer coordinate vector \(z\). With the Euclidean norm \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^m v_i^2)^{1/2}\), define
\[
\lambda_1(\Lambda(B))=
\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2.
\]
Full rank makes this a discrete lattice in its linear span, so the positive minimum is attained.

Successful output is a finite binary encoding of a nonzero integer vector \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\) with \(\|Bz\|_2=\lambda_1(\Lambda(B))\). Equivalently, it satisfies the exact rational inequalities
\[
\forall u\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\},\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m(Bz)_i^2\le\sum_{i=1}^m(Bu)_i^2.
\]
Any minimizer is acceptable, including either sign and any of several shortest vectors. The integer coordinates refer to the input basis. An approximate length, a short vector with a factor greater than one, or a real-valued coordinate approximation is not this output. The algorithm may report failure or return a nonoptimal vector on unsuccessful executions; all executions remain subject to both resource bounds.

Use a uniform probabilistic multitape Turing machine with read-only input, write-only output and a one-way stream of independent fair random bits. Working space counts every used work-tape bit, including saved random bits, counters, intermediate vectors, basis transformations and precision data. The random source cannot be revisited as free writable storage. No external writable memory, preprocessing oracle or nonuniform advice is available. Input and final output tapes are not counted as working storage, but every operation reading or writing them counts toward time. All arithmetic is charged in bit operations; arbitrary-precision arithmetic is not a unit-cost instruction.

The success probability is at least \(2/3\) separately for every fixed valid input, over the machine’s internal random bits. The time and space bounds are worst-case over those bits, including unsuccessful executions, and include preprocessing and all precision management. The same constants \(C,d\) apply to all ranks, ambient dimensions and coefficient lengths. Different fixed polynomial exponents for time and space can be absorbed into one \(d\). A deterministic algorithm qualifies as a special case.

No uniqueness, reduced-basis, random-lattice or special-lattice promise is imposed. The desired exponential base is any absolute constant \(2^C\); no particular base such as two is required. The task is an exact search-algorithm existence proposition, not a separate numerical approximation of \(\lambda_1\).
answer_criterion:
Supply an algorithm and complete Lean-checked proofs of both simultaneous resource bounds and its exact success probability on every valid rational basis. Alternatively, supply a complete Lean-checked proof that no algorithm and absolute constants \(C,d\) satisfy the displayed requirements.

A single-exponential algorithm using exponential space, a polynomial-space algorithm with \(2^{\Theta(n\log n)}\) time, a heuristic or average-case guarantee, or an approximation algorithm does not settle the question. A counterexample to one enumeration or sieving procedure does not rule out all algorithms. A lower bound conditional on an unproved lattice-hardness assumption is not an unconditional negative resolution.

title: Optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance tradeoff
summary: A binary code is any nonempty set of equal-length bit strings with a prescribed minimum pairwise Hamming distance. The function \(R_2(\delta)\) is the limsup of the maximum information rate at relative distance \(\delta\), allowing nonlinear codes and arbitrary subsequences of block lengths. Determine this function at every real distance strictly between zero and one half, with absolute error at most 0.01 information bits per transmitted bit. A complete Lean proof must establish both lower and upper guarantees throughout the domain, without any code-construction or evaluation-time bound. The checked 2026 papers improve the upper bounds but do not supply this certified whole-curve approximation; polynomial code-size improvements also leave the leading rate unchanged.
formal:
Determine the optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance function
\[R_2(\delta)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)}{n},\qquad 0<\delta<\frac12,\]
where \(A_2(n,d)\) is the largest cardinality of any nonempty binary code of length \(n\) whose distinct codewords have Hamming distance at least \(d\). Supply an unambiguous real-valued approximation \(g:(0,1/2)\to\mathbb R\), with a complete Lean proof that
\[\forall\delta\in(0,1/2),\qquad |g(\delta)-R_2(\delta)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The error is absolute rate error in information bits per transmitted bit. Codes may be nonlinear and have no construction, encoding or decoding efficiency requirement. The same error bound must hold on the entire real domain.
definitions:
Finite codes. For integers \(n\ge1\) and \(0\le d\le n\), a binary length-\(n\) code is a nonempty subset \(C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\). Its elements are codewords. For \(x,y\in\{0,1\}^n\), define their Hamming distance by
\[d_H(x,y)=|\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i\ne y_i\}|.\]
The distance requirement means \(d_H(x,y)\ge d\) for every distinct pair \(x,y\in C\). A singleton satisfies it vacuously; no minimum over an empty set needs to be chosen. Define
\[A_2(n,d)=\max\{|C|:\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ \forall x,y\in C,\ x\ne y\Rightarrow d_H(x,y)\ge d\}.\]
This is a finite maximum over a nonempty collection, and \(1\le A_2(n,d)\le2^n\). The rate of \(C\) is \(r(C)=\log_2|C|/n\). The distance parameter \(d/n\) is a required relative separation, not the fraction of independent random channel errors. All logarithms are base two.

Asymptotic convention. Fix the real parameter \(\delta\) before taking the block length to infinity. The integer \(\lceil\delta n\rceil\) is the smallest integer at least \(\delta n\). For \(0\le\delta\le1\), write \(a_n(\delta)=\log_2 A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)/n\). Explicitly,
\[R_2(\delta)=\inf_{N\in\mathbb N_{>0}}\ \sup_{n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge N} a_n(\delta).\]
Every term is in \([0,1]\), so the tail suprema and infimum are well-defined finite real numbers. The limsup allows a favorable infinite subsequence of block lengths and does not assert that the ordinary limit exists. The optimum ranges over all codes, without linearity or a single effective code-family generator. The requested domain is exactly \((0,1/2)\); the same definition outside it gives the known regimes \(R_2(0)=1\) and \(R_2(\delta)=0\) for \(1/2\le\delta\le1\).

Conventions for bounds. A lower curve \(L\) satisfies \(L(\delta)\le R_2(\delta)\) precisely when, for each fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\), every \(\varepsilon>0\) and every integer \(N\ge1\), there are an integer \(n\ge N\) and a valid code of length \(n\), distance at least \(\lceil\delta n\rceil\), and rate at least \(L(\delta)-\varepsilon\). An upper curve \(U\) satisfies \(R_2(\delta)\le U(\delta)\) precisely when, for each fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), some integer \(N\ge1\) has the following property: for every \(n\ge N\), every valid code at that distance has rate at most \(U(\delta)+\varepsilon\). Block length thresholds may depend on \(\delta\) and \(\varepsilon\); a common threshold for all real distances is not required. These existence bounds do not impose polynomial-time code construction.

For the background bounds, the binary entropy is \(h_2(t)=-t\log_2t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t)\) on \([0,1]\), with each endpoint term \(0\log_2 0\) interpreted as zero.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified function \(g:(0,1/2)\to\mathbb R\) and a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of \(|g(\delta)-R_2(\delta)|\le1/100\) for every real \(\delta\) in that domain, using the finite-code maximum, rounding, limsup and normalization above. This requires both \(g(\delta)-1/100\le R_2(\delta)\) and \(R_2(\delta)\le g(\delta)+1/100\); the preceding quantified code statements specify the corresponding lower and upper guarantees. Alternatively, certified curves \(L,U\) satisfying \(L(\delta)\le R_2(\delta)\le U(\delta)\) and \(U(\delta)-L(\delta)\le1/50\) everywhere qualify through their midpoint. A formula, certified evaluation rule or another unambiguous mathematical description may specify the answer; no predetermined formula grammar or evaluation-time bound is imposed. Merely renaming the defining optimization or limsup does not supply the requested determination. An exact determination qualifies, but exact equality to the Gilbert–Varshamov curve is not required. Finitely many samples, an uncertified numerical plot, a bound on only one side, or a result restricted to linear codes or to some distances does not establish the stated whole-domain guarantee.

title: Capacity of the general broadcast channel
summary: One transmitter sends two independent private messages through a memoryless channel to receivers with different noisy observations. The target is the weighted support function of the average-error capacity region for every finite rational channel table and rational weight between zero and one. All rates are measured in bits per channel use, and the two individual capacities do not determine the joint tradeoff. Classical and recent work provides achievable regions, converse bounds and special cases, while the August 2026 Marton-suboptimality preprint is a narrower unverified claim. A complete Lean proof must certify a supplied function within absolute error 1/100 over the entire stated domain.
formal:
Determine the function
\[F(W,\lambda)=\sup_{(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(W)}\bigl(\lambda R_{1}+(1-\lambda)R_{2}\bigr)\]
for every finite discrete memoryless broadcast channel \(W\) with a rational transition table and every \(\lambda\in\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]\). Here \(C(W)\) is the capacity region for two independent private messages, deterministic codes, vanishing joint average decoding error, and no feedback, as defined below. The required accuracy is absolute \(1/100\) bit per channel use throughout this entire domain.
definitions:
For a positive integer \(m\), write \([m]=\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\). The domain contains all positive integers \(a,b,c\), alphabets \(\mathcal X=[a]\), \(\mathcal Y=[b]\), \(\mathcal Z=[c]\), and arrays \(W(y,z\mid x)\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) such that \(\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y,z\in\mathcal Z}W(y,z\mid x)=1\) for every \(x\). Alphabet sizes are unbounded, and zero transition probabilities are allowed. There is no conditional-independence requirement on the two outputs in a single use. For each block length \(n\ge1\), the channel law is
\[\Pr(Y^{n}=y^{n},Z^{n}=z^{n}\mid X^{n}=x^{n})=\prod_{t=1}^{n}W(y_{t},z_{t}\mid x_{t}).\]
The table specifies the whole channel; it has no additional state or memory.

An \((n,K_{1},K_{2})\) code, with positive integer message sizes, consists of maps \(f:[K_{1}]\times[K_{2}]\to\mathcal X^{n}\), \(d_{1}:\mathcal Y^{n}\to[K_{1}]\), and \(d_{2}:\mathcal Z^{n}\to[K_{2}]\). The messages \(M_{1},M_{2}\) are independent and uniform, the encoder transmits \(f(M_{1},M_{2})\), and the receivers output \(d_{1}(Y^{n})\) and \(d_{2}(Z^{n})\). Its joint average error is
\[P_{e}=\Pr\bigl[d_{1}(Y^{n})\ne M_{1}\ \text{or}\ d_{2}(Z^{n})\ne M_{2}\bigr],\]
where the probability averages over both messages and the specified channel randomness. No worst-case-over-messages error requirement is imposed. The encoder knows both messages; each decoder observes only its own output block. There is no common message, feedback, receiver communication, shared randomness, secrecy condition, or input-cost constraint. Codes are arbitrary deterministic maps with no uniform construction or complexity bound. Dependence among the transmitted symbols and deterministic time sharing are allowed.

All logarithms defining rates have base two; rates and the target function are measured in bits per channel use. A pair \((R_{1},R_{2})\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{2}\) is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes, indexed by \(j\ge1\), with \(n_{j}\to\infty\), \(P_{e,j}\to0\), and \(\liminf_{j\to\infty}\log_{2}(K_{i,j})/n_{j}\ge R_{i}\) for both \(i=1,2\). Define \(C(W)\) as the Euclidean closure of the achievable pairs. It is a nonempty compact convex downward-closed subset of \([0,\log_{2}b]\times[0,\log_{2}c]\); these properties and the endpoint weights make \(F\) a finite real function, including when an alphabet has size one. A supremum in the definition does not require a finite code attaining a boundary rate. Its exact values at all rational weights determine the closed region; the benchmark below requires only their stated approximation.

If an answer is given as an algorithm, its finite input is the three alphabet sizes followed by the full table in lexicographic order and the weight, with integers in binary and rational numbers as reduced numerator/positive-denominator pairs separated by delimiters. All valid inputs in this encoding are included. No time bound or fixed grammar for a mathematical answer is imposed.
answer_criterion:
Supply one unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on the entire domain above and a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[\forall W\ \forall\lambda\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,1],\qquad |g(W,\lambda)-F(W,\lambda)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The proof must match the code model, average error, limiting convention, units, and unbounded range of alphabet sizes. It must justify both sides of the error guarantee against the operational capacity definition. Certified bounds \(L(W,\lambda)\le F(W,\lambda)\le U(W,\lambda)\) with \(U-L\le1/50\) qualify through their midpoint. An exact determination also qualifies. Any submitted evaluation algorithm must terminate for every valid input and certify its returned value; a mathematical expression is not required to have a prescribed computational complexity. Sampled agreement, an uncertified numerical optimizer, a one-sided achievable or converse bound, and a renaming of the defining supremum or an unevaluated limiting characterization do not suffice. Resolving whether one particular inner bound is exact is not by itself the requested function, and an impossibility result for a different evaluation task does not replace this answer.

title: Li–Li conjecture
summary: An undirected network carries independent messages, each from one source to one destination, with a common capacity budget for both directions of every edge. The Li–Li conjecture asks whether arbitrary causal zero-error network coding has exactly the same closed rate region as optimal fractional multicommodity routing. The card fixes independent finite uniform messages, deterministic encoding, exact decoding and the sum of the two whole-transcript entropies on each edge. A complete Lean proof must establish the universal equality or certify a finite coding instance whose supported rate is outside the fractional routing region. Recent restricted topology results and a corrected session-interaction framework leave the general question open, while undirected multicast separations rely on shared messages with multiple receivers.
formal:
For every network instance \(I\) defined below, is
\[\mathcal C(I)=\mathcal R(I)?\]
Here \(\mathcal C(I)\) is the closure of the rate vectors supported by finite deterministic causal zero-error network codes, with an entropy capacity shared between the two directions of every undirected edge. The region \(\mathcal R(I)\) consists of all rates supported by fractional multicommodity routing. The quantification includes every finite network size, every positive rational capacity vector, every finite list of independent unicast sessions, every finite message and symbol alphabet, every causal schedule and every nonlinear local encoding function.
definitions:
Network and sessions. An instance is \(I=(G,c,((s_i,t_i))_{i=1}^k)\). The supply graph \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, connected, simple and undirected, with at least two vertices; an edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices. Each edge \(e\) has a capacity \(c_e\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\). The number of sessions \(k\) is a positive integer, and \(s_i,t_i\in V\) with \(s_i\ne t_i\). Different sessions may share either endpoint, have opposite directions, or have the same ordered endpoint pair. Such sessions still carry independent messages, each required at its own single destination.

Messages and initial knowledge. Choose a nonempty finite alphabet \(A_i\) for each session. The random variables \(M_i\) are independent and uniformly distributed on \(A_i\); singleton alphabets are allowed. Initially, a vertex \(v\) knows exactly the tuple of messages with \(s_i=v\), along with the fixed instance and code. Thus a destination can also know messages of other sessions for which it is itself a source. There is no additional message-dependent initial information and no private or shared random seed. Local computation and storage have no resource bound.

Causal finite code. Before messages are sampled, fix a nonnegative integer \(L\), a schedule \((u_\ell,v_\ell)_{\ell=1}^L\) with \(\{u_\ell,v_\ell\}\in E\), and nonempty finite transmitted-symbol alphabets \(\Sigma_\ell\). At step \(\ell\), the sender \(u_\ell\) sends \(Z_\ell\in\Sigma_\ell\) to \(v_\ell\). Its encoding function is an arbitrary deterministic function of all messages initially at \(u_\ell\) and the tuple of symbols received there at steps strictly less than \(\ell\). Previously sent symbols are already functions of that information. The schedule and alphabets do not depend on the messages; timing and unrecorded silence carry no extra information. For each \(i\), a deterministic decoder at \(t_i\), applied to its initially known messages and all symbols received there, must output \(M_i\) for every tuple in \(\prod_{j=1}^k A_j\). This is exact recovery with zero error. Linear encoding is not required.

Entropy and supported rates. All probabilities come from the uniform product distribution of the messages. For a finite random variable \(Z\), write
\[H(Z)=-\sum_{z:\Pr[Z=z]>0}\Pr[Z=z]\log_2\Pr[Z=z].\]
Entropy is measured in bits, so \(H(M_i)=\log_2|A_i|\). For each orientation \(u\to v\) of an edge, let \(X_{u\to v}\) be the ordered tuple of all symbols sent in that direction during the whole schedule; the empty tuple has entropy zero. For a real scale \(b>0\), a code supports \(r\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^k\) if
\[H(M_i)\ge b r_i\quad(1\le i\le k),\qquad H(X_{u\to v})+H(X_{v\to u})\le b c_{\{u,v\}}\quad(\{u,v\}\in E).\]
Each directional transcript is measured jointly across its uses, and the two directional entropies are then added. This is not the entropy of their combined bidirectional tuple, nor a separate full-capacity allowance in each direction. The positive scale normalizes messages and edge budgets together. It may depend on the code and need not be an integer. No bound on the schedule length or on the alphabets is imposed in terms of this scale.

Coding region. Let \(\mathcal C_0(I)\) be the set of supported rate vectors over all such finite codes, alphabets and positive scales, and let \(\mathcal C(I)=\overline{\mathcal C_0(I)}\) in the ordinary topology of \(\mathbb R^k\). Explicitly, \(r\in\mathcal C(I)\) means \(r\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^k\) and, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is \(r'\in\mathcal C_0(I)\) with \(\max_i|r_i-r'_i|<\varepsilon\). The closure allows limiting rates; it does not allow decoding errors. This card fixes the inherited entropy-capacity model. Equivalence with a fixed-length bit-budget or vanishing-error definition is not assumed.

Routing region. Let \(\mathcal P_i\) be the finite set of simple paths from \(s_i\) to \(t_i\) in \(G\). A vector \(r\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^k\) belongs to \(\mathcal R(I)\) exactly when there are real numbers \(f_{i,P}\ge0\), one for every \(i\) and \(P\in\mathcal P_i\), such that
\[\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_i}f_{i,P}\ge r_i\quad(1\le i\le k),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{\substack{P\in\mathcal P_i\\e\in P}}f_{i,P}\le c_e\quad(e\in E).\]
A unit of flow consumes one unit of capacity on every edge of its path, regardless of the traversal direction. Each commodity may split among arbitrarily many of these paths. Flows need not be integral. The region is a closed bounded polytope, since the graph, path lists and capacities are finite and every source differs from its destination. Multicast delivery of one common message to several receivers and recovery of functions instead of messages are different tasks.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal equality or its negation. An affirmative proof must cover all the specified instances, independent finite messages, deterministic causal nonlinear codes and positive scales, and must justify passage to the closure. The familiar inclusion \(\mathcal R(I)\subseteq\mathcal C(I)\) is also part of the checked equality; the substantive conjecture is the reverse inclusion.

A negative answer may give one finite instance, a finite code, a positive scale and a supported rate vector outside \(\mathcal R(I)\). The checked proof must establish every encoder's causality, exact decoding on every message tuple, the transcript-entropy capacity inequalities, and infeasibility of the fractional routing constraints at that rate. This finite-code form loses no possible counterexample: a point of the coding closure outside the closed routing region has a neighborhood disjoint from that region and hence contains a supported finite-code rate.

Beating a particular routing algorithm, integral paths, or a cut bound does not establish a separation from the optimal fractional region. A result for directed edges, correlated messages or multicast does not refute this statement. An impossibility result only for linear encoders does not prove it. Any use of a different error or capacity convention requires a checked implication to the model above. There is no additive numerical tolerance on this exact yes-or-no equality.

title: Capacity of the general two-user interference channel
summary: Two independent senders communicate with their own receivers through one interfering channel. Each sender knows only its own message and receives no feedback. The capacity region contains the asymptotically reliable pairs of rates under average block error. Its weighted upper support values describe the entire tradeoff in bits per joint channel use. The benchmark asks for these values on every finite channel with a Lean-certified absolute error at most 0.01.
formal: Determine \[F_{\mathrm{IC}}(W,\lambda)=\sup_{(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal C_{\mathrm{IC}}(W)}\bigl(\lambda R_1+(1-\lambda)R_2\bigr)\] for every finite-alphabet discrete memoryless two-user interference channel \(W\) and every \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), with independent private messages and no feedback.
definitions: A channel has nonempty finite alphabets \(\mathcal X_1,\mathcal X_2,\mathcal Y_1,\mathcal Y_2\) and arbitrary real probabilities \(W(y_1,y_2\mid x_1,x_2)\ge0\), summing to one over outputs for each input pair. Conditional on input sequences, an \(n\)-use output sequence has law \(\prod_{t=1}^n W(y_{1,t},y_{2,t}\mid x_{1,t},x_{2,t})\). Messages \(M_1,M_2\) are independent and uniform on \([K_{1,n}]\) and \([K_{2,n}]\), where \([K]=\{1,\ldots,K\}\) and message counts are positive integers. Encoder \(i\) is a deterministic map \([K_{i,n}]\to\mathcal X_i^n\); its decoder is a deterministic map \(\mathcal Y_i^n\to[K_{i,n}]\). Error means at least one incorrectly decoded message, averaged over both messages and channel randomness. A pair \((R_1,R_2)\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^2\) is achievable if there are codes with block lengths \(n_j\to\infty\), error tending to zero, and \(\liminf_{j\to\infty}n_j^{-1}\log_2K_{i,n_j}\ge R_i\) for both users. The capacity region \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{IC}}(W)\) is the closure of these achievable pairs. The channel and both codebooks are known to all terminals. There is no common message, feedback, terminal cooperation, input cost or computational bound. Predetermined time sharing is allowed. The region is compact, convex and downward closed, so all its nonnegative upper supporting values determine it. The function is measured in weighted bits per joint channel use. Channel laws and weights are mathematical real objects; no finite-precision input or algorithmic evaluation model is imposed.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function \(g(W,\lambda)\) on the entire stated domain and a Lean proof of \(|g(W,\lambda)-F_{\mathrm{IC}}(W,\lambda)|\le1/100\) for every channel and weight. The proof must control both sides of the error; exact determination also qualifies. The guarantee concerns the support value in bits per joint use, with the coding model unchanged. Sample values, a plot or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit are insufficient. No prescribed formula syntax or polynomial evaluation-time bound is required.

title: Binary codes beyond the Gilbert–Varshamov bound
summary: Binary error-correcting codes store information in words whose pairwise Hamming distances are large. The Gilbert–Varshamov bound guarantees a familiar asymptotic rate at each fixed relative distance. This question asks whether some fixed distance permits a fixed positive rate improvement for unbounded block lengths. Codes may be nonlinear and need not have an efficient construction or decoding algorithm. Known finite-length gains and recent explicit-construction or upper-bound papers do not settle that constant-gap existence question.
formal:
Do binary error-correcting codes have an asymptotic rate strictly above the Gilbert–Varshamov bound at some fixed positive relative Hamming distance?

Precisely, do there exist real constants \(0<\delta<1/2\) and \(\eta>0\) such that for every integer \(N\ge1\) there are an integer \(n\ge N\) and a nonempty code \(C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) satisfying
\[\forall x,y\in C,\quad x\ne y\ \Longrightarrow\ d_H(x,y)\ge\lceil\delta n\rceil,\]
\[\frac{\log_2|C|}{n}\ \ge\ 1-H_2(\delta)+\eta?\]
The constants precede the block length and code. Codes may be nonlinear, and neither an efficient construction nor an efficient decoder is required.
definitions:
A binary word of block length \(n\) is a function from \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) to \(\{0,1\}\). Its Hamming distance from another word is
\[d_H(x,y)=|\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i\ne y_i\}|.\]
A code is a nonempty subset of this finite set of words, with distinct elements counted once. The pairwise distance condition is vacuous for a singleton, which has rate zero and cannot meet the stated positive-rate target. The ceiling \(\lceil\delta n\rceil\) is the least integer at least \(\delta n\); using the real threshold \(\delta n\) is equivalent because distance is integral.

The rate of \(C\) is \(\log_2|C|/n\), measured in information bits per transmitted binary symbol. No assumption that \(|C|\) is a power of two is made. The binary entropy function is
\[H_2(t)=-t\log_2 t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t)\quad(0<t<1),\]
with endpoint values \(H_2(0)=H_2(1)=0\). All logarithms in the statement are base two. The comparison \(1-H_2(\delta)\) is the binary Gilbert–Varshamov asymptotic rate benchmark at relative minimum distance \(\delta\).

For integers \(n\ge1\) and \(0\le d\le n\), define
\[A_2(n,d)=\max\{|C|:\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ d_H(x,y)\ge d\text{ for all distinct }x,y\in C\}.\]
The maximum exists because the cube is finite. Equivalently, the target asks whether
\[\exists\delta\in(0,1/2):\quad R_2^*(\delta)>1-H_2(\delta),\qquad R_2^*(\delta)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)}{n}.\]
Here the limit superior of the bounded sequence \(a_n\) means \(\inf_{N\ge1}\sup_{n\ge N}a_n\). An unbounded sequence of successful lengths suffices; codes need not be supplied at every length. The additive improvement \(\eta\) must remain a fixed positive constant. Letting the distance fraction or the improvement depend on \(n\) does not satisfy the displayed quantifiers.

This is an existence problem over ordinary finite subsets, with no time, space, randomness, encoding or decoding constraint. A linear binary code, meaning a vector subspace over the two-element field, is allowed but not required. Error distance concerns coordinate substitutions; insertions, deletions, erasures and quantum errors define other tasks. The target is a pairwise minimum-distance condition, not a list-decoding radius or the capacity of a channel with independently random errors.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed existence proposition or its full logical negation. A positive answer must establish fixed constants \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\), \(\eta>0\) and suitable binary codes for unbounded lengths, with the stated distance and rate. A negative answer must show that for every such \(\delta\) and every \(\eta>0\), some integer \(N\ge1\) satisfies: every \(n\ge N\) and every eligible binary code of distance at least \(\lceil\delta n\rceil\) has rate strictly less than \(1-H_2(\delta)+\eta\). The universal upper bound must cover nonlinear codes as well as linear ones. A finite-length gain, a gain tending to zero in normalized rate, or a result for a different alphabet or error metric does not establish the positive answer. No algorithmic efficiency is required.

title: Polynomial-length constant-query locally decodable codes
summary: A binary locally decodable code lets a decoder recover any requested message bit from a few bits of a corrupted codeword. The target is a fixed constant number of probes with a fixed positive fraction of arbitrary errors. The stored length may be any fixed polynomial in the message length, and nonlinear encodings are allowed. The question concerns existence, without an extra demand for an efficient uniform construction. A complete Lean-checked answer must establish this family or rule out all such constant-query polynomial-length families.
formal:
Do there exist an integer \(q\ge1\), real constants \(C\ge1\), \(d\ge1\) and \(0<\delta<1/2\), such that for every integer message length \(k\ge1\) there are an integer \(n\) with \(k\le n\le Ck^d\), an injective encoding
\[
 E_k:\{0,1\}^k\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^n,
\]
and randomized local decoders \(D_{k,i}\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), satisfying
\[
 \Pr[D_{k,i}^{\,z}=x_i]\ge\frac23
\]
for every message \(x\in\{0,1\}^k\) and every received word \(z\in\{0,1\}^n\) differing from \(E_k(x)\) in fewer than \(\delta n\) coordinates, while each decoder reads at most \(q\) bits of \(z\) on every execution?
definitions:
Here \(k\) counts message bits and \(n\) counts stored codeword bits. The Hamming distance between two length-\(n\) words is the number of coordinates where they differ. The allowed corruptions are precisely the words at Hamming distance strictly less than \(\delta n\), as in the source definition. In particular the uncorrupted codeword is included. The constants \(q,C,d,\delta\) are fixed before \(k\); they do not depend on the message, requested coordinate, corruption or code length. The blocklength \(n=n(k)\), encoding and decoder descriptions may depend on \(k\). Polynomial blocklength does not require constant rate or a polynomial of any prescribed degree.

This is an existence question in the classical randomized bit-query model. For fixed \(k,n,i,E_k\), a deterministic query procedure is a finite binary decision tree of depth at most \(q\). Each internal node is labelled by a coordinate \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\); the oracle returns the single bit \(z_j\), and this chooses the next child. Each leaf is labelled by the output bit zero or one. A randomized decoder is a probability distribution over such trees, fixed independently of \(x\) and \(z\). This describes adaptive queries: later coordinates may depend on earlier answers. Repeated queries count toward the same bound, and early stopping is allowed. The tree distribution may depend on the requested index and the code, but the only information it learns about the actual received word is through the queried bits.

The probability in the statement is solely over that decoder's private randomness. The guarantee holds separately for every triple \((x,z,i)\); a single random choice need not decode all message coordinates at once. Corruptions may depend on the full encoding and message and are computationally unrestricted, but \(z\) is fixed before the decoder draws its randomness. There is no secret key or randomness shared with the channel. The output is one bit: an erasure symbol, a candidate list or success only averaged over requested indices does not meet the definition.

Encoding linearity, systematic form and local correction of every codeword coordinate are not required. There is no bound on encoding time, decoder computation between queries or description length, and no additional requirement that one efficient uniform program construct the family. The finite decision-tree formulation makes the query resource explicit without granting access to any unqueried received bits. Codes must be available for every message length under one set of constants; a finite catalogue or a query bound growing with \(k\) does not suffice.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of this existence statement, specifying or proving the existence of the encodings and decoders and verifying the common constants, polynomial blocklength, worst-case query bound and all corruption/success quantifiers; or give a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation.

An efficient explicit construction is sufficient but is not required. A negative proof must rule out every fixed query count and every polynomial degree, including nonlinear codes and the unrestricted decoder model. A lower bound only for two or three queries, only for matching-vector constructions, or only for locally correctable codes does not establish that negation. Relaxed, approximate, list or amortized decoding and growing-alphabet symbol queries require a proved conversion meeting the exact binary single-bit requirements. No approximation tolerance applies to the yes/no target.

title: Decidability of unconditional entropy inequalities
summary: The input is one rational linear inequality involving the Shannon entropies of subsets of variables. It must be tested against every joint distribution on arbitrary finite alphabets, with no conditional premises. The question asks whether one algorithm can always halt and decide exact validity, including equality cases. Decidability for restricted inequalities and undecidability for conditional statements concern different problems. A complete Lean-checked answer must provide a total decision procedure or prove undecidability of this precise input language.
formal:
Does one deterministic Turing algorithm exist that always halts and decides the following problem? Its input is an integer \(n\ge1\) and rational coefficients \(a_S\) for the nonempty subsets \(S\subseteq[n]\). It must answer YES exactly when
\[
 \sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq[n]}a_S H(X_S)\ge0
\]
holds for every joint distribution of \(n\) finite-valued discrete random variables. The finite alphabet sizes are unrestricted, and the inequality has no premises or affine constant.
definitions:
Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input gives \(n\) in binary and a finite list of pairs \((S,a_S)\) with distinct nonempty subsets of \([n]\). A subset is encoded as an increasing list of its binary indices, and a coefficient as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Missing subsets have coefficient zero. Zero coefficients and an empty coefficient list are allowed. All delimiters and list lengths are explicitly encoded; malformed inputs may be rejected. This is a finite rational input, with no real-number oracle or distribution description.

For the semantic validity test, independently quantify over every choice of positive integers \(r_1,\ldots,r_n\) and every joint probability mass function
\[
 p:\prod_{i=1}^n\{1,\ldots,r_i\}\longrightarrow[0,1],
 \qquad \sum_x p(x)=1.
\]
The probability values may be arbitrary real numbers. Let \(X_i\) be coordinate \(i\) of a tuple sampled from \(p\). For a nonempty \(S\subseteq[n]\), \(X_S\) is the tuple of coordinates with indices in \(S\), in increasing order. Its marginal mass function \(p_S\) is obtained by summing over the other coordinates. Define Shannon entropy in bits by
\[
 H(X_S)=-\sum_z p_S(z)\log_2 p_S(z),\qquad 0\log_2 0=0.
\]
All these sums are finite. An alphabet size may be one, and zero-probability outcomes are allowed. The integers \(r_i\) are quantified over, not bounded by the input or supplied to the deciding algorithm.

Validity means the displayed non-strict inequality holds for every such distribution. Invalidity means that at least one finite-alphabet distribution gives a strictly negative value. No numerical separation from zero is promised. In particular, valid inequalities can achieve equality, and a total decider must handle those boundary cases.

There are no assumptions of independence, conditional independence, functional dependence, prescribed marginals, bounded support or bounded alphabet size. Coefficients of either sign are allowed. The input expresses one homogeneous linear inequality with right-hand side zero. It does not express an implication with entropy constraints as premises, a Boolean combination of inequalities, a nonzero affine term or a nonlinear function of entropies.

The term entropy inequality here includes all universal linear inequalities in Shannon entropies. It is not restricted to the class often called Shannon-type inequalities, meaning those deducible by nonnegative combinations of the elementary conditional-entropy and conditional-mutual-information inequalities. Deciding membership in that narrower class is a different problem.

A decision algorithm is a single finite deterministic Turing program returning the correct YES or NO answer after finitely many steps on every valid finite encoding, for every input value of \(n\). No polynomial or other prescribed running-time or space bound is requested. Separate procedures for only finitely many values of \(n\), a semidecision procedure that may fail to halt, or an oracle for a noncomputable real quantity do not meet this definition.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked construction of a total decision algorithm and a proof of its termination and exact semantic correctness for every input; or give a complete Lean-checked proof that the set of valid input inequalities is undecidable.

A new valid inequality, a counterexample to one candidate inequality, or an incomplete proof-generation procedure answers only individual instances. A procedure requiring a promised numerical gap, a fixed alphabet bound or a fixed number of variables is insufficient unless a proved effective reduction covers the full unrestricted problem. Undecidability for conditional inequalities or a richer input language does not settle this question without a valid reduction to this exact homogeneous unconditional form. There is no numerical approximation tolerance on the validity decision.

title: Computability of graph Shannon capacity
summary: A graph records which transmitted symbols can be confused. Its Shannon capacity is the limiting number of distinguishable messages per use when arbitrarily long blocks are allowed. The question asks for one terminating algorithm that approximates this quantity to any requested absolute accuracy on every finite graph. Known examples show that fixed finite prefixes and finite-power attainment do not supply a general stopping guarantee. The target concerns computability itself, with no required running-time bound.
formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine A such that, for every finite simple undirected graph G and every integer \(k\ge 1, A\) on input \((G,k)\) halts and outputs integers a and \(b>0\) with \(|a/b- \Theta (G)|\le 2^{- k}\)? No bound on running time is imposed.
definitions: Encode G with vertices \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}, n\ge 0\), by n and its symmetric zero-diagonal \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix; encode k, a and b as signed or unsigned binary integers as appropriate. For \(m\ge 1\), the strong power \(G^{\boxtimes m}\) has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}^{m}\). Distinct tuples x,y are adjacent exactly when, for every coordinate j, either \(x_{j}=y_{j}\) or \(\{x_{j},y_{j}\}\) is an edge of G. An independent set contains no adjacent pair; \(\alpha (H)\) is its maximum cardinality, with \(\alpha\) of the graph with no vertices equal to zero. Define \(\Theta(G)=\sup_{m\ge1}\alpha(G^{\boxtimes m})^{1/m}\). For nonempty G the supremum equals the limit as \(m\to \infty\), and \(1\le \Theta (G)\le n\); set \(\Theta (G)=0\) when \(n=0\). The desired output approximates \(\Theta\) itself, not its logarithm. The same machine must work for all graphs and precision requests, with no oracle or graph-dependent advice. It may use arbitrarily much finite time and memory on each input.
answer_criterion: A positive answer supplies a single algorithm and proves termination and the stated absolute-error bound for every valid graph and precision. A negative answer proves that no such uniform algorithm exists. Hardness of exact independent-set computation, failure of a particular approximation scheme, or failure of any finite power to attain the limit does not by itself answer this computability question.

title: Efficient explicit constant-rate tree codes
summary: A binary tree code assigns output labels to every possible input history as that history unfolds. After two histories first differ, their output suffixes must disagree on a fixed positive fraction of positions. A fixed output alphabet keeps the information rate bounded below by a positive constant. The encoder and decoder must both run in polynomial time. Dittmer and Ostrovsky construct the required encoder over a fixed alphabet, leaving efficient recovery under suffix errors open.

Both \(|\Sigma|\) and the two positive distance parameters must be independent of \(N\). The binary information rate \(1/\log_2|\Sigma|\) is therefore a positive constant. The precise causal and decoding requirements are specified below.

Fix an integer \(q=|\Sigma|\ge2\) and identify \(\Sigma\) with \(\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\), represented by fixed-length binary symbols. Thus an output symbol cannot depend on future input bits. For every \(N\ge1\), \(1\le\ell\le N\), and distinct \(x,y\in\{0,1\}^{\ell}\), let \(j\) be the first input position where \(x_j
e y_j\). The tree-distance requirement is \[ igl|\{t\in\{j,\ldots,\ell\}:C_N(x)_t
e C_N(y)_t\} igr|\ \ge\ \delta(\ell-j+1).\] Divergence is defined using the input histories, even if some output labels coincide. For equal-length \(u,v\in\Sigma^\ell\), \(\ell\ge1\), define suffix distance \[d_{\mathrm{sfx}}(u,v)=\max_{1\le j\le\ell} rac{|\{t\in\{j,\ldots,\ell\}:u_t
e v_t\}|}{\ell-j+1}.\] A decoder receives \(1^N\) and any \(w\in\Sigma^\ell\), \(1\le\ell\le N\), and returns a binary string of length \(\ell\), or a failure symbol. No correctness requirement is imposed outside this promise, but the decoder must still halt within its time bound. The promise bounds errors in every suffix of the received prefix. It is not a bound on total Hamming error alone, which would not separate paths that diverge close to their end. The encoder and decoder are two fixed finite deterministic Turing-machine programs, with constants \(K,k\), each using at most \(K(N+1)^k\) bit steps per invocation on valid inputs. Encoding receives \(1^N\) and the currently available input prefix \(x\), and outputs \(C_N(x)\). The known horizon \(N\) is allowed; the code families for distinct horizons need not agree. All preprocessing, symbol calculations and output writes count toward the time bound, and there is no separately supplied table, advice, random seed, oracle or graph of the exponentially large tree. An existence proof for labels without efficient encoding and decoding does not fulfill the target. A growing alphabet, vanishing distance or decoding guarantee for selected input histories alone is insufficient. A limitation of an additional property not required above does not refute the stated existence claim.

title: Positive-rate binary codes against adversarial deletions
summary: A binary deletion code must identify every transmitted word after an adversary removes an allowed fraction of its bits without revealing their positions. Positive rate means that codebook size grows exponentially along infinitely many block lengths with one fixed positive exponent. The target is the supremum deletion fraction for which such zero-error uniquely decodable code families exist, with no efficiency requirement. The checked bounds run from the square root of two minus one to one half minus ten to the minus fortieth power, and are too far apart to supply the required approximation. An accepted answer must determine this real threshold within 1/100 and prove the accuracy in Lean, without requiring that the supremum be attained.
formal:
Determine the real zero-rate threshold
\[
p^*=\sup\{p\in[0,1]:\operatorname{Ach}(p)\},
\]
where
\[
\operatorname{Ach}(p)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\exists r\in(0,1]\ \forall N\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\exists n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\
\left[n\ge N\ \land\ |C|\ge 2^{rn}\ \land\
\operatorname{Correct}(C,\lfloor pn\rfloor)\right].
\]
Here \(\operatorname{Correct}(C,t)\) means that every codeword in \(C\) can be recovered uniquely, with zero error, after any choice of at most \(t\) deleted positions. Deleted positions are not revealed, and the adversary may know the entire code and transmitted word. The positive rate \(r\) may depend on \(p\), but must remain fixed along the unbounded sequence of block lengths. This is a question about arbitrary code families, with no efficiency, linearity or uniform construction requirement. Benchmark acceptance is absolute error at most \(1/100\) in \(p^*\).
definitions:
A binary word of length \(n\) is a sequence \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\), with each symbol represented by one bit. A code \(C\) is a nonempty subset of these words. It may be represented by its duplicate-free lexicographically ordered list of words; no bound on the size of this representation is imposed. A message can be identified with an integer in \(\{1,\ldots,|C|\}\), encoded as the corresponding word in this list. The information rate, in bits per transmitted bit, is
\[
R(C)=\frac{\log_2|C|}{n}.
\]
Only positive block lengths \(n\ge1\) are used.

A word \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\) is a subsequence of \(x\) if there are indices \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_m\le n\) with \(y_j=x_{i_j}\) for every \(j\). The empty word is a subsequence. No surviving bit is changed or reordered. For \(0\le t\le n\), define the possible received words
\[
\mathcal D_t(x)=
\{y:\ y\text{ is a subsequence of }x,\quad n-t\le |y|\le n\}.
\]
Thus
\[
\operatorname{Correct}(C,t)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\forall x,x'\in C,\quad x\ne x'\Longrightarrow
\mathcal D_t(x)\cap\mathcal D_t(x')=\varnothing.
\]
Equivalently, a deterministic decoder from the binary words of lengths \(0,\ldots,n\) to \(C\cup\{\bot\}\) can satisfy \(D(y)=x\) for every \(x\in C\) and every \(y\in\mathcal D_t(x)\), where \(\bot\) denotes failure on other inputs. The decoder may know \(C,n,t\), but receives no deletion locations. Its computation time and storage are unrestricted. Success is required for every transmitted word and every allowed deletion pattern, rather than with a small average or probabilistic error.

For two words \(x,x'\), their longest-common-subsequence length \(\operatorname{LCS}(x,x')\) is the largest integer \(m\ge0\) for which some length-\(m\) word is a subsequence of both. The correction condition is equivalent to
\[
\forall x\ne x'\in C,\qquad
\operatorname{LCS}(x,x')<n-t.
\]
For \(t=\lfloor pn\rfloor\), this is also equivalent to \(\operatorname{LCS}(x,x')<(1-p)n\), since the LCS length is an integer and \(n-\lfloor pn\rfloor=\lceil(1-p)n\rceil\). This fixes the source's suppressed rounding conventions exactly.

The predicate \(\operatorname{Ach}(p)\) uses infinitely many, equivalently arbitrarily large, block lengths. It does not require a code at every sufficiently large length. The quantified codes may be arbitrary nonlinear subsets and need not be generated by a single algorithm. The model has no shared secret, public key, feedback, random channel, stochastic encoder or list output. It is the information-theoretic unique-decoding model.

The supremum exists as a real number: the achievable set is contained in \([0,1]\) and contains \(0\), witnessed by the full binary codes. Correcting a larger deletion budget implies correcting every smaller one, so achievability is downward closed. The definition does not assert that \(p^*\) itself is achievable, or that one fixed positive rate works for fractions approaching it.
answer_criterion:
Supply a specified real number \(a\), or an unambiguous mathematical expression defining it, and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[
|a-p^*|\le\frac{1}{100}
\]
for the exact model and quantifiers above. The answer need not be an integer or an exactly attained deletion fraction. Merely repeating the supremum that defines \(p^*\) does not determine it.

One sufficient form is a certified interval: supply reals \(0\le l\le u\le1\), prove \(l\le p^*\le u\) and \(u-l\le1/50\), and take \(a=(l+u)/2\). The two bounds can be made fully explicit as follows:
\[
\forall p\in[0,l)\ \exists r\in(0,1]\
\forall N\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\exists n\ge N\ \exists\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\
\left[|C|\ge2^{rn}\land
\operatorname{Correct}(C,\lfloor pn\rfloor)\right],
\]
and
\[
\forall p\in(u,1]\ \forall r>0\
\exists N\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\forall n\ge N\ \forall\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\
\left[\operatorname{Correct}(C,\lfloor pn\rfloor)
\Longrightarrow |C|<2^{rn}\right].
\]
All block-length variables in these statements are integers. The lower statement allows rates and families to depend on \(p\), and the upper statement ranges over every code. Neither requires attainment at an endpoint. The Lean development must establish the stated correction property and its asymptotic quantifiers, not merely verify codes at finitely many lengths.

Exact determination is welcome but is not required. A one-sided estimate, a result for efficient or linear codes alone, a different alphabet, list decoding, or probabilistic deletion errors does not by itself meet this criterion.

title: Do nonlinear binary codes have a strictly better asymptotic rate?
summary: Binary linear codes are vector subspaces, while arbitrary codes can be any sets of binary words. At each fixed relative minimum distance, compare their largest possible asymptotic information rates. The question asks whether arbitrary codes have a strictly higher rate at even one distance between zero and one half. Any fixed positive rate gap counts, but a finite-block advantage or a comparison with one construction does not. The source motivates the comparison through linear-programming hierarchies, and the checked later bound does not resolve it.
formal:
Does there exist a fixed real \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\) such that
\[
R_2(\delta)>R_2^{\mathrm{lin}}(\delta),
\]
where these are the optimal asymptotic rates of arbitrary binary codes and binary linear codes, respectively, at relative minimum Hamming distance \(\delta\), as defined below? Any fixed strictly positive gap qualifies.
definitions:
For integers \(n\ge1\) and \(0\le d\le n\), let
\[
A_2(n,d)=\max\{|C|:\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,
\ \forall x\ne y\in C,\ \Delta(x,y)\ge d\},
\]
where \(\Delta(x,y)=|\{j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_j\ne y_j\}|\). Let \(A_2^{\mathrm{lin}}(n,d)\) be the same maximum restricted to vector subspaces \(C\le\mathbb F_2^n\), where addition is coordinatewise modulo two. The one-word code is allowed, and its pairwise distance condition is vacuous. Both finite maxima are well defined.

For a fixed real \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\), define
\[
R_2(\delta)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 A_2(n,\lfloor\delta n\rfloor)}{n},\qquad
R_2^{\mathrm{lin}}(\delta)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 A_2^{\mathrm{lin}}(n,\lfloor\delta n\rfloor)}{n}.
\]
These bounded-sequence limit superiors are real numbers in \([0,1]\), measured in message bits per transmitted bit. The limsup of \((a_n)\) means \(\inf_{N\ge1}\sup_{n\ge N}a_n\). No assumption that the ordinary limits exist is made. The distance fraction is fixed before taking either limit superior.

All finite codes are eligible regardless of encoding, decoding, description or construction complexity. The arbitrary-code side includes linear codes. The linear side permits every binary subspace and every dimension. Affine translates do not change attainable cardinality and distance, so permitting affine codes on that side gives the same maximum.

A positive answer establishes \(R_2(\delta)\ge R_2^{\mathrm{lin}}(\delta)+\eta\) for some fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\) and \(\eta>0\). Neither constant has a prescribed magnitude. A negative answer proves equality of the two rates for every \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\), since the reverse inequality always follows from inclusion. An isolated finite-block advantage, a subexponential size advantage, or a comparison with one particular linear construction is not sufficient. This is a binary existence question, not a request to approximate the two entire rate curves.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of a fixed relative distance with a strictly positive asymptotic rate gap. A positive result must compare with all binary linear codes, and a negative result must establish equality throughout (0,1/2). No minimum improvement such as 1/100 is imposed.

title: Effective classification of polynomially testable hereditary graph properties
summary: A finite family of forbidden induced graphs specifies a hereditary graph property. The question asks whether a total algorithm can decide from that family whether its canonical one-sided test has polynomial reciprocal-distance sample complexity. Every query is an adjacency check, while rejection must exhibit a forbidden pattern with both its edges and its nonedges. Known structural conditions and quantitative container equivalences do not give the total finite-input classifier required by this card. Algorithmic decidability is the inherited editorial specification, and its status is uncertain rather than attributed verbatim as a conjecture of the structural survey.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine that, on input a finite list \(\mathcal F\) of finite simple graphs, always halts and correctly decides whether \(\mathcal F\) has the polynomial sampling property below? The input is the finite list of forbidden induced patterns. No running-time bound is imposed on this classification algorithm. The constants in the sampling property may depend on the whole fixed list, but must hold simultaneously at every graph order and proximity parameter.
definitions: A finite simple graph is an undirected graph with no loops or multiple edges. Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A valid input list \(\mathcal F=(F_1,\ldots,F_r)\), \(r\ge0\), is encoded by the orders and full Boolean adjacency matrices of its members on \([|V(F_i)|]\); the matrices are symmetric with zero diagonal. Integer orders and list lengths are binary encoded with delimiters. Repeated graphs and the graph of order zero are allowed. For \(n\ge1\), let \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}\) consist of all graphs on \([n]\) with no induced copy of any \(F_i\). An induced copy of \(F_i\) is an injection \(\phi:V(F_i)\to[n]\) such that for every distinct \(u,v\), \(\{u,v\}\in E(F_i)\) if and only if \(\{\phi(u),\phi(v)\}\in E(G)\). For a graph \(G\) on \([n]\), define \[d_{\mathcal F}(G)=\frac{1}{n^2}\min_{H\in\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}}|E(G)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)|\] when the set is nonempty, and \(d_{\mathcal F}(G)=+\infty\) otherwise. Symmetric difference counts each added or deleted undirected edge once. A graph is \(\varepsilon\)-far if \(d_{\mathcal F}(G)>\varepsilon\), with strict inequality. For an integer \(s\ge1\), the canonical sampling test chooses a uniformly random subset \(S\subseteq[n]\) of size \(\min\{n,s\}\), queries all \(\binom{|S|}{2}\) adjacency bits within it, and rejects exactly when \(G[S]\) contains an induced member of \(\mathcal F\). Local sampling and finite pattern checking are not charged as adjacency queries. The polynomial sampling property means that there exist integers \(C,a\ge1\) such that for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), every \(n\ge1\), and every \(\varepsilon\)-far graph \(G\), this test with \(s=\lceil C\varepsilon^{-a}\rceil\) rejects with probability at least \(2/3\). Probability is solely over the uniform subset. For every member of \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}\), the test accepts with probability one. There is no extra promise on the host graph. The empty forbidden list defines all graphs; if the list contains the order-zero graph, every test rejects since the empty induced copy exists in every sample. These conventions also specify empty property classes at individual orders. The classifier takes only \(\mathcal F\), not \(n,\varepsilon,C\) or \(a\), and need not output the constants. It is one finite program with no advice or oracle, required to output YES exactly for lists with the sampling property and NO for all other valid lists. It may reject malformed encodings; it must halt on every input string.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that such a total classifier exists, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such classifier exists. The affirmative answer must establish termination and both directions of correctness on every finite forbidden list. The negative answer must rule out every deterministic Turing program as a total correct classifier. An equivalent condition that still quantifies over unbounded host graphs and all accuracy parameters is not by itself a decision algorithm. Proving polynomial testability for one family or a finite collection of families does not meet the universal classification target.

title: Polynomial testability versus distance estimation
summary: A dense-graph tester distinguishes membership in a property from graphs that require many edge changes to satisfy it. A distance estimator must approximate that repair cost on every input, including graphs close to the property. The question asks whether a query bound polynomial in reciprocal accuracy for testing always entails a polynomial bound for estimation. The algorithms may use unlimited local computation, but must be uniform and obey query bounds independent of graph order. Known general conversions and positive special cases leave the polynomial-preservation target unresolved in the checked sources, and the stronger source question remains separately recorded.
formal: Is every polynomially testable property of finite simple graphs also polynomially estimable in the dense graph model? Precisely, for every graph property \(\mathcal P=(\mathcal P_n)_{n\ge1}\) satisfying the definitions below, does existence of a uniform randomized tester and integers \(C,a\ge1\) with worst-case adjacency-query bound \(Ct^a\) imply existence of a uniform randomized distance estimator and integers \(D,b\ge1\) with bound \(Dt^b\)? The guarantees must hold for every graph order \(n\), every integer \(t\ge2\), and every input graph, with proximity and additive accuracy \(\varepsilon=1/t\). Programs and polynomial constants may depend on \(\mathcal P\), but not on \(n,t\) or the input graph.
definitions: A finite simple graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is an undirected graph whose edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. For each integer \(n\ge1\), \(\mathcal P_n\) is a nonempty collection of these graphs invariant under every permutation of \([n]\). No closure under vertex or edge deletion is assumed. For \(n\ge2\), define \[d(G,\mathcal P_n)=\frac{1}{\binom n2}\min_{H\in\mathcal P_n}|E(G)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)|.\] Here \(E(G)\) is the edge set and symmetric difference \(\triangle\) counts each added or deleted edge once. Set \(d(G,\mathcal P_1)=0\). The minimum exists because \(\mathcal P_n\) is nonempty and finite. Distance lies in \([0,1]\); it is normalized by all possible unordered pairs, not by the number of present edges. A tester receives \(n,t\) in binary and can query whether any chosen pair of distinct vertices is an edge. Queries may depend on previous answers and independent fair random bits. It accepts each \(G\in\mathcal P_n\) with probability at least \(2/3\) and rejects each \(G\) with \(d(G,\mathcal P_n)\ge1/t\) with probability at least \(2/3\). Either answer is permitted when \(0<d(G,\mathcal P_n)<1/t\). An estimator has the same input and oracle access and outputs a binary-encoded rational number \(z\) such that \[\Pr\bigl[|z-d(G,\mathcal P_n)|\le1/t\bigr]\ge2/3\] on every graph, with no distance promise. Each algorithm is one finite probabilistic Turing oracle program with no advice or additional oracle. It must terminate on every execution. Local computation, storage and output length have no quantitative bound; the charged resource is the total number of adjacency queries, bounded on every input and every random execution. Each probability is over the program's random bits for the fixed input graph. The algorithm does not receive a description of \(\mathcal P\): its fixed program may depend on that property. The implication asks for existence of the estimator, not a uniform meta-algorithm taking a tester's code as input.
