Accuracy is required at every reciprocal integer; this discretization fixes the parameter encoding without imposing a graph-size-dependent bound.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated universal implication or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must provide the full estimator guarantees whenever the tester hypothesis holds. A negative proof must establish a property with a polynomial-query tester for which every uniform estimator fails every fixed polynomial query bound under the same model. A separation between particular algorithms, or a conversion with exponential rather than polynomial query overhead, is insufficient. This is a yes/no question about algorithms at arbitrarily small accuracy, not a request for one distance estimate at the numerical benchmark tolerance.

title: Sharp graph-removal bounds for fixed patterns
summary: For each fixed connected graph pattern, the question asks how few ordinary copies a graph can contain while still being far from avoiding that pattern. Distance is the fraction of adjacency-matrix entries that must change, and each vertex subset supporting the pattern is counted once. The target is matching constant-factor bounds in both the graph order and the proximity parameter, with constants allowed to depend on the pattern. The removal lemma guarantees positive density at every fixed distance, but the general quantitative bounds remain widely separated. Sharp bounds would quantify the worst-case visibility of local violations and the sampling cost of detecting them.
formal: Determine the asymptotic order of the extremal copy-count function \(M_H(\varepsilon,n)\) defined below, for every fixed connected finite simple graph \(H\) with at least two edges. Both the proximity parameter \(\varepsilon\) and the graph order \(n\) vary. The requested precision is matching upper and lower bounds up to multiplicative constants depending only on \(H\), uniformly over all feasible pairs \((\varepsilon,n)\). Thus the answer must specify bounds \(B_H(\varepsilon,n)>0\) and prove that, for each such \(H\), there are constants \(0<c_H\le C_H<\infty\) such that \[c_H B_H(\varepsilon,n)\le M_H(\varepsilon,n)\le C_H B_H(\varepsilon,n)\] for every feasible pair. The copies are ordinary subgraphs, with extra edges allowed.
definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(t=|V(H)|\). All graphs are undirected and have neither loops nor multiple edges. A graph is \(H\)-free if there is no injective map \(\phi:V(H)\to V(G)\) taking every edge of \(H\) to an edge of \(G\); nonedges of \(H\) impose no restriction. Let \(r_H(G)\) be the least number of edges that must be deleted from \(G\) to make it \(H\)-free. Allowing edge additions as well cannot decrease this minimum. Use the source's adjacency-matrix distance \(d_H(G)=2r_H(G)/n^{2}\): each changed undirected edge changes two matrix entries. Say that \(G\) is \(\varepsilon\)-far when \(d_H(G)>\varepsilon\), with a strict inequality. Define \(N_H(G)\) to be the number of \(t\)-element subsets \(S\subseteq[n]\) for which \(G[S]\) contains an ordinary copy of \(H\), counting each such subset once even if it supports several embeddings. This fixes the copy convention suggested by the source's random-subset test; counting injective labelled embeddings instead changes the count by factors between one and \(t!\). A feasible pair is a rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and an integer \(n\ge t\) for which at least one graph on \([n]\) has \(d_H(G)>\varepsilon\). On precisely this domain, set \[M_H(\varepsilon,n)=\min\{N_H(G):V(G)=[n],\ d_H(G)>\varepsilon\}.\] The minimum is over a nonempty finite set, so it is a positive integer. No value is requested for an infeasible pair. The constants in the matching bounds may depend on the whole fixed pattern \(H\), but not on \(n\) or \(\varepsilon\); in particular, \(\varepsilon\) may decrease with \(n\). The target is the growth of this extremal function, not the running time of enumerating graphs. No extra minimum-degree, regularity, randomness or sparsity promise is imposed on \(G\).
answer_criterion: Supply the matching asymptotic bounds in the formal statement and a complete Lean-checked proof of both inequalities for every permitted pattern and feasible parameter pair. The lower inequality must hold for every graph at the stated distance, and the upper inequality must establish existence of graphs with the claimed copy count. Merely restating the defining minimization, tabulating finitely many values, giving one-sided bounds, or establishing only that some positive removal bound exists does not meet this growth target. The precision here is a multiplicative constant factor depending only on the pattern, not additive \(1/100\) accuracy on a normalized copy density.

title: Polynomial-query submodularity testing
summary: Submodularity expresses diminishing returns for a real-valued function on all subsets of a finite ground set. The question asks whether a polynomial number of exact value queries can test this property with one-sided error. Distance is the fraction of table entries that must change to obtain a submodular function, regardless of change magnitude. Known general upper and lower bounds leave the polynomial-query question unresolved, and constant-query norm-distance results concern a different task. A resolution would determine how efficiently an oracle’s global diminishing-returns structure can be checked from limited access.
formal: Is there a uniform randomized one-sided-error tester for submodularity of arbitrary real-valued set functions using a number of value queries polynomial in the dimension and reciprocal distance? Precisely, do there exist one tester \(A\) in the model below and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), and every function \(f:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\), the algorithm \(A^{f}(n,\varepsilon)\) halts and makes at most \(C((n+1)/\varepsilon)^{k}\) value queries on every execution, accepts with probability one if \(f\) is submodular, and rejects with probability at least \(2/3\) if \(d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)\ge\varepsilon\)? The constants and program must work simultaneously for all parameters and functions.
definitions: Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(2^{[n]}\) is its set of all subsets, represented by their \(n\)-bit indicator vectors. The class \(\mathcal S_n\) consists of all functions \(g:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \[g(S)+g(T)\ge g(S\cap T)+g(S\cup T)\qquad(S,T\subseteq[n]).\] The distance is normalized Hamming distance on the full domain: \[d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)=\min_{g\in\mathcal S_n}2^{-n}\bigl|\{S\subseteq[n]:f(S)\ne g(S)\}\bigr|.\] This minimum exists because attainable disagreement counts form a nonempty subset of the finite set \(\{0,\ldots,2^n\}\). It measures how many table entries change, regardless of the magnitudes of the changes. There is no promise of monotonicity, nonnegativity, bounded range, integrality or normalization at the empty set. The input supplies \(n\) in binary and \(\varepsilon\) as a ratio of positive binary integers; the full value table is accessible only through queries. One value query chooses a subset \(S\) and returns the exact real number \(f(S)\), at cost one. Queries may depend on earlier answers and random bits. To specify computation on these exact values, use a finite program with integer and bit-string work storage, real registers initialized by rational constants, exact real addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by nonzero values, and exact order/equality comparisons. Division by zero is forbidden. The program can request independent fair random bits and can copy queried real values into registers. There is no real-valued advice, noncomputable primitive or other oracle. Only value queries are charged; intervening computation and storage have no quantitative bound, but every execution must terminate after finitely many steps. Acceptance probabilities are over the independent random bits, for each fixed input function. Behavior is unrestricted when \(0<d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)<\varepsilon\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of a tester with every guarantee in the formal statement, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A positive answer must cover arbitrary real-valued functions and all dimensions and proximity parameters with one finite program and fixed polynomial constants. A negative answer must exclude every such program and every fixed choice of polynomial constants, not only a particular local tester. A result for average value error, a restricted value range, a monotonicity promise, or a constant-dimensional grid does not settle this target.

title: Planar graphs from local neighborhoods
summary: The question compares two planar graphs through the rooted neighborhoods around all their vertices. It asks whether a radius depending only on the allowed error makes identical neighborhood multisets imply closeness under edge edits and vertex relabeling. No maximum-degree bound is imposed, so even a small-radius neighborhood may be large. The source proves the analogous result for outerplanar graphs, while bounded-degree planar theorems allow the radius to depend on the degree bound. This specific structural question replaces the original broad classification target by an explicitly selected yes/no assertion.
formal: For every real \(\varepsilon>0\), does there exist a positive integer \(D=D(\varepsilon)\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every pair of finite simple planar graphs \(G,H\) on \(n\) vertices, equality of their multisets of rooted radius-\(D\) neighborhoods implies \[\min_{\phi:V(G)\cong V(H)}\left|\phi(E(G))\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)\right|\le\varepsilon n?\] The minimum is over all vertex bijections, and \(\triangle\) denotes symmetric difference of edge sets. There is no maximum-degree bound; the radius may depend only on \(\varepsilon\).
definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph is a finite vertex set \(V\) and a set \(E\) of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Thus loops and multiple edges are excluded. A planar graph admits a drawing in the plane with distinct points for vertices and curves for edges whose interiors neither intersect one another nor meet a vertex. A drawing is not part of the data, and it is not used to compare neighborhoods. Graphs need not be connected. Their order is \(n=|V|\), and the two graphs in the question have the same order.

The graph distance \(\operatorname{dist}_G(u,v)\) is the minimum number of edges in a path from \(u\) to \(v\), with distance infinity when no path exists. The rooted radius-\(D\) neighborhood \(B_G(v,D)\) is the subgraph induced by \(\{u\in V(G):\operatorname{dist}_G(u,v)\le D\}\), together with the distinguished root \(v\). An induced subgraph retains every edge whose two endpoints belong to that set. Rooted graphs are isomorphic when a bijection of their vertices preserves edges and sends one root to the other. Vertex labels, the planar drawing, any ordering of neighbors, and edges leaving the neighborhood are not part of its rooted isomorphism type.

The multiset of radius-\(D\) neighborhoods records each rooted isomorphism type with its multiplicity among the \(n\) possible roots. Equality means that, for every finite rooted graph \(F\), the number of vertices \(v\) for which \(B_G(v,D)\) is isomorphic to \(F\) equals the corresponding number in \(H\). Thus multiplicities matter. Although corresponding roots can be paired, their individual neighborhood isomorphisms need not agree on overlapping vertices. In particular, such a pairing is not already a global graph isomorphism. Even a radius-one neighborhood may contain arbitrarily many vertices, because degrees are unrestricted.

For a vertex bijection \(\phi:V(G)\to V(H)\), define \(\phi(E(G))=\{\{\phi(u),\phi(v)\}:\{u,v\}\in E(G)\}\). The symmetric difference consists of edges in exactly one of its two arguments. Its cardinality counts edge deletions plus edge additions, each at unit cost, after a free relabeling of vertices. Taking the minimum over bijections gives the edit distance to isomorphism. There are no vertex edits or isolated-vertex padding in this equal-order question. Intermediate graphs during edge editing are not required to be planar. The permitted number of edits is at most \(\varepsilon n\), normalized by vertex count rather than by the number of possible edges or by a degree bound. For \(n=1\) the conclusion is automatic. No algorithm for finding the bijection, a computable bound on \(D\), or property-testing oracle is requested; this is a structural existence statement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal statement, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: there exists a fixed \(\varepsilon_0>0\) such that for every positive integer \(D\), there are some \(n\ge1\) and simple planar \(n\)-vertex graphs \(G,H\) with identical radius-\(D\) neighborhood multisets but edit distance strictly greater than \(\varepsilon_0 n\). The counterexample graphs and their orders may depend on \(D\); the same positive \(\varepsilon_0\) must work throughout. A proof restricted to bounded maximum degree or to outerplanar graphs does not establish the assertion for all planar graphs. Equality of the set of neighborhood types without multiplicities is a different hypothesis. A radius growing with \(n\) or maximum degree is insufficient. This is an exact yes/no implication, not a numerical approximation problem.

title: Sublinear testing of bounded-degree graph isomorphism
summary: The tester sees two bounded-degree graphs by asking for individual neighbors. It must accept isomorphic pairs and reject pairs far apart under every relabelling. Can it do so after inspecting a vanishing fraction of the input? Dror proved in 2026 that some targets require linearly many queries even when the tester already knows one of the graphs. An algorithm for two unknown graphs would also work with that known target, so the answer is no.
formal:
Can isomorphism between two arbitrary bounded-degree graphs be tested with a sublinear number of adjacency-list queries? Precisely, does there exist a uniform randomized tester \(A\), with explicit inputs \(n\ge1\), a degree bound \(d\ge1\), and an integer \(q\ge2\), satisfying the following guarantees for every pair of allowed \(n\)-vertex input graphs \(G_1,G_2\)?
\[G_1\cong G_2\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[A\text{ accepts}]\ge2/3,\]
\[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{iso}}(G_1,G_2)\ge1/q\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[A\text{ rejects}]\ge2/3.\]
For each fixed \(d,q\), its worst-case query bound \(Q(n,d,q)\) must satisfy
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{Q(n,d,q)}n=0.\]
Both graphs are given only through oracles. The graph model, distance and query accounting are specified below.
definitions:
The graphs \(G_i=([n],E_i)\), where \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), are undirected and simple, with maximum degree at most \(d\). Disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed. There is no expansion, hyperfiniteness, component-size or randomness promise on their structure.

Graph \(G_i\) is represented by an incidence oracle \(g_i:[n]\times[d]\to[n]\cup\{\bot\}\). Its first \(\deg_{G_i}(v)\) entries at vertex \(v\) list the distinct neighbors of \(v\) in an arbitrary fixed order, and the remaining entries are \(\bot\). The oracles are promised consistent with undirected simple graphs. One adjacency query chooses \(i\in\{1,2\}\), \(v\in[n]\), and \(j\in[d]\), and receives \(g_i(v,j)\). Queries may depend on earlier answers. Correctness must hold for every permitted neighbor ordering.

For a permutation \(\sigma\) of \([n]\), put \(\sigma(E_2)=\{\{\sigma(u),\sigma(v)\}:\{u,v\}\in E_2\}\). Define
\[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{iso}}(G_1,G_2)=\frac1{dn}\min_{\sigma\in S_n}|E_1\mathbin{\triangle}\sigma(E_2)|,\]
where \(S_n\) is the set of all permutations and \(\triangle\) denotes symmetric difference. Each deleted or added undirected edge counts once. Thus distance zero means graph isomorphism, and the rejection promise means at least \(dn/q\) edge edits are needed after the best vertex relabelling. Neighbor-list positions do not affect this distance. For nonisomorphic pairs at distance strictly below \(1/q\), either output is allowed.

The tester is a probabilistic oracle Turing algorithm given binary \(n,d,q\), access to both incidence oracles, independent fair random bits and a primitive returning an independent uniformly sampled vertex label in \([n]\). Count every incidence-oracle call and every such vertex-sampling call as one query. All other finite local computation is unrestricted, and the tester must halt. The bound \(Q(n,d,q)\) holds on every allowed pair, every representation and every sequence of random outcomes. Success probabilities include all internal randomness and vertex samples. No graph-dependent advice or full description of either graph is provided; any preprocessing uses only \(n,d,q\).

The degree and reciprocal proximity are fixed when taking the sublinear limit. There is no requirement for one bound uniform in growing \(d\) or \(q\), and no polynomial runtime requirement beyond the query guarantee. Using reciprocal integer accuracies covers all fixed positive proximities by choosing a smaller reciprocal threshold. The edge-edit normalization follows the saved card; the source also uses a convention with a factor of two in the edge threshold. That constant rescaling does not change the all-fixed-proximities existence question.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of a tester with the stated correctness, access and sublinear-query guarantees, or a Lean-checked refutation of that existence statement. A positive answer must cover every pair of bounded-degree input graphs and every fixed proximity, with two-sided error at most \(1/3\). A near-linear bound that is not \(o(n)\), a guarantee for almost all graphs, a known-target tester, or a result only for small connected components is insufficient. A lower bound of order \(n^{2/3}\) up to logarithmic factors alone does not rule out sublinear testing.

title: Polynomial-query adaptive tolerant monotonicity testing
summary: A monotone Boolean function never decreases when input coordinates increase. A tolerant tester must accept functions close to monotone, not just exactly monotone ones. The question asks whether adaptive tests need only polynomially many value queries for every fixed tolerance gap. Both thresholds are positive constants and the input distribution defining distance is uniform. Nonadaptive lower bounds do not automatically refute this assertion.
formal: For every pair of fixed rational constants \(0<a<b\le1/2\), do there exist constants \(C_{a,b}>0\) and \(q_{a,b}\in\mathbb N_0\) such that \[Q(n;a,b)\le C_{a,b}(n+1)^{q_{a,b}}\qquad\text{for every }n\ge1?\] Here \(Q(n;a,b)\) is the randomized adaptive value-query complexity, defined below, of accepting Boolean functions at uniform distance at most \(a\) from monotonicity and rejecting those at distance at least \(b\), with success probability at least \(2/3\). Computation between queries is unrestricted.
definitions:
The domain \(\{0,1\}^n\) has the coordinatewise partial order: \(x\le y\) if \(x_i\le y_i\) for all \(i\). A function \(g:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) is monotone if \(g(x)\le g(y)\) whenever \(x\le y\). For arbitrary \(f\), define \[\operatorname{dist}(f,\mathrm{MON}_n)=\min_{g\in\mathrm{MON}_n}2^{-n}|\{x:f(x)\ne g(x)\}|.\] The input function is unknown and is accessed by exact value queries at chosen vertices. Query locations may depend on all previous answers and internal randomness. Arbitrary computation between queries is free.

A tester must accept every function of distance at most \(a\) with probability at least \(2/3\), and reject every function of distance at least \(b\) with probability at least \(2/3\). No guarantee is imposed for distances strictly between the thresholds. Both types of errors are allowed. \(Q(n;a,b)\) is the smallest worst-case number of queries of any randomized decision tree satisfying these guarantees for all input functions. Probability is only over that tree's internal randomness. Repeated queries count as queries, and there is no free labelled sampling oracle; uniformly chosen test points can of course be queried. An entire truth-table query budget of \(2^n\) always makes the quantity finite.

The requested asymptotics take \(n\to\infty\) with \(a,b\) fixed; upper and lower multiplicative constants may depend on these thresholds. Since either the constant-zero or constant-one function differs from \(f\) on at most half the domain, every distance is at most \(1/2\). Therefore \(Q(n;a,b)=0\) when \(b>1/2\); those formal parameter pairs are trivial. The substantive regime has \(b\le1/2\).

A nonadaptive tester chooses all queried points before receiving any answers. A lower bound restricted to such testers does not automatically apply to the adaptive trees defining this card. Ordinary monotonicity testing is the separate case where the acceptance threshold is zero; tolerance here requires accepting all functions within positive distance \(a\).
answer_criterion: For each fixed tolerance pair \(a,b\), prove in Lean a polynomial adaptive query bound for the two promised classes at success probability \(2/3\), or exhibit one fixed pair for which every polynomial query bound fails.

title: Efficient black-box testing of high-dimensional convexity
summary: A membership oracle hides a set in high-dimensional Euclidean space. The tester must distinguish a convex set from one a fixed Gaussian distance away from every convex set. The card permits adaptive queries and two-sided error, measuring only the number of membership answers. Known lower bounds distinguish this model from tolerant or one-sided testing. The target asks whether convexity can be recognized from polynomially much black-box information.
formal: For each fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), is there a randomized adaptive membership-query tester that, for every dimension \(n\) and every Borel set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), distinguishes convexity from Gaussian distance at least \(\varepsilon\) to every convex set using at most \(C_\varepsilon n^{c_\varepsilon}\) queries and with error probability at most \(1/3\) on each promised input? This is ordinary two-sided testing, not tolerant testing.
definitions:
The standard Gaussian measure \(\gamma_n\) has density \((2\pi)^{-n/2}\exp(-\|x\|_2^2/2)\) on \(\mathbb R^n\). A set \(K\) is convex if \((1-t)x+ty\in K\) for every \(x,y\in K\) and \(t\in[0,1]\). Its distance from \(S\) is the Gaussian measure of the symmetric difference, \(\gamma_n(S\triangle K)\). Define distance to convexity as the infimum of this quantity over Borel convex sets \(K\), including the empty set and all of \(\mathbb R^n\).

An oracle returns the exact bit \(1_S(x)\) for a requested point \(x\). Queries can be chosen adaptively. The query model is an information model over exact real points: a randomized decision tree may choose points by measurable functions of its internal randomness and previous answer bits, with arbitrary measurable computation free. Independent Gaussian random points can be generated internally, but obtaining their membership labels costs queries. There is no oracle supplying samples conditioned on membership in \(S\), a boundary, a separation hyperplane or a finite description of the set.

The tester must accept every convex input with probability at least \(2/3\), and reject every input whose distance to convexity is at least \(\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(2/3\). Either output is allowed in the gap. Success probability is over its internal randomness on each fixed oracle, and the query bound is worst-case over oracles and random choices. Both false acceptance and false rejection are permitted. Constants and the polynomial degree may depend on the fixed accuracy but not on dimension or the set. This is an oracle-query claim, not a polynomial bound on finite-precision arithmetic or point representation.

Restricting to Borel inputs makes all measures and probabilities defined; the source's arbitrary measurable-set formulation is interpreted with this regularity convention. A tolerant tester would also have to accept nonconvex sets close to convexity. That additional promise is not required here.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked affirmative proof of a family of testers with the stated polynomial query bounds for every fixed accuracy, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A refutation must exclude adaptive two-sided testers, not only one-sided or nonadaptive procedures. A sample-only lower bound or a tolerant-testing lower bound is insufficient. A theorem about query count alone need not prove a comparable bound on all arithmetic operations.

title: Linear-query lower bound for sparse binary matrix rank estimation
summary: The matrix is binary and has bounded numbers of ones in each row and column. One query reveals the complete nonzero list of a selected row or column. The question asks whether some fixed sparsity and accuracy regime forces linearly many queries. Queries may be adaptive and all computation between them is free. The target is additive rank estimation, not exact rank or sublinear total machine time.
formal: Do there exist a fixed integer \(d\ge2\), a fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), constants \(c>0\) and \(n_0\ge1\), such that \[Q_d(n,\varepsilon)\ge cn\qquad\text{for every integer }n\ge n_0?\] Here \(Q_d(n,\varepsilon)\) is the minimum randomized adaptive row/column-query cost, defined below, for estimating the rank over \(\mathbb F_2\) of every \(n\)-by-\(n\) matrix having at most \(d\) ones per row and column, to additive error \(\varepsilon n\) with success probability at least \(2/3\).
definitions:
The field \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) uses arithmetic modulo two. Rank is the dimension of the span of the columns over that field, and belongs to \(\{0,\ldots,n\}\). Both row and column degree bounds are promises; there are no symmetry or graph-incidence promises. The all-zero matrix and zero rows or columns are allowed.

A row query gives a label \(i\in[n]\) and receives the complete list of indices j for which \(A_{ij}=1\), in increasing order. A column query analogously returns every i with \(A_{ij}=1\). Each list query costs one, and contains at most d indices. Query choices may depend on all previous answers and random coins. There is no free access to matrix-vector products or uniformly random nonzero entries. Random row or column labels can be chosen internally, but their lists still cost queries.

Define \(Q_d(n,\varepsilon)\) as the minimum worst-case number of queries of a randomized decision tree returning a real estimate r with \(\Pr[|r-\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F_2}(A)|\le\varepsilon n]\ge2/3\) on each eligible matrix. Arbitrary computation on the transcript is free. Query complexity is at most n by reading every row. The asymptotic limit is n tending to infinity with d and accuracy fixed; matching constants may depend on both. This is not an algorithm whose total time must be sublinear.

The original problem list includes rectangular matrices over finite fields; the imported card selected square matrices over \(\mathbb F_2\). For binary matrices, the neighbor lists determine all nonzero values, so the interface is complete. Its conjectured general linear lower bound should mean a fixed nontrivial degree and accuracy regime, not a claim for every d: the d=1 class, for example, has much simpler rank structure.
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean a linear row/column-query lower bound at every sufficiently large dimension for one fixed degree bound and precision. A refutation must negate this order of quantifiers using the same adaptive access and per-input success requirements.

title: Efficient characterization of instance-optimal identity testing
summary: The problem asks for an efficiently computable estimate of the optimal sample count for testing equality to a particular known distribution. The selected variant gives the reference probabilities and distance threshold explicitly as binary rational numbers. The estimate must match the information-theoretic optimum within one universal factor at exactly the requested distance. Existing instance-dependent bounds can disagree by arbitrarily large factors because their distance parameters differ. The card makes efficient evaluation precise while keeping the computation of the statistical test unrestricted.
formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluator \(\Phi\) and a universal constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every explicitly given finite rational probability vector \(q\) and rational \(0<\varepsilon\le1\),
\[C^{-1}n_*(q,\varepsilon)\le\Phi(q,\varepsilon)\le Cn_*(q,\varepsilon)?\]
The integer \(n_*(q,\varepsilon)\) is the smallest fixed number of independent samples needed to distinguish \(p=q\) from \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)>\varepsilon\), with each error probability at most \(1/3\), when the reference \(q\) is known and the unknown distribution \(p\) is otherwise arbitrary. Computation of the statistical test is unrestricted. Polynomial time is required of the evaluator of the characterization, in the binary input length of \((q,\varepsilon)\), and the multiplicative constant must hold at the same input \(\varepsilon\).

This is the finite, explicitly encoded version of the efficient-computability branch of the source's Open Question 1. The source also allows countably infinite domains and leaves “succinct” open to a closed-form interpretation; this card makes its computational interpretation and finite rational input scope explicit rather than treating those broader interpretations as equivalent.
definitions:
For an integer \(d\ge1\), write \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and \(\Delta_d=\{p\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{d}:\sum_i p_i=1\}\). The input lists every entry of \(q\in\Delta_d\cap\mathbb Q^d\), including zeros, and the rational number \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\). Rationals are represented by binary nonnegative numerators and positive denominators in lowest terms, with delimiters; let \(B\) be the total bit length, including the length encoding of the list. No oracle or compressed description replaces this list. The alternative \(p\) ranges over all of \(\Delta_d\), including irrational probabilities and mass on coordinates where \(q_i=0\). Total variation is
\[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{d}|p_i-q_i|.\]

For a nonnegative integer \(s\), a possibly randomized statistical test is specified by a function \(\tau:[d]^s\to[0,1]\); \(\tau(x)\) is its conditional probability of rejecting the null on sample sequence \(x\). There is no time, space or representation constraint on this finite table of real probabilities. The product law \(p^{\otimes s}\) means that all \(s\) observations are independent and have law \(p\). A valid test satisfies
\[\mathbb E_{q^{\otimes s}}\tau\le1/3,\qquad
\forall p\in\Delta_d\text{ with }d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)>\varepsilon:\quad \mathbb E_{p^{\otimes s}}\tau\ge2/3.\]
The same test must work for every alternative at that fixed \((q,\varepsilon)\); it cannot be chosen after learning \(p\). The minimum such \(s\) defines \(n_*\). It is finite on every permitted input. The sample count is fixed in advance, not an expected stopping time, and the two errors are bounded separately. Cases with \(0<d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)\le\varepsilon\) impose no condition.

The zero-sample case is included: \([d]^0\) is a singleton. The alternative is empty exactly when \(\varepsilon\ge1-\min_iq_i\), since the largest possible distance from \(q\) in this simplex is \(1-\min_iq_i\). In that case \(n_*=0\); otherwise \(n_*\ge1\). Thus the claimed multiplicative guarantee requires the evaluator to return exactly zero in empty-alternative cases, including \(d=1\). The strict inequality in the alternative is intentional.

The evaluator is a single finite-program deterministic multitape Turing machine. It outputs a nonnegative integer in binary and halts within \(K(B+1)^a\) steps for some fixed constants \(K,a\), independent of \(d,q,\varepsilon\); input reading, bit arithmetic and output writing all count. It has no advice or oracles, and must halt within the same bound on malformed encodings, whose outputs are irrelevant. The quantifier order is existence of the evaluator and constants, followed by all valid inputs. There is no permission for polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) in place of polynomial dependence on its encoded length. The statistical tester whose existence defines \(n_*\) is a separate object and need not be produced by this evaluator.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existence claim. A positive answer must specify the evaluator and prove its uniform polynomial running time and both bounds with one universal finite factor \(C\). A negative answer must refute the existence of every such evaluator and constant; failure of one proposed expression is insufficient. Neither defining \(\Phi\) by the minimum over all statistical tests without proving efficient evaluation, nor comparing upper and lower bounds at different multiples of \(\varepsilon\), satisfies this target. A conditional computational obstruction alone does not prove the unconditional negative claim. Countably infinite or implicitly described references are outside this explicitly selected variant.

title: Linear-in-state-count symmetric Markov-chain identity testing
summary: The tester observes one trajectory of an unknown symmetric Markov chain. It is also given the complete transition matrix of a reference chain. The question asks for a number of transitions proportional to the state count divided by the discrepancy tolerance. The guarantee must hold from every starting state without restarts or irreducibility promises. The spectral discrepancy avoids requiring distinctions that the observed trajectory cannot reveal.
formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized tester and a universal constant \(C>0\) that, for every integer \(n\ge2\), rational \(0<\varepsilon\le1/4\), and explicitly supplied symmetric reference transition matrix \(Q\), tests an unknown symmetric chain \(P\) using at most \(\lceil Cn/\varepsilon\rceil\) observed transitions of one trajectory? For every starting state it must accept with probability at least \(2/3\) when \(P=Q\) and reject with probability at least \(2/3\) when \[\Delta(P,Q)=1-\rho\!\left((\sqrt{P_{ij}Q_{ij}})_{i,j}\right)>\varepsilon.\] Here \(\rho\) is spectral radius. The access model below permits neither resets nor a chosen starting state; reducible chains are included.
definitions: A chain on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) has a transition matrix \(P\in[0,1]^{n\times n}\) with \(\sum_jP_{ij}=1\) for each \(i\). Symmetry means \(P_{ij}=P_{ji}\). Probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers, and zeros, holding probabilities and disconnected state spaces are allowed. For two such matrices set \[R(P,Q)_{ij}=\sqrt{P_{ij}Q_{ij}},\qquad \Delta(P,Q)=1-\rho(R(P,Q)),\] where \(\rho\) is the spectral radius, the maximum absolute value of an eigenvalue. The square root is entrywise; it is not a matrix square root. The resulting discrepancy lies in \([0,1]\), but it need not be a metric. The tester receives \(n\), rational \(\varepsilon\), the complete reference matrix \(Q\), and observations from one trajectory of an unknown symmetric matrix \(P\). For every initial state \(x\in[n]\), \(X_0=x\) and \[\Pr[X_{t+1}=j\mid X_0,\ldots,X_t]=P_{X_t,j}.\] The tester sees \(X_0\) without a transition cost; each subsequent observed transition costs one. It cannot choose the initial state, reset the chain, request a transition from an arbitrary state, or inspect entries of \(P\). It may stop early, but it must stop within the claimed worst-case number of transitions. It accepts with probability at least \(2/3\) if \(P=Q\), and rejects with probability at least \(2/3\) if \(\Delta(P,Q)>\varepsilon\), for every starting state. No guarantee is imposed for other unequal pairs. Probabilities include both the Markov trajectory and independent internal fair random bits. Correctness for every fixed starting state also covers every starting distribution. The tester is one finite uniform program across all \(n,\varepsilon,Q\), with integer and bit-string work storage and exact real registers holding the supplied entries of \(Q\). It has rational constants, exact arithmetic \(+,-,\times,\div\) with division by zero forbidden, nonnegative square root, and exact order/equality comparisons; it has no advice or other oracle. The integer and rational parameters use binary encodings. These conventions specify exact numerical access; no bit-time guarantee for arbitrary real input is being requested. Local computation, memory and access to the explicitly supplied \(Q\) are uncharged, but every execution terminates. For each \(n,\varepsilon\), let \(M(n,\varepsilon)\) be the least integer \(m\) attained as a worst-case transition bound by a uniform tester correct for every permitted parameter value, reference and unknown chain. The worst case includes every \(Q,P\), starting state and execution. Set \(M=+\infty\) if no finite bound exists. This is a worst-reference minimax quantity, rather than a reference-dependent hitting-time or mixing-time complexity. The full symmetric class in the original boxed problem is retained; irreducibility, aperiodicity and stationary initialization are not extra promises.
answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one tester with one universal \(C\) achieves both guarantees with at most \(\lceil Cn/\varepsilon\rceil\) transitions from every initial state, or refute that claim in the same single-trajectory model.

title: Finite-domain promise CSP dichotomy
summary: A finite promise CSP distinguishes inputs satisfying stronger local constraints from inputs failing even weaker constraints. The question asks whether every fixed finite template pair has a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm or is NP-hard under promise-preserving many-one reductions. The algorithm or reduction may depend on the pair, and no effective procedure for classifying input templates is required. New dichotomies cover finite digraphs without sources or sinks and Boolean templates with unate polymorphisms. The general question ranges over all pairs of finite relational templates.
formal: For every fixed pair of finite relational structures \(A,B\) of the same finite signature, with nonempty domains and a homomorphism \(A\to B\), is the decision promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\) either solvable by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm or NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one promise reductions? Its yes instances are the finite structures \(I\) with \(I\to A\); its no instances are those with \(I\not\to B\). The quantifier ranges over all finite signatures and template pairs. The algorithm or hardness reduction, including its polynomial bound, may depend on the fixed pair.
definitions:
A signature is an ordered finite list \(R_1,\ldots,R_s\), where \(s\geq0\) and each symbol has a fixed positive integer arity \(r_i\). A finite structure \(D\) for this signature has a finite domain and relations \(R_i^D\subseteq D^{r_i}\). The templates have domains \(A=\{1,\ldots,a\}\), \(B=\{1,\ldots,b\}\) for positive integers \(a,b\); their relation tables are fixed, not part of the varying input. Different template domains are allowed. For two structures of the same signature, a homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a map of domains satisfying
\[\forall i\;\forall(v_1,\ldots,v_{r_i})\in R_i^D:\ (h(v_1),\ldots,h(v_{r_i}))\in R_i^E.\]
Write \(D\to E\) if such a map exists, and \(D\not\to E\) if none exists. Homomorphisms need not be injective. Empty relations and repeated coordinates in a tuple are allowed.

An input structure \(I\) has domain \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Fix the following binary encoding. Write \(n\) as the unary prefix \(1^n0\). In signature order, write the number \(t_i\) of listed tuples of relation \(i\) as \(1^{t_i}0\), followed by its tuples in their listed order. Encode each coordinate \(v\) by \(1^{|w|}0w\), where \(w\) is the binary expansion of \(v\) without leading zeros and \(1\leq v\leq n\). Each tuple has exactly \(r_i\) coordinates. Duplicate tuples are permitted in the encoding and denote the same relation member; their bits still count. The input ends after the last relation list, with no trailing bits. Thus \(L\), the length of the entire encoding, accounts for the domain as well as all constraints. The empty-domain structure is valid only with all lists empty and is a yes instance. Any encoding polynomial-time equivalent to this explicit representation gives the same question.

For a fixed pair, define \(Y_{A,B}=\{I:I\to A\}\) and \(N_{A,B}=\{I:I\not\to B\}\). The assumption \(A\to B\) makes these sets disjoint. A valid decision algorithm accepts every input in \(Y_{A,B}\) and rejects every input in \(N_{A,B}\). It may give either answer when \(I\to B\) but \(I\not\to A\). Polynomial time means a single deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, no advice or oracle, halting on every binary input of length \(L\) within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,k\). It returns reject on malformed encodings; even instances outside the promise must obey the time bound. Reading, writing and manipulating bits all count. The constants and machine may depend on \(A,B\) and their signature, but not on \(I\).

NP-hardness here means that one uniform deterministic polynomial-time map sends every 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\) to a valid input structure \(I_\varphi\) and satisfies
\[\varphi\text{ satisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\to A,\qquad
\varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\not\to B.\]
A 3-CNF formula is a finite conjunction of clauses, each the disjunction of three signed Boolean variables; repeated variables and literals are allowed. For definiteness, encode its number of clauses in unary followed by three literals per clause, each a sign bit and a positive variable index encoded by the same length-prefixed binary convention as coordinates above. A positive literal is true when its variable is 1, and a negative literal when its variable is 0. The reduction's bound is polynomial in the entire formula encoding, including the time and bits needed to output \(I_\varphi\). Malformed formula encodings may map to the empty input structure. Both satisfiable and unsatisfiable formulas must map into the promise.

The question is the inclusive disjunction of these two possibilities for each fixed pair; it assumes neither \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) nor that the alternatives are disjoint. It does not request an algorithm that, given template tables, identifies the alternative, nor a common polynomial bound over all pairs. Producing a \(B\)-valued homomorphism on every input promised to map to \(A\) is the separate search task. Counting assignments, weighted objectives, allowing a fraction of violated constraints and robustness to broken promises are not part of this decision problem.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated dichotomy for every fixed finite pair, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must establish a fixed finite signature and pair \(A\to B\) whose decision promise problem admits neither any qualifying deterministic polynomial-time decider nor any qualifying polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3-SAT. Both failures must be proved; a presently unclassified pair is not a counterexample. The positive answer need not effectively classify templates, but must establish the full quantified disjunction without an unproved complexity assumption. A dichotomy only for a restricted family, a conditional general classification, or a theorem only about the search task does not settle this target.
references: https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.13538v1 | https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.03021v2 | https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.01914v11 | https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.01937v2 | https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2019.57 | https://www.karlin.mff.cuni.cz/~barto/Articles/DoNotPromise.pdf | https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09815v1 | https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2026.184 | https://hexagonmath.org/abs/2611.01095v1

title: Constant-colour polynomial-time colouring of 3-colourable graphs
summary: The input is a graph known to admit a three-colouring, without a supplied witness. The question asks whether one fixed larger palette permits a randomized polynomial-time algorithm on every such graph. Successful outputs must colour every vertex properly, with probability at least two thirds for each input. A direct reduction from 3-SAT now establishes hardness for every fixed palette. Excluding the randomized algorithms unconditionally would also separate NP and RP.
formal: Do there exist an absolute integer \(C\geq3\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph promised to be \(3\)-colourable, outputs a proper colouring using at most \(C\) colours with probability at least \(2/3\)? The same palette bound and finite program must work for all graph sizes. This card retains the explicitly adopted randomized version of the constant-palette problem.
definitions:
The input is an explicit finite simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), with \(n\geq1\), a unary size header and an adjacency matrix. There are no loops or parallel edges; isolated vertices count toward \(n\). The binary input length \(N\) is of order \(n^2+1\). The promise asserts the existence of a proper colouring with at most three colours, but supplies no colouring or other witness.

A proper \(k\)-colouring is a function \(c:[n]\to[k]\) with \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). A successful output explicitly lists one binary colour index in \([C]\) for each vertex, in vertex order. The algorithm may instead output a failure symbol. A candidate can be checked against the palette bound and all edges in polynomial time; invalid candidates can be converted to failure. Successful runs must colour every vertex and leave no monochromatic edge.

Use one randomized multitape Turing machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(K,d\) such that every computation takes at most \(K(N+1)^d\) bit operations on every graph and every random-bit sequence. All arithmetic precision, output and random-bit generation are included. The random bits are independent and fair, there are polynomially many of them in each run, and the machine has no advice or oracle. Deterministic algorithms are included. No correctness or success-probability requirement is imposed outside the three-colourability promise, but the time bound still applies.

For every promised graph, the probability of a valid \(C\)-colouring must be at least \(2/3\), over the internal bits alone. This is a guarantee for each individual input, not an average over random graphs. The existentially chosen \(C,K,d,A\) are fixed before the graph: \(C\) cannot depend on \(n\), degree, density or the particular input. The exponent and constants may depend on the selected palette bound because only one constant palette is required. Independent repetition can amplify the success probability after checking outputs; exact recognition of the three-colourability promise is not required.

There is no planarity, bounded-degree, expansion, forbidden-subgraph, random-input or supplied-decomposition assumption. A palette of six, one hundred or any other fixed integer could establish a positive answer. A number of colours growing with \(n\), however slowly, does not satisfy the constant-palette requirement.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of at least one such constant \(C\) and algorithm, or a proof in Lean that no such pair exists. A positive answer must verify all-input worst-case polynomial bit complexity and, for every promised graph, success probability at least \(2/3\) with a proper colouring of the full graph using that one palette.

A negative answer must exclude every absolute \(C\geq3\) and every uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm with the stated guarantee. Unconditional NP-hardness of each three-versus-\(C\) decision promise would give a complexity-theoretic obstruction, but deducing nonexistence of these randomized algorithms from it additionally requires \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\). An unproved separation or Label Cover hypothesis cannot be treated as established in an answer to this unconditional question. Hardness for five colours alone, fixed-point-logic inexpressibility, an algorithm with a growing palette, partial colouring, or a restricted input family does not settle the full target.

title: Bodirsky–Pinsker conjecture
summary: The conjecture asks for a P-versus-NP-complete dichotomy for all finite-signature first-order reducts of countable finitely bounded homogeneous structures. Inputs are finite constraint systems, while their possible values lie in a fixed domain that may be infinite. Homogeneity provides symmetry, and finitely many forbidden induced patterns provide polynomial-size certificates despite the infinite domain. Recent results simplify the conjecture’s scope or classify lower complexity boundaries, while the full tractability implication remains open in the checked sources. A resolution would determine whether this broad structural framework rules out intermediate NP complexity.
formal:
For every countable finitely bounded homogeneous relational structure \(A\) over a finite signature, and every first-order reduct \(B\) of \(A\) with a finite relational signature, is
\[\operatorname{CSP}(B)\in\mathrm{P}\quad\lor\quad\operatorname{CSP}(B)\text{ is NP-complete}\ ?\]
NP-completeness uses deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The templates are fixed before the finite input is supplied. This is the unconditional complexity dichotomy, without requiring an algebraic criterion identifying the two sides.
definitions:
A finite relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a fixed positive integer arity. A structure \(D\) interprets an \(r\)-ary symbol as a subset \(R^D\subseteq D^r\) of tuples over its domain. Countable means finite or countably infinite. Empty domains, if admitted, have trivial CSPs and do not affect the question. Nullary relations can likewise be processed separately.

The induced substructure on a subset \(S\) of a domain restricts every relation to tuples from \(S\). An embedding is an injective map \(e:D\to E\) with \(\bar d\in R^D\) if and only if \(e(\bar d)\in R^E\) for every relation and tuple; it preserves both presence and absence of relation tuples. An isomorphism is a bijective embedding, and an automorphism is an isomorphism from a structure to itself. The structure \(A\) is homogeneous when every isomorphism between two finite induced substructures extends to an automorphism of \(A\).

The structure \(A\) is finitely bounded when there is a finite list \(\mathcal N\) of finite structures in its signature such that, for every finite structure \(D\) in that signature,
\[D\text{ embeds into }A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{no }N\in\mathcal N\text{ embeds into }D.\]
Thus the finite patterns occurring inside \(A\) are precisely those avoiding finitely many forbidden induced patterns. Homogeneity is an additional condition, not part of finite boundedness alone.

A first-order reduct \(B\) has the same domain as \(A\). Each of its finitely many relations is defined by a fixed first-order formula over the relations of \(A\) and logical equality, using Boolean connectives and quantifiers over elements of \(A\), without naming parameters. It may forget original relations and introduce newly definable ones. Both signatures, \(A,B\), the defining formulas and a finite bound list witnessing the hypothesis are fixed; none is an input to the individual CSP.

An input \(I\) has finite domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and an explicit list of tuples for each relation in the signature of \(B\). A homomorphism \(h:I\to B\) is any map such that \((i_1,\ldots,i_r)\in R^I\) implies \((h(i_1),\ldots,h(i_r))\in R^B\). It need not be injective and need not preserve absence of tuples. The decision problem accepts exactly when such a map exists. Repeated coordinates and isolated input elements are allowed; duplicate listed tuples are harmless. The empty input has the empty homomorphism.

Encode \(n\) in unary and each relation by a unary list length followed by binary tuple coordinates, in fixed signature order, with delimiters. Let \(L\) be total bit length. Invalid encodings are rejected. Polynomial time means a deterministic multitape Turing machine halts correctly on every input within \(C(L+1)^k\) bit steps for constants \(C,k\) depending on \(B\). No randomness, infinite-domain oracle, advice, supplied homomorphism, common polynomial exponent or algorithm choosing the correct side from template descriptions is required.

Use the shared definition of [NP](definitions.html#p-np). A problem \(Q\) is NP-hard under the stated reductions when, for every \(K\in\mathrm{NP}\), a total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) satisfies \(x\in K\) if and only if \(f(x)\in Q\). NP-complete means NP-hard and in NP. Every CSP in the displayed scope is already known to be in NP. The two alternatives are not required to be disjoint without a separation assumption: if \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), every such problem satisfies the first alternative.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition, or of its logical negation, retaining every permitted structure and reduct. A negative answer must establish one permitted \(A,B\) for which \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) is neither in P nor NP-complete under the stated many-one reductions; membership in NP already follows from the hypotheses. No separation assumption is added to the proposition. A classification for one reduct family, the first-order/logarithmic-space-hard boundary, or a procedure deciding an algebraic meta-problem does not prove the full dichotomy. The stronger algebraic tractability conjecture would suffice if proved, but is not substituted for the existing bare complexity target.

title: Algorithmic threshold for random k-SAT
summary: The input is a random conjunction of fixed-width clauses, with all literal positions sampled independently. The algorithm must find an assignment satisfying every clause with probability tending to one. The conjectured leading threshold is two to the clause width times its natural logarithm, divided by the width. Known algorithms reach this scale, while satisfying assignments exist at substantially higher densities. Existing overlap-gap and low-degree barriers do not establish optimality against every polynomial-time algorithm.
formal: Does the randomized polynomial-time satisfying-assignment threshold for random \(k\)-SAT satisfy \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(k)}{2^{k}\ln(k)/k}=1?\] For each fixed \(k\), \(\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(k)\) is the supremum of constant clause densities at which some polynomial-time algorithm finds a satisfying assignment with probability tending to one as the number \(n\) of variables tends to infinity. The distribution and quantifiers are specified below.
definitions:
Fix an integer \(k\geq3\) and a real constant density \(\alpha\geq0\). On Boolean variables \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\), generate \(m=\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\) ordered clauses. Each clause has \(k\) literal positions, each independently uniform among \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},\neg x_{1},\ldots,\neg x_{n}\). The formula is the AND of these OR clauses. Sampling is with replacement: repeated literals, tautological clauses and repeated clauses are allowed.

The algorithm receives the entire explicit formula, with variable indices in binary, together with \(n\). It must output one full assignment in \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) satisfying every clause. It may report failure otherwise. The input is sampled without conditioning on satisfiability and without planting or revealing any assignment.

A density \(\alpha\) is algorithmically attainable at width \(k\) if there is a classical randomized algorithm \(A\), with no advice depending on \(n\), such that its running time is bounded by a polynomial in the explicit input length and \(n\) on every input and random tape, and
\[\Pr_{\Phi,A}[A(\Phi)\text{ outputs a satisfying assignment of }\Phi]\longrightarrow1
\quad\text{as }n\to\infty.\]
The probability includes both the random formula and the algorithm's internal randomness. One fixed algorithm must work for all \(n\) at the chosen \(k,\alpha\). Its code, polynomial degree and constants may depend on those fixed parameters. They are not allowed to depend separately on each input length.

Let \(\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(k)\) be the supremum of all such densities. Attainment at the supremum is not required. First take \(n\to\infty\) at fixed \(k,\alpha\); only then consider the asymptotic behavior as \(k\to\infty\). Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm. This is a leading-order asymptotic question, not a request for an exact critical density at a particular small \(k\).

The target ranges over all randomized polynomial-time assignment-finding algorithms. It imposes no locality, stability, low-degree representation or restriction to a named heuristic. Deciding satisfiability without producing an assignment, satisfying only most clauses, or proving a barrier for a restricted algorithm family is a different guarantee.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed asymptotic equality, or refute it. The known algorithm gives the lower bound \(1-o_{k}(1)\) on the ratio, so the missing positive direction is the matching upper bound for all polynomial-time algorithms. A refutation must change the limiting leading-order behavior along arbitrarily large widths; an improvement confined to one fixed small width or a lower-order term does not suffice.

title: Search-to-decision equivalence for finite promise CSPs
summary: A finite promise CSP distinguishes strong constraints whose satisfiability is guaranteed from weaker constraints an output must satisfy. The decision problem separates strongly satisfiable inputs from those with no weak solution. The question asks whether every fixed template with a deterministic polynomial-time decider also permits deterministic polynomial-time construction on the original stronger promise. Hardness of rounding arbitrary relaxation-accepted inputs and undecidability of template recognition leave this implication unresolved. A resolution would clarify whether tractability of finite promise constraints always extends from recognizing feasibility to producing assignments.
formal: For every fixed pair \((A,B)\) of finite nonempty relational structures over the same finite signature with \(A\to B\), does polynomial-time solvability of the decision promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\) imply polynomial-time solvability of its search version? Decision must accept every finite \(X\) with \(X\to A\) and reject every \(X\) with \(X\not\to B\). Search receives \(X\) with the promise \(X\to A\) and must output an explicit homomorphism \(X\to B\). Both algorithms are deterministic and have polynomial worst-case running time on all inputs; the programs and polynomial bounds may depend on \(A,B\).
definitions:
A finite relational signature is a finite ordered list of relation symbols, each assigned a positive integer arity. A structure \(D\) consists of a domain and, for each symbol \(R\) of arity \(r\), a relation \(R^D\subseteq D^r\). A homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a function satisfying
\[(d_1,\ldots,d_r)\in R^D\ \Longrightarrow\ (h(d_1),\ldots,h(d_r))\in R^E\]
for every relation and tuple. It need not be injective. The notation \(D\to E\) asserts existence of such a map. Templates \(A,B\), including their finite relation tables and a numbering of their domains, are fixed constants, not part of the input. No stronger assignment is supplied with an input.

The input structure \(X\) has domain \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Repeated coordinates and empty relations are allowed. Encode \(n\) in unary, followed by the tuple lists in signature order with unary list lengths; each coordinate has \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Let \(N\) be the total bit length, which counts isolated variables. Duplicate listed tuples have no effect. A search output is the list of images of all \(n\) elements in the fixed domain of \(B\), or a failure symbol. The empty input has the empty homomorphism.

A decision algorithm returns one bit. If \(X\not\to A\) but \(X\to B\), either bit is permitted; this is the intermediate region of the promise. Since \(A\to B\), no input simultaneously requires both answers. On search inputs outside the promise \(X\to A\), any output is permitted, including failure. Both machines halt on every binary input within \(C(N+1)^k\) steps for positive integers \(C,k\); malformed strings may be rejected. Cost is measured on a deterministic multitape Turing machine, without advice, oracle or randomness.

The quantifier order is \(\forall(A,B)\,[\exists D\text{ with the decision guarantee}\Rightarrow\exists S\text{ with the search guarantee}]\). Constants and exponents can depend on the fixed template. There is no required effective procedure that recognizes tractable templates or constructs \(S\) from arbitrary \(A,B,D\), no common exponent over templates, and no requirement that \(S\) use \(D\) as a black-box subroutine. The target is the tractability implication between the two fixed-template problems.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication for every fixed finite template pair, or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish a search machine with the stated promised output and all-input polynomial bound whenever a qualifying decision machine exists. A negative proof must exhibit a fixed finite \(A\to B\), prove its decision promise solvable in deterministic polynomial time, and prove that no deterministic polynomial-time promised search algorithm exists. Hardness of rounding all inputs accepted by a particular relaxation, undecidability when the template varies, or failure of a particular black-box reduction does not refute this statement. A conditional separation is partial progress and must retain its unproved hypothesis; the target itself is unconditional.

title: Dichotomy for finite-domain restricted CSPs
summary: A restricted CSP asks whether a finite input maps to a fixed finite target, under the promise that it maps to another fixed structure. The restriction structure may be infinite, but the source requires its finite-input CSP to be decidable. The question asks whether every such promise problem is polynomial-time solvable or NP-hard when P differs from NP. Hardness must hold for every decidable completion of the promised answers, and the known dichotomy only covers finite restrictions. A resolution would determine whether decidable homomorphism promises preserve the finite-domain dichotomy or allow intermediate behaviour.
formal:
Assume \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\). For every finite relational signature \(\tau\), every finite \(\tau\)-structure \(A\), and every possibly infinite \(\tau\)-structure \(B\) for which \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) is decidable, must \(\operatorname{RCSP}(A,B)\) be either polynomial-time solvable or NP-hard in the source’s completion sense? Explicitly, let
\[\mathcal S_{A,B}=\{S\subseteq\{0,1\}^*:S\text{ is decidable and }S\cap\operatorname{CSP}(B)=\operatorname{CSP}(A)\cap\operatorname{CSP}(B)\}.\]
Is it always true that
\[\bigl(\exists S\in\mathcal S_{A,B}:S\in\mathrm{P}\bigr)\quad\lor\quad\bigl(\forall S\in\mathcal S_{A,B}:S\text{ is NP-hard}\bigr)?\]
The input is a finite structure \(X\) promised to map homomorphically to \(B\); on that promise the decision is whether \(X\) maps to \(A\).
definitions:
A finite relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols of positive integer arities. A \(\tau\)-structure \(D\) has a domain and a relation \(R^D\subseteq D^r\) for each \(r\)-ary symbol. The target \(A\) is finite; the restriction \(B\) may have an arbitrary infinite domain. A homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a function preserving every relation tuple: \((d_1,\ldots,d_r)\in R^D\) implies \((h(d_1),\ldots,h(d_r))\in R^E\). Write \(D\to E\) for existence of such a map. Maps need not be injective. Neither \(A\to B\) nor \(B\to A\) is assumed.

Input structures have domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed tuples for each relation. Encode \(n\) in unary, then the relation lists in signature order with unary list lengths and binary coordinate indices. Let \(N\) be the total bit length. Empty relations, repeated coordinates and isolated elements are allowed; repeated listed tuples are harmless. Define \(\operatorname{CSP}(D)\) as the set of valid encodings of finite \(X\) with \(X\to D\). Invalid encodings do not belong to this set. Empty template domains may be included; their trivial boundary cases do not alter the question.

For each problem \(A,B,\tau\) are fixed, and only \(X\) is supplied. An input in \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) must be accepted exactly when it lies in \(\operatorname{CSP}(A)\); outside the promise either answer is allowed. A completion \(S\) is a total decidable language with precisely this behaviour on the promise. Since \(A\) is finite, \(\operatorname{CSP}(A)\) is a decidable completion, so \(\mathcal S_{A,B}\) is never empty. Decidability of \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) is a hypothesis recovered from the source, not a polynomial-time promise-recognition assumption. No description, relation-table algorithm, homomorphism into \(B\), or oracle for \(B\) is supplied. Infinite restrictions are not limited to finitely presented or categorically specified structures.

A completion is in \(\mathrm{P}\) if a deterministic multitape Turing machine accepts exactly it and halts on every string of length \(N\) within \(C(N+1)^k\) bit steps for fixed positive integers \(C,k\). The machine and constants may depend on \(A,B\). Decidable means a deterministic machine halts and decides membership, without any time bound. No uniform procedure for constructing these machines from templates, common polynomial exponent, advice or randomness is requested.

A language is in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership has polynomially bounded certificates checkable in deterministic polynomial time. A language \(S\) is NP-hard here under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions: for every \(K\in\mathrm{NP}\), there is a total polynomial-time function \(f_K\) with \(x\in K\) if and only if \(f_K(x)\in S\). Equivalently, it suffices to reduce Boolean three-clause satisfiability, where each clause has at most three literals. This is hardness of the total language \(S\), not a claim that \(S\) itself lies in NP.

The promise-hardness quantifiers are \(\forall\text{ decidable completions }S\ \exists\text{ suitable reductions to }S\). Reductions may depend on \(S\); no single reduction whose images always satisfy \(X\to B\) is required by this definition. A uniform reduction landing inside the promise would suffice, but is not silently substituted for the source’s definition. Under \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) the two displayed alternatives are disjoint. If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), the first alternative already holds for every finite \(A\), since its ordinary CSP is in NP.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean, under the stated \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) hypothesis, that the displayed dichotomy holds for every permitted \(A,B\), or that it fails. A negative answer must establish a fixed finite \(A\) and a permitted possibly infinite \(B\) such that no completion is in P and at least one decidable completion is not NP-hard under the stated reductions. A positive answer must cover every infinite restriction with decidable CSP, retaining the completion quantifiers. Proving only the already known finite-restriction case, treating an arbitrary input class that is not \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\), or disproving a stronger uniform hardness requirement does not settle this question. No additional unproved hypothesis may replace the explicitly stated separation assumption.

title: Boolean decision-Holant dichotomy
summary: Boolean decision Holant asks whether edges of a graph can be assigned zero or one so that every local relation is satisfied. The question seeks a structural classification of all fixed finite relation families that admit polynomial-time decision. The source’s edge-CSP model makes each variable occur in exactly two distinct constraint scopes, without freely adding constants or unary relations. Known results handle the non-delta-matroid boundary, symmetric delta-matroids and even delta-matroids, while the arbitrary delta-matroid region remains the general obstacle. A complete answer would identify the full tractability boundary beyond ordinary Boolean CSP and matching.
formal:
Classify the polynomial-time solvable Boolean decision-Holant problems for all fixed finite families of Boolean relations. More precisely, under \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), determine the entire characteristic function
\[\chi_{\mathrm H}(\mathcal F)=\begin{cases}1,&\operatorname{DecHolant}(\mathcal F)\in\mathrm{P},\\0,&\operatorname{DecHolant}(\mathcal F)\notin\mathrm{P},\end{cases}\]
with absolute error at most \(1/100\) at every finite family \(\mathcal F\). The answer must give a substantive structural criterion on the allowed relations, with algorithms and complementary lower bounds, rather than merely restating the definition of polynomial-time solvability. The model is the source’s Boolean edge-CSP interpretation of decision Holant, specified below.
definitions:
A Boolean relation of arity \(r\geq1\) is a subset \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^r\), equivalently its zero-one indicator function \(f_R\). A signature family \(\mathcal F\) is a finite ordered list of such relations given by their full finite truth tables; empty relations and the empty family are allowed. For each decision problem the family and all arities are fixed before inputs are supplied. Arbitrarily large fixed arities are covered across the classification.

A signature grid is a finite undirected loopless multigraph \(G=(V,E)\), together with a label \(R_v\in\mathcal F\) at each vertex and an ordering \((e_{v,1},\ldots,e_{v,r_v})\) of its incident edges, where \(r_v\) equals the arity of \(R_v\). Parallel edges are permitted and are separate variables. The graph need not be planar or bipartite. Each edge has two distinct endpoints and appears exactly once at each endpoint. The incidence order is part of the input, since relations need not be symmetric. This is the explicit convention of Definitions 1–3 in the cited edge-CSP paper: a variable is in exactly two distinct constraint scopes, without a repeated coordinate within one scope.

A Boolean assignment is a map \(\sigma:E\to\{0,1\}\). It is satisfying when \((\sigma(e_{v,1}),\ldots,\sigma(e_{v,r_v}))\in R_v\) for every vertex. Define
\[H_{\mathcal F}(G)=\sum_{\sigma:E\to\{0,1\}}\prod_{v\in V} f_{R_v}(\sigma(e_{v,1}),\ldots,\sigma(e_{v,r_v})).\]
The task \(\operatorname{DecHolant}(\mathcal F)\) accepts exactly the grids with \(H_{\mathcal F}(G)>0\). It asks for one yes/no answer, not the number or a list of satisfying assignments. The empty graph has value one, by the empty-product convention. A grid containing an empty relation is unsatisfiable. Nullary indicators, if included, can be processed separately: zero rejects the instance and one is deleted, so restricting the signature tables to positive arities loses no tractability class.

Encode the numbers of vertices and edges in unary; list binary endpoint indices for each numbered edge, the fixed-family index at each vertex, and its ordered list of edge indices. Let \(N\) be total bit length. Validity of the encoding is checked in polynomial time; malformed strings are rejected. A polynomial-time algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine that halts with the correct answer on every input in at most \(C(N+1)^k\) bit steps, for positive constants \(C,k\) depending on \(\mathcal F\). There is no randomness, oracle or advice. Programs may depend on the fixed family, and no common running-time exponent across all families is requested.

No unary relation, pinning constant, equality relation, edge weight or graph restriction is freely added to \(\mathcal F\). The at-most-two-occurrences decision model used in the survey has the same complexity under this scope convention: remove unused variables, take two copies of the instance, and identify corresponding variables that occurred only once. This gives exactly two occurrences and preserves satisfiability without new relations. The target does not impose a uniform input-template algorithm or require a polynomial-time procedure for recognizing the tractable families from their truth tables.

Use the shared definitions of [P and NP](definitions.html#p-np). Every fixed-family problem above is in NP, with the edge assignment as certificate. NP-hardness, when used in the classification, means deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions from every language in NP; NP-complete means both NP-hard and in NP. This is an explicit reduction convention. The separation assumption makes a tractability classification nontrivial; if \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), the function is identically one. A rational answer within \(1/100\) of a zero-one value determines that value, but the requested result is the structural description of the whole function, not numerical experiments on selected families.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of an exhaustive structural characterization of \(\chi_{\mathrm H}\) with the stated absolute \(1/100\) accuracy, under the explicit \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) hypothesis. Prove correct polynomial-time decision algorithms for every family assigned one and a matching exclusion of polynomial time for every family assigned zero; NP-hardness under the stated reductions is a sufficient exclusion. The result must cover all finite Boolean signature families, including arbitrary delta-matroid relations, with the graph and occurrence conventions above. A characterization cannot simply rename the existence of a polynomial-time machine. Classifying only symmetric signatures, only even delta-matroids, planar inputs, weighted counting, or a language enlarged by freely available unary signatures does not answer the full question. If additional complexity cases arise instead of the expected polynomial-time/NP-complete dichotomy, identify and justify them rather than asserting that every nontractable case is NP-complete without proof.

title: Universal representation of NP by \(\omega\)-categorical CSPs
summary: The question asks whether every NP language is polynomial-time Turing equivalent to a CSP with a fixed omega-categorical template. Omega-categoricity means that each finite tuple length has only finitely many symmetry orbits, even when the domain is infinite. The reductions may use adaptive exact membership queries, and no uniform template-construction algorithm or effective template presentation is required. Universality is known for unrestricted infinite templates, while the known omega-categorical construction gives a weaker oracle upper bound. A resolution would determine whether this symmetry condition limits computational representation of NP problems.
formal:
For every language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) in \(\mathrm{NP}\), does there exist a countable \(\omega\)-categorical relational structure \(\Gamma\) in a finite relational signature such that
\[L\equiv_T^p\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\ ?\]
The relation \(\equiv_T^p\) means deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions in both directions. This reduction convention follows the source’s accompanying non-dichotomy results and the explicit definition in the later monograph; Question 2 itself abbreviates it as polynomial-time equivalence.
definitions:
A finite relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a fixed positive integer arity. A structure \(\Gamma\) has a nonempty finite or countably infinite domain and an interpretation \(R^\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma^r\) for each \(r\)-ary symbol. A homomorphism \(h:I\to\Gamma\) maps elements of \(I\) to domain values and preserves every positive relation tuple. It need not be injective and need not preserve absence of tuples.

An automorphism of \(\Gamma\) is a bijection of its domain preserving both membership and nonmembership in every relation. It acts on an ordered tuple by applying the same bijection to all coordinates. Two tuples are in the same orbit if some automorphism maps one to the other. The structure is \(\omega\)-categorical here if for every positive integer \(k\), there are only finitely many orbits of ordered \(k\)-tuples. For countably infinite structures in a finite signature, this is equivalent to their complete first-order theory having a unique countably infinite model up to isomorphism. Finite structures are admitted by the same orbit convention. The bound on the number of orbits can depend on \(k\); no fixed global bound, algorithm for orbits, homogeneity or finite list of forbidden patterns is assumed.

A CSP instance is a finite \(\tau\)-structure \(I\) with domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. It is accepted exactly when \(I\to\Gamma\). Repeated coordinates and isolated elements are allowed; duplicate tuples are harmless. The empty structure has the empty homomorphism. Encode \(n\) in unary, then in signature order each relation’s unary list length and its tuples of binary indices, with delimiters. Invalid encodings are rejected. This defines a total language \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) of finite bit strings. The signature and structure are fixed for this language; no infinite table, presentation algorithm or value from \(\Gamma\) is supplied with an instance.

A language lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership is witnessed by a certificate of length polynomial in the input bit length and checked by a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine. A reduction \(K\leq_T^p Q\) is a deterministic oracle Turing machine deciding membership in \(K\) using exact yes/no membership queries to \(Q\). On every input \(x\), all its computation, query writing and answer processing take at most \(C(|x|+1)^d\) bit steps for fixed positive constants \(C,d\). Thus query lengths and their number are polynomially bounded. The oracle supplies each membership bit at unit query cost; its own computation is not part of the reduction. Queries may depend on earlier answers, and answers may be negated. No randomness or advice is available.

Polynomial-time Turing equivalence means \(L\leq_T^p\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) and \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\leq_T^p L\). The two programs and their constants may depend on \(L,\Gamma\), but each works on every finite input. The quantifiers are \(\forall L\in\mathrm{NP}\ \exists\tau,\Gamma,M_1,M_2,C_1,C_2,d_1,d_2\). No uniform algorithm turning an NP verifier into a template or into these reductions is requested.
